# Chapter 1: The Stone Egg of Flower-Fruit Mountain and the Birth of the Monkey King

A poem says:

> Before the chaos split, the heavens and the earth were one,
> A vast and formless blur that no eye ever looked upon.
> But once Pangu had shattered through that primal murky shell,
> The pure and the impure were parted, and creation's order fell.
> All living things look up in awe to that supreme benevolence,
> Which brought forth every thing that is, and made each thing turn toward the good.
> Would you know the work of making, the turning of the great world's age?
> Then read this tale of *Journey to the West*, the chronicle that frees from woe.

It is said that the reckoning of heaven and earth runs in great cycles, each cycle of one hundred twenty-nine thousand six hundred years. Each such cycle is divided into twelve epochs, named for the twelve earthly branches — Zi, Chou, Yin, Mao, Chen, Si, Wu, Wei, Shen, You, Xu, and Hai — and each epoch lasts ten thousand eight hundred years.

Consider it by the measure of a single day. At the hour of Zi the vital force of yang first stirs; at Chou the cocks begin to crow. At Yin the light has not yet broken through; at Mao the sun comes up. At Chen, breakfast is past; at Si all is set in order. At Wu the sun stands at heaven's center; at Wei it begins to slip westward. At Shen comes the late afternoon, and the sun sets at You. At Xu falls the yellow dusk, and at Hai the world lies down to rest.

By analogy with the great reckoning: when the epoch of Xu draws to its close, heaven and earth grow dark and dim, and all things wither. Five thousand four hundred years onward, at the opening of the epoch of Hai, there is utter blackness, and between the two realms neither man nor thing remains. This is what is called chaos, the undivided murk. After another five thousand four hundred years, as the epoch of Hai nears its end, the constant turns once more toward the source, and as the epoch of Zi approaches, light gradually begins to return. Master Shao Kangjie said: "At the winter solstice, the midpoint of Zi, the heart of heaven does not shift. Where the single yang first quickens — that is the moment before the myriad things are born." At this point, heaven first has its root.

After another five thousand four hundred years, in the very midst of the epoch of Zi, the light and the pure rise upward, and there come to be sun, moon, stars, and constellations. Sun, moon, stars, and constellations are called the Four Images. Hence it is said: heaven opened in Zi. After another five thousand four hundred years pass, as the epoch of Zi draws toward its close and the epoch of Chou approaches, things gradually grow firm and solid. The *Book of Changes* says: "Great is the creative principle of Qian! Supreme is the receptive principle of Kun! The myriad things draw their life from it, obediently following heaven." At this point, the earth first congeals.

After another five thousand four hundred years, in the very midst of the epoch of Chou, the heavy and impure settle downward, and there come to be water, fire, mountains, stone, and soil. Water, fire, mountains, stone, and soil are called the Five Forms. Hence it is said: earth was opened in Chou. After another five thousand four hundred years, as the epoch of Chou ends and the epoch of Yin begins, the myriad things spring into being. The almanac says: "The breath of heaven descends; the breath of earth ascends. Heaven and earth join in union, and all the host of things is born." At this point, heaven is clear and earth is fresh, and yin and yang join in union. After another five thousand four hundred years, in the very midst of the epoch of Yin, there are born human beings, beasts, and birds — and so the three powers, heaven, earth, and humankind, take their fixed places. Hence it is said: humankind was born in Yin.

After Pangu opened the world, the Three Sovereigns ruled the age, and the Five Emperors set in order the human bonds. The world was then divided into four great continents: the Eastern Continent of Spiritual Excellence, the Western Continent of Cattle-Offering, the Southern Continent of Jambu, and the Northern Continent of Kuru. This book concerns the Eastern Continent of Spiritual Excellence alone.

Beyond its seas there lay a country called Aolai. The country bordered the great ocean, and out in the ocean there rose a famous mountain called Flower-Fruit Mountain. This mountain was the ancestral vein of the Ten Continents, the source-dragon of the Three Isles. It stood from the very parting of the pure and the impure, and took its shape when the primal murk was first cleft asunder. Truly it was a splendid mountain! There is a rhapsody to prove it. The rhapsody says:

> Its power overawes the boundless deep; its might brings peace to the jade-green sea.
> Its power overawes the boundless deep — the tide surges up in silver hills and the fish flee to their dens;
> its might brings peace to the jade-green sea — the waves roll over in drifts of snow and the sea-monsters quit their abyss.
> Where water and fire heap high at the corners, it lifts a soaring summit over the Eastern Sea.
> Cinnabar cliffs and grotesque stones, sheer escarpments and wondrous peaks.
> Upon the cinnabar cliffs, paired phoenixes call together; before the sheer escarpments, a lone unicorn lies at rest.
> On the peaks one hears in season the crowing of golden pheasants; in the stone caverns one ever watches dragons coming and going.
> In the forest dwell long-lived deer and fairy foxes; in the trees roost numinous birds and dark cranes.
> The fairy grasses and rare blossoms never fade; the green pines and emerald cypress keep eternal spring.
> The immortal peaches forever set their fruit; the slender bamboo perpetually holds the clouds.
> A single ravine runs thick with vines and creepers, and on every side the embankments wear fresh new green.
> This is indeed the heaven-bracing pillar where the hundred rivers meet, the unmoving root of the earth that ten thousand ages cannot stir.

Now upon the very summit of that mountain there sat a magic stone. The stone measured three zhang six chi and five cun in height, and two zhang four chi around. Its height of three zhang six chi and five cun corresponded to the three hundred sixty-five degrees of the heavens; its girth of two zhang four chi corresponded to the twenty-four solar terms of the calendar. Upon it were nine apertures and eight holes, corresponding to the Nine Palaces and the Eight Trigrams. On all four sides there were no trees to shade it, but to left and right grew sprigs of magic fungus and orchid for company.

Ever since the world's beginning, the stone had received the true essence of heaven and the fine flower of earth, the seed of the sun and the splendor of the moon. Having been quickened so long, it conceived at last a numinous purpose, and nurtured within itself a magic womb. One day it burst open and gave birth to a stone egg, round and large as a ball. Touched by the wind, the egg transformed into a stone monkey, complete in all five senses and whole in all four limbs. At once it learned to crawl and to walk, and bowed toward the four quarters. From its eyes shot forth two beams of golden light that pierced upward to the Palace of the Dipper.

The light startled the August One on high, the supremely compassionate and benevolent Jade Emperor, the Most High Lord of the Mysterious Vault, who sat enthroned upon his Spirit-Mist Treasure Hall within the Cloud Palace of the Golden Gate. He had gathered his immortal ministers, and seeing the blazing golden light, he straightway commanded Thousand-Mile Eye and Down-the-Wind Ear to open the Southern Gate of Heaven and look out. The two generals received the order, went out beyond the gate, looked clearly and listened plainly, and after a moment returned to report: "Your servants, obeying the command, observed and listened at the source of the golden light. It comes from the border of the little country of Aolai, east across the sea of the Eastern Continent of Spiritual Excellence. There is a mountain there called Flower-Fruit Mountain, and on the mountain a magic stone, and the stone has given birth to an egg. Touched by the wind, it became a stone monkey, which now bows toward the four quarters; from its eyes shot the golden light that pierced the Palace of the Dipper. But now that it has begun to take food and drink, the golden light is fading away." The Jade Emperor in his gracious mercy declared: "These creatures of the world below are born of the very essence of heaven and earth. It is nothing to wonder at."

The monkey in the mountains could already walk and leap and run about. It ate the grasses and the trees, drank from the brook and the spring, gathered the mountain flowers and sought out the fruits of the trees. It made companions of the wolves and the insects, ran in packs with the tigers and leopards, made friends of the river-deer and the stags, and counted the gibbons and apes as its kin. By night it slept beneath the stone cliffs; by day it roamed among the peaks and caves. Truly, "In the mountains there is no calendar; when the cold is gone, one does not know the year."

One day the weather turned scorching hot, and the monkey, together with the troop of monkeys, took refuge from the heat and played beneath the shade of the pines. Just look at every one of them:

> Leaping the trees and clambering the branches, plucking the blossoms and seeking the fruit;
> tossing pellets and playing with marbles; racing through the sand-pits, building little pagodas;
> chasing dragonflies, pouncing on lizards; bowing to old Heaven, worshipping the Bodhisattva;
> pulling at the kudzu vines, plaiting the grasses; catching their fleas, biting and pinching them;
> grooming their fur, picking at their nails. The pressing pressed and the rubbing rubbed,
> the shoving shoved and the squashing squashed, the dragging dragged and the hauling hauled —
> beneath the green pine forest they romped at will, beside the clear brook they bathed as they pleased.

When the troop had played a while, they went to bathe in that mountain brook. They saw how the brook-water came rushing down, churning truly like a boiling cauldron. The old saying goes: "Birds have the speech of birds, and beasts the words of beasts." All the monkeys said: "We do not know where this water comes from. Today, having nothing better to do, let us follow the brook up to its head and trace it to its source — that will be sport!" With a shout they all came running, tugging the males and leading the females, calling to younger brother and elder brother, scrambling up the mountain along the brook until they reached the very source: a leaping waterfall and a flying spring. They saw there:

> A sheet of white rainbow rises, a thousand fathoms of snowy waves take flight.
> The sea-wind cannot break it; the river-moon still shines upon it.
> Its cold breath divides the blue cliffs; its overflow waters the emerald slopes.
> Murmuring, it is named a waterfall — truly like a hanging curtain of pearls.

The monkeys clapped their hands and cried in praise: "Fine water! Fine water! So it reaches far down beneath the mountain's foot and joins straight to the waves of the great ocean." Then they said: "If any one of us has the ability to bore in and find the source-head and come out again unhurt, we will honor him as our king." Three times they raised the cry, and suddenly out from the throng leaped the stone monkey, answering with a loud shout: "I'll go in! I'll go in!" Ah, what a monkey! For him it was:

> Today his fair name is made plain;
> his hour has come, his great fortune flows.
> By destiny he dwells in this place;
> his king will send him into the immortal palace.

Just watch him: he shut his eyes, crouched low, and with one bound sprang straight into the waterfall and the spring. Then he opened his eyes, lifted his head, and looked — and there inside was neither water nor wave, but a bright and shining bridge of iron. He steadied himself and calmed his spirit, and looking more carefully, he saw that it was indeed a bridge of wrought iron plates. The water beneath the bridge poured through the gaps among the rocks and gushed out, hanging downward to screen the bridge's mouth. He bent and climbed up onto the bridgehead, and walking on and looking again, he saw that it seemed a very dwelling-place where folk might live — truly a fine spot. He saw there:

> Green mosses heaped like blue, white clouds floating like jade, the light shimmering in shred upon shred of rosy mist.
> Empty windows and quiet chambers; smooth benches where flowers seem to bloom upon the boards.
> Stalactites hang like dragon-pearls; rare blossoms wind in profusion over all the ground.
> Beside the cliff a stove still bears the trace of fire; against the table the wine-jars show the dregs of a feast.
> Stone seats and stone beds, truly lovable; stone basins and stone bowls, more to be praised still.
> And there too one or two stalks of slender bamboo, three or five sprays of plum blossom.
> A few green pines that ever wear the rain — altogether, just like a human household.

After he had looked a good while, he leaped to the middle of the bridge and gazed left and right. There in the very center stood a stone tablet, and on the tablet a line of large regular characters was carved: "The Blessed Land of Flower-Fruit Mountain, the Cave-Heaven of the Water-Curtain Cave."

The stone monkey was beside himself with joy. He hastily turned and made his way out, shut his eyes, crouched low, and leaped clear of the water. With two great chuckles he cried: "Great fortune! Great fortune!" The monkeys crowded round him and asked: "How is it inside? How deep is the water?" The stone monkey said: "There's no water! No water! It turns out there's a bridge of wrought iron, and beyond the bridge a household ready-made by heaven and earth." The monkeys said: "How can it be a household?" The stone monkey laughed and said: "This water pours through beneath the stone bridge and hangs down to screen the gateway. Beside the bridge there are flowers and trees, and there's a stone house. Within the house are a stone hearth, a stone stove, stone bowls, stone basins, a stone bed, and stone benches. In the center, on a stone tablet, is carved: 'The Blessed Land of Flower-Fruit Mountain, the Cave-Heaven of the Water-Curtain Cave.' Truly it is a place for us to settle. And inside it is broad and wide, with room for a thousand or more of us, old and young. Let us all go in and dwell there, and so spare ourselves the buffets of old Heaven. In here:

> When the wind blows there's a place to hide, when the rain falls a good shelter for the body.
> Frost and snow we need not fear at all; the thunder's voice is never heard.
> Mist and rosy clouds forever glow; auspicious vapors ever steam and warm.
> The pines and bamboo year by year stay fair; the rare flowers grow fresh day after day."

When the monkeys heard this, every one rejoiced. They all said: "You go first and lead us in! In, in!" Again the stone monkey shut his eyes, crouched low, and leaped inside, calling: "Follow me in, all of you! In, in!" Those monkeys with bold hearts all leaped in; the timid ones, one by one, craned their necks and drew them back, scratched their ears and rubbed their cheeks, shrieked aloud, and after fussing a while, in they all went too. They leaped over the bridgehead, and one and all began snatching basins and seizing bowls, claiming the stove and fighting over the bed, hauling things this way and shifting them that way — for monkeys by nature are restless and unruly, and not a one would keep still until they had worn themselves out and their spirits flagged. Only then did they stop.

The stone monkey took his seat at the head and said: "Gentlemen — 'a man without good faith, one does not know what he can be good for.' You yourselves just now said that whoever had the ability to get in and out again unhurt should be honored as king. Now I have gone in and come out, come out and gone in, and have found you this cave-heaven where you may sleep soundly and rest at ease, and where each may enjoy the blessing of a household ready-made. Why then do you not honor me as king?" When the monkeys heard this, they all folded their hands and bowed in submission without dissent. One by one they arranged themselves in order of age, drew up in ranks, and bowed in homage, all hailing him "Great King of a Thousand Years." From that time the stone monkey ascended to the throne. He set aside the word "stone" and styled himself the Handsome Monkey King. There is a poem to prove it. The poem says:

> The three yang join in harmony to bring forth the living host;
> the magic stone, its womb enwrapping the essence of sun and moon.
> Borrowing the egg to become a monkey, he fulfills the Great Way;
> taking on a name and a surname, he matches the cinnabar's completion.
> Looked at within, there is no knowing — for it is without form;
> joined with the outer world, one clearly sees it takes on shape.
> Through all the ages every man belongs to this same kind:
> calling himself king, calling himself sage, free to roam as he will.

The Handsome Monkey King led his troop of gibbons, macaques, and horse-monkeys, and assigned to each the rank of minister, lord, aide, or officer. By day they roamed Flower-Fruit Mountain; by night they lodged in the Water-Curtain Cave. United in fellowship and of one mind, they did not join the flocks of flying birds nor follow the ranks of running beasts. He was king all by himself, and his delight was boundless. And so:

> In spring they gathered the hundred flowers for food and drink;
> in summer they sought all manner of fruits to make their living.
> In autumn they harvested chestnuts and taro to mark the season;
> in winter they hunted out the yellow-essence herb to pass the year.

The Handsome Monkey King enjoyed his innocent pleasures, and so it went — who could have foreseen it? — for three or four hundred years. One day, in the midst of a merry feast with the troop of monkeys, he suddenly grew downcast and troubled, and let fall tears. The monkeys hurriedly bowed all around him and asked: "Great King, what is the cause of your grief?" The Monkey King said: "Though I am now in my time of joy, I have one small far-reaching worry, and that is why I grieve." The monkeys laughed again and said: "Great King, how easily you are dissatisfied! Day after day we hold merry gatherings, in fairy mountains and blessed lands, in ancient caves and spirit continents. We are not subject to the rule of the unicorn, nor governed by the phoenix, nor bound by any earthly king's authority. We are free and at ease, and ours is a blessing beyond measure. Why then this far-reaching worry, that you should grieve?" The Monkey King said: "Today, though we are not bound by the laws of any human king, nor in dread of the majesty of birds and beasts, yet in years to come, when we grow old and our blood runs thin, there is old King Yama working in secret who has us in his charge. Once the body perishes, shall we not have lived in this world in vain, unable to abide forever among the ranks of the gods?"

When the monkeys heard these words, every one of them covered his face and wept, all troubled by the thought of impermanence. Just then, out from the ranks leaped a Common-Backed Gibbon, who cried in a stern, loud voice: "If the Great King has thoughts so far-reaching as these, it is truly what is called the awakening of the heart that seeks the Way! Now among all the Five Kinds of living creatures, there are just three sorts that are not subject to old King Yama." The Monkey King said: "Do you know which three sorts?" The gibbon said: "They are the Buddhas, the Immortals, and the Holy Sages — these three. They escape the wheel of rebirth; they are neither born nor extinguished, and they live as long as heaven and earth, the mountains and the rivers." The Monkey King said: "Where do these three dwell?" The gibbon said: "They dwell only within the world of Jambudvipa, within ancient caves and fairy mountains." When the Monkey King heard this, his heart was filled with joy, and he said: "Tomorrow I shall take leave of you all and go down from the mountain. I shall roam by cloud to the corners of the sea, journey far to the ends of heaven, and seek out these three without fail, that I may learn the secret of deathless long life and forever escape the woe of King Yama." Ah! This one saying caused him to leap clear of the net of the wheel of rebirth, and led at last to the making of the Great Sage Equal to Heaven.

The monkeys clapped and cried in praise, all saying: "Excellent! Excellent! Tomorrow we will cross the ridges and climb the heights and gather a wide store of fruits, and set out a great banquet to see the Great King off." The next day the monkeys went indeed to pluck the immortal peaches and pick the rare fruits, to dig up the mountain yams and grub out the yellow-essence herb. Magic fungus and fragrant orchid, fairy grasses and rare blossoms — every sort and every kind, neatly and in good order, they laid out on the stone benches and stone tables, and arranged the immortal wine and immortal viands. You should have seen them:

> Golden pellets and pearly bullets, ones split red and ones grown yellow-ripe.
> Golden pellets and pearly bullets — the winter cherries, their color true and their taste sweet;
> split red and grown yellow-ripe — the ripened plums, their flavor fragrant and tart.
> Fresh dragon-eyes, sweet of flesh and thin of skin; fire-lychees, small of stone and red of pulp.
> Crab-apples in jade-green fruit, offered still on the branch; loquats in pale-yellow husk, held up with the leaves.
> Hare-headed pears and chicken-heart dates, that slake the thirst, dispel vexation, and sober a drunken head.
> Fragrant peaches and softened apricots, sweet as the jade-broth and jasper nectar of the gods;
> crisp plums and bayberries, tart and cool as cream and curds and clarified butter.
> Ripe watermelons with red rind and black seeds; great persimmons of four lobes and yellow skin.
> Pomegranates split open, their cinnabar grains showing like fiery crystal beads;
> chestnuts cracked apart, their hard kernels round like golden agate.
> Walnuts and ginkgo nuts to go with the tea; coconuts and grapes that can be made into wine.
> Hazelnuts, pine-nuts, torreya and quince heaped full on the platters; oranges, sugarcane, tangerines and bitter-oranges piled high upon the boards.
> Mountain yams roasted soft, yellow-essence herb stewed tender;
> poria and Job's-tears pounded fine, simmered to a broth over a low fire in the stone pot.
> Though the world of men may have its rarest delicacies, how can they match the calm contentment of the mountain monkeys?

The troop set the Handsome Monkey King in the seat of honor, and each according to his age ranged himself below. One by one they came up in turn to offer wine, to offer flowers, to offer fruit, and they drank deep all that day.

The next day the Handsome Monkey King rose early and gave the order: "Little ones, break me some dry pine boughs and weave them into a raft, take a bamboo pole for a punt-pole, gather some fruits and the like — I am going now." He boarded the raft alone, pushed off with all his strength, and went drifting and tossing straight out into the waves of the great ocean. With a heaven-sent wind behind him, he made his crossing toward the borders of the Southern Continent of Jambu. This voyage was truly:

> The heaven-born fairy monkey, deep in his cultivation of the Way,
> leaves the mountain, rides the raft, and takes the wind of heaven.
> Across the ocean, over the sea, he seeks the immortal Way;
> firm in will, with hidden heart, to build a great achievement.
> Having his share and his destiny, he sets aside worldly desires;
> free of sorrow, free of care, he meets the Origin-Dragon.
> Surely he must encounter one who knows the music of his heart,
> who will lay bare the source and stream, and all the myriad ways flow clear.

It was indeed that his fortune had come and his hour had ripened. From the day he boarded his wooden raft, the southeast wind blew strong for days on end and carried him to the northwest shore, which was the border of the Southern Continent of Jambu. Testing the water with his pole, he chanced upon a shallow, abandoned the raft, and leaped up onto the bank. There along the shore were people fishing, catching wild geese, digging clams, and panning for salt. He went up close, played a trick, and made himself out a tiger to frighten them — so that those folk threw down their baskets and abandoned their nets and scattered in all directions, fleeing. The one who could not run he seized, stripped off his clothes, and learned, like a man, to put them on his own body. Swaggering and strutting, he passed through districts and crossed prefectures, and in the marketplaces learned the manners of men and the speech of men. By morning he ate and by night he lodged, his whole heart set on inquiring after the Way of the Buddhas, the Immortals, and the Holy Sages, and on finding some recipe for deathless long life. But he saw that the people of the world were all men bent on fame and gain, and not one among them cared for his own life and destiny. It was indeed:

> Striving for fame and snatching at gain — when will it ever cease?
> Up early and to bed late, never their own masters.
> Riding the donkey and the mule, they dream of fine steeds;
> holding the office of prime minister, they hope for the rank of king.
> They worry only over food and clothing and steep themselves in toil,
> never fearing that King Yama will come to hook them away.
> Sons after them and grandsons in their shade, they scheme for wealth and rank,
> and not a single one is willing to turn his head and look back.

The Monkey King sought everywhere after the Way of the immortals, but found no destined meeting. Through the Southern Continent of Jambu he wandered, threading the great cities and roaming the little counties, until, before he knew it, eight or nine years had passed. Then suddenly he came to the great Western Ocean, and he thought to himself that beyond the sea there must surely be immortals. As before, he made himself a raft all alone, and drifted across the Western Sea until he reached the borders of the Western Continent of Cattle-Offering. He went ashore and searched about for a long while, until suddenly he saw a tall mountain, fair and lovely, its forests and foothills deep and secluded. Fearing neither wolves and insects nor tigers and leopards, he climbed to the very summit to look about. Truly it was a fine mountain:

> A thousand peaks ranged like halberds, ten thousand fathoms spread like a screen.
> The sun lights the mountain mist and lightly locks the green; the rain clears and the dark hue coldly holds the blue.
> Withered vines twine the old trees; an ancient ford marks off the secret path.
> Rare flowers and auspicious grasses, slender bamboo and towering pine.
> Slender bamboo and towering pine — for ten thousand years ever green, putting the blessed land to shame;
> rare flowers and auspicious grasses — never fading through the four seasons, outdoing fairy Penglai.
> The secret birds call near at hand; the spring at the source murmurs clear.
> Fold upon fold of valleys, ringed about with fungus and orchid; everywhere the steep cliffs grow with moss and lichen.
> The rolling crests are dragon-veins of good fortune — surely here some lofty man hides his name and dwells.

As he was gazing about, he suddenly heard, from the depths of the forest, the sound of someone speaking. Hurriedly he quickened his step, pressed into the wood, cocked his ear, and listened — and found it was the sound of singing. The song went:

> "Watching the chess, the axe-handle rots; chopping wood, the strokes ring out — *ding, ding*.
> By the cloud's edge, at the valley's mouth, I stroll at ease.
> Selling firewood to buy my wine, I laugh wild and delight in myself.
> The green path, the high autumn — facing the moon, I pillow my head on a pine-root,
> and sleep a sleep till the sky grows light.
> I know the old wood, climb the cliffs and cross the ridges,
> and with my axe cut the withered vines.
> When I have gathered a full load, I go singing along the market street
> and trade it for three measures of rice.
> No haggling, no contention — the price of the day is fair and even.
> I know no cunning schemes or clever reckonings;
> without glory or disgrace, in calm and plainness I lengthen out my life.
> Those I meet upon the way are immortals, or else followers of the Way,
> who sit in stillness and expound the *Yellow Court*."

When the Handsome Monkey King heard these words, his heart was full of joy, and he said: "So the immortals are hidden away in here!" At once he sprang inside, and looking carefully again, he saw it was only a woodcutter, raising his axe to chop firewood. But look how strangely he was dressed:

> On his head a broad bamboo hat, made of the sheath that a fresh bamboo-shoot has just cast off.
> On his body a cloth gown, made of the yarn that cotton has been twisted into.
> Round his waist a knotted girdle, made of the silk that the old silkworm's mouth has spun.
> On his feet straw sandals, woven of the stripped and dried sedge.
> In his hand a polished steel axe, and a hempen rope coiled at his side.
> For prying loose the pines and splitting the dead trees — what could be better than such a woodcutter?

The Monkey King drew near and called out: "Old immortal, your disciple makes his bow!" The woodcutter hastily threw down his axe and turned to return the courtesy, saying: "Not fitting, not fitting! I am a poor clumsy fellow who lacks even enough to eat and wear — how should I dare bear the two words 'immortal'?" The Monkey King said: "If you are no immortal, how is it you speak the words of immortals?" The woodcutter said: "What words of immortals did I speak?" The Monkey King said: "Just now, as I came to the forest's edge, I heard you say: 'Those I meet upon the way are immortals, or else followers of the Way, who sit in stillness and expound the *Yellow Court*.' The *Yellow Court* is a true scripture of the Way and its Power — if that is not an immortal, what is it?"

The woodcutter laughed and said: "I'll tell you truly and hide nothing: this song is called *Fragrance Fills the Courtyard*, and it was an immortal who taught it to me. That immortal lives next door to my poor cottage. Seeing how I am worn down by household toil and daily vexations, he taught me that whenever I meet with troubles I should chant this song over to myself — first to ease my mind, and second to dispel my weariness. Just now I had some hardships weighing on my thoughts, and so I was chanting it, never expecting that you would hear me." The Monkey King said: "Since your house is next door to an immortal's, why do you not follow him in his cultivation, and learn some recipe for not growing old? Would that not be well?" The woodcutter said: "My whole life has been bitter and hard. From my infancy I was raised and reared by my parents, and by the time I was eight or nine and had come to know the ways of men, my father, alas, died, and my mother lived on a widow. I have neither brothers nor sisters — only myself, and no help for it but to wait upon her morning and evening. Now my mother is old, and all the more I dare not leave her side. Besides, my fields and garden lie fallow, and we lack enough food and clothing. So I can do nothing but cut a couple of bundles of firewood, carry them to the marketplace, sell them for a few coins, buy a few measures of rice, and cook it myself to set out some plain tea and food and provide for my old mother. That is why I cannot cultivate the Way."

The Monkey King said: "By what you say, you are a gentleman who practices filial piety, and in time to come good things will surely come of it. But I beg you to point me to that immortal's dwelling, that I may go and pay him a visit." The woodcutter said: "It is not far, not far. This mountain is called the Mountain of the Spirit-Terrace and the Square-Inch; in the mountain there is a cave called the Cave of the Slanting Moon and Three Stars. In that cave there dwells an immortal called the Patriarch Subodhi. Of his disciples who have gone forth there is no counting the number, and even now there are some thirty or forty cultivating the Way under him. You have only to follow that little path southward for seven or eight li, and you will come to his house."

The Monkey King took hold of the woodcutter with his hand and said: "Elder brother, come along with me. If I gain some benefit from it, I will surely not forget your kindness in showing me the way." The woodcutter said: "What a thick-headed fellow you are! I have just now told you all this, and still you do not understand. If I were to go with you, would I not neglect my livelihood? And who then would provide for my old mother? I have my firewood to cut — you go on by yourself, go on!"

Hearing this, the Monkey King had no choice but to take his leave. He came out of the deep forest, found the path, passed over a hillside, and after some seven or eight li, sure enough, he caught sight of a cave-dwelling. He stood up straight and gazed at it — truly a splendid place! He saw:

> Mists and rosy clouds scatter their colors; sun and moon shake their light.
> A thousand ancient cypresses, ten thousand joints of slender bamboo.
> A thousand ancient cypresses, bearing the rain, blue-green and soft against the empty sky;
> ten thousand joints of slender bamboo, wrapped in mist, filling a whole ravine with their somber hue.
> Outside the gate, rare flowers spread like brocade; beside the bridge, fairy grasses breathe out their fragrance.
> The stone cliffs jut up, their green moss moist; the hanging walls stretch high, their emerald lichen long.
> Now and again one hears the cry of fairy cranes; ever one sees the soaring of phoenixes.
> When the fairy crane cries, its voice shakes the ninefold marsh and reaches the far heavens;
> when the phoenix soars up, its plumage of five colors glows like a rainbow cloud.
> Dark gibbons and white deer come and go half-hidden; golden lions and jade elephants roam or hide at will.
> Look closely on this blessed spirit-land — truly it rivals heaven itself.

He saw too that the cave-gate was tightly shut, all hushed and still, with no trace of anyone. Suddenly turning his head, he saw at the edge of the cliff a stone tablet standing, about three zhang and more in height and eight chi and more in breadth, and on it a single line of ten great characters: "The Mountain of the Spirit-Terrace and the Square-Inch; the Cave of the Slanting Moon and Three Stars." The Handsome Monkey King was greatly delighted, and said: "The people here are honest folk indeed — there truly is such a mountain and such a cave." He looked a long while, but did not dare to knock at the gate. Instead he leaped up to the tips of the pine boughs, plucked the pine-seeds, and ate them as he played.

After a little while, he heard with a creak the cave-gate open, and out from within came a fairy lad, truly of fair and noble bearing, of pure and uncommon looks, quite unlike the common run of worldly folk. Just look at him:

> His twin tufts of hair bound with cords of silk; his wide robe with the wind in both its sleeves.
> His features and his form set him apart; his heart and his appearance both were void.
> A long-lived guest beyond the things of this world, an ever-youthful lad of the mountains.
> No speck of dust could stain him at all; let the years and calendars wheel as they would.

The lad came out the gate and called aloud: "Who is it making a disturbance here?" The Monkey King leaped down from the tree with a flop, came forward, bowed low, and said: "Fairy lad, I am a disciple come to seek the Way and to learn to be an immortal. I would never dare make a disturbance here." The fairy lad laughed and said: "You are one seeking the Way?" The Monkey King said: "I am." The lad said: "My master has just now risen from his couch and mounted the dais to expound the Way. Before he had even told the reason, he sent me out to open the gate, saying: 'There is one cultivating the Way come outside — go and receive him.' It must surely be you?" The Monkey King laughed and said: "It is I, it is I." The lad said: "Come in with me, then."

The Monkey King straightened his clothes, composed himself with reverence, and followed the lad straight into the deep recesses of the cave-heaven to look about. Tier upon tier of deep towers and jasper pavilions, court within court of pearl palaces and conch-shell gateways — there was no telling the number of those quiet chambers and secluded dwellings. They came at last to the foot of a jasper terrace, where he saw the Patriarch Subodhi seated upright upon the dais, with thirty lesser immortals standing in attendance on either side below. Truly he was:

> The Great Enlightened Golden Immortal, of a form without stain, the Patriarch Bodhi of the wondrous likeness of the West.
> Unborn, undying, in the threefold-threefold practice; whole in vital force, whole in spirit, in his myriad-fold compassion.
> Empty and still, of himself he follows transformation; in true suchness, his original nature acts as it will.
> Of a majestic body that lives as long as heaven; a great Dharma-master whose heart shines clear through aeon upon aeon.

The moment the Handsome Monkey King saw him, he flung himself down and bowed, knocking his head upon the ground beyond all counting, his mouth saying only: "Master, master! Your disciple pays homage with his whole heart, pays homage with his whole heart!" The Patriarch said: "From what region do you come? First state your native place and your name clearly, and then bow again." The Monkey King said: "Your disciple is a native of the Water-Curtain Cave on Flower-Fruit Mountain, in the country of Aolai, in the Eastern Continent of Spiritual Excellence." The Patriarch shouted his command: "Drive him out! He is nothing but a fellow who deals in lies and deceit — how should such a one cultivate any fruit of the Way?" The Monkey King hastily knocked his head without ceasing and said: "Your disciple's words are honest; there is surely no falsehood or deceit." The Patriarch said: "If you are honest, how is it you speak of the Eastern Continent of Spiritual Excellence? Between that place and here lie two great oceans and the whole Southern Continent of Jambu — how could you ever have come here?" The Monkey King kowtowed and said: "Your disciple drifted across the oceans and over the seas, made landfall and roamed about, for some ten years and more, before at last I found my way to this place."

The Patriarch said: "Well, if you came gradually, step by step, that may pass. What is your surname?" The Monkey King said again: "I have no temper. If men curse me, I am not vexed; if they strike me, I am not angered. I merely make my apology and let it go. All my life I have had no temper." The Patriarch said: "I do not mean that kind of temper. I mean — what was your father's and mother's surname?" The Monkey King said: "I have no father or mother either." The Patriarch said: "If you have no father or mother, then you must have grown on a tree." The Monkey King said: "Though I did not grow on a tree, I grew out of a stone. I remember only that on Flower-Fruit Mountain there was a magic stone, and in that year the stone burst open, and so I was born."

When the Patriarch heard this, he was secretly pleased, and said: "Then you are a being formed by heaven and earth. Get up and walk about, and let me see you." The Monkey King sprang up and went hobbling and rolling about twice. The Patriarch laughed and said: "Though your body is coarse and mean, you are like nothing so much as a pine-nut-eating macaque. I will take a surname for you from your own body. My thought is to give you the surname *Hu*. If you take the beast-radical from the character *hu*, what remains is *gu* and *yue* — 'ancient' and 'moon.' But 'ancient' means old, and 'moon' belongs to the yin; and what is old and yin cannot transform and bring forth life. Better that I give you the surname *Sun*. If you take the beast-radical from the character *sun*, what remains is *zi* and *xi* — 'child' and 'small.' 'Child' means a young boy, and 'small' means an infant — which fits exactly the root meaning of the newborn babe. Let your surname be *Sun*."

When the Monkey King heard this, his heart was filled with joy, and he kowtowed up toward the dais and said: "Splendid! Splendid! Splendid! Today at last I know I have a surname! I beg the master in his mercy — since now I have a surname, grant me also a personal name, so that it will be convenient to call me." The Patriarch said: "Within my school there are twelve characters by which names are assigned in order, and you fall in the tenth generation of little disciples." The Monkey King said: "Which twelve characters?" The Patriarch said: "They are *Guang, Da, Zhi, Hui, Zhen, Ru, Xing, Hai, Ying, Wu, Yuan, Jue* — twelve characters. Counting down to you, it falls upon the character *Wu*, 'Awakened.' I will give you the Dharma-name Sun Wukong — 'Monkey Awakened to Emptiness.' How is that?" The Monkey King laughed and said: "Splendid! Splendid! Splendid! From this day on I am called Sun Wukong!" It was indeed:

> When the primal murk was first cleft, there was no surname at all;
> to shatter stubborn emptiness, one must awaken to emptiness.

And after all, there is no knowing what fruit of the Way he was to cultivate from this point on — so listen to the next chapter for the explanation.

<!-- chapter 2 -->
# Chapter 2: The Secret Word at the Third Watch

Now the Handsome Monkey King, having at last received both surname and religious name, was so overjoyed that he leapt and capered for delight, then bowed before the Patriarch Subhuti to give his thanks. The master at once ordered the assembled disciples to lead Sun Wukong out beyond the second gate, where they were to teach him how to sprinkle and sweep, how to answer when spoken to, and the proper manners of coming and going, advancing and withdrawing. The immortals obeyed and led him out. Once outside the gate, Wukong bowed again to all his elder brothers in the faith, and arranged himself a sleeping place within the corridors of the cloister. Early the next morning he set about learning speech and courtesy from his elder brethren, discussing the scriptures and debating the Way, practicing his brushwork and burning incense. So passed each day. In his idle hours he swept the grounds and hoed the garden, tended the flowers and pruned the trees, gathered firewood and tended the flames, drew water and carried it in buckets. Of all the chores that wanted doing, there was none he left undone. And so, scarcely noticing the passage of time, he dwelt in that cave for six or seven years.

One day the Patriarch mounted his lecture platform, took his lofty seat, and summoned all the immortals to hear him expound the Great Way. Truly it was a marvel:

> Heaven's blossoms came tumbling down,
> golden lotuses welled up from the earth.
> Subtle, he laid out the teaching of the Three Vehicles,
> in fine detail, the ten thousand methods complete.
> A slow wave of the whisk, and pearls and jade came spraying;
> the sound rolled like thunder, shaking the Ninefold Sky.
> A while he spoke of the Way, a while he discoursed on Chan—
> the three traditions joined as one, as is their nature.
> Open but a single word, and you grasp the principle of return and faith;
> follow his pointing finger, and you fathom the mystery of the deathless, deep nature.

Sun Wukong, listening from the side, was so delighted that he scratched his ears and rubbed his cheeks, his brows fairly blooming and his eyes laughing; he could not keep his hands from waving nor his feet from stamping in a dance. All at once the Patriarch caught sight of him and called out: "Sun Wukong! There you stand among the ranks—why do you leap and dance like a madman instead of listening to my lecture?"

"Your disciple was listening with all his heart," said Wukong, "and when he reached the place where the old master's wondrous voice grew most marvelous, I was so beside myself with joy that, before I knew it, I fell into this capering. I beg the master's pardon."

"Since you can recognize the wondrous voice," said the Patriarch, "let me ask you this: how long have you been in this cave?"

"Your disciple was always a dull-witted creature," said Wukong, "and cannot reckon how many seasons it has been. I only remember that whenever there was no fire under the stove, I would go off behind the mountain to gather kindling. There I found a fine hill of peach trees, and there I have eaten my fill of peaches seven times over."

"That hill is called Ripe Peach Mountain," said the Patriarch. "If you have eaten there seven times, then it must be seven years. And now what manner of the Way do you wish to learn from me?"

"That rests with my honored teacher's instruction," said Wukong. "If there is but a breath of the Way's true essence in it, your disciple will learn it gladly."

The Patriarch said: "Within the gate of this one word, 'Tao,' there are three hundred and sixty side-doors, and every side-door can lead to a proper fruition. I wonder—which of them would you study?"

"That is as my honored teacher pleases," said Wukong. "Your disciple will listen and obey with his whole heart."

"Suppose I teach you the Way that lies within the gate of the word 'Arts,'" said the Patriarch. "How would that suit you?"

"And what does the Way of the Arts gate mean?" asked Wukong.

"Within the gate of the Arts," said the Patriarch, "are such things as summoning immortals and consulting the planchette, casting fortunes and divining with yarrow stalks—the lore by which one may know how to seek good luck and shun misfortune."

"And by such means," asked Wukong, "can one win eternal life?"

"No, no," said the Patriarch.

"Then I won't learn it, I won't learn it," said Wukong.

The Patriarch went on: "Suppose I teach you the Way within the gate of the word 'Schools.' How would that be?"

"And what is the principle within the Schools gate?" Wukong asked again.

"Within the gate of the Schools," said the Patriarch, "are the Confucians and the Buddhists, the Taoists, the Yin-Yang masters, the Mohists and the Physicians—some who pore over the scriptures, some who chant the Buddha's name, and others who summon the true and call down the holy."

"And by such means," asked Wukong, "can one win eternal life?"

"If it's eternal life you want," said the Patriarch, "then this is like setting a pillar inside a wall."

"Master," said Wukong, "I am a plain, honest fellow, and I don't follow the cant of the marketplace. What do you mean, 'setting a pillar inside a wall'?"

"When folk build a house," said the Patriarch, "and want it to stand firm, they set an upright pillar in among the walls. But the day the great hall begins to topple, that pillar is sure to have rotted away."

"By that account," said Wukong, "it does not last long. I won't learn it, I won't learn it."

The Patriarch said: "Suppose I teach you the Way within the gate of the word 'Stillness.' How about that?"

"And what proper fruition lies within the Stillness gate?" asked Wukong.

"This," said the Patriarch, "is fasting from grain and guarding the body's emptiness, pure quietude and non-action, sitting in Chan meditation, holding silence and keeping abstinence; some practice their merit lying down, some standing up, along with entering trance and sealing oneself in retreat."

"And can such practices win eternal life as well?" asked Wukong.

"They are like an unfired brick of clay on a kiln," said the Patriarch.

Wukong laughed: "The master is full of riddles! Just now I told you I can't follow the marketplace cant, and here you go again. What do you mean, 'an unfired brick of clay on a kiln'?"

"It is just like a brick or tile of clay shaped upon the kiln," said the Patriarch. "Though it has already taken its form, it has not yet been tempered by water and fire; and when one day the rain comes pouring down in torrents, it is sure to dissolve into mud."

"That does not last long either," said Wukong. "I won't learn it, I won't learn it."

The Patriarch said: "Suppose I teach you the Way within the gate of the word 'Action.' How about that?"

"And what then is the Way of the Action gate?" asked Wukong.

"This is the path of doing and contriving," said the Patriarch: "drawing on the yin to nourish the yang, drawing the bow and treading the crossbow's lever, massaging the navel and circulating the breath, compounding elixirs by formula, firing the cauldron over a grass blaze, ingesting red lead and refining 'autumn stone,' and such things as drinking a woman's milk."

"And by such means as these can one win eternal life?" asked Wukong.

"To seek long life this way," said the Patriarch, "is like fishing for the moon in the water."

"There the master goes again," said Wukong. "What do you mean, 'fishing for the moon in the water'?"

"The moon hangs in the vast sky," said the Patriarch, "and its reflection lies in the water. Though you can see it plainly, there is nothing there to grasp or seize; in the end it comes to nothing at all."

"Then I won't learn that either, I won't learn it," said Wukong.

When the Patriarch heard this, he gave a sharp cry—"Tcha!"—and sprang down from the high platform. Grasping his ruler-rod in his hand, he leveled it at Wukong and said: "You ape! This you won't learn and that you won't learn—what is it you're waiting for, then?" He strode forward and struck Wukong three times upon the head. Then, clasping his hands behind his back, he walked off into the inner quarters, shut the middle gate, and left the whole assembly standing there. This so alarmed all those who had come to hear the lecture that every one of them was terrified, and they fell to scolding Wukong: "You wretched monkey! You have no manners at all. The master would have handed you the methods of the Way—why wouldn't you learn them? Why must you talk back to him? Now that you've provoked him, there's no telling when he'll come out again!" One and all they reviled him and heaped reproach upon him, despising and detesting him. But Wukong was not the least bit vexed; his whole face was wreathed in smiles. For the truth was that the Monkey King had already cracked the riddle hidden in the master's words and kept it secret in his heart, and that was why he would not quarrel with the others but only held his peace in silence. The Patriarch's three blows on his head meant: be mindful at the hour of the third watch; and the clasping of his hands behind his back as he walked into the inner rooms and shut the middle gate meant: enter by the back door, and there in secret he would pass the Way to him.

That day Wukong made merry with the rest before the Cave of the Three Stars, watching the sky and impatient for the dark, which seemed it would never come. When dusk at last fell he went to bed with the others, but only feigned to close his eyes, steadying his breath and gathering his spirit. In the mountains there was no watchman's drum or arrow-clock to mark the hours, so he could not tell the time; he only regulated the breath that passed in and out of his own nostrils. When it drew near the hour of the Rat, he rose ever so softly, put on his clothes, stealthily opened the front door, slipped away from the sleepers, and went out. He lifted his head and looked about, and this is what he saw:

> The moon shone bright, the clear dew cold,
> and to the eight far quarters, no speck of dust.
> Deep in the trees the hidden birds were roosting,
> and at its source the water purled and flowed.
> The flitting fireflies scattered their drifting glow,
> and passing wild geese ranged in script across the clouds.
> Just at the moment of the third watch's depth—
> the very hour to seek the truth of the Way.

Watch him now, following the old familiar path to the place behind the rear gate, where he found the door standing half open and half closed. Wukong rejoiced: "So the old master truly means to pass me the Way—that is why he has left the door open." With long quiet strides he drew near, turned himself sideways, and slipped inside, going straight on until he stood beneath the Patriarch's sleeping couch. There he saw the master lying curled up, asleep with his face to the wall. Wukong dared not disturb him, but knelt down before the couch. Before long the Patriarch awoke, stretched out both his legs, and murmured to himself:

> "Hard! Hard! Hard! The Way is most profound—
> do not treat the Golden Elixir as a trifling thing.
> Unless you meet a perfected man to pass the wondrous secret,
> you weary your mouth with empty words and dry your tongue!"

At this Wukong answered aloud: "Master, your disciple has been kneeling here in waiting a long while." The Patriarch, hearing that the voice was Wukong's, at once rose and pulled on his robe, sat cross-legged, and barked: "You ape! Why aren't you sleeping out in front? What are you doing here behind?"

"Master," said Wukong, "yesterday at the lecture platform, before all the others, you promised your disciple that at the hour of the third watch you would pass me the Way by the back door. That is why I have made so bold as to come straight here and kneel beneath your couch."

When the Patriarch heard this he was greatly pleased, and thought secretly to himself: "This creature is indeed something engendered by Heaven and Earth—how else could he have cracked the dark riddle hidden in my words?"

"Here there are no other ears to hear," said Wukong, "none but your disciple alone. I beg the master in his great mercy to grant me the Way of eternal life, and I shall never forget the kindness."

"You have an affinity now," said the Patriarch, "and I too am glad to speak. Since you have read the hidden riddle, come closer and listen carefully, and I shall pass to you the wondrous Way of eternal life." Wukong kowtowed his thanks, washed out his ears, fixed his whole mind upon it, and knelt beneath the couch. The Patriarch chanted:

> The true and wondrous secret, manifest and hidden, perfect and all-pervading,
> guards nature and life—there is nothing else to say.
> It all comes down to essence, breath, and spirit:
> hold them firm, lock them deep, let nothing leak away.
> Let nothing leak away, but store it in the body,
> and the Way I pass to you will of itself grow great.
> Keep the oral formula in mind—much good it brings;
> banish lewd desire, and win the cool serenity.
> Win the cool serenity, the light pure and bright,
> and turn toward the elixir-terrace to savor the shining moon.
> The moon hides the jade hare, the sun hides the crow;
> of themselves the tortoise and serpent coil and entwine.
> Coiled and entwined, nature and life stand firm—
> and you can plant the golden lotus within the very fire.
> Gather and reverse the Five Phases in their working,
> and when the work is done, become a Buddha or an immortal as you will.

In that moment the very root and source were laid bare, and Wukong, his spirit quickened and his good fortune arrived, fixed the formula firmly in his heart. He bowed to the Patriarch in deep gratitude, then went out by the back door and looked about him. The east was just beginning to pale with white, and along the western road a great golden light shone forth bright. Following the old path, he came round to the front door, pushed it softly open, went in, and sat down in his usual sleeping place. Then he deliberately shook the bedstead so it rattled, and called out: "It's light! It's light! Time to get up!" The rest were still fast asleep, never knowing that Wukong had won this fine thing. That day he went about and mingled with the others as usual, secretly nurturing his attainment, and morning and evening, before noon and after, regulating his own breath.

In no time three more years had slipped by, and the Patriarch once again ascended his treasure-seat to expound the Dharma to the assembly. He spoke of the public cases and parables, and discoursed on the outer forms and the husks that wrap them. Suddenly he asked: "Where is Wukong?" Wukong came forward and knelt down: "Your disciple is here."

"What sort of Way have you been cultivating all this while?" asked the Patriarch.

"Of late your disciple's spiritual nature has grown fairly clear," said Wukong, "and the root and source are gradually growing firm."

"Since you have penetrated the nature of the Dharma and grasped the root and source," said the Patriarch, "and have already settled your spirit-body, you must now guard yourself against the perils of the Three Calamities."

Hearing this, Wukong brooded for a long while, then said: "Master, surely your words are mistaken. I have always heard that one of lofty Way and abundant virtue is coeval with Heaven itself; that when water and fire are brought into harmony, no illness can arise. How then can there be these 'perils of the Three Calamities'?"

"This," said the Patriarch, "is no ordinary Way. It robs Heaven and Earth of their very work of creation; it usurps the hidden workings of the sun and moon. Once the elixir is achieved, ghosts and spirits cannot abide it. Though it keeps your youth and lengthens your years, yet after five hundred years Heaven will send down a thunder-calamity to strike you. You must see your nature and make your mind clear, and dodge it beforehand. If you can dodge it, your life span will equal Heaven's; if you cannot, there your life is cut off. After another five hundred years Heaven will send down a fire-calamity to burn you. This is no fire of Heaven, nor any common fire; it is called the 'yin-fire.' It kindles up from the Bubbling Spring point beneath the soles of your own feet, drives straight up to the Niwan Palace in the crown of the head, reduces the five viscera to ashes and the four limbs to rot, so that a thousand years of bitter cultivation are all turned to illusion. After yet another five hundred years a wind-calamity will be sent down to blow upon you. This is no wind of east or south or west or north, no mild or scorching wind off the metal autumn, nor any wind through flowers and willows, pines and bamboo; it is called the 'Mighty Wind.' It blows in through the crown of the head into the six bowels, passes the elixir-field and pierces the nine apertures; flesh and bone melt and disperse, and the body of itself comes undone. All of these, therefore, must be dodged."

When Wukong heard this his hair stood on end and a shudder ran through him; he kowtowed and bowed, saying: "I beg the old master to take pity and pass me the method for dodging the Three Calamities. To the very end I shall never dare forget the kindness."

"This is not so hard," said the Patriarch. "Only, you are different from other men, and so it cannot be passed to you."

"But I too have a round head reaching up to Heaven and square feet treading the Earth," said Wukong. "I have the same nine apertures and four limbs, the five viscera and six bowels. How am I different from other men?"

"Though you have the likeness of a man," said the Patriarch, "you are short in the cheeks compared with others." For the truth was that this monkey had a hollow-cheeked, pointed-jawed face, a sunken visage and a sharp snout. Wukong put up his hand, felt about, and laughed: "The master hasn't reckoned right. True, I'm short in the cheeks, but I have more than other men in this gullet-pouch of mine, and that may serve to make up the difference."

"Very well, then," said the Patriarch. "Which sort would you learn? There is one set after the number of the Heavenly Ladle, which comprises thirty-six transformations; and there is one set after the number of the Earthly Fiends, which comprises seventy-two transformations."

"Your disciple would rather cast a wider net," said Wukong. "Let me learn the Earthly Fiends' transformations."

"In that case," said the Patriarch, "come forward and I shall pass you the oral formula." Then he put his mouth to Wukong's ear and murmured low—who knows what wondrous method he spoke? But this Monkey King was one in whom, once a single aperture opened, all hundred apertures opened together; and there and then he learned the formula, cultivated and refined it himself, and mastered all seventy-two transformations entire.

Then one day the Patriarch and his disciples were amusing themselves before the Cave of the Three Stars, enjoying the evening scene. The Patriarch said: "Wukong, have you accomplished it yet or not?"

"By the master's boundless grace," said Wukong, "your disciple's labor and fruit are complete, and I can already rise on the rosy mists and soar aloft."

"Try flying up for me to see," said the Patriarch.

Wukong displayed his skill: he hunched his body, gave a tumbling somersault, sprang up some fifty or sixty feet from the ground, trod the clouds and mists for about the time it takes to eat a meal, came and went, and covered not quite three miles before dropping down again before them. He folded his hands and said: "Master, that is what they call soaring on the clouds!"

The Patriarch laughed: "That can't be counted as cloud-soaring—it can only be called cloud-crawling. As the old saying goes: 'An immortal roams the Northern Sea at dawn and reaches Cangwu by dusk.' But you, in half a day, have gone not even three miles; that can't even be reckoned as cloud-crawling."

"What does it mean," asked Wukong, "to 'roam the Northern Sea at dawn and reach Cangwu by dusk'?"

"Those who soar upon the clouds," said the Patriarch, "rise in the early morning from the Northern Sea, roam across the Eastern Sea, the Western Sea, and the Southern Sea, and come round again to Cangwu. Now Cangwu is the speech-name for Lingling on the Northern Sea. To traverse the whole expanse beyond the Four Seas in a single day—that may be reckoned as cloud-soaring."

"This is hard indeed, hard indeed," said Wukong.

"In all the world there is no thing too hard," said the Patriarch; "only fear a man of resolve."

When Wukong heard these words he kowtowed and bowed, and said: "Master, when one does a thing for another, one should do it through to the end. Of your great mercy, be generous and pass me this method of cloud-soaring as well, and I shall surely never dare forget the kindness."

"When all the immortals soar upon the clouds," said the Patriarch, "they all rise by stamping off their feet—but you are not like that. Just now I watched you go: you had to scramble up by tumbling somersaults. Now then, working from this very posture of yours, I shall pass you the Somersault Cloud." Wukong bowed again and begged earnestly, and the Patriarch passed him this further formula: "For this cloud, make the secret hand-sign, recite the true words, clench your fists tight, give your body a shake, and leap up—and with one somersault you'll cover a hundred and eight thousand miles."

When the assembly heard this, every one of them tittered and laughed: "What luck for Wukong! If he can work this trick, he could hire himself out as a courier-runner, carrying documents and delivering dispatches—wherever he went, he'd never want for a meal." Master and disciples then dispersed, each to his own quarters, as the sky grew dark.

That night Wukong worked his spirit and refined the method, and mastered the Somersault Cloud. From then on, day by day, he was free of all restraint, at ease and roaming as he pleased—and this too was one of the joys of eternal life.

One day, when spring was passing into summer, the assembly had been gathered a long while beneath the pine trees, discoursing together. They said to him: "Wukong, what affinity from a former life have you cultivated to deserve this? The other day the old master put his mouth to your ear and whispered low, and passed you the methods for dodging the Three Calamities and the transformations. Have you really mastered them all?"

Wukong laughed: "I'll not deceive you, elder brothers. For one thing it was the master's teaching, and for another it was my own diligence night and day—and I have mastered every one of those several skills."

"Now is a fine time," said the assembly. "Try giving us a demonstration—let us have a look."

Hearing this, Wukong roused his spirit and prepared to show off his arts: "Elder brothers, set me a subject. What would you have me change into?"

"Change into a pine tree, then," they said. Wukong made the secret sign, recited the spell, gave his body a shake, and changed into a pine tree. Truly it was:

> Lush and dense, breathing mist through all four seasons,
> rising straight above the clouds in a fine, upright form.
> Not the least trace of the goblin-monkey about it—
> nothing but boughs that have braved the frost and borne the snow.

When the assembly saw it they clapped their hands and roared with laughter, all crying out: "What a fine monkey! What a fine monkey!" Their clamor and uproar, before they knew it, disturbed the Patriarch. He came hurrying out of his door, dragging his staff, and demanded: "Who is making this racket here?" At his call the assembly hastily checked themselves, straightened their robes, and stepped forward. Wukong too resumed his true form and, lost among the crowd, said: "May it please the honored master: we were gathered here discoursing, and there were no outsiders making any noise."

The Patriarch shouted in anger: "Bawling and shouting like this—you do not in the least resemble men of cultivation! A man who cultivates the Way, when he opens his mouth, lets his spirit-breath disperse, and when he stirs his tongue, breeds right and wrong. How is it you are roaring with laughter here?"

"We dare not deceive the master," said the assembly. "Just now Sun Wukong was performing his transformations for sport. We told him to change into a pine tree, and a real pine tree it was. Your disciples were all praising and applauding him, and so our loud voices startled and offended the honored master. We beg your pardon."

"Off with you, all of you," said the Patriarch. Then he called: "Wukong, come here! What sort of spirit were you working? What manner of pine tree were you changing into? Is this a feat to be showing off in front of others? Suppose you saw someone else with such a skill—wouldn't you beg him for it? And when others see that you have it, they will surely beg it of you. If you fear the harm, you will have to teach them; and if you do not teach them, they will surely do you injury—and then you cannot keep your own life safe."

Wukong kowtowed and said: "I only beg the master to pardon me."

"I lay no blame on you," said the Patriarch, "but you must simply go."

When Wukong heard these words, his eyes brimmed over with tears: "Master, where would you have me go?"

"Wherever you came from," said the Patriarch, "back there you must go."

All at once Wukong understood, and said: "I came from the Water Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, in the Aolai Country, in the Eastern Continent of Superior Body."

"Hurry back there," said the Patriarch, "and preserve your life. To remain here is by no means to be permitted."

Wukong accepted his fault and pleaded with the honored master: "I have been away from home a full twenty years now. Though I long indeed to look upon my children and grandchildren of old, yet when I think how I have not yet repaid the master's deep kindness, I dare not go."

"What kindness or obligation is there to speak of?" said the Patriarch. "Only see that you stir up no trouble and do not drag my name into it—that is all I ask."

Seeing there was no help for it, Wukong could only bow his farewell and take his leave of the assembly. The Patriarch said: "On this going of yours, you are bound to come to no good. Whatever trouble you stir up or evil you commit, you are forbidden to say that you are my disciple. Let half a word of it out, and I shall know it at once, and I will flay this ape's hide and grind his bones, and banish his spirit-soul to the Nine Hells, so that through ten thousand ages he shall never turn over again!"

"I will never dare to breathe a word of the master," said Wukong. "I'll only say that I learned it all by myself, and there's an end of it."

Wukong gave his thanks and then drew himself together, made the secret sign, gave a tumbling spring, mounted the Somersault Cloud, and headed straight back to the Eastern Continent. In less than an hour he could already see the Water Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. The Handsome Monkey King, glad in his own heart, said to himself in secret:

> When I set out, my mortal bones and frame were heavy;
> now that I've won the Way, my body's light, my whole self light.
> In all the world there's none who'll set his will to it—
> set your will to cultivate the mystery, and the mystery clears of itself.
> When I went out, the waves were hard to press across;
> today, returning, how easy the journey is!
> The parting words of admonition still ring in my ears—
> who would have thought I'd see the Eastern Sea in a single breath?

Wukong pressed down his cloud-head and came straight to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, picking his way along. Suddenly he heard the cry of cranes and the wail of apes—the cranes' cries piercing beyond the clouds of heaven, the apes' wailing mournful and full of grief. At once he called out: "Children, I have come home!" From beneath the cliffs and the rock-clefts, out of the flowers and grasses and the trees, monkeys great and small came leaping out by the thousands and tens of thousands, surrounding the Handsome Monkey King in their midst. They kowtowed and cried: "Great King! How carefree you must be! How could you stay away so long? You left us stranded here, longing for you as for food and drink. Lately we have been bullied and oppressed by a fiend who insists on seizing our Water Curtain Cave for his own dwelling. We have fought him to the death, heedless of our lives. All this while that wretch has plundered our household goods and carried off many of our young, so that day and night we cannot sleep but must keep watch over our home. Happily the Great King has come! Had the Great King stayed away another year or two, we and the whole mountain cave would have fallen into another's hands!"

When Wukong heard this his heart blazed with rage, and he said: "What fiend is this, that dares behave so outrageously? Tell me the whole of it, and I'll go and hunt him down to avenge you."

The monkeys kowtowed: "We report to the Great King: the wretch calls himself the Monstrous King of Havoc, and dwells away to the due north."

"How far is it from here to his place?" asked Wukong.

"When he comes, it's on cloud," said the monkeys; "when he goes, it's on mist—now wind, now rain, now lightning, now thunder. We have no idea how far it is."

"If that's so," said Wukong, "then never fear; just go on with your play, and let me go and hunt him out."

Splendid Monkey King! He drew his body together, leapt up and away, and went tumbling somersault after somersault straight to the north to look about him. There he saw a high mountain, truly steep and perilous in the extreme. A fine mountain:

> Brush-tip peaks standing sheer, winding ravines sunk deep.
> The brush-tip peaks stand sheer, piercing the empty sky;
> the winding ravines sink deep, leading down to Earth's own gate.
> On the two cliffs, flowers and trees vie in their splendor;
> in many a place, pine and bamboo contend in their green.
> On the left, the dragons—tame and docile;
> on the right, the tigers—crouching low and still.
> Here one often sees the iron ox at plough,
> and there are ever golden coins for the planting.
> The hidden birds sing sweet and clear;
> the cinnabar phoenix stands facing the sun.
> The rocks lie jagged, the waters lie clear—
> strange and uncanny, fierce and forbidding indeed.
> Famous mountains in the world are past all counting,
> where the flowers bloom and fade and crowd again in throngs;
> but how can they match this scene that endures forever,
> through the eight festivals and four seasons utterly unmoved?
> Truly it is the Source-Pit Mountain of the Three Realms,
> the nourishing Water-Viscera Cave of the Five Phases.

The Handsome Monkey King was silently taking in the scenery when he heard the sound of someone speaking, and went straight down the mountain to seek it out. There, before the sheer cliff, was the Water-Viscera Cave. Outside its gate several little imps were dancing about; the moment they saw Wukong they took to their heels. "Stop!" said Wukong. "Lend me the speech of your mouths, that I may carry word of what's in my heart. I am the Lord of the Water Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, in the due south. What is this Bird-Fiend King of Havoc of yours, who has so many times bullied my children and grandchildren? I have come on purpose to seek him out and settle accounts with him face to face."

When the little imps heard this they rushed pell-mell into the cave to report: "Great King! Disaster!"

"What disaster?" asked the Fiend King.

"Outside the cave," said the imps, "there's a monkey-head who calls himself the Lord of the Water Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. He says you have bullied his children and grandchildren time and again, and he's come on purpose to seek you out and have it out with you face to face."

The Fiend King laughed: "I've often heard those monkey-spirits say they had a Great King who'd gone off to leave home and cultivate the Way. So he's come back at last. How is he got up? What weapons does he carry?"

"He has no weapon at all," said the imps. "His head is bare; he wears a single robe of red, with a yellow sash bound about him, and on his feet a pair of black boots. Neither monk nor layman, and not like a Taoist or an immortal either, bare-handed and empty-fisted, he's shouting outside the gate."

When the Fiend King heard this he said: "Fetch me my armor and weapons." The little imps brought them out at once.

The Fiend King donned his armor and helmet, grasped his saber in his hand, and came out the gate with the horde of imps. At once he cried out in a loud voice: "Which of you is the Lord of the Water Curtain Cave?" Wukong opened his eyes wide and looked, and beheld the Fiend King:

> On his head an iron-black helmet, gleaming in the sun;
> over his body a black gauze robe, fluttering in the wind.
> Below he wore black iron armor, bound tight with leather thongs;
> on his feet, patterned pleated boots—mighty as a great commander.
> Round the waist, ten spans broad; in stature, three rods tall.
> In his hand he gripped a saber, its edge most keen and bright.
> Styled the Monster of Havoc—a bold and savage figure.

The Monkey King roared: "You wretched fiend, with eyes so big—and yet you can't see Old Monkey!"

The Fiend King looked at him and laughed: "You're not four feet tall, you're not thirty years old, and you've not so much as a weapon in your hand. How dare you be so wild and reckless as to come seeking me out to have it out?"

Wukong cursed him: "You wretched fiend, so you're blind after all! You reckon me small, but to make myself big is no hard thing. You reckon me without a weapon, but these two hands of mine can hook down the moon at the sky's edge! Never fear—just take a punch from Old Monkey!" With a spring he leapt up and struck straight at the fiend's face. The Fiend King put up his hand to ward it off and said: "You're such a runt, and I'm so big and tall; you mean to use your fists, while I mean to use my saber. If I cut you down with my blade, even that would set folk laughing. Let me lay down the saber and try a round of fists with you."

"Well said," replied Wukong. "Now there's a brave fellow—come on, then!" The Fiend King let go his guard and struck out, and Wukong bored straight in, grappling and trading blows. The two of them punched and kicked, charging and ramming. Now a long reach is hollow and unwieldy, but short clinching blows are firm and sure. The Fiend King found Wukong digging at his short ribs and ramming into his groin, and after a few cracks at his joints he was badly battered. He dodged aside, snatched up his broad steel saber, and slashed straight down at Wukong's head. Wukong whipped his body away, and the stroke cut empty air. Seeing how fierce the fiend was, Wukong now used the Body-Outside-the-Body method: he plucked a fistful of hairs, threw them into his mouth and chewed them to bits, then spat them out into the air with a cry of "Change!" At once they became two or three hundred little monkeys, clustering all around.

For when one attains the immortal body, his spirit issues forth in transformations without measure. Now since this Monkey King had won the Way, there were upon his body eighty-four thousand hairs, and every single one of them could transform, answering to the need at the bidding of his mind. Those little monkeys, sharp-eyed and nimble at leaping, dodged the saber when it came and could not be wounded by the spear when it thrust. Watch them now, springing forward and leaping back, boring in and swarming up, surrounding the Fiend King: some hugged him, some hauled at him, some ducked into his groin, some grabbed at his legs, kicking and pummeling, plucking his hairs, gouging at his eyes, pinching his nose, hoisting him up and tumbling him about, beating him into one writhing heap. In that moment Wukong managed to wrest away the fiend's saber, parted his little monkeys, and brought it down full on the crown of the fiend's head, cleaving him into two halves. Then he led his band charging into the cave and wiped out every last fiend, great and small. He shook his hairs and gathered them back onto his body—and then he saw that some could not be gathered back, and these were the little monkeys the Fiend King had carried off from the Water Curtain Cave.

"How did you come to be here?" asked Wukong. There were some thirty to fifty of them, and they all said through their tears: "After the Great King went off to cultivate immortality, these two years that wretch made trouble and snatched us all away here. And aren't these the household goods from our own cave? Our stone basins and stone bowls were all carried off by that wretch."

"If they are our household goods," said Wukong, "then move them all out." Then he set a fire blazing in the cave and burned the Water-Viscera Cave dry to a cinder, reducing it all to one ruin. He said to them: "All of you, follow me home."

"Great King," said the monkeys, "when we came, we only heard the wind whistling in our ears, and we drifted hazily to this place; we never learned the road. How are we to get home again?"

"That's just a magic art he worked," said Wukong. "What's hard about it? Now that one aperture in me is open, all hundred apertures are open, and I too can work it. Close your eyes, all of you, and don't be afraid."

Splendid Monkey King! He recited the words of a spell, summoned a wild gale, and brought his cloud-head down to earth. "Children, open your eyes," he called. The monkeys set their feet on solid ground, recognized it for their own homeland, and every one of them rejoiced, all racing for the old path to the cave-mouth. The monkeys that had stayed in the cave came crowding out together to meet them, and they all went in, ranked themselves in order of age, and bowed in homage to the Monkey King.
