They set out wine and fruit to welcome him back and offer congratulations, and asked about the matter of subduing the fiend and rescuing their young. Wukong told them the whole of it in full detail, and the monkeys praised him without end, saying: "Great King, who would have thought that, going off to that far place, you would learn such powers!"

Then Wukong said: "When I parted from you in those days, I followed the waves and drifted with the current, blown across the great Eastern Ocean to the borders of the Western Continent of Cattle-Gift, and straight on to the Southern Continent of Jambu. There I learned to take on human form, put on these clothes and wore these boots, and swaggered and roamed about the clouds for eight or nine years and more, yet never found the Way. Then I crossed the great Western Ocean to the borders of the Western Continent of Cattle-Gift, and after long inquiry I had the good fortune to meet an old patriarch, who passed me the true and fruitful art of being coeval with Heaven, the great gateway of deathless eternal life."

The monkeys offered their congratulations, all saying: "Such fortune is not to be met with in ten thousand ages!"

Wukong laughed again: "Little ones, here's another happy thing—every one of this clan of ours now has a surname."

"What is the Great King's surname?" asked the monkeys.

"My surname now is Sun," said Wukong, "and my religious name is Wukong."

When the monkeys heard this they clapped their hands in delight, crying: "The Great King is the Elder Sun, and we are all the second Suns, the third Suns, the little Suns, the small Suns—a whole family of Suns, a whole nation of Suns, a whole nest of Suns!" And they all came forward to wait upon the Elder Sun, with great basins and little bowls of coconut wine and grape wine, immortal flowers and immortal fruits—truly the whole household was merry together. Ah!

> Threaded through into a single surname, the self returns to its root,
> awaiting only the glorious rise—a name on the immortal rolls.

But after all, there is no knowing how it will all turn out, nor how his abiding in this realm will end from first to last. Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 3 -->
# Chapter 3: The Four Seas and a Thousand Mountains Bow in Submission; The Nine Shades and the Ten Kinds Are Struck from the Rolls

Now, the Handsome Monkey King had returned in glory to his native mountain. Having destroyed the Demon of Havoc and carried off a great broadsword, he spent his days drilling in the arts of war. He set the little monkeys to cutting bamboo for spears and whittling wood for blades; they fashioned banners and pennants, blew whistles for the signal, advanced and retreated, pitched camp and raised stockades, and amused themselves at this for a long while.

Then one day, sitting quietly, the King fell to thinking. "Here we are at our games," he said to himself, "but I fear that play may turn to earnest. We may yet disturb some human king, or some Lord of Birds or Lord of Beasts may take offense and say that we are mustering troops in rebellion. They would raise an army and come to slay us — and you with your bamboo poles and wooden swords, how could you meet such a foe? We must have keen swords and sharp halberds before we are safe. What is to be done?"

When the monkeys heard this, every one of them was alarmed. "Your Majesty sees far ahead," they said, "but there is nowhere we can get such weapons." As they spoke, four old monkeys stepped forward — two of them bare-rumped roan-apes, and two long-armed gibbons — and came before him. "Your Majesty," they said, "to procure sharp weapons is a very easy thing." "How is it easy?" asked Wukong.

"East of this mountain of ours," answered the four, "across two hundred miles of water, lies the kingdom of Aolai. In that land there is a throne, and within its walls are soldiers and citizens beyond counting — surely there must be smiths who work in gold and silver, copper and iron. If Your Majesty would go there, you might buy or have made some weapons; then you could train us and guard our mountain stronghold. Truly that would be the way to lasting peace and security." Wukong was filled with delight. "You stay here at your sport," he said, "while I go and return."

Good Monkey King! He leapt at once onto his somersault cloud and in an instant had crossed the two hundred miles of water. There indeed he saw a walled city, with six avenues and three markets, ten thousand households and a thousand gates, the people coming and going beneath the open light of day. Wukong thought to himself, "There must be ready-made weapons here. I could go down and buy a few — but it would be better still to use a bit of magic and simply help myself."

So he made the magic sign and recited a spell, drew in a breath toward the southeast quarter, and blew it out with a great puff. At once a wind arose, flinging sand and rolling stones — a fearsome thing indeed:

> Where the cannon-clouds rise, heaven and earth are shaken;
> Black mists and gloomy fogs darken all the land.
> Waves churn the rivers and seas till fish and crabs cower;
> Trees snap in the mountain woods, and tigers and wolves take flight.
> In every trade no merchant or traveler stirs;
> In every walk of life not a soul is seen.
> The king upon his hall withdraws to his inner court;
> Before the steps, civil and martial officers scatter to their offices.
> The age-old treasure-thrones are all blown over,
> And the lofty Five-Phoenix Tower rocks to its very roots.

Where the wind blew, it scattered the king of Aolai in terror; through the three streets and six markets, every household slammed its gates and barred its doors, and no one dared to walk abroad. Only then did Wukong bring down his cloud and stride straight in through the palace gates, making his way directly to the armory and the weapons-stores. He threw open the doors and looked inside, and there were arms beyond number: sabers and spears, swords and halberds, axes and battle-axes, pikes and sickles, whips and rakes, bludgeons and maces, bows and crossbows, forks and lances — every kind complete.

Delighted at the sight, he said, "How many can one man carry? Better to use my body-dividing magic and move the lot." Good Monkey King! He plucked out a handful of his hairs, chewed them to bits in his mouth, and spat them out, reciting a spell and crying, "Change!" At once they became hundreds upon hundreds of little monkeys, all snatching and grabbing in a tumult — the strong ones taking five or seven pieces, the weaker ones two or three — until they had cleared the place out entirely. Then he mounted his cloud, worked a summoning spell, called up the wild wind, and led his little monkeys all back to their home.

Now, the monkeys great and small of the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit were just then sporting outside the cave entrance when suddenly they heard the howling of the wind, and saw the air filled with a dense, boundless swarm of monkey-spirits, swooping and tumbling overhead. Frightened, they all ran helter-skelter and hid. In a moment the Handsome Monkey King set down his cloud, gathered up the mists, shook his body, and recovered his hairs. The weapons he heaped in a great pile before the mountain, and called out, "Little ones, come and take your arms!"

When the monkeys looked, they saw Wukong standing alone on the open ground, and they all came running to kowtow and ask what had happened. Wukong told them the whole story of how he had raised the wild wind and carried off the weapons. When the monkeys had finished thanking him, they all rushed to grab sabers and seize swords, to snatch axes and fight over spears, to draw bows and bend crossbows — shouting and bawling, they made sport of it all day long.

The next day they formed up the camp as before. Wukong assembled the whole host of monkeys, and they numbered more than forty-seven thousand. This roused all the monstrous beasts of the mountain — wolves and serpents, tigers and leopards, river-deer and roe-deer, muntjac and elk, foxes and wildcats, badgers and raccoon-dogs, lions and elephants, lion-mastiffs and orangutans, bears and stags, wild boars and mountain oxen, antelopes and blue rhinoceros, cunning hares and divine hounds — every sort of monster-king. There were seventy-two caves of them in all, and they all came to pay homage to the Monkey King as their sovereign. Year by year they offered tribute, and four times a season they reported for muster. Some drilled with the ranks; some levied grain by the seasons. Trim and orderly, they made of the whole Mountain of Flowers and Fruit something like an iron cauldron, a fortress of gold. The monster-kings of every quarter, moreover, brought gongs and drums, brought bright banners, brought helmets and armor; in a busy bustle they practiced their drills and mustered their forces day after day.

The Handsome Monkey King was rejoicing in all this when he suddenly said to the assembly, "You are now well-versed in bow and crossbow and skilled with your weapons. But this saber of mine is truly clumsy and ill-suited to my hand. What is to be done?" The four old monkeys came forward and addressed him: "Your Majesty is an immortal sage, and common weapons are not fit for your use. But we do not know — can Your Majesty travel beneath the water?"

"Since I came to know the Way," said Wukong, "I have mastered the seventy-two earthly transformations, and my somersault cloud has boundless power. I am skilled in vanishing and concealing my body, in raising spells and summoning spells. To Heaven there is a road for me, and into the Earth there is a gate; I walk the sun and moon and cast no shadow, I pass through metal and stone without hindrance; water cannot drown me, fire cannot burn me. Is there anywhere I cannot go?"

"If Your Majesty has such powers," said the four monkeys, "then beneath this iron-plank bridge of ours the water flows clear through to the Dragon Palace of the Eastern Sea. If Your Majesty would go down there, seek out the old Dragon King and ask him for some weapon — would that not be just what you wish?" Wukong was overjoyed to hear it. "Wait while I go and return," he said.

Good Monkey King! He sprang to the head of the bridge, worked a water-parting spell, made the magic sign, and with a splash plunged into the waves. Cleaving open a path through the water, he went straight to the bottom of the Eastern Ocean. As he was traveling along, he suddenly came upon a sea-patrolling yaksha, who barred his way and demanded, "What divine being is this that comes pushing the waters aside? Speak plainly, that I may go and announce you and bid you welcome."

"I am Sun Wukong," said Wukong, "the Heaven-born Sage of the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit — your old Dragon King's near neighbor. How is it you do not know me?" When the yaksha heard this, he hurried back to the Crystal Palace and reported: "Your Majesty, outside there is one Sun Wukong, the Heaven-born Sage of the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. He calls himself Your Majesty's near neighbor, and he is just arriving at the palace."

Aoguang, Dragon King of the Eastern Sea, rose at once and came out with his dragon sons and dragon grandsons, his shrimp soldiers and crab generals, to welcome him. "Come in, honored Immortal, come in!" They went straight into the palace to meet, and when Wukong had been seated in the place of honor and served tea, the Dragon King asked, "When did the honored Immortal attain the Way? What magic arts did you receive?"

"From the time of my birth," said Wukong, "I left my home to practice cultivation, and I have won a body neither born nor perishing. Lately, because I have been training my children and grandchildren and guarding our mountain caves, I find I have no proper weapon. I have long heard that my worthy neighbor enjoys his jeweled halls and coral palaces, and must surely have some divine arms to spare; so I have come expressly to beg one of you."

Hearing this, the Dragon King could hardly refuse. He ordered the perch marshal to fetch a great long-handled saber and present it. "Old Sun does not know how to wield a saber," said Wukong. "I beg you, give me something else." The Dragon King then bade the eel commandant lead the cuttlefish strongmen to carry out a nine-pronged fork. Wukong leapt down, took it in his hands, ran through a few passes, and set it aside. "Light, light, light! And it doesn't suit my hand either. I beg you, give me something else."

The Dragon King laughed and said, "Honored Immortal, take a closer look — that fork weighs three thousand six hundred catties!" "It doesn't suit my hand," said Wukong, "it doesn't suit my hand." Now the Dragon King grew uneasy, and ordered the carp inspector-general and the bream commander-in-chief to carry out a painted-handle Square-Heaven halberd, weighing seven thousand two hundred catties. When Wukong saw it, he ran up, took it in his hands, struck a few stances, made a couple of flourishes, then planted it upright in the middle. "Still too light, too light, too light!"

The old Dragon King was thoroughly frightened now. "Honored Immortal, this halberd is the heaviest weapon in my whole palace — there is nothing else." Wukong laughed: "As the ancients say, 'Never fear that the Dragon King lacks treasures.' Go and search again. If you have anything to my liking, I'll pay any price for it, one and all." "Truly there is nothing more," said the Dragon King.

As they were speaking, the Dragon Mother and the Dragon Daughter slipped out from behind and said, "Your Majesty, looking at this sage, he is plainly no ordinary being. In our sea treasury there is that piece of divine iron that anchors the bed of the Heavenly River. These last few days it has glowed with brilliant rosy light and given off auspicious vapors — could it be that the thing is meant to come forth now, and has met its sage?"

"That," said the Dragon King, "is the rod that the Great Yu used in taming the floods, to measure the depths of the rivers and seas — a piece of divine iron. What use could it be to him?" "Never mind whether he can use it," said the Dragon Mother. "Just give it to him; let him do with it whatever he likes, so long as we send him out of the palace gate." The old Dragon King agreed, and told Wukong all about it. "Bring it out and let me see it," said Wukong. The Dragon King waved his hands: "It can't be lifted, it can't be carried — the honored Immortal must come and look at it himself." "Where is it?" asked Wukong. "Lead me to it."

The Dragon King duly guided him into the midst of the sea treasury, and suddenly there appeared ten thousand shafts of golden light. The Dragon King pointed: "That glowing thing is it." Wukong hitched up his robe and went forward, gave it a feel — it was an iron pillar, about as thick as a peck-measure and more than twenty feet long. He grasped it with both hands and heaved with all his might. "Too thick and too long," he said. "It should be a bit shorter and thinner to be of use." No sooner had he spoken than the treasure shortened by several feet and grew thinner by a span. Wukong hefted it again. "Thinner still would be better." And truly the treasure grew thinner by a few more parts.

Wukong was overjoyed. Carrying it out of the sea treasury to look at it, he found that the two ends were bands of gold, and the middle a length of black iron. Close against one band there was a row of words engraved, reading: "The As-You-Will Gold-Banded Cudgel — weight, thirteen thousand five hundred catties." His heart rejoiced secretly: "No doubt this treasure does just as one wishes." And as he walked along, thinking in his heart and speaking with his mouth and hefting it in his hand, he said, "Shorter and thinner still would be more wonderful yet." By the time he carried it outside, it was only some twelve feet long and as thick around as a rice bowl.

Just look at him work his magic! Making his flourishes, he came whirling through the Crystal Palace, until the old Dragon King quaked with terror, the young dragon sons lost their wits, and the turtles and tortoises, the soft-shells and alligators, all drew in their necks, while the fish and shrimp, the sea-bream and crabs, all hid their heads. Wukong held the treasure in his hand, sat down upon the dais of the Crystal Palace, and said to the Dragon King with a laugh, "Many thanks, worthy neighbor, for your kindness." "Don't mention it, don't mention it," said the Dragon King.

"This piece of iron," said Wukong, "is good to use, but there is one more thing." "What more has the honored Immortal to say?" asked the Dragon King. "If there had been no such iron to begin with," said Wukong, "then so be it. But now that I hold it in my hand, and have no fitting clothes upon my body, what's to be done? If you have any armor here, why not give me a suit as well, and I'll thank you for the whole lot together." "That," said the Dragon King, "I really do not have." "A guest cannot trouble two hosts," said Wukong. "If you haven't any, I certainly won't go out this door." "I beg the honored Immortal to try another sea," said the Dragon King. "Perhaps there it may be found." "Better to sit at one house than to trudge round three," said Wukong. "I implore you — get me one suit, by all means." "Truly there is none," said the Dragon King. "If there were, I would certainly present it." "Truly none?" said Wukong. "Then let me try this iron out on you!"

The Dragon King panicked. "Honored Immortal, don't raise your hand, don't raise your hand! Let me see whether my brothers have any, and I'll send you a suit." "Where are your brothers?" asked Wukong. "My brothers," said the Dragon King, "are Aoqin, Dragon King of the Southern Sea; Aoshun, Dragon King of the Northern Sea; and Aorun, Dragon King of the Western Sea." "Old Sun won't go, won't go," said Wukong. "As the saying goes, 'Three on credit are no match for two in hand.' I only ask that you make do high or low and send me a suit, and that's that."

"There's no need for the honored Immortal to go," said the old Dragon. "I have here an iron drum and a golden bell. Whenever there is some urgent matter, we beat the drum till it thunders and strike the bell till it rings, and my brothers come in an instant." "Then quick, go and beat the drum and strike the bell," said Wukong. And indeed the alligator general went to strike the bell, and the soft-shelled marshal came to beat the drum.

In a little while, where the bell and drum sounded, they did indeed rouse the three other Dragon Kings, who arrived in a moment and gathered outside. Said Aoqin, "Elder brother, what urgent matter is there, that you beat the drum and strike the bell?" "Worthy brother," said the old Dragon, "it's hard to say. There's some Heaven-born Sage of the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit who came this morning and claimed me for a neighbor. Then he demanded a weapon. I offered him a steel fork — he scorned it as too small; I presented a painted halberd — he scorned it as too light. He took up with his own hands that divine iron that anchors the bed of the Heavenly River and made a few flourishes with it. Now he sits in my palace and demands a suit of armor besides. I have none, so I sounded the bell and beat the drum to ask you, worthy brothers, to come. Have you any armor? Give him a suit and send him out the door, and have done with it."

When Aoqin heard this, he was furious. "Let us brothers call out our troops and seize him — wouldn't that be the thing?" "Don't speak of seizing him, don't speak of it," said the old Dragon. "Just brush against that iron and you're dead; just graze it and you're done for; touch it and your skin splits; rub against it and your sinews are torn." Said Aorun, Dragon King of the Western Sea, "Second brother must not come to blows with him. Let us just put together a suit of armor for him, send him out the door, and then draw up a memorial to lay before Heaven — Heaven itself will execute him." "Well said," agreed Aoshun, Dragon King of the Northern Sea. "I have here a pair of cloud-walking shoes of lotus thread." "And I," said Aorun of the West, "have brought a suit of chain-link golden armor." "And I," said Aoqin of the South, "have a phoenix-winged cap of purple gold."

The old Dragon was delighted, and led them into the Crystal Palace to meet Wukong and present these to him. Wukong put on the golden cap, the golden armor, and the cloud-walking shoes all properly, then set his As-You-Will cudgel in motion and went fighting his way out, calling back to the assembled dragons, "Sorry to trouble you! Sorry to trouble you!" The four Dragon Kings of the Four Seas were greatly aggrieved, and aside they conferred about presenting a memorial — but of that we'll say no more for now.

Just look at the Monkey King! He parted the waters and came straight back to the head of the iron-plank bridge, and bounded up out of it. There were the four old monkeys leading the host, all waiting at the bridgeside. Suddenly they saw Wukong leap out of the waves without a single drop of water on his body, gleaming golden as he came up onto the bridge. The monkeys all fell to their knees in awe. "Your Majesty, what splendor! What splendor!" Wukong, his face wreathed in springtime smiles, mounted high upon his throne and stood the iron cudgel upright in the midst of them.

Those foolish monkeys, knowing no better, all came to take hold of the treasure — but it was like dragonflies trying to shake an iron tree; not a hair's breadth could they stir it. One after another they bit their fingers and stuck out their tongues. "Grandfather! So heavy as this — however did you carry it back?" Wukong stepped up, reached out his hand, and snatched it up in a single grip. He said to them with a laugh, "Everything has its master. This treasure has lain hidden in the sea treasury for who knows how many thousands of years, and it just happened to shine forth this very year. The Dragon King took it for nothing but a lump of black iron, and called it the divine pearl-iron that anchors the bed of the Heavenly River. None of those fellows could so much as lift or carry it, and they had to ask me to go and take it myself. At that time this treasure was more than twenty feet long and as thick as a peck-measure. When I gripped it once, meaning to say it was too big, it grew smaller by a good deal; when I told it to be smaller, it grew smaller again; and again I told it smaller, and again it shrank. Holding it up to the daylight to see, I found a row of words on it: 'The As-You-Will Gold-Banded Cudgel, thirteen thousand five hundred catties.' Now all of you stand aside, and let me make it change once more."

He hefted the treasure in his hand and cried, "Small! Small! Small!" and at once it became like an embroidery needle, small enough to be tucked away inside his ear. The monkeys were astonished and cried out, "Your Majesty, bring it out again and play with it some more!" The Monkey King truly took it out of his ear and held it on his palm, calling, "Big! Big! Big!" and at once it grew again to a peck-measure's thickness and twenty feet in length. Carried away with delight, he leapt onto the bridge and walked out of the cave, gripped the treasure in his hand, and worked the magic of taking Heaven for his pattern and Earth for his model. Bending his waist, he cried, "Grow!" — and he grew ten thousand fathoms tall, his head like Mount Tai, his waist like a towering range, his eyes like flashing lightning, his mouth like a basin of blood, his teeth like swords and halberds; and the cudgel in his hand reached up to the Thirty-Third Heaven above and down to the Eighteenth Hell below. The tigers and leopards, wolves and serpents, all the monster-throngs of the mountain, and the monster-kings of the seventy-two caves were so terrified that they kowtowed and bowed in worship, trembling till their wits scattered and their souls flew away. In an instant he withdrew the magic form, turned the treasure back into an embroidery needle, hid it in his ear, and returned to his cave dwelling. In great alarm the monster-kings of every cave all came to pay their respects and congratulate him.

Then they flung wide the banners and drums, set the brass gongs ringing, spread out a lavish hundred-flavored feast of rare delicacies, and filled the cups brimming with coconut wine and grape liquor. They drank and feasted with the whole host for a long while, and afterward took up their drilling as before. The Monkey King appointed the four old monkeys as his stalwart commanders: the two bare-rumped roan-apes he named Marshal Ma and Marshal Liu, and the two long-armed gibbons he named General Beng and General Ba. All matters of pitching camp and raising stockades, of rewards and punishments, he handed over to the four stalwart commanders to manage.

His mind at ease, he passed his days riding the clouds and mounting the mists, roaming the Four Seas and disporting himself among a thousand mountains. He displayed his martial arts and sought out heroes far and wide; he worked his magic and made worthy friends in plenty. At this time he became sworn brothers with six others — the Bull Demon King, the Serpent Demon King, the Roc Demon King, the Lion-Camel King, the Macaque King, and the Marmoset King — making seven, counting himself, the Handsome Monkey King. Day after day they discoursed on letters and debated the arts of war, passed the wine-cups and the goblets round, played the strings and sang, piped and danced; off in the morning and back at evening, there was no kind of joy they did not taste. The ten thousand miles of distance they reckoned as no more than the path across a courtyard — as the saying goes, a nod of the head and three thousand miles are crossed, a twist of the waist and eight hundred more are spanned.

One day, in his own cave, he ordered the four stalwart commanders to lay out a banquet and invited the six kings to come and drink. They slaughtered oxen and butchered horses, made sacrifice to Heaven and offerings to Earth, set the monster-throng to dancing and singing, and all drank themselves blind drunk. After seeing the six kings off, he rewarded his officers great and small. Then he reclined in the shade of the pines beside the iron-plank bridge and in a moment fell asleep. The four stalwart commanders led the host in keeping watch around him, not daring to raise their voices.

But in his sleep the Handsome Monkey King saw two men approach carrying a warrant, on which were written the three characters "Sun Wukong." Coming up to his side, they allowed him not a word of protest, slipped a noose over him, and led his very soul away. Stumbling and reeling, he was dragged along until they came to the wall of a city. The Monkey King gradually felt the wine wearing off, and lifting his head, he saw upon that wall an iron placard bearing three great characters: "Region of Darkness." At once the Handsome Monkey King came to himself. "The Region of Darkness is where Yama dwells," he said. "Why have I come here?" The two men said, "Your span of earthly life is at an end this day; we two have taken the warrant and come to summon you."

When the Monkey King heard this, he said, "Old Sun has risen above the Three Realms and is no longer within the Five Elements. I am no longer subject to his authority — how dare you, blindly and confusedly, come to summon me?" But the two soul-takers only kept tugging and hauling at him, determined to drag him inside. At this the Monkey King's temper flared. He plucked the treasure from his ear, gave it a shake till it was as thick as a rice bowl, and with one easy lift of his hand beat the two soul-takers to a pulp. He undid his own noose, let his hands fly free, and wielding the cudgel, came smashing his way into the city. The ox-headed demons fled and dodged east and west; the horse-faced demons ran north and south. The demon underlings rushed up to the Hall of Judgment and reported, "Your Majesties, disaster! disaster! Outside there is some hairy-faced thunder-god come smashing his way in!"

In a fluster the Ten Kings of the Underworld hurriedly straightened their robes and came out to look. When they saw how fierce his features were, they at once arranged themselves in their ranks and called out together in loud voices, "Honored Immortal, your name! Honored Immortal, your name!" Said the Monkey King, "Since you do not even know who I am, how is it you sent men to summon me?" The Ten Kings said, "We dare not, we dare not. Surely the men we sent were mistaken." Said the Monkey King, "I am Sun Wukong, the Heaven-born Sage of the Water-Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. What official ranks are yours?" The Ten Kings bowed and said, "We are the Ten Kings of the Underworld, the sovereigns of the world of shades." "Quick, tell me your names," said Wukong, "and spare yourselves a beating." Said the Ten Kings, "We are King Qinguang, King of First Rivers, King of the Song Emperor, King of Revolting Officials, King Yama, King of Equality, King of Mount Tai, King of the Capital City, King of Biancheng, and King of the Turning Wheel."

"Since you have all attained the rank of king," said Wukong, "and are of the order of bright and responsive spirits, how is it you do not know good from ill? Old Sun has perfected the way of the immortals; my life-span is equal to Heaven's; I have risen above the Three Realms and leapt out of the Five Elements. Why did you send a man to lay hold of me?" "Let not the honored Immortal be wroth," said the Ten Kings. "There are many in all the world who share the same name and surname. Perhaps the soul-taker went astray." "Nonsense! Nonsense!" said Wukong. "As the common saying goes, 'Officials may err and clerks may err, but the man sent on the errand does not err.' Quick, fetch me the Registers of Life and Death, and let me see them!"

When the Ten Kings heard this, they at once invited him up onto the hall to examine the records. Wukong, gripping his As-You-Will cudgel, mounted straight up onto the Hall of Judgment and sat down in the very middle, facing south. The Ten Kings ordered the recording judge in charge of the files to bring out the documents for examination. The judge dared not be slow; he went to the records office and brought out five or six bundles of documents along with the registers of the ten kinds of beings, and went through them one by one. Among the bare-skinned creatures, the hairy creatures, the feathered creatures, the insects, and the scaled and shelled kinds, his name was nowhere to be found. Then they came to the category of monkeys: now this monkey was like a man, yet was not entered among the names of men; like a bare-skinned creature, yet did not dwell within any kingdom; like a running beast, yet was not under the rule of the qilin; like a flying bird, yet was not subject to the phoenix. There was a separate register, and this Wukong examined for himself, until at the number one thousand three hundred and fifty under the character "Soul," there at last was set down the name of Sun Wukong, reading: "Heaven-born stone monkey; allotted life-span, three hundred and forty-two years; a good and natural death."

"I don't bother to remember how many years my span is," said Wukong. "I'll just strike out the name and have done." He called for a brush. The judge hastily presented the brush, well-dipped in thick black ink. Wukong took up the register and, wherever there was a name among the category of monkeys, struck them all out, one and all. Then he flung down the register and said, "It's settled, it's settled! From now on I am no longer under your authority!" And wielding the cudgel all the way, he smashed his way out of the Region of Darkness. The Ten Kings dared not come near him; they all went to the Azure Cloud Palace, joined together in worship before the Bodhisattva Kshitigarbha, and conferred about drawing up a memorial to lay before Heaven — but of that we'll say no more.

As the Monkey King came smashing his way out of the city, he suddenly tripped over a clump of grass and stumbled headlong — and woke with a start. It had all been but a dream of the Southern Branch. Just as he was stretching himself, he heard the four stalwart commanders and the host of monkeys calling out, "Your Majesty, how much wine did you drink? You've slept the whole night through and still aren't awake!" Said Wukong, "Sleeping is a small matter, but I dreamed that two men came here to summon me, and carried me off to the gate of the city of the Region of Darkness. Only when I woke did I understand. There I displayed my powers, shouting my way clear to the Hall of Judgment, and quarreled with the Ten Kings. I looked over our register of life and death, and wherever there was a name of ours, I struck it out — so now none of us is under that fellow's rule!" The monkeys kowtowed and gave thanks. And from this time on, many of the mountain monkeys never grew old — because their names were no longer recorded in the Office of Shades.

When the Handsome Monkey King had finished telling all that had passed, the four stalwart commanders made it known to the monster-kings of every cave, who all came to offer congratulations. Within a few days the six sworn brothers came again to pay their respects, and when they heard the reason the names had been struck off, every one of them rejoiced; day after day they gathered for revels — but of that we'll say no more.

Now let us tell of the Most High Holy and Greatly Merciful Lord, the Jade Emperor, August Sovereign of the Mysterious Vault on high. One day he sat in court upon the precious throne of the Hall of Divine Mists in the Cloud Palace of the Golden Gate, with the immortal officers civil and martial gathered for the morning audience, when suddenly the Perfected One Qiu Hongji came forward and announced, "Your Majesty, outside the Hall of Universal Brightness, Aoguang, Dragon King of the Eastern Sea, has presented a memorial, and awaits the Heavenly Lord's summons." The Jade Emperor gave the command: "Let him be summoned in." Aoguang was led to the foot of the Hall of Divine Mists; when he had finished making his reverences, an immortal page beside the throne took up the memorial and handed it up. The Jade Emperor read it through from the beginning. It read:

"Your subject Aoguang, lowly Dragon of the Eastern Sea of the Eastern Continent of Superior Spirits, in the watery realm of the lower world, makes report to the Great Holy Sovereign, the Most High August Emperor of the Mysterious Vault: Of late, by reason of one Sun Wukong, a monstrous immortal born on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit and dwelling in the Water-Curtain Cave, your lowly dragon has been bullied and abused. He forced his way into the water-mansion and demanded weapons, working his magic and flaunting his might; he demanded armor, raging in his fierceness and his power. He has terrified the water-tribes and put the turtles and alligators to flight. The Dragon of the Southern Sea quakes with fear; the Dragon of the Western Sea is wretched and miserable; the Dragon of the Northern Sea has bowed his head in surrender. Your subject Aoguang prostrated himself and made obeisance, and presented the divine pearl-iron cudgel, the phoenix-winged golden cap, the chain-link armor, and the cloud-walking shoes, sending him out with all courtesy. Yet still he flourished his martial arts and displayed his powers, saying only, 'Sorry to trouble you! Sorry to trouble you!' Truly he has no equal and is most difficult to control. Your subject now lays this before you, humbly awaiting Your Holiness's decision. I earnestly beg that Heavenly troops be sent to capture this monstrous creature, that the seas and mountains may be made clean and peaceful and the lower realm secure. Respectfully submitted."

When the Holy Emperor had read it through, he gave the command: "Let the Dragon Spirit return to his sea; I shall presently dispatch a general to seize him." The old Dragon King touched his head to the ground in thanks and departed.

Then below, the Heavenly Master Ge Xianweng came forward and announced, "Your Majesty, there is a memorial sent up from the Underworld by King Qinguang, presented on behalf of the Lord of the Region of Darkness, the Bodhisattva Kshitigarbha." An attendant Jade Maiden took up the memorial and handed it up, and the Jade Emperor likewise read it through from the beginning. It read:

"The Region of Darkness is the shadowy office of the Earth. Heaven has its spirits and Earth has its ghosts; the bright and the dark turn in their cycles. Birds have their birth and beasts their death; male and female alternate in their courses. Life upon life, transformation upon transformation, conceiving daughters and bringing forth sons — this is the order of nature, and may not be altered. But now there is a monstrous monkey, Sun Wukong, born of Heaven in the Water-Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, who works wickedness and commits violence and will not submit to the summons. Working his magic, he beat down the ghostly envoys of the Nine Shades; relying on his might, he terrified and harmed the merciful Kings of the Ten Courts. He made a great uproar in the Hall of Judgment and forcibly struck out the names from the registers, so that the kind of the monkeys is now beyond all restraint, and the breed of macaques live long beyond their span; stillness and the wheel of rebirth alike are undone, and each is freed from life and death. Your poor monk presents this memorial, daring to offend the Heavenly Majesty. I humbly beg that divine troops be dispatched to subdue this monster, to set the bright and the dark in order and bring lasting peace to the realm of shades. Respectfully submitted."

When the Jade Emperor had read it through, he gave the command: "Let the Lord of the Underworld return to the realm of shades; I shall presently dispatch a general to seize him." King Qinguang likewise touched his head to the ground in thanks and departed.

The Great Heavenly Lord summoned the assembled immortal officers, civil and martial, and asked, "In what year was this monstrous monkey born, of what age did he come, that he should have attained the Way to such a degree?" Scarcely had he spoken when there stepped forth from the ranks the Thousand-Mile Eye and the Down-the-Wind Ear, who said, "This monkey is the Heaven-born stone monkey of three hundred years ago. At that time he was thought nothing of, and we do not know in what place he has these few years cultivated himself into an immortal, subduing dragons and taming tigers, and forcibly striking out the registers of death." The Jade Emperor asked, "Which divine general shall go down to the lower world to subdue him?"

Scarcely had he spoken when there stepped forth from the ranks the Great White Planet, the Star of Long庚, who bowed low and announced, "Most Holy One, of all beings in the Three Realms that possess the nine apertures, every one may cultivate immortality. But this monkey is a body nurtured by Heaven and Earth, a form conceived by the sun and the moon; he too treads the earth and bears up the sky; he feeds upon the dew and dines upon the rosy mists. Now that he has perfected the way of immortality and has the power to subdue dragons and tame tigers, in what is he different from a man? Your subject begs Your Majesty, in mindfulness of the merciful grace of all begetting and transformation, to send down an edict of amnesty and recruitment, summoning him up to the upper realm and granting him some office great or small, entering his name upon the rolls and so binding him here. If he accepts the Heavenly command, then afterward he may be promoted and rewarded; if he defies the Heavenly command, then he may be seized on the spot. In this way, first, the host need not be stirred nor the army wearied; and second, an immortal is gathered in by the way of the Way." The Jade Emperor was greatly pleased to hear it, and said, "We shall do as our minister proposes." So he ordered the Star Official of Literary Songs to draft the edict, and bade the Great White Planet of Venus carry out the recruitment.

The Planet of Venus received the edict, went out beyond the Southern Heaven Gate, brought down his auspicious cloud, and came straight to the Water-Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. He said to the little monkeys, "I am an envoy of Heaven, sent by Heaven, and I have a holy edict here. I ask that your great king come up to the upper realm. Quickly, make it known." The little monkeys outside the cave passed the word layer by layer into the depths of the cave-heaven: "Your Majesty, outside there is an old man carrying a roll of documents on his back, who says he is an envoy sent down by Heaven, and that he has a holy edict inviting you." The Handsome Monkey King was overjoyed to hear it. "These last two days I have just been thinking I'd like to take a trip up to Heaven," he said, "and here is a Heavenly envoy come to invite me!" He called out, "Quick, show him in!"

The Monkey King hastily put his cap and robes in order and went out beyond the gate to welcome him. The Planet of Venus came straight to the center and stood facing south. "I am the Great White Planet of Venus, of the West," he said. "By the Jade Emperor's edict of amnesty and recruitment I have come down to the lower world to invite you up to Heaven, there to receive the immortal rolls and an appointment." Wukong laughed and said, "Many thanks, venerable Star, for descending here." And he ordered the little ones to lay out a banquet to entertain him. "The holy edict is upon me," said the Planet, "I dare not linger long. Let me beg the great king to come along with me; once you have won your glorious advancement, there will be time enough at leisure for talk." "It is an honor that you have called," said Wukong. "I am sorry to send you off empty, sorry to send you off empty." At once he summoned the four stalwart commanders and charged them: "Carefully train my children and grandchildren. Let me go up to Heaven and take a look at the road, and presently I'll take you up there to dwell together with me." The four stalwart commanders gave their assent.

Then the Monkey King and the Planet of Venus mounted up on their clouds and rose into the heights of the empyrean. Truly it was a case of:

> Raised high to the rank of an immortal of the upper grade,
> His name set down in the cloud-borne ranks and the precious rolls.

But as to what office and what rank he was to receive — that you shall hear told in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 4 -->
# Chapter 4: A Stable-Keeper's Title Cannot Content Him; The Name "Great Sage Equal to Heaven" Leaves Heaven Uneasy

The Great White Planet Star and the Handsome Monkey King came out together from the deepest recesses of the cave-heaven and rose into the air on a single cloud. Now Wukong's somersault cloud was unlike any other — wondrously swift — so that he left the Planet Star trailing far behind and arrived first outside the Southern Gate of Heaven. Just as he was about to gather in his cloud and press forward, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, at the head of his mighty heavenly soldiers — Pang, Liu, Gou, Bi, Deng, Xin, Zhang, and Tao — with spears, swords, sabers, and halberds, blocked the gate of Heaven and would not let him pass.

"This old Planet Star is a treacherous fellow!" cried the Monkey King. "He invited me, old Monkey, himself — so why has he set men to brandishing blade and spear and barring the road?"

While he was still bawling, the Planet Star arrived in a flash. Wukong rounded on him at once, fierce-faced. "You old fellow — how dare you cozen me? You told me you came at the Jade Emperor's command to summon me to amnesty and office. So why have these men blocked the gate of Heaven and refused to let old Monkey in?"

The Planet Star laughed. "Calm your anger, Great King. You have never before come to this celestial palace; your name is not yet registered, and these heavenly soldiers have never made your acquaintance. How could they let you barge in as you pleased? Once you have seen the Celestial Venerable, received your immortal scroll, and had your office recorded, you may come and go thereafter as you wish, and who would dare block you then?"

"In that case," said Wukong, "never mind — I won't go in."

But the Planet Star caught hold of him by the hand. "You shall go in together with me."

As they neared the gate of Heaven, the Planet Star called out in a loud voice: "Gatekeepers and heavenly generals, officers and soldiers great and small — clear the way! This is an immortal from the lower world. I bear the Jade Emperor's sacred decree and have summoned him hither."

Only then did Heavenly King Virūḍhaka and his soldiers draw back their weapons and stand aside. Now at last the Monkey King believed the old man's words, and step by step he passed within with the Planet Star, taking in all he saw. And truly it was a sight to behold:

> First treading the upper realm,
> at last entering Heaven's hall.
> Ten thousand strands of golden light come rolling in red rainbow,
> a thousand wisps of auspicious vapor breathe forth a purple mist.
> See the Southern Gate of Heaven:
> deep-shining azure, wrought all of lapis glaze;
> dazzling bright, adorned with precious jade.
> On either side stand rows of marshals who guard the sky,
> each a pillar bearing the roof-beam,
> gripping ax-head, clasping standard;
> on all sides line a dozen gods in golden mail,
> each one holding halberd, swinging whip,
> bearing saber, leaning on sword.
> The outer courts are striking enough;
> within, the sight astounds.
> Along the inner walls rise great columns
> wound about with red-bearded dragons whose golden scales blaze in the sun;
> and there are long bridges
> where phoenixes with painted plumes and crimson crests wheel up into the void.
> Bright sunset clouds reflect the light of Heaven;
> emerald mists, dense and dim, veil the mouth of the Dipper.
> Here in the heavens are thirty-three celestial palaces —
> the Cloud-Dispatching, the Vaiśravaṇa, the Five Brilliances,
> the Palace of the Sun, the Palace of Flower and Joy —
> palace upon palace, each roof-ridge crowned with gold-swallowing beasts;
> and there are seventy-two layered treasure-halls —
> the Hall of Court Assembly, the Hall of Soaring Void,
> the Hall of Precious Light, the Hall of the Heavenly Kings,
> the Hall of the Numinous Officers —
> hall upon hall, each pillar ranged with jade unicorns.
> On the Terrace of the Star of Longevity bloom famous flowers
> that have not faded in a thousand thousand years;
> beside the elixir-refining furnace grow embroidered grasses
> evergreen through ten thousand thousand ages.
> Before the Tower of Sage-Audience:
> robes of crimson gauze, bright as scattered stars;
> caps like hibiscus, gleaming with gold and jade;
> jade pins and pearled slippers, purple sashes and golden seals.
> When the golden bell is struck,
> the spirits of the Three Bureaus bear their memorials up the vermilion steps;
> when the heavenly drum sounds,
> ten thousand saints pay court and worship the Jade Emperor.
> And at the Numinous Empyrean Treasure-Hall:
> golden studs stud the jade doors,
> painted phoenixes dance on the vermilion gates.
> Galleries and winding corridors,
> everywhere exquisite, carved through and through;
> triple eaves in fourfold clusters,
> tier upon tier where dragons and phoenixes soar.
> Above sits a great golden gourd-shaped dome,
> towering and purple, dazzling and bright,
> rounded and gleaming, blazing with light.
> Below, heavenly consorts hold up their fans,
> jade maidens bear immortal kerchiefs;
> fierce-eyed heavenly generals manage the court,
> spirited noble immortals guard the throne.
> In the very center, on a tray of lapis glaze,
> lie pile upon pile of Grand Monad elixirs;
> in agate vases stand sprigs
> of coral trees, curling and twisting.
> Indeed — every rare thing of the heavenly palace is here;
> not one of these has the world below.
> Golden towers, silver chariots, and the purple courts,
> jade flowers, gem-grasses, and blossoms of fine jade.
> By the altar where the Jade Hare grinds, the worshipers pass;
> beneath where the saints gather, the Golden Crow flies low.
> The Monkey King is fated to come to Heaven's realm,
> not to be stained with the muddy dust of the mortal world.

The Great White Planet Star led the Handsome Monkey King to the outer reaches of the Numinous Empyrean Hall and, without waiting for the summons to be announced, went straight up before the throne and bowed in homage. Wukong stood stiffly to one side, offering no obeisance whatever, but cocked his ear to listen as the Planet Star made his report.

"Your servant, in obedience to the sacred decree," the Planet Star announced, "has summoned the demon-immortal, and here he is."

The Jade Emperor lowered the screen and asked, "Which is the demon-immortal?"

Only then did Wukong bow from the waist and answer, "That'd be old Monkey here."

The noble immortals all went pale with astonishment. "This wild ape! Why does he not prostrate himself and pay homage, but dares answer like that — 'That'd be old Monkey here'? He deserves to die! He deserves to die!"

But the Jade Emperor handed down his command. "This Sun Wukong is a demon-immortal of the lower world, only newly come into human form; he does not know the rites of court. Let his offense be pardoned for now."

The noble immortals all cried, "We thank you for your grace." And the Monkey King, at last, made a great long bow toward the throne.

The Jade Emperor summoned the immortal officers of civil and military appointments to find whatever post stood vacant somewhere, that Sun Wukong might be installed in it. From the ranks the Star Lord of Wuqu stepped forward and reported, "In all the palaces and halls of the heavenly court, in every quarter and every region, there is no shortage of officers — save that the Imperial Stable lacks a chief to manage its affairs."

The Jade Emperor handed down his command. "Then let him be made a BanMaWen — a Keeper of the Horses." The assembled ministers cried their thanks, and he too merely made a great long bow toward the throne. The Jade Emperor then dispatched the Star Officer of the Wood Virtue to escort him to the Imperial Stable to take up his post.

The Monkey King went off cheerfully with the Star Officer of the Wood Virtue and arrived directly at his post; the matter done, the Star Officer returned to his palace. There in the stable Wukong assembled the deputy directors, the assistant directors, the registrar, the grooms, and all the officers and men great and small, examined the affairs of the office, and found that there were just a thousand heavenly horses. They were:

> Hualiu and Qiji, Lu'er and Xianli;
> Longmei and Ziyan, the wing-hung Sushuang;
> Jueti and Yinhua, Yaoniao and Feihuang;
> Taotu the feather-turner, Chitu that outraces light;
> Yuhui and Mijing, mist-leaping Shenghuang;
> Wind-chaser, Earth-render, Skyward-flying steeds;
> swift as the red lightning, the Bronze Sparrow that floats on cloud;
> the dappled, the dragon-marked, the dust-leaving Zilin —
> the great steeds of Dayuan from the four corners of the earth,
> the eight chargers and the nine fleet ones,
> coursers that leave the herd a thousand li behind.
> Such fine horses, each and every one,
> neigh at the wind and chase the lightning, strong of spirit;
> tread the mist and mount the clouds, long of strength.

The Monkey King examined the ledgers and checked the count of the horses. Within his office, the registrar managed the requisition and provision of fodder; the groom-officers managed the currying and washing of the horses, the cutting of grass, the watering, and the boiling of feed; the deputy and assistant directors helped urge the work along. The Keeper of the Horses neither slept by day nor by night, but tended his charges. By daylight there was sport enough; but at night he watched over them with diligence — chasing up any horse that lay sleeping to feed it grass, catching back any that strayed and tying it to the trough. The heavenly horses, when they saw him, laid back their ears and drew in their hooves, and were so well kept that they grew sleek and fat. And so a good half-month passed without his marking it.

One day, at leisure, all the officers of the stable arranged a banquet — partly to welcome him, partly to congratulate him. In the midst of their merry drinking the Monkey King suddenly set down his cup and asked, "This BanMaWen of mine — what rank of office is it?"

"The title is just that — Keeper of the Horses," they said.

"And what grade does this office hold?" he asked again.

"It has no grade at all," they said.

"No grade?" said the Monkey King. "I suppose that means it is exalted beyond all measure."

"Not great, not great," they said. "It is merely called 'unranked.'"

"What do you mean by 'unranked'?" asked the Monkey King.

"The very bottom," they said. "An office like this is the lowest and smallest of all — fit only for looking after horses. Even after Your Honor took up the post and tended so diligently that the horses grew fat, all you'll earn is a single word — 'Good.' Should they fall the least bit thin and weak, you'll be called to account; and should they suffer any serious harm, you'll be fined, made to pay restitution, and charged with the crime."

When the Monkey King heard this, fire flared up in his heart, and he ground his teeth in great fury. "So this is how they slight old Monkey! On my Flower-Fruit Mountain I am hailed as king and patriarch — and they've gulled me into coming to tend their horses for them! Horse-tending is the base drudgery of low-born striplings — is that any way to treat the likes of me? I'll not do it, I'll not do it! I'm off!"

With a clatter he overturned the official desk, drew the treasure from his ear, gave it a shake until it was as thick as a rice-bowl, and with a flourish of fighting moves battled his way clear out of the Imperial Stable, straight to the Southern Gate of Heaven. The heavenly soldiers, knowing he had received an immortal scroll and was the Keeper of the Horses, dared not stop him, and let him fight his way out of the gate.

In a moment he pressed down the head of his cloud and returned to Flower-Fruit Mountain. There he saw his Four Mighty Generals and the demon kings of the various caves drilling their troops. The Monkey King called out in a ringing voice, "Little ones — old Monkey is back!" The whole crowd of monkeys came to kowtow to him and welcomed him into the deep recesses of the cave-heaven, inviting the Monkey King to ascend his treasure-seat, while on one side they laid out wine to welcome him home.

"Congratulations, Great King!" they all said. "You went up to the upper realm for a dozen years or more — surely you've come home in triumph and high content?"

"I've been gone scarcely a half-month and more," said the Monkey King. "How could it be a dozen years?"

"Great King," said the monkeys, "up in Heaven you take no notice of the passing hours. One day in Heaven is a whole year in the world below. May we ask, Great King — what office did you hold?"

The Monkey King waved his hand. "Don't speak of it, don't speak of it — it shames a fellow to death! That Jade Emperor doesn't know how to use a man. He saw old Monkey looking the way I do and made me some sort of 'BanMaWen' — which turns out to be a horse-keeper for him, the kind of post that doesn't even rank in the grades. When I first took it up I didn't know, and just amused myself about the Imperial Stable. But today I asked my colleagues, and only then learned how base and lowly it was. My heart was sorely vexed — I overturned the banquet table, refused the title, and so came back down here."

"Welcome, welcome!" cried the monkeys. "Great King, being king in this blessed land and cave-heaven of ours is honor and pleasure beyond measure — why should you go and play groom for him?" And they ordered the little ones to fetch wine quickly, to dispel the Great King's gloom.

In the very midst of this merry drinking, someone came in to report: "Great King, outside the gate are two One-Horned Demon Kings who wish to see Your Majesty."

"Show them in," said the Monkey King.

The Demon Kings straightened their robes, ran into the cave, threw themselves down, and bowed.

"What is your business with me?" the Handsome Monkey King asked them.

"Long have we heard that the Great King seeks out men of worth," said the Demon Kings, "but we found no way to gain an audience. Now that we see the Great King has received the heavenly scroll and come home in triumph, we have brought a robe of russet-yellow as a gift to mark the occasion. If you will not scorn us as base and mean, but take us into your service, we too may render you the labor of dog and horse."

The Monkey King was overjoyed and put on the russet-yellow robe. The others gladly fell into ranks to do him homage, and at once he appointed the Demon Kings to be Vanguard Commanders of the Front Division. The Demon Kings, their thanks made, then spoke again: "The Great King was in Heaven a long while — what office were you granted?"

"The Jade Emperor makes light of the worthy," said the Monkey King, "and named me some sort of 'BanMaWen.'"

When the Demon Kings heard this, they advanced again to speak. "With supernatural powers such as yours, Great King, why should you tend his horses? Why not make yourself 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven'? What is to stop you?"

When the Monkey King heard this, his delight knew no bounds, and he cried, "Good! Good! Good!" several times over. He ordered the Four Mighty Generals: "Quickly set up a banner for me, and on the banner write the four great words 'GREAT SAGE EQUAL TO HEAVEN.' Raise the pole and hang it out. From this time forward, you are to call me only the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, and never again 'Great King.' Let word of this go out, too, to the demon kings of all the caves, that all may know." But of this no more for now.

Now the Jade Emperor held court the next day, and there came Heavenly Master Zhang, leading the deputy and assistant directors of the Imperial Stable, who bowed at the foot of the vermilion steps and reported: "Your Majesty, the newly appointed BanMaWen, Sun Wukong, disdaining the smallness of his office, fled the heavenly palace yesterday in revolt." Even as they spoke, there came also from outside the Southern Gate the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka with his soldiers, who likewise reported: "The BanMaWen, for reasons unknown, has fled out the gate of Heaven."

When the Jade Emperor heard this, he straightway handed down his command: "Let the spirits of both reports return each to his proper duty. We shall dispatch heavenly soldiers to capture this monster." From the ranks stepped forth the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King Li and his third son, the Prince Nezha, who came forward and reported above: "Your Majesty, though your servants are without talent, we beg the decree to subdue this monster." The Jade Emperor was greatly pleased, and at once made the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King Li Jing the Demon-Quelling Grand Marshal, and the third Prince Nezha the Great Spirit of the Three Altars and the Ocean Assembly, and bade them raise their host and go down to the lower world at once.

Heavenly King Li and Nezha kowtowed their thanks, took their leave, and went straight to their own palace, where they mustered their three armies and their captains. They named the Mighty Magic Spirit as vanguard, the Fish-Belly General as rearguard, and the Yaksha General to urge the troops along. In an instant they passed out the Southern Gate and came straight to Flower-Fruit Mountain. Choosing a level open place, they pitched their camp, and the order went forth for the Mighty Magic Spirit to give challenge.

Receiving the command, the Mighty Magic Spirit girt himself in good order, swung up his patterned battle-ax, and came to the mouth of the Water-Curtain Cave. There outside the little cave-gate were many demons and monsters — all manner of wolves and serpents, tigers and leopards — in jagged ranks, brandishing spears and whirling swords, leaping and snarling in combat-play. The Mighty Magic Spirit shouted: "You cursed beasts! Hurry and report to your BanMaWen: I am a great general of the upper heavens, come by the Jade Emperor's decree to subdue him. Tell him to come out at once and submit, lest you all be hacked to pieces."

The monsters went scrambling and stumbling to spread the word within the cave: "Disaster! Disaster!"

"What disaster?" asked the Monkey King.

"Outside the gate," said the demons, "is a heavenly general who calls out your title of 'Great Sage,' and says he comes by the Jade Emperor's decree to subdue you. He bids you come out quickly to surrender, and so spare our lives."

When the Monkey King heard this, he called for his armor. He set the purple-gold cap on his head, donned the golden mail, slipped on his cloud-treading shoes, took the As-You-Will Golden-Banded Cudgel in hand, and led his host out the gate, drawing up his battle-line. The Mighty Magic Spirit opened his eyes wide and gazed: a fine Monkey King indeed —

> His body clad in golden mail, gleaming and bright;
> on his head a golden cap, light flashing forth.
> In his hand he raises a golden-banded cudgel;
> on his feet, cloud-shoes that match it well.
> A pair of strange eyes like bright stars;
> two ears that pass his shoulders, keen and hard.
> Straight and tall, of many transformations;
> his voice rings clear as bell and chiming-stone.
> Sharp-mouthed, jutting-toothed BanMaWen —
> high-hearted, he would be the Great Sage Equal to Heaven.

The Mighty Magic Spirit cried out in a stern voice, "You insolent ape! Do you know who I am?"

Hearing this, the Great Sage asked sharply, "What hairy little spirit are you from what quarter? Old Monkey has never met you. Report your name and be quick about it."

"I'll get you, you deceitful baboon!" said the Mighty Magic Spirit. "So you don't know me. I am the Mighty Magic Heavenly General, vanguard under the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King Li of the High Numinous Empyrean, come by the Jade Emperor's decree to subdue you. Strip off your gear at once and submit to Heaven's grace, lest all the beasts of this mountain be put to the sword. Say half a word of refusal, and I'll grind you to powder in an instant."

When the Monkey King heard this, great rage rose in his heart. "Foul hairy spirit! Don't boast so big or wag so long a tongue. I had a mind to strike you dead with one blow of my cudgel — but then there'd be no one to carry the message. So I'll spare your life: hurry back to Heaven and tell the Jade Emperor that he sorely fails to use the worthy. Old Monkey has boundless powers — why does he set me to tending his horses? Look at the words on my banner there: if he'll promote me according to that title, I'll lay down my weapons and Heaven and earth will of themselves be at peace; but if he won't, I'll come straight up and beat upon the Numinous Empyrean Treasure-Hall, and he'll not sit easy upon his dragon-throne!"

When the Mighty Magic Spirit heard this, he opened his eyes against the wind and looked — and there indeed outside the gate stood a tall pole, and on the pole a banner, and on the banner the four great words "GREAT SAGE EQUAL TO HEAVEN." The Mighty Magic Spirit gave three cold laughs. "This insolent ape! So utterly ignorant of his place, so brazenly without manners — you would be a Great Sage Equal to Heaven? Then take this ax of mine, and welcome!" And he hacked straight at the Monkey King's head.

But the Monkey King, being a master of the art, was in no haste; he met the ax with his Golden-Banded Cudgel, weapon answering hand. And this was a fine fight:

> The cudgel named As-You-Will,
> the ax called Patterned-Blossom.
> The two of them, meeting for the first time,
> knew not each other's depth.
> Ax and cudgel crossed left and right.
> One concealed a marvelous craft;
> the other boasted with a great loud mouth.
> Wielding their arts, they breathed out cloud and mist;
> spreading their hands, they scattered earth and flung the sand.
> The heavenly general had his powers and his way,
> but the Monkey King's transformations were truly without bound.
> The cudgel raised was like a dragon at play in water;
> the ax that came was like a phoenix piercing flowers.
> The Mighty Magic Spirit's fame was known throughout Heaven —
> yet his skill, it turned out, was no match for the other:
> the Great Sage lightly swung his iron rod,
> and one blow to the head left him numb from crown to sole.

The Mighty Magic Spirit could not hold his ground. The Monkey King brought his cudgel down upon his head; in a panic the spirit threw up his ax to fend it off — but with a sharp crack the ax-handle was beaten clean in two, and he hastily turned and fled the field to save his life.

The Monkey King laughed. "Soft sack! Soft sack! I've spared you — now hurry off and carry the message, hurry off and carry the message!"

The Mighty Magic Spirit returned to the camp gate and went straight to the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King, where he dropped to his knees and stammered, "The BanMaWen truly has vast and far-reaching powers. Your servant could not fight him, and has returned defeated to beg punishment."

Heavenly King Li flew into a rage. "This wretch has blunted my army's keen spirit! Drag him out and behead him!"

But from the side stepped Prince Nezha, who bowed and pleaded, "Calm your anger, Father King, and pardon the Mighty Magic Spirit's offense for now. Wait until your child has gone forth on a single campaign, and we shall know the creature's measure." The Heavenly King heeded the counsel, and bade the spirit return to camp to await judgment and manage affairs.

Now Prince Nezha, with his armor all in order, sprang out of the encampment and rushed to the mouth of the Water-Curtain Cave. Wukong, just then drawing in his troops, saw how boldly Nezha came on. A fine prince —

> His forelocks scarce shading his brow,
> his soft hair not yet reaching his shoulders.
> Wondrously quick of wit and bright of mind,
> fine of bone and clear of feature.
> Truly a unicorn-child of Heaven,
> indeed an immortal phoenix of mist and sunset-cloud.
> Dragon-seed by nature, of no common cast;
> in his tender years, no creature of the dust.
> About him hung six kinds of divine weapons;
> his flying transformations boundless and wide.
> Now, by the golden decree from the Jade Emperor's lips,
> he is invested with the title of the Three Altars and the Ocean Assembly.

Wukong came forward to meet him and asked, "Whose little lad are you, that you press up to my gate? What is your business?"

Nezha shouted, "Insolent demon-ape! Do you not know me? I am Nezha, third prince of the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King, and I come by special commission of the Jade Emperor to seize you."

Wukong laughed. "Little prince, your milk-teeth aren't out yet and your baby-down isn't dry — how dare you talk so big? I'll spare your life, and not strike you. Only look at what title is written on my banner, and report it to the Jade Emperor: grant me that office, and there'll be no need to trouble the host — I'll submit of myself. But if it doesn't suit my heart, I'll surely beat my way up to the Numinous Empyrean Treasure-Hall."

Nezha raised his head and looked — there were the four words "Great Sage Equal to Heaven."

"What great powers can this demon-ape have," said Nezha, "that he dares lay claim to such a title? Fear not — take this sword of mine!"

"I'll just stand here and not move," said Wukong, "and you may hack at me with a few strokes, as you please."

Nezha, roused to fury, gave a great shout — "Change!" — and at once changed into three heads and six arms, fierce and terrible, his six hands gripping his six weapons: the demon-slaying sword, the demon-hacking saber, the demon-binding rope, the demon-subduing pestle, the embroidered ball, and the fire-wheel; and in jagged array he came hurtling at Wukong's face.

Seeing this, Wukong was startled at heart. "This little lad knows a trick or two after all. No insolence, now — watch my powers!" A fine Great Sage: he too gave a shout — "Change!" — and changed into three heads and six arms; with one shake of the Golden-Banded Cudgel he made it three cudgels, and his six hands took up the three rods to ward off the blows. This battle truly made the earth quake and the mountains shudder — a fine fight indeed:

> Six-armed Prince Nezha,
> the heaven-born fine stone Monkey King —
> meeting, they were true match for each other,
> coming to grips at the very source.
> The one, dispatched, had come to the lower world;
> the other, deceitful of heart, had stirred up Dipper and Bull.
> The demon-slaying treasure-sword, keen of edge;
> the demon-hacking saber, cruel enough to grieve gods and ghosts;
> the demon-binding rope, like a flying python;
> the great demon-subduing pestle, like a wolf's head;
> the fire-wheel flashing lightning, blazing red and hot;
> the embroidered ball rolling back and forth, again and again.
> The Great Sage's three As-You-Will cudgels
> warded front and guarded rear with cunning craft.
> They fought bitterly through many bouts, neither gaining the higher hand;
> and the prince's heart would not give over.
> He made his six weapons each transform
> into hundreds of thousands of millions, raining down upon the head.
> The Monkey King, unafraid, laughed aloud,
> and tumbled his iron rod about by his own design,
> turning one into a thousand and a thousand into ten thousand,
> till the whole sky swarmed with them, dancing like flying serpents.
> The demon kings of every cave shut fast their doors in fright;
> all over the mountain the ghosts and goblins hid their heads.
> The heavenly soldiers' rage made the clouds grow grim;
> the golden-banded iron rod went whistling through the air.
> On that side, the heavenly host raised a cry, and every man was afraid;
> on this side, the monkey-monsters shook their flags, and every one was anxious.
> Furiously the two sides matched their valor,
> and who could tell which was the harder, which the softer?

The third prince and Wukong each gave free rein to his divine might, and they fought a full thirty bouts. The prince's six weapons turned into thousands upon thousands; Sun Wukong's Golden-Banded Cudgel turned into ten thousands upon thousands. In the middle air they were like raindrops, like shooting stars — and there was no telling victory from defeat.

Now Wukong was quick of hand and sharp of eye. In the very thick of the confusion he plucked out a single hair, cried "Change!", and changed it into his own likeness, holding a cudgel and sparring with Nezha; while his true body, with one bound, slipped around behind Nezha's head and struck him a blow on the left arm. Nezha, in the midst of his sorcery, heard the wind of the cudgel-head whistle down; he tried to dodge, but could not bring his hands round in time, and took the blow. Wounded and in pain, he fled, gathered in his magic, drew his six weapons back into his body, and retreated in defeat.

From the field below, Heavenly King Li had already seen it, and was about to lead his troops up in support, when all at once the prince appeared before him, trembling, and reported, "Father King, the BanMaWen truly has skill! With all my powers, your child could not best him, and has been wounded in the arm."

The Heavenly King went pale with shock. "If the creature's powers are such as this, how are we to win?"

"Outside his cave-gate stands a pole with a banner," said the prince, "and on it the four words 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven.' With his own mouth he boasts: let the Jade Emperor invest him with the title of Great Sage Equal to Heaven, and all will be over; but should it not be that title, he will surely beat his way up to the Numinous Empyrean Treasure-Hall."

"If that is so," said the Heavenly King, "then for now let us not hold the field against him. Let us go up to the upper realm, report these words in our memorial, and request more heavenly soldiers to encircle and seize the wretch — it will not be too late." The prince, hurt and unable to fight on, accordingly returned to Heaven with the Heavenly King to make their report. But of this no more.

Now see the Monkey King, returning to his mountain in triumph. The demon kings of the seventy-two caves and his six sworn brothers all came to offer congratulations, and in the blessed land of the cave-heaven they feasted and made merry beyond compare. Then he said to his six brothers, "Younger brothers, since I have styled myself Great Sage Equal to Heaven, you too may take the title of Great Sage."

From among them the Bull Demon King suddenly cried out, "Well said, worthy brother! I shall style myself the Great Sage Who Pacifies Heaven."

The Flood-Dragon Demon King said, "I shall be the Great Sage Who Overturns the Sea."

The Roc Demon King said, "I shall be the Great Sage Who Confounds Heaven."

The Lion-Camel Demon King said, "I shall be the Great Sage Who Moves Mountains."

The Macaque Demon King said, "I shall be the Great Sage Who Carries the Wind."

The Lemur-Monkey Demon King said, "I shall be the Great Sage Who Drives the Spirits."

And so at this time the Seven Great Sages, each as he pleased, took their own titles and styled themselves as they would, and made merry a whole day before they each dispersed.

Now Heavenly King Li and the third prince, leading their generals, came straight to the Numinous Empyrean Treasure-Hall and reported: "Your servants, in obedience to the sacred decree, marched forth to the lower world to subdue the demon-immortal Sun Wukong; but his powers proved so vast and far-reaching that we could not prevail. We beg Your Majesty to send more troops to root him out."

"A mere demon-ape," said the Jade Emperor. "How much skill can he have, that you ask for more soldiers?"

The prince came forward again to report: "May Your Majesty pardon your servant's mortal offense. That demon-ape wields an iron rod; he first defeated the Mighty Magic Spirit, then wounded your servant in the arm. Outside his cave-gate he has set up a pole with a banner inscribed with the four words 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven.' He says that if he is invested with this office, he will lay down his arms and submit; but if it is not this office, he will yet beat his way up to the Numinous Empyrean Treasure-Hall."

When the Jade Emperor heard this, he exclaimed in astonishment, "How dares this demon-ape be so wild and presumptuous? Let the generals put him to death at once!"

Even as he spoke, the Great White Planet Star stepped forth again from the ranks and reported: "This demon-ape knows only how to throw out big words, with no sense of high or low. To send troops against him in battle — I think he cannot be subdued at once, and the host would only be worn out to no purpose. Better that Your Majesty extend your great mercy and grace, hand down once more a decree of amnesty, and simply let him be the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. Bestow on him only an empty title — an office without emolument — and there's an end to it."

"What do you mean by 'an office without emolument'?" asked the Jade Emperor.

"His name shall be Great Sage Equal to Heaven," said the Planet Star, "only give him no affairs to manage and no salary to draw, but keep him quietly somewhere between Heaven and earth, so as to gather in his wayward heart and let no wild presumption arise. Then the cosmos will be at peace, and the seas and skies will gain their calm."

When the Jade Emperor heard this, he said, "We will do as our minister advises." And he commanded that the decree be drawn up, and again sent the Planet Star to carry it down.

The Planet Star passed out the Southern Gate of Heaven once more and came straight to the mouth of the Water-Curtain Cave on Flower-Fruit Mountain to look about him. This time it was unlike before: an awe-striking majesty, a grim and murderous air, and demon-sprites of every sort — there was no kind that was not there. Each one gripped sword or hefted spear, took up saber or brandished staff, snarling and leaping. At sight of the Planet Star, they all came forward to lay hands on him.

"You captains there," said the Planet Star, "trouble yourselves to go and report to your Great Sage: I am a heavenly envoy sent by the Lord on High, and I bear a sacred decree to invite him."

The demons ran in at once to report: "Outside is an old man who says he is an envoy from the upper realm, and has a decree to invite you."

"Welcome, welcome!" said Wukong. "This must be that Great White Planet Star who came before. That time he invited me up to the upper realm — and though the office wasn't fit to hold, still I walked the heavens once and learned the roads within and without the gate of Heaven. Now he comes again — surely with good intent." And he ordered the captains to throw wide the banners and drums and form up ranks to receive him. The Great Sage then led his troop of monkeys forth; with cap on head and mail upon his body, the russet-yellow robe over the mail, and cloud-shoes on his feet, he hurried out the cave-gate, bowed from the waist, and called out loudly: "Old Star, come in, and forgive me the offense of failing to welcome you properly."

The Planet Star stepped briskly forward, went straight into the cave, and stood facing south. "Now I tell you, Great Sage," he said. "Some while ago, because the Great Sage disliked the smallness of his office, he left the Imperial Stable. The officers of the stable, great and small, reported it to the Jade Emperor, who handed down his command: 'In conferring office, all proceeds from low to high; why should he disdain the smallness?' Whereupon Heavenly King Li led Nezha down to the lower world to give battle. Not knowing the Great Sage's powers, they met with defeat, and returning to Heaven reported: 'The Great Sage has set up a banner and would be the Great Sage Equal to Heaven.' The military officers still wished to dispute it, but it was I, your old servant, who at the risk of offense made the report on the Great Sage's behalf, so as to spare the raising of the host, and begged that the Great King be granted the scroll. The Jade Emperor approved the memorial, and so I have come to invite you."

Wukong laughed. "Last time you put yourself to trouble; now again I'm favored with your kindness. My thanks, my thanks! But I do not know — will the upper Heaven grant me the office and title of Great Sage Equal to Heaven?"

"It was with this very title that I obtained the Emperor's approval before I dared come bearing the decree," said the Planet Star. "Should it not come to pass, let the blame rest on your old servant alone."

Wukong was overjoyed, and pressed him earnestly to stay for a banquet, which the Planet Star declined. So the two of them mounted an auspicious cloud and came outside the Southern Gate of Heaven, where the heavenly soldiers and generals all clasped their hands in welcome. They went straight in below the Numinous Empyrean Hall, and the Planet Star bowed and reported: "Your servant, in obedience to the decree, has summoned the BanMaWen Sun Wukong, who is now arrived."

"Let Sun Wukong come forward," said the Jade Emperor. "Today We proclaim you Great Sage Equal to Heaven. The office could not be higher — but on no account are you to behave wildly." The Monkey, again, merely made a long bow toward the throne and said, "I thank you for your grace."
