The Jade Emperor then commanded the master-builders Zhang and Lu, the two craft-officers, to raise, on the right-hand side of the Garden of Immortal Peaches, a Mansion of the Great Sage Equal to Heaven; and within the mansion to establish two bureaus — one named the Bureau of Peace and Quiet, the other the Bureau of Tranquil Spirit. Each bureau had its immortal clerks to attend him left and right. He further dispatched the Star Lords of the Five Bushels to escort Wukong to take up his post, and bestowed in addition two bottles of imperial wine and ten golden flowers, charging him to settle his heart and steady his will, and never again to behave wildly.

The Monkey King received the orders and obeyed. That same day he went with the Star Lords of the Five Bushels to his mansion, opened the bottles of wine, and drank them down together with his company. Then he saw the Star Officers back to their own palaces, and at last, his heart content and his wishes fulfilled, gladdened in earth and joyful in heaven, he took his pleasure in the heavenly palace, with never a care or a hindrance. Truly it is said:

> His immortal name forever set in the scroll of long life;
> no more to fall through the wheel of rebirth — handed down for all the ages.

And in the end, there is no knowing what came after; so listen to the telling in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 5 -->
# Chapter 5: The Great Sage Plunders the Peaches and Steals the Elixir; The Hosts of Heaven March to Seize the Monster

Now then — for all his grand title, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven was at bottom nothing but a monkey-spirit. He neither understood the ranks and gradations of office nor cared whether his stipend ran high or low; so long as his name was on the rolls, he was content. In the offices beneath his Equal-to-Heaven residence the two bureaus of immortal clerks waited upon him morning and night, while he himself knew only this: three meals by day, one bed by night, no cares to entangle him, free and at ease in every way. In his idle hours he visited his friends and roamed the celestial palaces, forging bonds and swearing brotherhoods. When he met the Three Pure Ones he addressed them as "Venerable"; when he encountered the Four Emperors he said "Your Majesty." With the Nine Luminaries, the Generals of the Five Quarters, the Twenty-Eight Constellations, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the Twelve Branches of Time, the Five Elders of the Five Regions, and all the starry hosts of heaven and the divinities of the River of Stars — with every one of them he stood as brother to brother, hailing them all as equals. Today he wandered east, tomorrow he roamed west, drifting with the clouds, coming and going as the whim took him, his comings and goings never fixed.

One day, as the Jade Emperor held his morning audience, the Perfected Man Xu Jingyang stepped forth from the ranks, bowed low, and made his report: "This Great Sage Equal to Heaven, having nothing to occupy him, idles his days away and consorts with all the stars and constellations of heaven, calling high and low alike his friend. I fear that, with nothing to do, he will one day breed mischief in his idleness. It would be better to set him over some single charge, so that no other trouble may arise."

The Jade Emperor heard this and at once issued a summons. The Monkey King came tripping in, all delight, and said, "Your Majesty — for what advancement or reward have you summoned Old Monkey?"

"Seeing that you are idle and unoccupied," said the Jade Emperor, "I give you a duty. Take charge for the present of the Garden of Immortal Peaches, and mind it well, morning and evening."

The Great Sage, overjoyed, gave thanks for the favor, made his bow before the throne, and withdrew.

He could scarcely wait, and at once went into the Peach Garden to inspect it. There a local earth-god barred his way and asked, "Where does the Great Sage go?"

"I am sent by the decree of the Jade Emperor," said the Great Sage, "to take charge of the Peach Garden, and I have come now to inspect it."

At once the earth-god made his bow, and summoned the whole company — the laborers who hoed the roots, the laborers who carried water, the laborers who tended the trees, the laborers who swept the grounds — to come and kowtow before the Great Sage, and they led him within. And there he beheld:

> Luxuriant and glowing, bough on bough, tree upon tree.
> Luxuriant and glowing, the blossoms crowd the branches;
> bough upon bough, the fruit weighs heavy on the limbs.
> The fruit upon the boughs hangs down like brocade pellets;
> the blossoms on the trees are clustered thick as rouge.
> Now flowering, now fruiting, ripened in a thousand years —
> without a summer, without a winter, slow-maturing through ten thousand ages.
> The early-ripened wear a flushed and wine-drunk face;
> the still-green keep their stems and pale unripened skins.
> The misty flesh shows green beneath;
> against the sun they bare their crimson glory.
> Beneath the trees rare flowers and strange herbs,
> through all four seasons never fading, every hue in even rank;
> to left and right, the towers and halls,
> their heights forever veiled in cloud and rainbow.
> No common stock of the mortal world is this —
> the Queen Mother of the Jade Pool planted it with her own hand.

The Great Sage gazed and reveled long, then asked the earth-god, "How many trees are there in this garden?"

"There are three thousand six hundred," said the earth-god. "The twelve hundred in front bear small blossoms and little fruit; they ripen once in three thousand years, and a man who eats of them becomes an immortal and attains the Way, his body hale, his frame made light. The twelve hundred in the middle bear layered blossoms and sweet fruit; they ripen once in six thousand years, and a man who eats of them ascends in rosy mists and flies aloft, deathless and unaging. The twelve hundred behind bear fruit with purple veins and pale yellow stones; they ripen once in nine thousand years, and a man who eats of them lives as long as heaven and earth, of one age with the sun and moon."

Hearing this, the Great Sage was beside himself with joy. That very day he made his count of the trees, looked over the pavilions and lodges, and returned to his residence. From that time on he came every three or five days to enjoy the sight, and he neither sought out his friends nor wandered elsewhere.

One day he saw that on the boughs of the older trees the peaches were ripe over more than half. He had a mind to taste a few and try the new fruit — but the earth-god, the laborers, and the immortal clerks of his own residence followed him too closely for comfort. Of a sudden he hit upon a scheme. "Step outside the gate, all of you, and wait there," he said. "Let me rest a little while upon this pavilion." The whole company duly withdrew. Then the Monkey King slipped off his cap and robes, climbed the great tree, picked out the largest, ripest peaches, plucked a great many, and there among the branches ate his fill at his leisure. When he had stuffed himself, he leapt down, set his cap on, donned his robes, and called his attendants and retinue back to the residence. And two or three days later he went again and contrived to steal the peaches, and indulged himself to his heart's content.

Now one morning the Queen Mother prepared a banquet, threw open her precious halls, and made ready in the Jade Pool the grand Festival of Immortal Peaches. She sent the immortal maidens in red, in green, in white, in black, in purple, in yellow, and in green — seven maidens each bearing a flower-basket — to the Peach Garden to pluck the peaches and lay the feast. The seven-robed maidens came straight to the garden gate, and there they found the earth-god, the laborers, and the two bureaus of immortal clerks from the Equal-to-Heaven residence all keeping the gate.

The maidens drew near and said, "By the gracious command of the Queen Mother, we have come to pluck the peaches for a banquet."

"Wait, fair immortals," said the earth-god. "This year is not as years gone by. The Jade Emperor has appointed the Great Sage Equal to Heaven to oversee this place, and we must inform the Great Sage before we dare open the garden."

"Where is the Great Sage?" asked the maidens.

"The Great Sage is within the garden," said the earth-god. "Being weary, he has gone off by himself to sleep upon the pavilion."

"If that is so," said the maidens, "let us go and find him, and not delay."

The earth-god went in with them. They searched all the way to the flower-pavilion and saw no one — only his cap and robes lying there, and no telling where he had gone; and search as they might in every quarter, there was no finding him. For the truth was that the Great Sage, after sporting awhile and eating his fill of peaches, had changed himself into a little manikin no more than two inches tall and fallen asleep beneath the dense leaves at the very top of one of the great trees.

"We came at the Queen Mother's command," said the seven-robed maidens, "and we cannot find the Great Sage. How dare we go back empty-handed?"

An immortal attendant standing by said, "Since you fair maidens come by command, you need not hesitate. Our Great Sage is much given to idle wandering, and has likely gone out of the garden to visit his friends. Go and pluck your peaches; we will answer for you."

The maidens did as he said and went down among the trees to pluck. From the front trees they took two baskets; from the middle trees, three; but when they came to the rear trees to pluck there, they found the blossoms and fruit grown sparse, and only a few green-skinned, hairy-stemmed peaches left. For all the ripe ones the Monkey King had eaten. The seven maidens looked this way and that, and saw on a southward bough but a single peach, half red and half white. The green-robed maiden pulled the branch down with her hand, the red-robed maiden plucked the fruit, and then they let the branch spring back upward.

Now it so happened that the Great Sage, transformed, lay sleeping upon that very branch, and the jolt woke him. At once he resumed his true form, drew the gold-banded cudgel from within his ear, shook it till it grew thick as a bowl, and roared out, "What sort of monsters are you, that you dare so boldly to steal and pluck my peaches?"

Terrified, the seven maidens fell to their knees together and cried, "Stay your wrath, Great Sage! We are no monsters, but the seven-robed maidens sent by the Queen Mother to gather the immortal peaches for the grand opening of her precious halls and the holding of the Festival of Immortal Peaches. We came here, and first met the earth-god and the other spirits of this garden, but could not find the Great Sage. Fearing to be late for the Queen Mother's command, we could wait for the Great Sage no longer, and so plucked the peaches here. We beg you to forgive our fault."

At these words the Great Sage turned from anger to delight and said, "Rise, fair maidens. This banquet the Queen Mother holds — who is invited?"

"The upper assembly has its old established custom," said the maidens. "Those invited are the Buddha of the Western Heaven, the Bodhisattvas, the holy monks, the Arhats; the Guanyin of the South Pole in the south; the Sage Emperor of Exalted Grace in the east, and the immortal sages of the Ten Continents and Three Islands; the Mystic Numen of the North Pole in the north; and the Great Immortal of the Yellow Horn at the center — these being the Five Elders of the Five Quarters. There are also the Star Lords of the Five Bushels; in the upper Eight Caves the Three Pure Ones, the Four Emperors, the Grand Unity and the celestial immortals; in the middle Eight Caves the Jade Emperor, the Nine Mounds, and the gods of sea and peak; in the lower Eight Caves the Lord of the Dark Underworld and the earthbound immortals who watch over the world; and the great and lesser honored gods of every palace and every hall — all alike will attend the splendid Feast of Peaches."

The Great Sage laughed and said, "And am I invited?"

"We have not heard you mentioned," said the maidens.

"I am the Great Sage Equal to Heaven," said he. "Why should not Old Monkey be invited to sit in the place of honor?"

"That is the old custom of the upper assembly," said the maidens. "What may be done at this present feast, we cannot say."

"You are right," said the Great Sage, "and no blame to you. Stand here awhile and let Old Monkey go ahead and find out the news — whether or not he is to be invited."

Good Great Sage! He made the magic sign, recited a spell, and said to the maidens, "Stay! Stay! Stay!" This was a body-fixing spell, and it left the seven-robed maidens, every one of them, standing rooted beneath the peach trees, eyes glazed and staring, blank-eyed and stiff. Then the Great Sage mounted an auspicious cloud, sprang out of the garden, and set off straight along the road to the Jade Pool. As he traveled, he saw, off to one side:

> Heaven all bright with auspicious haze, light wavering and aglow,
> five-colored clouds of blessing flying without cease.
> The white crane's cry resounds through the Nine Marshes;
> the purple fungus blooms in glory, parting a thousand leaves.
> And in their midst appears an immortal,
> his features heaven-formed, his bearing all his own.
> Spirit-dancing on the rainbow, he sweeps across the starry sky,
> at his waist a precious scroll, deathless and undying.
> The Barefoot Great Immortal is his name,
> come specially to the Peach Feast to add to the years of life.

The Barefoot Immortal came face to face with the Great Sage. The Great Sage lowered his head and laid his scheme: he meant to gull the true immortal so that he might go secretly to the feast in his stead, and so he asked, "Venerable Sir, where do you go?"

"By the Queen Mother's gracious invitation," said the Immortal, "I go to the splendid Feast of Peaches."

"Venerable Sir, you do not know," said the Great Sage. "Because Old Monkey's somersault cloud is so swift, the Jade Emperor has charged me to go by all five roads and invite the worthies, that they may first perform the rites of ceremony below the Hall of Universal Brightness, and afterward go on to the feast."

Now the Barefoot Immortal was an open and upright man, and took the Sage's lie for truth. "In years past," he said, "the rites of thanksgiving were performed at the Jade Pool itself. How is it that this year we first go to the Hall of Universal Brightness to perform the rites, and only then to the Jade Pool for the feast?" But there was no help for it, and so he turned his auspicious cloud about and made straight for the Hall of Universal Brightness.

The Great Sage, riding his cloud, recited a spell, shook himself, and changed into the very likeness of the Barefoot Immortal, then sped on to the Jade Pool. Before long he came right up to the precious halls, stayed his cloud, and softly, step by step, walked within. And there he saw:

> Rare incense curling, auspicious haze in profusion.
> The jasper terrace spread with colored knots,
> the precious halls awash in fragrant mist.
> Phoenixes soaring, simurghs in flight, their forms half-glimpsed;
> golden flowers and jade calyxes, their shadows floating, sinking.
> Set out above: the nine-phoenix screen of rosy cloud,
> the eight-jeweled stools of purple rainbow,
> the five-hued tables traced with gold,
> the thousand-flowered basins of green jade.
> Upon the tables, dragon-liver and phoenix-marrow,
> bear's paws and the lips of apes.
> Rare viands of a hundred flavors, each one delicious;
> strange fruits and choice morsels, each fresh in its own color.

Everything was laid out in perfect order — but not yet had a single immortal arrived.

The Great Sage could not take in all there was to see, when of a sudden a gust of wine-fragrance came stealing to his nose. He turned his head, and there beneath the long gallery on the right-hand wall were several wine-making immortal officers and dreg-turning laborers, leading a few water-carrying Daoists and fire-tending lads, washing the vats and scrubbing the jars — for they had already made the jade-fluid and jasper-nectar, the fragrant brew and the choicest vintage. The Great Sage could not keep the drool from the corners of his mouth, and longed to go and drink — but all those people were there. So he worked a piece of magic: he plucked a few hairs, tossed them into his mouth, chewed them small, spat them out, and recited a spell, crying, "Change!" At once they became several sleep-insects, which flew onto the faces of the company. And look — that crew, their hands went limp, their heads drooped, their brows knit and their eyes fell shut, and dropping their charges they all went off to doze. Then the Great Sage took some of the hundred-flavored delicacies, the choice morsels and the rare dishes, walked into the long gallery, and there beside the vats and against the jars he opened his gullet and drank deep, a long and hearty bout. When he had drunk a good long while, he was thoroughly fuddled with wine. He felt and fumbled at himself and said, "This is bad — this is bad! In a little while, when the invited guests arrive, will they not lay the blame on me? If I am caught here, how shall I fare? Better get home early and sleep it off."

Good Great Sage! Reeling and swaying, propped up by the wine, he blundered along just as the fancy took him. Soon he lost the road — and instead of the Equal-to-Heaven residence, he came to the Tushita Palace. The sight of it brought him to his senses with a start. "The Tushita Palace stands above the Thirty-Three Heavens," he said, "in the Heaven of Parted Sorrows, the dwelling of Lord Lao Tzu, the Supreme Patriarch. How have I blundered here? Well, no matter — I have long meant to call on this old gentleman and never managed it. Now that my idle steps have brought me, I may as well pay him a visit." So he straightened his clothes and barged in — but Lord Lao was nowhere to be seen, nor was there a soul in sight. For the truth was that Lord Lao and the Ancient Buddha Dipankara were expounding the Way upon the Vermilion Mound Cinnabar Terrace in the three-storied high hall, and all the immortal lads, immortal generals, immortal officers, and immortal clerks stood attending to left and right and listening. The Great Sage went straight into the elixir-chamber, but seek as he might, found no one. He saw only, beside the elixir-stove, fire still glowing in the brazier; and to left and right of the stove stood five gourds, and within the gourds was all the refined golden elixir.

"This stuff is the supreme treasure of the immortal folk!" the Great Sage said in delight. "Ever since Old Monkey attained the Way, I have grasped the principle that inner and outer are one and the same, and I too have meant to refine some golden elixir to succor mankind, but never had the leisure once I got home. Today fortune favors me, and I have stumbled on the very thing. While the old gentleman is away, let me eat a few pellets and try the new." So he tipped out all the gourds and ate the lot, crunching them down as one cracks roasted beans.

In a little while the elixir had cleared the wine from his head, and again he reckoned with himself. "This is bad — this is bad! This is a calamity bigger than the sky itself. If the Jade Emperor learns of it, my life is forfeit. Go — go — go! Better to go down to the world below and be a king there." So he ran out of the Tushita Palace, and not by the old road, but slipping out through the Western Heaven Gate by a spell of invisibility, he made his escape. He pressed down his cloud and returned to the bounds of the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. And there he saw banners flashing and halberds gleaming — for the Four Mighty Generals and the seventy-two cave-kings of monsters were drilling at their martial arts.

"My little ones, I am back!" the Great Sage called out in a loud voice. The whole horde of monsters threw down their weapons and fell to their knees. "How easy in heart the Great Sage is!" they said. "You left us so long and never came to look in on us."

"It was no long time," said the Great Sage. "No long time at all."

Talking and walking, he passed straight into the deep recesses of the cave-heaven. The Four Mighty Generals swept and made ready his resting place, kowtowed and paid their respects, and when that was done they all asked, "The Great Sage has been a hundred years and more in heaven. What office did you truly hold?"

The Great Sage laughed. "By my reckoning it was but half a year," he said. "How can you speak of a hundred years and more?"

"One day in heaven," said the Generals, "is a year in the world below."

"It is well, then," said the Great Sage, "that this time the Jade Emperor took such a liking to me. He did indeed enfeoff me as the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, raised up an Equal-to-Heaven residence for me, set up the two bureaus of Tranquillity and Spirit-Repose, with immortal clerks and guards in each. Later, seeing I had nothing to do, he set me to mind the Garden of Immortal Peaches. Now of late the Queen Mother held her grand Feast of Peaches, and never invited me. So I did not wait for her invitation, but went first to the Jade Pool, and her immortal delicacies and immortal wine — I stole and ate the whole of them. Coming out of the Jade Pool, staggering and lurching, I blundered into Lord Lao's palace by mistake, and there I stole and ate the golden elixir from his five gourds as well. But fearing the Jade Emperor would charge me with the crime, I made my way out of the heavenly gate just now."

At this the whole horde of monsters rejoiced greatly. At once they set out wine and fruit to welcome him, and brimmed a stone bowl with coconut wine and offered it up. The Great Sage took one sip and at once grimaced and bared his teeth, saying, "It has no taste — it has no taste at all."

The two generals Beng and Ba said, "The Great Sage in the heavenly palace drank immortal wine and ate immortal fare, so coconut wine is little to his liking. As the old saying has it, 'Sweet or not sweet, it's the water of home.'"

"And you," said the Great Sage, "are 'Kin or not kin, they're the folk of home.' When I was reveling this morning at the Jade Pool, I saw beneath the long gallery a great many bottles and jars, all full of jade-fluid and jasper-nectar — and none of you has ever so much as tasted it. Wait while I go and steal a few bottles back, and each of you shall drink half a cup, and every one of you shall be deathless and unaging."

The monkeys were overjoyed beyond measure. The Great Sage went out of the cave-mouth, turned another somersault, and using a spell of invisibility went straight to the Peach Feast and into the palace of the Jade Pool. There he found the few wine-makers, dreg-turners, water-carriers, and fire-tenders still snoring and not yet awake. He took the largest jars, tucked two under his arms, carried two in his hands, then turned his cloud about and went back. Gathering the monkeys in the cave, he held a feast of immortal wine, and each drank a few cups, and they made merry — but of that we say no more.

Now those seven-robed maidens, once the Great Sage had laid his body-fixing spell upon them, could not break free until a full day and night had gone round. Each took up her flower-basket and went back to report to the Queen Mother, saying, "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven worked his magic to bind us fast, and that is why we are so late in returning."

"How many peaches did you pluck?" asked the Queen Mother.

"Only two baskets of small peaches and three of middling," said the maidens. "When we came to the rear trees, there was not half a large peach to be found — all eaten, we think, by the Great Sage. And as we were searching, who should come out but the Great Sage himself, who fell upon us in a fury, and then asked who was invited to the feast. We told him over the matter of the upper assembly, and he fixed us where we stood and went off, none knows where. Only now have we come to ourselves and returned."

When the Queen Mother heard this, she went at once to the Jade Emperor and laid the whole affair before him. Scarcely had she finished when the company of wine-makers came in with their immortal officers and reported: "Someone — we know not who — has thrown the grand Feast of Peaches into confusion and stolen and drunk the jade-fluid and jasper-nectar; and the eight delicacies and hundred flavors, those too have all been stolen and eaten." Then came four Grand Celestial Masters to report: "The Supreme Patriarch of the Way has arrived." The Jade Emperor went out with the Queen Mother to greet him. When Lord Lao had finished his salutations, he said, "In this old Daoist's palace I had refined some Nine-Cycle Golden Elixir against the day Your Majesty should hold the Grand Elixir Assembly — but it has been stolen away by a thief, and I come expressly to make it known to Your Majesty." The Jade Emperor heard the report with dismay.

In a little while the immortal clerks of the Equal-to-Heaven residence came kowtowing and said, "Sun the Great Sage has neglected his charge. Since yesterday he has gone off roaming and to this hour has not returned, and there is no knowing where he is." This added still more to the Jade Emperor's misgivings. Then the Barefoot Great Immortal bowed low and reported: "By the Queen Mother's summons, your servant went yesterday to attend the feast, and by chance met the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, who told me that Your Majesty had decreed he should invite us all to perform the rites of ceremony first at the Hall of Universal Brightness, and only then go to the feast. Trusting his word, your servant returned at once to the foot of the Hall of Universal Brightness, but saw nothing of Your Majesty's dragon-carriage and phoenix-chariot, and so hastened here to wait." The Jade Emperor was more alarmed than ever. "This wretch has counterfeited a decree and gulled our worthy minister!" he said. "Quick — set the Inspecting Numinous Officer to track down the trail of this wretch."

The Numinous Officer received the command, went out from the hall, and made inquiry everywhere; and having learned the whole matter in full detail, he returned and reported: "He who has thrown the heavenly palace into confusion is the Great Sage Equal to Heaven." And he related the whole affair from beginning to end. The Jade Emperor was sore wroth, and at once dispatched the Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King Li and Prince Nezha; and he mustered the Twenty-Eight Constellations, the Nine Luminary Star-Officers, the Twelve Branches of Time, the Revealers of the Five Quarters, the Four Duty-Gods of the Watches, the stars of east and west, the deities of south and north, the gods of the Five Sacred Peaks and the Four Great Rivers, and all the starry hosts of heaven — a hundred thousand heavenly soldiers in all — to spread eighteen frames of heaven-and-earth net and descend to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, there to surround and besiege the wretch and seize him without fail for punishment.

The host of gods raised their army at once and departed the heavenly palace. And as they went, behold:

> Yellow wind rolling, rolling, darkens the very sky;
> purple fog surging, surging, blots the earth in gloom.
> All because a monkey-monster has flouted the High God,
> the assembled saints come down into the dust of the world.
> The Four Great Heavenly Kings, the Revealers of the Five Quarters:
> the Four Great Kings hold the supreme command,
> the Five Revealers marshal the many troops.
> Li, the Pagoda-Bearer, in the central host gives the signals;
> fierce Nezha leads the vanguard.
> Rahu the star takes the muster as chief;
> Ketu the star presses on towering behind.
> The star of the Moon's Essence is full of dash and vigor;
> the star of the Sun shines clear and bright.
> The stars of the Five Elements excel in valor;
> the Nine Luminary stars love best to strive.
> The Branch-stars of midnight, noon, dawn, and dusk —
> each and every one a mighty heaven-warrior.
> The Five Plagues and Five Peaks ranged east and west,
> the Six Ding and Six Jia marching left and right.
> The dragon-gods of the Four Rivers split above and below,
> the Twenty-Eight Constellations in dense and serried ranks.
> Horn, Neck, Root, and Room lead all the rest;
> Stride, Bond, Stomach, and Mane are practiced in the tumult.
> Dipper, Ox, Maid, Void, Roof, House, and Wall;
> Heart, Tail, and Basket — every star a champion.
> Well, Ghost, Willow, Star, Bow, Wing, and Axletree —
> brandishing spears and waving swords, they show their awesome might.
> Halting the clouds and lowering the mist, they came down to the mortal world,
> and pitched their camp before the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit.

A poem says:

> The heaven-born Monkey King, of myriad transformations,
> stole the elixir, stole the wine, made merry in his mountain den.
> Only because he threw the Peach Feast into confusion,
> a hundred thousand heavenly soldiers spread their net for him.

Now the Heavenly King Li gave his orders, and bade the host of heavenly soldiers strike camp and ring the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit so close that not a drop of water could leak through, and above and below they spread the eighteen frames of heaven-and-earth net. Then he sent the Nine Luminaries, those fierce stars, out to do battle first. The Nine Luminaries led their troops straight to the cave-mouth, where they saw monkeys great and small leaping and sporting at their play. The star-officers cried out in stern, loud voices: "You little fiends! Where is that Great Sage of yours? We are the heavenly gods dispatched from the realm above, come to subdue this rebel Great Sage of yours. Tell him to come quickly and submit — and if he so much as breathes a word of refusal, you shall all be put to the sword together."

In alarm the little fiends rushed the word within: "Great Sage — disaster! Disaster! Outside there are nine fierce gods, who call themselves the heavenly gods sent down from the realm above, come to subdue the Great Sage."

The Great Sage was just then sharing out the immortal wine with the seventy-two cave-kings and the Four Mighty Generals. Hearing this report, he paid it no heed at all, but said, "Today there is wine, today get drunk; never mind what's right or wrong at the door." Scarcely had he spoken when another band of little fiends came leaping in: "Those nine fierce gods are at the door with their foul and abusive talk, hurling challenges to battle!"

The Great Sage laughed. "Pay them no mind," he said. "With poems and wine I'll take my pleasure for today; as for rank and fame, ask not when they'll come to pass." But the words were hardly out of his mouth when yet another band of little fiends came running to report: "Father! Those nine fierce gods have broken down the door and are fighting their way in!"

The Great Sage flew into a rage. "These vile hairy gods! What gross effrontery! I had meant to take no quarrel with them — how dare they come to my very door to bully me?" At once he ordered the One-Horned Demon King: "Lead forth the seventy-two cave-kings to give battle. Old Monkey will follow after with the Four Mighty Generals." The Demon King swiftly led his fiend-soldiers out of the gate to meet the foe — but the Nine Luminaries, those fierce stars, fell upon them all together and pinned them down at the head of the iron-plank bridge, so that they could not break out.

In the thick of the uproar the Great Sage arrived, crying out, "Make way!" He whipped out his iron cudgel, shook it once till it was thick as a bowl and a good twelve feet long, threw himself into his stance, and came striking forth. Not one of the Nine Luminaries dared withstand him, and in a moment he beat them back. The Nine Luminaries planted their battle-line and called out, "You reckless, death-defying Protector of the Horses! You have committed the ten unpardonable crimes — first you stole the peaches, then you stole the wine, you threw the grand Feast of Peaches into confusion, you filched Lord Lao's immortal elixir, and you have stolen the imperial wine to make merry with here. Crime heaped upon crime — do you not know it?"

The Great Sage laughed. "These several matters — they are true, all true. But what of it now?"

"We bear the golden decree of the Jade Emperor," said the Nine Luminaries, "and have led our host here to subdue you. Submit at once and spare these living creatures their lives — and if not, we will trample this mountain flat and overturn this cave of yours!"

"What power have a pack of paltry hairy gods like you," the Great Sage roared in fury, "that you dare utter such wild words? Stand and take a taste of Old Monkey's cudgel!" The Nine Luminaries leapt forward all together — but the Handsome Monkey King, not in the least afraid, swung up his gold-banded cudgel, parrying left and warding right, and battered the Nine Luminaries till their sinews ached and their strength failed, and one by one they trailed their weapons and fled the field in rout, hastening into the central command-tent. There they said to the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King, "That Monkey King is fierce and brave indeed. We could not stand against him, and have come back beaten."

Then the Heavenly King Li sent forth the Four Great Heavenly Kings and the Twenty-Eight Constellations to march out in one body and give battle. And the Great Sage, plainly unafraid, called out the One-Horned Demon King, the seventy-two cave-kings, and his Four Mighty Generals, and drew them up in battle-line outside the cave-mouth. Behold this melee — a terrible sight indeed:

> Cold wind whistling, eerie fog hanging dark.
> On that side, banners flying their colors;
> on this side, halberds glittering bright.
> Helmets gleaming, rank on rank;
> armor flashing, fold on fold.
> Rank on rank of gleaming helmets caught the sun
> like silver chimes battering heaven;
> fold on fold of flashing armor walled the cliffs
> like icy peaks bearing down upon the earth.
> Great broadswords flew like cloud and lightning;
> white tasseled spears pierced fog and cloud.
> Square-heaven halberds, tiger-eye whips, ranged thick as a hemp-grove;
> green bronze swords, four-bright shovels, set close as a forest.
> Curved bows and stiff crossbows, eagle-feathered arrows;
> short cudgels and serpent-lances that snatched away the soul.
> The Great Sage's single As-You-Will cudgel,
> turning and overturning, fought the gods of heaven.
> They battled till in the sky no bird flew over,
> and through the mountains tigers and wolves fled;
> flung sand and rolling stones blackened heaven and earth,
> whirling earth and flying dust darkened all the universe.
> Only the clash and clatter, startling sky and ground;
> the fierce and awful fury, shaking gods and ghosts.

This battle was arrayed from the hour of the Dragon, and the slaughter raged on until the sun went down behind the western hills. By then the One-Horned Demon King and the seventy-two cave-monsters had all been taken captive by the host of heavenly gods. Only the Four Mighty Generals and the troop of monkeys got away, hidden deep at the bottom of the Water-Curtain Cave.

The Great Sage, with his single cudgel, held off the Four Great Heavenly Gods, Li the Pagoda-Bearer, and Prince Nezha, all in the middle air; and after a long bout of slaughter, seeing that the day was drawing to its close, he plucked out a handful of his hairs, threw them into his mouth, chewed them small, spat them out, and cried, "Change!" At once they became a thousand and a hundred Great Sages, each one wielding a gold-banded cudgel, and they beat back Prince Nezha and routed the five heavenly kings.

His victory won, the Great Sage gathered in his hairs and hastened back into the cave. There at the head of the iron-plank bridge the Four Mighty Generals met him, leading the host, and bowed in welcome; and the whole company wept three sobbing, choking sobs, and then laughed three loud, hearty laughs.

"You see me again," said the Great Sage, "and you both weep and laugh — why is that?"

"This morning," said the Four Mighty Generals, "when we led the host to do battle with the heavenly kings, the seventy-two cave-kings and the One-Horned Demon King were all taken captive by the host of gods, and we ourselves escaped only with our lives — and that is why we wept. Now that the Great Sage has returned victorious and unhurt, that is why we laughed."

"Victory and defeat are the common lot of soldiers," said the Great Sage. "The ancients say, 'Slay ten thousand of the foe, and lose three thousand of your own.' Besides, those captains who were carried off are creatures of the tiger and leopard, wolf and reptile kind, badgers and roebucks, foxes and raccoon-dogs — and of our own monkey-kin not one was harmed. Why should we fret? Though I beat them back with my body-dividing magic, they will still pitch camp at the foot of our mountain. Let us keep close watch and ward, eat our fill, sleep with easy hearts, and nurse our strength. Tomorrow, at daybreak, you shall see Old Monkey work a mighty magic, take these heavenly captains, and avenge our host." So the Four Generals and the troop of monkeys drank a few bowls of coconut wine and went to their rest with quiet minds — but of that we say no more.

As for the Four Great Heavenly Kings, they withdrew their troops and broke off the battle, and each reported his merits: some had taken tigers and leopards, some had taken lions and elephants, some had taken wolves and reptiles, foxes and raccoon-dogs — but not a single monkey-spirit had been caught. Then they pitched their barracks afresh and laid out a great encampment, rewarded the generals who had won merit, and gave their orders to the soldiers of the heaven-and-earth net; and each man shook his bell and called his watchword, ringing the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit about and waiting only for the great battle of the morrow. Each held to his command and kept strict guard at his post. Truly:

> The monkey-monster's rising shook both heaven and earth;
> they spread their net and kept their watch by day and night.

And how, after the dawn broke, the matter was dealt with — that you shall hear told in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 6 -->
# Chapter 6: Guanyin Comes to the Feast and Asks the Cause; The Little Sage Unleashes His Power to Subdue the Great Sage

Let us leave aside the heavenly soldiers ringing him round while the Great Sage took his ease. The tale turns instead to the Bodhisattva Guanyin — the Greatly Merciful, Greatly Compassionate Deliverer from Pain and Rescuer from Calamity, the Efficacious One Who Hears the Cries of the World — who dwells upon Mount Potalaka by the Southern Sea. Having been invited by the Queen Mother to attend the Grand Peach Festival, she had climbed together with her chief disciple, the pilgrim Huian, up to the jeweled pavilion beside the Jasper Pool. There she found the place forlorn and desolate, the banquet tables in ruins and disorder. A few heavenly immortals were present, but none of them had taken their seats; instead they stood about in noisy clusters, all talking at once.

When the Bodhisattva had exchanged greetings with the assembled immortals, they told her at length all that had happened. Said the Bodhisattva, "Since there is to be no grand feast, and no cups are being passed, you may all come with this humble nun to see the Jade Emperor." The immortals followed her gladly. Before the Hall of Penetrating Brightness they found the Four Grand Preceptors and the Barefoot Immortal and the rest, all waiting there, who came forward to receive her. They explained that the Jade Emperor was sorely vexed, that he had dispatched his heavenly armies to capture the monster, and that the troops had not yet returned. Said the Bodhisattva, "I wish to see the Jade Emperor. Pray be so good as to carry word in for me." At once the Preceptor Qiu Hongji entered the Hall of Divine Mists and announced her, and she was summoned inside. The Supreme Lord Lao Zi was seated above, and the Queen Mother behind.

The Bodhisattva led the others within, and when she had paid her respects to the Jade Emperor, she greeted Lao Zi and the Queen Mother as well, and all took their seats. Then she asked, "How fared the Grand Peach Festival?"

Said the Jade Emperor, "Every year the gathering is held in joy and gladness. This year a monstrous ape ran riot, and the invitations all came to nothing."

"Where did this monstrous ape come from?" asked the Bodhisattva.

The Jade Emperor replied, "The monstrous ape was hatched from a stone egg on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, in the Country of Aolai, in the Eastern Continent of Superior Spirit. At the moment of his birth his eyes flashed with golden light that shot up to the Palace of the Dipper. At first I gave it no mind; but he grew into a sprite, subdued dragons and tamed tigers, and struck his own name from the registers of the dead with his own hand. The Dragon Kings and Yama, King of the Dead, both sent up petitions. I meant to seize and arrest him, but the Star Spirit Changgeng petitioned, saying, 'Among the Three Realms, any creature possessed of nine orifices may attain immortality.' So I extended instruction and nurtured the worthy: I summoned him to the upper realm and appointed him to the office of Bimawen, Keeper of the Imperial Stables. But the wretch despised the post as too lowly, and rebelled, fleeing the Heavenly Palace. I then sent Heavenly King Li and Prince Nezha to subdue and capture him; yet I also issued a decree of pardon and conciliation, summoning him back to the upper realm, and bestowed upon him the title of Great Sage Equal to Heaven — though it was an office with rank but no stipend. Having nothing to occupy or administer, he wandered idly east and west. Fearing he might breed fresh trouble, I set him to oversee the Peach Orchard in my stead. But he heeded no law: he stole and devoured every great peach on the oldest trees. And when the feast was being arranged, since he was a person without stipend, he was not invited. So he contrived a scheme, hoodwinked the Barefoot Immortal, then took on that immortal's very likeness and entered the gathering, where he stole and ate up all the celestial viands and celestial wines. He stole Lao Zi's elixir of immortality as well, and made off with a quantity of royal wine besides, carrying it back to share in revelry with the apes of his own mountain. It is this that vexes my heart, and so I have mustered a hundred thousand heavenly soldiers, with Heaven-Net and Earth-Snare, to take him. A whole day has passed without report, and I do not know how the fight goes."

When the Bodhisattva had heard this, she straightway charged the pilgrim Huian, saying, "Go you quickly down from the Heavenly Palace to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, and spy out how the battle stands. If you meet the enemy, you may lend a hand and do some service; but be sure to bring back a truthful account."

The pilgrim Huian smoothed his robe and gown, took up an iron rod, and mounting a cloud departed the palace, going straight to the foot of the mountain. There he saw the Heaven-Net and Earth-Snare laid layer upon dense layer, the gate of every camp ringing its bells and crying its watchwords, the mountain hemmed round so tightly that not a drop of water could leak through. Huian halted and called out, "You sentinels at the camp gate, be so good as to pass on this word: I am Moksha, second prince of Heavenly King Li — Huian, chief disciple of Guanyin of the Southern Sea — come expressly to spy out the state of the war."

The spirit-soldiers of the Five Sacred Peaks within the camp passed the message inward through the gate of the headquarters. Presently the Star Spirits — Empty-Day Rat, Pleiades-Day Cock, Heart-Day Horse, and Room-Day Hare — carried his words to the central command tent. Heavenly King Li sent down his command flag, ordering the Heaven-Net and Earth-Snare opened to let him through. The east was just growing light as Huian followed the flag inside, where he saw the Four Heavenly Kings and Heavenly King Li, and bowed before them. When the bows were done, Heavenly King Li said, "My child, from what quarter have you come?"

Huian answered, "Your foolish son went with the Bodhisattva to attend the Peach Festival. The Bodhisattva, seeing the grand feast laid waste and the Jasper Pool deserted, led the immortals and your son to see the Jade Emperor. The Jade Emperor told us in full how my royal father and the rest had descended to the lower world to subdue the monstrous ape, and that a whole day had passed without report, the outcome unknown. So the Bodhisattva charged your son to come here and learn the truth of it."

Said Heavenly King Li, "Yesterday we arrived here, pitched our camp and set our palisades, and ordered the Nine Luminary Stars to challenge him. But this wretch worked his magic mightily, and the Nine Luminaries were all routed and fled back. Afterward we ourselves led out our troops, and the wretch too drew up his battle line. Our hundred thousand heavenly soldiers fought him in a great melee until evening, when he used a body-dividing trick to fight us off. And when we recalled the troops and made our count, we had captured only some wolves, vermin, tigers, and leopards — not so much as half a monstrous ape. Today he has not yet come out to fight."

Before he had finished speaking, someone came to report outside the headquarters gate: "The Great Sage is leading a band of ape-sprites and calling for battle out front!" The Four Heavenly Kings and Heavenly King Li and the prince were just conferring about sending out troops when Moksha said, "Royal father, your foolish son was charged by the Bodhisattva to come down and gather news, and she said that should I meet a battle I might lend a hand. Now, unworthy though I am, I beg leave to go and see what manner of Great Sage this is."

Said the Heavenly King, "My child, you have practiced cultivation these several years under the Bodhisattva; doubtless you too have some magic powers. But you must take the greatest care."

Brave prince! He whirled his iron rod two-handed, cinched up his embroidered tunic, leaped out the headquarters gate, and shouted aloud, "Which of you is the Great Sage Equal to Heaven?"

The Great Sage hefted his As-You-Will cudgel and answered, "Old Monkey is he. And who are you, that you dare so freely to ask after me?"

Said Moksha, "I am Moksha, second prince of Heavenly King Li, and now I serve before the jeweled throne of the Bodhisattva Guanyin as a disciple guarding the Faith; my religious name is Huian."

"Why have you left off your cultivation in the Southern Sea," said the Great Sage, "and come here to see me — for what?"

Moksha replied, "My master sent me to spy out the state of the war; and seeing you so rampant, I have come on purpose to capture you."

Said the Great Sage, "You dare to boast so big? Stay where you are, then, and taste old Monkey's cudgel!"

Moksha was not in the least afraid, and met him with his iron rod, blow for blow. The two of them, midway up the mountain and outside the headquarters gate, fought a splendid combat:

> Rod faced rod, yet the iron of each was unlike;
> arms clashed against arms, yet the men were not the same.
> One was the Great Sage, hailed as a Scattered Immortal of the Primal One;
> the other Guanyin's disciple, a true dragon of the prime essence.
> The wrought-iron rod, beaten under a thousand hammers,
> wielded by the spirit-might of the Six Ding and Six Jia gods;
> the As-You-Will cudgel, that once stilled the River of Heaven,
> the Sea-Calming divine treasure, mighty in its power.
> The two met as true and matched opponents,
> their passes and ripostes, coming and going, without end.
> This one's sinister-handed rod was savage past counting,
> coiling round the waist, swift as the wind;
> that one's clamping spear-strokes were never spent in vain,
> warding left, blocking right — how could they yield?
> On that side the banners flickered and flashed;
> on this side the war-drums thundered and boomed.
> Ten thousand heavenly generals ringed them about;
> a whole cavern of monstrous apes clustered in throngs.
> Weird mists and grieving clouds spread over the underworld;
> wolf-smoke and killing vapors shot toward the Heavenly Palace.
> Yesterday's melee was hard enough to bear;
> today's contention was fiercer still.
> Admirable the Monkey King's true prowess —
> Moksha was beaten again, and fled for his life.

The Great Sage and Huian fought some fifty or sixty rounds, until Huian's arms grew sore and numb and he could no longer hold the field. He made a feint, then turned and fled, beaten. The Great Sage too recalled his ape-soldiers and encamped outside the cavern gate. There at the camp gate of the Heavenly King, soldiers great and small received the prince, opened a broad path, and led him straight into the headquarters. Before the Four Heavenly Kings, the Pagoda-Bearer Li, and Nezha, panting and gasping, scarcely able to catch his breath, he said, "A mighty Great Sage! A mighty Great Sage! His magic powers are truly vast — your son cannot stand against him, and has come back beaten again!"

Heavenly King Li was alarmed at the sight, and at once ordered a memorial drawn up begging for aid. He dispatched the Mighty Magic Spirit King and Prince Moksha to ascend to Heaven and lay the matter before the throne.

The two dared not linger. They burst out through the Heaven-Net and Earth-Snare and rose upon auspicious vapors and propitious clouds. In a moment they came straight beneath the Hall of Penetrating Brightness, where they saw the Four Grand Preceptors, who led them to the Hall of Divine Mists, and they presented the memorial. Huian then paid his respects to the Bodhisattva, who asked, "How fared your spying?"

Huian answered, "When first I received the command and reached the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, I had the gate of the Heaven-Net and Earth-Snare opened, saw my father, and told him my master's purpose in sending me. My royal father said, 'Yesterday I fought one battle with that Monkey King, and captured only his tigers, leopards, lions, and elephants — not a single ape-sprite.' While we were still speaking, he came again to demand battle, and your disciple wielded an iron rod against him some fifty or sixty rounds, but could not prevail, and retreated to camp beaten. For this reason my father sent the Mighty Magic Spirit King together with your disciple to come to the upper realm and beg for help." The Bodhisattva bowed her head in thought.

Now the Jade Emperor had opened the memorial, and seeing the plea for aid, he laughed and said, "Insufferable! How great can this ape-sprite's powers be, that he dares stand against a hundred thousand heavenly soldiers? Heavenly King Li comes again begging for help — but which divine troops shall I send to aid him?" Before he had finished, Guanyin pressed her palms together and addressed the throne: "Let Your Majesty set his mind at ease. This humble nun will recommend a deity who can capture this ape."

"Whom do you recommend?" asked the Jade Emperor.

Said the Bodhisattva, "It is Your Majesty's own nephew, the True Lord Erlang of Manifest Sanctity, who now dwells at the Mouth of the Guan River in Guanzhou and enjoys the incense and worship of the lower world. In days past he slew six monsters by his strength; he has, moreover, his sworn brethren of Plum Mountain and the twelve hundred grass-headed spirits before his tent, and his magic powers are vast. But he answers only to summons, not to command. Let Your Majesty send down a decree of troop-mustering ordering him to lend his strength, and the ape may be taken."

When the Jade Emperor had heard this, he straightway issued the troop-mustering decree, and dispatched the Mighty Magic Spirit King to carry the summons.

The Spirit King, having received the decree, at once mounted a cloud and went straight to the Mouth of the Guan River; in less than half a watch he came directly to the True Lord's temple. The gate-guarding demon-judges hurried inside to report, "Outside there is a heavenly envoy, come bearing a decree." Erlang and his brethren came out the gate to receive it, burned incense, and read it aloud. The decree ran thus:

> The monstrous ape of the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, has made rebellion. Because he stole peaches, stole wine, and stole elixir within the palace, and threw the Grand Peach Festival into uproar, a hundred thousand heavenly soldiers and eighteen frames of Heaven-Net and Earth-Snare have hemmed the mountain to subdue him, yet have won no victory. We now expressly muster Our worthy nephew, together with his sworn brethren, to go at once to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit to lend their strength in the work of extermination. When the task is accomplished, there shall be high promotion and rich reward.

The True Lord rejoiced and said, "Heavenly envoy, you may return. I shall go at once and draw my blade to lend aid." The Spirit King went back to make his report — but of that no more.

The True Lord then summoned his six brethren of Plum Mountain — the four Marshals Kang, Zhang, Yao, and Li, and the two Generals Guo Shen and Zhi Jian — and gathered them before the hall, saying, "Just now the Jade Emperor has mustered us to go to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit to subdue a monstrous ape. Let us go together." His brethren were all glad to set out. They mustered their own spirit-soldiers, loosed the hawks and led the hounds, set their crossbows and drew their bows, and riding a furious gale crossed the Eastern Great Ocean in an instant, coming straight to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. Seeing the Heaven-Net and Earth-Snare laid layer upon dense layer so that they could go no farther, they called out, "Hark, you divine generals of the Heaven-Net and Earth-Snare: I am the True Lord Erlang of Manifest Sanctity, mustered by command of the Jade Emperor to capture the monstrous ape. Be quick to open your camp gate and let me pass." At once the deities passed the word inward, layer by layer. The Four Heavenly Kings and Heavenly King Li all came out the headquarters gate to receive him. When greetings were done and the matter of victory and defeat was raised, the Heavenly King laid out the whole affair from the beginning.

The True Lord laughed and said, "Since the Little Sage has come here, he must contend with him in transformations. Gentlemen, draw not the net over the top — keep it tight only on the four sides, and let me wager combat with him. If I lose to him, you need not aid me; I have my brethren to support me. And if I beat him, you need not bind him; I have my brethren to lay hands on him. I ask only that the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King hold up for me the demon-revealing mirror and stand in the air. Lest the wretch be beaten and flee elsewhere, you must shine it clear and bright for me, so that he does not escape." The Heavenly King took his post at the four quarters, and the heavenly soldiers all drew up in their ranks.

The True Lord, leading the four Marshals and two Generals — seven sworn brothers counting himself — came out of camp to give battle, ordering his other generals to guard the camp closely and keep the hawks and hounds in check. The grass-headed spirits received their orders. The True Lord came right up to the mouth of the Water-Curtain Cave, and there saw a band of apes drawn up neat and orderly in the formation of a coiling dragon. In the center of their host stood a single banner pole, and on it were written four words: GREAT SAGE EQUAL TO HEAVEN. Said the True Lord, "That foul monster — how dare he lay claim to a rank equal to Heaven?"

The six brethren of Plum Mountain said, "Spare your wonder, and go challenge him to battle."

When the little apes at the camp mouth saw the True Lord, they ran in haste to report it. The Monkey King at once drew out his gold-banded cudgel, set straight his golden armor, stepped into his cloud-walking shoes, settled his cap of purple gold, and sprang out the camp gate. With a sharp look he saw that the True Lord's features were indeed pure and rare, and his array fair and elegant. Truly:

> His bearing pure and noble, his face open and grand,
> two ears hanging to his shoulders, his eyes alight with fire.
> On his head a Three-Mountains flying-phoenix cap,
> his body clad in a robe of pale goose-yellow.
> Gold-threaded boots set off coiling-dragon stockings,
> a jade belt with rounded flowers, decked in the Eight Treasures.
> At his waist hung a pellet-bow shaped like the new moon,
> in his hand he gripped a three-pointed, double-edged spear.
> With an axe he once split Peach Mountain to rescue his mother;
> with a pellet he once felled twin phoenixes in the palm-grove.
> By his might he slew eight monsters, and his fame spread far;
> in sworn brotherhood he ranged with the Seven Sages of Plum Mountain.
> Lofty of heart, he disowned his kin in the house of Heaven;
> proud of nature, he returned to godhood and dwelt by the Guan River.
> The bright-souled holy one of Chicheng, manifest and merciful,
> his transformings without bound — and his name is Erlang.

When the Great Sage saw him, he lifted his gold-banded cudgel with a grin and shouted, "What petty general are you, that you dare so boldly come here to challenge me?"

The True Lord roared back, "You wretch, with eyes but no pupils — do you not know me? I am the Jade Emperor's nephew, the True Lord Erlang, by decree enfeoffed as King of Bright Mercy and Manifest Sanctity. By imperial command I have come to capture you — the Bimawen monkey who rebelled against the Heavenly Palace — and still you do not know whether you live or die!"

Said the Great Sage, "I recall how in years past the Jade Emperor's younger sister, yearning for the mortal world, came down to earth, mated with the lord Yang, and bore a son who split Peach Mountain with an axe — is that you? I'd half a mind to revile you a few times, but there is no quarrel between us; and I'd half a mind to give you a blow of my cudgel, but it would be a pity to spoil your young life. You young master, you stripling, hurry back and call out your Four Heavenly Kings for me!"

When the True Lord heard this, his heart blazed with fury. "Foul monkey! No more of your insolence — taste my blade!" The Great Sage dodged aside, swiftly raised his gold-banded cudgel, and returned the stroke blow for blow. The two of them fought a fine and deadly fight:

> The god of Bright Mercy, Erlang;
> the Great Sage of Heaven, Sun the Monkey.
> This one, high of heart, scorned his foe — the handsome Monkey King;
> that one, strange of face, would crush him down — a true pillar and beam.
> The two, meeting at first sight,
> each found his sport in the wager.
> Never before had they known the shallow from the deep;
> only today did they learn the light from the heavy.
> The iron rod rivaled a flying dragon;
> the divine blade was like a dancing phoenix.
> Warding left, attacking right;
> meeting in front, glancing behind.
> On that side the six brethren of Plum Mountain lent their ardor;
> on this side the four Generals of the Ma and Liu clans relayed commands.
> Banners waved and drums rolled, each side of one mind;
> war-cries and clanging gongs, all swelling the fervor.
> Their two keen blades watched for the opening,
> coming and going without a seam between.
> The gold-banded cudgel is a treasure of the sea,
> able through its transformings and soarings to win.
> Should the body but slow, life is forfeit;
> a single misstep, and all goes to ruin.

The True Lord and the Great Sage fought past three hundred rounds, and still the outcome was unknown. Then the True Lord roused his divine might: he gave his body a shake and transformed, growing to a height of ten thousand fathoms, his two hands lifting the three-pointed, double-edged divine blade. He was just like a peak atop Mount Hua — blue-faced, fanged, with hair of vermilion red — and savagely he hacked straight at the Great Sage's head. The Great Sage too worked his magic and transformed, making his body the very match of Erlang's, his face and features the same, and lifting his As-You-Will gold-banded cudgel like the Sky-Propping Pillar atop Mount Kunlun, he held the god Erlang off. So terrified were the Marshals Ma and Liu that they trembled and could not wave their banners; the Generals Beng and Ba quailed in fear and could not use their swords. On that side, Kang, Zhang, Yao, Li, Guo Shen, and Zhi Jian relayed the command and loosed the grass-headed spirits, who set the hawks and hounds upon the apes outside the Water-Curtain Cave, drew their crossbows and bent their bows, and fell on them all together in a slaughter. Pitiable! — they scattered the four valiant ape-commanders, and captured two or three thousand of the magic creatures. Those apes threw down their halberds and cast off their armor, dropped their swords and flung away their spears; the runners ran, the screamers screamed, those for the mountain made for the mountain, those for the cave returned to the cave — like night-owls startling birds at roost, scattering across the sky like a rain of stars. Of the brethren's victory we say no more.

Now while the True Lord and the Great Sage were locked in their heaven-spanning, earth-imaging combat, the Great Sage suddenly saw the apes of his own camp scattered in terror. His heart grew anxious of itself; he gathered in his magic form, hefted his cudgel, drew back his body, and turned to flee. The True Lord, seeing him flee defeated, strode after him in great steps, calling, "Where do you run? Surrender now, while you may, and I'll spare your life!" But the Great Sage clung to no further fighting and only ran with all his heart. As he neared the cave mouth, he ran headlong into the four Marshals Kang, Zhang, Yao, and Li and the two Generals Guo Shen and Zhi Jian, who all at once led their host to block him, crying, "Foul monkey! Where do you run?" The Great Sage lost his nerve. He pinched his gold-banded cudgel down to an embroidery needle and hid it in his ear, then gave his body a shake and changed into a sparrow, and flew up to perch fixed on a treetop. The six brethren, flustered and bewildered, hunted high and low and could not find him, and all together set up a shout: "The ape-sprite has got away! The ape-sprite has got away!"

While they were still clamoring, the True Lord arrived and asked, "Brothers, you chased him to this spot — where did he vanish?"

The deities said, "We had him surrounded here, and then he was gone." Erlang opened wide his phoenix eyes and looked about, and saw the Great Sage changed into a sparrow, perched on the tree. He drew in his magic form, set aside his divine blade, slipped off his pellet-bow, gave his body a shake, and changed into a hawk-falcon; shaking out his wings, he flew up to strike. The Great Sage saw him, and with a whir flew off, changing into a great cormorant that soared into the sky. Seeing this, Erlang quickly ruffled his feathers, shook his body, and changed into a great sea-crane, piercing up to the clouds to snap at him. The Great Sage then lowered his body, dropped into a ravine stream, and changed into a fish, plunging into the water. Erlang chased to the streamside but saw no trace, and thought to himself, "That ape has surely gone into the water, and changed into some fish or shrimp. Let me change again and catch him." So he changed into a fish-hawk, drifting on the wave-surface at the lower reach of the stream, and waited a while. The Great Sage, changed into a fish, was swimming with the current when suddenly he spied a bird in flight — like a blue falcon, but the feathers were not blue; like an egret, but with no plume on its crown; like an old stork, but the legs were not red. "That," he thought, "must be Erlang changed and lying in wait for me!" He quickly turned, splashed up a little flurry, and swam off. Erlang saw it and said, "That fish that splashed — like a carp, but its tail is not red; like a mandarin-fish, but I see no patterned scales; like a snakehead, but no stars on its head; like a bream, but no spine on its gills. Why did it turn back the moment it saw me? It must surely be that monkey transformed." He swooped up and pecked at it — but the Great Sage darted out of the water, changed, and became a water-snake, swimming to the bank and wriggling into the grass. Erlang, having missed his peck, saw in the splashing water a snake dart out, and knew it for the Great Sage. He turned swiftly and changed again, into a vermilion-crested grey crane, stretching out a long beak like a pair of sharp-pointed iron pincers, and came straight to devour the water-snake. The snake gave a hop and changed once more, into a spotted bustard, standing dull and stupid upon a sandbar amid the smartweed. Erlang, seeing him changed into so base a thing — for the bustard is the lowest and lewdest of birds, mating without distinction with phoenix, hawk, or crow alike — would not go near it. He resumed his true form, walked over, took up his pellet-bow, drew it full, and with one pellet sent the bustard tumbling head over heels.

The Great Sage, seizing the chance, rolled down the mountain cliff, lay low there, and changed again, into a little temple of the local god. His wide-open mouth was the temple gate; his teeth became the door-leaves; his tongue became the bodhisattva within; his eyes became the latticed windows. Only his tail was awkward to dispose of, so he stood it up behind and made it into a flag pole. The True Lord chased down to the foot of the cliff, but did not see the bustard he had felled — only a small temple. Sharply he opened his phoenix eyes and examined it closely, and seeing the flag pole standing up behind, he laughed and said, "It is that monkey! Now he means to fool me again. I have seen temples before, but never one with a flag pole standing up behind it. This is surely that beast playing tricks. If he means to lure me inside, he'll bite me with one snap of his mouth. Why should I go in? Let me first smash the windows with my fist, then kick down the doors." The Great Sage heard him and was alarmed in his heart: "How vicious! How vicious! The doors are my teeth, the windows are my eyes — if he breaks my teeth and smashes my eyes, what then?" With a tiger's leap he sprang up and vanished again into the air.

The True Lord chased about, front and back, when up came the four Marshals and two Generals all together, asking, "Elder brother, have you caught the Great Sage?"

The True Lord laughed and said, "That monkey just now changed into a temple to fool me. I was about to smash his windows and kick his doors when he gave a spring and vanished without a trace again. How strange! How strange!" They were all astonished, and looked in every direction, but there was no shadow of him. Said the True Lord, "Brothers, keep watch and patrol here. Let me go up to seek him." Swiftly he sprang up and rode a cloud, rising into mid-air. There he saw Heavenly King Li holding high the demon-revealing mirror, with Nezha standing at his side at the cloud's edge. Said the True Lord, "Heavenly King, have you seen the Monkey King?"

The Heavenly King said, "He has not come up here. I have him shining in the mirror." The True Lord told him the whole tale — the wager of transformations, the working of magic, the rout of the apes — then added, "He changed into a temple, and just as I was about to strike, he got away." Hearing this, Heavenly King Li shone the demon-revealing mirror about the four quarters, then laughed aloud and said, "True Lord, be quick, be quick! That monkey has used a body-concealing trick to slip out of the camp ring and has gone off to your own Mouth of the Guan River." Hearing this, Erlang took up his divine blade and turned back toward the Mouth of the Guan River in pursuit.

Now the Great Sage had already reached the Mouth of the Guan River. He gave his body a shake and changed into the very likeness of the lord Erlang, lowered his cloud-head, and went straight into the temple. The demon-judges could not tell the difference, and one and all kowtowed to receive him. He sat in the central seat and inspected the offerings: there were the three beasts that Li Hu had vowed in thanks, the prayers for blessing that Zhang Long had pledged, the petition of Zhao Jia praying for a son, the votive plea of Qian Bing reporting his illness. While he was looking them over, someone came to report, "Another lord has come!" The demon-judges hurried to look, and not one but was struck with alarm. The True Lord said, "Has there been any so-called Great Sage Equal to Heaven here just now?"

The demon-judges said, "We have seen no Great Sage — there is only one lord inside, going over the offerings."

The True Lord rushed in the door, and the Great Sage, seeing him, showed his true form and said, "Young master, save your shouting — the temple is named Sun now!" The True Lord at once lifted his three-pointed, double-edged divine blade and hacked straight at his face. The Monkey King used a deft body-trick to let the blade pass, drew out his embroidery needle, gave it a shake until it was as thick as a bowl, rushed forward, and returned the stroke face to face. The two, clamoring and brawling, fought their way out the temple gate; half in mist, half in cloud, fighting as they went, they battled all the way back to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. The Four Heavenly Kings and the rest were thrown into alarm and tightened their guard the more. The Marshals Kang and Zhang and the others met the True Lord, and joining their strength with one heart, ringed the Handsome Monkey King round — but of that no more.

The tale tells how the Mighty Magic Spirit King, having mustered the True Lord and his six brethren to lead their troops off to capture the demon, then ascended to the upper realm to report. The Jade Emperor, with the Bodhisattva Guanyin, the Queen Mother, and the assembled immortal ministers, were just then talking in the Hall of Divine Mists. Said the Emperor, "Since Erlang has already gone to give battle, why has a whole day passed with no report?"

Guanyin pressed her palms together and said, "Let this humble nun ask Your Majesty to go with the Patriarch of the Way beyond the Southern Heaven Gate and see for yourselves how the matter truly stands." Said the Jade Emperor, "Reasonably spoken." At once he ordered his carriage made ready, and together with the Patriarch Lao Zi, Guanyin, the Queen Mother, and the immortal ministers, came to the Southern Heaven Gate. Heavenly soldiers and strong men received them, opened the gate, and they gazed afar. They saw the heavenly soldiers spreading their net, hemming in all four sides; Heavenly King Li and Nezha holding up the demon-revealing mirror, standing in the air; and the True Lord with the Great Sage ringed in the midst, locked in furious combat.

The Bodhisattva opened her mouth and said to Lao Zi, "How fares the Erlang I recommended? Truly he has magic powers — he has already hemmed the Great Sage in, only he has not yet captured him. Let me now lend a hand, and I'll surely take him." Said Lao Zi, "What weapon would the Bodhisattva use? How will you aid him?"

Said the Bodhisattva, "I will cast down my pure vase of willow to strike the monkey's head; even if it does not kill him, it will knock him sprawling, so that the Little Sage Erlang may easily take him." Said Lao Zi, "That vase of yours is porcelain. Well enough if it strikes him; but if it misses his head, or fells on his iron rod, would it not shatter to bits? Stay your hand — let old Lao Zi lend the aid instead."

"What weapon do you have?" asked the Bodhisattva.

Lao Zi said, "I have, I have, I have." Rolling up his sleeve, he took from his left forearm a ring, and said, "This weapon is forged of kun-steel, refined and quickened by my Reverting Elixir until it nurtured a spirit-energy through and through. It excels at transformation, neither water nor fire can harm it, and it can lasso any thing. One name for it is the Diamond Snare; another, the Diamond Bracelet. In the old days, when I passed the Hangu Pass and 'converted the barbarians into Buddhas,' I owed much to it. Morning and night it is the best of guards for the person. Let me cast it down and give him a stroke."

When he had spoken, from atop the Heaven Gate he flung it down. Whirling and dropping, it fell straight into the camp on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, and landed square upon the Monkey King's head. The Monkey King, all his mind bent on the bitter fight against the Seven Sages, never knew that a weapon had dropped from the heavens, and it struck him on the crown. He could not keep his footing and went down in a tumble; but he scrambled up and ran. Then the slender hound of the lord Erlang overtook him, and with one bite at his calf dragged him down in another fall. He lay sprawled upon the ground, cursing, "You wretched cur! Why do you not go plague your own master, but come to bite old Monkey instead!" He twisted hastily to rise but could not, and the Seven Sages swarmed in and pinned him down. They bound him fast with cords, and ran a hooked blade through his pipa-bone collar so that he could transform no more.

Then Lao Zi recovered his Diamond Snare, and asked the Jade Emperor, Guanyin, the Queen Mother, and the assembled immortals to return with him to the Hall of Divine Mists. Below, the Four Heavenly Kings, Heavenly King Li, and all the deities recalled their troops and struck their camps, and came forward to congratulate the Little Sage, all saying, "This is the Little Sage's achievement!"

Said the Little Sage, "This is the vast blessing of the Heavenly Honored One and the awesome authority of all you deities — what achievement is mine?" Kang, Zhang, Yao, and Li said, "Elder brother, no more of such talk. Let us march this wretch up to the upper realm to see the Jade Emperor, and beg a decree for his sentence."

Said the True Lord, "Worthy brothers, you have not yet received the heavenly registers, and may not appear before the Jade Emperor. Let the armored spirit-soldiers escort him, while I go up with the Heavenly King and the rest to report the decree fulfilled. You lead the host here and search the mountain; when it is swept clean, return to the Mouth of the Guan River. When I have claimed my reward and reckoned my merit, I'll come back and we shall make merry together." The four Marshals and two Generals assented and obeyed. Then the True Lord and the others mounted their cloud-heads and, singing songs of triumph, returned victorious to Heaven. In a little while they reached the gate of the Hall of Penetrating Brightness. The Grand Preceptor announced, "The Four Heavenly Kings and the rest have captured the monstrous ape, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, and have come to await your summons." The Jade Emperor handed down a decree, ordering the Mighty Magic Spirit King and the heavenly soldiers to march the wretch to the Monster-Slaying Terrace and there hack his corpse to mincemeat. Ah! Truly it is said:

> For deceit and cunning he now meets the bitter rigor of the law;
> the hero's lofty spirit is brought, for the time, to an end.

And in the end, knowing not how the Monkey King's life would fare — listen to the next chapter told.

<!-- chapter 7 -->
# Chapter 7: The Great Sage Escapes the Eight-Trigrams Furnace, and the Mind-Monkey Is Pinned Beneath the Mountain of Five Phases

Riches, rank, fame, and merit are all portioned out by destiny's earlier ties — so let no man ever cheat his own heart. Walk upright and shining-clear, for loyalty and goodness ripen into ever-deeper fruit. The least breath of arrogance draws Heaven's rebuke, and the moment of reckoning, though slow to come, is sure to arrive. Ask the Lord of Spring: why should calamity now press in so close? Only because a heart climbing too high reached for the boundless, refusing to know high from low, throwing all good counsel into ruin.

Our tale turns to the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, hauled away by the hosts of Heaven to the foot of the Demon-Slaying Platform and bound fast to the Pillar of Subduing Monsters. They hacked at him with swords, chopped at him with axes, stabbed him with spears and gouged him with blades — yet not one stroke could so much as scratch his skin. The Star Lord of the Southern Dipper ordered the gods of the Fire Department to set him ablaze and roast him, but the flames would not take hold. Then the gods of the Thunder Department were called to drive their thunder-bolts into him, and still less could they harm a single hair.

The mighty Demon King and the others reported, "Your Majesty, this Great Sage — we know not where he learned this art of guarding his body. We hewed at him with sword and axe, scorched him with fire and battered him with thunder, and could not damage him in the slightest. What is to be done?"

The Jade Emperor heard this and said, "A creature like this — like this! — how are we to deal with him?"

At once the Most High Lord Lao Zi stepped forward to memorialize: "That monkey ate the peaches of immortality, drank the imperial wine, and stole the elixir besides. My five gourds of cinnabar, both the raw and the refined, he gulped down whole into his belly. There, by the working of his samadhi-fire, they have fused into a single mass, so that his whole frame has become a body of adamantine gold — it cannot easily be wounded. It would be best to let me, old Daoist, take him away and set him within my Eight-Trigrams Furnace. With civil and martial fires I shall smelt him — and when my elixir is drawn out of him, his body will of itself be reduced to ashes."

Hearing this, the Jade Emperor commanded the Six Ding and Six Jia spirits to loose him from the pillar and hand him over to Lord Lao. Lord Lao received the decree and departed.

Meanwhile the court summoned Erlang, the Illustrious Sage, and bestowed on him a hundred golden flowers, a hundred bottles of imperial wine, a hundred grains of restorative elixir, rare treasures, bright pearls, brocades and embroideries, bidding him share these with his sworn brothers. The True Lord gave thanks for the favor and returned to the mouth of the Guan River — but of that we say no more.

Lord Lao came to his Tushita Palace, unbound the Great Sage's ropes, withdrew the hook that had been thrust through his collarbone, and pushed him into the Eight-Trigrams Furnace. He charged the Daoist who tended the furnace and the boys who fanned the fire to raise the flames and begin the smelting. Now this furnace was divided according to the eight trigrams — Qian, Kan, Gen, Zhen, Xun, Li, Kun, and Dui. The Great Sage promptly squeezed himself down into the quarter of Xun. Xun is the trigram of wind, and where there is wind there is no fire. But the wind whipped the smoke about, and it so reddened both his eyes that they became sore and inflamed forever after — and from this came his famous "fiery eyes and golden pupils."

Truly time flies swiftly, and before anyone knew it the full forty-nine days — seven times seven — had passed, and Lord Lao's smelting was complete. One day the furnace was opened to take out the elixir. The Great Sage was just then covering his eyes with both hands, rubbing them and weeping, when he heard a clatter at the furnace head. He blinked, saw the daylight, and could bear it no longer — with a single bound he leaped clear of the furnace. With a thunderous crash he kicked the Eight-Trigrams Furnace over and made for the door.
