The fire-boys, the furnace-keepers, and the Ding-Jia guards came rushing to grab him, but he knocked them down one after another, like a white-browed tiger in a fit of madness, like a single-horned dragon driven wild by the wind. Lord Lao lunged and made one grab at him, but the Sage gave him a twist that sent him tumbling head-over-heels, and so broke free.

Then from his ear he drew out the As-You-Will cudgel. He waved it once into the wind and it grew thick as a bowl, and he gripped it in his hand again. Caring nothing for good or ill, he ran riot once more through the Halls of Heaven, beating until the Nine Luminary Stars shut their doors and bolted them fast, and the Four Heavenly Kings vanished without a trace. A fine monkey-spirit! There are verses to prove it:

*His primal substance, true and whole, accords with the prime of Heaven;*
*through ten thousand kalpas, a thousand turns, it remains but Nature itself.*
*Boundless, dim, in non-action — utterly the Great One;*
*serene, unmoving, thus and so — he is named the First Mystery.*
*Long smelted in the furnace, yet no mere lead and mercury;*
*beyond all things, deathless — he is the original immortal.*
*Endlessly he transforms, and transforms again past counting —*
*of the Three Refuges and Five Precepts let nothing more be said.*

And again:

*One point of numinous light pierces the Great Void;*
*so too is that staff of his.*
*Now long, now short, as the wielder wills,*
*crosswise or upright, ranged at random, rolled out or rolled up at his pleasure.*

And again:

*The ape's body, in the Way, is matched to the human mind;*
*the mind is the very ape — the meaning runs deep.*
*"Great Sage Equal to Heaven" — no idle boast,*
*yet the office of "Keeper of Horses" — how could it know his worth?*
*Let horse and ape work as one, mind and will in accord,*
*bound tight and tethered fast — seek them not outside yourself.*
*All forms return to the True from a single principle;*
*and the Tathagata, sharing that bond, dwells in the Twin-Tree Grove.*

This time the Monkey King recognized neither high nor low. With his iron rod he struck east and parried west, and there was not a single god who could withstand him. He fought his way at last into the Hall of Penetrating Brightness, right up to the doors of the Hall of Numinous Mists. Happily there stood on guard Wang Lingguan, the lieutenant of the True Lord Protector of the Sages. Seeing the Great Sage rampaging freely, he raised his golden whip and pressed forward to bar the way, crying, "Reckless monkey, where do you think you are going? I am here — do not run wild!" The Great Sage, without a word of argument, lifted his cudgel and struck, and Lingguan met him with the whip. The two of them grappled together before the Hall of Numinous Mists — a marvelous fight:

*One, of crimson loyalty and good faith, his fame is great;*
*one, who flouts Heaven and deceives his lord, his name is ruined.*
*The low against the worthy — happily they hold their ground;*
*hero against champion, locked in the same wager.*
*The iron rod is fierce, the golden whip is swift;*
*upright and selfless — how could he endure such insolence?*
*This one is the Reverend One of the Great Unity, the Thunder-Voice made manifest;*
*that one is the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, the monkey-monster.*
*Golden whip and iron rod, both houses skilled,*
*and both are the holy weapons of the immortal palaces.*
*This day before the Treasure Hall of Numinous Mists they flaunt their power,*
*each displaying his prowess — truly a thing to admire.*
*One, with a cheating heart, would seize the Palace of the Dipper and the Ox;*
*one, with all his strength, would uphold the realm of the Mysterious Sages.*
*Bitterly they strive, neither yielding, showing their divine arts —*
*whip and rod going back and forth, with neither winner nor loser.*

The two of them battled together with no decision in sight. Soon the True Lord Protector of the Sages dispatched his officers to send word to the Thunder Bureau, calling out the full Thirty-Six Thunder Generals to come at once. They surrounded the Great Sage in their midst, and each, fierce and savage, joined the desperate fray. Yet the Great Sage showed not a flicker of fear. Wielding his one As-You-Will cudgel, he shielded left and warded right, blocking behind and meeting in front. When he saw the press of the Thunder Generals' swords and spears, blades and halberds, whips and maces, hammers and bludgeons, battle-axes and golden melon-maces, banners, sickles, and moon-shaped shovels coming on hard, he gave his body a shake and transformed: he grew three heads and six arms. He waved the As-You-Will cudgel and it became three cudgels; with his six hands he plied the three of them, whirling like a spinning-wheel, round and round, dancing through the heart of the encirclement. None of the Thunder Gods could come near. Truly:

*Round and perfect, blazing with light,*
*it has endured since time began — how could men learn it?*
*Cast into fire, it cannot be burned;*
*plunged into water, when was it ever drowned?*
*A single shining mani-pearl,*
*untouched by sword or halberd, blade or spear.*
*It can be good, it can be evil;*
*good and evil, here and now, are his to do.*
*In goodness, he becomes a Buddha or an immortal;*
*in evil, he wears fur and bears horns.*
*With boundless transformations he troubled the Halls of Heaven —*
*the Thunder Generals and divine soldiers could not lay hold of him.*

So the gods pressed the Great Sage into one spot, yet could not get at his body, and there was nothing but a din of shouting and clashing. Word of it soon startled the Jade Emperor, who issued a decree sending the Roving Inspector Lingguan together with the True Lord Assisting the Sages westward, to beg the Ancient Buddha to come and subdue him.

The two sages, having received the decree, went straight to the holy realm of Spirit Mountain, before the precious temple of the Thunderclap. There they paid their respects to the Four Vajra Guardians and the Eight Bodhisattvas, then asked that their errand be conveyed within. The gods went up before the Precious Lotus Throne and made it known, and the Tathagata summoned them in. The two sages circled the Buddha three times in reverence and stood in attendance below the throne.

The Tathagata asked, "What matter has brought the two sages down here to trouble themselves?"

The two sages reported: "Some time ago, on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, a monkey was born who there worked his divine arts, gathered the monkey-hordes about him, and threw the world into confusion. The Jade Emperor sent down a decree of amnesty and appointed him Keeper of the Imperial Horses, but he scorned the office as too low and rebelled away. Li, the Heavenly King, and the Prince Nezha were sent to seize him and failed. He was offered amnesty again and made 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven' — a title with rank but no stipend. He was put in charge of the Garden of Immortal Peaches, whereupon he stole the peaches; then he went to the Jasper Pool and stole the viands and the wine and wrecked the great festival; emboldened by drink he slipped secretly into the Tushita Palace and stole Lord Lao's elixir, then broke out of Heaven. The Jade Emperor sent a hundred thousand heavenly soldiers, and still they could not subdue him. Then Guanyin recommended Erlang the True Lord, who with his sworn brothers pursued and fought him. The monkey changed shape in a thousand ways, but thanks to Lord Lao's flung diamond snare striking him down, Erlang was at last able to take him. He was brought before the throne and ordered executed, but sword and axe, fire and thunder could not harm him. Lord Lao obtained leave to take him away and smelt him with fire. After forty-nine days the cauldron was opened — and he leaped out of the Eight-Trigrams Furnace, beat back the heavenly guards, and pushed straight into the Hall of Penetrating Brightness, to the very doors of the Hall of Numinous Mists. There Wang Lingguan, lieutenant of the True Lord Protector of the Sages, barred his way in bitter combat, and the Thirty-Six Thunder Generals were called to hem him in — yet none could come near him. The matter is urgent, and so the Jade Emperor expressly entreats the Tathagata to come and rescue the throne."

When the Tathagata had heard this, he said to the assembled bodhisattvas, "All of you stay seated here in the Hall of the Law. Disturb not your meditation-seats. I shall go to subdue the demon and rescue the throne."

The Tathagata then called the two honored disciples Ananda and Kasyapa to accompany him, left the Thunderclap, and went straight to the gate of the Hall of Numinous Mists. Suddenly he heard shouts that shook the ear — it was the Thirty-Six Thunder Generals hemming in the Great Sage. The Buddha-Patriarch gave his sacred command: "Let the Thunder Generals lay down their weapons and open their ranks. Call that Great Sage out, and let me ask what powers he has." The generals duly withdrew. The Great Sage too put away his magic forms, resumed his true shape, and came forward, his anger blazing, and bellowed in a stern voice, "What manner of holy man are you, that you dare come to stop the fighting and question me?"

The Tathagata smiled and said, "I am Sakyamuni, the Honored One of the Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss. Namo Amitabha! I have heard that you, a wild and reckless rustic, have time and again rebelled against the Halls of Heaven. I do not know where you were born, in what year you attained the Way, or why you are so violent and overbearing."

The Great Sage said, "I am one who—

*Was born of Heaven and Earth, a numinous, primal immortal,*
*an old ape upon the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit.*
*In the Water-Curtain Cave I made my home and estate;*
*I sought out friends and masters and awoke to the Great Mystery.*
*I refined the arts of long life past all counting,*
*and learned transformations boundless and beyond all bounds.*
*Because the mortal world felt cramped and narrow to me,*
*I set my mind firmly on dwelling in the Jasper Heaven.*
*The Treasure Hall of Numinous Mists shall not be his for long —*
*through the ages, even mortal kings hand the throne about in turn.*
*The strong should be honored; the seat should yield to me;*
*the hero alone dares step forth to claim the foremost place.*"

The Buddha-Patriarch heard him and laughed a cold laugh: "Ha! You are nothing but a monkey turned spirit, and yet you dare to be so brazen — to seek the venerated seat of the Jade Emperor, the Supreme Lord! From his youth he cultivated the Way, enduring one thousand seven hundred and fifty kalpas. Each kalpa is a hundred and twenty-nine thousand six hundred years — reckon how many years that is before one may enjoy this boundless Great Way! And you, a beast newly come into your first life as a being of intelligence — how dare you speak so grandly? Shameful! Shameful! You are cutting short your own allotted span. Submit and take refuge at once, and talk no more nonsense — for I fear you may meet a cruel hand, and your very life be snuffed out in an instant. What a pity that would be for your original true face."

The Great Sage said, "Young or old in cultivation, he should not occupy that seat forever. As the saying goes, 'The emperorship is taken in turns — next year it comes to my house.' Let him only move out and yield the Halls of Heaven to me, and the matter is settled. But if he will not yield, I shall keep up the uproar, and there will never be peace."

The Buddha-Patriarch said, "Besides your arts of long life and transformation, what other powers have you, that you dare to seize the holy realm of Heaven?"

The Great Sage said, "My talents are many indeed! I have the seventy-two transformations and a life that does not age through ten thousand kalpas. I can ride the somersault cloud, and with one leap go a hundred and eight thousand leagues. Why should I not sit upon the throne of Heaven?"

The Buddha-Patriarch said, "Let me make a wager with you. If you have the skill to use one somersault to leap clear of the palm of my right hand, you win; and then, with no more need of swords and spears or bitter fighting, I shall ask the Jade Emperor to go and dwell in the West and yield the Halls of Heaven to you. But if you cannot leap out of my palm, then go back down to the lower world to be a monster, cultivate yourself for a few more kalpas, and come quarrel again."

When the Great Sage heard this, he laughed to himself: "This Tathagata is a thorough fool! With one somersault I, old Sun, go a hundred and eight thousand leagues — and his palm is not even a foot across. How could I fail to jump out of it?" Eagerly he spoke up: "Since you say so — can you make good on it?"

The Buddha-Patriarch said, "I can, I can." He stretched out his right hand, and it was about the size of a lotus leaf.

The Great Sage put away his As-You-Will cudgel, summoned his divine might, and with one bound stood in the center of the Buddha's palm. Then he called out, "I'm off!" Watch him — a streak of cloud-light, formless and shadowless, gone in an instant. The Buddha-Patriarch watched with his eye of wisdom and saw the Monkey King whirling on like a pinwheel, pressing ever forward.

As the Great Sage went on, he suddenly saw five flesh-colored pillars propping up a band of blue-green vapor. He said, "This must be the end of the road. When I go back now, with the Tathagata as witness, the Hall of Numinous Mists is surely mine to sit in." Then he thought again: "Wait — let me leave some mark here, so I'll have proof when I speak to the Tathagata." He plucked out a hair, blew on it a breath of immortal energy, and cried, "Change!" It became a brush thick with ink, and on the middle pillar he wrote in large characters a line: "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven was here." When he had finished, he took back the hair. Then, with no reverence at all, at the foot of the first pillar he let fly a puddle of monkey-piss. He flipped his somersault cloud about and went straight back to where he had started, stood in the Tathagata's palm, and said, "I went, and now I've come back. Tell the Jade Emperor to yield the Halls of Heaven to me."

The Tathagata cursed him: "You piss-spirit of a monkey! You never even left the palm of my hand."

The Great Sage said, "You don't know! I went to the very end of Heaven and saw five flesh-colored pillars propping up a band of blue-green vapor. I left a mark there — do you dare go with me and look?"

The Tathagata said, "No need to go. Just lower your head and look for yourself."

The Great Sage opened wide his fiery eyes and golden pupils, lowered his head, and looked — and there, on the middle finger of the Buddha-Patriarch's right hand, was written, "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven was here." And in the cleft of the thumb there still lingered the rank smell of monkey-piss. The Great Sage was startled and said, "Can such a thing be? Can such a thing be? I wrote those words on a pillar that props up the sky — how can they be on his finger? Surely he has some art of foreknowledge. I won't believe it — I won't! Let me go again and see."

Brave Great Sage! In haste he gathered himself for another leap. But the Buddha-Patriarch turned his palm over and gave him a single push, shoving the Monkey King out beyond the western gate of Heaven. He transformed his five fingers into the five elements — Metal, Wood, Water, Fire, and Earth — joined into five linked peaks, which he named the Mountain of Five Phases, and gently he pressed the Great Sage down beneath them. The Thunder Gods, with Ananda and Kasyapa, all pressed their palms together in praise and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!

*In that year, hatched from an egg, he learned to be a man;*
*he fixed his will on cultivation and won the true fruit of the Way.*
*Through ten thousand kalpas, unmoving, he dwelt in the holy realm;*
*but in one day he changed, and his vital spirit was scattered.*
*Flouting Heaven, deceiving his lord, he coveted the high seat;*
*affronting the sages, stealing the elixir, he overthrew the great order.*
*Now that his cup of evil is brimful, the reckoning has come —*
*and who knows on what day he may turn his body free again."*

Having destroyed the demon-monkey, the Buddha-Patriarch called Ananda and Kasyapa to return with him to the Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss. Just then the Heavenly Marshal of the Canopy and the Heavenly Protector hurried out of the Hall of Numinous Mists and said, "We beg the Tathagata to wait a little — our sovereign's great chariot is coming." Hearing this, the Buddha-Patriarch turned and gazed upward.

In a moment there appeared a phoenix-carriage of the eight scenes, a canopy of nine lights, with the sound of mystic songs and wondrous music, the chanting of measureless divine scriptures, scattering jeweled flowers and spreading true incense. It came right up before the Buddha, and the Jade Emperor gave thanks, saying, "We owe it to your great Law that this demon-fiend has been subdued and destroyed. We beg the Tathagata to tarry but one day, that we may invite all the immortals to hold a feast of thanksgiving."

The Tathagata dared not refuse, and pressing his palms together he said in thanks, "This old monk came here only at the bidding of the Great Heavenly Honored One — what power of mine was it? It was the boundless blessing of the Heavenly Honored One and all the gods. How dare I trouble you with thanks?"

The Jade Emperor then issued his decree, sending the gods of the Thunder Department to go in all directions and invite the Three Pure Ones, the Four Imperial Lords, the Five Elders, the Six Ministries, the Seven Primes, the Eight Poles, the Nine Luminaries, the Ten Capitals, the Thousand True Ones and the Myriad Sages, all to come to the feast and together give thanks for the Buddha's grace. He further commanded the Four Great Heavenly Teachers and the Nine Heavenly Maidens to throw wide the Golden Towers of the Jade Capital, the Treasure Palace of Supreme Mystery, and the Jade Hall of the Cavern of Yang, to invite the Tathagata to take the high seat upon a Numinous Dais of seven treasures, and to set out the ranked places, arranging dragon-livers and phoenix-marrow, jade nectar and immortal peaches.

In no time at all came the Heavenly Honored One of Jade Purity, the Primordial Beginning; the Heavenly Honored One of Upper Purity, the Numinous Treasure; the Heavenly Honored One of Grand Purity, the Way and Its Power; the True Lords of the Five Influences, the Star Lords of the Five Dippers, the Three Officers and the Four Sages, the True Lords of the Nine Luminaries, the Left Assistant and the Right Supporter, the Heavenly Kings and Nezha — every numinous and far-reaching power, in paired banners and twin canopies, all bearing bright pearls and rare treasures, longevity-fruits and wondrous flowers. They bowed before the Buddha and presented their gifts, saying, "We are grateful to the Tathagata's measureless power of the Law for subduing the demon-monkey. By the grace of the Great Heavenly Honored One a feast is laid, and we have all been called here to offer our thanks. Will the Tathagata bestow a name upon this gathering?"

The Tathagata, accepting the gods' request, said, "If a name is to be given, let it be called the Assembly for the Peace of Heaven." With one voice the immortals and elders all cried, "A fine 'Assembly for the Peace of Heaven'! A fine 'Assembly for the Peace of Heaven'!" So saying, each took his seat, and the goblets went round and the wine-cups passed. They wore flowers in their hair, struck the zithers — truly a splendid gathering. There are verses to prove it:

*A feast was set with immortal peaches — the monkey threw it into chaos;*
*the Assembly for the Peace of Heaven surpasses the Peach Feast itself.*
*Dragon-banners and phoenix-chariots, auspicious light glowing soft;*
*jeweled standards and pennoned canopies, lucky vapors drifting high.*
*Immortal music and mystic songs, their tones and rhythms sweet;*
*phoenix flutes and jade pipes ringing loud and high.*
*Fragrant jasper-incense curling, the throng of immortals gathered —*
*the cosmos clear and at peace, hailing the holy court.*

While all rejoiced in the happy gathering, behold — the Queen Mother of the West led in a troupe of immortal maidens, fairy girls, lovely consorts and beautiful women, who came floating and swaying in dance before the Buddha. Bowing, she said, "Lately the demon-monkey threw my Peach Feast into disorder, so that the gathering of immortals and Buddhas could not be completed. Now, by the Tathagata's great Law, that stubborn monkey has been smelted and chained, and we celebrate the joyous Assembly for the Peace of Heaven. Having nothing else to offer in thanks, I have with my own clean hands plucked several great peaches of immortality from the largest tree, to present to you." Truly:

*Half red, half green, breathing a sweet fragrance,*
*these glorious immortal roots that endure ten thousand ages.*
*Laughable are the seedlings sown at Wuling's spring-source —*
*how could they vie with the rarer, mightier fruit of the Heavenly Court?*
*Purple-veined, tender and delicate, few in all the world;*
*pale-kerneled, clear and sweet, with no match under heaven.*
*They lengthen life, extend the years, and can transform the body —*
*and one who is fated to eat them becomes a being beyond the ordinary.*

The Buddha-Patriarch joined his palms and gave thanks to the Queen Mother. She then bade the immortal maidens and fairy girls sing and dance, and the whole assembly of immortals praised them in admiration. Indeed:

*Faint, ethereal heavenly fragrance fills every seat;*
*riotous immortal blossoms and fairy flowers.*
*In the Golden Towers of the Jade Capital, glory beyond measure;*
*rare wares and wondrous treasures of priceless worth.*
*Pair upon pair, long-lived as Heaven itself;*
*couple upon couple, gaining ten thousand kalpas more.*
*Let the mulberry-fields and the blue seas change as they will —*
*they themselves know neither alarm nor amazement.*

While the Queen Mother had the immortal maidens singing and dancing, and the goblets and tallies passed back and forth, before long there came once more—

*A gust of strange fragrance reached every nose,*
*startling all the stars and constellations in the hall.*
*Heaven's immortals and the Buddha-Patriarch set down their cups;*
*each raised his head and gazed in welcome.*
*In the midst of the empyrean appeared an old man,*
*bearing in his hands the numinous fungus, soaring amid embroidered mists.*
*His gourd held hidden a ten-thousand-year elixir;*
*his treasured register inscribed a thousand-cycle span of life.*
*Within his cave, heaven and earth are his to roam at will;*
*in his gourd, sun and moon ripen at his pleasure.*
*Wandering the Four Seas, he delights in quiet leisure;*
*free and easy through the Ten Isles, he draws all together.*
*Many a time at the Peach Feast he has come and grown tipsy;*
*and waking, found the bright moon still as it was before.*
*Long of head and large of ear, short of body —*
*the South Pole's own, he is called the Old Star of Long Life.*

The Star of Longevity had arrived. Having paid his respects to the Jade Emperor, he turned also to the Tathagata and gave thanks, saying, "When I first heard that the demon-monkey had been led by Lord Lao to the Tushita Palace and smelted there, I thought peace was assured — never expecting that he would break out again. Happily the Tathagata has well subdued this fiend, and a feast of thanks has been laid; therefore, hearing the wind of it, I have come. I have nothing else to offer — only this purple fungus and jade-grass, this jade-lotus-root and golden elixir, which I present to you." His verse ran:

*Jade lotus-root and golden elixir I offer to Sakyamuni —*
*may the Tathagata's myriad years be as the sands of the Ganges.*
*Pure and peaceful, ever joyous in the brocade of the Three Vehicles;*
*hale and long-lived among the flowers of the Nine Ranks.*
*In the gate of formlessness, the true Lord of the Law;*
*in the heaven of form-and-emptiness, the home of immortals.*
*Through heaven and earth, the great land, all hail him as Patriarch —*
*his sixteen-foot golden body, with blessings and long life to spare.*

The Tathagata gladly accepted his thanks. The Star of Longevity took his seat, and as before the goblets and cups went round. Then came also the Barefoot Great Immortal, who bowed low before the Jade Emperor, and turning to the Buddha-Patriarch likewise gave thanks: "Deeply do I feel the power of your Law in subduing the demon-monkey. Having nothing to mark my respect, I present these two cross-pears and several fire-jujubes." His verse ran:

*The Great Immortal, barefoot, with fragrant jujubes and pears,*
*reverently offers them to Amitabha, that his life-span be long.*
*The seven-jeweled lotus dais, steady as a mountain;*
*the thousand-gold flower-throne, adorned like brocade.*
*To say his life equals heaven and earth is no falsehood;*
*to say his blessings outdo the vast waves is no wild talk.*
*Blessing and long life, exactly as he wished — truly so;*
*that quiet, supremely blissful land of the West.*

The Tathagata gave thanks again and bade Ananda and Kasyapa take up all the gifts that had been offered and store them away, one by one. Then he turned to the Jade Emperor to give thanks for the feast. All were thoroughly drunk. Just then a patrolling Inspector Lingguan came to report, "The Great Sage has stuck out his head!"

The Buddha-Patriarch said, "No matter, no matter." From his sleeve he drew out a slip of paper on which were six golden words: "Om Mani Padme Hum." He handed it to Ananda and bade him paste it on the mountaintop. The honored disciple took the slip, carried it out the gate of Heaven to the summit of the Mountain of Five Phases, and pasted it firmly upon a square stone. At once that mountain took root and its seams closed shut. The Great Sage could still draw breath and move his hand to claw it out a little, and could give a feeble struggle — but no more. Ananda returned and reported, "I have pasted the slip."

The Tathagata then took his leave of the Jade Emperor and all the gods, and with the two honored disciples went out beyond the gate of Heaven. Moved once more by compassion, he recited a true incantation and summoned a Local Spirit of the Mountain of Five Phases, who together with the Revealers of the Five Quarters was to dwell upon this mountain and keep watch over the prisoner. "When he is hungry," the Buddha ordered, "give him iron pellets to eat; when he is thirsty, give him molten copper to drink. When the days of his punishment are fulfilled, there will of itself be one who comes to save him." Indeed:

*The bold demon-monkey rebelled against the Halls of Heaven,*
*but was subdued at last by the Tathagata's hand.*
*Thirsty, he drinks molten copper to wear out the years;*
*hungry, he eats iron pellets to pass the time.*
*Suffering heaven's calamity, he endures the grinding torment;*
*through cold misfortune in human affairs, he is glad his life is long.*
*If ever the hero may put forth his strength again,*
*in some later year he shall serve the Buddha and go west.*

And again a verse:

*Vaunting his might, his great power flourished;*
*he tamed dragons and subdued tigers, plying his crafty skill.*
*Stealing peaches and stealing wine, he roamed the Heavenly Court;*
*receiving register and grace, he dwelt in the Jade Capital.*
*His cup of evil brimful, his body now is bound;*
*but his root of goodness unbroken, his spirit yet shall rise.*
*Surely, when he has slipped free of the Tathagata's hand,*
*he will wait for the Tang dynasty to send forth its holy monk.*

After all, no one knows in what year, what month, his calamity and punishment will at last be fulfilled — so listen to the next chapter for the explanation.

<!-- chapter 8 -->
# Chapter 8: The Buddha Forges the Scriptures, and Guanyin Sets Out for Chang'an

*Try if you can to test the gate of Chan—*
*Countless are they who have sought and questioned,*
*and time and again come to nothing, grown old in vain.*
*Grinding a brick to make a mirror,*
*hoarding snowfall for grain—*
*how many years of youth are lost in delusion?*
*A single hair swallows the great sea,*
*a mustard seed holds up Mount Sumeru,*
*and the golden-bodied ascetic faintly smiles.*
*In the moment of waking he soars past the Ten Stages and Three Vehicles,*
*while the heedless stay mired in the Four Births and Six Paths.*
*Who is there to listen, before the Cliff of No Thought,*
*beneath the Shadowless Tree,*
*when the cuckoo cries out the spring dawn?*
*The road to Caoxi is perilous,*
*the clouds over Vulture Peak hang deep,*
*and in such a place the voices of old friends fade away.*
*From cliffs of ice a thousand fathoms high,*
*where the five-petaled lotus opens,*
*the ancient hall's curtain droops as incense curls.*
*In that very season, once the source of all is seen through,*
*the Dragon King's Three Treasures stand revealed.*

This poem is set to the tune "Su Wu Slowly." Our tale tells how the Buddha, the Tathagata, having taken his leave of the Jade Emperor, returned to his precious temple of Thunderclap. There he beheld the Three Thousand Buddhas, the Five Hundred Arhats, the Eight Great Vajra Guardians, and Bodhisattvas beyond number—each one bearing banners and streamers, jeweled canopies, rare treasures, and immortal flowers—arrayed in welcome beneath the twin sala trees of the Spirit Mountain's blessed land. The Tathagata reined in his auspicious cloud and addressed the assembly:

"With my profound wisdom I have looked upon the Three Realms entire. The root nature, in its essence, is utter stillness and extinction. Like the form of empty space, it is wholly without substance. The vanquishing of the unruly monkey is a matter no one can fathom. It marks the beginning of birth and death; the marks of all phenomena are thus."

Having spoken, he released the radiance of the sacred relic, and forty-two rainbows of white light filled the sky, joining north to south. The whole congregation, beholding it, bowed down and worshiped. After a little while the auspicious clouds and bright mists gathered, and the Buddha ascended his lotus throne of the highest grade and seated himself in serene composure. Then the Three Thousand Buddhas, the Five Hundred Arhats, the Eight Vajra Guardians, and the Four Bodhisattvas came forward with palms pressed together, made their obeisance, and asked: "Who was it that threw Heaven into uproar and ravaged the Peach Banquet?"

The Tathagata replied: "That creature was a monstrous monkey born of the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, whose crimes overtopped the very sky and were beyond all telling. Not one of Heaven's gods and generals could subdue him. Though Erlang captured him and Lord Lao Zi smelted him in fire, even that could do him no harm. When I arrived, he stood amid the lords of thunder flaunting his might, vaunting his prowess, showing off his spirit. I stayed their weapons of war and asked him of his origins. He boasted of his magic powers, his arts of transformation, and his somersault cloud that carries him a hundred and eight thousand miles at a bound. So I made a wager with him; he could not pass beyond my hand, and with a single grasp I seized him, transformed my fingers into the Mountain of Five Phases, and sealed him there beneath it. The Jade Emperor flung wide the golden gates of his jasper palace, invited me to the seat of honor, and held a Great Banquet for the Peace of Heaven in my thanks. Only then did I take my leave and return."

The assembly, hearing this, rejoiced and praised him without end.

When the thanksgiving was done, they divided into their ranks and withdrew, each taking up his own task, all delighting together in the truth of their nature. Truly it was so:

*Auspicious haze drifts over the Indian realm,*
*rainbow light enfolds the World-Honored One.*
*The West is called the foremost of all lands,*
*the gate of the formless Dharma King.*
*Often the dark gibbons offer fruit,*
*the spotted deer bring flowers in their mouths;*
*the azure simurgh dances, the bright phoenix sings;*
*the holy tortoise bears longevity,*
*the immortal crane holds the magic fungus.*
*In peace they dwell in the Pure Land's grove,*
*enjoying the Dragon Palace, the realm of the Dharma.*
*Day after day the flowers open,*
*hour after hour the fruit ripens.*
*Practicing stillness, returning to the true,*
*meditating in Chan, perfecting the fruit—*
*neither perishing nor arising,*
*neither increasing nor diminishing.*
*The misted haze drifts faint as they come and go;*
*neither cold nor heat intrudes, and the years go uncounted.*

And the verse runs:

*Coming and going at ease, they roam at leisure,*
*with neither dread nor sorrow in their hearts.*
*In the field of Utmost Bliss all is open and broad;*
*in the vastness of the great cosmos there are no springs nor autumns.*

The Buddha-Patriarch dwelt within the precious temple of Great Thunderclap on Spirit Mountain. One day he summoned together all the Buddhas, Arhats, Guardians, Bodhisattvas, Vajra Lords, and the monks and nuns of his order, and said: "Since I subdued that unruly ape and brought peace to Heaven, I have lost all count of the months and years here; but I reckon that some five hundred years have passed in the mortal world. Today falls on the full moon of early autumn. I have a precious basin, and in it I have set out a hundred kinds of rare flowers and a thousand sorts of strange fruits, that you may share with me this Ullambana Feast. What say you?"

The whole assembly, each one of them, pressed their palms together and circled the Buddha three times in reverence and consent. The Tathagata then took the flowers and fruits and dainties from the precious basin, bidding Ananda hold them up and Kasyapa scatter them abroad. The multitude, moved with gratitude, each offered a poem in thanks.

The poem of Blessing ran:

*The Star of Blessing shines bright before the World-Honored One;*
*the store of blessing, deeper still, grows ever more far-reaching.*
*The virtue of blessing knows no bound, enduring as the earth;*
*the bond of blessing holds its joy, joined to the very heaven.*
*The field of blessing, widely sown, flourishes year by year;*
*the sea of blessing, vast and deep, stands firmer age by age.*
*With blessing filling heaven and earth, its sheltering grace is manifold;*
*blessing increased beyond all measure, forever whole and complete.*

The poem of Prosperity ran:

*Prosperity weighs heavy as a mountain, the bright phoenix sings;*
*prosperity rides on the seasons' peace, hailing the morning star.*
*Prosperity adds ten thousand measures, the body sound and strong;*
*prosperity gives a thousand goblets, the world serene and calm.*
*Prosperity's salary equals heaven's, lasting and secure;*
*prosperity's renown is like the sea, the purer and the clearer.*
*Prosperity's grace, far handed down, draws many an admiring gaze;*
*prosperity's rank without a bound, a glory to ten thousand realms.*

The poem of Longevity ran:

*The Star of Longevity offers its radiance before the Tathagata;*
*the realm of long life, in splendor, opens from this hour.*
*The fruits of longevity heap the platter, breeding auspicious haze;*
*the flowers of longevity, freshly picked, are set upon the lotus throne.*
*The verse of longevity, pure and elegant, is full of rare delight;*
*the song of longevity, tuned in measure, is crafted with fine skill.*
*The span of longevity, drawn out long, matches the sun and moon;*
*long life like mountains and seas, more boundless yet, and far.*

When the Bodhisattvas had finished offering their poems, they begged the Tathagata to make plain the root of all things and to unravel for them the source and stream. The Tathagata gently parted his benevolent lips, expounded the Great Law, and proclaimed the True Fruit. What he taught were the wondrous scriptures of the Three Vehicles, the Surangama of the Five Aggregates. And there one saw the heavenly dragons circling round, and a rain of flowers falling in profusion. Truly:

*The Chan mind shines clear as the moon on a thousand rivers;*
*the true nature holds pure within it the sky of ten thousand miles.*

When the Tathagata had finished his discourse, he addressed the assembly: "I have observed the four great continents, and the good and evil of their living beings differ from place to place. In the Eastern Continent of Superior Body, men revere Heaven and honor Earth; their hearts are bright and their dispositions even. In the Northern Continent of Kuru, though they are fond of slaughter, it is only to fill their bellies; their natures are crude and their feelings sparse, and they do little real harm. In my own Western Continent of Cattle-Gift, men neither covet nor kill; they nourish their breath and conceal their spirit, and though they have no supreme sages, every one of them attains a firm long life. But in that Southern Continent of Jambu, they are greedy and lustful, delighting in mischief; they kill much and quarrel much—truly a battleground of wicked tongues, a sea of strife and slander. Now I have the Three Stores of True Scriptures, by which men may be exhorted to do good."

Hearing this, the Bodhisattvas pressed their palms together in submission and, facing the Buddha, asked: "And what are these Three Stores of True Scriptures that the Tathagata possesses?"

The Tathagata said: "I have one Store of the Vinaya, which speaks of Heaven; one Store of the Sastras, which tells of Earth; and one Store of the Sutras, which redeems the dead. Together the Three Stores comprise thirty-five divisions, totaling fifteen thousand one hundred and forty-four scrolls. They are the scriptures of cultivating the truth, the very gateway to goodness. I should like to send them to the Eastern Lands; but I fear the living beings of that quarter are foolish and benighted—they would slander the true words, failing to know the essential meaning of my Dharma gate and despising the orthodox teaching of Yoga. How might I find one of magic power to go to the Eastern Lands and seek out there a good and faithful seeker, to teach him to journey in hardship over a thousand mountains and across ten thousand waters, until he comes to my dwelling to ask for the True Scriptures, that they may be handed down forever in the East and turn the multitudes toward good? That would be a blessing high as the mountains, a beneficence deep as the sea. Who is willing to make the journey?"

At this the Bodhisattva Guanyin drew near the lotus throne, circled the Buddha three times in reverence, and said: "Though your disciple is of small worth, she is willing to go to the Eastern Lands to seek out a scripture-pilgrim."

The whole assembly raised their heads to look, and this is what they saw of the Bodhisattva:

*Her understanding is rounded with the Four Virtues,*
*her wisdom fills her golden body.*
*Strings of pearls and kingfisher gems hang down,*
*a fragrant ring of jeweled brightness is clasped about her.*
*Dark clouds deftly piled in a coiled-dragon coiffure;*
*an embroidered sash floats light with bright phoenix plumes.*
*Buttons of green jade, a robe of plain silk,*
*wrapped round in auspicious light;*
*a brocaded skirt, a golden chain,*
*shrouded and met by lucky vapors.*
*Her brows are like a slender crescent moon,*
*her eyes are like a pair of stars.*
*Her jade face is born to joy,*
*her vermilion lips a single point of red.*
*The pure vase of sweet dew is full year after year,*
*the slanting willow sprig is green age after age.*
*She unbinds the Eight Calamities, she redeems the throngs of the living,*
*great in mercy and compassion:*
*so she keeps watch over the great mountain, dwells in the Southern Sea,*
*saving the afflicted, seeking out the voices of distress,*
*answering ten thousand calls with ten thousand replies,*
*a thousand-saint, a thousand-spirit presence.*
*Her orchid heart delights in the purple bamboo,*
*her gentle nature loves the fragrant vines.*
*She is the merciful mistress upon Potalaka Mountain,*
*the living Guanyin within the Tide-Sound Cave.*

The Tathagata, beholding her, rejoiced greatly in his heart and said: "No other could go. It must be the Honored Guanyin, whose magic powers are vast and far-reaching—only she may make the journey."

The Bodhisattva said: "What instructions does your disciple carry as she goes to the Eastern Lands?"

The Tathagata said: "On this journey you must survey the road by foot; you may not travel high in the empyrean. You must go half by cloud and half by mist, passing the mountains and rivers with your eyes, taking careful note of the distances of the route, so that you may instruct the scripture-pilgrim. But lest the good and faithful one find the way too hard, I shall give you five treasures." And at once he bade Ananda and Kasyapa bring out a brocaded cassock and a nine-ringed monk's staff, and said to the Bodhisattva: "This cassock and this staff may be given to the scripture-pilgrim for his own use. If he will set his heart firmly on coming here and will wear my cassock, he shall escape the wheel of rebirth; if he carries my staff, he shall not meet with poison or harm."

The Bodhisattva bowed in submission and received them. The Tathagata then brought out three fillets and handed them to the Bodhisattva, saying: "These treasures are called the Tightening Fillets. Though the three are all alike, each is used in a different way. I have three spells of golden binding and restraint. If along the road you should meet with demons of vast and far-reaching power, you must urge them to learn goodness and to follow the scripture-pilgrim as his disciples. If any of them will not submit to command, you may set this fillet upon his head, and of itself it will take root in the flesh. Recite the proper spell for the one you use, and his eyes will swell, his head will throb, his very skull will split—and that will surely bring him into my gate."

Hearing this, the Bodhisattva leapt for joy, made her bow, and withdrew. At once she summoned the disciple Hui'an to accompany her. This Hui'an wielded an iron rod of solid black metal weighing a thousand pounds, and he served at the Bodhisattva's side as a mighty demon-quelling guardian. The Bodhisattva made the brocaded cassock into a bundle and had him carry it on his back. She hid the golden fillets away, took up the monk's staff, and went straight down from Spirit Mountain. This journey was destined to bring it about that:

*The Buddha's son returns at last to fulfill his original vow,*
*and the Elder Golden Cicada is wrapped once more in sandalwood.*

When the Bodhisattva reached the foot of the mountain, the Great Immortal of the Golden Crown at the Jade Truth Abbey met her at the gate and invited her in to take tea. The Bodhisattva did not dare to linger, and said: "I have today received the Buddha's command to go to the Eastern Lands to seek a scripture-pilgrim."

The Great Immortal said: "When will this scripture-pilgrim arrive?"

The Bodhisattva said: "It is not yet fixed—perhaps in some two or three years he may come this far." Then she took her leave of the Great Immortal and went on, half by cloud and half by mist, marking the distances of the route. There is a poem to bear witness. The poem says:

*Across ten thousand miles she seeks her man and does not speak of it,*
*yet they say to fulfill one's purpose wholly is hard.*
*If to seek a man should ever be just so as this,*
*then is my whole life's labor mere chance and accident?*
*To preach the Way with method becomes idle talk;*
*to make it plain without faith is empty transmission too.*
*Willing to bare her heart and liver to find a kindred soul,*
*she reckons that up ahead there must be destined ties.*

As mistress and disciple journeyed on, they suddenly came upon a stretch of the Weak Water Three Thousand Leagues—the boundary of the Flowing Sands River. The Bodhisattva said: "Disciple, this is a hard place to cross. The scripture-pilgrim will be of muddy bone and common flesh—how will he ever get over?"

Hui'an said: "Master, how wide do you judge the river to be?"

The Bodhisattva halted her cloud-step and looked, and saw only this:

*Eastward it joins the desert sands,*
*westward it reaches the foreign tribes,*
*southward it runs to Wuge,*
*northward it links with the Tartars.*
*Straight across it stretches eight hundred miles;*
*up and down, ten million leagues in length.*
*The water flows as if the very earth turned over,*
*the waves roll up like mountains heaving their backs.*
*Vast and boundless, dim and limitless,*
*ten miles off one hears its thunder ten thousand fathoms high.*
*An immortal's raft could never reach this place,*
*and the lotus leaf can find no float upon it.*
*Withered grass in the slanting sun by the winding shore,*
*yellow clouds darkening the sun above the long embankment.*
*Where do merchants ever come and go?*
*When has a fisherman ever made his rest here?*
*On the level sands no wild goose alights;*
*on the far bank only the gibbon cries.*
*Only the red knotweed knows the season's hue,*
*and the white duckweed, faintly fragrant, drifts as it will.*

As the Bodhisattva was gazing about her, all at once there came a splashing crash from within the river, and out of the waves leaped a monster, hideous beyond measure. This was how he was made:

*Not green, not black, a face of ill-omened hue;*
*not tall, not short, a bare-footed, sinewy frame.*
*His eyes flashed and flickered like twin lamps beneath a stove;*
*the corners of his mouth forked open like a butcher's brazier.*
*His tusks thrust out like sword-blades,*
*his red hair was tangled and wild.*
*A single roar of his bellow was like a clap of thunder,*
*and his two feet rushed onward like a rolling gale.*

The monster, gripping a precious staff in his hands, came up the bank and made to seize the Bodhisattva—but Hui'an drew his solid iron rod to block him, shouting: "Stand and don't run!" The monster met him at once with his precious staff. The two of them fought a fearsome battle there on the shore of the Flowing Sands, a battle truly terrifying to behold:

*Moksa's solid iron rod*
*displayed the Dharma-guard's divine power;*
*the monster's demon-quelling staff*
*strained to show its heroic might.*
*Two silver pythons danced by the riverside,*
*a pair of holy monks clashed on the bank.*
*The one made his might to overawe the Flowing Sands;*
*the other strove to guard Guanyin and win great merit.*
*The one churned the waves and leaped the billows,*
*the other spat the mist and breathed forth the wind.*
*Churning waves and leaping billows darkened heaven and earth;*
*spitting mist and breathing wind dimmed the sun and moon.*
*That demon-quelling staff*
*was like a white tiger come down from the hills;*
*this solid iron rod*
*was like a yellow dragon stretched across the road.*
*When the one struck out, it was like beating the grass to start a snake;*
*when the other flung free, it was like a falcon scattering through the pines.*
*They fought till all was dim and dark,*
*the stars and constellations blazing;*
*till the mists came surging up,*
*and heaven and earth grew hazy.*
*The one, long dwelling in the Weak Water, was the fiercer there;*
*the other, newly come from Spirit Mountain, won his first great merit.*

The two of them went back and forth, fighting some twenty or thirty bouts, with neither gaining the upper hand. Then the monster fended off the iron rod and said: "What temple do you hail from, monk, that you dare come and stand against me?"

Moksa said: "I am Moksa Hui'an, second prince of the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King Li, and I am now escorting my master to the Eastern Lands to seek a scripture-pilgrim. What manner of monster are you, that you dare so boldly to block our way?"

The monster then came to himself and said: "I remember you—you cultivated the Way alongside Guanyin of the Southern Sea in the Purple Bamboo Grove. Why have you come here?"

Moksa said: "Is that not my master there upon the bank?"

Hearing this, the monster murmured assent again and again, put away his precious staff, and let Moksa lead him off to see Guanyin. He bowed his head to the ground and made his plea: "Bodhisattva, forgive my crime, and let me tell my tale. I am no fiend or demon. I was once the Curtain-Raising Marshal who attended the imperial carriage before the Hall of the Numinous Empyrean. Only because at the Peach Banquet I let slip my hand and shattered a crystal goblet, the Jade Emperor had me beaten eight hundred strokes and banished me down to this world, transformed into this monstrous shape. And further, once every seven days he sends a flying sword to pierce my breast and ribs a hundred times and more before it returns. Such is my torment. Helpless, unable to bear hunger and cold, every two or three days I come out from the waves and seize a passerby to eat. Today, in my ignorance, I never thought I should affront the great and merciful Bodhisattva."

The Bodhisattva said: "You sinned in Heaven and were banished here, and now you go on harming living things in this way—this is truly crime piled upon crime. I have now received the Buddha's command to go to the Eastern Lands to seek a scripture-pilgrim. Why do you not enter my gate, take refuge in the fruit of goodness, and follow the scripture-pilgrim as his disciple, journeying to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures? I will see to it that the flying sword no longer comes to pierce you. And when the work is accomplished, your sin shall be remitted and your former office restored. What say you to that?"

The monster said: "I am willing to take refuge in the true fruit." Then he came forward again and said: "Bodhisattva, in this place I have devoured beyond counting. Several scripture-pilgrims have come this way before, and I ate every one of them. The heads of those I ate I flung into the Flowing Sands, and they sank straight to the bottom—for in this water not even a goose feather will float. Only nine skulls of scripture-pilgrims float upon the surface and will not sink. I thought them strange things, so I strung them together with a cord and would take them out to play with in my idle hours. But on this journey, I fear the scripture-pilgrim may never get this far—and then would I not have ruined my own future after all?"

The Bodhisattva said: "How could there be no chance of his arriving? You may hang these skulls about your neck and wait for the scripture-pilgrim—there will be a use for them." The monster said: "If that is so, I am willing to receive your teaching." Then the Bodhisattva laid her hand upon his crown and gave him the precepts, taking "sand" for his surname, so that he was named Sha; and she gave him a religious name, calling him Sha Wujing—Sand-Awakened-to-Purity. From that hour he entered the Buddhist order, saw the Bodhisattva across the river, washed clean his heart and purged his thoughts, harmed living things no more, and waited single-mindedly for the scripture-pilgrim.

The Bodhisattva took her leave of him and, together with Moksa, hastened straight on toward the Eastern Lands. They traveled a good while, and again came upon a high mountain, over which a baleful vapor hung so thick that they could not climb it on foot. Just as they were about to ride their cloud over the mountain, all at once a wild wind sprang up, and out flashed another monster. He too was a thing most fierce and dangerous; this is how he looked:

*His snout hung down, fleshy and dangling like a lotus pod;*
*his ears were like rush-leaf fans, and his golden eyes shone bright.*
*His tusks were sharp and keen as a file of steel;*
*his long mouth gaped open like a brazier of fire.*
*A golden helmet was tightly strapped beneath his cheeks;*
*his armor was bound with cords, like the sloughed scales of a python.*
*In his hands he held a rake like a dragon's questing claws;*
*at his waist hung a curved bow like the half-disk of the moon.*
*Bristling with might, he overawed the very Year-Star;*
*soaring in spirit, he overbore the gods of Heaven.*

He charged up at them, and without regard for good or ill, lifted his rake against the Bodhisattva and struck. But Moksa the disciple blocked him, crying out in a great voice: "Vile monster, hold your insolence! Look to my rod!"

The monster said: "This monk does not know whether he is alive or dead. Look to my rake!" The two of them, at the foot of the mountain, charged and clashed, gambling on victory or defeat—and truly it was a fine battle:

*The monster fierce and savage,*
*Hui'an mighty and able.*
*The iron rod pounded at his heart,*
*the rake came chopping at his face.*
*Scattering earth and raising dust, they darkened heaven and earth;*
*flying sand and rolling stones startled the very gods and ghosts.*
*The nine-toothed rake,*
*flashing bright,*
*its double rings ringing loud;*
*the single rod,*
*black and blurred,*
*flying in his two hands.*
*This one was the Heavenly King's prince,*
*that one a marshal's wandering spirit.*
*The one is a Dharma-guard at Potalaka,*
*the other a goblin in a mountain cave.*
*This meeting was a contest for the higher hand—*
*who could tell which would lose and which would win?*

Just as the two of them had fought to the very pitch, Guanshiyin, from the midst of the air, cast down a lotus blossom that parted the rake and the rod. The monster, seeing it, was struck with alarm and asked: "What temple do you hail from, monk, that you dare conjure such tricks of flowers before my eyes to fool me?"

Moksa said: "You fleshly-eyed, common-born vile creature! I am the disciple of the Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea. This is a lotus blossom flung down by my master, and you do not even know it!"

The monster said: "The Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea—is that the Guanshiyin who sweeps away the Three Calamities and saves from the Eight Difficulties?" Moksa said: "Who else should it be?" The monster threw down his rake, bowed his head to the ground, and said: "Elder brother, where is the Bodhisattva? Pray trouble yourself to present me to her."

Moksa lifted his face and pointed: "Is that not she up there?" The monster knocked his head upon the ground and cried out in a loud voice: "Bodhisattva, forgive my crime! Forgive my crime!"

Guanyin brought her cloud down low, came forward, and asked: "What wild boar turned to a spirit are you, what old swine become a fiend, that you dare to block my way here?"

The monster said: "I am no wild boar, nor any old swine. I was in truth the Marshal of the Heavenly Reeds in the River of Heaven. Only because, in my cups, I made sport with the moon-goddess Chang'e, the Jade Emperor had me beaten two thousand strokes with the mallet and banished me to the mortal dust. My single true spirit went straight down to seize a dwelling and be born again; but I lost my way and entered into the womb of a sow, and so was changed into this shape. I bit the sow to death, slew the whole litter of swine, and here took possession of the mountain ground, living by devouring men. I never thought to run against the Bodhisattva—I beg you, save me, save me!"

The Bodhisattva said: "What is this mountain called?" The monster said: "It is called Mount Fuling. In the mountain there is a cave called the Cloud-Ladder Cave. In the cave there was once a maiden named Second-Sister Egg. Seeing that I had some skill in arms, she took me in as the master of her house—they call it 'marrying into the household.' But before a year was out she died, and the whole cave's possessions came to me to enjoy. Long years I have dwelt here, with no honest livelihood to support me, doing nothing but living by my old trade of eating men. I beg the Bodhisattva to forgive my crime."

The Bodhisattva said: "The ancients say, 'If you would have a future, do not do what has no future.' You broke the law in the upper realm, and now you still do not mend your savage heart but harm the living and breed sin—is this not to deserve punishment for both crimes at once?"

The monster said: "A future, a future! If I followed your way, you would have me feed on wind. As the saying goes: 'Follow the law of the magistrate and you will be beaten to death; follow the law of the Buddha and you will be starved to death.' Off with you, off with you! I had far rather catch myself a traveler, plump and juicy, and eat him whole—and what care I for two crimes or three, a thousand crimes or ten thousand!"

The Bodhisattva said: "'When a man has a good wish, Heaven will surely grant it.' If you are willing to take refuge in the true fruit, you shall have your own means of livelihood. The world has the five grains, which can relieve hunger—why must you live by eating men?"

Hearing these words, the monster was like a man waking from a dream, and he said to the Bodhisattva: "I would gladly follow the right, but 'whoever has sinned against Heaven has none to whom he may pray.'"

The Bodhisattva said: "I have received the Buddha's command to go to the Eastern Lands to seek a scripture-pilgrim. You may follow him as his disciple and make the journey to the Western Heaven, atoning for your crime by your merit, and I will surely see you delivered from your calamity and corruption."

The monster cried with all his heart: "I am willing to follow, I am willing to follow!" Then the Bodhisattva laid her hand upon his crown and gave him the precepts, taking his own body for his surname, so that he was named Zhu—Pig; and she gave him a religious name, calling him Zhu Wuneng—Pig-Awakened-to-Power. So he received the command and returned to the truth, keeping the fast and abstaining from meat, cutting himself off from the five strong herbs and the three forbidden meats, and waited single-mindedly for the scripture-pilgrim.

The Bodhisattva then took her leave of Wuneng, and with Moksa pressed on, half-raising cloud and mist. As they were going along, they saw in the air above them a jade dragon crying out. The Bodhisattva drew near and asked: "What dragon are you, suffering punishment here?"

The dragon said: "I am the son of Aorun, Dragon King of the Western Sea. Because I set fire to the bright pearls upon the hall, my royal father sent a memorial to the courts of Heaven, charging me with unfilial conduct. The Jade Emperor has hung me up here in the air, given me three hundred strokes, and within a few days I am to be executed. I beg the Bodhisattva to save me, to save me!"

When Guanyin heard this, she at once went up with Moksa through the Southern Gate of Heaven, where the Heavenly Masters Qiu and Zhang met her and asked: "Whither are you bound?"

The Bodhisattva said: "This poor nun wishes to have one audience with the Jade Emperor." The two Heavenly Masters at once went in to report it, and the Jade Emperor came down from his hall to receive her. The Bodhisattva stepped forward, made her obeisance, and said: "This poor nun has received the Buddha's command to go to the Eastern Lands to seek a scripture-pilgrim. On the road I met with a sinful dragon hung up in punishment, and I have come especially to make this request—that you spare his life and bestow him upon this poor nun, to serve the scripture-pilgrim as his means of conveyance."

When the Jade Emperor heard this, he at once issued a decree of pardon, and dispatched a heavenly general to loose the dragon and deliver him to the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva gave thanks for the grace and withdrew. The little dragon bowed his head and gave thanks for the gift of his life, and submitted himself to the Bodhisattva's command. She placed him in a deep ravine, there to wait only until the scripture-pilgrim should come, when he would change into a white horse and go to the West to win his merit. The little dragon received the command and hid himself away—of which no more.

The Bodhisattva, leading the disciple Moksa, passed over this mountain and again hastened toward the Eastern Lands. They had not gone far when suddenly they beheld ten thousand shafts of golden light and a thousand strands of auspicious vapor. Moksa said: "Master, that place where the light shines forth is the Mountain of Five Phases, and the Tathagata's sealing-charm is set upon it."

The Bodhisattva said: "Then this is where the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, who threw the Peach Banquet into uproar and ran riot through the Palace of Heaven, now lies crushed beneath."

Moksa said: "Just so, just so." Master and disciple climbed the mountain together to look at the charm, which was the six-syllable true mantra, "Om mani padme hum." The Bodhisattva, having read it, sighed and lamented without end, and composed a poem. The poem ran:

*Pitiable is the monster-monkey who would not serve the common good;*
*in years past, in his wild presumption, he played the hero bold.*
*With reckless heart he threw the Peach Banquet into uproar;*
*with brazen daring he stole into the Tushita Palace.*
*Amid a host of a hundred thousand he had no equal foe;*
*through the ninefold heaven above he carried his mighty pride.*
*But once he met the snares of my Buddha, the Tathagata,*
*on what day will he stretch himself again and show his merit anew?*

While master and disciple were speaking, they startled the Great Sage. From beneath the roots of the mountain the Great Sage cried out in a great voice: "Who is that up there on the mountain, chanting verses and laying bare my faults?"

When the Bodhisattva heard this, she went straight down the mountain to seek him out. There at the foot of the stone cliff she found the local Earth-God, the Mountain-Spirit, and the heavenly general who guarded the Great Sage, all coming forward to bow and receive her, and they led her before the Great Sage. She saw that he was indeed crushed within a casket of stone, able to speak with his mouth but unable to stir his body.

The Bodhisattva said: "You who are surnamed Sun—do you know me?"

The Great Sage opened wide his fiery eyes and golden pupils, nodded his head, and cried out in a loud voice: "How should I not know you? You are she of the Southern Sea, of Potalaka Mountain, who saves from suffering and rescues from distress—the greatly merciful, greatly compassionate Bodhisattva Guanshiyin. I am grateful for your visit, grateful indeed. Here I pass my days like years, and never has one acquaintance come to look in upon me. From where have you come?"

The Bodhisattva said: "I have received the Buddha's command to go to the Eastern Lands to seek a scripture-pilgrim, and passing this way I have spared a few weary steps to look in upon you."

The Great Sage said: "The Tathagata deceived me and crushed me beneath this mountain. For more than five hundred years now I have not been able to stir. I beg the Bodhisattva, of her kindness, to grant me some small grace and save your old Sun—save me!"

The Bodhisattva said: "Your sins and crimes are deep beyond measure, and I fear that if I freed you, you would only breed fresh disaster—which would turn out badly after all."

The Great Sage said: "I have already learned to repent. I only beg the great and merciful one to point out a road, and I will willingly take up cultivation." And this was truly so:

*Let the human heart but give birth to a single thought,*
*and Heaven and Earth shall know it through and through.*
*If good and evil met with no requital,*
*then surely there would be partiality in the cosmos.*

When the Bodhisattva heard these words, her heart was filled with gladness, and she said to the Great Sage: "The sacred scriptures say: 'If his words be good, then from a thousand miles away men answer to them; if his words be not good, then from a thousand miles away men turn against them.' Since you have this mind, wait until I have reached the great land of Tang in the Eastern Lands and found a scripture-pilgrim there. I will have him save you. You may follow him as his disciple, uphold and observe the teaching, enter my Buddhist gate, and once more cultivate the true fruit. What say you?"

The Great Sage cried again and again: "I am willing to go, I am willing to go!"

The Bodhisattva said: "Since you are bent on the fruit of goodness, let me give you a religious name."

The Great Sage said: "I already have a name—I am called Sun Wukong, Awakened-to-Emptiness."

The Bodhisattva rejoiced again and said: "I have already brought two others before to submission, whose names are likewise of the 'Wu—Awakened' rank. And you too are of the 'Wu' rank, which fits well with theirs—very good, very good. There is then no need for further charge. I take my leave." So the Great Sage, having seen his nature and made clear his heart, turned toward the Buddhist teaching, while the Bodhisattva, keeping her purpose in mind, went on to seek the holy monk.

She and Moksa left that place and went straight on to the east, and within a day or so they came to the great land of Tang at Chang'an. There they gathered in their mists and folded away their clouds, and master and disciple transformed themselves into two scabby, mangy wandering monks, and entered the city of Chang'an. Before they knew it, the day grew late. As they walked along beside the great market street, they saw a shrine of the local Earth-God, and the two of them went straight in. This so flustered the Earth-God that his heart leaped in fright and his ghost-soldiers trembled; knowing it was the Bodhisattva, they bowed their heads and received her in. Then the Earth-God hurried in haste to report to the City-God, the Local Spirit, and all the gods of every shrine throughout Chang'an, who all knew it was the Bodhisattva and came to pay their respects, saying: "Bodhisattva, forgive us gods the offense of our late reception."

The Bodhisattva said: "On no account let a breath of this leak out. I have received the Buddha's command, and have come here especially to seek out a scripture-pilgrim. I will borrow your shrine to lodge in for a few days, until I have found the true monk, and then I shall return." The several gods each went back to their own places, and they hustled the Earth-God off to lodge for the while in the City-God's temple. There master and disciple hid away their true forms.

And in the end there is no knowing what scripture-pilgrim they would seek out—so listen to the next chapter, where it will all be explained.

<!-- chapter 9 -->
# Chapter 9: The River-Float Monk and the Long Road to Vengeance

In the great land of Shaanxi stood the city of Chang'an, the capital chosen by emperors through age after age. Ever since the dynasties of Zhou, Qin, and Han, three districts had bloomed like brocade there, and eight rivers wound about the walls — truly a realm renowned for its beauty. It was in this place that the Emperor Taizong of the great Tang ascended the throne, changed the reign-title to Zhenguan, and had now ruled for thirteen years. The cyclical year was *jisi*; the empire was at peace, tribute flowed in from the eight directions, and the four seas acknowledged him as their lord.

One day, when the emperor had taken his seat and the civil and military officials had completed the rites of court audience, the Prime Minister Wei Zheng stepped forth from the ranks and made his report.

"The realm is now at peace," he said, "and the eight directions are tranquil. We should follow the ancient custom and open the examination halls, summoning worthy men and promoting the talented, that they may aid in the governance of the world."

"What you propose is sound, my worthy minister," replied Taizong. He thereupon issued a proclamation calling for the worthy, posting it throughout the empire: in every prefecture, district, and county, whether of military or common stock, any scholar of the Confucian school whose grasp of letters was clear and whose mastery of the three examinations was complete should come to Chang'an to sit for the tests.

The notice came in time to the region of Haizhou, where there lived a man named Chen E, styled Guangrui. When he had read the proclamation he returned home at once and spoke to his mother, Lady Zhang.

"The court has sent down its golden notice," he said, "decreeing that the southern hall be opened to select men of worth. It is my wish to go and sit for the examination. Should I win some office, however small, I would bring honor to my parents and glory to my name, secure rank for my wife and shade for my sons, and shed luster upon our gate. Such is my ambition, Mother, and I have come to tell you of it before I go."

"My son is a scholar," said Lady Zhang. "'In youth he studies; in his prime he goes forth to act.' This is exactly as it should be. But on the road to the examination you must take care, and once you have your office, come home to me quickly."

Guangrui thereupon bade his servant pack the baggage, took leave of his mother with a bow, and pressed on his journey. When he reached Chang'an the halls had just been thrown open, and he entered to sit the tests. When the examinations were done, he was among those chosen; and when he had answered the three palace questions, the Tang sovereign with his own brush conferred upon him first place — the rank of *zhuangyuan*. He was given a horse to parade through the streets for three days.

It happened, as he rode, that he passed before the gate of the Prime Minister Yin Kaishan. Now the minister had a daughter named Wenjiao, also called Mantangjiao, who was not yet betrothed. At that very moment she had raised a high tower hung with colored silk, from which she meant to cast an embroidered ball to choose her husband. Just as Chen Guangrui passed beneath the tower, the young lady caught sight of him. Seeing how his bearing surpassed other men, and knowing him for the newly crowned first scholar, her heart was filled with delight, and she let the embroidered ball fall — and it struck Guangrui squarely upon his black gauze cap.

At once a strain of pipes and flutes broke into delicate music, and a dozen maids and attendants came down from the tower, took hold of Guangrui's horse by the head, and led the first scholar into the minister's mansion to be wed. The minister and his lady came straightway into the hall, summoned the master of ceremonies, and gave their daughter in marriage to Guangrui. They bowed to Heaven and Earth, husband and wife bowed to one another, and then they made obeisance to the bride's father and mother. The minister ordered a feast set out, and they drank in joy through the night, and the two of them, hand in hand, withdrew together into the orchid chamber.

Next day, at the third mark of the fifth watch, Taizong took his seat upon the golden throne in the precious hall, and the civil and military officers hastened to court.

"To what office should the newly crowned first scholar, Chen Guangrui, be appointed?" the emperor asked.

Wei Zheng came forward and replied, "Your servant has searched the prefectures under our authority, and there is a vacancy for governor at Jiangzhou. I beg my lord to grant him that post."

Taizong thereupon named Guangrui governor of Jiangzhou and ordered him to set out at once and not miss the appointed term. Guangrui gave thanks for the grace and withdrew from court. Returning to the minister's mansion, he took counsel with his wife, bade farewell to his father- and mother-in-law, and together with her set out for his post at Jiangzhou. So they left Chang'an and took to the road.

It was the season of late spring, when mild breezes set the willows greening and a fine rain dappled the flowers red. Guangrui turned his way homeward, and together with his wife bowed before his mother, Lady Zhang.

"I rejoice for you, my son," said Lady Zhang, "and that you have brought a bride home as well."

"It was by leaning on Mother's blessings and protection," said Guangrui, "that I unworthily took first place. The court granted me the parade through the streets, and as I passed the gate of the Prime Minister Yin, I happened to be struck by the embroidered ball cast down — and the minister at once made me his daughter's husband. The court has appointed me governor of Jiangzhou, and now I have come to take Mother with me to my post."

Lady Zhang was overjoyed, and they made ready for the road.

After some days of travel they came to the inn of Liu the Younger, in the town of Ten Thousand Flowers, and there they lodged. Lady Zhang suddenly fell ill, and she said to Guangrui, "I am not well. Let us stay at the inn a day or two to recover, and then go on." Guangrui obeyed.

The next morning he saw a man at the inn door crying his wares — a golden carp held up for sale. Guangrui at once bought it for a string of cash, meaning to cook it for his mother. But then he saw the carp blink its eyes, again and again.

Marveling, Guangrui said, "I have heard that when a fish or a serpent blinks its eyes, it is surely no common creature." So he asked the fisherman, "Where was this fish caught?"

"It was taken from the Hong River, fifteen *li* from the prefectural town," the man replied.

Guangrui thereupon carried the fish to the Hong River and set it free, and returning to the inn he told his mother what he had done.

"To set a creature free is a good deed," said Lady Zhang. "My heart is much gladdened by it."

"We have lodged here three days now," said Guangrui, "and the imperial term presses hard. It is my thought to set out tomorrow — but I do not know whether Mother is well enough."

"I am still unwell," she answered, "and the road just now is hot and close; I fear it would only worsen my sickness. You may rent a room here for me to rest in, and leave me a little money for expenses. You and your wife go on ahead to take up the office, and when the cool of autumn comes, return for me."

Guangrui took counsel with his wife and so rented a dwelling, gave money to his mother, and with his wife bowed farewell and went on.

The road was hard, traveling by dawn and resting by night, until at last, before they knew it, they reached the Hong River ferry crossing. There they saw two boatmen, Liu Hong and Li Biao, who poled their boat to the bank to meet them. It was that in a former life Guangrui was fated to suffer this calamity, and so he fell in with these enemies. Guangrui bade his servant carry the baggage aboard, and just as husband and wife had together stepped onto the boat, Liu Hong fixed his eyes upon the lady Yin — her face like the full moon, her eyes like autumn waters, her small mouth like a cherry, her slender waist like a green willow. Truly she had a beauty to sink fishes and bring down wild geese, to shame the moon and put flowers to blush. A wolf's heart rose up in him at the sight, and he and Li Biao laid their plot, poling the boat to a place where no smoke of men rose.

They waited until the dead of the third watch, when all was still. First they slew the servant; then they beat Guangrui to death, and pushed both corpses into the water. When the lady saw her husband murdered, she made to throw herself into the river as well, but Liu Hong seized her in his arms.

"If you yield to me, all will be well," he said. "If you refuse — one stroke, and I'll cut you in two."

The lady, finding no way out, could only consent for the moment and so submit to Liu Hong. The villain poled the boat to the southern bank, handed it over to Li Biao to keep, and then, putting on Guangrui's robes and cap and taking up his official seal, went off with the lady to take the post at Jiangzhou.

Now the body of the servant whom Liu Hong had killed went floating off downstream; but the corpse of Chen Guangrui sank to the bottom and did not stir. A patrolling sea-yaksha at the mouth of the Hong River saw it and flew like a shooting star to report it in the Dragon Palace. The Dragon King had just taken his seat in the hall when the yaksha announced: "At the mouth of the Hong River, some person unknown has beaten a scholar to death and flung his body into the depths."

The Dragon King ordered the corpse carried in and set before him, and when he had looked at it closely he said, "Why, this is the very man who saved my life! How comes it that he has been murdered? As the saying goes, 'Repay kindness with kindness.' Today I must save his life, to requite the favor of those days past."

He at once wrote out a dispatch and sent the yaksha straight to the City God and the Earth God of Hongzhou, demanding that the soul of the scholar be brought to save his life. The City God and the Earth God thereupon called for a little demon to deliver up the soul of Chen Guangrui to the yaksha, who carried the soul back to the Crystal Palace and reported to the Dragon King.

"What is your name, scholar," asked the Dragon King, "and from what place do you come? How did you come here to be beaten to death?"

Guangrui made his bow. "I am Chen E, styled Guangrui, a man of Hongnong county in Haizhou. I had the unworthy honor of being made the new first scholar and was granted the governorship of Jiangzhou. As I traveled with my wife to take up the post, we boarded a boat at the riverside, and the boatman Liu Hong, coveting my wife, beat me to death and cast away my body. I beg Your Majesty to save me."

When the Dragon King heard this he said, "So that is how it stands. Sir, the golden carp you set free that day — that was none other than I. You are my benefactor, who saved my life; now that you are in trouble, how could I do otherwise than save you?"

So he set Guangrui's body aside against a wall, placed within its mouth a pearl that preserves the features so that it would not spoil, that one day he might return to life and take his revenge. "As for your true soul," he said, "let it stay for the time being in my water-realm and serve as a commander." Guangrui bowed his head in thanks, and the Dragon King held a feast in his honor — but of that no more.

Now the lady Yin loathed the villain Liu so bitterly that she could have eaten his flesh and slept upon his skin. But because she was with child, and did not yet know whether it would be a boy or a girl, she could do nothing but force herself, against all will, to go along with him. In the turn of an eye they came to Jiangzhou, where the clerks and runners all came out to meet them, and the officials of the district set a feast in the public hall to welcome the new governor.

"It is wholly through the great support of you gentlemen," said Liu Hong, "that this student has come to his post."

"You, our lord governor, are a man of high talent and the highest distinction," the officials replied. "Naturally you will look upon the people as upon your own children, so that lawsuits are few and punishments clean. We who serve beneath you have only to rely on you. Why do you speak so modestly?" When the feast was over, they all dispersed.

Time flew swiftly by. One day Liu Hong went off far away on official business. The lady, alone in the yamen, thought of her mother-in-law and her husband, and sighed and grieved upon the flower pavilion. Suddenly her body grew weary and a pain seized her belly; she fell to the ground in a swoon, and before she knew it she had given birth to a son. And a voice spoke beside her ear:

"Mantangjiao, hear what I charge you. I am the Star Lord of the Southern Pole, and by the command of the Bodhisattva Guanyin I have brought you this child. In days to come his fame shall be great and far-reaching, no common man. If the villain Liu returns, he will surely do this child harm — so guard him with all your heart. Your husband has been saved by the Dragon King; one day husband and wife shall meet again, mother and son shall be reunited, and the day will come when wrongs are cleansed and vengeance taken.
