Mark my words well. Wake now, wake now." And with that the voice was gone.

The lady woke, remembering every word, and held her son fast — yet she could think of no plan. Suddenly Liu Hong returned, and the moment he saw the child he wished to drown him.

"It is late in the day now," said the lady. "Let us wait until tomorrow to cast him into the river." By good fortune, early next morning Liu Hong was suddenly called away on urgent business.

The lady thought to herself: "If this child is here when the villain returns, his life is forfeit. Better to cast him into the river at once and leave him to live or die. If perhaps Heaven takes pity and someone saves and rears him, the day may yet come when we meet again." But fearing he could never be recognized, she bit her finger and wrote a letter in blood, setting down in full the names of his father and mother and all the circumstances of his origin. Then she bit off the little toe of the child's left foot, that it might serve as a token of proof, and wrapped him in an undershirt from against her own body. Taking advantage of the empty hour, she carried him out of the yamen.

It was fortunate that the yamen lay not far from the river. Reaching the bank, the lady wept aloud one bitter while. As she was about to cast the child away, she saw a plank of wood come floating up to the very edge of the bank. The lady bowed in prayer toward Heaven, laid the child upon the plank, bound him fast with a sash, tied the bloody letter at his breast, and pushed him out into the river, leaving him to go where he would. Then, choking back her tears, she returned to the yamen — but of that no more.

The child upon the plank went floating down with the current until at last it came to rest at the foot of the Temple of the Golden Mountain. The abbot of that temple was a monk named Faming, who had cultivated truth and awakened to the Way, and had attained the subtle secret of no-rebirth. As he sat in meditation, contemplating Chan, he suddenly heard the crying of an infant. His heart was stirred, and he hurried to the riverside to look — and there on a plank at the water's edge lay a sleeping babe. The abbot quickly rescued the child, and finding the bloody letter at his breast, he learned the whole story. He gave the boy a milk-name, calling him Jiangliu — "River-Float" — and entrusted him to others to be raised, while he himself kept the bloody letter carefully hidden away.

Time sped like an arrow, the sun and moon shuttling by, and before anyone marked it River-Float had grown to be eighteen years old. The abbot then had him shave his head and take up the religious life, giving him the dharma-name Xuanzang. He touched the crown of his head and bestowed the precepts upon him, and with a steadfast heart the young man cultivated the Way.

One day in late spring, the monks were gathered together beneath the shade of the pines, expounding the scriptures and contemplating Chan, discoursing on profound mysteries — and there a certain wine-and-meat monk found himself bested in argument by Xuanzang. In a great rage he cursed the youth: "You beast of bad karma! You don't even know your own name, you don't even know your own father and mother — what mischief are you stirring up here?"

Stung by such words, Xuanzang went into the temple, knelt before his master, and with tears streaming down both cheeks said, "A man born between Heaven and Earth, endowed with *yin* and *yang* and nourished by the five elements, owes his being wholly to a father's begetting and a mother's rearing. How can there be one who walks the world without father or mother?" Again and again he pleaded, begging to know the names of his parents.

"If you truly wish to seek your parents," said the abbot, "come with me to the abbot's chamber." Xuanzang followed him there. The abbot climbed to the cross-beam above and took down a small box; opening it, he drew out the bloody letter and the undershirt and handed them to Xuanzang. Xuanzang unfolded the letter and read it, and only then learned in full his parents' names and the whole tale of their wrongs.

When he had finished reading he fell weeping to the ground. "If I cannot avenge my father and mother's wrong," he cried, "how can I call myself a man? For eighteen years I knew not those who bore me, and only this day do I learn that I have a mother. Had my master not rescued and reared me, how should I have lived to this day? Let your disciple go and find his mother — and then, bearing the censer-bowl upon my head, I will rebuild this temple's halls and repay my master's deep kindness."

"If you would go to seek your mother," said his master, "take this bloody letter and this undershirt with you. Go in the guise of a monk begging alms, straight to the private yamen at Jiangzhou — only so will you be able to meet your mother."

Xuanzang received his master's instructions, and dressed as an alms-begging monk he made his way straight to Jiangzhou. It happened that Liu Hong was away on business — it was Heaven too that meant mother and son to meet — and Xuanzang came directly to the gate of the private yamen to beg.

Now the lady Yin had that very night dreamed a dream: she saw the moon, once waned, grow round again. To herself she thought: "I have no word of my mother-in-law; my husband was murdered by that villain; my own child was cast into the river. If anyone has saved and reared him, he would by my reckoning be eighteen years old now. Perhaps Heaven means today that we should meet — who can say?"

As she sat thus musing, she suddenly heard someone before the yamen chanting scripture and calling again and again for alms. Taking the chance, the lady came out and asked, "Where have you come from?"

"This poor monk," answered Xuanzang, "is the disciple of the Abbot Faming of the Temple of the Golden Mountain."

"Since you are the disciple of the abbot of the Golden Mountain Temple..." said the lady, and she called him into the yamen and gave him a vegetarian meal to eat. As she watched his bearing and listened to his speech, she saw how like he was to her husband.

She sent her serving-maids away and asked him, "Little master, did you leave home to become a monk in your childhood, or in your middle years? What is your name? And have you father and mother?"

"I did not leave home as a child," Xuanzang answered, "nor did I leave home in middle age. When I tell it — my wrong is great as Heaven, my grievance deep as the sea. My father was murdered, and my mother was seized by the villain. My master, the Abbot Faming, sent me to seek my mother within the yamen of Jiangzhou."

"What is your mother's surname?" the lady asked.

"My mother's surname is Yin," said Xuanzang, "and her name is Wenjiao. My father's surname is Chen, his name Guangrui. My milk-name was River-Float, and my dharma-name was given as Xuanzang."

"I am Wenjiao!" said the lady. "But what proof have you now?"

When Xuanzang heard that this was his mother, he fell upon both knees and wept piteously. "If my mother does not believe me, here are the bloody letter and the undershirt for proof." Wenjiao took them and looked, and they were indeed genuine. Mother and son embraced and wept.

"My son, go quickly!" she said.

"For eighteen years I have not known those who bore me," said Xuanzang, "and only this morning have I seen my mother. How can I bear to tear myself away?"

"My son," she said, "you must withdraw at once. If the villain Liu returns, he will surely take your life. Tomorrow I will feign an illness and say that years ago I vowed to give away a hundred pairs of monk's shoes, and have come to your temple to fulfill the vow. Then I shall have words to say to you." Xuanzang obeyed and took his leave with a bow.

Now after the lady had seen her son, her heart was at once full of sorrow and of joy. One day she feigned sickness, would touch neither tea nor rice, and lay upon her bed. When Liu Hong returned to the yamen and asked the reason, the lady said, "When I was young I once made a vow to give away a hundred pairs of monk's shoes. Five days ago I dreamed of a monk holding a sharp blade, demanding the shoes — and ever since I have felt unwell."

"Such a small matter," said Liu Hong. "Why did you not say so sooner?" He went up to the hall and ordered Clerk Wang of the left office and Clerk Li of the right: every household in the city of Jiangzhou was to make one pair of monk's shoes, to be delivered within five days. The people all complied and delivered them in full.

"The shoes are made," the lady said to Liu Hong. "Is there any temple hereabouts where I may go to fulfill my vow?"

"There are the Golden Mountain Temple and the Burnt Mountain Temple here in Jiangzhou," said Liu Hong. "You may go to whichever you choose."

"I have long heard that the Golden Mountain Temple is a fine one," said the lady. "I will go there." Liu Hong at once called Clerks Wang and Li to make ready a boat. The lady took her trusted attendants and went aboard, and the boatmen poled off and headed for the Golden Mountain Temple.

Now Xuanzang had returned to his temple and told the Abbot Faming all that had passed, and the abbot was greatly pleased. The next day a maidservant came ahead to announce that the lady was coming to the temple to fulfill a vow, and all the monks came out to greet her. The lady went straight in at the temple gate, paid her devotions to the Bodhisattva, and set out a great offering-feast. She bade her maid place the monk's shoes and stockings upon a tray, and carried them to the dharma-hall, where she again lit incense in worship and had the Abbot Faming distribute them among the monks.

When Xuanzang saw that the monks had dispersed and there was no one left in the dharma-hall, he drew near and knelt down. The lady bade him take off his shoes and stockings, and looked — and there, sure enough, the little toe was missing from his left foot. Then again the two embraced and wept, and gave thanks to the abbot for the kindness of rearing him.

"Now that mother and son have met," said Faming, "I fear the treacherous villain may come to know of it. You must withdraw quickly, lest disaster fall."

"My son," said the lady, "I give you this incense-ring. Go straight to the region northwest of Hongzhou — some fifteen hundred *li* — and there you will find the inn of Ten Thousand Flowers. There I once left your grandmother, Lady Zhang; she is your father's own mother. I will write you another letter as well: take it straight to the imperial city of the Tang sovereign, to the household of the Prime Minister Yin Kaishan, to the left of the golden hall — they are my own father and mother. Give my letter to your grandfather and bid him petition the Tang king to send forth troops, seize and slay this villain, and avenge your father. Only then can your old mother's body be delivered. I dare not stay longer now, for I fear the villain will hold it against me if I return too late." And so she went out from the temple, boarded her boat, and departed.

Xuanzang wept his way back into the temple, took counsel with his master, and at once bade him farewell and set out straight for Hongzhou. Coming to the inn of Ten Thousand Flowers, he asked the innkeeper, Liu the Younger, "Years ago, the traveler Chen of Jiangzhou left a mother lodging at your inn. How does she fare now?"

"She was indeed at my inn," said Liu the Younger. "But afterward her eyes grew dim, and for three or four years she paid me no rent at all. Now she lives in a ruined tile kiln by the south gate, going out each day to beg on the streets to keep herself alive. That traveler went off long ago, and to this day there has been no word of him — I cannot tell why."

When Xuanzang heard this he hurried to the ruined kiln by the south gate and found the old woman.

"Your voice is much like my son Chen Guangrui's," she said.

"I am not Chen Guangrui," said Xuanzang. "I am Chen Guangrui's son. The lady Wenjiao is my mother."

"Why have your father and mother not come?" she asked.

"My father was beaten to death by a brigand," said Xuanzang, "and my mother was seized by the brigand for his wife."

"How did you come to know to seek me out?" she asked.

"My mother sent me to find you, Grandmother. Here is a letter from her, and an incense-ring as well." The old woman took the letter and the ring and wept aloud.

"My son went off for the sake of rank and honor," she said, "and I had thought he had turned his back on duty and forgotten kindness. Little did I know he had been murdered. Yet I am glad that Heaven has taken pity and not cut off my son's line — that today there is still a grandson to come and seek me."

"Grandmother," Xuanzang asked, "how is it your eyes have grown so dim?"

"It was through longing for your father," she said. "Day after day I watched for him and never saw him come, and so I wept until both my eyes grew dark."

Xuanzang knelt down and prayed toward Heaven: "I, Xuanzang, am now eighteen years old, and I have not been able to avenge my parents' wrong. Today, at my mother's bidding, I have come to seek my grandmother. If Heaven looks with pity upon your disciple's sincerity, restore the light to my grandmother's eyes." His prayer done, he licked her eyes with the tip of his tongue. In a moment, both eyes were licked open and were as they had been before.

The old woman looked at the little monk. "You are indeed my grandson," she said. "You are the very image of my son Guangrui." And she was at once joyful and grieved. Xuanzang then led his grandmother out from the kiln and back to Liu the Younger's inn, where he paid some rent to take a room for her to dwell in, and gave her money for expenses.

"I will be gone only a month or so before I return," he told her. And so he took leave of his grandmother and went straight on toward the capital.

Finding his way to the mansion of the Prime Minister Yin on the eastern street of the imperial city, he said to the gatekeeper, "This poor monk is a kinsman, come to call upon the minister." The gatekeeper reported this to the minister.

"I have no kinsman among the monks," said the minister.

But the lady said, "Last night I dreamed that our daughter Mantangjiao came home. Could it be that our son-in-law has sent some word back?" So the minister had the little monk brought into the hall.

When the little monk saw the minister and his lady, he fell weeping to the ground in obeisance, and from within his robe he drew a letter and handed it to the minister. The minister opened it and read it through from the beginning, and then wept aloud.

"My lord, what is the matter?" asked the lady.

"This monk is your grandson and mine," said the minister. "Our son-in-law Chen Guangrui was murdered by a brigand, and Mantangjiao was seized by the brigand for his wife." When the lady heard this, she too wept without ceasing.

"Do not grieve, my lady," said the minister. "Tomorrow I shall lay the matter before our sovereign, and I myself will lead troops and surely avenge our son-in-law."

The next day the minister went to court and made his report to the Tang king: "Your servant's son-in-law, the first scholar Chen Guangrui, was leading his household to take up his post at Jiangzhou when he was beaten to death by the boatman Liu Hong, who seized his wife for his own, falsely took my son-in-law's place, and has held office for many years. This is a thing of monstrous strangeness. I beg Your Majesty to send forth troops at once and root out the bandit."

When the Tang king heard the report he was greatly angered, and dispatched sixty thousand of the imperial guard, with the Prime Minister Yin to command the army and lead it forth. The minister received the edict and left the court; going to the parade ground, he mustered the troops and set out straight for Jiangzhou. Traveling by dawn and resting by night, beneath falling stars and flying birds, they came at last to Jiangzhou, where the minister's troops encamped on the northern bank.

In the dead of night he sent a golden tablet to summon the assistant prefect and the district magistrate of Jiangzhou. The minister told them of the matter and bade them raise their own soldiers to help, and together they crossed the river. While it was yet dark they surrounded Liu Hong's yamen. Liu Hong was deep in a dream when he heard the boom of a cannon and the clash of gongs and drums all at once; the soldiers stormed into the private yamen, and Liu Hong, taken unawares, was seized before he could lift a hand. The minister gave the order, had Liu Hong and his accomplices bound and marched off to the execution-ground, and commanded the rest of the army to make camp outside the city.

The minister went straight into the yamen and seated himself in the main hall, and called for the lady to come out and meet him. The lady wished to go out, yet was ashamed to face her father, and made to hang herself. Xuanzang heard of it and hurried to save his mother. Falling on both knees, he said to her, "Your son and his grandfather have led troops here to avenge my father. Now the villain is taken — why, Mother, do you instead seek death? If you die, how can your child live on?" The minister too came into the yamen to comfort her.

"I have heard," said the lady, "that 'a woman follows one husband to the end.' My husband, alas, was slain by the villain — how could I, with brazen face, have followed the villain? It was only because I bore his child in my womb that I endured shame and stole a wretched life. Now happily my son is grown, and I see my old father has brought troops to avenge us. But as a daughter, with what face can I look upon you? There is nothing left but to die, to requite my husband."

"This was no changing of your fidelity for the sake of fortune," said the minister. "It was all forced upon you by necessity. How can it be counted shame?" Father and daughter embraced and wept, and Xuanzang too could not cease his bitter weeping.

The minister wiped away his tears. "Do not, you two, give way to grief," he said. "I have now captured the enemy villain; let me go and deal with him." He rose and went to the execution-ground. Just then the assistant prefect of Jiangzhou had also sent scouts who had caught the river-bandit Li Biao and brought him in. The minister was greatly pleased, and bade the guards bring forth Liu Hong and Li Biao, and had each given a hundred heavy blows of the rod. He took their confessions, and they admitted the whole truth of how they had wickedly plotted years before to murder Chen Guangrui. First Li Biao was nailed to a wooden donkey and pushed off to the marketplace, where he was sliced a thousand cuts and beheaded as a warning to the crowd. Then Liu Hong was brought to the ferry crossing of the Hong River, the very place where years before he had beaten Chen Guangrui to death. There the minister, with the lady and Xuanzang — all three — went down to the riverside and made their offering toward the sky; they cut out the living heart and liver of Liu Hong, offered them to Guangrui, and burned a written eulogy.

As the three of them wept toward the river, their grief soon stirred the water-realm, and a patrolling sea-yaksha brought the eulogy before the Dragon King. When the Dragon King had read it, he sent his Marshal Turtle to invite Guangrui to come to him.

"Sir, I give you joy! I give you joy!" he said. "Your lady, your son, and your father-in-law are all at the riverside making offerings to you. Now I shall send you back to life, and grant you besides one wish-fulfilling pearl, two rolling-tray pearls, ten lengths of fine silk gauze, and a belt set with bright pearls and jade. Today you may be reunited, husband and wife, mother and son." Guangrui gave thanks again and again. The Dragon King then bade the yaksha bear Guangrui's body out to the river-mouth and restore him to life, and the yaksha went off to obey.

Now the lady Yin, having wept her offering over her husband, again wished to throw herself into the water and die, so that Xuanzang, in alarm, clung to her with all his strength. In the very midst of their confusion, a corpse suddenly came floating upon the water's surface and drew near the bank. The lady hurried forward to look, and knew it for her husband's body, and burst into wailing without end. Everyone came to look — and they saw Guangrui unclench his fists and stretch out his legs, his body little by little beginning to move; then all at once he scrambled up and sat. They were all struck with the greatest astonishment.

Guangrui opened his eyes, and there before him he saw the lady Yin, his father-in-law the Prime Minister Yin, and the little monk, all weeping at his side.

"Why are you all here?" said Guangrui.

"Because you were beaten to death by the villain," said the lady, "and afterward I bore this child. By good fortune the abbot of the Golden Mountain Temple raised him to manhood, and he came to find me. I bade him seek out his grandfather, and when my father learned of it he reported it to the court and led troops here, and we have captured the villain — just now we cut out his living heart and liver and made our offering toward the sky for you, my husband. But how is it, husband, that you have come back to life?"

"It is all because of the golden carp you and I bought and set free that year at the inn of Ten Thousand Flowers," said Guangrui. "Who would have thought that carp was the Dragon King of this place? Later, when the traitor pushed me into the water, it was wholly thanks to him that I was saved. And just now he has granted me return to life and bestowed these treasures upon me — they are here upon my body. Little did I imagine you had borne this son, and that my father-in-law would avenge me. Truly, bitterness ended turns to sweetness — there is no greater joy."

When the officials heard of it, they all came to offer congratulations. The minister had a feast prepared to thank the local officials, and that same day the army began its homeward march. Coming to the inn of Ten Thousand Flowers, the minister gave the order to encamp. Guangrui, with Xuanzang, went to Liu's inn to seek his mother.

The old woman had that very night dreamed a dream: she saw a withered tree break into bloom, and behind the house magpies chattering again and again. "Could it be my grandson coming?" she thought. The words were scarcely out when there, outside the inn door, came Guangrui and his son together.

"Is this not my grandmother?" said the little monk, pointing. When Guangrui saw his old mother, he hastened to bow down before her. Mother and son embraced and wept aloud, and he told her all that had happened. They settled the rent with Liu the Younger and set out, returning to the capital.

Entering the minister's mansion, Guangrui with the lady, and the grandmother with Xuanzang, all came to greet the minister's wife. The lady's joy was beyond measure, and she bade the servants set out a great banquet of celebration.

"Today's feast," said the minister, "may be named the Feast of Reunion." And truly the whole household rejoiced together.

The next day at the early audience, when the Tang king took his seat, the Prime Minister Yin came forth from the ranks and laid the whole affair, from first to last, in full before the throne, and recommended Guangrui as a man fit for high employment. The Tang king approved the petition and at once commanded that Chen E be raised to the rank of Academician, to serve at court in the governance of affairs. Xuanzang, set in his resolve to practice meditation, was sent to cultivate the Way at the Temple of Vast Blessings. Afterward, the lady Yin in the end quietly took her own life; and Xuanzang returned to the Golden Mountain Temple to repay the kindness of the Abbot Faming.

What befell hereafter is not yet known — listen, and the next chapter will make it clear.

<!-- chapter 10 -->
# Chapter 10: The Old Dragon King's Reckless Scheme Breaks Heaven's Law; Minister Wei Sends a Letter to the Officer of the Dead

Let us set aside for now the tale of Guangrui fulfilling his office and Xuanzang pursuing his cultivation. Instead, let us tell of two worthy men who lived beyond the walls of Chang'an, on the banks of the Jing River. One was a fisherman named Zhang Shao; the other a woodcutter named Li Ding. They were scholars who had never sat for the examinations, mountain hermits who happened to be lettered.

One day, having sold the firewood from his shoulders and traded away the carp in his basket, the two of them went together into a wine shop, drank until they were half-tipsy, and then, each carrying a bottle, strolled slowly homeward along the bank of the Jing River.

Said Zhang Shao, "Brother Li, when I consider the men who scramble after fame, they lose their lives because of fame; those who snatch after profit perish for the sake of profit; those who receive titles sleep as though embracing a tiger; those who bask in imperial favor walk as though a snake were hidden in their sleeve. Reckon it up, and none of them comes near to us — clear waters and green hills, free and unfettered, content with our plain fare, drifting along as fortune carries us."

"Brother Zhang speaks with reason," said Li Ding. "Yet your clear waters cannot match my green hills."

"Your green hills are no match for my clear waters," replied Zhang Shao. "I have a lyric to the tune *Butterflies Love Flowers* to prove it. The words run:

> A small skiff upon ten thousand miles of misty waves,
> quietly leaning against the lonely awning,
> while a voice as sweet as Xishi's lingers all around.
> Washed clean of cares, washed clean of name and gain,
> I idly pluck the smartweed plumes and reed-grass blades.
>
> A few dots of sandy gulls — there is the Way to delight in,
> willowed banks and reedy coves,
> wife and child laughing together in joy.
> One sound sleep, and wind and waves are stilled —
> no glory, no disgrace, and not a single care."

Said Li Ding, "Your clear waters cannot match my green hills. I too have a lyric to the same tune *Butterflies Love Flowers* for proof. The words run:

> A stretch of cloud-wreathed forest, pine pollen drifting full,
> and silently I listen to the orioles cry,
> their clever tongues like tuned pipes.
> Reds thinning, greens fattening — spring is at its warmest,
> then suddenly the summer solstice turns the light.
>
> Again comes autumn, easy in its change,
> yellow blossoms fragrant, fit for delight.
> Swiftly stern winter passes like a snap of fingers —
> through all four seasons I roam free, with no man to rule me."

Said the fisherman, "Your green hills cannot match my clear waters, where I take my pleasure in fine things. I have a lyric to the tune *Partridge Sky* for proof:

> Among the immortals' clouds and waters my whole living lies,
> I work the oar and turn my boat — and that is home.
> Fresh-scaled fish carved alive, green turtles stewed,
> purple crabs steamed at once, red shrimp set boiling.
>
> Green reed-shoots, water-fern sprouts,
> water-chestnuts and gorgon-fruit are worthier still.
> Tender lotus-root, old lotus, celery leaves so green,
> arrowhead, wild rice-stem, and the heron-flower bloom."

Said the woodcutter, "Your clear waters cannot match my green hills, where I take my pleasure in fine things. I too have a lyric to *Partridge Sky* for proof:

> Towering steep peaks that touch the edge of heaven,
> a thatched hut, a grass-roofed cell — that is my home.
> Salted and cured fowl beat any crab or turtle,
> river-deer, hare, and deer surpass your fish and shrimp.
>
> Fragrant toon leaves, golden chinaberry sprouts,
> bamboo shoots and mountain tea are worthier still.
> Purple plums, red peaches, ripe apricots and mei,
> sweet pears, sour jujubes, and the osmanthus flower."

Said the fisherman, "Your green hills truly cannot match my clear waters. I have yet another, to the tune *Immortal of Heaven*:

> A single leaf of a boat goes wherever it lodges,
> ten thousand folds of misty wave, and not a trace of fear.
> I drop the hook and cast the net to take the fresh-scaled fish —
> no sauce, no grease, and yet a flavor all its own,
> while old wife and young child gather round in joy.
>
> When the fish are many, I sell them in Chang'an's market,
> and trade for fragrant brew to drink myself to bliss.
> My straw cape for a quilt, I lie upon the autumn river,
> snore upon snore I sleep,
> with not a worry,
> never coveting the world's glory and rank."

Said the woodcutter, "Your clear waters still cannot match my green hills. I too have one to the tune *Immortal of Heaven*:

> A thatched cottage of a few rafters built below the hill,
> with pine and bamboo, plum and orchid — truly to be loved.
> Through the woods, over the ridges, I seek out the dry kindling,
> and no man blames me;
> I sell as I please,
> a little or a lot, just as the world will have it.
>
> I take the coin and buy my wine, glad as my heart desires,
> with earthen bowl and crockery cup, wholly at my ease.
> Dead drunk, I lie down in the shade of the pines,
> with nothing to bind me,
> nothing to harm me,
> heedless of the world's rising and its fall."

Said the fisherman, "Brother Li, your trade in the mountains is not so merry as my livelihood upon the water. I have a lyric to *The Moon over the West River* for proof:

> Red smartweed blossoms thick, mirrored in the moon,
> yellow reed-leaves wildly tossing in the wind.
> The azure sky stretches clear above the empty Chu River,
> and a tug of the line sets a whole pool of stars trembling.
>
> Great fish swim into the net in schools,
> small mandarin-fish swallow the hook in shoals.
> Brought home and cooked, the flavor is the richer —
> I laugh aloud, proud lord of river and lake at my carousing."

Said the woodcutter, "Brother Zhang, your trade upon the water is not so merry as my livelihood in the mountains. I too have a *Moon over the West River* for proof:

> Withered leaves and dry vines fill the path,
> broken branch-tips and old bamboo crowd the hills.
> The wild creeper and dry kudzu tangle and clamber,
> I cut them down, gather the rope, and lash my load.
>
> Worm-eaten, hollow-hearted elm and willow,
> wind-snapped, headless pine and nanmu.
> I gather them, pile them up against the winter cold,
> and trade them for wine, trade them for coin, as I please."

Said the fisherman, "Your mountains may be a match, yet they cannot equal the secluded grace of my clear waters. I have a lyric to *Immortal by the River* for proof:

> When the tide ebbs I shift my lonely skiff away,
> and deep in the night I cease the oar and come singing home.
> Straw cape under a waning moon — how secluded and serene!
> The roosting gulls, startled, do not rise,
> and at the sky's rim the bright clouds open.
>
> Weary, I lie upon the reed-isle with not a care,
> the sun three poles high, and still I lie at ease.
> As heart and whim incline, I arrange my own affairs —
> while courtiers shiver, waiting for the dripping clock to call them,
> how can their lot compare to my broad ease of mind?"

Said the woodcutter, "The secluded grace of your clear waters still cannot match the deeper seclusion of my green hills. I too have an *Immortal by the River* to prove it:

> Down the mossy path, autumn high, I drag my axe away,
> and in the cool of evening shoulder my load back home.
> Wildflowers tucked at my temples — stranger still and finer!
> I push aside the clouds to find my road out,
> and wait upon the moon to call the gate to open.
>
> Young children and mountain wife greet me with glad smiles,
> grass bed and wooden pillow where I lean and rest.
> Steamed pears and millet cooked are spread out in a moment,
> and in the jar the new-brewed wine is ripe —
> truly it swells the secluded heart."

Said the fisherman, "These are but the trades by which the two of us feed ourselves; yet you cannot match the good of my idle hours. I have a poem for proof. The poem runs:

> Idle I watch the azure heaven where white cranes fly,
> I moor my boat by the brook and close my plain gate fast.
> Leaning on the awning I teach my son to twist his fishing line,
> the oar laid by, with my wife I dry the netting ring.
> The temper settled is indeed like waters calm,
> the body at peace will feel the wind itself grow soft.
> Green straw cape and blue bamboo hat I wear as the hour requires —
> better than wearing the purple-corded robes of court."

Said the woodcutter, "Your idle hours are still not so good as my idle hours. I too have a poem for proof. The poem runs:

> Idle I watch the faint white clouds that float on high,
> alone I sit in my thatched cell and shut the bamboo gate.
> With nothing to do I teach my son and open up a book,
> and now and then with a guest I set the chessmen out.
> When joy comes I take my staff and sing along the fragrant lane,
> when the mood rises I carry my zither up the verdant slopes.
> Straw sandals, hempen cord, and a quilt of coarse cloth —
> a heart at ease is better far than wearing gauze and silk."

Said Zhang Shao, "Li Ding, the two of us are truly fit to be intimate companions in our soft chanting; we have no need of clappers and golden goblets. But to scatter off mere lyric verses is nothing rare. Let us each link a few lines and see how our fisher-and-woodcutter parley turns out." Said Li Ding, "Brother Zhang's words are most apt. I beg my brother to chant first." So Zhang Shao began:

> My boat lies moored amid green water's misty waves,
> his home is set deep in the mountains' open wilds.
> I love above all the brook-bridge when the spring waters rise,
> he loves above all the rocky crags veiled in dawn cloud.
> Fresh carp from the Dragon Gate I stew from time to time,
> worm-eaten dry kindling he sets ablaze each day.
> The hook and net, in all their kinds, can keep a man to his old age,
> the carry-pole and rope — two things — can see one through to the end.
> In my little boat, lying back, I watch the wild geese fly,
> on the grassy path, leaning aside, he hears the wild swans cry.
> In the wrangling-grounds of gossip I have no part,
> in the seas of right and wrong few are my footprints found.
> By the brook I hang and dry my net like a brocade,
> upon the rock he grinds his axe again to a keen edge.
> Under the bright autumn moon I often fish alone,
> on the silent spring mountains he meets no man at all.
> Fish in plenty I trade for wine and drink it with my wife,
> kindling to spare he sells for a jug and shares it with his son.
> Each of us sings to himself, pours for himself, abandoned and free,
> long we sing, long we sigh, careless of the whirling wind.
> Calling our brothers, hailing our mates, we summon the boat-fellows,
> taking friends, leading comrades, we gather the country elders.
> Playing the wine-game, guessing fingers, we pass the cup round and round,
> breaking the dominoes, spelling the words, we idly pass the chime.
> Boiling shrimp and cooking crab, each morning is a joy,
> frying duck and braising chicken, each day is a feast.
> My homely wife brews the tea, her manner free and light,
> his mountain wife cooks the rice, her bearing calm and slow.
> At dawn I lift my pole to dredge through the light waves,
> at sunrise he shoulders his wood across the great divide.
> After the rain I don my cape and catch the living carp,
> before the wind he plies his axe and fells the withered pine.
> Hiding our tracks, shunning the world, we play the dull and foolish,
> concealing our names, burying our surnames, we feign the deaf and dumb."

Said Zhang Shao, "Brother Li, just now I presumed to lead off with the opening lines. Now it falls to my brother — you too lead off with a couplet, and I, your younger brother, will continue it." So Li Ding began:

> Feigning madness in wind and moon, a wild fellow of the hills,
> lodging his pride in river and lake, an old man past his prime.
> The pure and idle have their share of free and easy ways,
> with no gossip in our ears, we delight in the great peace.
> On moonlit nights my body sleeps secure in its thatched hut,
> when the sky darkens I cover myself with a light bamboo cape.
> Forgetting the world, I make my friends of the pine and the plum,
> gladly I bind in fellowship with the gull and the egret.
> In my heart no scheming after name and gain,
> at my ear no sound of shield and spear.
> As the hour permits, a single cup of fragrant brew,
> to pass the day, three meals of wild-herb broth.
> Two bundles of kindling are my means of life,
> a single rod and line are my whole livelihood.
> Idly I call my young son to grind the steel axe sharp,
> quietly I summon my simple boy to mend the old net.
> When spring comes I love to watch the willows turn green,
> when the season thaws I gladly see the reeds grow blue.
> In summer's heat I trim fresh bamboo for the cool,
> in the sixth month, taking the air, I pluck the tender water-chestnuts.
> When frost descends the chickens are fat and often slaughtered,
> at the Double Ninth the crabs are plump and stewed in season.
> When winter comes, the sun risen, I still sleep sound,
> through the deepest cold the sky is high, yet of myself I feel no chill.
> Through the eight festivals in the mountains I follow my nature,
> through the four seasons on the lake I please my mood at will.
> In gathering firewood there is the joy of the immortals' households,
> in dropping the hook there is nothing of the world's vulgar form.
> Beyond my gate the wildflowers bloom fragrant and bright,
> at my boat's prow the green waters lie level and calm.
> The body at ease, I speak not of the rank of the Three Dukes,
> the temper settled is stronger than a city walled ten miles round.
> A city walled ten miles high must guard against the watch-commands,
> the high office of the Three Dukes must heed the herald's proclamations.
> To delight in mountains, to delight in waters — this is rare indeed.
> Thanks be to Heaven, thanks be to Earth, thanks be to the gods!"

When the two of them had each spoken their lyric verses and linked their poems together, they came to the place where their roads parted, and bowing, they took their leave. Said Zhang Shao, "Brother Li, take care along the way. As you go up the mountain, watch closely for tigers. If some peril should befall you, then indeed 'on the street tomorrow there will be one old friend the fewer.'"

At these words Li Ding flew into a great rage. "You worthless rascal!" he cried. "A good friend would lay down his life for me — how can you curse me so? If I should meet a tiger and come to harm, then you are bound to meet the waves and be capsized in the river!"

"I shall never in all my life be capsized in the river," said Zhang Shao.

"'The sky holds unforeseen winds and clouds; a man holds sudden fortune and disaster,'" said Li Ding. "How can you be so sure of coming to no harm?"

"Brother Li," said Zhang Shao, "though you talk this way, it is you who can take no measure of your trade — whereas my livelihood I can take the measure of, and I shall surely meet no such mishap."

"Your business on the water," said Li Ding, "is most perilous, most dangerous, hidden and dark — what measure can you possibly take of it?"

"You do not understand," said Zhang Shao. "In the city of Chang'an, on the street by the West Gate, there is a fortune-teller. Every day I bring him a golden carp, and he gives me a reading from his sleeve. I follow the directions he gives, and it is a hundred casts, a hundred hauls — never a miss. Today I went again to buy a reading, and he told me to cast my net on the east side of the bend in the Jing River, and to throw my hook on the western bank, and I shall surely come home with a full load of fish and shrimp. Tomorrow I'll go up to the city, sell them for coin, buy wine, and we'll meet again, old brother." And so the two parted.

Now this is just the case of "words spoken on the road, with someone hidden in the grass." For it happened that in the water-palace of the Jing River there was a patrolling yaksha on the night-watch, who, hearing those words of "a hundred casts, a hundred hauls," went hurrying back to the Crystal Palace and reported to the Dragon King in a panic, "Disaster! Disaster!"

"What disaster?" asked the Dragon King.

Said the yaksha, "Your servant, patrolling the waters, came to the riverbank, and there I heard two men, a fisherman and a woodcutter, in conversation. As they parted, their words were exceedingly dangerous. The fisherman said that in the city of Chang'an, on the street by the West Gate, there is a fortune-teller whose reckonings are most exact. Every day he brings the man a carp, and the man gives him a reading from his sleeve, telling him a hundred casts, a hundred hauls — never a miss. If by such accurate reckoning he goes on, then will not all our water-tribe be utterly fished out? How then shall we keep the grandeur of the water-palace? How then shall we leap the waves and overturn the billows to aid Your Majesty's might?"

The Dragon King was enraged. He seized his sword at once and was about to go up to Chang'an to slay this fortune-teller, when forth stepped the dragon-sons and dragon-grandsons, the shrimp-ministers and crab-officers, the shad field-marshal, the mandarin-fish vice-minister, and the carp prime-minister, who all together submitted, "Let Your Majesty restrain your wrath. As the old saying goes, 'Words that pass the ear should not be believed.' If Your Majesty goes thus, you must be attended by clouds and aided by rain, and we fear you would alarm the common folk of Chang'an, and Heaven above would call you to account. Your Majesty appears and vanishes past all fathoming, and changes without fixed form — so let us merely transform into a single scholar and go into the city of Chang'an to make inquiry. If such a man truly exists, there will be time enough to slay him; but if there is no such man, would it not be a wanton injury to an innocent person?"

The Dragon King heeded their counsel, and so he laid aside his precious sword, raised neither cloud nor rain, went up onto the bank, and with a shake of his body transformed himself into a scholar in white. Truly:

> His bearing handsome and heroic, towering aloft as if to brush the clouds.
> His steps proper and composed, observing measure and rule.
> His speech followed Confucius and Mencius, his courtesy embodied the rites of King Wen.
> His body clad in jade-colored gauze and silken robes, his head crowned with a free-and-easy single-band kerchief.

Taking to the road, he spread out his cloud-stride and went straight to the great street by the West Gate of Chang'an. There he saw a knot of people, crowded and jostling, noisy and clamorous. Among them one was holding forth grandly: "He whose fate-sign is the Dragon, and he whose sign is the Tiger, are in conflict. The signs of Tiger and Dragon, Snake and Pig — though they are called a harmonious set, what is feared most is when the day offends the Lord of the Year." When the Dragon King heard this, he knew at once that this was the place of divination. He came forward, parted the crowd, and looked within. He saw:

> The four walls hung with pearls and jade, the whole hall filled with embroidered silks.
> The treasure-duck censer never ceasing its incense, the porcelain vase with water so clear.
> On either side arrayed the paintings of Wang Wei, above the seat hung high the portrait of Guiguzi.
> An inkstone of Duanxi, golden smoke-ink, set off against the great frost-tipped brush;
> the Fire-Pearl Grove text, the calculations of Guo Pu, faced squarely by the new Classic of the Terrace's governance.
> Versed in the Six Lines, perfect in the Eight Trigrams,
> he could know the principles of Heaven and Earth, and well understood the ways of ghosts and gods.
> The compass-board with its meridian fixed and set, his breast full of stars laid out in clear array.
> Truly the things to come, the things gone by, he viewed as in a moon-bright mirror;
> how many houses prosper, how many fall, he discerned as clear as a god.
> He knew ill and fixed good fortune, foretold death and spoke of life.
> Opening his talk, the wind and rain rushed forth; setting down his brush, the very ghosts and gods were startled.
> The signboard bore his name in writing — Master Yuan Shoucheng, the diviner of spirit-readings.

Who was this man? He was, in fact, the uncle of Master Yuan Tiangang, Director of the Imperial Astronomical Bureau at court — this Yuan Shoucheng. The master was indeed of rare appearance and elegant bearing, his name famed throughout the great realm, his art unmatched in all Chang'an. The Dragon King came in at the door and greeted the master. The courtesies done, he invited the Dragon to take the seat of honor, and a serving-boy brought tea. The master asked, "On what business has the gentleman come to inquire?"

Said the Dragon King, "I beg a reading concerning the matter of fair weather and foul in the heavens."

The master at once drew a reading from his sleeve and pronounced, "The clouds shroud the mountain-peaks, the mist veils the forest-tops. If you would divine the rain, it falls for certain tomorrow morning."

"At what hour tomorrow will it rain?" asked the Dragon King. "And how much rain — how many feet and inches?"

Said the master, "Tomorrow the clouds will spread at the hour of the Dragon, the thunder will break at the hour of the Snake, the rain will fall at the hour of the Horse, and the rain will be complete at the hour of the Goat — altogether three feet, three inches, and forty-eight drops of water."

The Dragon King laughed and said, "These words are not to be taken in jest. If it indeed rains tomorrow according to the hours and amounts you have pronounced, I will send you fifty taels of gold as my reading-fee in thanks. But if there is no rain, or if it does not match your hours and amounts, then I tell you plainly: I will surely smash the front of your shop, tear your signboard to pieces, and drive you out of Chang'an this instant, never to deceive the multitude here again."

The master answered cheerfully, "That shall be entirely as you please. Go now, go now. Tomorrow, after the rain, we will meet again."

The Dragon King took his leave, left Chang'an, and returned to the water-palace. The water-spirits great and small received him and asked, "How did Your Majesty fare in seeking out that fortune-teller?"

Said the Dragon King, "There is one, there is one, there is one — but he is only a glib-tongued fellow peddling forecasts of spring. I asked him when it would rain, and he said it would rain tomorrow. I asked him at what hour and in what amount, and he said the clouds would spread at the hour of the Dragon, the thunder break at the hour of the Snake, the rain fall at the hour of the Horse, and the rain be complete at the hour of the Goat — altogether three feet, three inches, and forty-eight drops of water. I made a wager with him: if it should fall exactly as he says, I'll send him fifty taels of gold in thanks; but if it differs by the least bit, I'll smash the front of his shop, drive him on his way, and never let him deceive the people of Chang'an again."

The water-tribe laughed and said, "Your Majesty is the chief commander of the Eight Rivers, the great Dragon-Spirit who governs the rain. Whether there is rain or no rain, Your Majesty alone knows it. How dare he talk such nonsense? That fortune-teller is certain to lose — certain to lose!"

Just then, while the dragon-sons and dragon-grandsons, the fish-lords and crab-officers, were still laughing and talking gleefully of this matter, there came a cry from the middle air: "Let the Dragon King of the Jing River receive the decree!" All looked up, and there was a strongman in golden robes, holding in his hands the edict of the Jade Emperor, coming straight toward the water-palace. In a fluster the Dragon King set his garments straight, composed himself with all solemnity, burned incense, and received the decree. The golden-robed strongman returned through the air. The Dragon King gave thanks for the grace, broke the seal, and looked. There it was written:

> By imperial command to the Commander of the Eight Rivers:
> drive the thunder, hurl the lightning forth;
> tomorrow morning send down the rain
> to bless and save the city of Chang'an.

The hours and the amounts named in the decree did not differ by a hair's breadth from what the master had judged. The Dragon King was so startled that his soul flew off and his spirits scattered. After a moment he came to himself and said to the water-tribe, "That there should be in the dusty mortal world a man of such power, who can truly penetrate the principles of Heaven and Earth — am I then to lose to him?"

The shad field-marshal submitted, "Let Your Majesty set his mind at ease. To beat him — where is the difficulty? Your servant has a small scheme that will surely silence that fellow's mouth." The Dragon King asked his plan, and the field-marshal said, "Let the rain be sent at the wrong hour and short of the proper count — then that fellow's reading will be wrong, and how can he fail to be beaten? Then we smash his signboard and drive him on his way — what is hard in that?"

The Dragon King took his counsel, and so set aside his worry.

The next day, he summoned the Earl of Wind, the Duke of Thunder, the Cloud-Lads, and the Mother of Lightning, and went straight up to the nine heavens above the city of Chang'an. He held off until the hour of the Snake before spreading the clouds, let the thunder break at the hour of the Horse, sent the rain down at the hour of the Goat, and stopped the rain at the hour of the Monkey — and even so let fall only three feet and forty drops. Thus he altered the hour by one watch, and cut short the count by three inches and eight drops. When the rain was done he dismissed the spirit-officers and sent his troops home. Then he pressed his cloud-head down again, transformed himself once more into the scholar in white, and going to the great street within the West Gate, burst into Yuan Shoucheng's divining shop. Without a word of explanation, he smashed the signboard, the brushes, the inkstones, and all to pieces. The master sat in his chair without stirring. The Dragon King then snatched up a door-plank to strike him, cursing, "You sorcerer who lies about fortune and disaster! You wretch who deludes the people's hearts! Your reading was false, your words were wild and absurd. The hour and the count of today's rain that you spoke of were all wrong. And yet you sit there grandly aloft! Get out at once, and I'll spare you the death you deserve!"

Yet Shoucheng remained utterly unafraid, not in the least. He turned his face up to heaven and laughed coldly, saying, "I am not afraid, I am not afraid. I have no crime worthy of death — but I fear that it is *you* who have a crime worthy of death. Others you may deceive, but it is hard to deceive me. I know you: you are no scholar — you are the Dragon King of the Jing River. You have defied the decree of the Jade Emperor, altered the hours, and cut short the count — you have broken the law of Heaven. On the Dragon-Quartering Terrace, I fear, you can scarcely escape the blade. And here you stand cursing me?"

When the Dragon King heard this, his heart quailed and his courage failed, his hair stood on end and his flesh crept. He flung away the door-plank at once, straightened his robes, made his obeisance, and knelt down before the master, saying, "Master, do not blame me. My earlier words were spoken in jest — how could I know that the make-believe would become real, and that I should truly break the law of Heaven? What am I to do? I beg the master to save me, to save me — and if you do not, then in death I will not let you go!"

Said Shoucheng, "Save you I cannot — but I can point out to you a path to life, that you may find your way." Said the Dragon, "I beg you to instruct me." The master said, "Tomorrow, at the third quarter of the hour of the Horse, you are to be brought for sentence of beheading before the officer of human affairs, Wei Zheng. If you truly wish to keep your life, you must go at once, with all speed, and plead with the present sovereign, Emperor Tang Taizong — that will be best. For this Wei Zheng is the prime minister beneath the throne of the Tang king; if you can win from him some favor, then your safety is assured."

The Dragon King heard this, took his leave with bows and brimming tears, and departed. Before he knew it, the red sun was sinking in the west and the moon-star had risen. There was to be seen:

> Mist gathers, mountains turn purple, the homing crows grow weary,
> travelers on the distant road put in at their inns.
> By the ferry-head the new wild geese roost on the sandy shoals,
> the Milky Way appears,
> the watch-tally is sounded,
> and in the lonely village the lamplight burns without a flame.
> The wind curls the censer-smoke about the quiet temple yard,
> in the butterfly's dream the dreamer is nowhere seen.
> The moon shifts the shadows of the flowers up onto the railing,
> the starlight scatters,
> the dripping-clock changes its tally,
> and unawares the deep, deep night is already half gone.

This Dragon King of the Jing River did not return to his water-palace, but stayed up in the air. He waited until about the hour of the Rat, then gathered up his cloud-head, drew in his horns of mist, and went straight to the gate of the imperial palace. At that very time the Tang king was dreaming that he had walked out beyond the palace gate and was strolling under the moon in the shade of the flowers. Suddenly the Dragon King, in the form of a man, came forward, knelt and bowed, and cried out, "Your Majesty, save me, save me!" Said Taizong, "Who are you? I will surely save you." Said the Dragon King, "Your Majesty is the True Dragon; your servant is a doomed dragon. Because I have broken the law of Heaven, I am to be beheaded by Your Majesty's worthy minister, the officer of human affairs, Wei Zheng — and so I have come to make my plea, hoping Your Majesty will save me, will save me." Said Taizong, "Since it is Wei Zheng who is to behead you, I can save you. Set your heart at ease and go." The Dragon King rejoiced, kowtowed his thanks, and departed.

Now when Taizong woke from his dream, he kept the matter fixed in his mind. Already it was the third point of the fifth watch. Taizong held court and gathered the two ranks of civil and military officials. There was to be seen:

> Mist enwreathing the phoenix-towers, fragrance hovering over the dragon-halls.
> The light shimmers, the vermilion screens stir; the clouds brush the kingfisher-plumed canopies as they flow.
> Sovereign and ministers in concord, like Yao and Shun; their rites and music, stern in majesty, near to Han and Zhou.
> The attendants' lamps, the palace-maids' fans, pair upon pair reflecting bright colors;
> the peacock screens, the unicorn hall, everywhere the light floats high.
> They cry "Ten thousand years!" to the hills, they wish a thousand autumns of glory.
> The silencing-whip cracks three times, and the capped and gowned bow to the crown.
> Palace blossoms blazing bright, the heavenly fragrance wafts; the dike-willows soft and gentle, the imperial music sings.
> The pearl curtains, the kingfisher curtains, drawn up high on golden hooks;
> the dragon-and-phoenix fans, the mountains-and-rivers fans, where the treasure-carriage halts.
> The civil officials handsome and refined, the military generals fierce and rousing.
> The royal way divides high from low, the vermilion steps array the ranks of office.
> Golden seals and purple cords ride upon the three elephants —
> long as earth, enduring as heaven, ten thousand thousand autumns.

When the officials had finished their court-salutations, they each took their places by rank. The Tang king opened his phoenix-eyes and dragon-pupils and looked them over one by one. Among the civil officials he saw Fang Xuanling, Du Ruhui, Xu Shiji, Xu Jingzong, Wang Gui, and the rest; among the military he saw Ma Sanbao, Duan Zhixuan, Yin Kaishan, Cheng Yaojin, Liu Hongji, Hu Jingde, Qin Shubao, and the rest — each one of awesome and solemn bearing. But the prime minister Wei Zheng was nowhere to be seen. The Tang king summoned Xu Shiji up to the hall and said, "Last night I had a strange dream. I dreamed that a man came forward to make me his obeisance, calling himself the Dragon King of the Jing River. He said that he had broken the law of Heaven and was to be beheaded by the officer of human affairs, Wei Zheng, and he begged me to save him, and I gave my promise. Today, of all those before the court, only Wei Zheng is not to be seen. Why is this?"

Shiji answered, "This dream foretells the truth. Wei Zheng must be summoned to court, and Your Majesty must not let him go out of the door. Keep him past this one day, and the dragon of the dream may be saved." The Tang king rejoiced, and at once issued an order that the officer on duty should summon Wei Zheng to court.

Now the prime minister Wei Zheng, in his own residence, had been observing the celestial signs by night and burning precious incense, when he heard the cry of a crane in the nine heavens — it was a heavenly messenger sent by the gods, bearing a golden decree of the Jade Emperor, charging him at the third quarter of the hour of the Horse to behead in a dream the old dragon of the Jing River. The prime minister gave thanks for Heaven's grace, fasted and bathed, and in his residence tested the blade of wisdom and exercised his primal spirit — and for this reason he had not gone to court. When suddenly he saw the officer on duty come bearing the summons, he was filled with dread; yet not daring to delay the sovereign's command, he could only make haste, set his garments and girdle straight, and go in with the summons to the court, where before the imperial presence he kowtowed and begged pardon for his fault. Said the Tang king, "I absolve my minister of all blame." At that time the other officials had not yet withdrawn from court; now the king commanded the screens be rolled up and the court dismissed. He kept Wei Zheng alone, summoned him up to the golden throne-room, called him into the side hall, and first discussed with him the strategies for securing the realm and the plans for settling the state.

When the time drew near the end of the hour of the Snake and the beginning of the hour of the Horse, the king commanded the palace attendants, "Bring over the great chessboard. I will play a game with my worthy minister." The palace ladies fetched the chessboard and set it out upon the imperial table. Wei Zheng gave thanks for the grace, and at once played against the Tang king, each setting down a piece in turn, laying out their formations. It accorded well with the *Classic of the Rotted Axe-Handle*, which says:

> The way of chess prizes care and rigor. The strong play to the center, the weak to the edges, the middling to the corners — this is the common method of the chess-master. The rule says: "Rather lose a single stone than lose a single move." Strike to the left while watching the right; attack behind while looking before. There is a leading that comes after, and a following that comes first. Where two are alive, do not cut them; where all are alive, do not connect them. Be not too sparse in your openness, nor too crowded in your density. Better than clinging to a stone in search of life is to abandon it and take the victory; better than going alone with nothing to do is to make yourself firm and repair your own. When the enemy is many and you are few, first contrive your own survival; when you are many and the enemy few, strive to spread out your force. The good winner does not contend; the good arrayer does not fight; the good fighter is not defeated; the good loser is not thrown into disorder. For chess begins by joining with the orthodox and ends by winning through the unexpected. When an enemy with nothing to do mends his own position, he has a mind to invade and cut you off; when he abandons the small and does not save it, he has a heart set on the great; he who plays as his hand falls is a man without a plan; he who responds without thought takes the road to defeat. The *Book of Songs* says: "Anxious and careful, as if standing at the edge of an abyss." This is what is meant.
>
> The poem runs:
> The chessboard is the earth, the stones are heaven,
> their colors set by yin and yang, the work of creation complete.
> Played to the subtle point where the changes are fathomed through,
> one laughs and boasts of that immortal of the bygone Rotted Axe.

The two of them, sovereign and minister, played on, and the game came just to the third quarter of the hour of the Horse, with a single ruined position not yet finished, when Wei Zheng suddenly bent down upon the edge of the table and fell fast asleep, snore upon snore. Taizong laughed and said, "My worthy minister is truly wearied with the toil of upholding the altars of state, and spent with the labor of founding the realm — and so without knowing it he has dozed off." Taizong let him sleep on and would not call to him. After no long while, Wei Zheng woke, prostrated himself upon the ground, and said, "Your servant deserves ten thousand deaths, your servant deserves ten thousand deaths! Just now I was overcome with weariness and knew not what I did — I beg Your Majesty to forgive your servant the crime of slighting his sovereign." Said Taizong, "What crime of slighting have you? Get up now, and clear away the ruined game, and we will play afresh."

Wei Zheng gave thanks for the grace and had just taken a stone into his hand when suddenly there came a great shouting and clamor from outside the court gate. It was Qin Shubao, Xu Maogong, and the others, who bore in a dripping dragon's head and flung it down before the throne, submitting, "Your Majesty, that the seas should run shallow and the rivers run dry has been seen before, but such a marvel as this has never been heard of!" Taizong and Wei Zheng rose and said, "Where did this thing come from?" Said Shubao and Maogong, "South of the Thousand-Pace Gallery, at the crossroads, this dragon's head fell down from the midst of the clouds, and your servants dared not fail to report it." The Tang king, startled, asked Wei Zheng, "What is the meaning of this?" Wei Zheng turned, kowtowed, and said, "It is the dragon that your servant just now beheaded in his dream."

When the Tang king heard this, he was greatly astonished and said, "When my worthy minister was dozing, I saw you neither move your body nor stir your hands, and you had neither blade nor sword — how then did you behead this dragon?" Wei Zheng submitted, "My sovereign, my body was before my king, but my dream departed from Your Majesty's side. My body before my king faced the ruined game, my eyes closed in a drowsy haze; my dream departed from Your Majesty, riding an auspicious cloud, my spirit roused and vigorous. That dragon, upon the Dragon-Quartering Terrace, was bound fast by the heavenly troops and generals. And I said: 'You have broken the law of Heaven, and the crime deserves death. I bear the mandate of Heaven, to behead your remaining life.' The dragon, hearing, wailed in misery; your servant roused his spirit. The dragon, hearing, wailed in misery — it laid down its claws and drew in its scales and willingly received death; your servant, rousing his spirit, hitched up his robe, stepped forward, and raised the frost-bright blade. With a clashing stroke the blade swept down, and the dragon's head thereby fell into the empty air."

When Taizong heard this, his heart was divided between sorrow and joy. He was glad, for he praised Wei Zheng as a fine minister: with such a hero in his court, why should he fear that the realm would not be secure? He was sorrowful, for he had in the dream promised to save the dragon, and had not expected it would come to be slain after all. He could only force up his spirits and issue a decree that Shubao should hang the dragon's head in the marketplace to make it known to the common folk of Chang'an. On the one hand he rewarded Wei Zheng, and the officials dispersed.

That evening he returned to the palace, his heart heavy with melancholy. He thought of the dragon of the dream, that had wept and wailed and begged for its life — little knowing that impermanence is hard to escape, that this calamity could not be avoided. He brooded on it for a long while, and gradually felt his spirit grow weary and his body unwell. That very night, at about the second watch, he heard the sound of wailing and weeping outside the palace gate, and Taizong grew the more terrified. Just as he lay in a drowsy half-sleep, he saw again that Dragon King of the Jing River, holding in his hand a dripping, bloody head, crying aloud, "Tang Taizong, give me back my life! Give me back my life! Last night your mouth was full of promises to save me — how is it that at daybreak you turned about and summoned the officer of human affairs to behead me? Come out, come out! You and I will go before the King of the Underworld and argue this out!" He seized hold of Taizong and clamored again and again, refusing to let go. Taizong's mouth was sealed, he could not speak, and only struggled until the sweat ran down his whole body.

Just at this moment of hopeless deadlock, behold, in the southern sky fragrant clouds came curling and colored mists came drifting, and a female immortal came forward and with her hand waved a willow-branch — whereupon that headless dragon, weeping and wailing piteously, went off straight to the northwest. Now this was none other than the Bodhisattva Guanyin, who, bearing the Buddha's command, had come to the Eastern Land to seek out the pilgrim who would fetch the scriptures, and was lodging here in the city-god's temple of Chang'an. Hearing by night the ghost's weeping and the spirit's cries, she had come on purpose to drive back the doomed dragon and rescue the emperor. The dragon went straight to the courts of the underworld to lodge its complaint — but of that, no more for now.

Now when Taizong came to himself, he could only cry, "A ghost! A ghost!" In a fright the queens of the Three Palaces and the consorts of the Six Courts, together with the attendant eunuchs, trembled and quaked, and not one of them slept the whole night through.

Before they knew it, it was the third point of the fifth watch, and all the civil and military officials of the court waited outside the court gate for the audience. They waited until full daylight, yet still no audience was held, and one and all were struck with alarm and hesitation. When the sun was three poles high, at last a decree came forth, saying, "My heart is unwell; the officials are excused from audience." Five or seven days passed unawares; the officials grew anxious and fearful, and were just about to force the gate and seek an audience to inquire after the emperor's health, when there came an order from the Empress Dowager summoning the court physician into the palace to administer medicine. The crowd waited outside the court gate for news. After a little while the physician came out, and they asked what the illness was. Said the physician, "His Majesty's pulse is irregular — empty, and yet rapid; he raves wildly and sees ghosts. And I find that the pulse skips once in every ten beats: the five viscera are without vital force, and I fear the worst is to be feared within seven days."

When the officials heard this, they were stricken pale with dismay.

In the midst of their dismay, they heard another decree from the Empress Dowager summoning Xu Maogong, the Duke who Guards the Realm, and Yuchi Gong to an audience. The three lords obeyed the summons and hurried in to the foot of the Detached Palace Tower. When the obeisances were done, Taizong, composing his face and forcing himself to speak, said, "My worthy ministers, at nineteen I led troops, campaigning south and warring north, blocking the east and clearing the west; through bitter years of hardship I never once saw the least trace of evil spirits — yet today I see ghosts." Said Yuchi Gong, "In founding the realm you slew men beyond all counting; why then fear ghosts?" Said Taizong, "You do not believe it. Outside the door of my sleeping-chamber, when night comes, they fling bricks and rattle the tiles, the demons and goblins cry and howl, and it is truly past enduring. The daytime is bearable, but the dark of night is not to be borne." Said Shubao, "Set your heart at ease, Your Majesty. Tonight your servant and Jingde will stand guard at the palace gate and see what manner of ghost it is." Taizong granted the request. Maogong gave thanks for the grace and withdrew.

That day, when evening came, the two of them took up their armor and accoutrements, donned their helmets and cuirasses in full array, grasped the golden mace and the battle-axe, and stood guard outside the palace gate. What fine generals! See how they were arrayed:

> On their heads gleaming golden helmets, dazzling bright; their bodies cased in scaled armor like dragon-mail.
> The heart-guarding treasure-mirrors flash with auspicious clouds, the lion-buckled belts drawn tight, the embroidered sashes fresh with rosy light.
> This one's phoenix-eyes turned skyward make the very stars and constellations quail; that one's ringed eyes, mirroring the lightning, set the moonlight afloat.
> They were heroes and stalwarts, old ministers of merit — and so they came to be, for a thousand years, hailed as the Guardians of the Gate, and through all ages to serve as the Gods of the Door.

The two generals stood guard beside the gate, and through the whole night until dawn there was not the least sign of any evil. That night Taizong slept in the palace in peace and untroubled. When morning came he summoned the two generals and rewarded them richly, saying, "Since I fell ill, for several days I could get no sleep, and tonight, by the might of the two generals, I have been wholly at peace. Go now and rest yourselves, and tonight stand guard once more." The two generals gave thanks for the grace and withdrew.

Thus for two or three nights the watch was kept and all was peaceful. But the imperial meals dwindled, and the illness grew the heavier. Taizong, unwilling that the two generals should be so wearied, summoned Shubao and Jingde, together with Du and Fang and the other lords, into the palace, and charged them, saying, "These two days, though I have been at peace, it has been a hardship for the two generals Qin and Hu to keep watch through the whole night. I wish to summon a skilled painter to take the true likeness of the two generals and paste it on the door, to spare them the toil. How would that be?" The officials at once obeyed the order, chose two who were skilled at portraiture, and had the two lords Hu and Qin armored as before, and painted to the life, and the likenesses pasted on the door. And through the night there was again no trouble.

So it went for two or three days. Then there came from the rear palace gate a clattering and banging, bricks and tiles rattling in confusion. When morning came he at once summoned the officials and said, "These last days the front gate has happily been quiet, but tonight the rear gate clamors again — does it not nearly frighten me to death?" Maogong came forward and submitted, "When the front gate was troubled, Jingde and Shubao guarded it; for the rear gate's trouble, Wei Zheng should stand guard." Taizong granted the request, and summoned Wei Zheng to guard the rear gate that night. Wei Zheng received the command, and that night, accoutered in full array, grasping the precious sword with which he had slain the dragon, stood guard before the rear palace gate. Truly a fine hero! See how he was arrayed:

> A black kerchief of fine silk bound across his brow, a brocade robe with jade-girt belt hanging at his waist.
> The wind-catching cape's wide sleeves flutter like frost; he outdoes in aspect the very gods of the gate.
> His feet in black boots, seated firm; in his hand the keen blade, fierce and bold.
> His two eyes glaring round, peering on every side — what evil spirit dares come near?

The whole night through, bright as day, there was no demon either. And though front gate and rear gate were now both at peace, still his body grew steadily heavier.

One day, the Empress Dowager again issued a decree, summoning the officials to deliberate on the affairs of the funeral and interment. Taizong once more summoned Xu Maogong, charged him with the great affairs of state, and enjoined him after the manner of the Lord of Shu entrusting his orphan. When he had finished speaking, he bathed and changed his garments, and only awaited his hour. Then forth stepped Wei Zheng at his side, who took hold of the dragon-robe with his hand and submitted, "Let Your Majesty set your heart at ease. I have one thing that will surely secure Your Majesty's long life." Said Taizong, "The sickness has already entered the vitals, and my life is in peril — how can it be secured?" Said Wei Zheng, "Your servant has a letter which I present to Your Majesty, to carry down to the underworld and deliver to the Judge of Fengdu, Cui Jue." Said Taizong, "Who is Cui Jue?" Said Wei Zheng, "Cui Jue was a minister before the throne of the late former emperor. He first received the post of Magistrate of Cizhou, and was later promoted to Vice-Minister of Rites. In his lifetime he and your servant swore brotherhood with eight bows, and our friendship was deep. He is now dead, and serves in the underworld as the Judge of Fengdu in charge of the registers of life and death; in my dreams he often meets with me. If on this journey you give him this letter, then mindful of his slight bond with your servant, he will surely send Your Majesty back. I warrant that the soul shall return to the world of the living, and that the dragon-countenance shall surely come again to the imperial city." When Taizong heard this, he took the letter in his hand, tucked it into his sleeve, and then closed his eyes and died.

The queens of the Three Palaces and the consorts of the Six Courts, the empress and the imperial concubines, the chief attendants and the heir apparent, and the two ranks of civil and military officials, all raised the wail of mourning and donned their mourning weeds. And in the Hall of the White Tiger the coffin was laid in state — but of that, no more.

And as for how, in the end, Taizong returned to life — listen to the next chapter as it is told.

<!-- chapter 11 -->
# Chapter 11: The Emperor's Soul Journeys Through the Underworld and Returns to Life; Liu Quan Bears Melons to the Dead and Wins a New Bride

A poem says:

>   A hundred years of light and shadow flow away like water;
>   a whole life's labors are no more than bubbles on the stream.
>   Yesterday the face was flushed with the color of peach blossoms;
>   today the snowflakes drift and gather at the temples.
>   Only when the white-ant armies crumble is their pomp shown false;
>   when the cuckoo's cry grows urgent, turn back early.
>   Since ancient times, hidden good deeds can lengthen a life;
>   do good without begging for pity, and Heaven looks after all.

Now we tell how Emperor Taizong, dim and dazed, drifted in a faint, his soul slipping out from before the Tower of the Five Phoenixes. There he saw the cavalry of the Imperial Forest Guard, who begged the great carriage to ride forth from court and go hunting. The Emperor cheerfully consented and went off into the mist and haze. He traveled a long while — and then men and horses alike vanished. He was left all alone, wandering across desolate moors and weedy wilds.

Just as he was floundering in alarm, unable to find the road, he saw someone off to one side who cried out in a loud voice: "Great Tang Emperor — come this way! Come this way!" Hearing him, Taizong lifted his head and looked, and saw a man whose appearance was thus:

On his head a cap of black gauze; about his waist a sash of rhinoceros horn. The black gauze cap with its soft fluttering bands; the rhinoceros-horn sash set in gleaming gold. In his hand he gripped an ivory tablet, wrapped in auspicious vapors; on his body he wore a silken robe, glowing with hidden good omen. On his feet a pair of white-soled boots that trod the clouds and hastened the mists; in his breast he carried a Register of Life and Death, fixing who should live and who should die. His side-locks were tousled, drifting above his ears; his whiskers flew and curled about his cheeks. In days gone by he had been a minister of the Tang realm; now he kept the records as an officer attending King Yama.

When Taizong drew near, he saw the man kneel and bow beside the road, calling out: "Your Majesty, forgive your servant the offense of failing to come farther to welcome you." Taizong asked, "Who are you? And on what business have you come forward to receive me?" The man said, "Half a month ago, in the Hall of Endless Shadows, I saw the ghost-dragon of the Jing River accuse Your Majesty of promising to save him and then having him put to death instead. King Qinguang of the First Hall at once dispatched ghostly couriers to summon Your Majesty, that the case might be tried before the Three Tribunals. Knowing this, I came here to wait and welcome you. I did not expect to arrive late today — I beg you, forgive my fault, forgive my fault." Taizong said, "What is your surname and given name? What office do you hold?" The man replied, "While I lived, in the world of light I served before the late sovereign's throne as magistrate of Cizhou, and afterward was raised to Vice-President of the Board of Rites. My surname is Cui, my name is Jue. Now in the shadow realm I have been granted the post of Records Judge of Fengdu." Taizong was greatly pleased. He stepped forward and, with his own imperial hand, hastily raised the man up, saying, "Sir, you have toiled far on my account. My minister Wei Zheng entrusted me with a letter addressed to you, sir — and now, how fortunate, we have met!" The judge gave thanks and asked where the letter might be. Taizong reached into his sleeve, drew it out, and handed it over. Cui Jue received it with a bow, broke the seal, and read. The letter said:

>   With unworthy affection, your younger brother Wei Zheng bows his head and presents this letter to the desk of the Senior Records Officer, his sworn elder brother, the venerable Cui:
>   I remember our old fellowship; your voice and face are still before me. In a flash several years have passed, and I have heard nothing of your wise teaching. Always at the festival seasons I have set out vegetable offerings in sacrifice — though I cannot tell whether you have partaken. And then, not disdaining me, you appeared to me in a dream, and only then did I learn that you, my elder, had risen high. Yet, alas, the realms of light and shadow keep us apart, the heavens set us in separate quarters, and we cannot meet face to face. Now, because my Emperor Taizong, the Civil and Cultured, has suddenly passed away — I reckon his case is to be tried before the Three Tribunals, and surely he will come to meet with you, elder brother. I beg you, in remembrance of our lifelong friendship, to grant some small accommodation, and let my sovereign return to the world of light. That would be a singular kindness. I shall thank you again hereafter. Words cannot say it all.

When the judge had read the letter, his heart was filled with joy, and he said, "I already knew long since of how the human officer Wei beheaded the old dragon in his dream the other day — it is a deed beyond all praise.
