And he has so kindly looked after my children and grandchildren morning and evening. Now that this letter has come, let Your Majesty set your heart at ease. Your humble servant will see Your Majesty back to the world of light, that you may again ascend the jade throne." Taizong gave his thanks.

While the two of them were talking, there came a pair of blue-robed page-boys bearing pennants, banners, and a precious canopy, who called out: "King Yama requests your presence — your presence is requested." So Taizong, together with Judge Cui and the two boys, stepped forward and advanced. Suddenly there appeared a city, and over its gate hung a great placard inscribed with seven large golden characters: "The Gate of Ghosts of the Dark and Dismal Region of the Dead." The blue-robed boys shook out their pennants and led Taizong straight into the city, walking down the street. There along the roadside stood his late father Li Yuan, his late elder brother Jiancheng, and his dead younger brother Yuanji, who came forward crying: "Shimin has come! Shimin has come!" And Jiancheng and Yuanji rushed up to seize him and demand back their lives. Taizong could not dodge in time and was caught fast in their grasp. Luckily Judge Cui summoned a green-faced, fang-toothed ghost-courier, who bellowed Jiancheng and Yuanji back, and only then did Taizong win free and get away. Before he had gone many li, he saw a tower of emerald tiles, truly grand and splendid. Behold:

>   Drifting and heaped, ten thousand folds of colored sunset clouds;
>   dim and shadowed, a thousand strands of red mist appear.
>   Bright and shining, monster-heads soar from the eaves;
>   gleaming and glowing, five-layered mandarin-duck tiles.
>   Through the gate run rows of red-gold studs;
>   on the threshold lies one bar of white jade.
>   The lattice-windows let the dawn-smoke's brightness through;
>   the bamboo blinds flash bright as bolts of red lightning.
>   The tower soars high to touch the blue empyrean;
>   the corridors stretch level, joined to courts of treasure.
>   From beast-shaped censers the incense-clouds sweep over royal robes;
>   in crimson gauze the lantern-fires light the palace fans.
>   To the left, fierce and grim, are ranked the Ox-Heads;
>   to the right, towering and rugged, stand the Horse-Faces.
>   Receiving the dead and sending off the ghosts, the gold tablets turn;
>   guiding the souls and summoning the spirits, white streamers hang.
>   This is called the Great Assembly Gate of the Shadow World —
>   below it, old Yama's Hall of Endless Shadows.

While Taizong was looking on from outside, he heard the tinkling of girdle-pendants from inside the walls, and a strange and rare immortal fragrance. Two pairs of attendants came bearing candles, and behind them descended the Ten Kings of the Underworld, coming down the steps to meet him — the Ten Kings of the Ages, namely: King Qinguang, King Chujiang, King Songdi, King Wuguan, King Yama, King Pingdeng, King Taishan, King Dushi, King Biancheng, and King Zhuanlun. The Ten Kings came forth from the Treasure Hall of Endless Shadows, bowing low with arched backs to welcome Taizong. Taizong, in humility, dared not go forward. The Ten Kings said, "Your Majesty is a king of men in the world of light; we are ghost-kings of the world of shadow. Such is the proper order of things — why need you yield so much?" Taizong said, "I have given offense at your court — how should I dare to argue the ways of light and shadow, of men and ghosts?" And he deferred without end. At last he went forward, entered the Hall of Endless Shadows, exchanged courtesies with the Ten Kings, and they took their seats, host and guest in their proper places.

After a little while, King Qinguang clasped his hands and spoke: "The ghost-dragon of the Jing River accuses Your Majesty of promising to save him and then killing him instead. Why was this?" Taizong said, "I did indeed dream one night that the old dragon begged for rescue, and I truly granted that no harm should come to him. I did not expect that, having committed a crime that merited execution, he was to be beheaded by my human officer Wei Zheng. I had summoned Wei Zheng into the hall to play chess with me, and I did not know that in a single dream he carried out the beheading. This was the divine working of that human officer's mysterious power, and likewise it was that the Dragon King had committed a crime that merited death — how can it be counted my fault?" When the Ten Kings heard this, they prostrated themselves in courtesy and said, "Even before that dragon was born, it was already recorded in the Register of Death of the Southern Dipper Star that he was fated to be slain at the hand of a human officer. We have long known it. But because he so stubbornly disputed the matter here, insisting that Your Majesty be brought to face the case before the Three Tribunals, we have already sent him into the Wheel of Transmigration to be reborn. Now we have troubled Your Majesty to descend to us — we beg you, forgive our fault in summoning you." This said, they ordered the Records Judge who held the Register of Life and Death to fetch the book at once, and see how many years of earthly life and Heaven-allotted fortune Your Majesty should have. Judge Cui hurried back to the records office, took up the master register of the Heaven-allotted fortunes of all the kings of all the myriad nations, and examined it one by one. There he found that the Emperor Taizong of Great Tang, of the Southern Continent of Jambudvipa, was recorded as fated for thirteen years of the Zhenguan reign. Judge Cui gave a start, and quickly took up a thick brush dipped in heavy ink, added two strokes atop the character "one," and then presented the book. The Ten Kings looked it over from the top, and saw that beneath Taizong's name was recorded "thirty-three years." King Yama asked in surprise, "How many years has Your Majesty sat upon the throne?" Taizong said, "I came to the throne, and now it has been thirteen years." King Yama said, "Then set your heart at rest, Your Majesty, and have no worry — you still have twenty years of earthly life remaining. Now that this case has been clearly tried, we beg you to return to your roots and go back to the world of light." Hearing this, Taizong bowed and gave thanks. The Ten Kings of Yama dispatched two officers, Judge Cui and Grand Marshal Zhu, to escort Taizong back to life.

As Taizong left the Hall of Endless Shadows, he again raised his hands and asked the Ten Kings, "How fare the old and young of my palace?" The Ten Kings said, "All are well — but we fear the lifespan of the imperial sister may not be long." Taizong bowed once more and gave his thanks: "When I return to the world of light, I have nothing with which to repay you — only melons and fruit, that is all." The Ten Kings said happily, "Here we have plenty of winter-melons and watermelons — we lack only southern melons, the pumpkins." Taizong said, "When I return, I shall send them at once — I shall send them at once." And so, with bows of farewell, they parted.

Then the Grand Marshal took up a soul-leading banner and went ahead to guide the way, while Judge Cui followed behind, escorting Taizong, and they went straight out of the dark offices. Taizong raised his eyes and looked — it was not the old road. He asked the judge, "Is this the wrong way?" The judge said, "It is not wrong. In the shadow realm it is just so: there is a way out, but no way back in. Now we escort Your Majesty so that you may issue forth from the Wheel of Transmigration. First, that Your Majesty may tour and behold the Region of the Dead; second, that Your Majesty may be carried over into rebirth." Taizong had no choice but to follow the two of them as they led the way forward.

When they had gone a few li, they suddenly saw a high mountain, where dark clouds hung down to the ground and black mists blotted out the sky. Taizong said, "Master Cui, what mountain is that yonder?" The judge said, "It is the Mountain of the Dark and Dismal Shadow-Side." Taizong said in terror, "How shall I get across it?" The judge said, "Set your heart at ease, Your Majesty — we will lead you." Trembling and shaking, Taizong followed the two of them up the mountain crags. Lifting his head to look, he saw:

>   Its shape all hollows and bumps, its slopes still more rugged and steep.
>   Sharp as the ranges of Shu, high as the cliffs of Lu.
>   No famous mountain of the world of light, but a perilous place of the shadow realm.
>   In thicket upon thicket of brambles lurk ghosts and monsters;
>   among the glittering stone crags hide demons and fiends.
>   To the ear comes no cry of beast or bird;
>   to the eye appear only the walking shapes of ghosts and goblins.
>   The shadow-wind sighs and whistles; the black mist rolls and spreads.
>   The shadow-wind sighs and whistles — it is the smoke piped from the mouths of spirit-soldiers;
>   the black mist rolls and spreads — it is the breath spewed by ghosts in the dark.
>   Look far, high and low, and there is no scenery;
>   look about, left and right, and all is savage ruin.
>   There are mountains here, and peaks, and ridges, and caves, and ravines —
>   only the mountains grow no grass, the peaks pierce no sky,
>   the ridges bear no travelers, the caves hold no clouds,
>   the ravines run with no water.
>   On the slopes before are all goblins; below the ridges, all demons;
>   the caves take in the wild ghosts; the ravine-bottoms hide the evil souls.
>   Before the mountain and behind, the Ox-Heads and Horse-Faces clamor in confusion;
>   half-hidden, half-concealed, the hungry ghosts and ruined souls weep to each other.
>   The life-hastening judges hurry and bustle, passing on their summons-tickets;
>   the soul-pursuing marshals shout and bellow, speeding their official documents.
>   The swift-footed runners roll along like whirlwinds;
>   the arresting officers swirl thick in the black mist.

Relying wholly on the judge's protection, Taizong crossed the Shadow Mountain.

Going onward, they passed through many more government offices, and at every one of them mournful cries rang in the ears, and hideous monsters startled the heart. Taizong asked again, "What place is this?" The judge said, "These are the Eighteen Layers of Hell, behind the Shadow Mountain." Taizong said, "Which are the eighteen layers?" The judge said, "Listen, and I will tell you:

>   The Hell of the Hanging Sinews, the Hell of Dark Injustice, the Hell of the Fire-Pit — silent and forlorn, fretful and full of woe — these are all for the thousand kinds of evil done in life, whose punishments are reckoned and paid after death.
>   The Hell of Fengdu, the Hell of the Tongue-Pulling, the Hell of the Flaying — weeping and wailing, wretched and grim — for the disloyal and unfilial who wounded the principles of Heaven, who had Buddha's mouth and a serpent's heart, and fell through this gate.
>   The Hell of the Grinding, the Hell of the Pounding-Pestle, the Hell of the Crushing Cart — skin split and flesh torn, mouths wiped and teeth bared — for those who deceived their own hearts and dealt unjustly, who with clever words and flowery speech secretly ruined others.
>   The Hell of the Freezing Ice, the Hell of the Shell-Stripping, the Hell of the Gut-Drawing — grime-faced and tangle-haired, brows knit and eyes wrinkled — these are all for the big measures and little scales that cheated the foolish and dull, bringing calamity heaped upon their own heads.
>   The Hell of the Oil-Cauldron, the Hell of the Utter Darkness, the Hell of the Mountain of Knives — quaking and shuddering, grieving and sorrowing — all because the violent oppressed the good and gentle; now they huddle and shrink their necks in bitter loneliness.
>   The Hell of the Pool of Blood, the Avici Hell, the Hell of the Steelyard Beam — skin stripped and bones laid bare, arms broken and sinews snapped — these too are for those who plotted to seize wealth and took life, who butchered beasts and slaughtered the living; fallen for a thousand years, hard to release, sunk forever, never to turn back.
>   Each one is bound fast and chained tight, wound about with cords and ropes. There are dispatched red-haired ghosts and black-faced ghosts with long spears and short swords; Ox-Head ghosts and Horse-Face ghosts with iron tablets and brazen mallets — beating them till their faces wrinkle in pain and the blood streams down, calling on earth and heaven with none to answer. Truly it is:

>   In life, then, let no one deceive his own heart;
>   gods and ghosts shine forth — whom do they let off?
>   Good and evil in the end are surely repaid;
>   the only question is whether it comes early or late."

When Taizong heard this, his heart was struck with horror.

Going on a little farther, he saw a band of ghost-soldiers, each bearing pennants and banners, who knelt by the roadside and said, "The Bridge Officers have come to receive you." The judge ordered them to rise, then led Taizong forward, and they crossed by way of a golden bridge. Taizong saw, off to one side, a silver bridge, upon which walked several men of loyalty, filial piety, virtue, and worth — fair, upright, and great-hearted people — who were also met and led across with pennants and banners. And over yonder was yet another bridge, where a cold wind rolled and waves of blood surged, and the sound of weeping and wailing never ceased. Taizong asked, "What is the name of that bridge?" The judge said, "Your Majesty, that is called the Bridge of No Recourse. When you return to the world of light, be sure to record it. Below that bridge are all these:

>   Rushing, surging waters; a perilous, narrow road.
>   It looks like a bolt of silk laid across the long river, yet seems a fire-pit floating up to the world above.
>   The shadow-vapor presses on you, cold through to the bone;
>   the reeking wind strikes the nose, its stench boring to the heart.
>   The waves roll and the billows churn, yet to and fro there is no ferryboat to carry men across;
>   barefoot and tangle-haired, all who pass in and out are sin-laden ghosts.
>   The bridge is several li long, but only three spans wide; a hundred feet high, yet a thousand layers deep.
>   Above there is no handrail or balustrade; below there are vicious monsters who snatch at men.
>   Bound in cangues and fetters, they are driven onto the perilous road of the Bridge of No Recourse.
>   Look how fierce and brutal are the spirit-generals at the bridge's edge, how truly wretched are the sinful souls within the river.
>   On the forking trees hang the silken garments of green, red, yellow, and purple;
>   crouched before the cliff-walls are the lewd, shrewish women who cursed their husbands' parents.
>   Brazen serpents and iron dogs feed on them at will;
>   fallen forever into the River of No Recourse, with no way out."

A poem says:

>   At times the ghosts' weeping and the spirits' howling are heard;
>   the muddy waves of blood-water rise ten thousand fathoms high.
>   Countless Ox-Heads and Horse-Faces,
>   ferocious and grim, stand guard at the Bridge of No Recourse.

While they spoke, the several Bridge Officers had already gone back. Taizong's heart was alarmed again; he nodded and sighed to himself, grieving silently. Following the judge and the marshal, they soon passed over the foul waters of the River of No Recourse and the bitter region of the Bowl of Blood. Then they came to the City of the Wrongfully Dead. There he heard only an uproar of shouting people, plainly saying: "Li Shimin has come! Li Shimin has come!" When Taizong heard the cries, his heart quailed and his courage shook. He saw a band of phantoms — some dragging their waists, some with broken arms, some with legs but no heads — who came forward to block his path, all crying out: "Give me back my life! Give me back my life!" Terrified, Taizong dodged and hid, calling only: "Master Cui, save me! Master Cui, save me!" The judge said, "Your Majesty, these are all the ghost-souls of the princes and chieftains of the sixty-four places of dust and tumult and the seventy-two haunts of grass-bandits. They are all wrongfully dead, with no one to gather them and no one to keep them, unable to be reborn, and having no money or means for the road — all of them lonely, destitute, hungry ghosts. If Your Majesty will give them some money, then I can save you." Taizong said, "I came here empty-handed — where am I to get any money?" The judge said, "Your Majesty, in the world of light there is a man who has deposited a great sum of gold and silver here in our shadow realm. Your Majesty may put your name to a bond, with this humble judge as guarantor, and borrow one storehouse of his to scatter among these hungry ghosts — then you may pass." Taizong asked, "Who is this man?" The judge said, "He is a man of Kaifeng prefecture in Henan, surnamed Xiang, named Liang. He has thirteen storehouses of gold and silver here. If Your Majesty borrows of his, you need only repay him when you reach the world of light." Taizong was very glad, and willingly put his name to the loan. So he drew up a document with the judge, borrowed one storehouse of gold and silver, and bade the marshal scatter the whole of it. The judge then instructed the ghosts: "This gold and silver — you may divide and use it among yourselves, and let your Great Tang sovereign pass. His earthly span is still far from spent. I have received the Ten Kings' command to send him back to life, and to bid him hold, when he reaches the world of light, a Grand Mass of Land and Water to deliver you all into rebirth. Make no more trouble." When the ghosts heard this and had got the gold and silver, they all murmured assent and withdrew. The judge ordered the marshal to wave the soul-leading banner, and led Taizong out of the City of the Wrongfully Dead, onto the broad level road, where they drifted and floated away.

After going on for some time, they came at last to the place of the Six Paths of Transmigration. There he saw those who rode the clouds, draped in rosy cloud-capes; those who had received the registers of ordination, with golden fish-tokens hung at their waists. Monks and nuns, Taoists and laymen, running beasts and flying birds, goblins and demons — all of them, in a teeming flood, hastened down beneath the Wheel of Transmigration, each entering his own path. The Tang king asked, "What does this mean?" The judge said, "Your Majesty, with a clear mind perceiving your own nature, you must surely remember this and make it known to the people of the world of light. This is called the Six Paths of Transmigration: those who did good ascend and are transformed into the Path of the Immortals; the wholly loyal rise to be reborn into the Path of the Noble; the filial are reborn into the Path of Blessing; the fair and just return to be born again into the Path of Men; those who heaped up virtue are reborn into the Path of Wealth; the wicked and venomous sink down into the Path of Ghosts." Hearing this, the Tang king nodded and sighed:

>   How good, how truly good!
>   Do good, and the fruit is free of disaster.
>   Let the good heart be ever earnest;
>   let the path of good be opened wide.
>   Do not let evil thoughts arise,
>   and you will surely have fewer crooked troubles.
>   Say not that there is no requital —
>   gods and ghosts have it all arranged.

The judge escorted the Tang king right up to the gate of the Path of the Noble Reborn, and bowing, called out to him: "Your Majesty, this is the place of emerging into the world. Your humble judge takes his leave and returns; let Grand Marshal Zhu escort you the rest of the way." The Tang king thanked him, saying, "I have troubled you, sir, to come so far." The judge said, "When Your Majesty reaches the world of light, be sure by all means to hold a Grand Mass of Land and Water to deliver those masterless, wronged souls. Do not forget. If in the shadow realm there are no voices of grievance, then the world of light may enjoy the blessings of great peace. In every place where there is anything not good, let it be amended, point by point. Exhort all the people of the world to do good, and I warrant your posterity shall be long and unbroken, your realm and altars forever secure."

The Tang king assented to every word, took leave of Judge Cui, and went in through the gate together with Grand Marshal Zhu. Inside the gate the marshal saw a bay sea-horse, saddle and harness all in readiness, and hastily begged the Tang king to mount, supporting him on left and right. The horse went like an arrow, and soon they reached the bank of the Wei River. There, on the surface of the water, was a pair of golden carp turning the waves and leaping in play. The Tang king, seeing them, was delighted at heart, and reined in his horse to gaze, unwilling to part with the sight. The marshal said, "Your Majesty, hasten on a little; let us make speed and reach the city in good time." But the Tang king only kept on gazing, unwilling to go forward. Then the marshal seized him by the feet and cried aloud, "Why won't you go? What are you waiting for?" — and with a splash thrust him down off the horse into the Wei River. And so he slipped free of the shadow realm and returned straight to the world of light.

Now we tell how the ministers of the Tang court — Xu Maogong, Qin Shubao, Hu Jingde, Duan Zhixuan, Ma Sanbao, Cheng Yaojin, Gao Shilian, Li Shiji, Fang Xuanling, Du Ruhui, Xiao Yu, Fu Yi, Zhang Daoyuan, Zhang Shiheng, Wang Gui, and the rest, both files of civil and military officers — were guarding the Crown Prince of the Eastern Palace together with the Empress, the imperial consorts, the palace maidens, and the chief attendants, all keeping mourning in the Hall of the White Tiger. On the one hand they discussed issuing the proclamation of mourning, to make it known to the empire, intending to set the Crown Prince upon the throne. At that time Wei Zheng was standing by, and he said, "My lords, hold a moment — it must not be, it must not be. If we alarm the prefectures and counties, I fear something unforeseen may arise. Let us wait and watch one more day; my sovereign will surely return to life." Then up stepped Xu Jingzong from below, who said, "Prime Minister Wei speaks most absurdly. Since ancient times it is said: 'Spilt water cannot be gathered up; the dead do not return.' How can you still utter such empty words, confusing men's hearts? What sense is there in it?" Wei Zheng said, "To tell you the truth, Master Xu, I from my youth was instructed in the immortals' arts, and my reckoning is most clear. I warrant Your Majesty will not die."

While they were speaking, they suddenly heard from within the coffin a loud, repeated cry: "You're drowning me! You're drowning me!" It so frightened the civil officers and military officials that their hearts were thrown into confusion, and the Empress and consorts trembled in terror. Every one of them:

>   Faces like the yellow mulberry leaves after autumn,
>   waists like the tender willow withes before spring.
>   The heir-apparent's legs went weak — he could scarcely lean on the mourning-staff to complete the rites of grief;
>   the chief attendants' souls flew off — how could they don the ridged caps and keep the filial ceremony?
>   The consorts stumbled and fell, the colorfully dressed maids tottered and swayed.
>   The consorts stumbled and fell, like wild wind blowing down the withered lotus;
>   the maids tottered and swayed, like a sudden rain beating crooked the delicate lotus-buds.
>   The ministers were struck with dread, their bones soft and their sinews numb.
>   Quaking and shuddering, dumbstruck and tongue-tied —
>   the whole Hall of the White Tiger was like a bridge with a broken beam;
>   the mourning platform was like a collapsed and ruined temple.

At that moment all the palace folk ran clean away, and who dared go near the bier to tend the coffin? It was thanks to the upright Xu Maogong, the principled Prime Minister Wei, the bold Qin Qiong, and the headlong, fierce Jingde that they came forward to hold the coffin, calling out: "Your Majesty, if there is anything weighing on your heart, tell it to us — do not play the ghost and so terrify your kin." Wei Zheng said, "It is no playing the ghost — this is His Majesty come back to life. Quick, fetch tools." They pried open the coffin lid, and there indeed they saw Taizong sitting up inside, still crying: "I'm drowned! Who will save and pull me out?" Maogong and the others came forward and raised him up, saying, "Your Majesty, recover yourself; do not be afraid. We are all here to guard Your Majesty." Only then did the Tang king open his eyes and say, "What bitter straits I have just been through: barely escaping the wicked ghosts' troubles in the shadow realm, then meeting with the calamity of losing my life upon the water." The ministers said, "Set your heart at ease, Your Majesty, and have no fear — what flood-calamity could there be?" The Tang king said, "I was riding my horse, going along, and had just reached the bank of the Wei River, where I saw twin fish at play. Then Grand Marshal Zhu, with deceitful heart, thrust me down off my horse, and I fell into the river and was all but drowned." Wei Zheng said, "Your Majesty's ghost-vapor is not yet dispelled." He hurriedly bade the Imperial Medical Academy bring soul-soothing, spirit-settling decoctions and medicines, and prepared gruel and food besides. After taking it once or twice, the Emperor at last returned to his roots and recovered his true self, and came to know human affairs again. Reckoning it up, the Tang king had been dead three days and nights, and now had come back to the world of light to be sovereign. There is a poem as proof:

>   Through all the ages the rivers and hills have changed how many times;
>   through the generations the tallies of failure and success have run.
>   Zhou and Qin, Han and Jin had many marvelous matters —
>   but who, like the Tang king, died and came to life again?

That day the sky had already grown dark, and the ministers begged the king to retire to rest, and each dispersed.

Early the next morning, they doffed their mourning garments and changed into colored robes — every one in red gown and black cap, every one with purple sash and golden seal — and waited outside the gate of the court for the summons.

Now we tell how Taizong, since taking the soul-soothing, spirit-settling potions and drinking gruel-broth several times, had been helped by the ministers into his bed-chamber, where he slept soundly through the night, nourishing his vital spirit, and did not rise until daybreak. Then he shook out his majestic dignity. See how he was arrayed:

>   He wore a Heaven-piercing crown, and a robe of reddish-ochre yellow.
>   He bound on a belt of green Lantian jade, and trod a pair of "Founding-the-Realm, Free-of-Care" shoes.
>   Stately of countenance, surpassing the courts of old;
>   awesome and fierce, renewing the glory of this day.
>   What a fine, fair, and well-governed Great Tang king —
>   the Emperor Li, dead and brought back to life again!

The Tang king went up to the Golden Chimes Treasure Hall and assembled both files of civil and military officers. When the cries of "Long live the King!" were done, they took their ranks by grade. Then was heard the imperial command proclaimed: "Let any who have business come forth from the ranks and report; those with no business, the court is dismissed." From the eastern wing stepped forth Xu Maogong, Wei Zheng, Wang Gui, Du Ruhui, Fang Xuanling, Yuan Tiangang, Li Chunfeng, Xu Jingzong, and others; from the western wing stepped forth Yin Kaishan, Liu Hongji, Ma Sanbao, Duan Zhixuan, Cheng Yaojin, Qin Shubao, Hu Jingde, Xue Rengui, and others. Together they came forward, and before the white-jade steps they bowed low and reported: "How is it that Your Majesty, after a former dream, took so long to awaken?" Taizong said, "Some days ago, after I received Wei Zheng's letter, I felt my soul go out from the hall, and saw the Imperial Forest Guard begging me to come out hunting. As I was riding along, men and horses vanished without a trace, and then I saw my late royal father and my late brothers quarreling and clamoring. Just when I could not resolve it, I saw a man in a black cap and dark gown — it was Judge Cui Jue — who bellowed my late brothers back. I handed Wei Zheng's letter to him. As I was reading, I again saw a blue-robed one bearing pennants and banners, who led me within, to the Hall of Endless Shadows, where I sat in converse with the Ten Kings of the Ages. They spoke of how the Jing River dragon had falsely accused me of promising to save him and then killing him instead, and I laid out the whole prior matter to them. They said the case had already been tried before the Three Tribunals, and quickly ordered the Register of Life and Death brought, to examine my earthly span. Then Judge Cui handed up the register, and when King Yama had looked at it, he said I had thirty-three years of Heaven-allotted fortune, of which thirteen had passed, so that twenty years of earthly life were still owed me. At once he had Grand Marshal Zhu and Judge Cui escort me back. I took leave of the Ten Kings, and promised to send them melons and fruit in thanks for their grace. After I came out of the Hall of Endless Shadows, I saw in the shadow realm the disloyal and unfilial, the unmannerly and unjust, those who wasted the five grains, who cheated openly and deceived in secret, who used big measures and little scales, the lewd, the thievish, the false and treacherous — suffering the tortures of grinding, burning, pounding, and chopping, the punishments of searing, scorching, hanging, and flaying — thousands upon thousands of them, more than the eye could take in. Then I passed through the City of the Wrongfully Dead, where there were countless wronged souls, all the grass-bandits of the sixty-four places of dust and tumult and the souls of the rebels of the seventy-two haunts, who blocked my homeward road. Luckily Judge Cui stood guarantor, and I borrowed one storehouse of gold and silver from old Xiang of Henan, bought off the ghost-souls, and only so was able to go on. Judge Cui charged me that, on returning to the world of light, I should by all means hold a Grand Mass of Land and Water to deliver those masterless lonely souls — these words he urged on me again and again. After parting and coming out from beneath the Six Paths of Transmigration, Grand Marshal Zhu begged me to mount, and we went, as if flying, to the bank of the Wei River, where I saw twin-headed fish at play. Just as I was delighting in the sight, he seized me by the feet and thrust me down into the water — and so I was able to return to life." When the ministers heard these words, there was not one but offered congratulations. And so it was set down and proclaimed throughout the empire, and the officials of every prefecture and county sent up memorials of felicitation — but of this we will say no more.

Now we tell how Taizong further issued a decree pardoning the criminals of the empire. He also reviewed the grave offenders in the prisons. At that time the presiding officers, having examined the prisoners of the Board of Punishments condemned to strangling or beheading, found upward of four hundred names and presented them. Taizong released them and pardoned them to go home, to take leave of their parents and brothers, to entrust their property to their kin, sons, and nephews, and on this same day the next year to come to the courts and there receive the punishment they had earned. The prisoners gave thanks for the grace and withdrew. He also issued a proclamation of relief for orphans. And he reviewed the palace women, old and young, of whom there were three thousand in all, and issued an order to match them in marriage with the soldiery. From this time, within the palace and without, all was good. There is a poem as proof. The poem says:

>   The great Tang king's grace and virtue were vast;
>   his Way surpassed Yao and Shun, and the myriad people flourished.
>   Four hundred condemned to death all left their cells;
>   three thousand resentful women were released from the palace.
>   The many officials of the empire wished him long life;
>   the assembled ministers of the court hailed him as the Primal Dragon.
>   One single thought of a good heart, and Heaven sent its blessing —
>   and the shelter of that fortune was to pass down through seventeen reigns.

When Taizong had thus released the palace women and freed the death-row prisoners, he issued besides a proclamation of his own composing, spread throughout the empire. The proclamation said:

>   Heaven and earth are vast; the sun and moon shine and judge with clearness. The universe is broad; Heaven and earth will not harbor the wicked clique. Scheme with cunning and use of tricks, and the retribution falls within this very life; spread shallow goodness and beg for little, and you gain blessing — speak not of the world to come. A thousand clever plots are not as good as being a man within one's lot; ten thousand kinds of violent men are no match for following circumstance and living thriftily. Let the heart act in mercy and goodness — what need to labor over reading the scriptures? But if the mind would harm others, then in vain has one read the whole Tripitaka of the Buddha!

From this time, under all of Heaven there was not one person who did not do good. On the one hand, he issued a proclamation calling for worthies, summoning someone to bear melons and fruit into the shadow realm; on the other, he took one storehouse of gold and silver from the treasure-store and dispatched Yuchi Gong and Hu Jingde to Kaifeng prefecture in Henan, to seek out Xiang Liang and repay the debt.

The proclamation had been posted several days when there came a worthy man, willing to undertake the bearing of melons and fruit. He was a native of Junzhou, surnamed Liu, named Quan, and his household had a fortune of ten thousand strings of cash. It happened that his wife, Li Cuilian, had drawn the golden hairpin from her hair at the gateway to give alms to a monk, and Liu Quan had cursed her for it, saying she did not keep the way of a wife, presuming to step beyond the women's quarters. Unable to bear the shame of it, Lady Li hanged herself and died, leaving behind a young son and daughter who wept day and night. Liu Quan could not bear to look upon it, and at his wits' end, he resolved to give up his own life — abandoning his household estate, leaving his children — and willingly, by his own death, to bear the melons. He tore down the imperial proclamation and came before the Tang king. The king issued his command, bidding him go to the Golden Pavilion Lodge, to balance a pair of southern melons upon his head, to carry paper money in his sleeve, and to hold medicine in his mouth.

Liu Quan indeed swallowed the poison and died. His single soul, bearing the melons and fruit upon his head, soon arrived at the Gate of Ghosts. The ghost-courier who kept the gate bellowed, "What man are you, daring to come to this place?" Liu Quan said, "I come on the imperial commission of the Great Tang Emperor Taizong, sent expressly to present melons and fruit for the enjoyment of the Ten Kings of the Ages." The ghost-courier gladly received and led him in. Liu Quan went straight to the Treasure Hall of Endless Shadows, and seeing King Yama, presented the melons and fruit, saying, "By the command of the Tang king, I have borne melons and fruit from afar, to thank the Ten Kings for the grace of their leniency." King Yama was greatly pleased, and said, "What a faithful and virtuous Emperor Taizong!" And so he accepted the melons and fruit. Then he asked the melon-bearer's name and what region he came from. Liu Quan said, "Your humble servant is registered among the people of Junzhou city. My surname is Liu, my name is Quan. Because my wife, Lady Li, hanged herself and left behind our children with no one to tend them, your servant willingly gave up his home and forsook his sons, offering up his body to repay his country, and came expressly to present melons and fruit to my king's order, to thank you great kings for your bounteous grace." When the Ten Kings heard this, they ordered the case of Liu Quan's wife, Lady Li, to be looked into. The ghost-courier swiftly brought her to the foot of the Hall of Endless Shadows, and there husband and wife, Liu Quan and Lady Li, were reunited. When they had told over the former matters, they turned and gave thanks to the Ten Kings for the grace of their pardon. Then King Yama, examining the Register of Life and Death, found that this husband and wife both had the lifespan of those destined to become immortals, and quickly dispatched a ghost-courier to send them back. The ghost-courier reported, "Li Cuilian has been long in the shadow realm, and her body no longer exists — to what shall her soul attach itself?" King Yama said, "The Tang emperor's imperial sister, Li Yuying, is fated to die just now; you may borrow her body, and let Lady Li return to life by means of it." The ghost-courier received the command, and at once brought Liu Quan and his wife back to life, and together they went forth out of the shadow realm.

In the end we do not yet know how the husband and wife returned to life — so listen to the explanation in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 12 -->
# Chapter 12: The Borrowed Body and the Bodhisattva's Sign

Now, the ghostly envoy led Liu Quan and his wife out of the realm of shades, and a cold, swirling wind carried them straight to the great capital of Chang'an. There the envoy thrust Liu Quan's soul into the golden pavilion of the courier station, while he bore Cuilian's soul into the inner courts of the imperial palace. It happened that the Princess Yuying was just then walking beneath the shade of the flowering trees, stepping slowly across the green moss, when the envoy rushed straight into her and knocked her sprawling to the ground. He seized her living soul and pressed Cuilian's soul into Yuying's body. Then the envoy turned back to the underworld — but of that no more need be said.

Meanwhile the waiting-maids of the court, great and small, saw that Yuying had fallen dead, and ran in haste to the golden throne hall to report to the empresses of the three palaces: "The princess has fallen dead!" The empresses were aghast and sent word at once to Emperor Taizong. When the emperor heard, he nodded and sighed: "So it is true after all. I once asked the Kings of the Ten Courts of Hell, 'Are the old and young of my house safe?' And they answered, 'All are safe, save that we fear the emperor's sister has but a short span left.' Their words have come to pass."

All the household came weeping, and they hurried to the shade of the flowers to look — and behold, the princess still breathed faintly. The Tang emperor said, "Do not weep! Do not weep! You will startle her." He came forward, lifted her head with his own royal hand, and called, "Sister, wake! Wake!" The princess suddenly rolled over and cried, "Husband, walk slower — wait for me!" Taizong said, "Sister, it is we who are here." The princess raised her head, opened her eyes, looked about, and demanded, "Who are you, that you dare lay hands on me?" Taizong said, "I am your royal brother, and this your royal sister-in-law." The princess said, "Where would I get a royal brother or a royal sister-in-law? My maiden family is surnamed Li, and my childhood name was Li Cuilian. My husband is surnamed Liu, named Quan, and we are both folk of Junzhou. Three months ago I drew the gold pin from my hair to give alms to a monk at our gate. My husband blamed me for stepping unbidden past the inner door and breaking the rules of a wife. He scolded me with a few sharp words, and my breast filled with such rage that I hung a white silk sash from the beam and strangled myself, leaving behind a son and a daughter to weep day and night. Now, because my husband was sent by the Tang emperor to carry melons and fruit to the underworld, the King of Hell took pity and released us both to return. He walked ahead, and because I came late and could not catch him up, I stumbled and fell. You people are rude! You do not even know my name — how dare you seize me?"

When Taizong heard this, he said to the assembled household, "It seems my sister was stunned by the fall and is babbling nonsense." He commanded the Imperial Academy of Medicine to bring potions, and Yuying was helped into the palace.

The Tang emperor sat in his hall when suddenly the officer on duty announced, "Your Majesty, the man Liu Quan who carried the melons and fruit has returned to life, and now waits outside the palace gate for your command." The Tang emperor was astonished and quickly ordered Liu Quan summoned in. The man prostrated himself before the vermilion steps. Taizong asked, "How fared the matter of the melons and fruit?" Liu Quan said, "Your servant bore the melons and fruit straight to the Gate of Ghosts, was led up to the Hall of Judgment, and there beheld the Kings of the Ten Courts of Hell. I presented the offering and conveyed in full my king's earnest gratitude. The Kings were greatly pleased, and bowed many times to honor my king, saying, 'Truly Taizong is an emperor of faith and virtue!'" The Tang emperor said, "And what did you see in the underworld?" Liu Quan said, "Your servant did not travel far and saw little. I only heard the King of Hell ask my native place and my name. I told him how I had abandoned home and children because my wife had hanged herself, and how I had volunteered to carry the melons. He swiftly dispatched a ghostly envoy who brought my wife, and we met below the Hall of Judgment. Then they examined the Registers of Life and Death, declared that we both still had the span of immortals before us, and sent us back by the envoy. I walked ahead, my wife behind, and by good fortune I have returned to life. But I do not know into what place my wife has gone." The Tang emperor asked with alarm, "Did the King of Hell say anything about your wife?" Liu Quan said, "The King said nothing, but I heard the envoy say, 'Li Cuilian has long been among the dead; her corpse no longer survives.' And the King said, 'The Tang emperor's sister, Li Yuying, is fated to die soon — let Cuilian borrow Yuying's body and return to life that way.' I do not know where this 'Tang emperor's sister' lives, nor in what house, and I have not yet been able to go seek her out."

When the Tang emperor heard this report, his heart was filled with joy, and he said to his many officials, "When I took my leave of the King of Hell, I asked after the affairs of my palace. He said, 'The old and young are all safe, save that we fear the emperor's sister has but a short span.' And indeed, just now my sister Yuying fell dead beneath the flowering trees. I hurried to lift her, and in a little while she revived, crying, 'Husband, walk slower — wait for me!' I took it for the babble of one stunned by a fall. But when I questioned her further, her words matched Liu Quan's exactly." Wei Zheng came forward and said, "If the emperor's sister chanced to come to the end of her span, and revived to speak such words, this is the matter of Liu Quan's wife borrowing a body to return to life. Such things do happen. Let the princess be brought out, that we may see what she has to say." The Tang emperor said, "I have just sent the Academy of Medicine to give her physic — I do not know how she fares." So he ordered the consorts to go into the palace and fetch her. But the princess within was shouting wildly: "What medicine should I take? Whose house is this? My home is of cool tiled roofs, not this jaundice-yellow chamber with its gaudy painted doors! Let me out! Let me out!"

While she was still shouting, four or five court women and two or three eunuchs came supporting her, all the way up into the hall. The Tang emperor said, "Do you recognize your husband?" Yuying said, "What kind of talk is that? The two of us have been wedded since childhood and have borne sons and daughters together — how could I not know him?" The Tang emperor ordered an attendant to help her down. The princess descended from the throne hall and went straight to the foot of the white jade steps. When she saw Liu Quan she seized him fast and cried, "Husband, where were you going, that you would not even wait for me? I stumbled and fell, and all those unreasonable people surrounded me and shouted at me — what is the meaning of this?" Liu Quan heard the words of his wife from her mouth, but saw that the face was not his wife's face, and he dared not own the kinship.

The Tang emperor said: "Truly, when mountains crumble and the earth splits, someone may witness it — but to catch the living standing in for the dead is a thing hard to meet with." A king of true virtue indeed: he granted Liu Quan the whole of his sister's dowry — her garments, her jewels, her ornaments — exactly as a wedding portion. He also gave a royal decree exempting him forever from corvée and taxes, and bade him take the princess home. The two of them gave thanks for the grace at the foot of the steps and returned joyfully to their native place. There is a poem to prove it:

> A man's life and a man's death are the bond of a former age;
> short or long, each has his appointed years.
> Liu Quan carried the melons and returned to the world of the living;
> Li Cuilian borrowed a body and her soul came home.

The two of them took their leave of the king and went straight to the city of Junzhou. They found their old estate and their children all well, and the couple spread the fame of good karma far and wide — but of this no more.

Now, of the storehouse of gold and silver: the general Yuchi Gong took it to Kaifeng prefecture in Henan to seek out one Xiang Liang. This Xiang Liang, it turned out, made his living selling water, and together with his wife, of the Zhang family, peddled black crockery and earthenware at their gate. Whatever small coins they earned, they kept only enough for their daily needs; the rest they spent on alms to monks, on buying paper gold and silver ingots, recording them to a treasury and burning them. And so this good fruit had ripened upon him: in the world of the living he was a poor man fond of doing good; in that other world he was a wealthy elder with heaped jade and piled gold. When Yuchi Gong brought the gold and silver to his door, it so frightened the old husband and wife that their souls flew out of them. With prefectural officials besides, and carriages and horses crowding outside their thatched hut, the old couple, dumb and dazed as idiots, knelt on the ground doing nothing but knock their heads and bow.

Yuchi Gong said, "Old folk, please rise. Though I am an imperial envoy, I have brought my king's gold and silver to repay you." Trembling, the old man answered, "Your humble servant has no gold or silver out at interest. How should I dare receive this wealth of unclear origin?" Yuchi Gong said, "I have looked into it and learned you are a poor man — only that you gave alms to monks and spent all you had on it, and bought paper gold and silver ingots and burned them, recording them to the underworld. In the underworld there is the money you laid by. When our Emperor Taizong died for three days and then revived, he borrowed in the underworld a storehouse of your gold and silver, and now repays it to you to the last coin. Take it, every piece, so that I may go back and report." But the two of them only worshipped toward heaven and dared not receive it, saying, "If we humble folk took this gold and silver, we should die the sooner. True, we burned paper and recorded it to a treasury, but that is a matter of the dark unseen world. And besides — that His Majesty borrowed gold and silver in the other world, what proof is there of it? We dare by no means receive it." Yuchi Gong said, "His Majesty said the thing he borrowed of you is warranted by Judge Cui as surety. Take it." Xiang Liang said, "Even unto death we dare not receive it."

Seeing how bitterly they refused, Yuchi Gong had no choice but to draw up a memorial and send a man to report. When Taizong saw the memorial and learned that Xiang Liang would not take the gold and silver, he said, "This is truly a good and worthy elder." At once he decreed that Yuchi Gong should use the gold and silver to repair temples and raise a living shrine, and invite monks to do good works on Xiang Liang's behalf — counting it the same as repaying him. On the day the decree arrived, Yuchi Gong bowed toward the palace in thanks and proclaimed it, and all knew of the matter. So with the gold and silver he bought a parcel of ground within the city, unencumbered by soldier or commoner, fifty mou broad on every side, and there set the work in motion. He raised up a temple and named it "The Imperially Founded Xiang Kingdom Temple," and at its left set the living shrine of the old man and his wife, with a carved tablet and an inscribed stone that read "Built under the supervision of Yuchi Gong." This is the very temple now called the Great Xiang Kingdom Temple.

When the work was finished and reported, Taizong was greatly pleased. Then he gathered his many officials again, posted notices to summon monks, and ordered the building of a Great Mass of Land and Water to deliver the orphaned souls of the dark courts. The notices went out over all the realm, charging the officials of every region to choose virtuous high monks and send them up to Chang'an for the assembly. Within a month's span, monks from all under heaven had arrived. The Tang emperor decreed that the Grand Astrologer Fu Yi should select the high monks and undertake the Buddhist rites. But when Fu Yi heard the command, he at once submitted a memorial to stop the building of pagodas, arguing that there was no Buddha. His memorial read:

The teaching of the Western Lands knows neither prince and minister nor father and son; with its Three Paths and Six Ways it deludes the foolish. It chases after sins long past and peers after blessings yet to come; men mumble its Sanskrit syllables hoping to steal away from their due. Yet life and death, long span and short, are rooted in nature itself; punishment and virtue, awe and reward, belong to the lord of men. Now I hear the common herd lean on it idly, all saying it comes from the Buddha. From the Five Emperors and Three Kings there was no Buddha-law, yet rulers were enlightened and ministers loyal, and the years of the dynasties ran long. Not until Emperor Ming of the Han was the barbarian god first set up — and even then only the monks of the Western Lands passed on their own teaching. In truth it is the barbarian encroaching upon the Middle Kingdom, and not worthy of belief.

When Taizong heard this, he cast the memorial down before his assembled ministers for debate. Then the chancellor Xiao Yu stepped from the ranks, bowed low, and submitted: "The Buddha-law has flourished through dynasty after dynasty; it spreads good and stems evil, secretly aiding the state — there is no reason to cast it aside. The Buddha is a sage. To be no sage and yet defy the law deserves a heavy punishment." Fu Yi disputed with Xiao Yu, saying, "Ritual is rooted in serving one's parents and one's prince; yet the Buddha turns his back on his parents and leaves home, sets a common man against the Son of Heaven, and as heir defies those who bore him. Xiao Yu was not born of a hollow mulberry, yet he follows a teaching that has no father — this is precisely what is meant by saying the unfilial have no parents." Xiao Yu only pressed his palms together and said, "Hell was established precisely for such men as this."

Taizong summoned the Grand Coachman Zhang Daoyuan and the Secretariat Director Zhang Shiheng, and asked them how the merit of Buddhist rites might answer. The two ministers replied, "The Buddha lies in purity, benevolence, and forbearance; the true fruit is the Buddha-emptiness. Emperor Wu of the Zhou ranked the Three Teachings in their order; the Chan master Dahui has praises that reach into the far and deep; through all the offerings of the multitudes none has gone unmanifested; the Fifth Patriarch entered the womb, Bodhidharma showed his form. From of old all have said the Three Teachings are most venerable and may not be defamed, may not be cast aside. We humbly beg Your Majesty's sagely discernment and clear judgment." Taizong was greatly pleased and said, "The words of my ministers accord with reason. Whoever speaks further against this shall be punished." So he charged Wei Zheng, together with Xiao Yu and Zhang Daoyuan, to invite the various Buddhist monks and to choose one of great virtue and conduct to be master of the altar and set up the place of the Way. All bowed their heads in thanks and withdrew. From this time forth a law went out: whoever defamed monks or slandered the Buddha would have his arm struck off.

The next day the three court ministers gathered the monks together in the Altar of Mountains and Rivers, and one by one, from first to last, examined and chose them. Among them they selected one high monk of great virtue and conduct. And who do you think he was?

> His spirit-pervading true title was once Golden Cicada,
> only because he listened heedlessly to the Buddha's preaching.
> Cast down to the dusty mortal world to suffer grinding pain,
> born into the common age to fall into the net of snares.
> Entering the womb and dropping to earth, he met with violence at once;
> before he was even born, he stood among wicked men.
> His father was Chen, top graduate of Haizhou;
> his grandfather a Commander-in-Chief, an elder of the reigning court.
> Born under a star of the fate of "falling into the river,"
> he drifted with the current, tossed upon the waves.
> At Gold Mountain isle there lay a great affinity;
> the monk Qian'an took him in and reared him.
> At eighteen years he sought out his true mother,
> and made his way to the capital to seek his grandfather.
> The Commander opened the campaign and led the great army,
> at Hongzhou he wiped out the bandits and slew the wicked crew.
> Graduate Guangrui escaped the heavenly net;
> father and son, reunited, were worthy of all joy and reward.
> He went again before the reigning lord and received his grace,
> and his worthy name rang out upon the Tower of Mist.
> Honored with office, he would not take it, but vowed to be a monk;
> at Hongfu temple he sought the Way among the sands.
> His small name was River-Float, the Old Buddha's child;
> his dharma name was called Chen Xuanzang.

That day they brought forth before the assembly the Dharma Master Xuanzang. This man had been a monk from his youth; from the moment he left his mother's womb he kept the fasts and held the precepts. His grandfather was Yin Kaishan, a Commander-in-Chief of the reigning court; his father Chen Guangrui had been top graduate and was appointed Grand Academician of the Hall of Profound Letters. Yet Xuanzang's whole heart cared nothing for glory or splendor and delighted only in cultivating quietude and extinction. They found his origins good and his virtue lofty besides; in the thousand scriptures and ten thousand classics there was nothing he had not penetrated; of the Buddha's chants and the immortals' tones there was no kind he could not perform.

The three ministers led him before the throne, where he stirred the dust in dance and bowed. Their bows done, they reported: "Your servants Xiao Yu and the rest, by Your Majesty's command, have chosen one high monk, Chen Xuanzang." When Taizong heard the name he pondered a long while, then said, "Could this be Xuanzang, the son of the Academician Chen Guangrui?" River-Float knocked his head and said, "Your servant is indeed he." Taizong said with joy, "Truly the choice was not amiss. Here is a monk of virtue and conduct, of a Chan heart indeed. I bestow upon you the offices of Left Controller of Monks, Right Controller of Monks, and Grand Controller of Monks of all the realm." Xuanzang bowed his head in thanks and received the great offices of Controller. The emperor further granted him a five-colored cassock woven with gold and a Vairocana cap, and bade him take care to bow again to the enlightened monks, to arrange the order of the abbot's company, to draw up the decree, and to proceed to the Temple of Transformation-Birth, there to choose an auspicious day and propitious hour to begin the expounding of the scriptures.

Xuanzang bowed again, received the command, and went out. Then he came to the Temple of Transformation-Birth, gathered the many monks, had Chan couches built, fitted out the appointments of merit, and set the music in order. He chose enlightened monks great and small, twelve hundred in all, and divided them among the three halls — upper, middle, and lower. Before every image of the Buddha the implements were all complete, and each thing was in its proper sequence. They chose the third day of the ninth month of that year, an auspicious day of the zodiac, to open the Great Mass of Land and Water, to last seven times seven, forty-nine days. The matter was duly set down in a memorial and reported. Taizong, with the civil and military officials and the imperial kinsmen, all came to the assembly on the appointed day to offer incense and hear the preaching. There is a poem to prove it:

> In the thirteenth year of Zhenguan the dragon gathers;
> the king proclaims to the multitude the discoursing of the scriptures.
> The place of the Way opens to expound the measureless Law;
> through cloud and mist the light bears up the great vow's shrine.
> By imperial command and grace the high temple is built;
> the Golden Cicada slips its shell to be transformed in the western sphere.
> Good fruit is spread abroad to lift up the sunken;
> upholding the teaching, it is proclaimed to all the generations, past and to come.

In the thirteenth year of Zhenguan, the year of jisi, the ninth month of jiaxu, on the third day, the auspicious hour of guimao, the Grand Controller Dharma Master Chen Xuanzang gathered twelve hundred high monks, all in the Temple of Transformation-Birth in the city of Chang'an, to begin expounding the various wondrous scriptures. The emperor, his morning audience done, led his many civil and military officials, and riding in phoenix carriage and dragon car, came out from the golden throne hall and went straight up to the temple to offer incense. And how was that imperial cortège? Truly it was thus:

> A whole sky of auspicious vapor, ten thousand beams of blessed light. The kindly breeze drifts soft and light, the transforming sun shines uncommon bright. A thousand officials in their girdle-jades, ranked before and behind; the Five Guards with banners and standards arrayed on either side. They bear the golden melon-maces, lift the axes and halberds, in pair upon pair; crimson gauze candles, the imperial censer's incense, in solemn order, hall upon hall. Dragons soaring, phoenixes dancing, ospreys commended, hawks aloft. The sage and enlightened Son of Heaven is upright; his loyal and righteous great ministers are good. Their blessing surpasses a thousand years of Shun and Yu; their peace outdoes ten thousand ages, rivaling Yao and Tang. And then are seen the bent-handle parasol, the rolling-dragon robe, their splendor shooting back and forth; the linked jade rings, the painted-phoenix fans, their blessed haze floating on the air. Pearled crowns and jade girdles, purple cords and golden seals. A thousand companies guard the carriage; two ranks flank the imperial chariot. This emperor, bathed and reverent, honors the Buddha; taking refuge in good fruit, he gladly offers incense.

The Tang emperor's great cortège soon reached the temple gate, and there he had the music and instruments stilled. He stepped down from his carriage, led his many officials, and worshipped the Buddha with offered incense. The three circuits done, he raised his head and looked, and truly it was a fine place of the Way. Behold:

> Banners and streamers fluttering and dancing, jeweled canopies winging with light. Banners and streamers fluttering and dancing — against the void they shake, ray after ray of colored cloud; jeweled canopies winging with light — reflecting the sun, fluttering, red lightning shoots clean through. The World-Honored One's golden image is fair of face; the arhats' jade visages are stern with might. Vases set with immortal flowers, censers burning sandal and aloeswood. Vases set with immortal flowers — brocade trees gleaming, spreading over the jeweled temple; censers burning sandal and aloeswood — fragrant clouds in haze piercing the clear empyrean. Fresh seasonal fruits heaped on vermilion plates, strange shapes of sugar and pastry piled on painted tables. The high monks ranked in rows chant the true scriptures, vowing to pluck the orphaned souls from their misery.

Taizong and his civil and military officials each offered incense, bowed to the Buddha's golden body, and paid homage to the arhats. Then they saw the Grand Controller Dharma Master Chen Xuanzang lead the assembled monks in bowing low to the Tang emperor. The rites done, they divided into ranks and each took his Chan seat. The Dharma Master offered up the proclamation for the deliverance of the orphaned souls for Taizong to read. The proclamation said:

The utmost virtue is vast and dim; the Chan school is silence and extinction. Pure and spirit-pervading, it circulates through the Three Realms. With its thousand changes and ten thousand transformations it governs yin and yang. Its substance and function, true and constant, are without limit or end. Behold those orphaned souls — deeply do they merit pity and compassion. Now, by Taizong's sage command: we gather the various monks to practice Chan and preach the Law. We open wide the gate of expedient means, broadly ply the boat and oar of mercy, universally save the host of beings in the sea of bitterness, and free them from the lingering sickness of the Six Ways. We lead them back to the true road, that they may roam the boundless; in stillness and motion alike doing nothing, they merge into pure simplicity. By this good cause we invite them to feast at the cinnabar towers of the pure capital; riding upon our victorious assembly, they slip free of hell's mortal cage. Soon they shall ascend to the Land of Bliss to wander at ease, going and coming in the Western Region as they please.

> And the poem said:
> One censer of incense of everlasting life;
> a few scrolls of the register that delivers from rebirth.
> The boundless wondrous Law is proclaimed;
> the limitless grace of heaven bathes us.
> Grudges and karmic burdens are wholly dissolved;
> the orphaned souls all come out of prison.
> May it keep safe our land and house,
> at peace and clear, with blessing ten-thousand-fold.

That night's evening scene we leave untold. Next morning the Dharma Master ascended his seat again, gathered the assembly, and chanted the scriptures — but of that no more.

Now, the Bodhisattva Guanshiyin of Potalaka Mountain in the Southern Sea had received the command of the Tathagata Buddha and was in the city of Chang'an, searching out a good man to fetch the scriptures. For many days she had met no one truly virtuous. Then suddenly she heard that Taizong was proclaiming good fruit, choosing high monks, and opening a great assembly. And she saw that the Dharma Master and altar-master was none other than the monk River-Float — the very son of the Buddha who had come down from the Land of Bliss, the very abbot whom she herself had once guided to enter the womb. The Bodhisattva was greatly pleased. So she took up the treasures the Buddha had bestowed and carried them out into the long street, to sell them with Moksha. And what treasures were these? There was one rare and precious brocade cassock and a nine-ringed monk's staff. There were also the three golden fillets — the Gold, the Tight, and the Forbidding — which she kept hidden close away, to await later use. Only the cassock and the staff did she put up for sale.

In the city of Chang'an there was a foolish monk who had not been chosen, but who happened to have a few strings of country cash. Seeing the Bodhisattva transformed into a scabby, mange-ridden shape — body wrapped in a tattered robe, barefoot and bald-headed, holding the cassock fast, all aglow with brilliant light — he came up and asked, "You scabby monk, how much do you ask for that cassock?" The Bodhisattva said, "The cassock is worth five thousand taels, the staff two thousand taels." The foolish monk laughed: "These two scabby monks are madmen! Idiots! These two coarse things, sell for seven thousand taels of silver? Unless putting them on made a man live forever and never grow old, or made him a Buddha or a patriarch on the spot, they would never be worth so much! Take them away! There's no sale here!"

The Bodhisattva did not argue, but went on ahead with Moksha. After they had walked a good while they came before the Donghua Gate, and there they ran straight into the chancellor Xiao Yu, returning from the morning court, his outriders shouting to clear the street. The Bodhisattva, openly and without stepping aside, stood in the middle of the road holding the cassock and went straight up to meet the chancellor. Xiao Yu reined in his horse to look, and seeing the cassock glowing with brilliant light, he had his men ask the seller his price. The Bodhisattva said, "The cassock five thousand taels, the staff two thousand taels." Xiao Yu said, "What virtue has it, that it is worth so high a price?" The Bodhisattva said, "The cassock has its good points and its bad points; there are times it costs money and times it costs nothing." Xiao Yu said, "What is its good, and what its bad?" The Bodhisattva said, "He who wears my cassock will not sink into the round of death, will not fall into hell, will not meet with the harm of venom and malice, will not encounter the calamity of tiger and wolf — that is its good. But the foolish monk who is greedy for lust and gladdened by misfortune, the monk who keeps no fast and holds no precept, the common man who defames the scriptures and slanders the Buddha — these can never look upon the face of my cassock. That is its bad." He asked again, "And how does it cost money, or cost nothing?" The Bodhisattva said, "He who does not follow the Buddha's Law, who does not revere the Three Treasures, and would force the purchase of cassock and staff — for him the price is fixed at seven thousand taels. That is when it costs money. But he who reveres the Three Treasures, who rejoices at the sight of goodness, who takes refuge in my Buddha — to such a one I am willing to give the cassock and staff freely, and forge a bond of good karma with him. That is when it costs nothing."

When Xiao Yu heard this, his face filled with springlike joy, for he knew this was a good man. He at once dismounted and greeted the Bodhisattva with proper courtesy, calling out, "Great Dharma Elder, forgive the offense of Xiao Yu! Our Tang emperor is exceedingly fond of doing good, and there is not an official in all the court who does not practice it. Just now he has begun the building of a Great Mass of Land and Water, and this cassock would be just the thing for the Grand Controller, Dharma Master Chen Xuanzang, to wear. Come, you and I, into the court to see His Majesty."

The Bodhisattva gladly consented, turned her steps, and went straight in at the Donghua Gate. The Gate Officer reported, and a command came summoning them to the throne hall. Seeing Xiao Yu lead in two scabby monks who stood below the steps, the Tang emperor asked, "What has Xiao Yu to report?" Xiao Yu prostrated himself before the steps and said, "Your servant, coming out before the Donghua Gate, chanced upon two monks selling a cassock and a staff. Your servant thought the Dharma Master Xuanzang might wear this robe, and so brought the monks to your presence." Taizong was greatly pleased and asked the price of the cassock. The Bodhisattva and Moksha stood below the steps, offered no obeisance, and when asked the cassock's price, answered, "The cassock five thousand taels, the staff two thousand taels." Taizong said, "What good has the cassock, that it is worth so much?" The Bodhisattva said:

This cassock — let a dragon wear a single thread of it, and it escapes the calamity of being devoured by the roc; let a crane hang a single strand upon it, and it gains the wonder of passing beyond the common into the holy. Wherever its wearer sits, ten thousand spirits come to do him homage; in every motion, the Seven Buddhas attend his body. This cassock is spun from the drawn silk of the ice-silkworm, twisted into thread by a skilled craftsman, woven by immortal maidens, completed on the loom of a goddess. Patch upon patch, the embroidered flowers are sewn; piece upon piece, brocade heaped upon brocade. Delicate and scattered, the blossoms vie in adornment; bright and shimmering, the light gushes forth in jeweled splendor. Put on, it wreathes the whole body in red mist; taken off, it flies away a stretch of colored cloud. Beyond the Three Heavens' Gate it shines with primal light; before the Five Sacred Peaks it breeds a precious vapor. Layer on layer the Western lotuses are set in; gleaming and bright the pearls hang in the likeness of the stars and constellations. At its four corners are night-shining pearls; at its crown a single grandmother-emerald. Though it does not shine forth its whole original substance, still it has the light-breeding cluster of eight treasures. This cassock, in idle times is folded away; only when meeting a sage is it worn. Folded in idle times, its thousand layers wrap up and shine through the rainbow; worn at the meeting of a sage, it startles all the heavens, and gods and ghosts take fright. Upon it are the wish-granting pearl, the mani pearl, the dust-repelling pearl, the wind-stilling pearl; and there are red agate, purple coral, night-shining pearls, and relic-beads. They steal the moon's whiteness, contend with the sun's redness. Strand upon strand, immortal vapor fills the sky; cluster upon cluster, blessed light upholds the holy. Strand upon strand, immortal vapor fills the sky, and lights clean through the gate of heaven; cluster upon cluster, blessed light upholds the holy, and casts its image over all the world. It lights the mountains and rivers, startling tiger and leopard; it shadows the sea-isles, stirring fish and dragon. Along its borders run two cords of inwrought gold; at its collar are linked rings of white jade rings.

> And the poem said:
> Lofty and lofty the Three Treasures, the Way is to be honored;
> the Four Births and Six Ways are all weighed and judged.
> Clearing the heart, it knows how to nurture the law of men and gods;
> seeing the nature, it can pass on the lamp of wisdom.
> Guarding the body, majestic, in the golden world;
> body and mind made pure, like jade-pot ice.
> Ever since the Buddha first ordained the cassock,
> through ten thousand kalpas who has dared cut off the monkhood?

When the Tang emperor heard this, he at once had the cassock spread open and examined it closely from head to foot. Truly it was a fine thing. He said, "Great Dharma Elder, I will not deceive you. I have now opened wide the teaching of goodness and broadly sown the field of blessing. In yonder Temple of Transformation-Birth many monks are gathered, expounding the scriptures and the Law. Among them is one of great virtue and conduct, whose dharma name is Xuanzang. I would buy these two treasures of yours to bestow upon him for his use. What price do you truly ask?" When the Bodhisattva heard this, she and Moksha pressed their palms together in homage, intoned the Buddha's name, and bowing low said, "Since there is one of such virtue and conduct, this poor monk is willing to give them to him, and will by no means take money." So saying, she turned to go. The Tang emperor quickly had Xiao Yu hold her back, and rising in his seat he asked, "You first said the cassock was five thousand taels and the staff two thousand. Now that you see me wish to buy them, you will take no money. Do you mean to suggest that I, leaning upon the position of my throne, would seize your goods by force? There is no such reason. I will repay you by your original price — you must not refuse and evade." The Bodhisattva raised her hands and said, "This poor monk made a vow beforehand: I said that if there were truly one who reveres the Three Treasures, who rejoices at the sight of goodness, who takes refuge in my Buddha, I would take no money, but give them gladly. Now I see that Your Majesty is of clear virtue and given to goodness, honoring my Buddha's gate; and moreover that the high monk is of virtue and conduct, proclaiming the great Law. By rights I should offer them up; I will by no means take money. This poor monk is willing to leave these things behind and take my leave." When the Tang emperor saw how earnest she was, he was greatly pleased. He at once ordered the Court of Imperial Entertainments to lay out a great vegetarian feast in thanks. But the Bodhisattva firmly declined to receive it, and went away contented, returning as before to hide herself in the local shrine of the city god — but of this no more.

Now, Taizong held a noon audience and ordered Wei Zheng to bear a command summoning Xuanzang into court. The Dharma Master was just then gathering the assembly upon the altar, chanting scriptures and reciting verses, when he heard the command. He at once came down from the altar, straightened his robes, and went with Wei Zheng to see the emperor. Taizong said, "I have troubled you, Dharma Master, in seeking the proof of good works, and have had nothing to repay you. This morning Xiao Yu met two monks who wished to give me a rare and precious brocade cassock and a nine-ringed staff. Now I have specially summoned you, Dharma Master, to take them for your use." Xuanzang knocked his head in thanks. Taizong said, "Dharma Master, if you do not disdain it, put it on and let me see." The Elder then shook out the cassock and draped it over his body, took the staff in his hand, and stood waiting before the steps. Prince and ministers, every one, were filled with delight. Truly he was a son of the Tathagata Buddha. Look at him:

> Stern and majestic of countenance, refined and fair,
> the Buddha-robe fits his body as though cut to measure.
> Its radiant brilliance fills heaven and earth;
> its woven colors in profusion gather up the cosmos.
> Bright, bright the pearls ranged above and below;
> layer on layer the gold threads run before and behind.
> On all four sides the tula-down edges the brocade;
> ten thousand rare wonders spread out in figured silk.
> The eight treasures adorn the flowers, bound with knotting threads;
> golden rings clasp the collar, fastened with woolen loops.
> Buddhas of heaven, great and small, ranged high and low;
> stars and constellations, noble and humble, divided left and right.
> Dharma Master Xuanzang has a great affinity;
> this thing before him he is worthy to receive.
> Wholly like a living arhat of the Land of Bliss,
> surpassing the true awakened sages of the West.
> The staff goes ringing, its nine rings vying;
> the Vairocana cap shines forth, rich and full.
> Truly he is a son of the Buddha — no false report;
> better than bodhi, with no deceit or error.

Then the civil and military officials before the steps shouted their applause. Taizong was beyond measure pleased, and at once had the Dharma Master put on the cassock and take the precious staff. He further granted him two files of ceremonial attendants and ordered his many officials to escort him out of the palace gate, bidding him walk the great street in procession on his way back to the temple, exactly like a top graduate showing off his office. At this Xuanzang bowed again in thanks and went down the great street in dazzling, thunderous splendor, swaying and stately. Look now, in the city of Chang'an: merchants traveling and merchants in their shops, young lords and sons of kings, men of letters and men of ink, grown men and little women — there was not one who did not vie to look and to praise, all saying, "What a fine Dharma Master! Truly a living arhat come down, a living Bodhisattva descended to the mortal world!"

Xuanzang reached the temple, and the monks came down from their couches to meet him. As soon as they saw him wearing this cassock and holding this staff, they all said the King Kṣitigarbha had come, and each took refuge and waited upon him to left and right. Xuanzang went up into the hall, burned incense, and worshipped the Buddha. He spoke to the assembly, recounting the emperor's grace, and when that was done they each returned to their Chan seats. And again, before anyone knew it, the red wheel of the sun sank into the west. Truly it was:

> The sun sets, mist veils grass and trees; in the imperial city the bells and drums first sound. Ding, ding, three strokes, and the people's walking stops; before and behind, the streets fall silent. In the high temple the lamps and fires blaze; the lonely village lies cold and soundless. The Chan monk enters meditation and tends the worn scriptures — just the time to refine away the demons and nurture the nature.

The days slipped through the fingers, and now came the seventh day, the chief assembly. Xuanzang again drew up a memorial inviting the Tang emperor to offer incense. By this time the fame of goodness filled all under heaven. Taizong at once arrayed his cortège and led the civil and military officials, the empresses and consorts and imperial kin, early to the temple. And the whole city, great and small, noble and humble, all came to the temple to hear the preaching.

Then the Bodhisattva said to Moksha, "Today is the chief assembly of Land and Water; one seven joined to seven sevens — it is enough. You and I will mingle in the crowd: first, to see what this assembly is like; second, to see whether the Golden Cicada's son has the blessing to wear my treasure; and third, to hear what gate of scripture-law he expounds." So the two of them went into the temple. Truly it was, with affinity one meets an old acquaintance; the Prajñā returns to its own place of the Way. Entering the temple to look, truly it was: a great realm of the heavenly court, surpassing even the Sahā world; outdoing the Jeta Grove and Śrāvastī, no less than the noblest temple-ground. There a strain of immortal music rang clear and loud, and the Buddha's name resounded in clamor.

The Bodhisattva went straight up to the side of the many-jeweled dais, and there indeed was the very likeness of the wise and enlightened Golden Cicada. The poem said:

> Ten thousand phenomena clear and bright, without a speck of dust;
> at the great rite Xuanzang sits upon the high dais.
> The orphaned souls he delivers come secretly in the dark;
> the lofty ones who hear the Law come from the marketplace.
> Giving things as the moment requires, his heart's road runs far;
> bringing forth life at will, the Tripitaka's gate swings open.
> Facing one another, he expounds the measureless Law;
> old and young, every one, gives way to joy of heart.

> And again the poem said:
> Roaming the Dharma-world, within the lecture hall,
> he meets a knowing friend, not of the common sort.
> They tell of the thousand, ten thousand things now present;
> they speak of the many merits across the dusty kalpas.
