> The Dharma-clouds drift, unfurling over the ranges of mountains;
> the teaching-net is spread, filling the great void.
> Examining human life, returning to the thought of goodness,
> in confusion the rain of heaven falls in red blossoms.

The Dharma Master upon the dais chanted for a while from the *Scripture for Receiving Life and Delivering the Dead*, discoursed for a while upon the *Seal of Heavenly Treasure for Securing the Realm*, and proclaimed for a while the *Scroll Exhorting Cultivation and Merit*. Then the Bodhisattva drew near, struck the precious dais, and called out in a stern, loud voice: "You, monk! You only know how to discourse on the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle. Can you discourse on the Greater Vehicle?" When Xuanzang heard this, his heart was filled with joy. He turned and leapt down from the dais, raised his hands to the Bodhisattva, and said, "Old master, this disciple has been remiss — many are my faults. The assembled monks before us all preach the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle. I do not know how the teaching of the Greater Vehicle goes." The Bodhisattva said, "This Lesser Vehicle teaching of yours cannot deliver the dead to ascend on high; it can only let one drift along with the common dust. I have the Three Baskets of the Greater Vehicle Buddha-Law, which can deliver the dead to ascend to heaven, can save the suffering from their misery, can cultivate a body of measureless life, and can make one neither come nor go."

While they were thus discoursing, the incense-officer who patrolled the hall reported in haste to the Tang emperor: "The Dharma Master was just discoursing on the wondrous Law when two scabby wandering monks pulled him down and are talking wild nonsense." The king ordered them seized. So many people pushed and crowded the two monks into the rear Hall of the Law. When they saw Taizong, the monks neither raised their hands nor bowed, but lifted their faces and said, "What does Your Majesty ask of us?" The Tang emperor recognized them and said, "Are you not the monks who gave me the cassock the other day?" The Bodhisattva said, "We are." Taizong said, "Since you came here to hear the preaching, you should have eaten a little of the vegetarian fare and let it be. Why did you talk wild with my Dharma Master, disturbing the scripture-hall and spoiling my Buddhist rites?" The Bodhisattva said, "Your Dharma Master preaches the teaching of the Lesser Vehicle, which cannot deliver the dead to ascend to heaven. I have the Three Baskets of the Greater Vehicle Buddha-Law, which can deliver the dead from suffering and give a body of life that does not decay." Taizong, his face turning grave with pleasure, asked, "Where is this Greater Vehicle Buddha-Law of yours?" The Bodhisattva said, "It is in the Western Heaven, in the Country of India, at the Temple of the Great Thunderclap Sound, in the place of my Buddha the Tathagata. It can untie the knots of a hundred grievances and dispel calamities undeserved." Taizong said, "Can you remember it?" The Bodhisattva said, "I remember it." Taizong said in great joy, "Let the Dharma Master lead you up; I beg you to ascend the dais and expound it."

Then the Bodhisattva, taking Moksha with her, flew up onto the high dais, and treading upon blessed clouds rose straight to the ninth empyrean. There she revealed her true body, the Deliverer from Suffering, holding the pure vase and the willow sprig. On her left was Moksha Huian, gripping his staff, his spirit fierce and rousing. This so delighted the Tang emperor that he worshipped toward heaven, and the civil and military officials all knelt to the ground and burned incense. Throughout the temple, monks and nuns, Daoists and laymen, scholars, craftsmen, and merchants — there was not one who did not bow and pray, "What a Bodhisattva! What a Bodhisattva!" There is a hymn of praise to prove it. Behold:

> The auspicious haze scatters in profusion, blessed light guards the Law-body. In the ninth empyrean's flowery Milky Way appears the female sage. This Bodhisattva: upon her head she wears a fringe of hanging pearl-strings — gold-leaf clasps, kingfisher-flower spread, casting golden light, breeding blessed vapor; on her body she wears a pale-hued, lightly adorned, gold-coiled-dragon, soaring-painted-phoenix robe of plain blue silk; before her breast hangs a fragrant set of ringing girdle-pendants, facing the bright moon, dancing in the clear wind, of mingled jewels and pearls, clustered emerald and jade; about her waist is bound an embroidered woolen skirt of ice-silkworm silk, woven with gold edging, treading the colored clouds, hastening over the jasper sea. Before her she leads a yellow-feathered, red-billed white parrot that flies over the Eastern Ocean, roams the whole world, grateful for grace and practicing filial piety. In her hand she holds a precious vase that gives grace and saves the world, and in the vase is set a willow sprig that sprinkles the blue empyrean, scatters great evils, and sweeps away the lingering mist. The jade rings thread the embroidered clasps; deep beneath her tread the golden lotuses. Through the Three Heavens she goes in and out at will. This indeed is Guanshiyin, who saves from suffering and rescues from disaster.

So delighted was the Tang Taizong that he forgot his realm; so smitten the civil and military officials that they neglected the court etiquette; and all the assembled multitude chanted, "Namo Bodhisattva Guanshiyin!" Taizong at once issued a decree that a skilled painter should sketch the Bodhisattva's true likeness. The word was no sooner spoken than there was chosen one who could paint the divine and write the holy, of far sight and high skill — Wu Daozi (this is the very man who later painted the meritorious ministers on the Tower of Mist). At once he spread out his wondrous brush and painted the true form. The Bodhisattva's blessed cloud gradually drew off, and in a moment the golden light was gone. But there was seen, fluttering down out of mid-heaven, a single slip of paper, on which were written a few lines of verse, clear and plain. The verse said:

> We greet on high the lord of the Great Tang;
> in the West there is a wondrous text.
> The road is a hundred and eight thousand li;
> let the Greater Vehicle be earnestly sought.
> When this scripture returns to your land,
> it can deliver ghosts and lift them from the crowd.
> If there be one willing to go,
> he shall seek the true fruit and a body of gold.

When Taizong saw the verse, he at once commanded the monks: "For now, close the goodly assembly. Wait until I have sent someone to fetch the Greater Vehicle scriptures back, and then, with renewed sincerity, we will cultivate the good fruit anew." Not an official but obeyed. Then, there in the temple, he asked, "Who is willing to take up my command, to go to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures?" Before the question was done, the Dharma Master stepped forth from the side, made obeisance before the emperor, and said, "This poor monk, though without talent, is willing to render the service of a dog or a horse, to seek the true scriptures for Your Majesty, and to pray that my king's realm be forever secure." The Tang emperor was overjoyed. He came forward and lifted him up with his own royal hand, saying, "Dharma Master, if you can indeed exhaust this loyalty and worth, fearing neither the long road nor the toil of crossing mountains and rivers, I am willing to bow with you as sworn brothers." Xuanzang knocked his head in thanks. The Tang emperor was indeed a man of great worth and virtue: he went there before the Buddha in the temple and bowed four times to Xuanzang, calling him "Imperial Younger Brother, the Holy Monk." Xuanzang gave thanks without end and said, "Your Majesty, what virtue, what ability have I, that I should dare receive such favor of heavenly grace? On this journey I am resolved to give my body to the utmost effort, going straight to the Western Heaven. If I do not reach the Western Heaven and obtain the true scriptures, then though I die I will not dare return to my country, but will fall forever into the sinking hell." Then before the Buddha he offered incense, and made this his vow. The Tang emperor was greatly pleased and at once ordered the cortège to return, to choose a fortunate, propitious day and hour, to issue the travel papers and set out — and so the imperial carriage went back and all dispersed.

Xuanzang too returned to Hongfu Temple. The many monks of that temple, with several of his disciples, had already heard of the scripture-fetching errand, and all came to see him. They asked, "Is it true that you have vowed to go up to the Western Heaven?" Xuanzang said, "It is true." His disciples said, "Master, we have often heard it said that the road to the Western Heaven is far, and there are many tigers, leopards, and demons besides. We fear that you go and do not return, that your life can hardly be kept safe." Xuanzang said, "I have already made a great vow and a mighty oath: if I do not fetch the true scriptures, I will fall forever into the sinking hell. In the main, it is that I have received the king's favor and grace, and cannot but exhaust my loyalty to repay the country. This journey of mine is truly vague and uncertain; good fortune and ill are hard to foretell." And he added, "Disciples, after I have gone — in two or three years, or in five or seven years — if you see the branch-tips of the pine within the mountain gate turn toward the east, then I am coming back; if not, then surely I shall not return." The disciples all engraved these words earnestly upon their hearts.

The next morning Taizong held court and gathered the civil and military officials. He had the scripture-fetching travel papers written out and stamped with the great seal of free passage. An official of the Bureau of Astronomy reported, "Today the stars are in their lucky station, fit for a man to set out upon a far road." The Tang emperor was greatly pleased. Then the Gate Officer reported, "The Imperial Younger Brother, the Dharma Master, waits outside the palace gate for your command." At once he was summoned up to the throne hall, and the emperor said, "Imperial Brother, today is the lucky day to set forth. Here are the passage papers. I have also a purple-gold alms-bowl to give you, for begging your food along the way. And I have chosen two attendants for the long road, and a horse with reddish-white markings to bear you on your far journey. You may set out at once." Xuanzang was greatly pleased, gave his thanks, received the things, and showed no thought of lingering. The Tang emperor arrayed his cortège and, with his many officials, escorted him to beyond the pass. There the monks of Hongfu Temple and his disciples were waiting beyond the pass with Xuanzang's winter and summer clothing. When the Tang emperor saw this, he first had the baggage and horse put in order, and then had an official take up a flagon and pour the wine. Taizong raised the cup and asked again, "What elegant title does the Imperial Brother go by?" Xuanzang said, "This poor monk is one who has left the household; I have not dared take a title." Taizong said, "The Bodhisattva said the Western Heaven has the scriptures in three baskets — the Tripitaka. Imperial Brother, you may take your title from the scriptures and be styled Tripitaka. How would that be?" Xuanzang gave thanks again, took the royal wine, and said, "Your Majesty, wine is the very first of a monk's prohibitions. Since I became a man I have never drunk wine." Taizong said, "Today's journey is not like other matters; this is a plain, unfermented wine — drink only this one cup, that I may fulfill my wish of seeing you off." Tripitaka dared not refuse and took the wine. Just as he was about to drink, he saw Taizong stoop, pinch up a bit of dust with his royal fingers, and flick it into the wine. Tripitaka did not understand his meaning. Taizong laughed and said, "Imperial Brother, on this journey, when you reach the Western Heaven, in how long can you return?" Tripitaka said, "In only three years I shall come straight back to my country." Taizong said, "The days are long and the years deep, the mountains far and the road distant. Imperial Brother, drink this wine: rather cherish a pinch of dust from your own homeland than love ten thousand taels of gold from another land." Then Tripitaka understood the meaning of the pinched dust, gave thanks once more, drank the cup dry, took his leave, and went out beyond the pass. And the Tang emperor's carriage returned.

After all, no one knows how this going fared. Listen to the next chapter, and it shall be made clear.

<!-- chapter 13 -->
# Chapter 13: Into the Tiger's Pit, and the Mountain Lord's Welcome

A poem says:

> Great was the Tang king who sent the imperial decree,
> dispatching Xuanzang to seek the Chan truth's seed.
> With steadfast heart he chiseled toward the dragon's lair,
> with single mind he labored up toward Vulture Peak.
> Through borderlands and distant realms past counting,
> through cloud-wreathed ranges folded ten thousand deep —
> from this day forth he parts from court and turns toward the West,
> upholding the teaching, awakening to the Great Void.

Now, we left off with Tripitaka. On the thirteenth day of the ninth month of the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan reign — three days before the full moon — the Tang king and a host of officials had seen him off beyond the gates of Chang'an. For a day or two his horse never paused, and he soon arrived at the Temple of the Law Gate. The abbot of the temple and the senior monks led out more than five hundred of the brotherhood, who lined up in two ranks to receive him and brought him within, where they greeted one another and offered tea. After tea came a vegetarian meal, and before they knew it, evening had fallen. It was just as the verse describes:

> Shadows stir as the River of Stars draws near;
> the moon shines bright, not a speck of dust to see.
> Wild geese cry across the far Milky Way,
> and washing-blocks ring rhythm from the western lane.
> Returning birds roost in the withered trees,
> the Chan monks chant their Sanskrit melodies.
> Upon a single couch with cushion of rush
> they sit until the night has split toward dawn.

By lamplight the monks debated the settled purpose of the Buddha's gate, and the reasons for the journey to fetch the scriptures from the Western Heaven. Some said the waters were far and the mountains high; some spoke of roads thick with tigers and leopards; some warned of sheer ridges and steep cliffs impossible to cross; others, of venomous demons and vicious monsters hard to subdue. Tripitaka sealed his lips and said nothing — he only pointed with his finger to his own heart, and nodded several times. The monks could not fathom his meaning, and pressing their palms together, they asked: "Master, why do you point to your heart and nod?"

Tripitaka answered: "When the heart is born, every kind of demon is born; when the heart is extinguished, every kind of demon is extinguished. I, your disciple, once vowed a mighty oath before the Buddha at the Temple of Transformation, and I cannot help but exhaust this heart of mine. On this journey I am bound for the Western Heaven, to behold the Buddha and seek the scriptures, that the Wheel of the Law may turn once more, and that the imperial throne may stand secure forever." When the monks heard these words, every one of them admired him, and every one proclaimed his praise. They cried out together: "A loyal and true-hearted master of the great teaching!" Their praise was without end, and they invited him to his couch to rest.

Soon the bamboo struck the waning moon down, and the cock's crow raised the dawn-clouds. The monks rose to set out the tea and water and the morning meal. Xuanzang then donned his cassock, climbed to the main hall, and bowed before the Buddha, saying: "I, your disciple Chen Xuanzang, go to the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures. But these eyes of flesh are dull and deluded, and I cannot recognize the true form of the living Buddha. Now I make this vow: that along the road, wherever I meet a temple I will burn incense, wherever I meet a Buddha I will bow, wherever I meet a pagoda I will sweep it. I pray only that our Buddha in his mercy may soon reveal his sixteen-foot golden body, and bestow the true scriptures to be handed down in the Eastern Land." His prayer finished, he returned to the abbot's quarters for the meal. When it was done, his two attendants prepared the saddle and horse and urged the journey onward. Tripitaka came out the mountain gate and bid the monks farewell. Unable to bear the parting, they walked with him fully ten miles, then turned back with tears welling in their eyes. And Tripitaka pressed straight on toward the West.

It was the season of late autumn, and this is what met his eye:

> In a few villages the leaves have fallen, reed-blossoms shattered;
> on scattered trees the maple and willow drop their crimson leaves.
> The road runs through smoke and rain, old friends grow scarce;
> the yellow chrysanthemum is lovely, the mountain's bones grow thin.
> The water turns cold, the lotus breaks, and men grow gaunt with care.
> White duckweed, red knotweed under a frost-white sky like snow;
> the sinking glow, a lone wild duck plunging down the endless air.
> Faint and somber the wild clouds fly,
> the swallows depart, the guest-geese come,
> their crying, crying, sob-broken cries that splinter through the night.

For several days master and servants traveled, until they came to the city of Gongzhou, where the assembled officials and townsfolk came out to welcome them in. They rested for a night, and early the next morning set out from the city again. Along the way they ate when hungry and drank when thirsty, lodging at night and walking at dawn. After two or three days they reached the garrison of Hezhou — the very border of the great Tang's mountains and rivers. The frontier commander and the local monks and Taoists, hearing that this was the imperial envoy and sworn brother of the emperor, a master bound westward to behold the Buddha, all received him with reverence. They brought him in and provided for him, and the head of the monks invited him to lodge at the Fuyuan Temple. The temple's monks came one by one to pay their respects and arranged an evening meal. When it was done, Tripitaka instructed his two attendants to feed the horse well, for they would set out before daybreak.

When the cock had only just begun to crow, he roused his attendants — and this in turn startled the temple monks, who set about preparing tea and a meal. When it was eaten, they departed beyond the border. But the master's heart was anxious, and he had risen far too early. For it was now deep autumn, and the cocks crowed early; in truth it was no more than the fourth watch of the night. The three travelers, with the horse making four, set their faces against the clear frost and walked beneath the bright moon. After some tens of miles they came upon a mountain ridge, where they had to part the grass to seek the path — and words cannot tell how rough and hard the going was. Fearing they had strayed from the trail, they hesitated in doubt — and then suddenly their feet gave way, and all three men together with the horse tumbled down into a pit.

Tripitaka's heart leapt in terror; his attendants shook with fear. And while they were still trembling, they heard from within a roaring and howling, a voice that cried: "Bring them in! Bring them in!" Then a wild wind came rolling, and out swarmed fifty or sixty fiends, who seized Tripitaka and his attendants and dragged them up. The master, quaking and shivering, stole a glance — and the demon king seated above was monstrously fierce. Truly he was:

> Majestic in his might, his body grave and grim,
> savage in his temper, terrible in form.
> His lightning eyes shot dazzling flame,
> his thunder-voice shook all four quarters wide.
> His saw-teeth jutted past his lips,
> his chisel-fangs bared along his jaws.
> Brocade wrapped round his body,
> a striped pelt cloaked his spine.
> His steel-stiff whiskers showed scarce a hint of flesh,
> his hooked claws were keen as frost.
> The Yellow Duke of the Eastern Sea would dread him —
> the White-Browed King of the Southern Hills.

This drove Tripitaka's soul to flee his body and scatter, and left his two attendants limp in bone and slack in sinew. The demon king shouted the order to bind them, and all the fiends together lashed the three with ropes. They were just about to set them out and devour them when a clamor arose outside, and someone came to report: "Mountain Lord Xiong and Squire Te, the two of them, have arrived!"

Hearing this, Tripitaka raised his head and looked. The one walking in front was a black fellow. And what was his appearance? Hear it:

> Bold and full of daring,
> nimble yet thick of frame.
> Crossing water, sheer brute force;
> ranging the woods, he flaunts his wrathful might.
> Long ago a sign of auspicious dreams,
> today alone he shows his hero's bearing.
> The green trees he can bend and snap,
> he knows the cold and aptly tells the season.
> Where his true spirit plainly shows,
> for this he bears the name of Mountain Lord.

And then he saw the one coming behind — a stout fellow. And what was his appearance? Hear it:

> Towering, with a crown of double horns,
> grave and stately, his shoulders and back upraised.
> Quiet by nature, robed in steady blue,
> his hoofed step often slow and lingering.
> By his line his sire is called the bullock,
> by his stock his dam is called the heifer.
> Able to do the labor of the fields,
> for this he bears the name of Squire Te.

These two came swaggering and swaying in, and the demon king rushed out in a fluster to greet them. Mountain Lord Xiong said: "General Yin, you have been in fine form of late — congratulations, congratulations!" Squire Te said: "General Yin, your bearing surpasses the ordinary — how delightful, how delightful!" The demon king said: "And how have you two gentlemen been these past days?" The Mountain Lord said: "I merely keep to my simple ways." The Squire said: "I merely follow the times as they come." Their greetings done, each took a seat to talk and laugh.

Now the attendants, bound in agony, wept and wailed bitterly. The black fellow said: "Where did these three come from?" The demon king said: "They delivered themselves to my very door." The Squire laughed and said: "Might they serve to entertain your guests?" The demon king said: "I am honored to oblige, honored to oblige." The Mountain Lord said: "There is no need to use them all up. Eat two, and one may be kept." The demon king assented, and at once called to his attendants left and right. They cut open the bellies of the two servants and dug out their hearts, hacking the corpses to pieces. The heads and the hearts and livers they offered to the two guests; the four limbs the demon king ate himself; and the rest of the bones and flesh he shared out among the fiends. Nothing was heard but the sound of gnawing and gulping — truly like tigers devouring lambs — and in a moment all was eaten. The master was very nearly frightened to death. This indeed was the first trial of suffering since leaving Chang'an.

In the midst of their grief and terror, the east gradually grew pale. The two monsters did not disperse until daybreak, and they said: "Today we have imposed greatly upon you; another day we will repay your hospitality with all our hearts." Then they crowded out and withdrew.

Before long the red sun rose high. Tripitaka was in a daze, unable to tell east from west, north from south. Just as he hung between life and death, he suddenly saw an old man approaching, leaning on a staff. The old man walked up, gave a single sweep of his hand, and all the ropes fell broken. He blew a breath upon Tripitaka's face, and the monk revived. Tripitaka knelt and bowed to the ground, saying: "Many thanks, venerable grandfather, for saving this poor monk's life." The old man returned the bow and said: "Rise. Have you lost anything?" Tripitaka said: "My attendants have already been devoured by the monsters. I only do not know where my baggage and my horse have gone." The old man pointed with his staff: "Yonder — is that not a horse and two bundles?" Tripitaka turned to look, and indeed they were his own things, nothing lost. Only then did his heart settle a little.

He asked the old man: "Venerable grandfather, what place is this? And how is it you are here?" The old man said: "This is Twin-Fork Ridge, a den of tigers and wolves. How did you come to fall in here?" Tripitaka said: "At cockcrow I set out beyond the Hezhou garrison. I did not expect to rise so early, and braving the frost and brushing the dew, I suddenly fell into this place. I met a demon king, monstrously fierce, who bound me and my two attendants. Then came a black fellow who called himself Mountain Lord Xiong, and a stout fellow who called himself Squire Te. They came in and addressed the demon king as General Yin. The three of them ate my two attendants, and did not disperse until daylight. I cannot imagine what great destiny and fortune I possess, that I should be blessed with your coming to save me."

The old man said: "The Squire is the spirit of a wild ox; the Mountain Lord is the spirit of a bear; General Yin is the spirit of an old tiger. The fiends to either side are all hill-sprites and tree-ghosts, monstrous beasts and gray wolves. It was only because your true nature is fundamentally bright that they could not eat you. Come with me, and I will set you on your road."

Tripitaka, overcome with gratitude, slung his bundles upon the horse, took the reins, and followed the old man straight out of the pit and up onto the great road. He tethered the horse to a clump of grass beside the way and turned to bow his thanks to the venerable one — whereupon the old man changed into a gust of clear wind, mounted a white crane with a vermilion crest, and rose into the sky and away. From the wind there fluttered down a single slip of paper, on which were written four lines of verse:

> I am the Great White Star of the Western Heaven,
> come on purpose to save your living soul.
> Ahead there will be holy disciples to aid you —
> do not, for hardship's sake, resent the scripture-quest.

Tripitaka read it, then bowed toward heaven and said: "Many thanks, Venus, Star of Gold, for delivering me from this peril." His bow finished, he led the horse and pressed on alone — solitary and forlorn — bitterly forward. Upon this ridge, truly it was so:

> Cold and gusting, the wind through the rain-soaked woods;
> murmuring and rushing, the water down the gorge.
> Fragrant and rich, the wildflowers in bloom;
> dense and heaped, the tumbled jumble of rocks.
> Clamoring and noisy, the deer and the apes;
> in troops and herds, the river-deer and roe.
> Loud and jangling, the many voices of birds;
> silent and still, no trace of human affairs.
> That master — trembling and quaking, his heart unquiet;
> this horse — feeble and faltering, its hooves hard to lift.

Tripitaka risked his life and pressed up into that steep ridge. He traveled half a day and still saw no sign of cooking-smoke, no village, no cottage. For one thing his belly was hungry; for another the road was uneven. Just in this moment of crisis, he saw before him two fierce tigers roaring, and behind him several long snakes coiling. To his left were venomous insects, to his right monstrous beasts. Alone and helpless, Tripitaka could only let go of body and mind and resign himself to heaven's will. And to make matters worse, the horse went weak in the back and bent at the hoof; it knelt down and lay flat upon the ground, and beat it as he might, it would not rise; pull it as he might, it would not move. The poor master had nowhere to turn — truly in the deepest distress, already counting himself as good as dead, and able to do nothing.

But though he was beset by calamity, rescue was at hand. Just as he hung between life and death, he suddenly saw the venomous insects scurry off, the monstrous beasts take flight, the fierce tigers slink away, and the long snakes vanish. Tripitaka raised his head and looked — and there was a man, a steel trident in his hand, a bow and arrows at his waist, coming around from before the mountain slope. Truly he was a fine, stout fellow. Look at him:

> Upon his head a cap of mugwort-patterned, dappled leopard skin;
> on his body a robe of brocade woven from lamb's wool;
> round his waist a belt clasped with a lion's-mask buckle;
> on his feet a pair of boots of roe-deer hide.
> His ringed eyes were round and full, like a mourner come to call;
> his curling whiskers wild and tangled, like the constellation Kui.
> A pouch of poisoned arrows and bow he carried;
> a great pole-trident of pointed steel he gripped.
> His thunder-voice could shatter the gall of mountain vermin;
> his fierceness could blast the souls of the wild pheasants.

When Tripitaka saw him drawing near, he knelt by the roadside, pressed his palms together, and cried out loudly: "Great king, save my life! Great king, save my life!" The fellow came up, set down his steel trident, and helped him up with his hand, saying: "Master, do not be afraid. I am no villain. I am a hunter of these mountains; my surname is Liu and my name is Boqin, and my nickname is the Mountain-Guarding Defender. I came just now to seek a couple of mountain beasts for my food, and did not expect to meet you. I have given you a fright." Tripitaka said: "I am a monk, the imperial envoy under the Tang court, going to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. Just now I came to this place and met with wolves, tigers, snakes, and insects that ringed me on all sides so that I could go no further. Suddenly I saw you, Defender — and all the beasts fled, and you saved my life. Many thanks, many thanks." Boqin said: "I live here and make my living by hunting these wolves and tigers, catching these snakes and insects to get by; that is why the beasts feared me and ran. Since you have come from the Tang court, you and I are countrymen. This is still the territory of the great Tang, and I too am a subject of Tang; you and I drink the same water and tread the same soil of our sovereign — we are truly people of one country. Do not be afraid; come with me, rest your horse at my dwelling, and tomorrow morning I will set you on your road." Hearing this, Tripitaka's heart was full of joy. He thanked Boqin, led his horse, and went along.

When they had passed the slope, they heard again a whistling of wind. Boqin said: "Master, do not move — sit here. Where the wind whistles, a mountain cat is coming. Let me catch it to take home and entertain you." Hearing this, Tripitaka was again terrified and dared not stir a step. The Defender gripped his steel trident, strode out, and went up to meet it. And there was a striped tiger that came face to face with him. Seeing Boqin, it quickly turned its head to flee. The Defender gave a thunderclap of a shout and barked: "Where do you go, you cursed beast!" The tiger, seeing the pursuit close, turned and swung its claws and pounced. The Defender raised his three-pronged trident to meet it in battle. The sight left Tripitaka collapsed and limp upon the grass — never since he came forth from his mother's belly had this monk seen so perilous a thing. The Defender and the tiger grappled there below the slope, man and tiger locked together, and truly it was a fine fight. Behold:

> Wrath upon wrath, wild wind upon wind.
> Wrath upon wrath — the Defender, hair bristling under his cap, full of brawn;
> wild wind upon wind — the striped beast, flaunting its force, spewing red dust.
> The one bares its fangs and flails its claws;
> the other shifts his step and turns his body.
> The three-pronged trident hoists to the sky and dazzles the sun;
> the thousand-flowered tail stirs the mist and sends the clouds aflight.
> The one stabs wildly at the chest;
> the other comes to swallow him face-on.
> Whoever dodges may live to tell of it;
> whoever is struck will surely meet King Yama.
> One hears the striped beast roar and howl;
> one hears the Defender's voice grow savage.
> The striped beast roars and howls, splitting the hills and rivers, startling the birds and beasts;
> the Defender's voice grows savage, shouting open the heavenly courts to reveal the stars.
> The one thrusts out his golden eyes in fury;
> the other summons his courage and breeds his rage.
> Lovable is Liu the Mountain-Guarding Defender;
> praiseworthy is this lord of beasts who holds the ground.
> Man and tiger, each greedy for life, contend for victory —
> the least slack, and three souls are lost.

The two of them fought for the space of a full watch, until at last the tiger's claws went slack and its waist loosened, and the Defender raised his trident and ran it level through its chest, throwing it down. Pitiful — the steel trident's point pierced clean through its heart and liver, and in a moment the blood ran all over the ground. Seizing it by the ears, he dragged it up onto the road. A fine man — his breath unhurried, his color unchanged — he said to Tripitaka: "What luck, what luck! This mountain cat is enough to feed you for a day." Tripitaka praised him without end: "The Defender is truly a mountain god!" Boqin said: "What skill have I that I should merit such praise? This is the master's own great good fortune. Come along — let us hurry and skin it, and cook some meat to entertain you."

With one hand gripping the trident and the other dragging the tiger, he led the way ahead. Tripitaka led the horse and followed behind. Winding along over the slope, they suddenly came upon a mountain farmstead. Before its gate, truly it was:

> Ancient trees reaching to the sky, wild vines sprawling across the path.
> In ten thousand ravines the wind and dust are cold;
> on a thousand cliffs the air and aspect are strange.
> One trail of wildflower fragrance steals upon the body;
> a few stalks of secluded bamboo, green and lush, lean close.
> A thatched gate-tower, a hedge-fenced yard — fit to be painted, fit to be sketched;
> a stone-slab bridge, white earthen walls — truly joyful, truly rare.
> The autumn face is bleak and bare, the bracing air lone and lofty.
> By the road the yellow leaves fall; over the ridge the white clouds drift.
> In the thin woods the mountain fowl chatter and squawk;
> outside the farm gate the slim hounds bay and yelp.

When Boqin reached the gate, he flung down the dead tiger and called: "Where are you lads?" Out came three or four household servants, all of monstrous and ugly aspect, who came forward and hauled and tugged the tiger inside. Boqin instructed them to skin it quickly and prepare it to entertain his guest. Then he turned back to welcome Tripitaka in, and they greeted one another, and Tripitaka again bowed his thanks for Boqin's deep kindness and mercy in saving his life. Boqin said: "We are men of the same homeland — why trouble yourself with thanks?" When they were seated and had finished their tea, an old dame appeared, leading a young wife, to pay their respects to Tripitaka. Boqin said: "This is my mother, and my humble wife." Tripitaka said: "Pray, let your honored mother take the seat of honor, and let me make my bows to her." The old dame said: "Master, you are a guest from afar — pray spare yourself; there is no need for bows." Boqin said: "Mother, he is under the Tang king's command, sent to the Western Heaven to behold the Buddha and seek the scriptures. Just now I met your son upon the ridge-top, and your son, thinking of him as a man of our own country, invited him home to rest his horse, and tomorrow I will set him on his road." Hearing this, the old dame was greatly pleased and said: "Good, good, good! Even had we wished to invite him, it could not have fallen out so well. Tomorrow is the anniversary of your father's death. Let us trouble the master to perform some good works and recite a scroll of scripture, and the day after we shall send him off." Now this Liu Boqin, though a slayer of tigers and the Defender who guarded the mountain, had some measure of filial devotion in him. Hearing his mother's words, he set about preparing incense and paper, and kept Tripitaka there.

As they were talking, the day unknowingly drew toward evening. The servants set out tables and stools and brought up several platters of well-cooked tiger meat, steaming hot, and placed them on the table. Boqin invited Tripitaka to make do with it for now, and said he would prepare more food. Tripitaka pressed his palms together at his breast and said: "Mercy! I will not deceive you, Defender — from the time I came out of my mother's womb I have been a monk, and I have never known how to eat meat." Hearing this, Boqin pondered a long while and said: "Master, for generations my household has never known how to eat vegetarian fare. Even when we have a few bamboo shoots, or gather some wood-ear fungus, or find some dried vegetables, or make some bean curd — they are all fried in the fat of river-deer, deer, tiger, or leopard, and there is nothing truly vegetarian about them. Even my two cooking-stoves are soaked through with grease. What is to be done? It is I who have done you wrong by inviting you." Tripitaka said: "Defender, do not trouble yourself overmuch — pray, enjoy your own meal. Even if I, a poor monk, go three or five days without eating, I can endure the hunger; only I dare not break my vow of abstinence." Boqin said: "But what if you should starve to death?" Tripitaka said: "By the Defender's heaven-sent grace I have been rescued from the den of tigers and wolves. Even to starve to death would be better than to be fed to the tigers."

Boqin's mother, hearing this, called out: "Son, do not waste idle words with the master. I have vegetarian things of my own that can serve to entertain him." Boqin said: "Where would vegetarian things come from?" His mother said: "Never you mind — I have my own." She bade the young wife take down the small pot and burn off its grease with fire; they scrubbed it and scrubbed it again, washed it and washed it again, then set it back upon the stove. First they boiled half a pot of water for another use. Then they took some mountain elm-leaves and steeped them in water to make a tea. After that they took some yellow millet and cooked it into rice, and boiled some dried vegetables until they were done. They filled two bowls and brought them out and spread them on the table. The old mother said to Tripitaka: "Master, please take your meal. This tea and rice my daughter-in-law and I have prepared with our own hands, perfectly clean and pure." Tripitaka came down and thanked them, then took his seat.

Boqin set out a separate place, laying out tiger meat without salt or sauce, fragrant river-deer meat, python meat, fox meat, rabbit meat, and dried strips of minced venison — bowls and platters heaped full — to keep Tripitaka company at his meal. But just as he sat down and was about to lift his chopsticks, he saw Tripitaka press his palms together and chant a sutra, which so startled Boqin that he dared not move his chopsticks but rose hastily and stood at the side. Tripitaka had chanted only a few lines when he bade Boqin take his meal. Boqin said: "So you are a monk who recites a short scripture?" Tripitaka said: "That was no scripture — it was a single scroll of grace before meat." Boqin said: "You who have left home certainly have many fine particulars — you must chant and chant even just to eat a meal."

When the meal was eaten and the bowls and platters cleared away, the day gradually grew late. Boqin led Tripitaka out of the central house and back to the rear for a stroll. Passing through a narrow lane, they came to a thatched pavilion. He pushed open the door and they went inside. On the four walls hung several strong bows and stiff crossbows, with quivers of arrows thrust among them; over the beams were draped two blood-reeking tiger hides; at the foot of the wall were stuck many spears, knives, tridents, and staves; and in the very center stood two seats. Boqin invited Tripitaka to sit a while. But seeing how fierce and unclean it all was, Tripitaka dared not sit long, and so came out of the thatched pavilion. Walking on further to the rear, they came to a great garden, where there was no end to the clumps of chrysanthemum heaping up their yellow, and the trees of maple and willow hung with crimson. Then, with a sudden rush, out bounded a dozen or so fat deer and a great herd of yellow river-deer, who, seeing the men, only blinked dully and showed no fear at all. Tripitaka said: "Are these river-deer and deer creatures the Defender has kept tame?" Boqin said: "Just as in your city of Chang'an the wealthy households hoard up treasure and the landed ones gather up grain, so we who hunt can only keep and raise some wild beasts, to provide against the days of foul weather." The two of them talked and strolled idly, and before they knew it dusk had fallen, and they turned back to the front house to rest.

Early the next morning the whole household, old and young, all rose and prepared a vegetarian feast to entertain the master, and asked him to begin reciting the scriptures. The master washed his hands, and together with the Defender lit incense before the family altar and bowed to it. Then Tripitaka struck the wooden fish, and first chanted the true words for purifying the karma of the mouth, then the spirit-charm for purifying body and mind, and after that opened a scroll of the Sutra for Delivering the Dead. When that was finished, Boqin asked him to write out a memorial for the departed soul, and then to open and chant the Diamond Sutra and the Guanyin Sutra, each recited aloud in a clear, high voice. When these were done, they ate the midday meal, and then chanted the Lotus Sutra and the Amitabha Sutra, several scrolls of each, and a scroll of the Peacock Sutra, and discussed the story of the cleansing of karma — and again the day grew late. They offered up all manner of incense and burnt offerings, burned the paper horses for the spirits, and burned the memorial document for the departed. The Buddhist service complete, each retired to rest.

Now the soul of Boqin's father, delivered up out of the depths of perdition, came as a ghost to his own house and entrusted a dream to the whole family, old and young, saying: "In the underworld I suffered torments I could not escape, and for long days I could not be reborn. Now, by good fortune, the holy monk has chanted the scriptures and dissolved my sins; King Yama has dispatched men to send me to the rich land of China, to be reborn into a house of consequence. You must thank and see off the master well — do not be remiss, do not be remiss. I am going now." This indeed was: the myriad laws, in their solemn majesty, surely have their purpose — delivering the dead from suffering, lifting them out of perdition.

The whole family woke from their dreams just as the sun was rising in the east. Boqin's wife said: "Defender, last night I dreamed Father came home and said that in the underworld he suffered torments he could not escape, and for long days could not be reborn. Now, by good fortune, the holy monk chanted the scriptures and dissolved his sins; King Yama dispatched men to send him to the rich land of China, to be reborn into a house of consequence. He bade us thank the master well and not be remiss with him. Having spoken, he went straight out the door and drifted away. We called to him but he did not answer; we tried to keep him but could not. Then I woke, and it was a dream." Boqin said: "I too had just such a dream, the very same. Let us rise and tell Mother." The two of them were just about to go and tell her when the old mother called out: "Boqin my son, come here — I have something to say to you." The two came before her, and the old mother, sitting on her bed, said: "Son, last night I had a happy dream. I dreamed your father came home and said that, all thanks to the master's deliverance, his sins were already dissolved, and he was bound for the rich land of China, to a house of consequence, to be reborn." Husband and wife both laughed aloud: "My wife and I both had this very dream, and were just coming to report it — and unexpectedly Mother calls us, and it is the same dream too." Then they called the whole household, young and old, to rise and arrange their thanks, and to ready the horse for him. They all came forward and bowed in gratitude, saying: "Many thanks to the master for delivering our departed father from suffering and lifting him to rebirth — our gratitude is beyond repaying." Tripitaka said: "What power have I, that you should trouble yourselves to thank me?"

Boqin recounted to Tripitaka the dreams of all three, and Tripitaka too rejoiced. Early they had prepared a vegetarian meal, and they also offered a tael of silver in thanks. Tripitaka would not accept a single coin. The whole family pleaded with him most earnestly, but in the end Tripitaka accepted nothing at all. He only said: "If you are willing to show mercy and see me on my way a short distance, I shall be deeply moved by your kindness." Boqin and his mother and wife, having no choice, hastily made some coarse-flour baked cakes for travel-provisions, and bade Boqin see him far on his road. Tripitaka gladly accepted them. The Defender, taking his mother's command, also summoned two or three household servants, each bearing hunting gear, and together they set out upon the great road. There was no end to the wild scenery of the mountains, the splendor of the ridges.

When they had traveled half a day, they saw before them a great mountain — truly it rose to touch the blue heavens, towering and perilous and sheer. In no long time Tripitaka came to its foot. The Defender climbed this mountain as though walking on level ground. When they had come just to the middle of the slope, Boqin turned about and stood below the path, saying: "Master, pray go forward by yourself; I must now take my leave and turn back." Hearing this, Tripitaka rolled from his saddle and dismounted, saying: "I beg you, Defender, by all means, see me a little further on." Boqin said: "Master, you do not understand. This mountain is called the Mountain of Two Borders. Its eastern half belongs to the rule of our great Tang; its western half is the territory of the Tartars. The wolves and tigers over there will not submit to my taming, and I cannot cross the border. You must go on by yourself." At this Tripitaka's heart leapt with fear. He flung out his arms and clutched at Boqin's clothes and sleeves, his tears falling, unable to part. And just at this moment of earnest, lingering farewell, there came from the foot of the mountain a shout like thunder, crying: "My master has come! My master has come!" It so startled Tripitaka that he was struck dumb, and Boqin too was thrown into confusion.

After all, there is no knowing who it was that shouted — so listen to the explanation in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 14 -->
# Chapter 14: The Mind-Monkey Returns to the Right, and the Six Thieves Leave No Trace

A poem says:

> The Buddha is the mind, the mind is the Buddha,
> yet mind and Buddha both depend on things.
> Know that there is no thing and no mind,
> and you are the true-mind, the Dharma-body Buddha.
>
> The Dharma-body Buddha has no shape at all —
> a single round of light enfolding all forms.
> The bodiless body is the one true body,
> the formless form is the form that is real.
>
> Not matter, not void, and not "not-void,"
> not coming, not going, not turning back.
> No difference, no sameness, no being, no non-being,
> hard to renounce, hard to grasp, hard to hear or behold.
>
> The sacred light, within and without, is everywhere the same;
> a whole Buddha-land lies in a single grain of sand.
> One grain of sand contains the thousandfold worlds;
> one body-and-mind holds all the laws as one.
>
> To know this you must master the no-mind secret:
> undefiled, unhindered — that is pure karma.
> A thousand strands of good and evil, yet doing nothing at all —
> that is the homage, Namo Sakyamuni.

Now the story tells how Liu Boqin and the Tang Monk Tripitaka, in their fright and alarm, again heard a voice cry out, "Master, you have come!" The household servants said, "That call must be the old ape in the stone box at the foot of the mountain." The Guardian said, "It is he, it is he." Tripitaka asked, "What old ape is this?" The Guardian replied, "This mountain was once called the Mountain of Five Phases. But when our great Tang Emperor went west and pacified the realm, its name was changed to the Mountain of Two Frontiers. In years past I heard the old folk say that, in the days when Wang Mang usurped the Han, Heaven sent down this mountain and pressed beneath it a divine monkey who fears neither cold nor heat, eats no food nor drinks, but is kept under guard by an earth-spirit who feeds him iron pellets when he hungers and molten bronze when he thirsts. From ancient times until now he has neither frozen nor starved to death. That cry must surely be his. Do not be afraid, Elder; let us go down the mountain and look."

Tripitaka could only consent, and led his horse down. Before they had gone two or three miles, there, sure enough, in the stone box was a monkey, his head bared, his hand thrust out, waving wildly and crying, "Master, why have you come only now? You have come well, you have come well! Free me from here, and I will guard you all the way to the Western Heaven." The Elder drew near and looked closely. And how did the creature appear?

> A pointed snout and sunken cheeks,
> with golden pupils and eyes of fire.
> Moss heaped upon his head,
> creeping vines sprouting in his ears.
> By his temples little hair, but much green grass;
> beneath his chin no beard, but emerald sedge.
> Dirt in his brows, mud in his nose-hollows —
> a thoroughly wretched sight.
> Thick at the fingertips, heavy in the palms,
> caked with the grime of ages.
> Yet the eyes were glad enough to roll,
> the throat and tongue to sound out sweet.
> Quick though his speech might be,
> his body could not stir.
> This was the Great Sage of five hundred years ago,
> who this day, his ordeal fulfilled, escapes the net of Heaven.

The Guardian Liu, truly bold of heart, stepped forward and plucked away the grass at the monkey's temples and the sedge beneath his chin, asking, "What is it you wish to say?" The monkey answered, "I have nothing to say to you. Have that master come up; I have a question to ask him." Tripitaka said, "What would you ask me?" The monkey said, "Are you the one sent by the great lord of the Eastern Land to fetch the scriptures from the Western Heaven?" Tripitaka said, "I am indeed. Why do you ask?" The monkey said, "I am the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, who five hundred years ago made the great uproar in the Palace of Heaven. Because I committed the crime of deceiving my superiors, the Buddha-Patriarch pressed me down in this place. Some time ago a Bodhisattva, the Guanyin, came bearing the Buddha's command to seek out a scripture-pilgrim in the Eastern Land. I begged her to save me, and she counseled me to do no more violence, to take refuge in the Buddha's Law, and with all my heart to protect the scripture-pilgrim on his journey west to worship the Buddha — promising that when the work was done there would be good reward. So day and night I have kept my heart on guard, from dawn to dusk I have hung in suspense, awaiting only a master to come and set me free. I am willing to protect you on your quest for scriptures and to be your disciple."

When Tripitaka heard this he was filled with joy and said, "Though you have such a good heart, and have received the Bodhisattva's instruction, and wish to enter the gate of the Buddha, yet I have neither axe nor chisel — how am I to free you?" The monkey said, "No need for axe or chisel. Only be willing to save me, and I will come out by myself." Tripitaka said, "I am willing to save you — but how will you get out?" The monkey said, "On the summit of this mountain is the Tathagata's gold-lettered seal-slip. Only climb up and peel away the slip, and I shall come out at once." Tripitaka did as he was told, and turning back, entreated Liu Boqin: "Guardian, I would have you make the climb up the mountain with me." Boqin said, "I do not know whether what he says is true or false." The monkey called out loudly, "It is true! I would never dare to lie."

Boqin had no choice but to summon his servants to lead the horses, while he himself supported Tripitaka and once more ascended the high mountain. Clutching at vines and clinging to creepers, they climbed until they reached the very topmost peak, where indeed they saw ten thousand beams of golden light and a thousand strands of auspicious vapor. There was a great four-square boulder, and on it was pasted a paper seal bearing six golden words: Om Mani Padme Hum. Tripitaka drew near and knelt down, gazing at the golden words upon the stone, made several bows, and facing west prayed aloud: "Your disciple is Chen Xuanzang, sent by imperial command to seek the scriptures. If indeed it is my lot to have a disciple, let me peel away these golden words, free the divine monkey, and together attain the Spirit Mountain. But if it is not my lot to have a disciple — if this is some fierce and stubborn monster seeking to deceive your disciple, with no good fortune to follow — then let the slip refuse to lift." Having prayed, he bowed again; and his bows finished, he stepped forward and gently peeled the six golden words away.

At once a gust of fragrant wind arose and snatched the seal-slip from his very hand up into the sky, and a voice cried, "I am the guard set over the Great Sage. This day his ordeal is fulfilled; we now return to see the Tathagata and to give back this seal-paper." Tripitaka and Boqin and all their company, terrified, bowed toward the empty sky. Then they went straight down the high mountain and came again to the stone box, and Tripitaka said to the monkey, "The seal is peeled away; come out now." The monkey rejoiced and called, "Master, please stand back a little, so I can come out — I would not startle you."

Hearing this, Boqin led Tripitaka and all the company back eastward at a run. When they had gone some five or seven miles, again they heard the monkey shout, "Further, further!" Tripitaka went on a good way more and came down off the mountain — and then there was a thunderous crash, as though the earth split and the mountains crumbled. Everyone shook with terror. And there was the monkey, already arrived before Tripitaka's horse, kneeling stark naked and crying, "Master, I have come out!" He bowed to Tripitaka four times, then sprang up and made a great salute to Boqin, saying, "Thank you, elder brother, for escorting my master, and for weeding the grass from my face." His thanks done, he set to gathering up the luggage and saddling the horse. But when the horse saw him, its loins went soft and its hooves buckled, and trembling it could not stand still — for the monkey had once been the Heaven-Stable Master, Bimawen, who tended the dragon-horses of Heaven and knew certain arts, so that ordinary horses are afraid of him.

Seeing that the monkey was truly of good intent and indeed had the bearing of a man of the Buddhist gate, Tripitaka called to him, "Disciple, what is your surname?" The Monkey King said, "My surname is Sun." Tripitaka said, "Let me give you a religious name, so that you may be called by it." The Monkey King said, "There is no need to trouble your kindness, Master — I already have a religious name. It is Sun Wukong, 'Awakened to Emptiness.'" Tripitaka said joyfully, "Why, that fits our own lineage perfectly! And as for your appearance — you look just like a little novice mendicant. Let me give you a common nickname too, and call you Pilgrim. Will that do?" Wukong said, "Good, good, good!" And from that time he was also called Pilgrim Sun.

When Boqin saw that Pilgrim Sun was wholeheartedly packing up and eager to go, he turned to Tripitaka and made a bow, saying, "Elder, you are fortunate to have gained so fine a disciple here — I am most glad, most glad. This fellow will surely serve. But now I must take my leave." Tripitaka bent in courteous thanks: "I have given you great trouble; my gratitude is beyond words. When you return home, please convey my many regards to your honored mother and your good wife. I have imposed greatly upon your household; when I return I shall come to thank you in person." Boqin returned the courtesy, and so the two parted ways.

Now Pilgrim Sun invited Tripitaka to mount, while he himself went ahead, the luggage on his back, stark-bodied, striding along. Before long they had crossed the Mountain of Two Frontiers, when suddenly a fierce tiger came roaring and lashing its tail. Tripitaka, on his horse, was struck with fear. But Pilgrim, by the roadside, rejoiced and said, "Master, do not fear him — he has come to bring me a set of clothes." He set down the luggage, drew a needle from his ear, faced the wind and gave it a shake, and behold — it was an iron rod as thick as a bowl. Taking it in hand he laughed and said, "This treasure I have not used in more than five hundred years; today I bring it out to earn myself a suit of clothes." Watch how he opened his stride and went to meet the fierce tiger, crying, "Cursed beast! Where do you think you're going?" The tiger crouched low and pressed itself into the dust, not daring to stir. The monkey brought the rod down full on its head, and the brains burst out in ten thousand points of peach-red, the teeth spattered out like beads of jade. So terrified was Chen Xuanzang that he tumbled from the saddle, bit his finger, and cried, "Heaven! O Heaven! The brindled tiger that Guardian Liu fought the other day kept him at it half a day — and today Sun Wukong, without a struggle, beats this tiger to a pulp with a single blow! Truly, beyond the strong there is always the stronger!"

Pilgrim dragged the tiger over and said, "Master, sit a while and rest; let me peel off his clothes and put them on to walk in." Tripitaka said, "Where does he have any clothes?" Pilgrim said, "Never mind me, Master — I have my own way." Good Monkey King! He plucked out one of his hairs, blew on it a breath of magic, and cried, "Change!" — and it became a sharp ox-ear knife. With it he slit the skin along the tiger's belly, stripped it downward, and peeled off the whole hide in one piece. He chopped off the claws and cut away the head, then trimmed the hide into a neat square. Holding it up and measuring it, he said, "A bit too wide — one panel will make two." So he took up the knife and cut it into two panels, stowed one away, and wrapped the other around his waist. He pulled a length of vine from the roadside, bound it tightly, and so covered his lower body, saying, "Master, let us go, let us go. When we reach some house, I'll borrow a needle and thread and sew it up properly — it won't be too late." He gave the iron rod a twirl, and it became a needle again, which he tucked into his ear. Then he shouldered the luggage and invited his master to mount.

As the two went forward, the Elder asked from his horse, "Wukong, that iron rod with which you just slew the tiger — where has it gone, that I cannot see it?" Pilgrim laughed, "Master, you do not understand. This cudgel of mine was got from the Dragon Palace in the great Eastern Ocean. It is called the Divine Treasure Iron that Stills the Bed of the Heavenly River, and also the As-You-Will Gold-Banded Cudgel. In the old days when I rebelled against Heaven, I owed much to it. It changes at my will — when I want it big, it grows big; when I want it small, it shrinks small. Just now I made it into the likeness of an embroidery needle and stowed it in my ear. When there is need, I take it out again." Tripitaka heard this and was secretly delighted. He asked further, "Just now, when that tiger saw you, why did it not move at all, but let you strike it at your leisure? How do you explain that?" Wukong said, "Not to deceive you, Master — never mind a tiger; even a dragon, seeing me, would not dare be insolent. I, old Sun, have no small skill in subduing dragons and taming tigers, in overturning rivers and stirring the seas. I read faces and judge their colors, I hear voices and discern their meaning. Made large, I can measure with the universe; made small, I can withdraw into a single hair. My transformations are without limit, my comings and goings beyond all reckoning. To peel off this tiger's hide — what is there strange in that? Wait till we come to some place of real difficulty, and then you shall see my true powers." Hearing these words, Tripitaka was all the more set at ease, free of care, and urged his horse onward.

Master and disciple went along the road, talking as they went, until before they knew it the sun sank in the west. And they beheld:

> The flaming slant of sunset throwing back its glow;
> at the world's edge, at the sea's far corner, the clouds returning home.
> On a thousand peaks the birds cried frequent and shrill,
> seeking their roosts, plunging into the woods in flocks.
> The wild beasts went in pairs and couples,
> returning to their dens in clans and herds.
> A hook of new moon broke the dusk;
> ten thousand points of bright stars haloed the sky.

Pilgrim said, "Master, step lively — the day grows late. There among those dense-clustered trees there must be some farmstead; let us hurry on early and beg a night's lodging." Tripitaka indeed urged his horse forward and made straight for the dwelling, dismounting before the gate of the farmstead. Pilgrim flung down the luggage, went up, and called out, "Open the gate! Open the gate!" From within an old man came leaning on a staff, and with a creak he opened the gate. But when he saw Pilgrim's evil looks — a tiger-skin tied at his waist, for all the world like the Duke of Thunder — his legs went weak and his body numb, and he stammered out, "A ghost has come! A ghost has come!" Tripitaka stepped forward and steadied him, saying, "Old patron, do not be afraid. He is this poor monk's disciple, not a ghost or a demon." The old man raised his head, and seeing Tripitaka's clear and noble features, at last stood firm and asked, "From what temple are you, monk, that you bring this evil fellow to my door?" Tripitaka said, "This poor monk has come from the Tang court, journeying to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek scriptures. Passing this way as night fell, I have come to your honored dwelling to beg a single night's lodging; tomorrow before daybreak I shall be on my way. I beg only a little kindness." The old man said, "Though you may be a man of Tang, that evil one is no man of Tang."

Wukong cried out in a stern voice, "Old fellow, you have no eyes at all! The man of Tang is my master; I am his disciple. And I am no 'sugar-man' nor 'honey-man' either — I am the Great Sage Equal to Heaven! There are people in these parts who know me. I have seen you before, too." The old man said, "Where did you ever see me?" Wukong said, "When you were small, did you not gather firewood before my face? Did you not pick vegetables upon my very cheeks?" The old man said, "This rascal talks nonsense! Where do you live? Where do I live? And I came before your face to gather firewood and pick vegetables?" Wukong said, "It's my own child who talks nonsense! You don't know me — but I am the very Great Sage from the stone box of this Mountain of Two Frontiers. Look again." The old man at last understood, and said, "You do indeed look somewhat like him. But how did you get out?" So Wukong told the old man in full how the Bodhisattva had counseled him to virtue and bidden him wait for the Tang Monk to peel away the seal and set him free.

Only then did the old man bow down, and he invited the Tang Monk inside, calling his old wife and his sons and daughters all to come and pay their respects. He told them the whole matter, and every one of them was glad. He ordered tea brought, and when the tea was done, he asked Wukong, "Great Sage, you must be well on in years?" Wukong said, "And how old are you this year?" The old man said, "In my foolishness I have reached one hundred and thirty." Pilgrim said, "Then you'd still be my great-great-grandchild! I cannot recall the year of my birth; but I have been at the foot of this mountain more than five hundred years already." The old man said, "True, true. I remember my grandfather saying that this mountain came down from Heaven and pressed down a divine monkey — and only now, this very day, have you escaped the flesh. When I saw you in my childhood, you had grass on your head and mud on your face, and I was not afraid of you. Now there's no mud on your face and no grass on your head, and you look a little thinner — but with that great tiger-skin draped at your waist, how do you differ much from a goblin?" When the whole household heard this, they all roared with laughter.

This old man was quite the worthy soul, and at once ordered a vegetarian meal prepared. After they had eaten, Wukong said, "What is your family's surname?" The old man said, "Our humble house bears the surname Chen." Hearing this, Tripitaka at once came down and clasped his hands, saying, "Old patron, you and this poor monk are of one clan." Pilgrim said, "Master, you are of the Tang surname — how are you of one clan with him?" Tripitaka said, "In my lay family I too was surnamed Chen, a man of the Juxian Village in Hongnong Prefecture of Haizhou, in the Tang realm. My religious name is Chen Xuanzang. It was only because our great Tang Emperor Taizong bestowed on me the title of Imperial Brother Tripitaka, taking 'Tang' as my surname, that I am called the Tang Monk." When the old man heard they shared a surname, he was the more delighted.

Pilgrim said, "Old Chen, I've troubled your house every which way, and I haven't bathed in over five hundred years. Could you go and heat some water, so my master and I may wash ourselves? When we leave, we'll thank you all the more." The old man at once ordered water heated and basins brought, and lit the lamps. When master and disciple had bathed, they sat before the lamp, and Pilgrim said, "Old Chen, there's one more thing to trouble you with: have you a needle and thread I might use?" The old man said, "Yes, yes, yes," and at once bade his wife fetch needle and thread and hand them to Pilgrim. Now Pilgrim had a sharp eye: seeing that his master, while bathing, had taken off a short white cloth tunic and not put it on again, he pulled it over and threw it about himself. Then he took off the tiger-skin, stitched it into one piece, made a horse-face pleat in it, wrapped it about his waist and bound it with the vine, and came before his master, saying, "How does old Sun's get-up today compare with yesterday?" Tripitaka said, "Good, good, good! Dressed like this, you finally look like a real pilgrim." And he added, "Disciple, if you don't mind its being worn and old, you may keep that tunic and wear it." Wukong made a bow and said, "I accept the gift, I accept the gift." Then he went and found some fodder to feed the horse. By then all the chores were done, and master, disciple, and the old man each went to their rest.

Early next morning Wukong rose and asked his master to take the road. Tripitaka dressed, and bade Pilgrim pack up the bedding and luggage. Just as they were about to take their leave, the old man had already prepared face-water for washing, and a vegetarian meal besides. When the meal was over, they at last set out. Tripitaka mounted, Pilgrim led the way; and without their marking it they ate when hungry and drank when thirsty, lodging by night and traveling by dawn. It was now early winter, and they beheld:

> Frost has withered the red leaves; a thousand groves grow thin.
> On the ridges a few pines and cypress keep their grace.
> Plum buds, not yet open, scatter a faint, hidden fragrance;
> the days are warm and short — the little spring of the season.
> The chrysanthemums are spent, the lotus gone, but the mountain camellia thrives;
> by cold bridges the ancient trees vie branch against branch.
> Down winding gullies the spring-water trickles and purls;
> pale clouds, heavy with coming snow, drift and fill the sky.
> The north wind gusts suddenly, tugging at sleeve and hem —
> toward evening the cold strikes hard: how is a man to bear it?

Master and disciple had been traveling a good while when suddenly, by the roadside, there came a sharp whistle, and out burst six men, each gripping a long spear or a short sword, a keen blade or a stout bow, and shouting in a great voice, "Where do you think you're going, monk? Leave your horse and set down your baggage at once, and we'll spare your life to pass!" So terrified was Tripitaka that his souls flew off and scattered; he tumbled from his horse and could not utter a word. Pilgrim helped him up with his hand and said, "Master, rest easy — it's nothing at all. These men have come to bring us clothes and traveling money." Tripitaka said, "Wukong, your ears must be a little stopped up. They say we are to leave our horse and baggage, and you turn round and ask them for clothes and money?" Pilgrim said, "You keep watch over the clothes, the baggage, and the horse; let old Sun have a bout with them and see how it goes." Tripitaka said, "A good fist is no match for two fists, and two fists no match for four hands. There are six big men over there, and you such a small little person — how dare you contend with them?"

But Pilgrim's daring was great from birth, and brooking no argument he stepped forward, folded his hands before his breast, and saluting the six men said, "Sirs, for what cause do you block this poor monk's road?" The men said, "We are the great kings of the highway, the goodly lords of this mountain. Our great names have long been famous — surely you must have heard. Leave your things at once and we'll let you pass; but utter so much as half a 'no,' and we'll grind you to pulp and powder your bones!" Pilgrim said, "I too am a great king by ancestral descent, a mountain-lord of long standing — yet I have never heard that you sirs have any great names." The men said, "You don't know? Then let me tell you: one of us is called Eye-That-Sees-and-Delights; one, Ear-That-Hears-and-Rages; one, Nose-That-Smells-and-Craves; one, Tongue-That-Tastes-and-Longs; one, Mind-That-Perceives-and-Desires; and one, Body-That-Is-the-Root-of-Care." Wukong laughed and said, "So you're six petty hair-thieves! You fail to recognize that this man of religion is your true master — yet you come to block the road. Bring out the precious loot you've plundered, and I'll split it with you in seven shares and let you off." At this the thieves — the glad one glad, the angry one angry, the craving one craving, the longing one longing, the desiring one desiring, the careworn one careworn — all rushed forward together, yelling, "This monk has no manners! You've nothing at all of your own, and now you turn round and ask us to share our things!" They whirled their spears and brandished their swords and crowded forward in a mass, hacking at Pilgrim's head — bang, clang, bang — for seventy or eighty strokes. Wukong stood there in the midst of them as though he knew nothing of it. The thieves said, "What a monk! Truly his head is hard!" Pilgrim laughed, "It'll pass well enough. You've worn your hands out striking — now it's old Sun's turn to take out a little needle and play." The thieves said, "This monk must be some acupuncture-doctor in disguise. We've no illness — what's this talk of plying a needle?"

Pilgrim reached into his ear and drew out an embroidery needle, gave it a shake in the wind, and lo, it was an iron rod, fully as thick as a bowl. Taking it in hand he said, "Don't run — let old Sun strike one blow just to try his hand!" So terrified were the six thieves that they scattered and fled in every direction. But he opened his stride, ran them down all around, and beat each and every one of them to death. He stripped off their clothes, seized their traveling money, and came back smiling, saying, "Master, please proceed — those thieves have all been wiped out by old Sun." Tripitaka said, "What a calamity you have wrought! Though they were highway robbers, even if they had been taken to the magistrate it would not have been a capital crime. With all your skill, you needed only to drive them off — why beat them all to death? This is taking lives without cause! How can you be a monk? A man who has left the household sweeps the floor for fear of harming an ant's life, and shades the lamp with gauze out of pity for moths. How could you, drawing no distinction of black from white, beat them all dead in a single bout? You have not a single shred of mercy or love of goodness. It is well that this is wild country with no one to make inquiry; but if we came to a town, and someone gave you a moment's affront and you fell to your savagery, swinging your cudgel and wounding men at random — I could hardly stand by clean. How then should we escape?" Wukong said, "Master, if I had not beaten them to death, they would have beaten you to death." Tripitaka said, "I, a man of religion, would sooner die than dare to do violence. Even if I died, it would be but one body; but you have killed six men — how do you reason that away? If this matter were brought to the magistrate, then even if your own father held the office, it could not be talked round." Pilgrim said, "Not to deceive you, Master — five hundred years ago, in the days when I held sway as a monster-king on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, I cannot tell how many men I killed. By your reckoning, if it had all gone to the magistrate, there'd have been some fine indictments." Tripitaka said, "It was precisely because you were unrestrained and unmanaged, raging savagely through the world, bullying Heaven and deceiving your superiors, that you suffered that ordeal of five hundred years. Now that you have entered the gate of religion, if you go on doing violence as you did then, killing living things at every turn, you cannot reach the Western Heaven, you cannot be a monk. Too wicked! Too wicked!"

Now this monkey, all his life, could never endure a scolding. Hearing Tripitaka go on nagging and muttering, he could not hold down the fire that flared in his heart, and burst out: "Since you say I cannot be a monk and cannot reach the Western Heaven, then have done with this endless carping and railing at me — I'll go back, and that's that!" Tripitaka made no reply. And the monkey, giving way to his temper, leapt up with a bound, cried, "Old Sun's off!" — and was gone. Tripitaka quickly raised his head, but already he was nowhere to be seen; he heard only a whoosh, and away the monkey went eastward. The Elder was left utterly alone, nodding to himself and sighing, grieving and lamenting without end: "That fellow! So past all teaching — I said only a few words to him, and he goes off without form or shadow, straight back where he came from! Enough, enough, enough! It must be that it is not in my fate to win a disciple or gather any companion. Now if I wished to seek him there is no place to seek; if I wished to call him he would not answer. On, then, on." Indeed:

> Staking body and life, he turns toward the West alone —
> leaning on no other, he must be his own master.

The Elder had no choice but to gather up his luggage, sling it on the horse, and not even riding but going on foot — one hand propping the priest's pewter staff, the other clutching the reins — pressed on westward, forlorn and desolate. He had not gone far when, on the mountain road ahead, he saw an aged mother holding out a cotton-padded garment, and upon the garment a flowered cap. When Tripitaka saw her draw very near, he hurriedly led his horse aside and stood to the right to let her pass. The old mother asked, "Where are you from, Elder, that you go all alone and forlorn in this place?" Tripitaka said, "Your disciple is one sent by the great Tang of the Eastern Land to journey to the Western Heaven, to worship the living Buddha and seek the true scriptures." The old mother said, "The Buddha of the West is at the Temple of Great Thunderclap, in the land of India; the way thither is a hundred and eight thousand miles. With you traveling thus, a single man and a lone horse, with no companion and no disciple, how can you ever get there?" Tripitaka said, "Some days ago I gained a disciple, but he was savage and headstrong, and when I spoke a few words to him he would not take instruction, and went off into the void." The old mother said, "I have here a cotton tunic and a gold-inlaid flowered cap that once belonged to my son. He was a monk for but three days when, alas, his life was cut short and he died. I have just been to his temple to weep for him, and taken leave of his master, and brought away these two things — the garment and the cap — to keep as a remembrance. But since you have a disciple, Elder, let me make you a gift of this garment and cap." Tripitaka said, "I am grateful for your generous gift, old mother, but my disciple has already gone, and I dare not receive it." The old mother said, "Which way did he go?" Tripitaka said, "I heard a whoosh, and he went off eastward." The old mother said, "My own home is not far to the east; he has surely gone that way. I have besides a spell, called the Spell of the Settled Mind, also named the Tight-Fillet Spell. You should silently con it until you know it by heart, fix it firmly in your mind, and never let a single soul learn of it. I will go and overtake him and bid him come back and follow you again, and you shall give him this garment and cap to put on. If he will not obey your command, only recite this spell in silence, and he will never again dare to do violence, nor ever again dare to leave you."

Hearing this, Tripitaka bowed his head in grateful thanks. The old mother changed into a beam of golden light and went off eastward. Then Tripitaka knew in his heart that it was the Bodhisattva Guanyin who had bestowed this true spell upon him, and hastily he gathered earth in place of incense and burned it, bowing earnestly toward the east. His bows done, he took up the garment and cap and hid them in the middle of his bundle. Then, sitting by the roadside, he conned and practiced the Spell of the Settled Mind, reciting it over and over a number of times until he had it letter-perfect and fixed firm in his breast — but of that we say no more.

Now the story tells how Wukong, having parted from his master, took a single somersault of cloud and went straight back to the great Eastern Ocean. Pressing down his cloud-head, he parted the watery way and came straight to the front of the Crystal Palace. Soon the Dragon King, alarmed, came out to receive him and brought him within to be seated. The courtesies done, the Dragon King said, "Of late I have heard that the Great Sage's ordeal was fulfilled — my congratulations, belated though they be! No doubt you are putting in order your fairy mountain and returning to your ancient cave?" Wukong said, "I had such a mind, but I have become a monk besides." The Dragon King said, "A monk? How so?"
