Pilgrim said, "I owe it to the Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea, who counseled me to virtue and bade me attain the right fruit, following the Tang Monk of the Eastern Land westward to worship the Buddha, taking refuge in the Buddhist gate; and I am called Pilgrim now." The Dragon King said, "This is truly to be congratulated, to be congratulated! This is indeed to forsake the crooked and return to the straight, to chasten the heart toward goodness. But since it is so, why are you not going west — why have you come back east?" Pilgrim laughed and said, "It's that the Tang Monk does not understand a man's nature. There were a few hair-thieves robbing the highway, and I beat them to death; but the Tang Monk went nagging and muttering and reckoned up no end of my faults. You may imagine — can old Sun bear such stifling reproaches? So I left him, meaning to go back to my own mountain, and came first to pay you a visit and beg a cup of tea." The Dragon King said, "I am honored, I am honored." And straightway the dragon-sons and dragon-grandsons brought up fragrant tea and presented it.

When the tea was done, Pilgrim turned his head and saw, hanging on the rear wall, a painting of "The Presenting of the Shoe at the Yi Bridge." Pilgrim said, "What scene is this?" The Dragon King said, "Great Sage, you came before; this event came after — that is why you do not know it. This is called 'Thrice Presenting the Shoe at the Yi Bridge.'" Pilgrim said, "What is 'Thrice Presenting the Shoe'?" The Dragon King said, "The immortal here is Huang Shigong, and the young man is Zhang Liang of the Han age. Shigong was sitting on the Yi Bridge when of a sudden his shoe fell off below the bridge, and he called Zhang Liang to fetch it. The young man at once fetched it and knelt to present it before him. This happened three times, and Zhang Liang showed not the least hair of arrogance or sloth. So Shigong, loving his diligence and respect, gave him by night a heavenly book and charged him to uphold the Han. Afterwards he did indeed plan strategy within the tent and decide victory a thousand miles away. When peace was won, he gave up his office and returned to the mountains, roamed with Master Red Pine, and awakened to the Way of immortals. Great Sage, if you do not protect the Tang Monk, do not give your full diligence, do not accept instruction, then in the end you will be but a goblin-immortal — never think to attain the right fruit." Wukong heard this and brooded in silence a good while, saying nothing. The Dragon King said, "Great Sage, you must decide for yourself; do not, for the sake of present ease, ruin your future." Wukong said, "Say no more — old Sun will go back and protect him, and there's an end." The Dragon King said joyfully, "Since it is so, I dare not keep you long. I beg the Great Sage early to show his mercy, and not stay parted too long from your master."

Pilgrim, seeing him press him to be gone, hastily sprang up, left the sea-treasury, mounted his cloud, and took leave of the Dragon King. As he went, he met the Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea. The Bodhisattva said, "Sun Wukong, why is it that you do not take instruction, do not protect the Tang Monk, but come to do business here?" In a fluster, Pilgrim made obeisance upon his cloud and said, "Some time ago I received the Bodhisattva's good words, and indeed a Tang monk came, peeled away the seal, saved my life, and I followed him as his disciple. But he blamed me for being savage and headstrong, so I gave him the slip for a moment; and now I am going to protect him again." The Bodhisattva said, "Go quickly, then, before you lose your resolve." With that, each went their way.

In a moment Pilgrim saw the Tang Monk sitting downcast by the roadside. He went up and said, "Master, why are you not on the road? What are you still doing here?" Tripitaka raised his head and said, "Where have you been? You left me neither daring to go on nor daring to stir; I could only sit here waiting for you." Pilgrim said, "I went to the house of the old Dragon King in the great Eastern Ocean to beg a cup of tea." Tripitaka said, "Disciple, a man of religion should not tell lies. You'd been gone from me scarcely an hour, and you say you went to the Dragon King's house for tea?" Pilgrim laughed, "Not to deceive you, Master — I can ride the somersault cloud, and a single somersault carries a hundred and eight thousand miles. That's how I could go and come back so quick." Tripitaka said, "I spoke to you a trifle too heavily, and you took offense at me and went off in a temper, abandoning me. For one of your gifts, you may go and get a cup of tea; but one like me, who cannot go anywhere, can only sit here enduring hunger. You ought to feel some shame!" Pilgrim said, "Master, if you're hungry, I'll go and beg some food for you." Tripitaka said, "There's no need to beg. There's still some dry provision in my bundle, given me by Guardian Liu's mother. Go and fetch the alms-bowl, find some water, and let me eat a little so we can be on the road."

Pilgrim went to unfasten the bundle, and in the midst of the wrappings he saw several coarse-flour cakes, which he took out and handed to his master. And he also saw the glossy, glowing cotton tunic and the gold-inlaid flowered cap. Pilgrim said, "Did you bring this garment and cap from the Eastern Land?" Tripitaka glibly answered offhand, "These are what I wore when I was small. With this cap on, even untaught one can recite the scriptures; with this garment on, even unrehearsed one can perform the rites." Pilgrim said, "Good Master, give them to me to wear." Tripitaka said, "I only fear they may not fit; but if you can wear them, then put them on." So Pilgrim took off his old white cloth tunic, donned the cotton tunic — and it was just as if it had been cut to his measure — and set the cap upon his head. When Tripitaka saw him put the cap on, he stopped eating his dry provision and silently recited the Tight-Fillet Spell once through. Pilgrim cried, "My head aches, my head aches!" The master recited it again and again without stopping, until Pilgrim was rolling on the ground in pain and had clawed the gold-inlaid flowered cap to tatters. Then Tripitaka, fearing he would snap the gold fillet, ceased and recited no more; and when he stopped, the pain ceased too. Pilgrim reached up to feel his head, and there, like a thread of gold, it was clamped tight upon him — it could not be taken off nor snapped through, for it had already taken root. He took the needle out of his ear, thrust it into the fillet, and pried wildly to get it out. Tripitaka, fearing he would pry it apart, recited the spell again; and at once the pain was upon him as before, so that he stood on his head, turned somersaults, his ears red and his face crimson, his eyes bulging and his body numb. Seeing him in such a state, the master could not bear it, and once more ceased; and the pain left his head. Pilgrim said, "This head of mine — so it's Master that has put a curse on me!" Tripitaka said, "I was reciting the Tight-Fillet Scripture — when did I ever curse you?" Pilgrim said, "Recite it again and see." Tripitaka did indeed recite it again, and Pilgrim was indeed in pain again, crying only, "Stop, stop! The moment you start it, I hurt. What's the meaning of this?" Tripitaka said, "Will you now heed my teaching?" Pilgrim said, "I will heed it." "And will you do no more violence?" Pilgrim said, "I dare not."

Though he answered so with his mouth, his heart still harbored ill intent; and giving the needle a shake — bowl-thick again — he made to bring it down on the Tang Monk. In a fright the Elder recited the spell two or three times more, and the monkey toppled to the ground, dropped the iron rod, and could not lift his hand, crying only, "Master, I understand! Recite no more, recite no more!" Tripitaka said, "How dare you, with such a treacherous heart, try to strike me?" Pilgrim said, "I never dared strike you. I ask you, Master — who taught you this trick?" Tripitaka said, "It was an old mother just now who handed it down to me." Pilgrim flew into a rage and said, "No need to say more — that old mother is surely none other than that Guanshiyin! How could she harm me so? Let me go up to the Southern Sea and beat her!" Tripitaka said, "Since it was she who taught me this spell, she must surely know it already. If you go looking for her, and she recites it, won't you be done for?" Pilgrim saw the reason in this and truly dared not stir, but turned his heart, knelt, and pleaded piteously: "Master, this is her device to keep me in check and make me go west with you. I won't go provoke her — and you, don't take it for a common matter to keep reciting. I am willing to protect you, with never again a thought of turning back." Tripitaka said, "Since it is so, then help me to mount and let us go." And only then did Pilgrim, his heart wholly given over, brace up his spirit, gird tight the cotton tunic, saddle the horse, gather up the luggage, and press on toward the west.

What more befell on this journey, and what was said hereafter — listen to the explanation in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 15 -->
# Chapter 15: The Hawk-Grief Gorge and the Dragon-Horse

We left off with Wukong attending upon the Tang Monk as they pressed westward. For several days they journeyed on, and it was now the cold of the last month of the year, with a bitter north wind howling and ice slicking every surface. Their road wound along sheer cliffs and broken precipices, over folded ridges and tier upon tier of perilous peaks. Tripitaka was upon his horse when, from far off, he heard the rushing of water clamoring in his ears. He turned his head and called, "Wukong, where is that water sounding?"

Wukong answered, "I recall that this place is called Coiled-Snake Mountain, and the stream here is the Hawk-Grief Gorge. That must be the gorge water making the noise." Before he had finished speaking, the horse reached the bank, and Tripitaka reined in to look. What he saw was this:

> A trickling cold vein winds and pierces the clouds,
> Clear deep waters mirror the sun in crimson.
> Its voice stirs like night rain heard in a hidden valley,
> Its colors flare like dawn glow dazzling the empty sky.
> Down a thousand fathoms the spray flies, spitting shattered jade,
> A single pool roars and answers the pure wind.
> The flow returns at last to vast leagues of misty waves,
> Where gull and egret forget themselves, far from any angler's line.

While master and disciple were both gazing, all at once the middle of the gorge gave a great roar, and out bored a dragon. Pushing the waves and heaving up the swells, it shot from the cliffside straight at the elder. In his fright Wukong dropped the luggage, snatched his master down off the horse, and ran. But the dragon could not catch up to them — so instead it swallowed the white horse, saddle, bridle, and all, in a single gulp, and once more sank down and hid its tracks beneath the water.

Wukong settled his master on a high mound to sit, then went back to fetch the horse and shoulder the load. But there was only the one load of luggage — the horse was nowhere to be seen. He carried the baggage over and set it before his master, saying, "Master, that wicked dragon has vanished without a trace. It has only frightened my horse away."

Tripitaka said, "Disciple, how then can we find the horse again?"

"Rest easy, rest easy," said Wukong. "Let me go and have a look." He gave a whistle and leapt into the air. With his fiery eyes and golden pupils he shaded his brow with his hand and searched in all four directions, but nowhere could he see a sign of the horse. He brought his cloud down and reported, "Master, our horse has certainly been eaten by that dragon. I can see nothing of it anywhere."

Tripitaka said, "Disciple, how big a mouth can that creature have, that it could swallow a horse that size, saddle and bridle and all? More likely it was startled and slipped its rein, and has bolted into some fold of the mountains. Look again, and look closely."

Wukong said, "You don't know my powers. With these two eyes of mine, in broad daylight I can commonly see fortune and disaster a thousand li off. Within that thousand li, if a dragonfly so much as spreads its wings, I would see it — how then could I fail to see a horse that big?"

Tripitaka said, "If indeed the thing has eaten it, how am I to go forward? Pity me — through all these thousand mountains and ten thousand rivers, how am I ever to travel?" And as he spoke, his tears fell like rain.

When Wukong saw him begin to weep, he could not hold back his hot temper, and he shouted aloud, "Master, don't carry on in this spineless way! Sit there, sit there, and let old Sun go find that creature and make it give back our horse — that's all there is to it."

But Tripitaka caught hold of him and said, "Disciple, where will you go to find it? What if it comes lunging out from some hidden place behind you, and harms me too? Then both man and horse would be lost — what good would that be?"

At these words Wukong grew angrier still, and bellowed like thunder, "You're useless, useless! You want a horse to ride, yet you won't let me go — at this rate I'll sit here minding the baggage until I grow old!"

He was raging fiercely and could not master his fury, when all at once they heard a voice speaking from the air, calling, "Great Sage Sun, do not be vexed; royal younger brother of Tang, do not weep. We are the host of guardian deities dispatched along this road by the Bodhisattva Guanyin, come in secret to protect the seeker of scriptures." Hearing this, the elder hastily made his bows.

Wukong said, "Which of you are you? Report your names, that I may take the roll."

The gods said, "We are the Six Ding and Six Jia, the Guardians of the Five Quarters, the Four Sentinels of the Hours, and the eighteen Protectors of the Faith — each of us taking turns to stand watch by day and await your commands."

Wukong said, "Today, beginning with whom?"

The Guardians said, "The Ding and Jia, the Sentinels, and the Protectors serve in rotation. As for us, the Guardians of the Five Quarters — only the Gold-Headed Guardian stays close by your side day and night without leave."

Wukong said, "Very well. Those not on duty may withdraw. Leave the Six Ding spirit-generals and the Day-Sentinel of the Hours, together with the Guardians, to keep watch over my master. Let old Sun go and find that wicked dragon in the gorge and make it return my horse." The host of gods obeyed.

Only then did Tripitaka set his heart at ease and sit down upon the stone cliff, charging Wukong to be careful. "Just keep your mind at rest," said Wukong.

What a fine Monkey King! He girt up his cotton tunic, hitched up his tiger-skin kilt, gripped his gold-banded iron cudgel, roused his spirits, and went straight down to the gorge. Half on cloud and half on mist, he hovered over the water's face and shouted aloud, "You filthy mud-loach, give me back my horse! Give me back my horse!"

Now that dragon, having eaten Tripitaka's white horse, lay coiled in the middle of the gorge bottom, nursing its spirit and tending its nature. But hearing someone above cursing and demanding the horse, it could not keep down the fire blazing in its heart. With a sudden bound it leapt up through the waves and broke the surface, crying, "Who dares come here mouthing such big talk to do me injury?"

When Wukong saw it, he gave a great shout — "Don't run! Give me back my horse!" — and whirling his cudgel, struck straight at its head. The dragon bared its fangs and lashed its claws to seize him. The two of them fought a bout there at the edge of the gorge, and it was a valiant contest indeed. Behold:

> The dragon stretched its keen claws,
> The monkey raised his gold-banded staff.
> The one's whiskers hung like threads of white jade,
> The other's eyes flashed like lamps of red gold.
> The one's barbel-pearl spat out a rainbow mist,
> The other's iron rod danced up a wild wind.
> The one was an unfilial whelp that shamed its sire and dam,
> The other a spirit who had bullied the hosts of Heaven.
> Both, through misfortune, had endured their torments,
> And now, to win merit, each displayed his might.

Back and forth they went, battling for a long while, circling and wheeling, until the dragon's strength softened and its sinews went slack, and it could resist no longer. With a single twist it dove again into the water, sank deep to the gorge bottom, and would not show its head — though the Monkey King railed at it without cease, it only played deaf.

Wukong, having no recourse, could only go back to Tripitaka and say, "Master, I cursed that monster out, and it fought me for a good while, then turned coward and fled. Now it skulks in the middle of the water and won't come out again."

Tripitaka said, "But are you certain it was truly that creature that ate my horse?"

Wukong said, "Listen to you! If it hadn't eaten it, would it still be willing to come out and answer me, and pit itself against old Sun?"

Tripitaka said, "When you slew that tiger the other day, you said you had the art of subduing dragons and taming tigers. How is it that today you cannot subdue this one?"

Now this monkey could not bear to be pressed. When he heard Tripitaka throw this rebuke in his face, his divine fury blazed up and he said, "Say no more, say no more! Let me go and have it out with him once again."

The Monkey King strode off and sprang to the gorge's edge, and there he worked his sea-overturning, river-churning magic. The waters of that bottomlessly clear Hawk-Grief Gorge he stirred up until they surged like the flooding waves of the Yellow River winding through its nine bends. Down in the deep gorge the wicked dragon could neither sit nor lie in peace, and thought in its heart, "Truly, blessings come not in pairs, and disasters never come singly. I have only just escaped the death sentence of Heaven's law; for not even a year I have been passing my days here as fate allows, and now I run into this loutish demon come to do me harm." The more it thought, the angrier it grew, until it could no longer endure the affront. Gritting its teeth, it leapt forth and cursed, "What lout of a demon are you, come from who-knows-where, to bully me like this?"

Wukong said, "Never mind where I'm from or not from — just give back my horse, and I'll spare your life."

The dragon said, "Your horse is down in my belly. How am I to vomit it up again? I won't give it back — what of it?"

Wukong said, "If you won't return the horse, then look out for my cudgel. I'll simply beat you to death, and you can pay for my horse with your life — that will settle it." And the two of them fought another bitter battle beneath the mountain cliff. But after only a few exchanges the little dragon truly could not hold out. With a flick of its body it changed into a little water-snake and slithered away into the grass.

The Monkey King chased after with his cudgel, parting the grass in search of the snake, but not the least sign of it could he find. So vexed was he that the three corpse-spirits within him leapt and the smoke poured from his seven orifices. He recited the syllable "Om" and at once summoned the local Earth-god of that district and the Mountain-spirit of that place. Together they came and knelt, saying, "The Mountain-spirit and the Earth-god come to attend you."

Wukong said, "Stick out your shanks — five strokes apiece to greet me, and let old Sun ease his temper."

The two gods knocked their heads and pleaded, "We beg the Great Sage's indulgence; let your humble spirits speak."

"Speak, then," said Wukong. "What is it?"

The two gods said, "The Great Sage was long pent up, and your humble spirits did not know when you would come forth, which is why we failed to meet you. We beg ten thousand pardons for the offense."

Wukong said, "Very well, I'll not beat you. But let me ask you: that monster dragon in the Hawk-Grief Gorge — where is it from? And how did it come to snatch and eat my master's white horse?"

The two gods said, "Great Sage, you never had a master before. You were originally a primal immortal who would submit neither to Heaven nor to Earth. How could you come to have any master's horse?"

Wukong said, "You two simply don't know. It was for the matter of my deceiving Heaven above that I suffered five hundred years of misery. Now, by the grace of the Bodhisattva Guanyin's exhortation to virtue, a true monk under the Tang court's commission has rescued me out, and bidden me follow him as his disciple, to journey to the Western Heaven and worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. Because our road passed this place, my master lost his white horse."

The two gods said, "So that is how it stands. There never was any demon in this gorge before — only that it is deep, steep, broad, and wide, and the water gleams clear to the very bottom, so that even crow and magpie dare not fly across; for the clear water shows them their own reflections, which they take for birds of their own flock, and again and again they hurl themselves into the water. That is why it is named the Steep Hawk-Grief Gorge. Only that some years ago, when the Bodhisattva Guanyin was traveling to seek out the scripture-pilgrim, she saved a jade dragon and sent it here, bidding it await that pilgrim and commit no evil deeds. It only, when hungry, comes up onto the bank to snatch a few birds to eat, or to catch some river-deer for its food. We do not know how, in its ignorance, it has today collided with the Great Sage."

Wukong said, "The first time, it traded blows with old Sun and circled with me a few rounds. The second time, old Sun cursed and railed, but it would not come out again. So I worked a river-churning, sea-overturning spell and muddied up its gorge water, and then it came leaping forth, still bent on contending. But it could not withstand the weight of old Sun's cudgel, and changed into a water-snake and slithered into the grass. I chased after to find it, but there was no trace."

The Earth-god said, "Great Sage, you don't know. This gorge has ten thousand passages all connecting through, which is why its currents run so deep and far. There must be just such a passage here too, and down it the dragon has slipped. There is no need for the Great Sage to rouse his temper and hunt here. To capture this creature, you need only invite the Bodhisattva Guanyin to come, and naturally it will submit."

Hearing this, Wukong called the Mountain-spirit and Earth-god to come together with him to see Tripitaka, and he laid out the whole matter. Tripitaka said, "But if we are to go and invite the Bodhisattva, when will we ever get her back? Your poor monk — how am I to endure the cold and hunger?" Before he had finished, they heard the Gold-Headed Guardian call out of the empty air, "Great Sage, you need not stir from your place. Your humble spirit will go and invite the Bodhisattva."

Wukong was overjoyed and called out, "What trouble for you, what trouble! Go quickly, go quickly!" The Guardian at once mounted his cloud and went straight up toward the Southern Sea. Wukong charged the Mountain-spirit and Earth-god to guard his master, sent the Day-Sentinel of the Hours to seek out provisions, and himself went back to patrol the gorge bank — but of that no more.

Now the Gold-Headed Guardian, riding his cloud, soon arrived at the Southern Sea. He pressed down his auspicious light and went straight into the Purple Bamboo Grove of Potalaka Mountain. There he had the gold-armored devas and Moksha the Hui'an page convey his message, and was granted an audience with the Bodhisattva.

The Bodhisattva said, "On what errand have you come?"

The Guardian said, "The Tang Monk, at Coiled-Snake Mountain by the Steep Hawk-Grief Gorge, has lost his horse, and the Great Sage Sun is so beset that he can move neither forward nor back. When they questioned the local earth-spirits, it was said that the wicked dragon the Bodhisattva placed in the gorge has swallowed it. So the Great Sage sent me to come and beg the Bodhisattva to subdue this wicked dragon and restore their horse."

Hearing this, the Bodhisattva said, "This creature is the son of Aorun, Dragon King of the Western Sea. Because he set a fire and burned the bright pearls upon the palace hall, his father accused him of unfilial defiance, and in the Court of Heaven he was condemned to death. It was I who saw the Jade Emperor in person and begged him down, that he might serve as the Tang Monk's mount and bearer. How is it that, on the contrary, he has eaten the Tang Monk's horse? If that is how it is, then let me go myself."

The Bodhisattva descended from her lotus throne, left her immortal grotto, and with the Guardian rode upon the auspicious light, crossing over the Southern Sea. There are verses to attest it. The verses say:

> The Buddha preached the Paramita Tripitaka scriptures;
> The Bodhisattva spread goodness to fill the Long Wall.
> The Mahā wondrous words pass through Heaven and Earth;
> The Prajñā true mantras rescue ghost and spirit.
> Thereby the Golden Cicada cast off his shell anew,
> And so Xuanzang was made to cultivate again.
> Only because the road was barred at Hawk-Grief Gorge,
> The dragon's son returned to truth and took the form of a horse.

In no great while the Bodhisattva and the Guardian arrived at Coiled-Snake Mountain. There in mid-air they halted their auspicious cloud, and looking down, they saw Sun Wukong at the gorge's edge cursing and railing. The Bodhisattva bade the Guardian go and summon him. The Guardian brought his cloud down and, not passing by Tripitaka, went straight to the gorge bank and said to Wukong, "The Bodhisattva has come."

Hearing this, Wukong sprang up on his cloud into the air and shouted at her, "You — teacher of the Seven Buddhas, compassionate founder of the faith — how could you cook up such a scheme to do me harm?"

The Bodhisattva said, "You insolent horse-monkey, you boorish bare-bottomed simpleton! With all my care, again and again, I won you a scripture-pilgrim, and earnestly charged him to save your life. How is it that, instead of coming to thank me for the grace of sparing you, you come to make an uproar at me?"

Wukong said, "You've served me well indeed! When you set me free, you should have let me roam wherever I pleased and amuse myself in peace. The other day you met me upon the sea and wounded me with a few words, telling me to come and serve the Tang Monk with all my heart and strength — well and good. But why did you give him a flowered cap to trick me into wearing it on my head, to suffer for it? You've made this band grow fast into old Sun's very skull, and taught him besides some 'Tight-Band Spell.' That old monk recites it again and again, and my head aches and aches — is this not your doing me harm?"

The Bodhisattva laughed and said, "You monkey! If you will not obey instruction and will not accept the true fruit, then unless you are bound like this, you'll go deceiving Heaven and bullying above again — how would you know good from ill? If once more you go blundering into calamity as before, who would there be to take you in hand? Only by getting this 'demon-headband' will you be willing to enter the gateway of my yoga."

Wukong said, "Well, count that affair as my own demon-band, then. But why have you taken that guilty wicked dragon and set it here to work mischief and eat my master's horse? This too is letting a wrongdoer loose to do evil — most unkind of you!"

The Bodhisattva said, "That dragon I personally petitioned the Jade Emperor for, and begged him down here expressly to serve the scripture-seeker as a mount and bearer. Consider — how could a common horse from the Eastern Land ever survive these ten thousand rivers and thousand mountains? How could it reach that Buddha-land of Spirit Mountain? Only by getting this dragon-horse can the journey be made."

Wukong said, "But as for this creature, who fears old Sun so that it skulks and won't come out — what's to be done about that?"

The Bodhisattva called to the Guardian, "Go down to the gorge bank and call out, 'Third Prince Jade Dragon, son of Dragon King Aorun, come forth — the Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea is here.' Then it will come out."

The Guardian indeed went to the gorge bank and called twice. The little dragon broke through the waves and leapt out of the water, changing into human form. Treading a cloud, it rose into the air, bowed to the Bodhisattva, and said, "I thank the Bodhisattva for the grace of saving my life. I have waited here a long while, yet have heard no tidings of any scripture-pilgrim."

The Bodhisattva pointed at Wukong and said, "Is this not the chief disciple of the scripture-pilgrim?"

The little dragon looked and said, "Bodhisattva, this is my adversary! Yesterday, hungry in my belly, I truly ate his horse. Trusting in some strength of his, he battled me until I lost heart and fled, and then cursed me until I dared not come out of my door. He never once mentioned a single word about 'seeking scriptures.'"

Wukong said, "You never asked me my surname or my name — how was I to say?"

The little dragon said, "Did I not ask you, 'What lout of a demon are you, come from where?' And you bawled, 'Never mind where from or not from — just give me back my horse!' When did you so much as utter half the word 'Tang'?"

The Bodhisattva said, "That monkey-head trusts only in his own strength and is never willing to praise another. From now on, going forward, there will be more who join you. If they ask, first bring up the words 'seeking scriptures,' and then, without need of any toil, they will submit of themselves."

Wukong gladly accepted the teaching. The Bodhisattva stepped forward and plucked the bright pearl from beneath the little dragon's throat. Dipping her willow sprig in the sweet dew, she sprinkled it over the dragon's body, blew upon it a breath of immortal vapor, and cried, "Change!" At once the dragon changed into a horse with hair and markings exactly like the old white horse. Then she gave it her charge in words: "You must devote your whole heart to working off your karmic debt. When the merit is achieved, you shall rise above the rank of common dragons and be granted a golden body and the true fruit." The little dragon took the bit-bone crosswise in its mouth and assented with all its heart.

The Bodhisattva bade Wukong lead it to see Tripitaka. "I am returning to the sea," she said. But Wukong clutched at her and would not let go, saying, "I won't go on! I won't go on! The road to the West is so rugged, and guarding this mortal monk — when will we ever arrive? With torments and tribulations like these, old Sun's own life is hard to keep whole — how am I ever to achieve any merit or fruit? I won't go on, I won't go on!"

The Bodhisattva said, "In years past, before you had attained the Way of man, you were still willing to cultivate enlightenment with all your heart. Now that you have escaped your heavenly calamity, how is it you turn so slothful? In our gate, it is by stilling and extinction that one attains the truth; you must keep faith to win the true fruit. If you should come to some place of bodily injury and bitter torment, I grant that you may call upon Heaven and Heaven will answer, call upon Earth and Earth will respond. And if at the very last you reach some pass from which there is no escape, I myself will come in person to save you. Come here — let me grant you one more power." The Bodhisattva plucked three leaves from her willow, set them at the back of Wukong's head, and cried, "Change!" At once they changed into three life-saving hairs. She told him, "When you come to a time of utter helplessness with no master to turn to, you may transform these as the moment requires, to rescue you from urgent and bitter calamity."

Hearing all these kind words, Wukong at last gave thanks to the greatly merciful, greatly compassionate Bodhisattva. And the Bodhisattva, wreathed in fragrant winds and drifting colored mists, turned straight back toward Potalaka and was gone.

Only then did Wukong bring his cloud down, grasp the dragon-horse's forelock, and come to Tripitaka, saying, "Master, the horse is here."

The moment Tripitaka saw it he was greatly delighted and said, "Disciple, how is it this horse is even plumper and sleeker than before? Where did you find it?"

Wukong said, "Master, you must still be dreaming. Just now the Gold-Headed Guardian invited the Bodhisattva to come, and she transformed that dragon of the gorge into our white horse. The hair and markings are the same — only it lacks saddle and bridle. Old Sun led it here." Tripitaka was astonished and said, "Where is the Bodhisattva? Let me go and bow my thanks to her."

Wukong said, "By now the Bodhisattva has reached the Southern Sea — no use troubling yourself." Still, Tripitaka gathered up a pinch of earth for incense and bowed toward the south. His bows finished, he rose, and together with Wukong made ready to press on. Wukong dismissed the Mountain-spirit and Earth-god, gave his charges to the Guardian and the Sentinel, and then invited his master to mount.

Tripitaka said, "But how can one ride a horse without saddle or bridle? Let us wait and find a boat to cross the gorge, and then make further arrangements."

Wukong said, "What an impractical master you are! In this wild mountain waste, where would a boat come from? This horse has lived here a long while and must know the lay of the water. Just ride it, and let it serve as your boat across."

Tripitaka, having no choice, did as he said and bestrode the dragon-horse. Wukong shouldered the baggage, and they came to the gorge bank. There, on the upper reach of the stream, they saw an old fisherman poling a raft of dead wood down along the current. When Wukong saw him, he beckoned with his hand and called, "Old fisher, come here, come here! I am from the Eastern Land, going to fetch the scriptures. My master has reached this place and cannot get across — come and ferry him over."

Hearing this, the fisherman at once poled in close. Wukong asked his master to come down from the horse and supported him on either side. Tripitaka stepped onto the raft, the horse was led aboard, and the luggage was settled. The old fisherman poled the raft off, and swift as the wind, swift as an arrow, before they knew it they had crossed the Steep Hawk-Grief Gorge and come up on the western bank.

Tripitaka bade Wukong open the bundle, take out a few cash of Great Tang coin, and offer them to the old fisherman. But the old fisherman gave his raft a single shove with the pole and said, "I'll take no money, I'll take no money," and off he went into the midstream, dim and far away. Tripitaka felt most uneasy and kept pressing his palms together in thanks. Wukong said, "Master, no need to make so much of it. Don't you recognize him? He is the water-spirit of this gorge. He never came to meet old Sun, and old Sun was minded to beat him for it! Letting him off the beating is reward enough — how would he dare to take money?" The master half believed and half doubted, but could only mount the dragon-horse once more and follow Wukong, heading straight onto the main road and pressing west. Truly this is it:

> By the broad and great True Suchness he gains the far shore;
> With a sincere heart, his nature made clear, he climbs Spirit Mountain.

As master and disciple journeyed on together, before they knew it the red sun sank into the west and the daylight grew late. Behold:

> Pale clouds in disarray, the mountain moon grown dim;
> A whole sky of frost-color breeds the cold,
> And on every side the sound of wind pierces the body.
> When the lone bird departs, the gray islet stretches wide;
> Where the falling glow gleams bright, the far mountains lie low.
> A thousand trees of the thin forest roar;
> On the empty ridge a solitary gibbon cries.
> Along the long road no trace of any traveler;
> For ten thousand li the homeward boat enters the night.

Tripitaka, gazing afar from his horse, suddenly saw a manor by the roadside. He said, "Wukong, there is a household ahead. We might lodge there for the night and travel on at dawn."

Wukong raised his head and looked, then said, "Master, that is no household manor."

"How is it not?" said Tripitaka.

Wukong said, "A household manor has no ridge-beasts of soaring fish and crouching creatures on its roof. That is surely a temple or a hermitage."

While master and disciple were still talking, they had already reached the gate. Tripitaka dismounted, and saw above the gate three great characters: "Shrine of the Local Earth-god." So he went in through the gate. Within was an old man with a string of prayer-beads about his neck, who came forward with palms pressed together to welcome them, calling, "Master, please be seated."

Tripitaka hastily returned the courtesy, went up into the hall, and made his obeisance before the holy image. The old man then called a boy-attendant to bring tea. When the tea was finished, Tripitaka asked the old man, "Why is this shrine called the 'Local Earth-god's'?"

The old man said, "This humble place lies within the borders of the country of Habi, in the western lands. Behind this temple is a manor of households, who all, with reverent hearts, raised up this shrine. Li means the soil of one village and district; she means the earth-god of one parish. At every season — spring plowing, summer weeding, autumn harvest, winter storing — each household prepares the three sacrificial beasts, with flowers and fruit, and comes here to sacrifice to the she-god, that the four seasons may be clear and auspicious, the five grains abundant, and the six kinds of livestock thriving."

Hearing this, Tripitaka nodded and praised it: "Truly, 'three li from home and already another district's ways.' Where I come from, the people have no such good custom."

The old man then asked, "Master, what blessed land is your home?"

Tripitaka said, "Your poor monk is from the country of Great Tang in the Eastern Land, sent by imperial decree to go to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. Passing your precious district as the sky grows late, I have come especially to your holy shrine to beg lodging for one night; at first light I will go on."

The old man was greatly pleased, said several times, "I have failed to welcome you properly," and again called the boy to prepare a meal. When Tripitaka had eaten, he gave thanks.

Now Wukong's eye was sharp, and he spied a clothesline hanging beneath the eaves. He went over, gave it a yank to break it off, and used it to tie the horse's legs. The old man laughed and said, "Where did you steal this horse?"

Wukong said angrily, "You old fellow, you don't know high from low in your talk! We are holy monks come to worship the Buddha — how would we steal a horse?"

The old man laughed, "If it isn't stolen, why has it no saddle, bridle, or rein, that you must come and break off my clothesline?"

Tripitaka made his apologies: "This rascal — he's only of a hasty temper. If you wanted to tie the horse, you should have asked the old gentleman nicely for a rope. Why break off his clothesline? — Old sir, don't take offense, don't take offense. This horse of mine — to tell you the truth — is no stolen beast. Yesterday, coming from the east, we reached the Steep Hawk-Grief Gorge, where I had a white horse to ride, complete with saddle and bridle. Unexpectedly there was a wicked dragon in that gorge, grown into a spirit, and it swallowed my horse, saddle and bridle, in one gulp. Luckily my disciple here has some powers, and we were favored that the Bodhisattva Guanyin came to the gorge bank to capture that dragon, and bade it change into the very white horse I used to ride — hair and markings all the same — to carry me to the West to worship the Buddha. We have just now crossed the gorge, not yet a full day past, and have already come to your holy shrine; we have not yet had a chance to procure a saddle and bridle."

The old man said, "Master, don't take offense — your old fellow was only making a joke, who knew your honored disciple would take it in earnest. When I was young I had a bit of country money and rather liked to ride a fine horse myself. But through years of misfortune, suffering bereavement and a fire, I came at last to this state with nothing left, and so I serve as temple-keeper, tending the incense, getting by on the alms of the donor families of the manor behind. As it happens, I still have a saddle and bridle here — a thing I have cherished all my life, and even in this poverty I have never been willing to sell it. Now, hearing the venerable master's words — that even the Bodhisattva should rescue a divine dragon and turn it into a horse to bear you — how can your old man fail to lend a little help? Tomorrow I will fetch that saddle and bridle and gladly present them to the venerable master, to be fitted upon the horse's back for the road. I beg you to accept them with a smile."

Hearing this, Tripitaka thanked him without end. Soon the boy brought out the evening meal. When the meal was done, the lamps were lit, the bedding laid out, and each lay down to rest.

By early the next morning Wukong rose and said, "Master, that old temple-keeper promised us a saddle and bridle last night. Ask him for them, and don't let him off." Before he had finished, the old man indeed came bearing a saddle, bridle, saddle-cloth, rein, halter, and the like — everything needed for a horse, all complete — and set them down beneath the corridor, saying, "Master, I present the saddle and bridle."

When Tripitaka saw them, he received them with delight, and bade Wukong take them up and put them on the horse to see whether they suited. Wukong stepped forward and lifted them up one piece at a time to examine — they were indeed fine things. There are verses to attest it. The verses say:

> The carved saddle gleams bright with silver stars;
> The precious stirrups flash their light, gold threads ablaze.
> The saddle-cloth, layer on layer of folded felt;
> The leading-rein, three plies of purple silk cord.
> The bridle-head's leather worked with rosettes, dazzling;
> The cloud-flaps drawn in gold, dancing with beast-forms.
> The ring-bit forged of tempered, well-hammered iron;
> And hanging down on both sides, water-dipped tassels of hair.

In his heart Wukong was secretly pleased. He set the saddle and bridle upon the horse, and they fit as though made to measure. Tripitaka bowed his thanks to the old man, but the old man hastily raised him up, saying, "How embarrassing, how embarrassing! Why trouble yourself with thanks?" The old man did not detain them further, but invited Tripitaka to mount. The elder came out the gate, took hold of the saddle, and mounted. Wukong shouldered the luggage. The old man then drew from his sleeve a riding-whip — a handle of fragrant rattan studded with leather, and a lash strung and knotted of tiger-tendon silk — and standing by the roadside, offered it up with cupped hands, saying, "Holy monk, I have besides a hand-whip; let me give you that as well."

Tripitaka, on his horse, took it and said, "Many thanks for your charity, many thanks for your charity."

But just as he was exchanging these courtesies, all at once the old man was nowhere to be seen. And when he looked back at the Shrine of the Local Earth-god, it was a patch of bare ground. He only heard, from out of the air, a voice speaking: "Holy monk, forgive my poor reception. I am the Mountain-spirit and Earth-god of Potalaka Mountain, sent by the Bodhisattva to deliver the saddle and bridle to you. Strive on westward, and do not for a moment grow slack." In alarm Tripitaka tumbled out of the saddle and down from the horse, bowing toward the sky and saying, "Your disciple has but fleshly eyes and a mortal frame, and did not recognize the honored spirit's honored face. I beg ten thousand pardons. Pray convey my message to the Bodhisattva — I am deeply favored by her gracious protection." And look at him — he kept knocking his head toward Heaven beyond all counting.

By the roadside the Great Sage Sun was fairly toppled over with laughter, beside himself with mirth — that fine Handsome Monkey King! He came forward and took hold of the Tang Monk, saying, "Master, get up. He's already gone far off — he can't hear your prayers, he can't see you knocking your head. What are you bowing for?"

The elder said, "Disciple, while I knock my head like this, you not only fail to bow even once, but stand there at the side merely grinning and sneering — what is the meaning of that?"

Wukong said, "What do you know of it? For one who plays hide-and-seek like this, head tucked and tail showing, he ought by rights to get a good beating! Only out of regard for the Bodhisattva's face I spare him the beating — that is plenty for him. How would he dare receive old Sun's bow? From a boy, old Sun played the hero and never learned to bow to anyone. Even before the Jade Emperor and Lord Lao Zi I do no more than make a salute — that's the end of it."

Tripitaka said, "You graceless creature, don't talk such empty nonsense. Get up at once, and don't delay our journey." So the master rose, gathered up their things, and they set off toward the west.

From here they traveled two months of peaceful road, meeting only Lolo tribesmen, Hui folk, wolves, serpents, tigers, and leopards. Time sped swiftly by, and it was early spring again. They saw the mountain forests in brocade green, grass and trees putting out green sprouts; the plum blossoms all fallen, the willow's eyes first opening. As master and disciple traveled, taking pleasure in the spring scenery, again they saw the sun sinking into the west. Tripitaka reined in his horse and gazed afar, and in a fold of the mountains saw the shadowy forms of towers and terraces, halls and pavilions sunk deep among the hills. He said, "Wukong, what sort of place do you see over there?"

Wukong raised his head and looked, then said, "That is no palace hall — it must surely be a monastery. Let us hurry on and beg lodging there for the night." Tripitaka gladly agreed, gave the dragon-horse its head, and headed straight toward it.

And after all, there is no knowing what sort of place this was that they went to — so listen to the explanation in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 16 -->
# Chapter 16: The Monks of Guanyin Temple Scheme for the Treasure, and the Fiend of Black Wind Mountain Steals the Cassock

Now the story tells how master and disciple urged their horse onward until they came right up to the temple gate to take a look — and indeed it was a true monastery. Behold:

> Hall upon hall, terrace upon terrace,
> cloister upon cloister, range upon range.
> Beyond the triple gate, ten thousand towering paths
> of bright-hued cloud hung veiled across the sky;
> before the Hall of the Five Blessings, a thousand strands
> of vivid red mist coiled and wreathed about.
> Pine and bamboo lined the two approaches;
> juniper and cypress filled a single grove.
> The pine and bamboo, ageless and unrecorded,
> kept their own clear and secluded calm;
> the juniper and cypress, rich in hue and color,
> stood proud and lovely as their nature pleased.
> One saw besides the high bell-and-drum tower,
> the steep and soaring pagoda spire.
> The meditating monks composed their natures still;
> the birds that cried among the trees sang idle and free.
> Lonely and dustless — truly a place of stillness;
> pure and void, possessed of the Way — and so truly pure and void.

A poem says:

> A lofty cloister, a Jeta Grove hidden in green hollows,
> a sanctuary whose splendor rivals the world beyond.
> Indeed such Pure Lands are rare among mankind —
> of all the famous mountains under heaven, the monks claim most.

The elder dismounted; Pilgrim set down the carrying-pole. They were just about to step through the gate when out from within came a whole company of monks. Look at how they appeared:

> On their heads, the left-pinned caps;
> on their bodies, the spotless robes.
> Bronze rings hung double from their ears;
> silken sashes bound their waists.
> Steady they came in their straw sandals,
> wooden fish gripped in their hands.
> Their mouths forever murmured the chants —
> all taking refuge in the Prajna.

When Tripitaka saw them he stood waiting respectfully beside the gate and offered a courteous greeting. The monks hastily returned his salute and said with a smile, "Forgive us for not noticing you sooner." Then they asked, "Where have you come from? Please come inside the abbot's quarters and take some tea." Tripitaka said, "I am a disciple of the Buddha, sent by imperial commission from the Land of the East, bound for the Thunderclap Monastery to bow to the Buddha and seek the scriptures. Reaching this place as the day grows late, I should like to borrow the shelter of your noble temple for a single night." The monks said, "Please come in and be seated, please come in and be seated." Only then did Tripitaka call to Pilgrim to lead the horse inside.

But when the monks suddenly caught sight of Pilgrim's features, they grew rather afraid and asked, "What sort of thing is that, leading the horse?" Tripitaka said, "Softly, softly! He is quick-tempered. If he hears you call him a 'thing' he'll take offense. He is my disciple." The monks gave a shiver and, biting their fingers, said, "Such an ugly, monstrous-looking head — and you took him as a disciple?" Tripitaka said, "You can't tell by looking. Ugly he may be, but he is exceedingly useful."

So the monks had no choice but to enter the gate together with Tripitaka and Pilgrim. Inside the gate, upon the main hall they saw four great characters written: "Meditation Temple of Guanyin." Tripitaka rejoiced again and said, "Time and again I have felt the holy grace of the Bodhisattva, yet never managed to give thanks. Now that I have come upon her meditation temple, it is as good as seeing the Bodhisattva herself — a fine chance to bow my gratitude." Hearing this, the monks at once ordered a lay servant to open the hall doors and invited Tripitaka to make his obeisance. Pilgrim tethered the horse, flung down the baggage, and went up into the hall with Tripitaka. Tripitaka stretched out his back and limbs, pressed his breast to the ground, and bowed his head before the golden image. The monks went to beat the drum; Pilgrim went to strike the bell. Tripitaka lay prostrate before the altar, pouring out his heart in prayer. When his prayers and bows were done, the monks left off the drum — but Pilgrim kept right on striking the bell without stopping, now fast, now slow, ringing it for a good long while. The lay servant said, "The worship is finished — why are you still ringing the bell?" Pilgrim at last let go of the bell-hammer and laughed, "What would you know! This is a case of: 'Be a monk for a day, ring the bell for a day.'"

By this time the clanging had startled all the monks of the temple, high and low, great and small. Hearing the wild ringing of the bell, they came crowding out together, crying, "What wild man is in here banging the bell and drum about?" Pilgrim leapt out and with a shout cried, "It's your Grandpa Sun, ringing it for sport!" When the monks saw him they tumbled and rolled in terror and groveled on the ground, crying, "Lord Thunder-God! Lord Thunder-God!" Pilgrim said, "The Thunder-God is my great-grandson. Get up, get up, don't be afraid. We are lords come from the Great Tang in the Land of the East." Only then did the monks make their bows. When they saw Tripitaka, their hearts were eased and they were afraid no longer. Among them the abbot of the temple invited them, saying, "My lords, come to the abbot's quarters at the rear and take some tea." So they loosed the reins and led the horse, took up the baggage, passed around the main hall, and went straight into the rear chambers, where they sat in due order.

The abbot offered tea and then had a vegetarian meal prepared. The daylight was still early; Tripitaka had not finished expressing his thanks when from behind, two young acolytes came supporting an aged monk. See how he was got up:

> On his head a Vairocana square cap,
> its cat's-eye gem-knob gleaming with light;
> on his body a brocaded velvet tunic,
> kingfisher-feathered with bright gold edging.
> A pair of monk's shoes set with the Eight Treasures,
> a single staff inlaid with cloud-and-star.
> His face all furrowed with wrinkles —
> like the Old Mother of Mount Li;
> his pair of dim and clouded eyes —
> like the Dragon Lord of the Eastern Sea.
> His mouth could not hold the wind, his teeth being gone;
> his back was bent and humped from cramping sinews.

The monks said, "Our Patriarch has come." Tripitaka bowed and made his greeting, saying, "Venerable Abbot, your disciple makes his salutation." The old monk returned the courtesy, and they took their seats together. The old monk said, "Just now the little ones told me that lords had come from the Tang court of the Land of the East — so I have come out to pay my respects." Tripitaka said, "I have intruded carelessly upon your noble mountain, knowing no better — forgive me, forgive me." The old monk said, "Don't say so, don't say so." Then he asked, "My lord, how many miles is it from the Land of the East to here?" Tripitaka said, "From the borders of Chang'an it is somewhat more than five thousand miles. Crossing the Mountain of Two Frontiers, I took on a young disciple; coming along the road, I passed through the Western foreign kingdom of Habi, and after two months and another five or six thousand miles, I have only now reached your honored place." The old monk said, "Then it is a journey of ten thousand miles and more. I, your disciple, have idled my whole life away and never so much as stepped beyond the temple gate — truly what they call 'sitting in a well to look at the sky,' a worthless and rotten old stump." Tripitaka then asked, "Venerable Abbot, what is your honored age?" The old monk said, "I have foolishly reached the age of two hundred and seventy." Pilgrim heard this and said, "Then he's still a grandson of mine, ten thousand generations down." Tripitaka shot him a glare and said, "Mind your tongue! Don't go about not knowing high from low and offending people." Then the monk asked, "My lord, and how many years have you?" Pilgrim said, "I daren't say."

The old monk took this only for some mad talk, paid it no mind, and asked no further, but only called for tea to be served. A little page brought out a tray of mutton-fat jade bearing three teacups of cloisonné enamel rimmed with gold. Another page carried a white-bronze pot and poured out three cups of fragrant tea — and truly its color shamed the pomegranate blossom for brightness, its flavor surpassed the cassia flower for sweetness. When Tripitaka saw it he praised it without end, saying, "Fine things, fine things — truly fine food in fine vessels." The old monk said, "They offend the eye, they offend the eye. My lord comes from the celestial Tang, a superior realm, and has gazed widely on rare and precious things — what are vessels such as these, that you should overpraise them? My lord, coming from a superior land, surely you have some treasure you might lend your disciple to behold?" Tripitaka said, "Alas, in my Land of the East there is nothing of any worth; and even were there, the road is so long I could not carry it." Pilgrim, at his side, spoke up: "Master, the other day in the bundle I saw that cassock of yours — isn't that a treasure? Why not take it out and show it to him?" When the monks heard "cassock," every one of them gave a cold smile. Pilgrim said, "What are you smirking at?" The abbot said, "My lord just now said a cassock is a treasure — the words are truly laughable. If we speak of cassocks, men like us have no fewer than twenty or thirty apiece; and as for our Patriarch, who has been a monk in this place for two hundred and fifty or sixty years, he has a good seven or eight hundred." And he called out, "Bring them forth to see!"

The old monk too, in a fit of showing off, ordered the lay servants to open the storeroom, and the ascetics carried out the chests — twelve in all — and set them down in the courtyard and unlocked them. Clothes-racks were set up on either side, ropes strung all around, and the cassocks shaken open one by one and hung up for Tripitaka to view. Indeed, the whole place was a hall of damask embroidery, the four walls draped in silk and gauze.

Pilgrim looked them over one by one — all flower-stitched, brocade-padded, embroidered and gold-worked things — and laughed, "Good, good, good. Put them away, put them away. Now bring out ours for a look too." Tripitaka caught hold of Pilgrim and said softly, "Disciple, don't go contesting wealth with people. You and I are alone out here; I only fear something may go wrong." Pilgrim said, "Where's the harm in just looking at a cassock?" Tripitaka said, "You don't understand. The ancients had a saying: 'A rare and precious treasure must not be shown to the greedy and the false.' Once it meets the eye, it stirs the heart; once the heart is stirred, schemes are born. You, who shrink from trouble — if they demand it, you must answer their demand; otherwise, ruin of body and loss of life all spring from this. It is no small matter." Pilgrim said, "Rest easy, rest easy — it's all on old Sun's shoulders."

Look at him — without another word he went hurrying off, undid the bundle, and at once rays of rosy light came bursting out, for there were still two wrappings of oiled paper around it. He stripped off the paper and took out the cassock, and when he shook it open, red light filled the room and colored vapors flooded the courtyard. When the monks saw it, there was not one whose heart did not leap and whose mouth did not praise — truly a fine cassock! Upon it:

> A thousand cunning marvels, hung with bright pearls;
> ten thousand rarities, clustered with the Buddha's gems.
> Above and below, dragon-whiskers spread the colored damask;
> on all four sides, tula-cotton bordered the brocade.
> Wear it, and goblins and demons are thereby destroyed;
> don it, and ogres and sprites are sent to the Yellow Springs.
> A transformed celestial wrought it with her own hands —
> none but a true monk dares to put it on.

When the old monk beheld so rich a treasure, his heart was indeed seized with wicked greed. He stepped forward, knelt down before Tripitaka, and with tears falling from his eyes said, "Your disciple is truly luckless." Tripitaka raised him up and said, "Venerable Abbot, what have you to say?" He said, "My lord, this treasure of yours has only just been spread out, but the day has grown dark, and alas, my eyes are dim and clouded so that I cannot see it clearly — is that not to be luckless?" Tripitaka said, "Bring up a lamp, and you may look again." The old monk said, "My lord's treasure is already radiant; light a lamp on top of that and it will only dazzle the more, and I shall never make it out clearly." Pilgrim said, "How would you like to look at it, then?" The old monk said, "My lord, if in your broad mercy you would set your heart at ease and let your disciple take it back to the rear chamber to study carefully through the night, I would return it to you tomorrow morning to send you on your way westward. I do not know what your honored will may be?" Hearing this, Tripitaka was startled and reproached Pilgrim, "It's all your doing, all your doing!" Pilgrim laughed, "What's there to fear from him? Let me wrap it up and let him take it away to look at. If there's any mishap, old Sun will see to it all." Tripitaka could not stop him; he handed the cassock to the old monk and said, "As you please, look at it. Only return it to me as it was tomorrow morning, with not the least bit of damage or stain." The old monk, full of joy, had a page take the cassock inside. Then he instructed the monks to sweep clean the front meditation hall, fetch two rattan beds, lay out bedding, and invite the two lords to rest; and on the other hand he had them prepare a morning meal to see them off. So all dispersed, and master and disciple shut up the meditation hall and lay down to sleep — of which no more.

Now the story tells how the old monk, having cheated the cassock into his hands, carried it to the rear chamber under the lamp and there wept and wailed bitterly over it, so that the monks of the temple dared not go to sleep first. Even the little page did not know why, but went to report to the others, saying, "Grandfather has wept until the second watch and still won't stop." Two grand-disciples whom he dearly loved came forward and asked, "Master, why do you weep?" The old monk said, "I weep at my own ill-luck — that I cannot look upon the Tang Monk's treasure." The young monks said, "Grandfather, you've gone overboard in your old age. His cassock lies right before you; you need only undo it and look — why all this bitter weeping?" The old monk said, "But I cannot look at it for long. This year I am two hundred and seventy, and for nothing have I scraped together several hundred cassocks. How shall I ever come by one like his? How shall I ever become a Tang Monk?" The young monks said, "Grandfather, you're mistaken. The Tang Monk is a wandering pilgrim who has left his home and forsaken his native village. You, at your great age, enjoying such comforts — that should surely be enough; yet you wish to become a wandering pilgrim like him? Why?" The old monk said, "Though I sit at home in ease and delight in the comforts of my declining years, I shall never get to wear his cassock. If you could let me wear it for but a single day, I would close my eyes in death content — it would mean I had been a monk to some purpose in this mortal world." The monks said, "What nonsense. If you want to wear his, where's the difficulty? We'll keep him here a day tomorrow, and you wear it for a day; keep him ten days, and you wear it for ten days — and that's that. Why this bitter weeping?" The old monk said, "Even if we kept him a year, I could wear it only for a year; in the end I'd not have it for good. When he means to go, we'd just have to let him go — how can we keep it forever?"

While they were talking, a little monk named Guangzhi (Broad Wisdom) put himself forward and said, "Grandfather, if you want it forever, that's easy too." The old monk, hearing this, brightened up at once and said, "My child, what brilliant notion have you?" Guangzhi said, "Those two Tang men are travelers, utterly worn out from the road, and by now they're fast asleep. Let us gather a few strong fellows, take spears and knives, break open the meditation hall, and kill them. We'll bury the corpses in the back garden, and only our own household will know. Then we make off with his white horse and his baggage besides, and keep the cassock here as an heirloom treasure for our line — is that not a plan for the lasting prosperity of our descendants?" When the old monk heard this he was overjoyed, and wiping away his tears he said, "Good, good, good — this plan is masterly!" And he set about readying spears and knives.

But among them was another little monk named Guangmou (Broad Scheme), the younger brother in religion of Guangzhi, who stepped forward and said, "This plan won't do. If you mean to kill them, you must first see how things stand. That white-faced one looks easy enough, but that hairy-faced one looks hard. If by chance we fail to kill him, won't we bring disaster down on ourselves instead? I have a method that uses neither blade nor spear — I do not know how it sits with your honored will." The old monk said, "My child, what method is that?" Guangmou said, "By your grandson's reckoning, let us now summon the heads of all the dormitories on the eastern hill, great and small, and have each bring one bundle of dry firewood. We'll sacrifice those three rooms of the meditation hall and set them ablaze, so that the men have no door to flee by, and burn them, horse and all. Even if the households before and behind the mountain see it, they'll only say the men were careless themselves and let a fire get loose that burned down our meditation hall. Won't both monks be burned to death? And it nicely hoodwinks everyone besides. Will the cassock not then be our heirloom treasure?" When the monks heard this, there was not one who was not delighted, and they all said, "Strong, strong, strong — this plan is even better, even better!" So they ordered the dormitory heads to carry firewood over. Alas! This one scheme was precisely the cause that:

> the long-lived old monk was fated to meet his end,
> and the Meditation Temple of Guanyin turned to dust.

It turned out that within this temple there were seventy or eighty dormitories, and great and small the monks numbered more than two hundred. That very night they came crowding to haul firewood, piling it all around the meditation hall, front and back, hemming in all four sides until there was no way through, making ready to set the fire — of which no more.

Now the story tells how master and disciple had settled down to rest. But Pilgrim, being a spirit-monkey, though he had lain down, was only nourishing his spirit and refining his breath, his eyes drowsing half-awake. Suddenly he heard people moving about outside without cease, and the rustling and crackling of firewood in the rising wind. His heart grew suspicious, and he thought, "It is the dead of night, all is still — how is it there's the sound of footsteps? Could it be thieves and robbers come to do us harm?" In one bound he sprang up, meaning to open the door and go out to look — but feared to wake his master. So look at him work his wonders: with a shake of his body he changed into a honeybee. Truly:

> Sweet-mouthed and venom-tailed,
> slim of waist and light of frame.
> Threading flowers, skimming willows, it flies like an arrow;
> clinging to catkins, seeking fragrance, it falls like a star.
> Its tiny little body can bear a heavy load;
> its faint and humming wings can ride upon the wind.
> Out from beneath the rafter-edge
> it slipped, to see the matter plain.

He saw the whole crowd of monks hauling firewood and dragging straw, already ringing the meditation hall and setting it alight. Pilgrim laughed to himself, "So it's just as my master said! They want to take our lives and scheme for my cassock — that's why they've conceived this poisonous plot. I'd like to take my cudgel and beat them, but the pitiful wretches can't stand a beating; one round of the cudgel and I'd kill them all, and then my master would blame me for cruelty. Enough, enough, enough — I'll do them a 'lead the sheep away as the hand passes,' turn their own scheme against them, and see to it they can't go on living here!"

Good Pilgrim! With one somersault he leapt up into the Southern Heaven Gate. The startled guardians Pang, Liu, Gou, and Bi bowed; Ma, Zhao, Wen, and Guan arched their backs, all crying, "This is bad, this is bad! The one who made havoc in Heaven has come again!" Pilgrim waved his hand and said, "My lords, spare the ceremony, don't be alarmed. I've come looking for the Broad-Eyed Heavenly King." He had hardly finished when the Heavenly King himself arrived, and coming to meet Pilgrim said, "Long time, long time! I heard lately that the Bodhisattva Guanyin came to see the Jade Emperor and borrowed the Four Duty-Gods, the Six Ding and Six Jia, the Revealers and the rest, to guard the Tang Monk on his journey west to fetch the scriptures — and that you had become his disciple. How is it you've found the leisure to come here today?" Pilgrim said, "Never mind catching up. The Tang Monk has met evil men on his road who have set a fire to burn him — the matter is desperate beyond measure. I've come specially to borrow your Fire-Averting Cover to save him. Quick, hand it over for me to use, and I'll return it at once." The Heavenly King said, "You've got it wrong. If evil men have set a fire, you should borrow water to save him — why a fire-averting cover?" Pilgrim said, "How would you know the inside of it? Borrow water to save it, and the fire won't catch — which would only suit them. No, I'll use this cover to shield the Tang Monk from harm, and the rest I don't care about — let it all burn. Quick, quick! By now I fear it may already be too late — don't spoil the business I have below." The Heavenly King laughed, "This monkey is still as unkindly-minded as ever — he looks only to his own and cares nothing for others." Pilgrim said, "Hurry, hurry, don't wag your tongue and wreck the whole affair!" The Heavenly King dared not refuse, and so handed the cover over to Pilgrim.

Pilgrim took it and, pressing down the head of his cloud, came straight to the ridgepole of the meditation hall and covered over the Tang Monk, the white horse, and the baggage. Then he went and sat upon the roof of the rear abbot's chamber where the old monk lodged, to protect the cassock. When he saw the men start the fire, he turned and made a magic sign, recited a spell, and facing the southeast drew in a breath and blew it out — and a gust of wind sprang up that fanned the flames into a roaring blaze. Fine fire, fine fire! Behold:

> Black smoke spreading thick, red flames leaping high.
> Black smoke spreading thick — in all the vast sky not a single star;
> red flames leaping high — the whole earth lit, a thousand miles of red.
> At first, glittering golden serpents;
> after, fierce and bloody horses.
> The Three Spirits of the South display their valor,
> and Huilu, the great Fire-God, plies his power.
> Dry tinder kindled the fierce nature of the blaze —
> what need to speak of Suiren drilling wood?
> Hot oil before the gate scattered colored flames,
> outdoing the Patriarch when he opened his furnace.
> Truly when heartless fire breaks out,
> how can it withstand a willful wickedness?
> Far from quelling the disaster, it abetted the cruelty.
> Wind followed the fire's force — flames flew a thousand fathoms high;
> fire borrowed the wind's might — ashes burst beyond the ninefold clouds.
> Crack and bang, like firecrackers at year's end;
> sputter and crackle, like cannon-fire in the camp.
> It burned so that the Buddha-images in the hall could not escape,
> and the temple-guardians of the eastern courts had nowhere to hide.
> It outdid the night-long battle at Red Cliff,
> it surpassed the fire within the Epang Palace.

This was indeed a case of a single spark able to set ablaze ten thousand acres of field. In a moment the wind raged and the fire flourished, and the whole Temple of Guanyin glowed red from end to end. Look at the crowd of monks, hauling chests and lugging baskets, snatching tables and clutching pots, the whole courtyard filled with wails of misery to heaven. Sun the Pilgrim guarded the rear abbot's chamber, the fire-averting cover shielded the front meditation hall, and all the rest, front and back, blazed in a great conflagration — truly red flames glaring brilliant to the sky, golden light shining through the very walls.

It happened that, as the fire rose, it disturbed a beast-fiend of the mountains. Some twenty miles due south of the Temple of Guanyin there stood a Black Wind Mountain, and within it a Black Wind Cave, and in the cave there dwelt a goblin who had just woken from sleep and was turning over. Seeing brightness through the window, he took it for daybreak; but rising to look, he found it was the glare of a fire to the north below. The goblin was greatly startled and said, "Aha! That must be a fire broken out in the Temple of Guanyin. What careless monks! Let me go and lend them a hand to put it out." Good goblin — he leapt up on his cloud and came straight down beneath the smoke and flame. Truly the fire reached to the sky; the halls in front stood empty, while the two cloisters were just then alight with smoke and fire. He strode in with great steps, and was just calling for water to be brought when he saw that the rear chamber had no fire, and that on its roof-ridge a man sat raising the wind. At this he understood how things stood, and hurried inside to look — and saw in the midst of the abbot's chamber a rosy glow and colored vapors, and on the writing-table a bundle wrapped in green felt. He undid it and looked, and saw it was a brocade cassock, a rare treasure of the Buddhist gate. Truly, "wealth stirs the human heart": he no longer fought the fire, no longer called for water, but seized the cassock and, taking advantage of the uproar to loot, drew back his cloud-steps and went straight off to the eastern mountain.

That fire burned only until the fifth watch and the break of day, and then at last died out. Look at the crowd of monks, stark naked and stripped bare, weeping and wailing, all going to search the ashes for copper and iron, raking through the rotted charcoal, scrabbling for gold and silver. Some, within the broken walls, propped up makeshift sheds; some, at the foot of a scorched wall, set up pots to cook their rice. They cried out their wrongs and their grievances, jabbering and quarreling in confusion — of which no more.

Now the story tells how Pilgrim took the fire-averting cover and with one somersault sent it back up to the Southern Heaven Gate, handing it over to the Broad-Eyed Heavenly King with thanks: "Thank you for the loan, thank you for the loan." The Heavenly King took it back and said, "The Great Sage is most honest. I was just worrying you wouldn't return my treasure and I'd have nowhere to seek it — and to my joy, here you bring it back." Pilgrim said, "Is old Sun the sort to swindle a thing to its owner's face? This is what they call: 'Borrow well and return well, and the next loan comes easily.'" The Heavenly King said, "We haven't met in a long while — won't you come into my palace and sit a moment?" Pilgrim said, "Old Sun isn't as he was in the old days, lounging on broken benches and holding forth in lofty talk. Now I'm guarding the Tang Monk and have no leisure of body. Some other time, some other time." Hastily he took his leave and dropped down on his cloud, and saw the sun-star already rising. He came straight back before the meditation hall, shook his body and changed into a honeybee, flew inside, and resuming his true form to look, found his master still sound asleep.

Pilgrim called out, "Master, it's daylight — get up." Only then did Tripitaka wake, and turning over he said, "So it is." He put on his clothes, opened the door, and stepped out — and lifting his head, suddenly saw nothing but toppled walls and reddened brick, the towers and halls all gone. Greatly alarmed, he cried, "Aiya! How is it the halls are all gone, and everything is red walls? What's happened?" Pilgrim said, "You're still dreaming. There was a fire here tonight." Tripitaka said, "How is it I knew nothing of it?" Pilgrim said, "It was old Sun who guarded the meditation hall; seeing the master deep in sleep, I didn't disturb you." Tripitaka said, "You had the power to guard the meditation hall — why then did you not save the other rooms from the fire?" Pilgrim laughed, "Let me tell you, master, the truth: it was just as you said yesterday. They coveted our cassock and plotted to burn us to death. If old Sun hadn't been aware of it, by now we'd be nothing but charred bones." Hearing this, Tripitaka was afraid and said, "Was it they who set the fire?" Pilgrim said, "If not they, then who?" Tripitaka said, "Could it not be that they slighted you, and this is some doing of yours?" Pilgrim said, "Is old Sun so worthless a fellow as to do such a base thing? It was truly their household that set the fire. Old Sun, seeing their hearts were poisonous, indeed did not help put out their fire — I only helped them along with a little wind." Tripitaka said, "Heavens, heavens! When a fire starts, you should help it with water — how could you turn and help it with wind?" Pilgrim said, "You know the ancients' saying: 'If a man bears no harming heart toward the tiger, the tiger bears no harming mind toward the man.' Had they not played with fire, how would I have stooped to play with wind?" Tripitaka said, "Where is the cassock? It's surely not burned up, is it?" Pilgrim said, "It's all right, it's all right — it can't have burned; the abbot's chamber where the cassock was kept had no fire." Tripitaka said resentfully, "I'll have none of your excuses; if there's the least bit of damage to it, I'll just recite that little spell of mine over and over — and you'll be a dead monkey." Pilgrim took fright and said, "Master, don't recite, don't recite — I'll see to it your cassock is found and returned, that's all. Just let me go and fetch it, and we'll be on our way." Then Tripitaka led the horse and Pilgrim shouldered the load, and they came out of the meditation hall and went straight to the rear abbot's chamber.

Now the story tells how the monks, in the very midst of their grief, suddenly saw master and disciple come leading their horse and shouldering their burden, and were so terrified that the souls fled from every one of them. "The wronged ghosts have come to claim our lives!" Pilgrim shouted, "What wronged ghosts claiming lives? Quick, return my cassock!" The monks all fell to their knees together, kowtowing and saying, "My lord, a wrong has its wronger, a debt has its debtor. If you'd claim lives, it's no concern of ours — it was Guangmou and the old monk who laid the plot to harm you; don't seek your lives' payment from us!" Pilgrim gave a snort and said, "I'll have at you, you death-deserving beasts — who's asking any of you for a life? Just hand over the cassock and let us be on our way!" Among them were two monks of greater courage who said, "My lord, you were already burned to death in the meditation hall — and now you come again asking for the cassock. Are you really men, or ghosts?" Pilgrim laughed, "You spawn of sin — where's there any fire? Go to the front and have a look at the meditation hall, then come back and talk." The monks scrambled up and went to look in front, and the doors and windows and lattices outside the meditation hall had not been so much as singed in the least. The crowd was awestruck, and only then did they recognize that Tripitaka was a holy monk of divine breed and Pilgrim a venerable guardian of the Law. Together they came forward, kowtowing and saying, "We had eyes but no pupils and failed to know the true men come down to the world. Your cassock is at the rear, in the abbot's chamber, with the old Patriarch." Tripitaka passed by three or five layers of ruined walls and broken partitions, sighing without end. And indeed the abbot's chamber had no fire. The monks rushed inside and called out, "Grandfather, the Tang Monk is a divine being and was not burned to death — and now you've only ruined your own household's property. Hurry and bring out the cassock and return it to him."

It turned out that the old monk could not find the cassock, and had besides burned down the temple's own buildings, and was in a state of utter vexation and feverish distress. Hearing these words, how could he dare to answer? Finding no way out, with no road forward or back, he flung open his stride, bent his back, and dashed his head with all his force against the wall — and pitiable to tell, he only smashed his skull and spilled his brains, his soul scattered, his throat's breath cut off, dyeing the red sand crimson. There is a poem to prove it. The poem says:

> Lament the old monk, his nature dull and benighted,
> who lived in vain his span as a graybeard of the world.
> He wished the cassock to pass to far-off ages —
