> how could he know the Buddha's gem is no common thing?
> Taking the easy way, he thought to make it last;
> but bleakness and ruin were sure to be his reward.
> What use were Broad Wisdom and Broad Scheme in the end?
> To harm others for one's own gain comes all to nothing.

The horrified monks wept, crying, "Grandfather has dashed himself to death, and still the cassock is nowhere to be seen — what are we to do?" Pilgrim said, "I suppose you lot have stolen and hidden it. Come out, all of you, and draw up a register of every name, so old Sun can check you off one by one." The abbots of the upper and lower dormitories drew up two registers of the temple's monks, ascetics, pages, and lay servants — high and low, great and small, two hundred and thirty persons in all. Pilgrim asked his master to sit in the high seat, while he himself called the names over from the top one by one, having each open the lapels of his robe and pass clearly inspected — but there was no cassock. He then searched again, item by item, through all the chests and boxes and goods the dormitory heads had snatched out — but nowhere was there any trace of it.

Tripitaka's heart was vexed, and his resentment of Pilgrim was endless; sitting up above, he began to recite the spell. Pilgrim toppled flat to the ground with a thud, clutched his head in unbearable agony, and could only cry, "Don't recite, don't recite — I'll see the cassock found and returned!" When the monks saw it, every one of them trembled with fear and came forward to kneel and plead, and only then did Tripitaka close his mouth and cease. Pilgrim sprang up with a bound, whipped the iron cudgel from his ear, and was about to strike the monks, but Tripitaka shouted him down, "You monkey-head! Your head still aches, and you're still afraid of nothing? Stay your hand — don't harm anyone — and question them once more for me." The monks kowtowed and bowed, beseeching Tripitaka, "My lord, spare our lives! We truly never saw it. This is all the fault of that dead old wretch. Last night, gazing on your cassock, he wept until the depth of the watches, and dared not so much as look at it, for he was scheming to keep it forever and make it an heirloom treasure for his line. He laid the plot and fixed the plan to burn you, my lord, to death. From the moment the fire arose, a wild wind blew up, and every man looked only to fighting the fire and snatching out the goods — none of us knows where the cassock went."

Pilgrim was greatly enraged. He strode into the abbot's chamber, dragged out the corpse of the wretch who had dashed himself to death, stripped it bare and examined it closely — but nowhere on the body was that treasure. He dug down three feet into the floor of the abbot's chamber — but there was not a shadow of it. Pilgrim pondered a good while, then asked, "Is there any goblin or fiend hereabouts that has become a spirit?" The abbot said, "My lord, had you not asked, we'd never have thought to tell you. Due southeast of here there stands a Black Wind Mountain, and within the Black Wind Cave there lives a Black Great King. This dead old wretch used often to discuss the Way with him — and he is a goblin. There's nothing else of the sort." Pilgrim said, "How far is that mountain from here?" The abbot said, "Only twenty miles — that mountain peak you can see is the one." Pilgrim laughed, "Set your heart at ease, master, no need to say more. Beyond a doubt it's that black fiend who's stolen it." Tripitaka said, "His place is twenty miles from here — how can you be so sure it's him?" Pilgrim said, "You didn't see the fire in the night — its light surged ten thousand miles, its brightness pierced the threefold heavens. Never mind twenty miles, it would have been seen at two hundred. It stands fixed that he saw the dazzling glare of the fire, and seizing the chance came secretly here; and seeing our cassock was a treasure, he surely took advantage of the uproar to carry it off. Let old Sun go and look for him." Tripitaka said, "If you go, on whom am I to rely?" Pilgrim said, "Have no fear of that — in the unseen there are spirits to protect you, and in the seen I'll have these monks wait upon you." At once he called the monks over and said, "Some of you go and bury that old ghost; some wait upon my master and tend my white horse." The monks assented.

Pilgrim went on, "And don't you go answering me with your lips only and then, once I'm gone, fail to attend him. Those who look after my master must wear cheerful, pleasant faces; those who tend the white horse must keep his water and fodder evenly supplied. If there's the least thing amiss, here's the kind of cudgel I'll show you." He drew out his cudgel and, against the fire-scorched brick wall, gave a single thump — and smashed the wall to powder, and the shock toppled seven or eight courses of wall besides. When the monks saw it, every one of them went soft in the bones and limp in the body, and knelt kowtowing with dripping tears, saying, "My lord, go in peace — we will serve our lord with all our strength and a true heart, and dare not be in the least remiss."

Good Pilgrim! He swiftly mounted his somersault cloud and went straight up Black Wind Mountain to seek out the cassock. Truly it was that:

> The Golden Dhyana sought the right and left the capital lands,
> staff in hand, turned westward, crossing the green ranges.
> Where tigers, leopards, wolves, and serpents roamed at large,
> merchants, craftsmen, scholars, travelers were rarely seen.
> On the road he met the foolish monk of a foreign land, all envy;
> he leaned wholly on the might of the Great Sage Equal to Heaven.
> Fire broke out, wind arose, the meditation temple lay in ruin;
> and a black bear by night stole the brocade-bordered robe.

After all, this journey — whether the cassock be found or no, and whether the outcome be fortune or ill — listen to the next chapter told.

<!-- chapter 17 -->
# Chapter 17: The Black Wind Mountain and the Bear Who Stole the Robe

When Sun Wukong leapt up into the air with a single somersault, the monks of the Guanyin Temple—great and small alike, together with the ascetics, the serving boys, and the Daoist hangers-on—were so terrified that every one of them bowed toward heaven and cried out, "Master, oh Master! So he was a holy one come down to earth, riding the clouds and harnessing the mist—no wonder fire could not harm him. Curse that blind old skinflint of ours, who schemed and plotted with his crafty heart, and today has only brought ruin upon himself."

Tripitaka said, "Rise, gentlemen, and trouble yourselves no further with cursing. If we recover the cassock, the whole matter is finished. But should it not be found, my disciple has something of a difficult temper, and I do not know what may become of your lives—I fear not one of you would escape." Hearing these words, the monks were each gripped with dread, and they called upon heaven and made vows, asking only that the cassock be found so that their lives might be spared. But of this no more.

Now the Great Sage, having risen into the void, gave his waist a single twist and arrived at once upon Black Wind Mountain. Halting his cloud, he looked carefully, and indeed it was a fine mountain—and the season being the full glory of spring, this was what he saw:

> Ten thousand ravines vie in their streaming,
> a thousand cliffs contend in their splendor.
> Birds call, yet no man is seen;
> blossoms fall, yet the trees keep their fragrance.
> After rain, the sky meets the green wall's gleam;
> wind comes, and the pines unfurl a kingfisher screen.
> Mountain grasses sprout, wild flowers open
> upon hanging cliffs and sheer ridges;
> creeping vines grow, lovely trees shine
> over towering ranges and level downs.
> No hermit is met—then who shall seek the woodcutter?
> Beside the brook two cranes drink;
> upon the rocks the wild apes run mad.
> Heaped and heaped, the conch-shell peaks arrayed in dark eyebrow-hue;
> lofty and lofty, embracing emerald, toying with the haze's light.

While the Pilgrim was admiring the mountain scenery, he suddenly heard voices coming from the slope of fragrant grass before him. Lightly he crept, treading in stealth, and slipped beneath an overhang of rock to peer out with a sidelong eye. There he saw three fiends sitting upon the ground. At the head sat a swarthy fellow; to his left was a Daoist; to his right was a scholar in white. All three were holding forth grandly, discoursing on setting up cauldrons and tending furnaces, on rolling cinnabar and refining mercury, on "white snow" and "yellow sprouts"—the heterodox arts of the side-doors and outer ways.

In the midst of their talk, the swarthy fellow laughed and said, "The day after tomorrow is the anniversary of my mother's travail—my birthday. I trust you two gentlemen will favor me with your presence." The scholar in white replied, "Year after year we have come to wish the Great King long life; how could this year be any different?" The swarthy fellow said, "Last night I came into a treasure—a Buddha-robe of brocade, called the Cassock of the Embroidered Gauze. It is truly a marvelous thing to delight in. Tomorrow I mean to make it the centerpiece of my festivities: I shall throw open a grand banquet, invite the Daoist officials of every mountain, and celebrate the Buddha-robe. We shall call it the 'Buddha-Robe Assembly.' What say you?" The Daoist laughed, "Splendid, splendid, splendid! Tomorrow I shall come first to offer my birthday wishes, and the day after I shall return for the feast."

When the Pilgrim heard the words "Buddha-robe," he was certain at once that this was his cassock. He could not contain his fury. Bounding out from beneath the rock, he raised the golden-banded cudgel in both hands and shouted, "I'll have at you, you pack of thieving fiends! You stole my cassock, and now you mean to hold some Buddha-Robe Assembly? Bring it back to me this instant!" With a roar of "Don't run!" he whirled the cudgel and brought it crashing down toward their heads. In a panic the swarthy fellow turned to wind and fled; the Daoist mounted a cloud and was gone; and only the scholar in white was struck dead by a single blow. Dragging the body over to look at it, the Pilgrim found it was a white-flowered serpent-spirit. For good measure he hoisted it up and tore it into five or six pieces. Then he made straight into the deep mountain to hunt down the swarthy fellow.

Rounding a sharp peak and skirting a steep ridge, he saw before a sheer cliff a cave-dwelling rising up. And this was the sight of it:

> Mists and rosy vapors, faint and far;
> pines and cypress, dense and deep.
> Mists and vapors, faint and far, fill the gateway with their gleam;
> pines and cypress, dense and deep, ring the doors in green.
> The bridge is trodden over a weathered, withered log;
> the peak's crown is wound about with creeping vine.
> Birds bearing red petals fly to the cloudy ravine;
> deer treading the fragrant thickets climb the stone terrace.
> Before that gate the seasons hasten the flowers to bloom,
> and the wind carries their scent abroad.
> Along the dyke green willows turn to golden orioles;
> beside the bank tender peaches flutter the powdered moths.
> Though a wild and open place, not to be boasted of,
> still it rivals the scenes below the Penglai hills.

The Pilgrim came to the gate and saw two leaves of stone door shut very fast. Above the door was a horizontal slab of stone, plainly inscribed with six great characters: "Black Wind Cave of Black Wind Mountain." At once he raised his cudgel and shouted, "Open the door!" Inside, a little imp who kept the gate opened it and came out, asking, "Who are you, that dares to come pounding upon our immortal cave?" The Pilgrim cursed him: "You death-courting beast! What sort of place is this, that you dare call it an 'immortal cave'? Is the word 'immortal' yours to claim? Get inside quickly and report to your swarthy master—tell him to send out your old grandfather's cassock at once, and I'll spare the whole nestful of your lives."

The little imp ran hurriedly back inside and reported, "Great King, the Buddha-Robe Assembly cannot go forward—there is a hairy-faced, thunder-god-beaked monk at the gate demanding a cassock." Now the swarthy fellow, having been chased home from the fragrant-grass slope by the Pilgrim, had only just barred his door and had not yet settled himself when he heard this report. He thought to himself, "I don't know where this fellow has come from, that he should be so insolent as to come bawling at my very door." He called for his armor, and when he had buckled it on, he took up a black-tasseled spear and strode out the gate. The Pilgrim slipped to one side, gripped his iron cudgel, opened his eyes wide, and looked—and indeed the monster was ferociously made:

> A bowl-shaped iron helmet, lacquer-bright;
> black-gold armor, dazzling and brilliant.
> A black silk gown girt with a wind-flap sleeve,
> a dark-green silken sash, its tassels long.
> In his hand a single black-tasseled spear;
> on his feet a pair of black-leather boots.
> His eyes flashed golden pupils like lightning—
> truly this was the Black Wind King of the mountain.

The Pilgrim laughed to himself: "This fellow looks for all the world like one fresh from a kiln, no different from a coal-heaver—he must make his living shoveling charcoal here. How else could he be so black from head to foot?" The monster shouted in a stern voice, "What sort of monk are you, that you dare be so bold in this place of mine?" The Pilgrim, gripping his iron cudgel, rushed up to his face and bellowed, "No idle chatter! Give back your old grandsire's cassock, and be quick about it!" The monster said, "From what temple are you a monk? Where did you lose this cassock of yours, that you dare come demanding it from me?"

The Pilgrim said, "My cassock was kept in the rear abbot's quarters of the Guanyin Temple, due north of here. Because that temple caught fire, you took the chance amid the uproar to loot and plunder, and you stole it away to hold your Buddha-Robe Assembly in celebration of your birthday. How dare you deny it? Give it back quickly, and I'll spare your life. But if you so much as let half a 'No' grind out between your teeth, I'll topple Black Wind Mountain, trample Black Wind Cave flat, and grind every fiend in this den to powder."

When the monster heard this, he laughed coldly, "Ho, ho! So you reckless creature—it was you who set last night's fire, then. You worked your mischief upon that abbot's rooftop, raising the wind, and it was I who carried off a single cassock. What of it? Where do you come from? What is your surname and name? What manner of powers have you, that you dare spout such vast boasting and reckless talk?" The Pilgrim said, "It seems you don't even recognize your own grandfather. Your grandfather is the disciple of the Imperial Younger Brother, the Tripitaka Master who serves before the throne of the Great Tang in the Upper Kingdom. My surname is Sun, my name is Wukong, the Pilgrim. And if you ask after old Sun's powers—why, once I tell them out, they'll scatter your soul and shatter your wits, and you'll die where you stand." The monster said, "I've never had the acquaintance. What powers have you? Tell them out and let me hear." The Pilgrim laughed, "My boy, stand still and listen carefully. I—

> From my youth my powers and arts were high;
> riding the wind, I changed and transformed, a hero bold.
> I nurtured my nature and cultivated truth, enduring the suns and moons,
> leaping clear of the wheel of rebirth, escaping with my life.
> With a single point of sincere heart I once went seeking the Way,
> on the Mountain of the Spirit Terrace I gathered the herbs of medicine.
> On that mountain dwelt an old immortal elder,
> a hundred and eight thousand years in span of life.
> Old Sun bowed to him as master and teacher,
> and he pointed me to the one road of long life.
> He said the elixir lies within the body itself,
> and to seek it outside is labor spent in vain.
> I received the Great Grade Heavenly Immortal's secret formula—
> yet without the root and ground, it is truly hard to bear.
> Turning the light to shine within, I sat with stilled mind;
> in my body the sun and moon, the trigrams Kan and Li, conjoined.
> Thinking on nothing, with desires made few,
> the six senses pure, the body firm and sound.
> To turn from age back to youth is easily had;
> the road from the common to the sage is not far off.
> In three years, without leakage, I formed the immortal body,
> no longer like the vulgar herd to suffer the boiling pot.
> Through the Ten Continents and Three Isles I went roaming at play,
> to the sea's corners and sky's edges I made a circuit round.
> Fated to live three hundred years and more,
> yet I could not soar aloft into the Ninefold Empyrean.
> I went down into the sea, subdued the Dragon, won a true treasure—
> and so I came by this one golden-banded cudgel.
> Before the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit I was the chief commander,
> in the Water-Curtain Cave I gathered my host of fiends.
> The Jade Emperor sent down his summoning decree
> and titled me Equal to Heaven, of the highest rank.
> Several times I made great havoc in the Hall of Divine Mists;
> more than once I stole the peaches of the Queen Mother.
> A hundred thousand heavenly soldiers came to subdue me,
> ranged layer upon layer, dense with spear and blade.
> I beat back the Heavenly King, who returned to the upper realm;
> Nezha, nursing his wounds, led his troops in flight.
> The Illustrious Sage, the True Lord, could change and transform—
> yet old Sun matched him hard and threw him to a draw.
> The Daoist Ancestor, Guanyin, and the Jade Emperor too
> watched from the Southern Heaven's Gate as they subdued the fiend.
> But then Lord Lao lent his aid in one assault,
> and Erlang seized me, hauling me to the Heavenly Court.
> They bound my body to the Fiend-Subduing Pillar
> and ordered the divine soldiers to strike off my head.
> Blades hacked, hammers pounded—they could do me no harm;
> then they had thunder strike and fire come to burn.
> Old Sun, in truth, has powers,
> and I was not afraid by half a hair.
> They sent me into Lord Lao's furnace to be smelted,
> and the Six-Ding divine fire slowly seared me.
> When the days were full and the furnace opened, I leapt out,
> iron cudgel in hand, and ran circling all of heaven.
> Crosswise and lengthwise, nowhere was there a barrier;
> through the Thirty-Three Heavens I made havoc all the way.
> Then my Buddha, the Tathagata, brought his Dharma-power to bear,
> and the Mountain of Five Phases pressed down upon old Sun's waist.
> A full five hundred years I was pinned beneath it,
> till happily I met Tripitaka setting out from the Tang.
> Now I have turned to the right path, going west,
> climbing on to Thunderclap to behold the Jade Brow.
> Go ask through heaven and earth and the four seas around—
> I am, through all the ages, the most famous demon, first of all!"

When the monster heard this, he laughed, "So you're that Bimawen who made havoc in Heaven's Palace, are you?" Now what most enraged the Pilgrim was to be called Bimawen—"Keeper of the Heavenly Stables." Hearing that name, his heart blazed with fury, and he cursed, "You thieving fiend! You stole the cassock and won't return it, and instead you'd wound your master! Don't run—watch the cudgel!" The swarthy fellow dodged aside, took up his long spear, and met the blow hand to hand. A fine fight the two of them made:

> The compliant cudgel, the black-tasseled spear—
> the two before the cave mouth flaunted their strength.
> One stabs splitting the heart, slashing the face;
> one strikes the arm, aiming at the head.
> This one whirls a sinister sideways cudgel-stroke;
> that one drives straight, three sudden spear-thrusts.
> A white tiger climbing the hill comes probing with its claws;
> a yellow dragon lying across the road turns swiftly round.
> They blow out colored mists, spit out radiant light—
> two fiend-immortals beyond all measure.
> One is the cultivated and corrected Sage Equal to Heaven;
> one is the Black Great King grown into a spirit.
> This struggle here within the mountains
> was all for a cassock, and neither of them right.

The monster and the Pilgrim battled for a dozen-odd rounds without deciding the victory, and gradually the red sun stood at noon. The swarthy fellow raised his spear to fend off the iron cudgel and said, "Sun the Pilgrim, let us two break off for now. Wait until I've had my meal, and then I'll wager battle with you again." The Pilgrim said, "You beast—and you call yourself a man? What kind of man fights half a day and then must eat? Why, when old Sun lay pinned beneath the mountain root for five hundred years and more, he never so much as tasted soup or water—where was the hunger in that? Don't make excuses. Don't run. Give back my cassock, and then I'll let you go eat." The monster made a feint with his spear, then drew back his body, slipped into the cave, barred the stone door, and called in his little imps. He set about arranging a banquet and writing out invitations, summoning the demon kings of the various mountains to the celebration—but of this no more.

Now the Pilgrim, unable to break open the door by assault, had no choice but to return to the Guanyin Temple. The monks of that temple had already buried the old abbot and were all in the abbot's quarters waiting upon the Tang Monk. The morning meal being finished, they had laid out the midday meal as well. They were just there refilling soup and changing water when they saw the Pilgrim descend from the air. The monks bowed and ushered him in, and he came before Tripitaka. Tripitaka said, "Wukong, you've come back? What of the cassock?"

The Pilgrim said, "I've found the root of the matter. It's well we did not wrong these monks—it was indeed a fiend of Black Wind Mountain who stole it. Old Sun went secretly to seek him out, and there I found him sitting before a fragrant-grass slope, talking with a scholar in white and an old Daoist. He was a self-confessing monster, too: all at once he came out with it, saying the day after tomorrow is the anniversary of his mother's travail, his birthday, and that he'd invited all the fiends to come celebrate; that last night he'd come by a brocade Buddha-robe and meant to make it his birthday centerpiece, throwing a grand banquet he called the Buddha-Robe Assembly. Old Sun charged up to his face and struck him a blow; the swarthy fellow turned to wind and fled, the Daoist also vanished, and only the scholar in white I beat to death—he turned out to be a white-flowered serpent grown into a spirit. Then I hurried to his cave mouth and called him out to do battle. He's admitted it—he's the one who carried it back. We fought half a day, neither prevailing. The monster went back into his cave, wanting to eat, and barred his stone door, too cowardly to come out and fight. So old Sun has come back to look in on my master and bring this news first. We now know the whereabouts of the cassock; there's no fear he won't return it."

When the monks heard this, those who could press their palms together pressed their palms, those who could kowtow kowtowed, and all chanted aloud, "Namo Amitabha! Today we have learned its whereabouts—now at last our lives are safe." The Pilgrim said, "You needn't be so glad and easy yet. I haven't got it in hand, and my master hasn't yet gone out the door. Only when the cassock is recovered, and my master is sent off well on his way, will you have your place of peace. But if there's the least mishap, old Sun is not a master to be trifled with! Has there been good tea and food for my master? Has there been good fodder for the horse?" The monks all answered with their mouths full of assurances, "Yes, yes, yes—we have not been the least bit remiss with the Master."

Tripitaka said, "In the half-day since you left, I have already had tea three times and two vegetarian meals; they have not dared to slight me. Only put your whole heart and strength into fetching back the cassock." The Pilgrim said, "Don't fret. Since we know its whereabouts, I'll surely seize this fellow and return your property. Rest easy, rest easy."

As they were speaking, the head of the upper hall once more set out a vegetarian offering and invited Master Sun to eat. The Pilgrim took a little, then mounted his auspicious cloud again and went off in search. As he traveled, he saw a little imp coming along the main road, a pear-wood box tucked under his left arm. The Pilgrim reckoned there must be some letter or note inside the box, raised his cudgel, and brought it down on the creature's head. Pity the imp—he could not bear the blow, and was beaten flat as a meat-cake. The Pilgrim dragged him to the roadside, opened the box, and looked—and indeed, there was an invitation. The card read:

> Your humble younger student, Xiongpi the Bear, with bowed head, respectfully addresses the elixir-chamber of the venerable Elder of the Golden Pool, Great Master and Spreader of the Faith: Repeatedly have I received your kind favors, and I am moved to the depths. Last night I beheld the calamity of the Fire God's wrath, and I failed to come to your rescue—yet I trust that, with your immortal contrivance, no harm has come to you. By chance I have come into a single Buddha-robe, and I wish to hold an elegant gathering. I have humbly prepared a few cups of flowered wine and beg the honor of your refined appreciation. When the day comes, I most earnestly entreat your immortal carriage to pass by for a meeting. This is my hope. Sent two days in advance.

When the Pilgrim read it, he laughed aloud, "Ho, ho! That old skinflint—he didn't die one whit unjustly; he was in league with fiends after all. No wonder he lived to two hundred and seventy: I suppose that monster taught him some petty breath-nurturing arts, and so he came by such long years. Old Sun still remembers his looks. Let me change into that monk and stroll into the cave to see where my cassock is kept. If I can lay hands on it, I'll carry it straight back—that will save some effort."

A fine Great Sage! He chanted his spell, faced the wind, and with one transformation became the very likeness of the old monk. Hiding his iron cudgel, he strode along and came straight to the cave mouth, calling, "Open the door!" The little imp opened it, and seeing this figure, hastily turned and reported, "Great King, the Elder of the Golden Pool has come." The monster was greatly startled. "I only just sent the little one off with the invitation to ask him," he thought, "and by now the imp can't even have reached him—how has the Elder come so quickly? It must be that the imp never met him, and that this is surely Sun the Pilgrim, conjured here to demand the cassock. Steward—hide the Buddha-robe; don't let him see it."

The Pilgrim came in through the front gate and saw in the courtyard pines and bamboo crossing their jade-green, peaches and plums vying in their bloom, clump upon clump of opening flowers, cluster upon cluster of fragrant orchids—truly a cave-heaven of a place. He also saw, upon the inner gate, a matched couplet that read: "Quietly secluded deep in the hills, no worldly cares; / dwelling apart in the immortal cave, delighting in heaven's truth." The Pilgrim thought to himself, "This fellow too is a creature who has shed the dirt and left the dust, who knows his allotted fate." Passing through the gate and going farther forward, he reached the third tier of doors, all painted beams and carved rafters, bright windows and colored casements.

There he saw the swarthy fellow, dressed in a black-green ramie-silk lined jacket, draped with a crow-blue patterned-damask cloak, wearing a soft hat of black horn and a pair of black deerskin boots. Seeing the Pilgrim come in, he straightened his clothes and cap, descended the steps to receive him, and said, "Old friend of the Golden Pool, I have been wanting in attentiveness these past days. Please be seated, please be seated." The Pilgrim returned his courtesy. When the greetings were done, they sat; when they were settled, tea was served. After the tea, the monster bowed slightly and said, "Just now I sent a little note to invite you for a meeting the day after tomorrow. Why does my old friend favor me with his visit today?"

The Pilgrim said, "I was on my way to pay my respects when, unexpectedly, I met your splendid letter upon the road. Seeing there was to be an elegant Buddha-Robe Assembly, I hurried here in haste, wishing to beg a glimpse of it." The monster laughed, "Old friend, you are mistaken. This cassock belongs to the Tang Monk. He was lodging at your place—surely you have already seen it; why come to me to look at it?" The Pilgrim said, "Your poor monk only borrowed it, and as it was late at night, I had not yet spread it out to look, when unexpectedly the Great King carried it off. And then the fire burned my humble mountain temple and I lost my household goods. That Tang Monk's disciple, moreover, is something of a fierce fellow, and in all the confusion I searched everywhere and could not find it. It turns out it was the Great King's great good fortune that gathered it in—so I have come especially to have a look."

Just as they were talking, a mountain-patrolling imp came in and reported, "Great King, disaster! The little scout who carried the invitation has been beaten to death by Sun the Pilgrim on the high road, and he has taken the note and changed himself into the Elder of the Golden Pool to come and cheat you of the Buddha-robe!" When the monster heard this, he thought to himself, "I said—how is it the Elder came today, and came so fast? It is indeed him." Swiftly he sprang up, snatched his spear, and thrust at the Pilgrim. The Pilgrim quickly drew his cudgel from his ear, showed his true form, fended off the spear-point, and went leaping out from the central hall, fighting from the courtyard out beyond the front gate. The fiends within the cave were so terrified their courage failed them, and the old and young of the household were all frightened out of their wits. A fine struggle they fought there upon the mountaintop, and this time it was different from before. A fine fight:

> That Monkey King, bold of gall, played the monk;
> this swarthy fellow, sharp of wit, hid away the robe.
> Words went and words came, the chance contrived with skill;
> meeting each turn with a turn, never a step amiss.
> He longed to see the cassock, but no way could he see it—
> a treasure dark and subtle, truly wondrous and fine.
> The little fiend patrolling spoke of the disaster,
> and the old fiend, kindling rage, displayed his divine might.
> Turning his body, he fought out of Black Wind Cave;
> spear and cudgel grappling to tell the right from wrong.
> The cudgel parrying the long spear rang out clear and loud;
> the spear meeting the iron cudgel flashed its gleaming light.
> Wukong's transformations are rare among men;
> the monster's divine powers are scarce in this world.
> This one would make the Buddha-robe his birthday celebration;
> that one, without the cassock, would never willingly yield.
> This bitter fight was hard indeed to part—
> even a living Buddha come to earth could not have broken the siege.

The two of them fought from the cave mouth up to the mountaintop, and from the mountaintop out beyond the clouds, spitting fog and blasting wind, flinging sand and rolling stones, until the red sun sank in the west, and still neither had won or lost. The monster said, "Sun—stay your hand. It's late today, and no good for grappling. Go, go; come again early tomorrow, and we'll settle life and death." The Pilgrim shouted, "Boy, don't run! If you'll fight, fight like a fighter, and don't put me off with 'it's late.'" He laid on, heedless of head or face, working his cudgel down upon him. But the swarthy fellow changed once more into a pure breeze, turned back into his own cave, and shut the stone door fast, coming out no more.

The Pilgrim, having no stratagem to do anything about it, had no choice but to return again to the Guanyin Temple. Lowering his cloud, he called out, "Master." Tripitaka, who had been gazing for him with anxious, longing eyes, was overjoyed to see him before him of a sudden—but seeing no cassock in his hand, was afraid again. He asked, "How is it you still have no cassock this time?" The Pilgrim drew from his sleeve a little note and handed it to Tripitaka, saying, "Master, that monster and the dead old skinflint were friends. He'd sent a little imp with this note, inviting him to come to the Buddha-Robe Assembly. Old Sun beat the little imp to death, changed into that old monk, and went into his cave, where I was cheated of a cup of tea to drink. I meant to ask him for the cassock to look at, but he wouldn't bring it out. Just as we were sitting, some mountain-patrol fellow let the wind out of the secret, and so he fell to fighting me. We battled until just now, neither above the other. Seeing it was late, he slipped back into his cave and shut the stone door fast. Old Sun, with no help for it, has come back for the moment."

Tripitaka said, "How do your powers compare with his?" The Pilgrim said, "I'm not much harder than he—we only fought to a draw." Tripitaka then read the note, and handed it on to the temple's head and said, "Could it be that your own master was a fiend too?" The head of the temple knelt down in alarm and said, "Master, my teacher was a man. It was only because that Black Great King had cultivated his way to the human path, and would often come to the temple to expound the scriptures with my teacher, and taught my teacher certain arts of nurturing the spirit and ingesting the breath, that they addressed each other as friends." The Pilgrim said, "This pack of monks has no fiendish air about it—every one of them has a round head crowning heaven and square feet treading earth; they're only a bit fatter and taller than old Sun, and no fiends. But look here—the note is signed 'humble younger student, Xiongpi the Bear.' This creature must surely be a black bear grown into a spirit."

Tripitaka said, "I have heard the ancients say, 'The bear and the orangutan are of one kind.' Both are beasts. How, then, did he become a spirit?" The Pilgrim laughed, "Old Sun is of the beast kind, and look—I'm made the Great Sage Equal to Heaven. How is he any different? Generally, of all things in the world, whatever has the nine apertures can cultivate itself and become an immortal." Tripitaka said again, "You just said his abilities are a match for yours—how then will you win, and fetch back my cassock?" The Pilgrim said, "Don't worry, don't worry—I have a way to deal with it."

While they were deliberating, the monks laid out the evening meal and invited master and disciple to eat. Tripitaka ordered the lamps lit and went again to the meditation hall at the front to rest. The monks all bunked along the walls and leaned against the partitions, throwing up makeshift shelters, and each lay down to sleep, leaving only the rear abbot's quarters for the heads of the temple to lodge in. By now the night was still, and this was the sight of it:

> The River of Heaven shows its image;
> the jade firmament is without dust.
> The whole sky's stars are brilliant;
> on the one water the wave-marks are gathered in.
> All the ten thousand voices are stilled;
> on a thousand hills the birds are silent.
> Beside the brook the fisher-fires are out;
> on the pagoda the Buddha-lamps grow dim.
> Last night the monks' bells and drums resounded;
> tonight, one round of weeping is heard.

That night he lodged in the meditation hall. But Tripitaka, brooding over the cassock, could not sleep soundly there. Suddenly he turned and saw the window paling white outside, and he rose hastily and called, "Wukong, day has broken—go quickly and seek the cassock." The Pilgrim rolled to his feet in a single bound. Seeing the monks standing in attendance and offering up soup and water, he said, "You take care to wait well upon my master—old Sun is off." Tripitaka got down from the bed and caught hold of him, "Where are you going?" The Pilgrim said, "I've been thinking—this whole business is the fault of the Bodhisattva Guanyin's want of reason. She has this meditation temple of hers here, receiving the incense and offerings of the people hereabouts, and yet she lets that monster live as a neighbor. I'm going to the Southern Sea to find her, to have it out with her, and make her come in person to demand the cassock from the fiend and return it to me." Tripitaka said, "When you go like this, when will you be back?" The Pilgrim said, "At the least, by the time the meal is done; at the most, by noon, the thing will be accomplished. Those monks can wait on you well enough. Old Sun is off."

No sooner had he said "off" than he was gone without a trace. In a moment he reached the Southern Sea, where he halted his cloud to look. And this was the sight of it:

> The boundless ocean stretching far,
> the press of waters joined to the sky.
> Auspicious light enwraps the universe;
> propitious vapors shine on mountain and stream.
> A thousand layers of snow-billows roar to the blue empyrean;
> ten thousand folds of misted waves surge in the white day.
> Water flies to the four quarters,
> waves roll all around.
> Water flying to the four quarters cracks like rolling thunder;
> waves rolling all around peal like the thunderbolt.
> Speak not of the water's force—look rather to the midst.
> Five-colored, hazy, the treasure-heaped hill:
> red, yellow, purple, black, green, and blue.
> Now is seen Guanyin's true and surpassing realm—
> behold the Potalaka Mountain of the Southern Sea.
> A fine place! The mountain peaks soar high,
> their crowns piercing the void.
> In the midst are a thousand kinds of rare flowers,
> a hundred sorts of auspicious herbs.
> The wind sways the treasure-trees;
> the sun reflects on golden lotuses.
> Guanyin's hall, roofed with glazed tile;
> the Tide-Sound Cave, its doorway paved with tortoise-shell.
> In the shade of green willows the parrot speaks;
> in the purple bamboo grove the peacock cries.
> Upon the figured stone, the Dharma-guardians stand in majesty;
> before the agate strand, Moksha stands stalwart.

The Pilgrim could not look his fill at these strange and uncommon scenes. He lowered his cloud straight down and came beneath the bamboo grove. At once the various devas came to receive him, saying, "The Bodhisattva, before the assembly, has greatly proclaimed that the Great Sage has turned to the good—she has praised it much. Now that you are guarding the Tang Monk, how do you find the leisure to come here?" The Pilgrim said, "Because of guarding the Tang Monk, I have met with a certain matter on the road, and have come specially to see the Bodhisattva. I trouble you to announce me." The devas then went to the cave mouth to report, and the Bodhisattva summoned him in. The Pilgrim proceeded according to the rule, and bowed beneath the precious lotus dais.

The Bodhisattva asked, "What have you come for?" The Pilgrim said, "My master, on the road, came upon your meditation temple. You receive the incense of the human world there, yet you let a black-bear spirit dwell as a neighbor, and he has stolen my master's cassock. I have demanded it of him several times and he won't give it up. So I've come especially to ask it of you." The Bodhisattva said, "This monkey talks with no manners at all. If the bear-spirit stole your cassock, why come and demand it of me? It's all because you, you reckless monkey, were so bold as to make a show of the treasure, taking it out for a small-minded man to see; and then you worked your violence, called up the wind and started the fire, and burned my Cloud-Lodging Lower Court—and now you come to my place to play your tricks." When the Pilgrim heard the Bodhisattva say this, he knew that she understood matters past and future, and he bowed in haste, "Bodhisattva, I beg you to forgive your disciple's fault—it is indeed just so. But I'm vexed that the monster won't give me the cassock, and my master wants to recite that little spell of his, and old Sun can't bear the headache. That's why I've come to trouble the Bodhisattva. I beg the Bodhisattva, of her compassionate heart, to help me capture that monster, recover the robe, and go westward." The Bodhisattva said, "That monster has a great many divine powers—he's no less than your equal. Very well—for the Tang Monk's sake, I'll go and make a turn with you." When the Pilgrim heard this, he gave thanks and bowed again. Then he asked the Bodhisattva out the door, and together they mounted the auspicious cloud, and soon reached Black Wind Mountain. They lowered the cloud and followed the path to find the cave.

As they were going along, they saw a Daoist come out from before the mountain slope, carrying a glass tray in his hand, in which were set two pellets of immortal elixir, walking straight ahead. The Pilgrim ran full into him, drew out his cudgel, and brought it down on his head with a single blow, beating the brains out and the blood spurting from his frame. The Bodhisattva was greatly startled, "You monkey, still as wild and lawless as ever! He never stole your cassock, he's no acquaintance of yours, and there's no grudge or feud between you—why have you just beaten him to death?" The Pilgrim said, "Bodhisattva, you don't know him. He's a friend of that black-bear spirit. Yesterday he and a scholar in white were both sitting and talking before the fragrant-grass slope. The day after tomorrow is the black spirit's birthday, and they were invited to come celebrate the Buddha-Robe Assembly. Today he comes first to offer his birthday wishes; tomorrow he'd come to celebrate the Buddha-robe. That's how I knew him—surely today he was going to wish the fiend long life on the fiend's behalf." The Bodhisattva said, "If that's how it is, then never mind." The Pilgrim then went and lifted up the Daoist to look, and found he was a gray wolf. Beside him, on the underside of the tray, were carved some words, reading "Made by the Master of Soaring Emptiness."

When the Pilgrim saw it, he laughed, "Good fortune, good fortune! Old Sun is in luck, and the Bodhisattva is spared some labor too. This fiend may be said to have confessed without being struck, and that fiend has appointed his own undoing today." The Bodhisattva said, "Wukong, what do you mean by that?" The Pilgrim said, "Bodhisattva, old Sun has a word for it—it's called 'turning the enemy's scheme to your own advantage.' I don't know whether the Bodhisattva will be willing to go along with me." The Bodhisattva said, "Speak." The Pilgrim said, "Bodhisattva, you see, in this tray are two pellets of immortal elixir—those will be our gift of introduction to the fiend; and the four characters carved on the back of the tray, 'Made by the Master of Soaring Emptiness'—that will be our hook into him. If the Bodhisattva will go along with me, I can lay out a plan for you, and then there'll be no need to set spear and shield in motion, no need to toil at battle: the monster will meet his doom on the spot, and the Buddha-robe will appear on the spot. But if the Bodhisattva won't go along with me, then the Bodhisattva goes west and old Sun goes east; the Buddha-robe may as well be a gift bestowed, and Tang Tripitaka may as well come to nothing." The Bodhisattva laughed, "This monkey has a glib tongue." The Pilgrim said, "I wouldn't dare—it really is a plan." The Bodhisattva said, "And how does this plan of yours go?"

The Pilgrim said, "On this tray is carved 'Made by the Master of Soaring Emptiness.' I should think this Daoist was himself called the Master of Soaring Emptiness. Bodhisattva, if you'll go along with me, you can change into this Daoist, and I'll eat one of these elixir-pellets and change into the other—made a little larger. Bodhisattva, you take up this tray with its two pellets and go to wish the monster long life; give the larger pellet to the fiend. When the fiend swallows it at one gulp, old Sun will do his work from inside: if he won't hand over the Buddha-robe, old Sun will weave him one straight out of his bowels." The Bodhisattva, having no other way, could only nod her head and go along with him. The Pilgrim laughed, "Well, then?"

At that, the Bodhisattva, with her vast compassion and boundless Dharma-power, her hundred million transformation-bodies—with mind meeting intention, and intention meeting body—in the space of a flicker changed into the immortal Master of Soaring Emptiness:

> The crane-feather robe, the immortal wind blowing brisk;
> wafting and floating, about to step the void.
> The aged countenance, old as pine and cypress;
> a comeliness unequaled in past or present.
> Going and going, yet without abiding;
> thus and thus, of itself set apart.
> All comes at last to one single Dharma—
> it is only the husk of the body that divides.

The Pilgrim looked and said, "Marvelous, marvelous! Is it the fiend who is the Bodhisattva, or the Bodhisattva who is the fiend?" The Bodhisattva laughed, "Wukong—Bodhisattva and fiend, both are a single thought; and as for the original ground, both belong to non-being." The Pilgrim's heart was suddenly enlightened, and turning his body he changed into a single pellet of immortal elixir:

> Rolling on the tray, never coming to rest;
> round and bright, yet without a fixed shape.
> Three threes conjoined in the Goulou rite;
> six sixes weighed in the Shaoweng's count.
> The tile-fragment with the yellow-gold flame;
> the relic-pearl with the broad-day light.
> The lead and mercury without—
> not lightly may their measure be discussed.

The Pilgrim having changed into the pellet, it came out, after all, a little larger. The Bodhisattva marked it well, took up the glass tray, and went straight to the mouth of the fiend's cave to look. And truly it was:

> The cliffs deep, the grottoes perilous; clouds rising over the ridges.
> The cypress dark, the pines green; wind blowing through the woods.
> The cliffs deep, the grottoes perilous—indeed where fiends come and go and human smoke is rare;
> the cypress dark, the pines green—here too the immortal true may cultivate and hide, rich in the Way's own mood.
> The mountain has its ravine, the ravine its spring:
> the murmuring running water sobs like a sounding lute—fit to wash one's ears;
> the cliff has its deer, the wood its crane:
> the deep and secret immortal piping stirs among the peaks—fit too to please the heart.
> This is the fiend-immortal who has his portion to descend to Bodhi,
> and the great vow, boundless, that lets down its pity.

The Bodhisattva looked, and secretly rejoiced in her heart, "This beast has seized this mountain cave, but he has, after all, something of a portion in the Way." And so a compassion was already in her heart.

She came to the cave mouth, and the little imps who kept the cave all somewhat recognized her, saying, "The immortal elder, the Master of Soaring Emptiness, has come!" While one passed word in, another ushered her forward. The monster had already come out to meet her at the door: "Master of Soaring Emptiness, I am obliged for the trouble of your immortal carriage's precious visit—my humble cottage is honored by your light." The Bodhisattva said, "This poor Daoist respectfully presents a single pellet of immortal elixir, and ventures to wish you a thousand years of life." When the two of them had finished their bows and just settled into their seats, they began again to speak of yesterday's affair. The Bodhisattva did not answer, but hastily took up the elixir-tray and said, "Great King, let me first show you my poor intention." She fixed her eye on the larger pellet and pushed it toward the fiend, saying, "I wish the Great King a thousand years of life." The fiend likewise pushed a pellet across and handed it to the Bodhisattva, saying, "I would share it with the Master of Soaring Emptiness."

The yielding done, the fiend was just about to swallow when the pill rolled straight down his throat. The Pilgrim revealed his true form and braced himself into the four-square stance, and the fiend tumbled to the ground. The Bodhisattva showed her true appearance and demanded the Buddha-robe of the fiend. The Pilgrim had already come out through his nostrils. And the Bodhisattva, fearing the fiend might still be unruly, flung a band onto the fiend's head. The fiend rose up and lifted his spear to thrust, but the Pilgrim and the Bodhisattva had already risen into the air, and they began to recite the True Words. The monster's head ached as before; he threw down his spear and rolled about all over the ground. In the half-sky the lovely Monkey King laughed himself over, and on the level ground the black-bear fiend rolled himself ruined.

The Bodhisattva said, "Beast—will you submit now and take refuge in the faith?" The fiend cried with his mouth full, "My heart is willing to take refuge—only spare my life!" The Pilgrim, fearing it would delay the work, meant to strike him then and there. But the Bodhisattva hastily stopped him, "Don't harm his life—I have a use for him." The Pilgrim said, "A monster like this—if you don't beat him to death, what use will you keep him for?" The Bodhisattva said, "Behind my Potalaka Mountain there's no one to keep watch—I mean to take him to be a guardian deity of the mountain." The Pilgrim laughed, "Truly you are a merciful Lord who saves from suffering—not one soul lost. If old Sun had a spell like that, I'd recite the wretched thing on him a thousand times over. This little while there'd be no end of black bears, all of them brought to book!" Now the fiend, having revived a good while, could no longer in fairness bear the pain, and had no choice but to kneel upon the ground and plead, "Only spare my life, and I'll take refuge in the true fruit." The Bodhisattva then lowered her auspicious radiance, laid her hand upon his crown and gave him the precepts, and bade him take up the long spear and follow at her side. And the black bear—now in a single day his wild heart was settled, and his boundless stubborn nature was in this hour gathered in.

The Bodhisattva instructed him, "Wukong, you may go back now. Wait well upon the Tang Monk, and henceforth no more slacking off or making trouble." The Pilgrim said, "I'm deeply grateful the Bodhisattva has come so far—your disciple ought to see you off a way." The Bodhisattva said, "Spare yourself the trouble." The Pilgrim then took up the cassock, knocked his head in farewell, and parted. The Bodhisattva also led off the bear, Xiongpi, and went straight back to the great sea. There is a poem in proof. The poem says:

> Auspicious light, soft and dense, congeals the golden image;
> ten thousand rays in radiant profusion, truly to be admired.
> Broadly she succors the people of the world, letting down her pity;
> everywhere she beholds the Dharma-realm, manifesting the golden lotus.
> Now she has come mostly for the sake of conveying the scriptures;
> and going hence, there was, from the first, no blemish or flaw.
> Subduing the fiend and bringing it to truth, she returns to the great sea—
> and the gate of emptiness has again recovered its brocade cassock.

In the end we do not yet know how the matters that follow will turn out; listen, and the next chapter will explain it.

<!-- chapter 18 -->
# Chapter 18: The Tang Monk Escapes His Trouble at Guanyin Monastery; The Great Sage Subdues a Monster at Gao Village

Sun Wukong took his leave of the Bodhisattva, lowered his cloud, and hung the brocade cassock upon a fragrant nan-wood tree. Then he drew out his iron rod and went smashing his way into the Black Wind Cave—but not a single small imp was to be found within. The truth was that, having seen the Bodhisattva reveal herself and bring the old fiend writhing helplessly to the ground, every one of them had scattered and fled. Wukong, with his blood up, piled dry kindling against the several layers of gates within the cave, front and back, and set it all ablaze at once, turning the Black Wind Cave into a Red Wind Cave. Then he took up the cassock, mounted the auspicious light, and turned back toward the north.

Now Tripitaka had been waiting and watching, and when Wukong did not quickly return, his heart filled with doubt. He could not tell whether the Bodhisattva had refused to come, or whether Wukong had made some excuse and run off for good. While he was lost in these wild guesses and uneasy musings, all at once a glory of bright-colored mist came shimmering down from the middle air, and Wukong suddenly dropped to his knees before the steps and said, "Master, the cassock has come back!" Tripitaka rejoiced greatly, and the assembled monks, too, were one and all delighted. "Wonderful, wonderful!" they cried. "Only now, this very day, are our lives made whole again." Tripitaka received the cassock and said, "Wukong, when you went off this morning you reckoned to be back by noon at the latest. Why do you return now, with the sun in the west?" So Wukong recounted in full how he had invited the Bodhisattva, how she had worked her transformations, and how the monster had been subdued. When Tripitaka heard it, he set out an incense table, bowed to the south in thanks, and then said, "Disciple, since we have the Buddha-robe again, let us pack up at once and be on our way."

"No hurry, no hurry," said Wukong. "It is growing late, and this is no time to be traveling. Let us wait and set out early tomorrow." The monks all knelt down together. "Master Sun speaks rightly," they said. "For one thing, the day is far gone; for another, we have certain vows to fulfill. Now that all is safe and the treasure recovered, let us pay our vows, and we beg the elder to share his blessings with us. Tomorrow morning we will see you off again on your westward road." "Just so, just so," said Wukong. And so you should have seen those monks empty out their purses to the very bottom, gathering whatever scraps of property they had snatched from the fire, each contributing what he could; they laid out a vegetarian feast, burned paper offerings for peace and safety, and chanted several scrolls of scriptures to dispel calamity and undo misfortune. That evening the matter was finished.

Early the next morning they groomed and saddled the horse, packed up the baggage, and set out. The monks accompanied them a long way before turning back. Wukong led the road ahead. It was now the season when spring was at its mellowest, and behold what they saw:

> Soft grass cushioned the white horse's hoofprints;
> willows swayed their golden threads, fresh with dew.
> Peach and apricot filled the woods, vying in loveliness;
> creeping vines wreathed the path and put forth their vigor.
> On the warm sandy banks the mandarin ducks drowsed;
> in the mountain streams, fragrant with blossom, butterflies grew tame.
> Thus autumn had gone, winter waned, and spring was half over—
> yet who knew in what year their pilgrimage would be fulfilled and the true scriptures won?

Master and disciples traveled some five or seven days along wild roads. Then one day, toward dusk, they spied far off a village of houses. Said Tripitaka, "Wukong, look—there's a hamlet close by yonder slope. Suppose we go and beg a night's lodging, and travel on again tomorrow?" "Wait until old Monkey has gone to look whether the omens are good or ill," said Wukong, "and then we'll decide what to do." The master reined in his silken bridle, and Wukong fixed his eyes and looked. Truly it was a place where—

Bamboo fences stood thick, thatched roofs clustered close. Wild trees, towering to the sky, greeted the gate; a winding brook and a stream-bridge mirrored the doors. Beside the road the willows hung green and tender; within the gardens the flowers opened with rich fragrance. At this hour the setting sun was sinking westward, and everywhere through the mountain woods the birds and sparrows clamored; evening smoke rose from the cookfires, and along every lane the oxen and sheep came winding home. He saw, too, the well-fed chickens and pigs drowsing in the corners of the houses, and a tipsy old neighbor coming along singing in his cups.

When Wukong had finished looking, he said, "Master, ride on—it is surely a village of good folk, and just the place to borrow a night's rest." The elder urged the white horse forward, and they soon reached the head of the street. There they saw a young fellow, his head wrapped in cotton cloth, dressed in a blue jacket, carrying an umbrella and a pack on his back, his trousers tucked up and bound, his feet shod in a pair of three-eared straw sandals—a brisk, vigorous lad striding hurriedly out of the village. Wukong reached out and grabbed him fast. "Where are you off to? Let me ask you for a bit of news: what place is this?" The man only struggled and shouted, "Is there nobody else in my village, that you must question me?" Wukong said with a smile, "Don't be angry, good sir. 'Do another a kindness, and you do yourself one.' What harm is there in telling me the name of this place? I might even be able to relieve your troubles." The man could not pull his hand free, and stamped about in a fury. "Bad luck, bad luck! I can't bear the unjust temper of my master, and now I run smack into this bald-pate and have to swallow his impertinence too!" "If you have the strength," said Wukong, "pry my hand open, and then you may go—and good riddance." The man twisted left and right, but he could not budge it; it was as though an iron pincers had clamped him fast. So enraged was he that he flung down his bundle, tossed aside his umbrella, and came clawing at Wukong with both hands like falling rain. Wukong steadied the baggage with one hand and fended the man off with the other, and however the fellow flailed and dodged, he could never lay a finger on him. The more he struggled, the tighter Wukong held, until the man fairly crackled with rage like thunder.

Tripitaka said, "Wukong, isn't someone else coming yonder? Ask that man instead, and have done. Why keep dragging this one about? Let him go." Wukong laughed and said, "Master doesn't understand. If I ask someone else, there'll be no profit in it. It must be this one—there's business to be done here." The man, finding himself held and not released, had no choice but to speak. "This is the land within the borders of the Kingdom of Wusi-Tibet, and it is called Gao Village. More than half the families in the village are surnamed Gao, and so it is called Gao Village. Now let me go!"

"By your traveling gear," said Wukong, "you're no man bound on a short errand. Tell me truly where you mean to go and what business you're really about, and then I'll let you go." Helpless, the man had to tell the truth. "I am a servant of Squire Gao, and my name is Gao Cai. My master has a youngest daughter, twenty years old this year, who has never been betrothed to anyone. Three years ago she was seized by a monster, who has been her husband these three years. My master is far from pleased, and says, 'A daughter married to a monster is no lasting arrangement: for one thing it ruins the family's name, and for another there's no proper in-law to come and go with us.' All along he has wanted to be rid of this monster, but the creature won't go—indeed he has shut my mistress away in his back apartments, and for nearly half a year now has not let her out to see any of the household. My master gave me a few taels of silver and sent me to seek out a master of spells to capture the fiend. All this while I've had no rest; I've gone here and there and engaged three or four men—but all of them were useless monks and weak-bellied Taoists, and none could subdue the creature. Just now my master cursed me roundly, saying I'm good for nothing, and gave me five mace of silver for traveling expenses and told me to go off again and fetch a capable exorcist. Then I run into you, you ill-starred jinx, and you grab hold of me and hold up my journey—so I get it from inside and out, and that's why, in my helplessness, I shouted at you. And now it turns out you've got some grip on you, and I can't break free, and so I've told you the whole truth. Let me go!"

"Your luck's in!" said Wukong. "This is right in my line of work—the very thing, as neat as four-plus-six making ten. You needn't travel far, and you needn't waste your silver. We are no useless monks nor weak-bellied Taoists. We have real skill, and we're old hands at catching monsters. As the saying goes, 'First, the physician is well looked after; second, the eyes are well cured.' Be so good as to go back and tell your master that we are holy monks—the imperial brother sent under commission from the Land of the East, journeying to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures—and that we are well able to subdue fiends and bind monsters."

Gao Cai said, "Don't you go fooling me. I'm a man with a bellyful of grievance already; if you've lied to me and have no skill, and can't lay hold of the monster, then you'll only drag me into more trouble." "I promise I won't let you down," said Wukong. "Lead me to your master's gate." The man, having no other choice, picked up his bundle and his umbrella, turned about, and led the master and disciple to the gate. "Reverend sirs," he said, "sit a moment on the mounting-block while I go in and tell my master." Only then did Wukong let go his hand. He set down the load, led the horse aside, and master and disciple sat and stood by the gate, waiting.

Gao Cai went in through the main gate and walked straight on to the central hall, where, as it happened, he ran square into Squire Gao. The old man scolded him: "You barbarian-hided beast! Why haven't you gone to find someone? What have you come back for?" Gao Cai set down his pack and umbrella and said, "Allow me to report, master: I had just gone out to the head of the street when suddenly I ran into two monks—one riding a horse, one carrying a load. He grabbed hold of me and wouldn't let go, asking where I was bound. I refused, again and again, to tell him; but he pestered me past all bearing, and I couldn't get my hand loose, so at last I told him the whole of your business. He was overjoyed at it, and wants to catch the monster for us." "Where do they come from?" asked the old man. "He says they are holy monks—the imperial brother dispatched by decree from the Land of the East—on their way to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek scriptures." Said the squire, "Since they are monks come from afar, perhaps they really have some skill. Where are they now?" "Waiting outside the gate," said Gao Cai.

The squire hurriedly changed his clothes and came out with Gao Cai to receive them, calling, "Reverend elder!" Tripitaka heard, turned quickly, and there the old man was, already before him. He wore a black silk-gauze cap, a robe of onion-white Shu brocade, a pair of calf-leather boots the color of brown rice, and a girdle of black-green cord; he came out with smiling words to greet them, saying, "Reverend elders, my respects to you." Tripitaka returned the courtesy, but Wukong stood stock-still and did not move. Seeing how fierce and ugly his features were, the old man did not dare bow to him. "Why don't you make your bow to old Monkey?" demanded Wukong. The old fellow, somewhat frightened, said to Gao Cai, "You little wretch, you'll be the death of me! There's an ugly-mugged, monstrous-headed son-in-law in the house already that we can't get rid of—why have you led in this very Thunder God to plague me?"

"Old Gao," said Wukong, "you've lived to such a great age and still haven't learned sense. If you judge people purely by their looks, you'll go clean wrong. Ugly I may be, but I have some abilities. I'll capture the monster for your house, seize the fiend, take hold of your son-in-law, and give you back your daughter—and that will be a good thing done. Why need you keep harping on a man's looks?" The squire, hearing this, trembled and shook, but mustered his spirits as best he could and called, "Please, come in." Seeing the invitation, Wukong led the white horse in, had Gao Cai shoulder the baggage, and went in with Tripitaka. Caring nothing for ceremony, he tied the horse to a pillar of the open hall, dragged over a polished-lacquer folding chair, and bade his master be seated; then he pulled over another chair and sat down at his side. Said old Gao, "This little reverend makes himself quite at home." "If you'll only let me stay half a year," said Wukong, "I'll be more at home still."

When they were seated, old Gao asked, "My servant said just now that you two reverends are come from the Land of the East?" "Just so," said Tripitaka. "I am sent by imperial command to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures, and passing your honorable village, I would beg one night's lodging and be on my way in the morning." "If you two only came to lodge," said old Gao, "how is it you speak of catching the monster?" "Since we're lodging here anyway," said Wukong, "we'll catch a monster or two for sport while we're about it. May I ask how many monsters there are in your house?" "Heavens above!" said old Gao. "How could we put up with any more? This one monster of a son-in-law has worn us to a frazzle already." "Tell me from the beginning," said Wukong—"the whole story of this monster, and how great his powers are—so that I may catch him for you."

Old Gao said, "From ancient times down to now, this village of ours has never known any ghost or goblin, any specter or evil spirit working mischief. It was only my own misfortune that I had no son, but only three daughters: the eldest named Xianglan, the second Yulan, the third Cuilan. The two elder ones were betrothed in childhood to families of this very village. Only the youngest I wished to keep at home with a husband taken into our house—I'd hoped he would live here with me and support me in my old age, hold up the household, and do the work and the labor. But three years ago there came a fellow, of really rather handsome appearance, who said he was a man from the Fuling Mountains, surnamed Zhu, with no parents above him nor brothers below, and that he was willing to marry into a household as a son-in-law. Seeing him to be a man without root or tie, I took him in. And when first he came, he was diligent enough: he plowed the fields and harrowed the ground without need of oxen or tools; he reaped the grain without knife or sickle; he came in at dusk and went out at dawn, and truly all was well. There was only this one thing—he had a way of changing his face."

"Changing it how?" asked Wukong. Said old Gao, "When he first came he was a stout, dark fellow; but afterward he turned into an idiot creature with a long snout and great ears, a tuft of bristles down the back of his head, a body coarse and frightful, and a face for all the world like a hog's. And his appetite is huge: at a single meal he must eat three or five pecks of rice, and for a morning's snack alone he wants a hundred-odd baked cakes before he's satisfied. Luckily he keeps a vegetarian diet still; if he took to meat and wine besides, why, the whole of my estate and lands and all would be eaten clean away inside half a year." "Because he does so much," observed Tripitaka, "that's why he eats so much." "The eating is the lesser matter," said old Gao. "What's worse, he has lately learned to make winds—coming in clouds and going in mist, sending stones rolling and sand flying—and he has so frightened my whole household and all the neighbors that none can live in peace. And he has shut my young daughter Cuilan away in the back apartments, so that for half a year now she's not been seen face to face, and we don't even know whether she's alive or dead. By this we know he is a monster, and so we wished to engage some exorcist to drive him off."

"That's no hard matter," said Wukong. "Set your mind at rest, old man. This very night I'll catch him for you, make him write a deed of divorce, and give you back your daughter. How's that?" Old Gao rejoiced greatly. "It mattered little enough that I took him in," he said, "but how much of my good name he's ruined, how many of my kinsfolk he's estranged! Only catch him—what need of any deed? Just be so good as to root the creature out for me." "Easy, easy," said Wukong. "When night falls, you'll see how things stand."

The old man, overjoyed, had the tables and chairs wiped clean and a vegetarian feast laid out. When the meal was over and evening drew on, the old man asked, "What weapons do you need? How many men to attend you? Best to get them ready early." "I have my own weapon," said Wukong. "But you have only that single monk's staff," said the old man. "How can a monk's staff strike down the monster?" Wukong thereupon took from inside his ear a tiny embroidery needle, rolled it between his fingers, and with one shake into the wind it became an iron rod, bound with gold, as thick as a rice bowl. He held it out toward old Gao and said, "Look at this cudgel—how does it compare with the weapons in your house? Will it serve to beat that monster or no?" Old Gao said again, "Since you have a weapon, do you want men to go with you?" "I need no men," said Wukong, "only a few aged, virtuous old gentlemen to sit and keep my master quiet company, so that I may slip away from him. Let me bring the monster back, and before them all extract his confession, and root him out for you." The old man at once summoned his houseboys and invited in several friends and kinsfolk. When all had soon arrived and the greetings were done, Wukong said, "Master, sit easy and rest secure—old Monkey is off."

Now see him grip his iron rod and tug at old Gao: "Take me to the back apartments where the monster lives, and let me have a look." So old Gao led him to the door of the rear chambers. "Go and fetch the key," said Wukong. "Just look at it," said old Gao. "If a key were any use, I'd not have sent for you." Wukong laughed: "Old man, you may be great in years, but you can't take a joke. I only said it to tease you a little, and you take it in earnest." He stepped up, felt about—the lock turned out to be one poured solid with bronze. So with a furious thrust of his gold-banded rod he burst the door-leaves open. Within it was black as a cave. "Old Gao," said Wukong, "call out to your daughter and see if she's inside." The old man, screwing up his courage, cried, "Third sister!" The girl recognized her father's voice and, faint and feeble, answered, "Father, I'm here." Flashing his golden eyes into the darkness, Wukong looked her over closely. And how do you suppose she looked? Behold:

> Her cloudy tresses lay tumbled, uncombed;
> her jade-fair face, unwashed, was stained with grime.
> Her one orchid-pure heart was as before,
> but all her tender grace was fallen to ruin.
> Her cherry lips had not a trace of color;
> her slender waist bent, cowering and bowed.
> Sorrow-knit her brow, the moth-wing eyebrows pale;
> thin and shrinking, her voice gone low and weak.

She came forward, and seeing old Gao she seized him, buried her head against him, and wept aloud. "Don't cry, don't cry," said Wukong. "Let me ask you—where has the monster gone?" The girl said, "I don't know where. These days he goes off at daybreak and comes back at nightfall, in clouds and mists, coming and going I know not whither. Because he's aware that my father wants to be rid of him, he's always on his guard, and so he comes at dusk and leaves at dawn." "No need to say more," said Wukong. "Old man, take your daughter off to the front rooms and have your long-deferred talk together, and leave old Monkey here to wait for him. If he doesn't come, don't blame me; but if he does come, I'll surely cut him off at the root for you." So old Gao, happy and glad, led his daughter away to the front.

Then Wukong worked his magic: he shook himself and changed, taking on the very form of the girl, and sat alone in the room awaiting the monster. Before long, up came a gust of wind—and truly it sent stones rolling and sand flying. A fine wind it was:

> At first it came soft and gentle, swaying;
> later it grew vast and boundless, dim.
> Soft and gentle—yet heaven and earth were great with it;
> vast and boundless—and nothing could withstand it.
> Withering flowers, snapping willows, like crushing hemp;
> toppling trees, flattening woods, like pulling up greens.
> It churned the rivers and stirred the seas till ghosts and gods grieved;
> it split rocks and crumbled hills till Heaven and Earth marveled.
> The flower-grazing deer lost track of their way;
> the fruit-plucking apes were stranded abroad.
> Seven-storied iron pagodas leaned against the Buddha's head;
> eight-sided banners and pennants tore the precious canopies.
> Golden beams and jade pillars rocked at their roots;
> roof-tiles flew like swallows whirled away.
> The boatman, plying his oar, vowed offerings in fear;
> the ferryman, casting off, hastened to pledge pigs and sheep.
> The local earth-god abandoned his shrine;
> the Dragon Kings of the Four Seas bowed up toward heaven.
> Along the shore a yaksha's boat was dashed to wreck,
> and half a stretch of the Great Wall was blown flat.

Where that wild wind passed, there appeared in mid-air a monster, and an ugly one indeed: a black face with short bristles, a long snout and great ears; he wore a cotton-weave gown neither quite green nor quite blue, and bound about him a kerchief of flowered cloth. Wukong laughed to himself: "So this is the article!" Now Wukong, like a good fellow, neither went to meet him nor questioned him, but lay upon the bed feigning illness, groaning and moaning without ceasing. The monster, not knowing true from false, came into the room, threw his arms about "her," and would have a kiss. Wukong chuckled inwardly: "So he really means to come making sport of old Monkey!" He used a wrestling trick, caught hold of the monster's long snout, gave it a quick twist—a little throw they call it—wrenched the head over, and flung him sprawling off the bed with a thump. The monster scrambled up and, steadying himself against the bedside, said, "Sister, why are you cross with me today? I suppose it's because I came back late?" "Not cross, not cross," said Wukong. "If you're not cross with me," said the monster, "why throw me down like that?" Wukong said, "Why must you be so common, grabbing me to kiss the moment you come in? I'm a bit out of sorts today; if I were well as usual, I'd have got up and opened the door to wait for you. Just take off your clothes and lie down."

Not catching the meaning, the monster truly went to undress. Wukong sprang up and sat on the chamber-pot. The monster came groping back to the bed as before, felt about, and finding no one there, called, "Sister, where've you gone? Come, take off your things and lie down." "You first," said Wukong. "Wait till I've eased myself." So the monster did indeed take off his clothes first and got into bed.

Then Wukong suddenly heaved a sigh and exclaimed, "What rotten luck!" "What's eating you?" said the monster. "How can your luck be rotten? Since I came into your family, though I've eaten a bit of your food, I've not eaten it for nothing: I've swept your floors and cleared your drains, hauled brick and carried tile, rammed earth and built walls, plowed the fields and harrowed the ground, sown wheat and set out rice-seedlings—I've made your house and built your fortunes. Now you wear brocade on your back and gold in your hair, with flowers and fruit to enjoy in all four seasons and fresh vegetables cooked at every festival. What is there still not to your liking, that you sigh and groan like this and talk of rotten luck?" "It isn't that," said Wukong. "Today my parents, just on the other side of the wall, were flinging bricks and tiles, abusing me roundly and cursing me." "Why should they beat and curse you?" said the monster. "They say," said Wukong, "that since you and I became man and wife, you, being a son-in-law of their house, have shown not the least propriety. A man with such an ugly mug, who can't be presented to his wife's relations nor shown to the kin—and who knows where you come from, riding clouds and mists, what family you belong to, what your name is—you ruin their good name and disgrace their house, and that's why they beat and curse me so, and that's what grieves me."

"Ugly I may be," said the monster, "yet if it's good looks you want, that's no hard matter. When first I came, I made it plain to them, and only then, willingly, did they take me in. Why bring all this up today? My home is in the Cloud-Ladder Cave on the Fuling Mountains. I take my surname from my looks, and so my surname is Zhu—Hog—and my given name is Zhu Ganglie, Hog the Stiff-Bristles. If they ask you again, just tell them this." Wukong rejoiced in secret: "What an honest monster! No need for torture—he's confessed it all this plainly. Now that I have his place and his name, I'll catch him whatever happens."

Wukong said, "They mean to invite an exorcist to come and catch you." The monster laughed: "Go to sleep, go to sleep, and pay no mind to them. I have the transformations of the Heavenly Ladle's number—thirty-six of them—and a nine-toothed muckrake; what do I care for exorcists, monks, or Taoists? Even if your old father were earnest enough to call down the Patriarch Exorcist of the Nine Heavens himself, I've been acquainted with him too, and he'd not dare do anything to me." "They say," said Wukong, "that they'll invite a certain one surnamed Sun—the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, who five hundred years ago made his great uproar in the Heavenly Palace—to come and catch you." The moment the monster heard that name, he was three parts frightened. "If that's how it is," he said, "I'd best be off—our marriage is at an end." "Why should you go off?" said Wukong. "You don't know," said the monster. "That Protector of the Horses who made the uproar in Heaven has real abilities, and I'm afraid I'd be no match for him; I'd lose my good name and cut a poor figure."

So saying, he pulled on his clothes, opened the door, and started straight out. But Wukong seized him fast, wiped a hand across his own face to reveal his true form, and bellowed, "Fine monster—where do you think you're going? Lift your head and see who I am!" The monster turned his eyes and saw Wukong's jutting fangs and gaping jaws, his fiery eyes and golden pupils, his butting brow and hairy face—the very image of a living Thunder God. He was so terrified that his hands went numb and his legs grew weak; with a ripping tear he burst clean out of his clothes, turned himself into a wild wind, and made his escape. Wukong hurried forward, raised his iron rod, and struck a blow at the wind. The monster turned into ten thousand shafts of fiery light and went straight back to his own mountain. Wukong mounted a cloud and gave chase behind, crying, "Where do you run? If you climb to the sky, I'll chase you to the Palace of the Dipper and the Ox; if you go into the earth, I'll pursue you to the Hell of the Unjustly Dead!"

Ah!—but there is no telling, in the end, to what place this chase will lead, nor what the victory or defeat will be. Listen, and the next chapter will make it clear.

<!-- chapter 19 -->
# Chapter 19: The Cloud-Ladder Cave, Where Wukong Wins the Hog; Vulture Peak, Where Tripitaka Receives the Heart Sutra
