We left off with the monster racing ahead in a streak of fire, while the Great Sage came close behind on his banner of rosy cloud. As they flew, a high mountain suddenly reared up before them. The monster gathered his red glow into one knot, resumed his true shape, and plunged into a cave. From within he fetched out a nine-pronged muckrake and turned to fight.

"Vile creature!" Wukong roared. "What demon are you, and from where? How do you come to know old Sun's name? Tell me plainly what powers you have, and I may yet spare your life."

"So you don't know my abilities either," the monster said. "Step up and stand your ground, and I'll tell you. Listen:

> From my very birth my nature was crude and dull,
> Greedy for idleness, slothful, never resting.
> I never nourished my spirit nor cultivated truth,
> But muddled my heart and squandered the suns and moons.
> Then one idle day I met a true immortal,
> Who sat and spoke with me of warmth and cold,
> And urged me to turn back and not fall to the common world,
> For harming life heaps up boundless sin.
> When the great limit comes and the breath of life is spent,
> The Eight Hardships and Three Paths leave no time for regret.
> Hearing his words, my mind turned toward the Way;
> Hearing his counsel, my heart sought the marvelous secret.
> By destiny I bowed there and took him as my master,
> Who showed me the gates of Heaven and the doors of Earth.
> I learned the Nine-Cycle Great Reverting Elixir,
> And labored at it night and day without a pause.
> Up to the Mud-Pellet Palace in the crown of the head,
> Down to the Bubbling-Spring point in the soles of the feet.
> The kidney water flowed round into the Floriate Pool,
> And the Cinnabar Field was warmed to a gentle heat.
> The Infant and the Fair Maiden joined yin and yang,
> Lead and mercury combined, dividing sun and moon.
> The Li dragon and Kan tiger were harmonized,
> The numinous tortoise drank dry the golden crow's blood.
> The Three Flowers gathered at the crown and returned to the root,
> The Five Breaths faced the origin, flowing clear and through.
> My merit complete, my practice full, I rose in flight,
> And immortals came in pairs to welcome me.
> Bright colored clouds were born beneath my feet,
> Light of body, sound of limb, I attended the golden gates.
> The Jade Emperor held a feast for the assembled immortals,
> Ranking each by grade and arraying us in rows.
> By decree he made me Marshal of the Heavenly River,
> Commander of all the water troops, bearing the rod of office.
> But when the Queen Mother held her Feast of Peaches,
> Spreading a banquet at the Jasper Pool and inviting the guests,
> That day I grew drunk and my wits went dim,
> Lurching east and west, raising a drunken brawl.
> In my swagger I blundered into the Vast Cold Palace,
> Where the lovely fairy maiden came to receive me.
> Seeing her beauty that steals away men's souls,
> My old mortal heart could not be quenched.
> Forgetting all rank, high and low, I lost all reverence,
> Seized hold of Chang'e and demanded she lie with me.
> Three times, four times, she would not consent,
> Dodging east and hiding west, her heart displeased.
> My lust grew bold as the sky, I bellowed like thunder,
> And nearly shook down the very gates of Heaven.
> The Inspector-General reported me to the Jade Emperor,
> And on that day my fortune was wretched indeed.
> The Vast Cold was ringed about, no breath of wind let through,
> No door to advance or retreat, no way to escape.
> Then the host of gods laid hold of me,
> But, with wine still in my breast, I felt no fear.
> Hauled up to the Hall of Divine Mists before the Jade Emperor,
> By the law I was sentenced to be put to death.
> I owe my life to the Great White Planet, Li the Gold Star,
> Who stepped from the ranks, bowed low, and pleaded for me.
> My sentence was changed to two thousand heavy blows;
> My flesh was split, my skin laid open, my bones near broken.
> Spared and banished, I was driven out of Heaven's gate,
> And below Mount Fuling I sought to make a home.
> Because of my sin I was thrown into the wrong womb,
> And so my common name is Zhu Ganglie, the Bristled Hog."

When Wukong heard this he said, "So you are the Water God, Marshal Tianpeng, fallen to the lower world. No wonder you knew old Sun's name."

"Hah!" cried the monster. "You insolent Bimawen, you Keeper of the Heavenly Horses! When you stirred up that calamity back then, you've no idea how many of us you dragged down with you. And now here you come again, bullying others. Enough of your rudeness — taste my rake!"

Wukong was hardly inclined to mercy. He lifted his cudgel and struck straight at the monster's head. The two of them fought there halfway up the mountain, in the black of night. It was a fine battle:

> The Monkey's golden eyes flashed like lightning,
> The demon's ringed eyes glittered like silver flowers.
> This one spat colored mist from his mouth,
> That one breathed out red clouds from his lungs.
> Red clouds breathed out lit up the dark,
> Colored mist spat gave the night its glow.
> The gold-banded cudgel, the nine-pronged rake —
> Two heroes truly worth the praising:
> One the Great Sage come down to the mortal world,
> One the Marshal banished to the ends of the sky.
> That one, for losing his dignity, had become a monster;
> This one, having luckily escaped his torments, had joined the holy order.
> The rake came in like a dragon stretching its claws,
> The cudgel met it like a phoenix piercing the flowers.
> That one cried, "Wrecking a man's marriage is like killing his father!"
> This one cried, "Raping a young girl deserves arrest!"
> Idle words and wild shouting,
> Back and forth, cudgel against rake.
> They fought on until the sky began to lighten,
> And the monster felt both his shoulders go sore and numb.

The two of them battled from the second watch of the night clear through till the east turned white. The monster could fight no longer; beaten, he fled, changed once more into a wild gust of wind, and bolted straight back to his cave, where he barred the door fast and would not show his head again.

Outside the cave Wukong saw a stone tablet inscribed with three characters: Cloud-Ladder Cave. Since the monster would not come out, and it was now full daylight, he thought to himself, "My master may be anxious and waiting. I had best go back and let him see me, then return to catch this fiend — there's no harm in waiting that long." So with a single step on the cloud he soon arrived at the Gao Family Village.

Now Tripitaka had passed the whole night talking with the old men of past and present, never sleeping a wink. He was just wondering why Wukong had not returned when, all at once, Wukong appeared standing in the courtyard. Wukong put away his iron cudgel, straightened his robe, and stepped up into the hall. "Master, I'm back," he called.

The old men, flustered, all bowed together and thanked him: "Such trouble for you, such trouble!"

Tripitaka asked, "Wukong, you've been gone the whole night — where is the monster you caught?"

"Master," said Wukong, "that monster is no common evil spirit of the mortal world, nor a wild beast of the mountains. He is the Marshal of the Heavenly Reeds come down among men. Only because he was cast into the wrong womb, his face is shaped like a wild boar — yet his spiritual nature still remains. He told me he takes his very form for his surname and is called Zhu Ganglie, the Bristled Hog. Old Sun went after him with the cudgel from the rear courtyard, but he turned into a gust of wind and got away. I caught him with one blow as he rode the wind, and he changed into a streak of fire and made straight for his home cave. There he fetched out a nine-pronged muckrake and fought me a whole night. Just now, as the sky was about to brighten, he lost his nerve and fled, barring his cave door tight and refusing to come out. I wanted to break the door open and have it out with him for good, but I feared you might be here worried and waiting, so I came first to bring you word."

When he had finished, old Gao came forward and knelt. "Reverend Sir, there's no help for it. You may have driven him off, but after you've gone he'll come back again — then what's to be done? Better, I beg you, that you take the trouble to seize him for me and pull him up by the roots, so there's no future trouble. I, old fellow that I am, will not be ungrateful: I'll have my kinsmen and friends draw up a deed, and divide my whole estate — house, land, and goods — equally with you, Reverend. Only cut the grass and dig out the root, and don't let my honest house's good name be spoiled."

Wukong laughed. "Old man, you don't know your limits. That monster himself told me that, big eater though he is, in exchange for the tea and rice he ate at your house he also did a great deal of good work — these past years he's built up a fine fortune for you, all by his own strength. He didn't eat your food for nothing, so why are you so set on driving him off? By his own account he's a heavenly spirit come down to the lower world to slave away keeping your house, and he never once harmed your daughter. A son-in-law like that is well matched to your family, and does no harm at all to your reputation or your good name. Truly, you might as well keep him."

"Reverend Sir," said old Gao, "though he does no harm to public morals, the name of it sounds none too pleasant. At every turn people say, 'The Gao family has taken on a monster for a son-in-law.' How is anyone to bear a saying like that?"

Tripitaka said, "Wukong, since you've already had one round with him, finish the business and see it through to the end, so there's a proper beginning and a proper close."

"I was only testing him a little, for sport," said Wukong. "This time I'll surely bring him back for you all to see — don't fret." He called, "Old Gao, you take good care of my master; I'm off." And with that word he leapt, formless and shadowless, up to the mountain and came to the mouth of the cave. With a few strokes of his iron rod he smashed both leaves of the door to splinters, cursing aloud: "You chaff-eating clod! Come out quick and fight old Sun!"

The monster, panting and worn out, was just then asleep inside the cave. Hearing the door crash and hearing himself cursed as a chaff-eating clod, he could not master his fury. Dragging out his rake and rousing his spirits, he rushed out and railed in a fierce voice: "You Bimawen, you Keeper of Horses — what shameless gall! What business of yours is this, that you come breaking down my front gate? Go look at the law: forcing your way in through a man's front gate is a capital offense among the lesser crimes!"

Wukong laughed. "You blockhead! Even if I have broken your gate, there's an argument to be made for it. But you — seizing a man's daughter without the three matchmakers and six witnesses, without so much as a cup of tea or a gift of wedding wine — now that's a true crime, worthy of beheading!"

"Enough of this idle talk," said the monster. "Look out for old Hog's rake!"

Wukong fended it off with his cudgel and said, "Is this the same rake you used as a hired hand at old Gao's, digging the ground and planting vegetables? What's so fine about it that I should fear it?"

"You've mistaken it," said the monster. "Do you take this rake for a thing of the mortal world? Just listen while I tell you:

> This was forged from divine ice-iron,
> Ground and polished to a bright and gleaming work.
> Lord Lao himself wielded the hammer and tongs,
> And the Fire Star added the bits of charcoal with his own hands.
> The Five Emperors of the Five Quarters lent their thought,
> The Six Ding and Six Jia spirits spent their pains.
> They wrought nine teeth of pendant jade,
> And cast two rings with leaves of hanging gold.
> Its body adorned with the Six Luminaries, ranged with the Five Stars,
> Its frame conformed to the Four Seasons and the Eight Festivals.
> Its length and breadth, high and low, fix Heaven and Earth;
> Left and right, yin and yang, divide the sun and moon.
> The spirit-generals of the Six Lines follow Heaven's statutes,
> The stars of the Eight Trigrams are ranged like the Dipper.
> It is named the Supreme Treasure, the Gold-Steeped Rake,
> Presented to the Jade Emperor to guard the Cinnabar Court.
> Because I had perfected myself as a Great Luo Immortal,
> Become a deathless guest of eternal life,
> By decree I was made Marshal, titled Tianpeng,
> And granted this muckrake as my imperial badge.
> Lift it up, and it blazes with flame and radiant light;
> Bring it down, and a fierce wind scatters auspicious snow.
> The spirit-generals of the Heavenly Bureau are all dismayed,
> And Yama of the Underworld loses his nerve.
> Where in the mortal world is there a weapon like this?
> In all the earth there is no such iron.
> It changes its shape at will to suit my mind,
> Tumbling and turning as my spell directs.
> For several years it has gone with me, never parted;
> For many a year it has kept me company, no day apart.
> At my three daily meals it is never set aside;
> At my single night's sleep it is never put away.
> I have carried it to the Feast of the Peaches,
> And borne it to attend at the Imperial Court.
> But because I leaned on wine and turned to violence,
> Because I trusted in my strength and ran wild,
> Heaven banished me down to the mortal dust,
> And in the lower world I worked out my sins.
> In the stone cave my evil heart once devoured men,
> At Gao Village my fond heart made a marriage.
> This rake, plunged into the sea, overturns the dragons' and crocodiles' dens;
> Raised in the mountains, it tears apart the tigers' and wolves' lairs.
> Of all the other weapons let's say no more —
> There is none so keen as this rake of mine.
> To win the contest by it is no hard thing;
> To gain merit in the fight needs no saying.
> Though your head be bronze and your skull be iron, your whole body steel,
> When the rake strikes, your soul will flee and your spirit drain away."

Hearing this, Wukong put away his iron cudgel and said, "Stop your boasting, blockhead. Old Sun will stick his head out right here, and you give it one stroke — let's see if my soul flees and my spirit drains."

The monster truly raised his rake and brought it down with all his force. There was a loud crack; the rake threw off a shower of flickering sparks of fire — but it had not so much as stirred a hair of the scalp. The shock left his hands numb and his legs weak, and he cried out, "What a head! What a head!"

"You don't understand," said Wukong. "When old Sun made havoc in Heaven for stealing the elixir of immortality, robbing the peaches, and filching the imperial wine, I was captured by the Young Sage Erlang and held before the Dipper-and-Bull Palace. The host of heavenly gods hacked at me with axes, pounded me with mallets, slashed me with knives and stabbed me with swords, burned me with fire and struck me with thunder — and never harmed me a jot. Then Lord Lao the Supreme took me away and set me in his Eight-Trigrams Furnace, where he tempered me with divine fire and refined me into one with fiery eyes and golden pupils, a bronze head and iron arms. If you don't believe it, give me a few more strokes and see whether it hurts or not."

"Monkey," said the monster, "I remember that when you stirred up Heaven, your home was in the Water-Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, in the Aolai Country of the Eastern Continent of Superior Body. It's been so long since I've heard your name — how do you come to be here, knocking at my door to bully me? Could it be my father-in-law went and invited you?"

"Your father-in-law never invited me," said Wukong. "It's because old Sun has reformed from evil and returned to the right, given up the Way of the Tao for the order of monks, and now guards a holy man — the younger brother by imperial favor of the Great Tang in the Land of the East, a master of the Law called Tripitaka, bound for the Western Heaven to bow before Buddha and seek the scriptures. Passing through Gao Village, we lodged for the night, and when the old man brought up the matter in conversation, he begged me to rescue his daughter and seize you, you chaff-eating clod."

The moment the monster heard this, he flung down his rake and made a deep bow. "Where is this scripture-seeker? Pray take the trouble to introduce me."

"What do you want with him?" asked Wukong.

"It was the Bodhisattva Guanyin who exhorted me to do good," said the monster. "I took the vows from her, and here I keep a fast and abstain from meat, waiting for her command that I should follow the scripture-seeker to the Western Heaven, bow before Buddha and seek the scriptures, and so atone for my sins and win the true fruit. She told me to wait for him these several years, but I had heard no news. Now since you are his disciple, why didn't you say so at the start about the scriptures, instead of trusting to brute strength and coming to my door to thrash me?"

"Don't think you can trick me and soften me with cunning words, hoping for some scheme to slip free," said Wukong. "If you truly mean to protect the Tang Monk, with no falsehood, then swear an oath to Heaven, and I'll take you to see my master."

The monster dropped flat to his knees and, bowing toward the sky like a pestle pounding rice, kowtowed again and again: "Amitabha, Namo Buddha — if I am not sincere and true in heart, may I be charged with breaking the laws of Heaven and have my corpse hacked into ten thousand pieces."

Seeing him swear and vow so, Wukong said, "Very well. Then set a fire and burn down this dwelling of yours, and I'll take you along." The monster truly gathered up some reeds and brambles, lit a torch, and burned the Cloud-Ladder Cave until it was like a heap of broken tiles. He said to Wukong, "Now I've nothing left to hold me back. Lead me away, then."

"Hand me your rake to hold," said Wukong. The monster passed it over. Then Wukong plucked out a single hair, blew on it with a breath of immortal air, and cried, "Change!" At once it became a three-stranded hemp rope. He stepped over and bound the monster's hands behind his back. The monster truly let his hands be tied behind him and submitted to whatever binding Wukong chose. Then Wukong seized him by the ear and dragged him along, calling, "Hurry up, hurry up!"

"Go gently, won't you," said the monster. "Your hand's heavy — you're hurting the root of my ear."

"I can't go gently — there's no helping you," said Wukong. "As the old saying has it, 'A good hog is roughly handled.' Only when you've seen my master, and proved you truly mean it, will I let you go." So the two of them, half on cloud and half in mist, made straight back to the Gao Family Village. There is a verse to prove it:

> The hard, strong nature of metal can subdue wood;
> The Mind-Monkey has brought the Wood-Dragon to heel.
> Metal and wood, when they accord, become one;
> Wood, cleaving to metal's kindness, brings all to full play.
> Host and guest, the two, with no division between them;
> Three meetings, three unions, holding a subtle mystery.
> Nature and feeling alike rejoice when truth and origin are gathered;
> Together they prove the West — and the saying does not fail.

In a moment they reached the front of the village. Wukong, holding the rake and gripping the monster's ear, said, "Look — who is it sitting so solemnly there in the hall? That is my master." When old Gao and his kinsmen and friends saw Wukong bringing the monster along, hands bound behind and ear in hand, every one of them came joyfully to meet them in the courtyard, crying, "Reverend Sir, Reverend Sir — that's our son-in-law, sure enough!"

The monster stepped forward, fell to both knees, and, with his hands still bound behind him, kowtowed to Tripitaka, calling loudly, "Master, your disciple failed to welcome you! Had I known you were lodging at my father-in-law's house, I'd have come to receive you, and not put myself through all this trouble."

"Wukong," said Tripitaka, "how did you subdue him so that he comes to bow before me?"

Only then did Wukong let go his hand, and tapping the monster with the handle of the rake, he barked, "Blockhead — speak!" The monster then recounted in full how the Bodhisattva had exhorted him to do good.

Tripitaka was overjoyed and called, "Squire Gao, bring out an incense table." Old Gao hurried to carry one out. Tripitaka washed his hands, lit incense, and bowed to the south, saying, "My deep thanks for the Bodhisattva's holy grace." The old men too added incense and bowed together. When the worship was done, Tripitaka took the high seat in the hall and bade Wukong loose the monster's bonds. Wukong gave his body a shake and drew the hair back into himself, and the binding came undone of itself. The monster bowed anew to Tripitaka and vowed to follow him to the West. He bowed also to Wukong, and since Wukong had entered the order first, he called him elder brother, addressing him as Brother Wukong.

"Since you have entered my good fruit and wish to be my disciple," said Tripitaka, "let me give you a religious name, so it will be easy to call you morning and night."

"Master," he said, "the Bodhisattva already touched the crown of my head and gave me the vows, and named me Zhu Wuneng — Awakened to Power."

Tripitaka smiled. "Good, good. Your elder brother is called Wukong, and you are called Wuneng — truly you belong to the same lineage within my school."

"Master," said Wuneng, "I took the Bodhisattva's vows and cut off the five pungent roots and the three forbidden meats; at my father-in-law's house I kept a fast and abstained, never once touching meat. But now that I've seen you, my master, may I break my fast?"

"No, no," said Tripitaka. "Since you don't eat the five pungent roots and the three forbidden meats, let me give you another name as well — I'll call you Bajie, the Eight Prohibitions."

The simpleton, delighted, said, "I humbly obey my master's command." And so he was also called Zhu Bajie.

When old Gao saw him thus turn from evil and return to the right, he was all the more pleased, and ordered his servants to prepare a banquet to thank the Tang Monk. Bajie went up and caught hold of old Gao. "Father-in-law," he said, "won't you ask my poor wife to come out and pay her respects to her grandfather-in-law and uncles?"

Wukong laughed. "Worthy brother, now that you've entered the gate of Sand — become a monk — from this day on you mustn't bring up that talk of 'my poor wife' again. In this world there's only such a thing as a married Taoist priest; where did anyone ever hear of a married monk? Let's just take our seats in order, eat a vegetarian meal, and get an early start on the road west."

Old Gao laid out the tables and asked Tripitaka to take the place of honor; Wukong and Bajie sat to left and right, and the kinsmen took the lower seats. Old Gao opened a jar of vegetarian wine, filled a cup to the brim, poured a libation to Heaven and Earth, and then offered it to Tripitaka.

"To tell the truth, Squire," said Tripitaka, "this poor monk has been a vegetarian since the womb, and has never eaten meat from childhood."

"Knowing your reverence's pure abstinence," said old Gao, "I have not dared to serve any meat. This wine, too, is of the pure sort — surely there's no harm in one cup."

"I dare not take wine either," said Tripitaka. "Wine is the first of the prohibitions for us monks."

Wuneng grew flustered. "Master, I've kept the fast, but I never gave up wine."

"Old Sun's capacity is small — I can't manage a whole jar," said Wukong, "but I never gave up wine either."

"Well then," said Tripitaka, "let my two disciples drink a little of the vegetarian wine — only no drinking to drunkenness and spoiling our affairs." So the two of them took the first cups. Then all sat down again as before, and the vegetarian feast was spread. Words could not exhaust the splendor of the cups and dishes, the abundance of the fare.

When master and disciples had finished their feast, old Gao brought out a red-lacquered tray bearing two hundred taels of broken gold and silver, which he offered to the three reverends for their traveling expenses; he also brought three robes of padded cloth to serve as outer garments.

Tripitaka said, "We are mendicant monks, begging our rice at the villages and our meals wherever we go. How could we dare accept gold, silver, and silk?"

But Wukong stepped up, swept out his hand and grabbed a fistful, and called, "Gaocai! Yesterday you took the trouble to lead my master here, and today we've gained a disciple, but we've nothing to thank you with. Take this broken gold and silver as a guide's fee, and buy yourself some straw sandals. Hereafter, whenever there are monsters about, bring me a few more of these jobs, and there'll be more to thank you for." Gaocai took it, kowtowed, and thanked him for the reward.

Old Gao spoke again. "Since the reverends won't accept gold or silver, I hope you'll graciously receive these coarse garments, as a small token of my heart."

"We who have left the household life," said Tripitaka, "if we accept so much as a thread of bribe, will struggle through a thousand kalpas without attaining the Way. It will be quite enough to take along some of the cakes and fruit left over from the feast, as dry rations."

But Bajie spoke up from the side. "Master, brother — don't you two be so hasty. I've been a son-in-law in this house these several years; my back-pay alone ought to come to three measures of grain. Father-in-law! My cassock was torn by my brother last night — give me a robe of green brocade; and my shoes have split — give me a good new pair." Old Gao, hearing this, dared not refuse, and at once bought a new pair of shoes and a padded gown, exchanging them for the old worn things.

Then Bajie, swaggering this way and that, made a bow to old Gao and said, "Convey my respects to my mother-in-law, to the elder and younger aunts, to the uncles and all the kin: I'm off today to be a monk, and haven't time to take my leave to their faces — don't hold it against me. Father-in-law, take good care of my wife, won't you. For if we should fail to get the scriptures, I can always come back and return to lay life, and go on being your son-in-law as before."

"Clod!" Wukong shouted. "Don't talk such nonsense."

"It's not nonsense," said Bajie. "I'm only afraid that if there's some slip along the way, I'll have spoiled my chance both at being a monk and at having a wife — and be left empty-handed on both counts."

"Enough idle chatter," said Tripitaka. "Let's get an early start." So they packed up a load of luggage, which Bajie shouldered; saddled the white horse, which Tripitaka rode; and Wukong, his iron cudgel on his shoulder, led the way in front. The three of them together took leave of old Gao and all his kin and friends, and set off westward. There is a verse to prove it:

> Smoke and rosy mist filling the land, the tree-colors high;
> The Buddha's son of the Tang, toiling on in bitter labor.
> Hungry, he eats from one bowl the rice of a thousand homes;
> Cold, he wears against the chill one patched robe of a thousand stitches.
> Let the will-horse in your breast not run loose and wild;
> Let the mind-monkey, willful and wayward, not be allowed to howl.
> When feeling is calmed and nature is settled, all conditions accord;
> When the moon is full in the golden flower, the hair is trimmed away.

The three of them went on along the western road, and for a month or so all was smooth and steady. They passed beyond the borders of Tibet, when suddenly, looking up, they saw a high mountain. Tripitaka reined in his horse and said, "Wukong, Wuneng — the mountain ahead is high; you must be very, very careful."

"No matter," said Bajie. "This mountain is called Vulture Peak. In it lives a Zen Master of the Crow's Nest, who cultivates his practice here. Old Hog has met him before."

"What is his business?" asked Tripitaka.

"He has some attainment of the Way," said Bajie. "He once urged me to follow him in his practice, but I never went, and that was the end of it."

As master and disciples talked, before long they came up the mountain. A fine mountain it was! Behold:

> On the mountain's south, green pines and emerald cypress;
> On the mountain's north, green willows and red peach.
> Noisily, mountain birds answer one another;
> Fluttering in dance, immortal cranes fly together.
> Fragrant, fragrant, the flowers in a thousand hues;
> Green and luxuriant, the mingled grasses in ten thousand wonders.
> Below the ravine, water rushes green;
> Before the cliff, auspicious clouds in drifting flakes.
> Truly a place of uncommon quiet and grace,
> Still and silent, with never a traveler in sight.

The master, gazing far from his horse, saw before a fragrant cypress a nest of brushwood and grass; on the left a river-deer held a flower in its mouth, on the right a mountain monkey offered fruit; and in the treetops blue simurghs and colored phoenixes sang together, while dark cranes and brocade pheasants gathered all around. Bajie pointed and said, "There — isn't that the Crow's Nest Zen Master?" Tripitaka spurred his horse on and rode straight up beneath the tree.

Now when the Zen Master saw the three of them coming, he left his nest at once and leapt down from the tree. Tripitaka dismounted and made his bow. The Zen Master raised him up with his hand, saying, "Holy monk, please rise. Forgive my failure to welcome you." Bajie said, "Old Zen Master, my respects." The Zen Master started in surprise and asked, "Aren't you Zhu Ganglie of Mount Fuling? How have you come by such good fortune as to travel with this holy monk?"

"The year before last," said Bajie, "I had the grace of the Bodhisattva Guanyin's exhortation, and vowed to follow him as a disciple."

"Good, good, good!" cried the Zen Master with great joy. Then, pointing at Wukong, he asked, "And who is this one?"

Wukong laughed. "How is it, old Zen Master, that you know him, but don't know me?"

"Because I've had little acquaintance with you," said the Zen Master.

"He is my eldest disciple, Sun Wukong," said Tripitaka.

The Zen Master smiled apologetically. "My oversight, my oversight."

Tripitaka bowed again. "May I ask where the Great Thunderclap Monastery of the Western Heaven lies?"

"Far, far away," said the Zen Master. "The road is thick with tigers and leopards, and hard to travel."

Tripitaka pressed his inquiry earnestly, asking again, "Just how far is the road, in truth?"

"Far though the road may be," said the Zen Master, "in the end there will surely come a day of arrival — only the demon-miasmas are hard to dispel. I have a scroll of the *Heart Sutra*, fifty-four sentences in all, two hundred and seventy characters together. Whenever you come to a place of demon-miasma, only recite this sutra, and you'll suffer no harm."

Tripitaka prostrated himself on the ground and earnestly begged for it, and the Zen Master then recited and transmitted it to him by mouth. The sutra runs:

> *The Maha Prajna-paramita Heart Sutra*: When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara was practicing the deep Prajna-paramita, he illuminated and saw that the five aggregates are all empty, and so passed beyond all suffering and distress. Shariputra, form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, emptiness is itself form. So too are sensation, perception, volition, and consciousness. Shariputra, all these things are marked with emptiness: they neither arise nor cease, are neither defiled nor pure, neither increase nor decrease. Therefore in emptiness there is no form, no sensation, perception, volition, or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or thought; no realm of the eye, and so on up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance, and no ending of ignorance; and so on up to no old-age-and-death, and no ending of old-age-and-death. There is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, no path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, the Bodhisattva, relying on Prajna-paramita, has a mind without hindrance; and because there is no hindrance, there is no fear. Far removed from all confused dream-thoughts, he reaches the ultimate Nirvana. The Buddhas of the three ages, relying on Prajna-paramita, attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Therefore know that Prajna-paramita is the great divine spell, the great spell of light, the supreme spell, the spell beyond all spells, able to remove all suffering — true and not false. So he proclaimed the spell of Prajna-paramita, the spell that runs: "Gate, gate, paragate, parasamgate, bodhi svaha!"

Now this master of the Law of the Tang dynasty had a foundation of true roots, so that on hearing the *Heart Sutra* through but once, he could remember it; and so it has come down to the world to this day. This is the all-encompassing scripture of cultivating the truth, the gateway to becoming a Buddha.

When the Zen Master had transmitted the text of the sutra, he stepped onto the radiant cloud, meaning to return to his Crow's Nest. But Tripitaka caught hold of him again and would not let go, insisting that he tell him plainly the road that lay to the west. The Zen Master smiled and said:

> The road is not hard to travel;
> Just listen to my instructions.
> A thousand mountains, a thousand streams, deep;
> Many a miasma, many a demon-haunted place.
> If you come to a cliff that reaches the sky,
> Set your heart at ease and do not fear.
> When you reach the Ear-Rubbing Crag,
> Tread sidelong, planting your steps with care.
> Be wary of the Black Pine Forest,
> Where demon foxes throng to block the road.
> Sprites fill the cities and the towns,
> Demon-lords crowd the mountains where they dwell.
> Old tigers sit as masters in the hall,
> Gray wolves serve as registrars.
> Lions and elephants all call themselves kings,
> Tigers and leopards all act as courtiers.
> A wild boar shoulders the carrying-pole,
> A water-fiend you'll meet up ahead.
> An ancient stone monkey of many years —
> there harbors a smoldering wrath.
> Ask of one well acquainted there:
> he knows the road that runs to the west.

Hearing this, Wukong gave a cold laugh. "Let's be off. There's no need to ask him — ask me, and that's enough." Tripitaka still did not catch his meaning. The Zen Master changed into a beam of golden light and went straight up to his Crow's Nest. The elder bowed upward in thanks, but in his heart Wukong was greatly enraged, and he raised his iron cudgel and lashed wildly upward — only to see a thousand lotus blossoms spring forth and auspicious mists shield the nest in a thousand layers. Though Wukong had strength to churn the seas and overturn rivers, he could not so much as tug loose a single vine of the Crow's Nest.

When Tripitaka saw this he caught hold of Wukong. "Wukong, what do you mean by smashing a Bodhisattva's nest like this?"

"He cursed the two of us, my brother and me, and then went off," said Wukong.

"He was speaking of the road to the Western Heaven," said Tripitaka. "Whenever did he curse you?"

"How would you understand?" said Wukong. "When he said 'a wild boar shoulders the carrying-pole,' that was a jibe at Bajie; and 'an ancient stone monkey of many years' was a jibe at old Sun. How could you make out his meaning?"

"Brother, calm your anger," said Bajie. "This Zen Master knows the things of past and future too. Only let's see whether his words 'a water-fiend you'll meet up ahead' prove true or not. Let him be." Seeing the lotus blossoms and the auspicious mists about the nest, Wukong could only ask his master to mount, and they went down the mountain and on toward the west. And as they went:

> It surely makes pure blessings few among men,
> And causes calamity and demons to throng in the mountains.

In the end there is no knowing how the road ahead truly turned out — so listen to the next chapter for the explanation.

<!-- chapter 20 -->
# Chapter 20: The Yellow Wind Ridge and the Tiger Vanguard

> The Dharma is born from the mind, and from the mind it likewise dies.
> Birth and death — by whom are they decreed? Reader, judge for yourself.
> Since all of it is your own mind, why need another tell you so?
> Only set yourself to bitter toil, and wring the blood from iron.
> Thread the soft cord through the nose, and tie it fast in the empty void.
> Tether it to the tree of non-doing, and let it not run wild.
> Mistake not the thief for a son; let mind and Dharma both be wholly forgotten.
> Suffer him not to deceive you — strike him through with the first blow of your fist.
> When mind appears, there is no mind; when Dharma appears, Dharma too falls still.
> When neither man nor ox is seen, the blue sky shines clear and bright.
> Round as the autumn moon — and which is which, none can tell apart.

This verse is the hymn that the Master of the Law, Tripitaka, composed when he had pierced through to the heart of the *Heart Sutra*, when he had thrown open the door of understanding. The elder recited it always and held it close, so that a single point of holy light shone clear within him.

Now, the three of them ate the wind and slept by the water, journeyed beneath the moon and clad in the stars, until soon the season turned to the blazing heat of summer. And this is what they saw:

> The flowers all spent, no butterflies remained to court them;
> the trees grown tall, the cicadas shrilled their clamor.
> Wild silkworms spun their cocoons; the fiery pomegranate bloomed;
> and in the ponds the fresh new lotus rose.

One day, as they were walking, evening came on suddenly, and beside the mountain road they spied a village dwelling. Tripitaka said, "Wukong, look — the setting sun hides its mirror of fire behind the western hills, and the moon lifts its wheel of ice from the eastern sea. Luckily there is a household by the road. Let us beg a night's lodging here, and travel on tomorrow."

Zhu Bajie said, "Well said. Old Hog is getting a bit hungry too. Let's go to that house and beg some food, so we'll have strength to carry the luggage."

The Pilgrim said, "You homesick ghost — you've been away from home only a few days, and already you're full of complaints."

"Brother," said Bajie, "I'm not like you, who can live on wind and breathe in smoke. Since I joined the Master these past days, I've gone half-starved the whole while. Did you know that?"

Hearing this, Tripitaka said, "Wuneng, if your heart is so heavy with thoughts of home, then you are no true monk. You may as well go back."

The blockhead, frightened, dropped to his knees. "Master, don't listen to my elder brother. He has a way of slandering people. I never complained about anything, and he says I complain. I'm a plain, straight-gutted fool — I only said my belly was empty and we ought to find a house and beg some food, and he calls me a homesick ghost. Master, I have received the Bodhisattva's commandments, and I have your kind pity besides. I am willing to serve you all the way to the Western Heaven, and I swear I shall never turn back in regret. This is what they call 'enduring bitterness to cultivate the Way.' How can you say these are not the words of a true monk?"

"If that is so," said Tripitaka, "then get up."

The blockhead sprang to his feet, muttering and grumbling under his breath, shouldered the carrying-pole, and resigned himself to following along. Soon they reached the door of the roadside house. Tripitaka dismounted, the Pilgrim took the bridle, and Bajie set down the luggage, and they all stood waiting beneath the green shade. Tripitaka, leaning on his nine-ringed staff and straightening his rattan-woven bamboo hat, went first to the door. There he saw an old man reclining against a couch of bamboo, his lips murmuring the name of the Buddha. Not daring to speak loudly, Tripitaka called out softly, "Patron, my greetings to you."

The old man scrambled up in a single bound, hastily gathered his robe, and came out to return the greeting. "Reverend, forgive me for not welcoming you. Where have you come from, and why have you come to my humble door?"

"I am a poor monk of the Great Tang in the eastern land," said Tripitaka, "sent by the imperial decree to the Thunderclap Monastery to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. Reaching your honored region just as night fell, I had a mind to beg a single night's shelter at your gracious house. I beg you, grant us this small kindness."

The old man waved his hands and shook his head. "You cannot go. The scriptures of the Western Heaven are not to be had. If you must seek scriptures, go to the eastern heaven instead."

Tripitaka said nothing aloud, but inwardly he pondered: "The Bodhisattva pointed me westward — why does this old man say to go east? What scriptures could there be in the east?" Shy and uncertain, he stood for a long while without answering.

But the Pilgrim, fierce and headstrong by nature, could hold back no longer. He stepped forward and cried out, "You old fellow, with all those years on you, you understand nothing at all. We are men who have left the household life, come from far away to beg a night's lodging — and you try to scare me off with such dreary, dull talk. If your house is so cramped that there's nowhere to sleep, then we'll just sit out the night beneath the trees, and not trouble you at all."

The old man caught hold of Tripitaka. "Master, you say nothing, but that disciple of yours — that crook-faced, hollow-cheeked creature with the thunder-god's beak and the red eyes, that consumptive little devil — how dare he turn and affront an old man like me?"

The Pilgrim laughed. "You old man, you've got no eye for things at all. The handsome ones — they're what we call 'fine to look at but no good to eat.' Now old Sun, though I'm small, I'm tough as can be — every inch of me wrapped in sinew."

"You must have some skills, then," said the old man.

"I'll not boast," said the Pilgrim, "but I'll do well enough to get by."

"Where is your home," asked the old man, "and what made you shave your head and become a monk?"

"Old Sun's ancestral home," said the Pilgrim, "is the Water-Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, in the Aolai Country east of the sea, in the Eastern Continent of Superior Body. From my childhood I learned to be a monster, and I called myself Wukong. By my own abilities I made myself a Great Sage Equal to Heaven. But because I would not accept Heaven's registry, I rebelled in the great revolt against the Celestial Palace and brought down a great calamity upon myself. Now, having escaped that disaster and dissolved that doom, I have turned to the gate of the Buddha and seek the right fruit ahead. I am guarding this Master of mine, who serves under the Tang court, on his way to worship the Buddha in the Western Heaven. What do I fear of high mountains and perilous roads, of broad waters and wild waves? Old Sun can catch demons and subdue fiends, tame tigers and capture dragons, kick the sky and stir the wells — I know a little of all of it. And if there should be any brick-throwing or tile-flinging at your house, any pot that howls or door that opens of itself, old Sun can set it all at peace."

When the old man heard this speech, he laughed aloud. "So you're a glib-tongued monk who goes about knocking on doors begging alms."

"Your son's the glib-tongued one," said the Pilgrim. "Me — I've been so weary tramping the road after my Master all this time, I've even grown too lazy to talk."

"If you weren't weary, and weren't too lazy to talk," said the old man, "I dare say you'd chatter me clean to death. But since you have such skills, then the Western Heaven can be reached after all — yes, it can be reached. How many are there in your party? Come into my thatched hut and rest the night."

"Many thanks to you, old patron, for not driving us off," said Tripitaka. "There are three in my party."

"And where is the third?" asked the old man.

The Pilgrim pointed. "This old fellow's eyes are dim — isn't that him standing there under the green shade?"

The old man's eyes were indeed dim. He raised his head and looked carefully, and the moment he caught sight of Bajie's face, he was so terrified that he went stumbling and tripping at every step, running pell-mell into the house and crying, "Shut the door! Shut the door! A monster is coming!"

The Pilgrim ran up and caught hold of him. "Don't be afraid, old man. He's no monster — he's my fellow disciple."

Trembling all over, the old man said, "Well, well, well — each monk uglier than the last."

Bajie stepped forward. "Old sir, if you judge people by their looks, you're clean mistaken. Ugly we may be, but we're all of us useful."

While the old man stood at the door talking with the three monks, two young men from the southern end of the farmstead came home from transplanting rice, bringing with them an old woman and three or four small children, their clothes tucked up and their feet bare. Seeing a white horse and a load of luggage all clustered and clamoring at their door, and not knowing what manner of folk these were, they all rushed forward and demanded, "What are you doing here?"

Bajie turned his head, waggled his ears a few times, and stretched out his long snout — and the sight so terrified those people that they went toppling this way and that, scattering and tumbling in confusion. In a fluster, Tripitaka called out to them all, "Don't be afraid, don't be afraid! We are not evil men — we are monks going to fetch the scriptures."

Only then did the old man come out the door, and taking the old woman by the arm, he said, "Get up, granny, and don't be so frightened. This master comes from the Tang court. It's only that his disciples are a bit ugly of face — but they're foul of feature and fair of heart. Take the children indoors." The old woman then clung to the old man, and the two young men led the children inside.

Tripitaka sat down upon the bamboo couch in the gatehouse and grumbled, "Disciples — the two of you, with your ugly faces and coarse tongues, have frightened this whole household half to death. You're heaping sins upon me!"

"I'll not deceive you, Master," said Bajie. "Since Old Hog joined you, I've grown a good deal handsomer. Why, back in the old days at the Gao family village, if I jutted my snout out front and waggled my ears at both ends, I'd scare twenty or thirty people to death."

The Pilgrim laughed. "Blockhead, stop your nonsense — and tidy that ugliness away a bit."

"Listen to what Wukong says," said Tripitaka. "His looks are what he was born with. How do you expect him to tidy them away?"

"Tuck that rake-snout of his into his bosom and don't let it out," said the Pilgrim, "and stick those fan-ears flat against the back of his head and don't let them flap — that's what I call tidying up."

So Bajie did indeed tuck in his snout and flatten his ears, and bowing his head he stood off to one side. The Pilgrim carried the luggage in through the door and tethered the white horse to a post.

Presently the old man, leading a young man who carried a wooden tray, came to offer three cups of clear tea. When the tea was done, he gave orders for a meal to be prepared. The young man fetched an old table, full of holes and with no lacquer left on it, and set out two broken-backed, splay-legged stools in the courtyard, inviting the three of them to sit in the cool. Tripitaka then asked, "Old patron, what is your honored surname?"

"My humble name is Wang," said the old man.

"And how many sons have you?"

"Two boys, and three little grandsons."

"Congratulations, congratulations," said Tripitaka. "And how old are you?"

"I have foolishly reached sixty-one years."

"Good, good, good," said the Pilgrim — "you've come round to a second cycle of the sixty-year span."

Tripitaka asked again, "Old patron, why did you say at first that the scriptures of the Western Heaven are hard to fetch?"

"It is not the scriptures that are hard to fetch," said the old man, "but the road that is rough and hard to travel. About thirty li west of here there is a mountain called the Yellow Wind Ridge, eight hundred li across, and in that mountain there are many monsters. That is why I said it would be hard. But if this little reverend truly has such skills as he claims, then it can be done."

"No matter, no matter," said the Pilgrim. "With old Sun and this fellow disciple of mine, no monster — whatever it may be — will dare to trouble us."

While they were speaking, the son brought in the rice and set it on the table, saying, "Please, eat." Tripitaka pressed his palms together and began to chant the grace before meals. But Bajie had already gulped down a whole bowl, and before the elder had finished the few lines of his grace, the blockhead had bolted down three bowls more.

"This chaff-guzzler," said the Pilgrim — "he must have run smack into a hungry ghost."

Old Wang, knowing how things stood and seeing how fast he ate, said, "This reverend must be truly famished. Quick, bring more rice." And indeed the blockhead's gullet was vast — never lifting his head, he downed a dozen bowls one after another, while Tripitaka and the Pilgrim each ate scarcely two. Still the blockhead would not stop, but kept on eating.

"We had no relish ready on short notice, and dare not press you hard," said old Wang. "Do take another mouthful."

"Enough for us," said Tripitaka and the Pilgrim both.

But Bajie said, "Old man, what are you dithering about? Who's asking you to cast my fortune, prattling on about five lines and six lines? If there's rice, just keep bringing it." And so the blockhead at one sitting ate up every last grain in the whole household's stores, and still claimed he was only half full. Then the cooking things were cleared away, and beneath the gatehouse a bamboo bed and plank pallet were made up, and they lay down to sleep.

The next day at dawn, the Pilgrim went to saddle the horse, and Bajie went to arrange the luggage. Old Wang had the old woman prepare a few cakes and some hot broth to send them on their way, and then the three thanked him and took their leave. "If you should meet with any mishap on the road ahead," said the old man, "be sure to come back to my hut."

"Old man," said the Pilgrim, "speak no foolish words. We who have left the household never walk the road back." And so they whipped the horse and shouldered the load, and set off westward.

Ah! Going on like this — west toward the Western Region there is surely no good road, and there must be some evil fiend to bring down a great disaster. The three had not gone half a day before they came indeed upon a high mountain, towering and exceedingly steep. When Tripitaka rode his horse up to the brink of the cliff and tilted his precious hat to look, he saw truly:

> High were the mountains; sheer were the ridges;
> steep were the cliffs; deep were the gorges;
> loud were the springs; bright were the flowers.
> The mountain — how high? Its peak touched the blue empyrean.
> The ravine — how deep? At its bottom one could glimpse the underworld.
> Before the mountain rolled banks of white cloud, and jutted grotesque crags,
> and there stretched, beyond all telling, cliffs a thousand and ten thousand fathoms high that clutched at the very soul.
> Behind the cliffs wound a twisting Hidden-Dragon Cave,
> and within the cave, drip by drip, a dripping water-ledge.
> There one saw branching, antlered deer, and dull, gazing river-deer that stared at men;
> coiling red-scaled pythons, and frisking, white-faced apes.
> At dusk the mountain tigers sought their lairs;
> at dawn the dragons churned the waves and rose from the water,
> so the cave-mouth boomed and roared.
> Birds in the grass flapped whirring up; beasts in the forest went loping by.
> Suddenly a pack of wolves and serpents passed,
> and a man's heart pounded and quaked with terror.
> Truly, fold upon fold of caverns, cavern upon overturned cavern,
> caves overturning upon the mountain.
> The dark green pigment dyed a thousand fathoms of jade;
> the azure gauze shrouded ten thousand mounds of mist.

The Master gently spurred his silver-grey horse; the Great Sage Sun halted his clouds and walked slowly; and Zhu Wuneng dragged his load along at a measured pace. Just as they were gazing at the mountain, a sudden whirlwind sprang up in a great blast. Tripitaka, on his horse, grew alarmed at heart and said, "Wukong, the wind is rising."

"A wind — what's there to fear in that?" said the Pilgrim. "It's only one of Heaven's four seasonal airs. What is there to dread?"

"This wind is fierce and foul," said Tripitaka, "not at all like a heavenly wind."

"How can you tell it's not a heavenly wind?" asked the Pilgrim.

"Look at this wind," said Tripitaka:

> Vast and surging, howling and whirling,
> dim and boundless, it issues from the azure heights.
> Crossing the ridges, one hears a thousand trees roar;
> entering the forest, one sees ten thousand stalks sway.
> On the bank the willows shake, stirred to their very roots;
> in the garden it blows the blossoms, scattering them with their leaves.
> The fishing boats that gather their nets all fasten their cables tight;
> the passenger skiffs that lower their sails all cast their anchors down.
> Halfway along the road the traveler loses his way;
> in the mountains the woodcutter can scarcely shoulder his load.
> Among the immortal fruit-groves the monkeys scatter;
> within the rare-flower thickets the deer take flight.
> Before the cliff the cypress and juniper topple one by one;
> below the ravine the pine and bamboo wither leaf by leaf.
> It flings up earth and raises dust, the sand spurting and flying;
> it overturns the rivers and stirs the seas, the billows surging and rolling.

Bajie stepped up and seized the Pilgrim by the hand. "Elder brother, the wind is terribly strong — let's just dodge aside and be clear of it."

The Pilgrim laughed. "Brother, you're no good. The moment the wind blows hard, you want to hide. But if we should come face to face with a demon, what then?"

"Brother," said Bajie, "haven't you heard the saying, 'Shun lust as you would shun an enemy; shun the wind as you would shun an arrow'? If we dodge aside a bit, no one's the worse for it."

"Say no more," said the Pilgrim. "Let me grab a fistful of this wind and have a sniff at it."

Bajie laughed. "There you go telling tall tales again, brother. Who can grab a wind and sniff it? And even if you grabbed it, it'd be gone in an instant."

"Brother," said the Pilgrim, "you don't know that old Sun has a method for grabbing the wind." Splendid Great Sage — he let the head of the gust go by, caught hold of the tail of the wind, and gave it a sniff. There was something rank about it. "It's truly no good wind," he said. "The flavor of this wind isn't a tiger's wind — it's surely a monster's wind. There's something amiss here, beyond a doubt."

Before he had finished speaking, there leapt out from the foot of the slope, flicking its tail and bounding on its hooves, a brindled fierce tiger. So alarmed was Tripitaka that he could not sit firm in his carved saddle but tumbled head over heels off the white horse and lay slumped at the roadside, truly with his three souls scattered and his seven spirits flown.

Bajie threw down the luggage, whipped out his nailed rake, and — not letting the Pilgrim get ahead of him — gave a great shout: "Cursed beast, where do you think you're going!" And he charged forward to strike straight at its head. But the tiger reared up bolt upright, raised its left forepaw, hooked its own breast, and with a downward rip — *slick!* — peeled off its hide and stood by the roadside. And what a hideous shape it took! Just look at that figure:

> Its bared red body, raw and dripping with blood;
> its bent and ringed legs, an angry crimson.
> The fiery tufts at its temples bristling wild;
> its two stiff eyebrows standing straight up.
> Four steel fangs, white and gleaming;
> a pair of golden eyes, blazing and bright.
> In a towering rage it roared with all its might;
> ferocious and grim, it shrieked aloud.

It shouted, "Slow down, slow down! I am no ordinary creature — I am the Vanguard of the Road under the Great King of the Yellow Wind. Today, by the King's strict command, I patrol the mountain to seize a few mortal men to be relish for his wine. What sort of monk are you, that you dare lift a weapon against me?"

Bajie cursed at him: "I'll have you, cursed beast! You don't know who I am. We're no passing mortals — we're the disciples of Tripitaka, the imperial younger brother of the Great Tang in the eastern land, sent by decree to worship the Buddha in the West and seek the scriptures. Get yourself far off to some other quarter and clear the road, and don't go startling my Master, and I'll spare your life. But if you keep up this insolence, then once my rake is raised, there'll be no mercy in it."

The monster gave him no time to argue, but stepped quickly close, struck a pose, and clawed straight at Bajie's face. Bajie dodged aside in haste and swung his rake to strike. The monster, having no weapon in hand, turned and fled. Bajie chased after him, and the monster, reaching the boulder-strewn thicket at the foot of the slope, drew out two red-bronze sabers, swiftly raised them, and turned to meet him. The two of them, back and forth, charge and clash, fought it out before the slope.

The Pilgrim, meanwhile, helped Tripitaka up. "Master, don't be afraid. Sit still here, and let old Sun go help Bajie. We'll knock the monster down and then be on our way." Tripitaka managed to sit up, trembling, and chanted the *Heart Sutra* under his breath — but no more of that.

The Pilgrim whipped out his iron rod and shouted, "Take that!" At this, Bajie summoned his spirits afresh, and the monster fell back in defeat. "Don't spare him," cried the Pilgrim. "Be sure to run him down." The two of them, raising rake and iron rod, chased him down the mountain. The monster, his hands and feet in a panic, played the trick of the golden cicada shedding its shell: he rolled over, revealed his true form, and once more became a fierce tiger. The Pilgrim and Bajie, unwilling to let him go, pursued the tiger, determined to root him out altogether. Seeing them close upon him, the monster again hooked his breast, peeled off his hide, draped it over a crouching-tiger rock, slipped out his true body, transformed into a blast of wild wind, and went straight back to the head of the road. There he suddenly saw the Master, still reciting the *Heart Sutra* — and with one grab he seized him, mounted the long wind, and carried him off. Pity poor Tripitaka — born to the river's current and fated to many torments, his merit and works hard to win within the gate of perfect quiescence!

The monster brought Tripitaka to the mouth of his cave, stilled the wild wind, and said to the gatekeeper, "Go report to the Great King that the Tiger Vanguard of the Road ahead has captured a monk and awaits his orders outside the gate."

The cave-lord gave the order to bring him in. The Tiger Vanguard, the two red-bronze sabers thrust in his belt, lifted Tripitaka up in both hands, came forward, and knelt. "Great King, your unworthy little general, having received your command to patrol the mountain, suddenly met a monk — he is Tripitaka, the Master of the Law and imperial younger brother under the Great Tang of the eastern land, going west to worship the Buddha and seek scriptures. I have captured him and present him to you, a small dish for your table."

When the cave-lord heard this, he was startled. "I have heard it said by people before now," he said, "that this Master Tripitaka is a holy monk sent by the Tang emperor's decree to fetch scriptures, and that he has a disciple named Sun the Pilgrim, of vast magic powers and high cunning and strength. How could you manage to capture him?"

"He has two disciples," said the Vanguard. "The first to come uses a nine-toothed nailed rake; he has a long snout and great ears. The other uses an iron rod bound with golden bands; he has fiery eyes and golden pupils. They were just bearing down hard on your little general when I used the trick of the golden cicada shedding its shell, slipped my body free, and seized this monk to offer to you, Great King — a small token toward a meal."

"Don't eat him yet," said the cave-lord.

"Great King," said the Vanguard, "to see food and not eat it — isn't that what they call being a contrary fool?"

"You don't understand," said the cave-lord. "Eating him is no great matter — but I'm only afraid those two disciples of his will come knocking at our door and making an uproar, and that wouldn't be safe. Let's bind him to the Wind-Stilling Stake in the back garden, and wait three to five days. If those two don't come to make trouble, then — first, his body will be clean; and second, there'll be no quarrel — and we can do just as we please. To boil him, or steam him, or fry him, or stir-fry him, and enjoy him at our leisure, won't be too late."

The Vanguard was delighted. "The Great King's deep schemes and far-sighted plans — it's truly well reasoned. You there, take him away!" Seven or eight binding-hands crowded up from the side and carried Tripitaka off — just as a hawk seizes a swallow, trussing him with cord and winding him with rope. Truly the ill-fated child of the river thought of the Pilgrim; the holy monk in his peril longed for Wuneng. He cried, "Disciples! I know not on what mountain you are seizing monsters, in what place subduing fiends, while I am taken by this fiend-chief to suffer this cruel harm. When shall we meet again? Oh, the bitterness of it! If you come soon, you may still save my life; but if you come too late, then surely I cannot be preserved." And on one hand he sighed, and on the other his tears fell like rain.

Now, the Pilgrim and Bajie had chased the tiger down the slope, and there they saw the tiger fallen and crouched flat before the cliff. The Pilgrim raised his rod and struck with all his might — and the blow jarred his own hands with pain. Bajie struck a blow with his rake, and the rake-teeth sprang back. For it was only a tiger's hide draped over a crouching-tiger rock!

The Pilgrim was aghast. "This is bad, this is bad — we've fallen for his trick!"

"What trick?" asked Bajie.

"This is what's called the golden-cicada-shedding-its-shell trick," said the Pilgrim. "He draped his hide here and made off himself. Let's get back quick and see how the Master is, and pray he hasn't come to harm."

The two hurried back — but Tripitaka was already gone. The Pilgrim cried out like thunder, "What's to be done? The Master's been carried off by him!"

Bajie at once led the horse, tears dropping from his eyes. "Heaven! Oh, Heaven! Where are we to look for him now?"

The Pilgrim lifted his head. "Don't weep, don't weep — weeping only blunts our spirit. He's surely somewhere on this very mountain. Let's go and search."

So the two of them plunged into the mountain, crossing ridges and climbing over peaks. After a good while they saw, rising up beneath a stone cliff, a cave-dwelling. The two halted to take in the sight, and it was fierce and forbidding indeed. They saw:

> Tiered barriers and pointed peaks; winding ridges and ancient paths.
> The green pines and emerald bamboo soft and lush; the green willows and azure phoenix-trees gently swaying.
> Before the cliff, grotesque rocks in pairs; within the forest, secluded birds two by two.
> Ravine-water flowing far to dash against the stone walls; mountain springs trickling fine to flood the sandy banks.
> Wild clouds in drifting wisps; jade-bright grasses lush and thick.
> Sly foxes and cunning hares darted to and fro like shuttles;
> antlered deer and fragrant river-deer vied together in valor.
> Cleaving the cliff, ten-thousand-year vines hung aslant;
> deep in the gorge, thousand-year cypresses hung half-suspended.
> Lofty and towering, it put Mount Hua to shame;
> with falling blossoms and crying birds, it rivaled the Terrace of Heaven.

The Pilgrim said, "Worthy brother, set the luggage down in some wind-sheltered hollow of the mountain, turn the horse loose, and don't show yourself. Let old Sun go to his door and fight it out with him. I must capture the monster — only then can we rescue the Master."

"No need to tell me twice," said Bajie. "Go quick."

Splendid Pilgrim — he straightened his cassock, cinched up his tiger-skin kilt, whipped out his rod, and rushed up to the door. There he saw six great characters upon the gate: "Yellow Wind Cave of the Yellow Wind Ridge." Planting his feet in a firm T-stance and gripping his rod, he shouted loudly, "Monster! Send my Master out at once, and spare me the trouble of overturning your nest and leveling your dwelling to the ground!"

When the little fiends heard this, they were all of them terrified, and went trembling and quaking into the cave to report: "Great King, disaster!"

The Yellow Wind Fiend, who was sitting within, asked, "What's the matter?"

"At the cave-mouth," said the little fiends, "there's come a monk with a thunder-god's beak and a hairy face, holding an iron rod thick as anything, demanding his Master."

The cave-lord was alarmed, and at once summoned the Tiger Vanguard. "I sent you to patrol the mountain — you should have caught only some mountain oxen, wild boars, fat deer, and goats. Why did you go and seize that Tang monk, and so bring his disciples here to make this uproar? How are we to deal with it now?"

"Great King, set your heart at ease, and rest easy with your head upon a high pillow," said the Vanguard. "Unworthy as I am, your little general is willing to lead fifty of the lesser troops out, and bring this Sun the Pilgrim, or whatever he calls himself, back to add to our feast."

"Besides my chief officers, great and small," said the cave-lord, "I have five or seven hundred lesser troops. Choose as you please — take however many you will. Only capture that Pilgrim, and then we may eat that monk's flesh at our leisure and ease, and I'll gladly bow with you as sworn brothers. But if you fail to take him, and instead come to harm yourself — then don't go blaming me."

"Rest easy, rest easy," said the Tiger Fiend. "Wait while I go." And he duly mustered fifty stout, vigorous little fiends, beat the drums and waved the flags, took up his two red-bronze sabers, and came charging out the gate, shouting in a fierce voice: "What sort of monkey-monk are you, that you come here bellowing and shrieking — and to what end?"

The Pilgrim cursed at him: "You skin-peeling beast! What shell-shedding tricks did you play, to carry off my Master, and then turn round and ask me what I'm about? Send my Master out, nice and proper, this instant, and I'll still spare you your life."

"Your Master I did capture," said the Tiger Fiend, "to make a dish to go with our King's rice. If you know what's good for you, go back. Otherwise I'll seize you too, and we'll eat the lot of you together — and isn't that buying one and getting one free?"

Hearing this, the Pilgrim's heart blazed with rage. He ground his steel teeth together with a grating sound and rolled his fiery eyes wide and round, whipped out his iron rod, and shouted, "How great are your skills, that you dare talk so big? Don't run — taste my cudgel!" The Vanguard hastily lifted his sabers to meet it. This was no gentle contest indeed; each displayed his might and prowess. A fine fight:

> The monster was a true goose-egg; Wukong, a goose-egg stone.
> The red-bronze sabers crossing the Handsome Monkey King
> were as if a heaped-up egg had come to strike a stone.
> How shall the magpie vie with the phoenix?
> How dare the wood-pigeon match the hawk and falcon?
> The monster spewed wind till the ash filled the mountain;
> Wukong belched mist till the clouds dimmed the sun.
> Back and forth, not three or five rounds gone by,
> and the Vanguard's waist went limp, his strength all spent.
> He turned to flee and save his life —
> but Wukong pressed him hard, to the death.

The Tiger Fiend, unable to hold his ground, turned and fled. But because he had boasted before the cave-lord, he dared not return to the cave, and made straight for the mountain slope to save his life. The Pilgrim would by no means let him go, but gripping his rod chased after him with all his heart, howling and roaring, his shouts never ceasing — until he had driven him to the wind-sheltered mountain hollow. Just then Bajie, raising his head, saw the Pilgrim there. Bajie had been pasturing the horse, and hearing the howling and shouting, he turned to look and saw that it was the Pilgrim driving the routed Tiger Fiend before him. So he flung the horse aside, lifted his rake, and struck a slanting blow straight at the creature's head.

Pity that Vanguard — slipping his body free and meaning to leap clear of the yellow silken net, who could have known he'd run instead into the fish-trapper? With one stroke of Bajie's rake, nine holes were opened, gushing fresh blood, and his whole skull was drained dry of its brains. There is a poem to prove it:

> Three or five years ago he returned to the orthodox sect,
> kept the fast and a plain diet, and woke to the truth of emptiness.
> With a sincere heart he meant to guard the Tang Tripitaka —
> first taking up the monk's vocation, he stood this merit here.

The blockhead set one foot on the creature's spine and, gripping the rake in both hands, struck again. Seeing this, the Pilgrim was overjoyed. "Brother, that's exactly it! He led out several dozen little fiends and dared fight it out with old Sun — and I beat him so that, rather than run back to the cave, he ran here to meet his death. Lucky you were here to catch him, or he'd have gotten away again."

"Was it this one," asked Bajie, "who worked the wind and carried off the Master?"

"The very one, the very one," said the Pilgrim.

"Did you ask him where the Master is?" said Bajie.

"This monster took the Master into the cave," said the Pilgrim, "to make a dish to go with some bird-king's rice. Old Sun got angry and fought him all the way here, where you put an end to his life. Brother — this merit goes to you. Now you stay and keep watch over the horse and the luggage, while I drag this dead monster off and go back to the cave-mouth to challenge them again. We must capture that old fiend himself before we can rescue the Master."

"Brother, that's well reasoned," said Bajie. "Go on, go on. And if you beat that old fiend and chase him back this way, Old Hog will cut him off and slay him."

Splendid Pilgrim — with one hand he held his iron rod, and with the other he dragged the dead tiger, and went straight to the cave-mouth. Truly:

> The Master of the Law in his peril met with a monster;
> their natures in harmony, they subdued the unruly fiend.

And in the end, whether on this venture he could subdue the monster and rescue the Tang Monk — listen to the explanation in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 21 -->
# Chapter 21: The Wind Demon and the Healing Salve

Now the fifty battered little demons, clutching their torn banners and broken drums, came tumbling back into the cave and reported: "Great King, Tiger Vanguard could not stand against that hairy-faced monk. He was driven down the eastern slope and away." When the old demon heard this, he was deeply troubled. He sat with his head bowed, saying nothing, silently turning over schemes in his mind, when another of the little demons who had been guarding the front gate came in and said: "Great King, Tiger Vanguard has been beaten to death by that hairy-faced monk. His body lies dragged before our gate, and the monk stands there shouting for battle."

At this the old demon grew more wretched still. "The wretch knows nothing," he said. "I never even ate his master, yet he turns around and slays my own vanguard. Hateful! Hateful!" He called for his armor. "I have only heard talk of some Sun Wukong. Let me go out and see what manner of monk this is, with his nine heads and eight tails. I shall seize him and bring him in to pay with his life for my Tiger Vanguard."

The little demons hurriedly carried out his armor, and the old demon dressed himself in full array. Grasping a three-pronged steel fork, he led the whole troop of demons leaping out of the cave.

The Great Sage stood waiting outside the gate, and when he saw the demon come striding forth, he found him truly fierce and martial. See now how he was arrayed:

> A golden helmet flashing in the sun,
> golden armor gleaming with frozen light.
> From the helmet streamed a pheasant-tail plume;
> a gauze robe of pale goose-yellow draped the mail.
> The cords that bound his plates coiled like dragons, bright;
> the heart-guard mirror dazzled the eyes around.
> Boots of deerskin dyed with sophora bloom;
> a brocade kilt soft as willow leaves.
> In his hand the keen three-pronged steel fork —
> no less than that immortal lord of bygone years.

Coming out at the gate, the old demon shouted harshly: "Which of you is Sun Wukong?" Wukong, his feet shod with the skin of the slain tiger and the obedient iron staff in his hand, answered: "Your Grandfather Sun is here. Send out my master."

The monster looked him over carefully and saw that the pilgrim was a mean little figure, gaunt of face and barely four feet tall. He laughed. "Pitiful, pitiful! I had thought you some unbeatable hero no man could throw, and here you are — a sickly little skeleton of a ghost."

Wukong laughed back. "You son of mine, your eyes are no good at all. Your grandfather may be small, but if you'll consent to crack me one across the head with that fork-handle, I'll grow six feet taller."

"Hold your head steady," said the monster, "and take my blow."

The Great Sage, wholly without fear, let the monster strike him a blow. He gave his waist a little bend — and shot up six feet, until he stood a full ten feet tall. So startled was the demon that he braced his fork upright and shouted: "Sun Wukong, why do you bring out before my gate these protective tricks of transformation? Enough of your conjuring! Come up here, and let me see what you can do."

Wukong laughed. "Son, as the old saying goes: spare your foe and your hand stays down; once your hand is raised, no foe is spared. Your grandfather's hand falls heavy — I only fear you can't bear a single stroke of my staff."

The monster gave him no room to talk. Twirling his steel fork, he stabbed straight at Wukong's chest. The Great Sage was the master who never hurries and never flusters; he opened up his iron staff, swung it in a "Black Dragon Sweeps the Ground" stance, knocked the fork aside, and aimed a blow at the monster's head. There at the mouth of the Yellow Wind Cave the two of them fought a magnificent battle:

> The demon king was wrathful, the Great Sage proud and bold.
> The demon king was wrathful — he would take the pilgrim to avenge his vanguard;
> the Great Sage stood proud — he would seize the sprite to save the elder monk.
> Fork came, staff parried; staff went, fork rose to meet it.
> One was the mountain's supreme commander,
> the other the Dharma-guarding Handsome Monkey King.
> At first they fought down in the dust,
> then both rose up into the air.
> The tempered fork was sharp and bright and keen;
> the obedient staff, black-bodied with bands of gold.
> Whatever the fork pierced went down to the shades;
> whatever the staff struck met King Yama for certain.
> All hung on quick hands and quicker eyes,
> on strength of arm and a hardy frame.
> Both sides forgot their lives and warred to the death —
> who could say which would come safe through, which take the wound?

The old demon and the Great Sage fought thirty rounds, and neither could gain the upper hand. Then Wukong, wanting to show his skill, used his "body-outside-the-body" art. He plucked a handful of hairs, chewed them to fragments in his mouth, spat them upward, and cried "Change!" — and a hundred and more little Wukongs appeared, all dressed alike, each wielding an iron staff, ringing the monster round in the air.

The monster took fright and worked a trick of his own. He turned quickly, faced the southeast quarter, opened his mouth three times, and with a great "Whoosh!" blew out a single breath — and all at once a yellow wind came howling up out of the sky. What a wind it was, truly terrible:

> Cold and keen, it changed both heaven and earth,
> a yellow whirlwind, shapeless, casting no shadow.
> It pierced the forests, snapped the ridgelines, toppled pine and plum,
> flung up the soil, scattered the dust, and crumbled mountain altars.
> The Yellow River's billows churned muddy to the bed;
> the Xiang's waters surged and turned their waves about.
> It rocked the Palace of the Plough in the blue-green sky,
> and nearly blew down the very Hall of King Yama.
> Five hundred arhats clamored to high heaven;
> the eight great Vajra-guardians shouted in confusion.
> Manjushri lost his blue-maned lion;
> Samantabhadra's white elephant could not be found.
> Zhenwu's tortoise and snake were parted from their kind;
> the mule of Zitong saw its saddle-cloth blown away.
> Wandering merchants cried out to the grey heavens;
> boatmen bowed and vowed every kind of vow.
> Lives floated lost upon the misty waves;
> the wreck of fame and gain went drifting with the water.
> Immortal hills and caverns turned to black,
> the sea-isles of Penglai to dim obscurity.
> Lord Lao could not tend his elixir furnace;
> the Star of Longevity put away his dragon-whisker fan.
> The Queen Mother, just then going to the Peach Feast,
> had girdle-sash and ringlets blown into disorder.
> Erlang lost his way back to Guanzhou town;
> Nezha could not draw the sword from out its case.
> The Heavenly King could not see the tower in his palm;
> Lu Ban let fall his golden-headed awl.
> Three tiers of the Thunderclap Tower came tumbling down;
> the stone bridge of Zhaozhou cracked clean in two.
> The one red sun was swept clear of its light,
> and all the stars of heaven were thrown into a daze.
> South-mountain birds flew off toward the northern hills;
> the eastern lake's waters poured over into the west.
> Mated pairs were torn apart and could not call;
> mothers and young, divided, could not cry out.
> The Dragon King combed the seas to find his yaksha;
> the Duke of Thunder searched everywhere for his lightning.
> The Ten Kings of the dead sought their judge in vain;
> in the underworld, Ox-Head chased after Horse-Face.
> This wind blew down the whole of Mount Potala
> and rolled up one whole scroll of Guanyin's scriptures.
> The white lotus blossoms scattered and flew along the shore;
> it toppled the Bodhisattva's twelve courts entire.
> From Pangu's time till now men have seen wind,
> but never a wind that came so ill as this.
> With a great roar — heaven and earth all but split and burst;
> and the rivers and hills of ten thousand miles stood trembling.

When the monster loosed this raging storm, the little Wukongs made of his hairs were whirled about in mid-air like so many spinning-wheels, with no way to swing a staff or steady themselves. In alarm, Wukong gave his fur a shake and drew the hairs back onto his body. Alone now, he raised his iron staff and pressed forward to strike — but the monster blew a mouthful of yellow wind full into his face, and his two fiery, golden eyes were buffeted shut, unable to open. With his eyes useless he could not wield the staff, and so he was driven from the field. The demon gathered up his wind and returned to his cave — but of that no more.
