Now while the yellow wind raged and heaven and earth lost their light, Zhu Bajie had led the horse and guarded the luggage, crouching in a hollow of the mountain. He dared not open his eyes nor lift his head, but kept reciting the Buddha's name and making vows without ceasing — for he had no idea whether Wukong had won or lost, nor whether the master was alive or dead. Just as he was caught up in these doubts, the wind died and the sky cleared. He raised his head and looked toward the cave gate, but saw no weapons there and heard no gong or drum. The blockhead dared not approach the gate, yet there was no one to mind the horse and baggage. Truly he could neither go forward nor back, and he fretted in great distress.

While he worried, he heard the Great Sage hallooing as he came up from the west. Bajie stirred himself and went to meet him. "Brother! What a tremendous wind! Where have you come from?"

Wukong waved his hand. "Terrible! Terrible! In all my born days I never saw such a wind. That old demon came at me with a three-pronged steel fork, and we fought above thirty rounds. So I worked my 'body-outside-the-body' trick and ringed him round to beat him. In his desperation he conjured up that wind. It was savage indeed — it buffeted me till I could not keep my feet, so I packed up my magic and fled before it. Faugh, what a wind! Faugh, what a wind! Old Sun can call up wind himself and summon rain too, but never have I met a wind as wicked as that monster's."

"Elder brother," said Bajie, "and how does the monster's fighting compare?"

"Passable enough," said Wukong. "His fork-work is well-ordered — he fought me to a draw. It is only that wicked wind that makes him hard to beat."

"If that's how it is," said Bajie, "how are we ever to rescue the master?"

"Saving the master can wait," said Wukong. "I don't know whether there's any eye-doctor hereabouts — I'd have him treat my eyes a little."

"What's wrong with your eyes?" asked Bajie.

"When that monster blew his wind in my face, it left my eyeballs aching and smarting, and now they keep running with cold tears."

"Brother," said Bajie, "we're halfway up a wild mountain and the day grows late. Never mind an eye-doctor — there isn't even a place to spend the night."

"Finding lodging is no hard matter," said Wukong. "I reckon the monster won't yet dare harm our master. Let's get back to the main road, find some house, stay the night, and tomorrow at first light come back to subdue the demon."

"Quite right, quite right," said Bajie.

So he led the horse and shouldered the load, and they came out of the hollow onto the road. By now dusk was gathering, and they heard the barking of a dog on a hillside south of the way. The two of them stopped and looked, and there was a farmstead, with the dim glow of lamplight showing. Caring nothing whether there was a path or none, they pushed through the grass straight to the gate. There they saw:

> Purple fungus, shadowy and dense; white stones, grey and pale.
> The purple fungus, shadowy and dense, amid much green grass;
> the white stones, grey and pale, half veiled in emerald moss.
> A few small fireflies glimmered with their flickering light;
> a grove of wild trees stood close and thick in rows.
> Fragrant orchids breathed their rich perfume;
> tender bamboo had been freshly set.
> A clear spring ran through the winding gully,
> and an ancient cypress leaned against the deep cliff.
> So remote the spot that no traveler ever came;
> before the gate only the wildflowers bloomed.

The two did not dare push in unbidden, but could only call out: "Open up! Open up!" From within an old man came, with several young farmhands, all carrying forks, rakes, and brooms. "Who are you? Who are you?" they demanded.

Wukong bowed and said: "We are disciples of the holy monk of the Great Tang in the Land of the East. We are bound for the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures, and passing this mountain, our master was carried off by the Great King of Yellow Wind. We have not yet been able to rescue him. The day is late, so we have come to beg a single night's lodging at your house. We earnestly hope you will oblige us."

The old man returned the bow. "Forgive our poor welcome. This is a place of much cloud and few people, and when we heard the knocking just now we feared it might be demon-foxes, tigers, or mountain bandits and the like. That is why these foolish lads of mine came out rudely and gave offense — we did not know it was two reverend elders. Please, come in, come in."

The brothers led the horse and carried the load inside, tethered the horse, set down the burden, and exchanged greetings with the old farmer and sat down. A servant brought tea, and when the tea was finished, several bowls of sesame rice were set out. After they had eaten, bedding was spread for them to rest.

Wukong said: "Not sleeping is well enough — but may I ask, good sir, does your honored district have anyone who sells eye-medicine?"

"Which of the reverend elders has ailing eyes?" asked the old man.

"To tell you the truth, sir," said Wukong, "we men of religion are by nature never ill, and have never known what it is to have sore eyes."

"If your eyes are not sore," said the old man, "why do you ask for medicine?"

"Today, at the mouth of the Yellow Wind Cave, we were trying to save our master," said Wukong, "when that monster blew a mouthful of wind at me unexpectedly, and it left my eyeballs aching and smarting, so that now they run with tears. That is why I seek eye-medicine."

The old man said: "Mercy, mercy! You are a young elder — how can you tell such a tale? That Great King of Yellow Wind — his wind is the most terrible thing. His wind is nothing like your spring or autumn winds, your pine-and-bamboo breeze, or the winds of east, west, south, or north —"

"It must be a brain-cramp wind, a sheep's-ear wind, a great-leprosy wind, or a half-and-whole migraine wind!" put in Bajie.

"No, no," said the elder. "It is called the Samadhi Divine Wind."

"How is it known to be so?" asked Wukong.

The old man said: "That wind can blow heaven and earth dark, and make ghosts and gods grieve; it splits stone and crumbles cliffs in its fury, and where it touches a man, his life is forfeit on the instant. If you had met the full of that wind, do you think you'd still be alive? Only an immortal could come through it unharmed."

"True, true," said Wukong. "We may not be immortals, but immortals are my juniors. This life of mine is not so easily ended — it has only left my eyeballs aching and smarting."

"If that is so," said the old man, "then you are indeed a person of some standing. In this poor place of mine there is no one who sells eye-medicine. But I too suffer cold tears in the wind, and once I met an extraordinary man who passed me a formula. It is called the Three-Flower Nine-Seed Salve, and it can cure every kind of wind-borne eye ailment."

Hearing this, Wukong bowed his head and made his salute. "I beg you to give me a little, that I might try it."

The old man consented, went within, and brought out a small agate-stone jar. He pried out the stopper, dipped a jade hairpin in, drew out a little of the salve, and applied it to Wukong's eyes, telling him not to open them but to rest his mind and sleep, and by morning he would be well. This done, he put away the stone jar and led his young lads off to the inner quarters.

Bajie undid the bundle, spread out the bedding, and invited Wukong to settle down. Wukong, his eyes shut, groped about blindly. Bajie laughed: "Sir, where's your blind-man's stick?"

"You drivel-stuffed blockhead," said Wukong, "you'd have me play the blind man, would you?" The idiot chuckled silently to himself and went to sleep, while Wukong sat up on the bedding and circulated his magic energies, not lying down until after the third watch.

Before he knew it, the fifth watch was nearly upon them. Wukong wiped his face, opened his eyes, and said: "That's truly fine medicine — my sight is a hundred times clearer than before." But when he turned his head and looked behind — why! Where were the rooms, the windows, the doors? He saw only old sophora trees and tall willows, and the brothers lying on a soft green carpet of grass.

Bajie woke. "Brother, what are you shouting about?"

"Open your eyes and look," said Wukong.

The idiot suddenly raised his head, saw the house was gone, and in a flurry rolled over and scrambled up. "Where's my horse?"

"Tied to that tree, isn't it?" said Wukong.

"And the luggage?"

"Set there beside your head, isn't it?"

"This family is downright lazy," said Bajie. "They've moved away, and why didn't they call us once? If they'd only let old Pig know, I'd have given them a little tea and fruit. They must be folk dodging the registers, afraid the village headman would find out, and so they moved off in the dead of night. — Ai! And we slept like the dead — how is it we never heard so much as a sound while they pulled their house down?"

Wukong gave a chuckling laugh. "Blockhead, stop your jabbering. Look — what's that paper notice on the tree?"

Bajie went up and pulled it down with his hand. On it were four lines of verse:

> This farmstead is no dwelling of common folk —
> a Dharma-guardian's hermitage, conjured for the hour.
> The wondrous salve has healed your aching eyes;
> bend all your heart to subdue the demon — do not waver.

"These ruffian-spirits!" said Wukong. "Ever since I got the dragon-horse I've never once mustered them, and now they come playing their conjuring tricks."

"Brother, don't put on airs," said Bajie. "How could they ever answer to your muster?"

"Brother, you don't yet understand," said Wukong. "These Dharma-guarding monastery-gods, the Six Ding and Six Jia, the Revealers of the Five Quarters, and the Four Sentinel Officers — they all, by the Bodhisattva's holy command, secretly protect our master. From the day they reported themselves to me, since I had you all this while, I never had need of them, and so never mustered them — that is all."

"Brother," said Bajie, "since they bear the holy command to protect the master in secret, they cannot show themselves openly, and so they conjured this immortal farmstead. Don't be vexed with them. Yesterday they did you the kindness of treating your eyes, and saw to it that we got a meal of fasting-fare besides — you may well say they did their utmost. Don't be vexed. Let us go and rescue the master."

"What you say is right, brother," said Wukong. "It's not far from here to the Yellow Wind Cave. Don't stir yourself — just stay in the woods to mind the horse and guard the load. Let old Sun go to the cave and find out what's become of the master, and then I'll fight the demon again."

"Exactly so," said Bajie. "Get one solid word, alive or dead. If the master is dead, each of us can go his own way and see to his own business; if he's not dead, then we'll bend every effort to save him."

"No more idle talk — I'm off," said Wukong.

With a single leap he went straight to the cave gate, which was still shut with all asleep behind it. Wukong did not knock, nor would he rouse the demons. Making a magic sign and reciting a spell, he shook himself and changed into a mottle-legged mosquito — truly small and deft. There is a poem to prove it:

> A tiny, restless shape with a keen-edged bill,
> humming a thread of sound thin as thunder.
> Through orchid chambers and gauze bed-curtains it slips at will,
> loving best the warm air of blazing summer.
> It fears only the smoking fumes and beating fans,
> and dotes most on the brightness of lamp and candle.
> Light and small, marvelously quick to pierce,
> it flew into the demon's cave.

He saw the gate-keeping demon snoring fast asleep. Wukong stung him once on the face, and the little demon rolled over and woke. "Ouch, ouch! What a great mosquito — one bite and it's raised a great welt!" Then he opened his eyes. "It's daylight." And with a creak the second gate was opened. Wukong went humming in, and there saw the old demon ordering each gate to keep careful watch while along one wall the weapons were being made ready. "I only fear yesterday's wind didn't blow Sun Wukong to death," the old demon was saying. "He's sure to come again today, and when he comes I'll see to it his life is ended for good."

Hearing this, Wukong flew past the great hall and on to the rear, where he saw a door barred fast and tight. He slipped in through the crack of the door, and found a great empty garden. Against the far wall, bound with rope and cord to the Wind-Quelling Stake, stood Tripitaka. The master's tears fell and fell, his heart fixed only on Wukong and Wuneng, with no notion of where either might be. Wukong folded his wings and lit upon the bald crown of his head, crying softly: "Master!"

The elder knew his voice. "Wukong! You'll be the death of me with longing. Where are you, that you call to me?"

"Master, I'm on your head," said Wukong. "Don't fret your heart, don't be troubled. We must take the demon before we can save your life."

"Disciple," said Tripitaka, "when will you ever take the demon?"

"The tiger-monster that seized you has already been killed by Bajie," said Wukong. "It's only the old demon's wind that's so fierce. I reckon it'll be this very day — I'll be sure to take him. Set your mind at ease, don't weep. I'm off now."

So saying, he flew humming back to the front, and there saw the old demon seated on high, mustering his various captains. Then a little demon-sprite came in from before the cave, brandishing a command-banner, and rushed up to the hall to report: "Great King, I was out patrolling the mountain, and had scarcely gone past the gate when I saw a long-snouted, big-eared monk sitting in the woods. If I hadn't run quickly, he'd all but have caught me. But the hairy-faced monk of yesterday was nowhere to be seen."

"If Sun Wukong is not about," said the old demon, "then likely the wind blew him to death; or else he's gone off somewhere to fetch reinforcements."

The demons said: "Great King, if you really blew him dead, that's our good fortune. But if the wind didn't kill him, and he's gone to fetch some divine troops, what shall we do then?"

"What's there to fear in any divine troops?" said the old demon. "If anyone can quell my wind, it could only be the Bodhisattva Lingji come in person. Aside from him, what is there to dread?"

Up on the roof-beam Wukong heard these very words and could not contain his delight. At once he drew off, flew out, resumed his true form, and came to the woods, crying: "Brother!"

"Brother, where have you been?" said Bajie. "Just now a demon with a command-banner came by, and I chased him off."

Wukong laughed. "Well done, well done. Old Sun changed into a mosquito and went into the cave to look for the master. He's bound to the Wind-Quelling Stake, weeping — and old Sun told him to weep no more. Then I flew up to the roof-beam and listened. That banner-bearer came puffing in to report — that you'd chased him, but I was nowhere to be seen. The old demon guessed wildly that old Sun was blown dead by the wind, or gone to fetch divine troops. And then he let slip the name of one person himself — most excellent, most excellent!"

"And whose name did he let slip?" asked Bajie.

"He said, what's there to fear in any divine troops — the only one who could quell his wind is the Bodhisattva Lingji. But I don't know where Lingji lives."

While they were thus consulting, an old gentleman came walking out from beside the main road. See now what manner of man he was:

> Hale of body, needing no staff to lean upon;
> icy whiskers and snowy temples, all tousled.
> Golden flowers dazzled his eyes to a dreamy haze;
> his bones were lean, his sinews worn, yet hard and strong.
> Bent-backed, head bowed, he walked at a slow pace;
> his brows were thick, his ruddy face like a child's.
> Look at his features — a man worthy of praise,
> as though the Star of Longevity had come out from his cave.

Bajie was overjoyed at the sight. "Elder brother, as the saying goes: to learn the road below the mountain, you must ask the man who comes and goes. Why not go forward and ask him?"

Indeed the Great Sage hid his iron staff, let down the skirt of his robe, and stepped forward, calling: "Old sir, my greetings to you."

The old man returned a half-hearted bow. "Where are you a monk from? What business have you in this wild waste?"

"We are holy monks seeking the scriptures," said Wukong. "Yesterday we lost our master hereabouts, and I've come especially to ask you a question, sir: where does the Bodhisattva Lingji dwell?"

"Lingji is away to the due south," said the old man. "It is three thousand miles from here. There is a mountain called Little Mount Sumeru, and in that mountain is a holy site, the Bodhisattva's hall for expounding the scriptures. Are you going to fetch scriptures from him?"

"I'm not going for his scriptures," said Wukong. "I have a matter to trouble him with — only I don't know which road to take."

The old man pointed south with his hand. "This sheep's-gut footpath is the way." But while he had tricked the Great Sage into turning his head to look at the road, the old gentleman dissolved into a clear breeze and was silently gone. Only beside the road he had left a slip of paper, on which were four lines of verse:

> A message for the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, attend:
> the old man is none but Li Changgeng.
> On Mount Sumeru is the Flying-Dragon Staff;
> Lingji long ago received the Buddha's host.

Wukong took up the note and turned back to the path. "Brother," said Bajie, "our luck's been low these last few days — twice now in broad daylight we've seen ghosts. Who was that old fellow who changed into a wind and vanished?"

Wukong handed the note to Bajie, who read it through. "Who is this Li Changgeng?" he asked.

"It's the title of the Great White Planet of the West," said Wukong.

Bajie hastily bowed toward the sky. "Benefactor, benefactor! Had not the Planet petitioned the Jade Emperor on my behalf, old Pig's life would not know what it might have been turned into."

"Brother," said Wukong, "so you do know how to feel gratitude. But keep your head down — just hide deep in this grove and mind the luggage and the horse with care. Let old Sun seek out Mount Sumeru and invite the Bodhisattva to come."

"I understand, I understand," said Bajie. "Just you go quickly. Old Pig has learned the way of the tortoise — when it's time to pull in my head, I'll pull it in."

The Great Sage sprang into the air, riding his cloud-somersault straight to the due south. Truly he was swift: a nod of his head carried him three thousand miles, a twist of his waist above eight hundred more. In a moment he saw a high mountain, halfway up which auspicious clouds appeared and lucky vapors gathered thick. In a hollow of the mountain there was indeed a Chan monastery, and he heard the bells and chimes ringing soft and clear and saw the incense-smoke drifting faint. The Great Sage came straight to the gate, where he saw a Taoist acolyte, a string of beads about his neck, reciting the Buddha's name.

"Greetings, acolyte," said Wukong.

The acolyte bowed and returned the courtesy. "Where has the old master come from?"

"Is this the place where the Bodhisattva Lingji expounds the scriptures?" asked Wukong.

"This is the very place," said the acolyte. "What is your business?"

"I trouble you, sir," said Wukong, "to carry word for me. I am the disciple of the Imperial Younger Brother, the Tripitaka Dharma-Master under the Great Tang of the East — the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, Sun Wukong the pilgrim. I have a matter on which I wish to see the Bodhisattva."

The acolyte laughed. "Old master, your words are many and your titles many — I can't remember them all."

"Just say that Sun Wukong, the disciple of the Tang Monk, has come," said Wukong.

The acolyte did as he was told and went up to the lecture hall to announce him. The Bodhisattva at once donned his cassock, added incense, and came to welcome him. The Great Sage stepped inside the gate and, looking about him, saw:

> The whole hall hung with brocade, the chamber filled with awe.
> The assembled disciples chanted in chorus the Lotus Sutra;
> the old precentor lightly struck the gold-cast chime.
> The offerings before the Buddha were all immortal fruits and flowers;
> the dishes set upon the table were all fasting-fare and meatless.
> Brilliant the precious candles — each golden flame shot rainbow light;
> rich the true incense — each thread of jade smoke flew in colored mist.
> This was the moment when, the lecture done and the mind at ease, he entered samadhi,
> while flake on flake of white cloud curled about the pine-tops.
> Stilled, he sheathed the sword of wisdom and the demon-heads were ended;
> high was his mastery of the prajna-paramita's grace.

The Bodhisattva straightened his robes and came out to greet him. Wukong mounted the hall, took the guest's seat, and tea was duly ordered. "Spare yourself the tea," said Wukong. "It is only that my master is in distress on the Mountain of Yellow Wind. I have come especially to beg the Bodhisattva to exert his great power, subdue the demon, and rescue him."

The Bodhisattva said: "I received the Tathagata's command and am stationed here to keep down the Yellow Wind demon. The Tathagata bestowed on me a Wind-Quelling Pellet and a Flying-Dragon Treasure-Staff. In those days I caught the creature, but spared his life and let him go to hide his nature and return to the mountain, on condition that he take no life and work no further sin. I did not know that today he meant to harm your master, in defiance of that command — the fault is mine." The Bodhisattva would have kept Wukong to share a vegetarian meal and talk, but Wukong earnestly declined. So the Bodhisattva took up the Flying-Dragon Staff, and together with the Great Sage rode off upon the clouds.

Before long they reached the Mountain of Yellow Wind. The Bodhisattva said: "Great Sage, this demon stands somewhat in fear of me. I'll stay fixed up here in the clouds; you go down and challenge him to battle, lure him out, and I'll work my power upon him." Wukong agreed, lowered his cloud, and without a word of warning swung his iron staff and smashed in the cave gate, shouting: "Monster! Give me back my master!"

In a fright the gate-keeping demons hurried to report. "This vile ape is utterly without manners," said the monster. "He still won't yield to kindness — now he comes and smashes my gate. This time I'll go out, loose my divine wind, and blow him dead for certain." Once more he put on his armor, grasped his steel fork, and came striding out the gate. Seeing Wukong, he wasted no words but twirled the fork and stabbed at his chest; the Great Sage dodged aside and, raising his staff, struck back face to face. Before they had fought many rounds the monster jerked his head about toward the southeast quarter, and just as he opened his mouth to call up the wind, down from the high air the Bodhisattva Lingji flung his Flying-Dragon Treasure-Staff. With some spell or other — none knew what he chanted — it became an eight-clawed golden dragon, which whirled open two of its claws with a snap, seized the monster, lifted him by the head, and dashed him two or three times against the rocky cliff at the mountain's edge. There he showed his true shape — a yellow-furred sable rat.

Wukong rushed up and raised his staff to strike, but the Bodhisattva stayed his hand. "Great Sage, don't take his life. I still must bring him before the Tathagata." Then he said to Wukong: "This creature was a rat that had attained the Way at the foot of the Spirit Mountain. Because he stole the pure oil from a glazed lamp-cup and so dimmed the lamp's flame, and feared the Vajra-guardians would seize him, he fled and came here to set himself up as a demon and work his mischief. The Tathagata, seeing all, judged that he did not merit death, and so charged me to keep him in custody. But since he has taken life and worked sin, I shall carry him up to the Spirit Mountain; and now that he has affronted the Great Sage and brought calamity on the Tang Monk besides, I'll take him before the Tathagata, where his crimes may be plainly judged — only then will this be reckoned a true merit."

Hearing this, Wukong thanked the Bodhisattva, and the Bodhisattva returned to the west — but of that no more.

Now Zhu Bajie, waiting in the woods and pondering over Wukong, heard a shout from below the mountain: "Brother Wuneng, bring the horse and the luggage up!" The idiot knew it for Wukong's voice, hastily gathered things up, and ran out of the woods. Seeing Wukong, he said: "Brother, how did the business go?"

"I invited the Bodhisattva Lingji," said Wukong, "and with a Flying-Dragon Staff he took the demon. The thing turned out to be a yellow-furred sable rat run to spirit, and the Bodhisattva has carried him off to the Spirit Mountain to see the Tathagata. Now you and I will go into the cave and rescue our master."

The idiot grew merry and glad. The two of them charged inside and, with rake and iron staff, beat to death the whole den of cunning hares, demon-foxes, fragrant river-deer, and antlered stags. Then they went to the rear garden and bowed to free their master. The master came out the gate and asked: "How did you two manage to take the demon? And how did you come to rescue me?" Wukong recounted from beginning to end the matter of inviting Lingji to subdue the demon, and the master's thanks were without end. The brothers prepared a little tea and rice from the vegetarian stores in the cave, ate their fill, and only then went out the gate and took the main road westward.

What befell them hereafter is not yet known — listen to the telling in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 22 -->
# Chapter 22: The Sands That Swallow Men — Pig of the Eight Precepts Battles the Flowing-Sand River, and Moksha by Holy Command Wins Over Wujing

We left the Tang Monk and his two disciples having escaped their last peril and pressing on westward. In less than a day they passed beyond the Yellow Wind Ridge, and beyond it the land opened into a broad, level plain. Time flew swiftly: summer gave way to autumn, and they saw the chill cicadas droning among the withered willows, while the great red star of summer slid down toward the west.

As they journeyed on, suddenly before them lay a vast expanse of water — a wild, raging flood, its turbid swells heaving and its waves churning. From his saddle Tripitaka cried out in alarm, "Disciples, look at that — the water ahead is so wide, and not a single boat in sight. How are we to cross?"

Pig looked and said, "It's a raging torrent, sure enough. No boat to ferry us over."

Then the Pilgrim, Sun Wukong, leapt up into the air, shaded his eyes with his hand, and gazed across — and even his heart sank. "Master," he said, "this is truly difficult, truly difficult! If it were only old Monkey crossing, I'd give my waist a single twist and be over in a flash. But for you, Master, it is a thousandfold hard to ferry, a ten-thousand-year hard to traverse."

"From here I can see no end to it," said Tripitaka. "How wide do you make it?"

"Some eight hundred li across, near as I can tell," the Pilgrim replied.

"Brother, how can you fix the distance so exactly?" asked Pig.

"I won't deceive you, worthy brother," said Wukong. "These two eyes of mine can make out the fortune and disaster on a road a thousand li off in broad daylight. Just now from up in the air I could not see how far this river runs upstream or down — but across, it's a full eight hundred li."

The Elder sat sighing in his distress, and turned his horse about. Just then he spied a stone tablet standing on the bank. The three of them came up together to read it, and found three seal-script characters carved at the top: **Flowing-Sand River**. Below, in small, neat script, ran four lines:

> Eight hundred li of flowing sand,
> three thousand fathoms of weakling water deep.
> A goose-feather will not float upon it,
> a reed-blossom sinks straight to the bed.

While master and disciples were still studying the inscription, they heard the waves surge up like mountains and the billows pile high like ridges, and from the very middle of the river a monster came slithering forth — hideous and ferocious beyond measure:

> A shock of flaming red hair, wild and unbound;
> two round eyes, gleaming bright as lanterns.
> A face neither black nor green, but indigo-blue;
> a voice like thunder, like a drum, like an old dragon's roar.
> Over his shoulders a cape of goose-down yellow;
> at his waist a doubled cord of pale white rattan.
> Nine skulls dangling from a string about his neck,
> and in his hand a fearsome treasure-staff.

The fiend came whirling up the bank in a gust of wind and lunged straight for the Tang Monk. In a panic the Pilgrim flung his arms around his master, scrambled up the high bank, and bore him away to safety. Pig set down his load, whipped out his nine-toothed muckrake, and swung it at the monster, who parried with his treasure-staff. The two of them, there on the bank of the Flowing-Sand River, each gave full play to his valor. It was a splendid fight:

> The nine-toothed rake, the demon-quelling staff —
> two warriors locked in battle on the river's shore.
> This one, once Marshal of the Heavenly Reeds;
> that one, the Curtain-Lifting Captain cast from grace.
> In years gone by they'd met in the Hall of Divine Mist;
> today they strive to prove which is the stronger.
> This rake darts in like a dragon clawing for its prey;
> that staff blocks like a tusked elephant grinding its teeth.
> Both stretch out wide in their four-square stance,
> then bore in close against the driving wind.
> This one claws blind for face and skull;
> that one strikes without a wasted blow or empty pause.
> One is the man-eating spirit who has long held the Flowing-Sand realm;
> the other is the warrior who keeps the faith and treads the path.

Back and forth they went, and after some twenty rounds neither had the advantage.

Now the Great Sage, guarding the Tang Monk and holding the horse, watching over the baggage, saw Pig trading blows with the fiend and ground his teeth with longing — rubbing his palms, cracking his knuckles, unable to hold himself back. Out came his iron cudgel. "Master, you sit here and don't be afraid," he said. "Let old Monkey go have a little sport with him." The Elder begged him in vain to stay. With a whistle he sprang to the front.

The monster and Pig were just at the thick of it, locked too tight to part, when the Pilgrim swung up his iron rod and brought it down straight at the fiend's head. The fiend twisted aside in a flash, dodged in a fright, and dived headlong back into the Flowing-Sand River.

Pig was beside himself, hopping with rage. "Brother! Who asked you to come? That monster's strokes were slowing — he could barely hold off my rake. Three or five more rounds and I'd have had him! He saw how fierce you looked, turned tail, and bolted. Now what?"

The Pilgrim laughed. "Brother, I won't lie to you. Ever since we subdued the Yellow Wind fiend and came down off the mountain, it's been a whole month since I had a chance to swing my cudgel. When I saw how sweetly you two were going at it, I just couldn't stand the itch in my feet, so I jumped in for a bit of fun. How was I to know the monster has no taste for sport, and bolted?"

Arm in arm, talking and laughing, the two went back and found the Tang Monk. "Did you catch the monster?" he asked.

"He couldn't stand up to the fight," said Wukong. "He broke off and burrowed back into the water."

"Disciple," said Tripitaka, "this fiend has lived here a long while — he must know the shallows and the deeps. With weakling water as boundless as this and no boat at all, we shall need someone who knows the water's ways to guide us across."

"Just so," said the Pilgrim. "As the saying goes, 'Who keeps near vermilion turns red; who keeps near ink turns black.' Living here, the creature surely knows the water. Let's capture him — but not kill him. We'll only make him ferry the Master across, and then settle the rest."

"Brother, no need to dither," said Pig. "You go take him first, and let old Hog watch over the Master."

The Pilgrim laughed. "Worthy brother, this is one job I dare not boast about. Doings underwater are not much in old Monkey's line. If I simply walk down, I have to make the hand-sign and chant the water-repelling spell before I can move at all; otherwise I must change myself into some fish, shrimp, crab, or turtle to go in. When it comes to contests of skill — up in the highest mountains, among the clouds, whatever strange and crooked business there is — old Monkey can do it all; it's just the trade underwater that's a bit awkward for me."

"In my day old Hog commanded the Heavenly River," said Pig, "and had eighty thousand water-troops under my hand, so I did learn something of the water's ways. But I'm afraid that down there the creature may have kinfolk, old and young — seven nests and eight generations of them all coming at once. Then I'd be no match for them, and like as not they'd drag me off."

"If you go down to fight him in the water," said the Pilgrim, "don't get drawn into a real battle. Lose on purpose, never win — lure him out, and old Monkey will be ready to lend a hand."

"Right you are. I'm off," said Pig. And with that he stripped off his green brocade robe, took off his shoes, gripped his rake in both hands, parted the waters, and using the old arts of his former days, leapt through the waves and plunged in, going straight down to the river's bed and pressing forward.

Now the fiend, having lost the fight and just got his breath back, heard someone pushing the water aside with a splashing din. He started up to look, and there was Pig with his rake, shoving through the current. The monster raised his staff and shouted in his face, "Where do you think you're going, monk? Watch out for this!" Pig blocked with his rake. "What sort of fiend are you, daring to bar the road here?"

"So you don't know me," said the monster. "I'm no common goblin or ghost, and I'm not some nameless nobody."

"If you're no goblin or ghost," said Pig, "then why are you here killing the living? Tell me your true name, plainly, and I'll spare your life."

"Listen, then," said the fiend. "I:

> From my youth my spirit and force were strong;
> across ten thousand li of heaven and earth I roamed.
> A hero who showed his power throughout the world,
> a champion held up as a model in men's homes.
> Through all the lands and the Nine Provinces I went as I pleased,
> across the Five Lakes and Four Seas I barged at will.
> All because I sought the Way I wandered to the sky's edge,
> only to find a master I traveled the broad earth.
> Year upon year my robe and bowl I kept close by me;
> day upon day my heart and mind I would not let stray.
> Over the land I drifted, cloud-borne, dozens of times,
> and idly walked to every place a hundred trips and more.
> So at last I met a True Immortal,
> who opened wide for me the great Way's golden radiance.
> First I gathered in the Infant and the Lovely Maid;
> then I set free the Wood Mother and the Metal Lord.
> The kidney-water of the Bright Hall I drew into the Flower Pool;
> the liver-fire of the storied tower I cast into the heart.
> When the three thousand merits were full, I bowed before Heaven's face,
> and with whole heart paid court, turned toward the bright and splendid.
> The Jade Emperor himself raised me in rank,
> and with his own lips named me Curtain-Lifting Captain.
> Within the Southern Heaven Gate I was held in honor;
> before the Hall of Divine Mist I was called a chief.
> At my waist hung the tiger-head tablet of command;
> in my hand I held this demon-quelling staff.
> Atop my head a golden helmet blazed like the sun;
> upon my body armor bright as rosy dawn.
> Coming and going, I led the imperial escort;
> at every audience I stood in the highest place.
> But because the Queen Mother brought down her peaches of immortality
> and spread a feast at the Jasper Pool, inviting all the captains,
> I let a crystal goblet slip and shatter,
> and every god in heaven was struck with terror.
> The Jade Emperor flew into a rage,
> and ordered the Minister of the Left at court:
> they stripped my cap, my armor, and my title,
> and thrust my body onto the execution ground.
> I owe my life to the Barefoot Great Immortal,
> who stepped from the ranks and pleaded that I be spared.
> Reprieved from death, brought back to life with no sentence carried out,
> I was banished to the eastern shore of the Flowing-Sand.
> When full, I lie sleeping in this hill;
> when hungry, I churn the waves to hunt for food.
> The woodcutter who meets me does not live;
> the fisherman who sees me loses his life.
> Back and forth I have eaten many men,
> over and over I have wrought a pestilence of slaughter.
> You dare bring your violence to my very door —
> today my belly has its hopes!
> Don't say you're too coarse and tough to eat;
> once I've caught you, I'll take my time and chop you into mince!"

When Pig heard this he flew into a fury and cursed him. "You filthy thing! You've not got a scrap of an eye in your head. Old Hog here can still pinch the froth of refinement from his own skin — and you dare call me coarse, and talk of chopping me into mince? It seems you've taken me for some worn-out old hide! No more of your insolence — taste your grandfather's rake!"

Seeing the rake come on, the fiend dodged with a move called "the phoenix nods its head." The two of them fought up from the water's bed to the surface, each treading the billows and riding the waves. This bout was unlike the last. Just look:

> The Curtain-Lifting Captain, the Marshal of the Heavenly Reeds —
> each displays his powers, a wonder to behold.
> That one swings the demon-quelling treasure-staff straight at the head;
> this one's nine-toothed rake follows quick as the hand can move.
> They leap the waves and shake the mountains and streams,
> they shove the billows till the whole world darkens.
> Fierce as the year-god ramming the banners and streamers,
> savage as the Death-Gate spirit ripping off the precious canopy.
> This one, heart loyal and stern, guards the Tang Monk;
> that one, steeped in crime, plays the water-fiend.
> The rake claws once and leaves nine furrowed wounds;
> the staff strikes home and routs the very soul.
> They strain in joyful contest, locked together,
> bending all their wits to win the wager.
> Reckon it up — it's all for the scripture-seeker's sake,
> their wrath pierces heaven, past all enduring.
> They stir the perch and carp and mandarin-fish to shed their fresh scales,
> bruise the soft shells of turtle, terrapin, and great soft-shelled tortoise;
> red shrimp and purple crabs all lose their lives,
> and all the spirits of the water-palace bow toward the sky.
> You hear only the waves churn and the billows roll like thunder-crash,
> sun and moon gone lightless, heaven and earth aghast.

The two fought for two full watches without a winner. This was truly a case of a copper basin meeting an iron broom, a jade chime answered by a golden bell.

Now the Great Sage, guarding the Tang Monk and standing close by, watched with anxious, longing eyes as the two struggled upon the water — but it was no place for him to lend a hand. Then he saw Pig feint with his rake, pretend defeat, and turn back toward the eastern bank. The fiend came after him, drawing near the shore. The Pilgrim could bear it no longer: he left his master, snatched up his iron rod, sprang to the river's edge, and struck straight down at the fiend's head. The creature dared not face him, and with a *whoosh* dived back into the river.

Pig bawled, "You Bimawen, you Stable-Boy-of-Heaven — you're nothing but a hot-headed, hasty monkey! If you'd just held off a little longer, I'd have coaxed him up onto high ground, and you could have blocked the river's edge so he couldn't turn back — and then we'd have had him! Now that he's gone in, when will he ever come out again?"

The Pilgrim laughed. "Idiot, stop your bellowing, stop your bellowing. Let's go back and see the Master."

So Pig went with the Pilgrim up onto the high bank and faced Tripitaka. The Elder bent forward. "You've had a hard time of it, disciple."

"Never mind the hardship," said Pig. "Only when we've subdued the fiend and got you across the river will the plan be wholly sound."

"How did your fight with the monster go?" asked Tripitaka.

"That fiend's skill is a fair match for old Hog's," said Pig. "We were right in the thick of it when I used a feigned defeat, and he chased me up to the bank. The moment he saw Elder Brother lift his cudgel, he ran."

"In that case, what are we to do?" said Tripitaka.

"Set your heart at ease, Master, and don't fret," said the Pilgrim. "It's late now. Sit here on the cliff-bank, and let old Monkey go beg some food. You'll eat and sleep, and tomorrow we'll see to it."

"Well said," replied Pig. "Be quick there and back."

The Pilgrim leapt up on his cloud, went straight to a household away to the north, begged a bowl of plain vegetarian food, and brought it back to offer his master. Seeing how quickly he had returned, the Master said, "Wukong, at this house where you begged the meal, why not ask them for some plan to cross the river? Wouldn't that be better than struggling with this fiend?"

The Pilgrim laughed. "That household is dreadfully far — five or seven thousand li off. What would they know of the water here? What good would it do to ask them?"

"Brother, you're spinning lies again," said Pig. "Five or seven thousand li — how could you go and come back so fast?"

"What do you know of it?" said Wukong. "Old Monkey's cloud-somersault carries me a hundred and eight thousand li at a single bound. A trip of five or seven thousand is no more than two nods of the head and one bow of the waist — there and back, where's the difficulty?"

"Brother," said Pig, "if it's that easy, then just carry the Master on your back, give two nods and a bow of the waist, and hop us across! Why bother fighting this fiend so bitterly?"

"Can't you ride a cloud yourself?" said the Pilgrim. "Why don't *you* carry the Master over?"

"The Master's mortal flesh and common bones are heavier than Mount Tai," said Pig. "How could a cloud-rider like me bear him up? It would take your somersault to manage it."

"My somersault is a cloud-riding too," said Wukong, "differing only in how far it goes. If you can't carry him, how could I? As the old saying has it, 'To shift Mount Tai is light as a mustard-seed, but to carry a mortal man past the red dust is hard.' These vile fiends and venomous monsters may use snatching-spells and conjure the wind, but it's all tugging and dragging, traveling along the ground — they cannot bear a man up into the empty air. That sort of trick old Monkey can also work. There are the spells of invisibility and of shrinking the road, every one of which old Monkey knows. But the Master must wear out the whole journey through these strange lands; he cannot leap clear of the sea of suffering — and so he must go inch by hard-won inch. You and I can only escort him, keep his body whole and his life safe; we cannot take these hardships off him, nor can we fetch the scriptures for him. Even if we went on ahead and saw the Buddha first, the Buddha would not be willing to hand the scriptures over to you or me. It is just as they say: 'What is got too easily is held too lightly.'"

Hearing this, the Idiot bowed his assent and took the words to heart. They ate a little of the plain, meatless food, and master and disciples rested at the foot of the eastern cliff of the Flowing-Sand River.

Early next morning Tripitaka said, "Wukong, how shall we manage today?"

"There's no managing it," said the Pilgrim, "except that Pig must go down into the water again."

"Brother," said Pig, "you only want to keep yourself clean and make old Hog do the diving."

"Worthy brother, this time I won't be so hasty," said the Pilgrim. "You just lure him up, and I'll block the riverbank and keep him from getting back. We must take him for certain."

Good Pig! He wiped his face, braced his spirit, gripped his rake in both hands, went to the riverbank, parted the waters, and once more went down to the lair.

The fiend had only just woken from sleep when he heard the splashing of the water pushed aside. He whipped his head around, opened his eyes wide, and saw Pig coming with his rake. Out he sprang, barred the way head-on, and bellowed, "Easy there, easy there — watch out for this staff!" Pig raised his rake to block. "What kind of mourner's staff is that," he jeered, "that you'd have your grandfather watch out for it?"

"You wretch, you know nothing," said the fiend. "This:

> This treasure-staff has a name of high renown,
> sprung from the sala-tree that grows within the moon.
> Wu Gang cut down a single branch of it;
> Lu Ban wrought it with the craftsman's perfect skill.
> Within runs a single core of gold;
> without, ten thousand strands of pearl-set jade.
> Its name, the Treasure-Staff, is good for quelling demons,
> forever keeping the Hall of Divine Mist, able to subdue all fiends.
> Because I was made a Great General,
> the Jade Emperor bestowed it for me to carry at my side.
> Long or short, it follows my heart's wish;
> thick or thin, it bends to my whim.
> It once guarded the throne at the peach-feast;
> it once attended court in the upper realm.
> On duty in the hall, the assembled saints beheld it;
> lifting the curtain, the immortals all bowed before it.
> A spirit-weapon, nurtured to numinous nature —
> no common tool of the mortal world.
> Since I was banished out the heaven gate,
> it roams the seas with me as I please.
> I'll not be so bold as to boast too far —
> but no spear or blade on earth can match it.
> As for that rusty nailed rake of yours,
> it's good for nothing but hoeing fields and digging vegetable beds!"

Pig laughed. "You under-thrashed, filthy thing! Never mind your vegetable-beds — I'm only afraid that one swipe of mine will leave you no place to stick a plaster, with all nine of your eye-holes streaming blood at once. And even if it doesn't kill you, it'll be a lifelong case of lockjaw!" The fiend threw open his guard, and there beneath the water he and Pig fought their way up to the surface again. This bout was truly different from the last. Just look:

> The treasure-staff swings, the nailed rake drives;
> their words don't agree, for they are not of one house.
> All because the Wood Mother bears down on the Blade-and-Sword,
> the two are set against each other in the fray.
> No winner, no loser, no give and take —
> churning waves and tossing billows, never at peace.
> How can this one's wrath be contained;
> how can that one bear the shame of his hurt?
> Rake comes, staff blocks — each plays the hero;
> the water boils, the flowing sand can do its venom.
> Spirits high, toil unceasing,
> all because Tripitaka journeys to the Western Realm.
> The nailed rake is mighty fierce;
> the treasure-staff is thoroughly practiced.
> This one grabs to drag the other up the bank;
> that one claws to souse the other in the water.
> The din is like a thunderclap that stirs the fish and dragons,
> clouds darken, the sky dims, gods and ghosts cower.

Back and forth this time, they fought thirty rounds with neither showing the stronger. Then Pig again worked his feigning-defeat trick, trailed his rake, and ran. The fiend came chasing after, riding the billows and seizing the waves, right up to the cliff's edge. Pig cursed him: "You filthy fiend! Come up here onto the high ground where there's solid earth underfoot — it'll be good fighting!" But the fiend cursed back: "You wretch, you're luring me up so your helper can come at me again! You come down — we'll fight it out in the water, as before." For the fiend had grown wary, and would by no means come up onto the bank; he only made his uproar at the river's edge against Pig.

Now the Pilgrim, seeing he would not come up, grew so hot and frantic with vexation that he longed to snatch him in one grasp. "Master," he said, "you sit here, and let me serve him a 'hungry hawk pouncing on its food.'" With that he leapt up in a somersault, sprang into mid-air, and came swooping down to seize the fiend. But the fiend, just then wrangling with Pig, suddenly heard the wind whistle, jerked his head around, saw the Pilgrim dropping from the clouds, drew in his staff, and with one plunge dived into the water — vanished without a trace.

The Pilgrim stood on the bank and said to Pig, "Brother, this fiend has grown slippery indeed. He won't come up on the bank any more — what's to be done?"

"Hard, hard, hard," said Pig. "I can't beat him. I've used up the very strength I sucked at my mother's breast, and I can only just hold him to a draw."

"Let's go see the Master," said the Pilgrim.

The two of them climbed again to the high bank and faced the Tang Monk, telling him in full how hard the fiend was to take. The Elder, his eyes brimming with tears, said, "With such difficulties as these, how are we ever to cross?"

"Master, don't grieve," said the Pilgrim. "This fiend lurks deep in the water, and truly it is hard going. Pig, you just stay here and guard the Master, and fight him no more. Let old Monkey go make a trip to the Southern Sea."

"Brother, what will you do at the Southern Sea?" asked Pig.

"This scripture-seeking business," said the Pilgrim, "was the doing of the Bodhisattva Guanyin from the start; and it was Guanyin too who delivered each of us. Now that our road is blocked at the Flowing-Sand River and we can go no further, without her how shall we set it right? Let me go ask her — it's far better than wrangling with this fiend."

"Yes, yes," said Pig. "Elder Brother, when you go, do be sure to put in a word for me: tell her I'm grateful for all her past instruction."

"Wukong," said Tripitaka, "if you're going to ask the Bodhisattva, then don't delay — be quick there and back."

The Pilgrim at once mounted his cloud-somersault and made straight for the Southern Sea. Marvelous! In less than half a watch he sighted the bounds of Mount Potalaka. In a moment he set down his somersault, and outside the Purple Bamboo Grove the Devas of the Twenty-Four Roads came forward to greet him. "Whence comes the Great Sage?"

"My master is in trouble," said the Pilgrim, "and I've come especially to see the Bodhisattva."

"Pray be seated, and allow us to announce you," said the Devas. The Deva on duty that day went straight to the mouth of the Tide-Sound Cave and reported, "Sun Wukong is here on business, seeking an audience." The Bodhisattva, who was just then leaning on the railing by the Treasure-Lotus Pool with the pearl-bearing Dragon Maiden, admiring the flowers, heard the announcement, turned back to the cloud-cliff, opened the door, and called him in. The Great Sage, solemn and reverent, made his obeisance.

"Why are you not guarding the Tang Monk?" asked the Bodhisattva. "What brings you here to see me again?"

The Pilgrim reported, "Bodhisattva, at the Gao Family Village my master took on another disciple, called Zhu Bajie, Pig of the Eight Precepts — to whom you graciously gave the religious name Wuneng. We have just crossed the Yellow Wind Ridge and have now come to the eight-hundred-li Flowing-Sand River, the three thousand fathoms of weakling water, which my master cannot hope to cross. And in the river there is a fiend of high martial skill. Thanks to Wuneng he has been fought three times upon the water, but we cannot prevail; the fiend bars our way, and we cannot cross. So I have come especially to tell you, Bodhisattva, in hope that you will take pity and grant us a means to get across."

"You monkey," said the Bodhisattva, "puffed up with your own self-satisfaction again — wouldn't you let on that you were the one escorting the Tang Monk?"

"We only meant to capture him and make him ferry my master over," said the Pilgrim. "Underwater work I can't manage finely. It was Wuneng who sought out his lair and spoke with him — and I suppose he never let out anything about the scripture-seeking."

"That fiend in the Flowing-Sand River," said the Bodhisattva, "is the Curtain-Lifting Great Captain come down to the mortal world — also one of the faithful whom I converted, charged to protect the scripture-seekers. Had you only let it be known that you are scripture-seekers from the Land of the East, he would surely never have fought you, but would certainly have submitted."

"The fiend now shrinks from battle and won't come up on the bank," said the Pilgrim. "He only lurks hidden in the water. How is he to be made to submit? And how is my master to cross the weakling water?"

The Bodhisattva at once called Huian, drew a little red gourd from her sleeve, and instructed him: "Take this gourd, go with Sun Wukong to the surface of the Flowing-Sand River, and simply call out 'Wujing' — and he will come forth. First lead him to take refuge with the Tang Monk. Then string those nine skulls of his together, arrange them according to the pattern of the Nine Palaces, and set this gourd in the middle. That will be a single dharma-vessel, able to ferry the Tang Monk across the bounds of the Flowing-Sand River."

Huian heard, respectfully obeyed his teacher's command, and with the Great Sage bore the gourd out of the Tide-Sound Cave; having received the holy order, they took their leave of the Purple Bamboo Grove. There is a poem to attest it:

> The Five Phases matched and joined return to heavenly truth;
> the old master of former days is recognized again.
> Refine the self, lay the foundation for the marvelous work;
> distinguish clearly the false and true, and see the root cause.
> Metal comes home to its nature, returning to its kind;
> Wood departs seeking feeling, and both sink back together.
> When the Two Earths' full merit is complete, all is stillness —
> water and fire harmonized, without a speck of dust.

In no long while the two of them brought down their clouds and came to the bank of the Flowing-Sand River. Pig recognized the Pilgrim Moksha at once, and led his master forward to welcome him. Moksha exchanged courtesies with Tripitaka, and then greeted Pig. "Honored One," said Pig, "thanks to your former guidance I came to see the Bodhisattva, and old Hog has indeed followed the holy teaching — and now, to my joy, has entered the gate of the faith. All this while I've been so taken up with the toils of the road that I never managed to thank you. Forgive me, forgive me."

"Let's not stand on long talk," said the Pilgrim. "Let's go call that fellow out."

"Call whom?" asked Tripitaka.

"I saw the Bodhisattva," said Wukong, "and set the whole matter before her. She says the fiend of the Flowing-Sand River is the Curtain-Lifting Great Captain come down to the mortal world. For a crime committed in Heaven he fell into this river and forgot his true form, turning into a fiend. He too was once converted by the Bodhisattva, and vowed to follow the Master to the Western Heaven. But because we never said anything about the scripture-seeking, he kept up the bitter struggle. Now the Bodhisattva has sent Moksha with this gourd to make the fellow into a dharma-vessel and ferry you across."

Hearing this, Tripitaka bowed in endless reverence, and made obeisance to Moksha, saying, "I beg the Honored One to proceed without delay."

Moksha, holding the gourd firm, rode half on cloud and half on mist straight to the surface of the Flowing-Sand River and cried in a ringing voice, "Wujing! Wujing! The scripture-seeker has been here a long while — why have you still not submitted?"

Now the fiend, in dread of the Monkey King, had gone back to the riverbed and was resting in his lair when he heard his religious name called. He knew at once it must be the Bodhisattva Guanyin; and hearing the words "the scripture-seeker is here," he no longer feared the axe and battle-axe, but quickly churned up through the waves and thrust out his head — and recognized the Pilgrim Moksha. See how, all smiles, he came forward and bowed. "Honored One, forgive me for failing to welcome you! Where is the Bodhisattva now?"

"My teacher has not come," said Moksha, "but sent me ahead to tell you to follow the Tang Monk at once as his disciple. You are to take the skulls hung about your neck, and with this gourd, arrange them by the pattern of the Nine Palaces into a dharma-vessel, and ferry him across this weakling water."

"Where is the scripture-seeker?" asked Wujing.

Moksha pointed. "Isn't that he, sitting there on the eastern bank?"

Wujing looked and saw Pig. "That one — I don't know where the filthy thing came from. He's fought me two whole days, and never once spoke a single word about scripture-seeking!" Then he saw the Pilgrim and said, "And that master there is his helper — a mighty dangerous one. I'll not go."

"That is Zhu Bajie, and this is Sun the Pilgrim," said Moksha. "Both are disciples of the Tang Monk, both converted by the Bodhisattva. Why fear them? Come, I'll take you to see the Tang Monk."

Only then did Wujing put away his treasure-staff, straighten his robe of yellow brocade, leap onto the bank, and kneel on both knees before the Tang Monk. "Master, your disciple has eyes but no pupils — I failed to know your honored face, and gave you much offense. I beg you, forgive me."

"You sack of pus," said Pig, "why didn't you submit at the start, instead of insisting on fighting me? What have you to say for yourself?"

The Pilgrim laughed. "Brother, don't blame him. It's only that we never spoke out about the scripture-seeking or our names."

"Are you truly willing, with a sincere heart, to take refuge in our faith?" asked the Elder.

"Your disciple was long ago instructed by the Bodhisattva," said Wujing. "She took the sand for my surname and gave me a religious name — Sha Wujing. How could I not follow you, Master?"

"In that case," said Tripitaka, and called, "Wukong, fetch the precept-knife and shave his head." The Great Sage did as he was told and shaved him at once. Then Wujing made his bows to Tripitaka, to the Pilgrim, and to Pig, and they settled their ranks of seniority. Seeing that he carried himself with all the bearing of a true monk, Tripitaka named him also Sha the Monk — Friar Sand.

"Since he has taken up the holy charge," said Moksha, "there's no need for more fuss. Make the dharma-vessel quickly and be off."

Wujing dared not delay. He took the skulls from about his neck, strung them with a cord into the pattern of the Nine Palaces, set the Bodhisattva's gourd in the center, and invited the Master down to the bank. The Elder stepped onto the dharma-vessel and sat upon it, and truly it was as steady as a light skiff. On the left Pig supported him, on the right Wujing held him up; Sun the Pilgrim came behind, leading the dragon-horse, following half on cloud and half on mist; and high overhead Moksha kept watch over them. So the Master floated calmly and steadily across the bounds of the Flowing-Sand River — the waves stilled, the wind laid, he passed over the weakling water. Truly it was swift as a flying arrow, and in no long while he set foot on the farther shore, escaped from the mighty flood — not so much as a smear of mud or trail of water on him, but, to his joy, with dry feet and dry hands, clean and serene in perfect repose. Master and disciples set their feet on solid ground.

Then Moksha brought down his auspicious cloud and gathered up the gourd. And lo — in that instant the skulls dissolved into nine streams of dark wind and, silent and still, vanished from sight. Tripitaka gave thanks to Moksha and made obeisance toward the Bodhisattva. Indeed:

> Moksha went straight back to the Eastern Ocean Sea;
> Tripitaka mounted his horse and turned again toward the west.

In the end there is no telling when at last they would win the true fruit and obtain the scriptures — so listen to the next chapter told.

<!-- chapter 23 -->
# Chapter 23: The Four Saints Test a Pilgrim's Heart

Bearing the Law, they journey west — the road runs long and far;
The autumn wind sighs softly down, and frost-flowers fall like stars.
The crafty ape is chained up tight — loose not the binding cord;
The stubborn horse is reined and curbed — spare it the goading rod.
The Wood Mother and the Metal Squire were one from the beginning;
The Yellow Dame and the Crimson Child were never two apart.
Bite open the iron pellet, and the true tidings come;
Through Prajñā-pāramitā you reach the farther shore at last.

This chapter tells how the way of fetching the scriptures is never separate from the single body's labor at its own root. We left our master and his three disciples awakened to True Suchness, the locks of the dust-world flung open all at once, leaping clear of the sea of nature and the flowing sands, free now of every entanglement, striking straight onto the great western road. They crossed green mountains and blue waters, gazed upon more wild grass and idle blossoms than the eye could take in. Truly time runs swift, and again the ninth-month autumn came upon them. They saw such sights as these:

> Maple leaves redden across the hills,
> Yellow chrysanthemums endure the evening gale.
> The old cicada's droning slows and tires,
> The grieving cricket frets without an end.
> The lotus tears its fan of pale green silk;
> The citron's fragrance hangs in golden clusters.
> How pitiful — a few thin lines of geese,
> Dot upon dot, ranged far against the empty sky.

As they journeyed on, evening came before they marked it. Tripitaka said, "Disciples, the daylight is failing again — where shall we lodge for the night?"

Monkey said, "Master, your words go astray. We who have left the household life dine on the wind and sleep on the water, lie beneath the moon and bed down in the frost — wherever we are is home. Why ask where to lodge?"

Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, you can talk! You go light along the road — what do you care for another man's burdens? Ever since we crossed the Flowing-Sands River, it's been climbing peaks and crossing ridges, with this heavy load on my shoulders the whole way — it's a hard road for a poor fellow to endure. We ought to find a household: first, to beg some tea and rice; second, to restore our spirits. That would be the sensible thing."

Monkey said, "Idiot, the way you talk, it sounds like you've a complaining heart. You'd still like to lounge about as you did at the Gao Village, idle and asking no blessing — well, that won't do anymore. Now that you've taken your vows as a true monk, you must eat bitterness and bear hardship — only so are you fit to be a disciple."

Bajie said, "Elder brother, just look how heavy this baggage is." Monkey said, "Brother, ever since we had you and Sha Monk along, I've never once carried it — how should I know how heavy it is?"

Bajie said, "Brother, just reckon the count of it:

> Four leaves of yellow rattan-matting,
> Eight ropes long and short to bind it;
> Then, to guard against the gloomy rains,
> Three or four layers of felt to wrap it.
> The flat carrying-pole frets you with slipping,
> So nails are driven in at either end.
> A nine-ringed staff of copper-mounted iron,
> And the great broad rain-cape wound in woven cane.

A load like this, so much of it — it's no easy thing for old Pig to carry day after day, while you, the favored one, play disciple to the Master and make a hired laborer of me!"

Monkey laughed: "Idiot, who are you talking to?"

Bajie said, "I'm talking to you, brother."

Monkey said, "You've mistaken your man. Old Monkey looks after the Master's welfare alone; you and Sha Monk are charged with the baggage and the horse. But if you slack off the least bit, you'll first taste a stout cudgel across your ankle-bone."

Bajie said, "Brother, don't talk of beating — beating is just using force to bully a man. I know that grand, haughty nature of yours; you'll surely never carry it. But that horse the Master rides is big and tall and well-fed, and it only bears one old monk. Let it carry a few pieces too — that'd be brotherly feeling."

Monkey said, "You call him a horse, but he's no ordinary horse. He is the son of Aorun, Dragon King of the Western Sea, and was named the Third Prince Dragon-Horse. Because he set fire to the bright pearl on his hall, his father charged him with unfilial conduct, and he broke the laws of Heaven — but for the grace of the Bodhisattva Guanyin, who saved his life. He waited long for the Master at the Eagle-Grief Steep Torrent, and by good fortune the Bodhisattva herself came, stripped away his scales, plucked off his horns, took the pearl from beneath his throat, and changed him into this very horse, that he might willingly bear the Master to the Western Heaven to worship Buddha. This is all his own merit in the working — don't go pestering him."

Sha Monk, hearing this, said, "Brother, is he truly a dragon?" Monkey said, "He is a dragon."

Bajie said, "Brother, I've heard the men of old say a dragon can puff out clouds and breathe forth mists, scatter earth and fling up sand; that he has the power to grip a mountain ridge, and the magic to overturn rivers and stir the seas. How is it, then, that today he plods along so slowly?"

Monkey said, "You want him to go fast? I'll make him go fast for you to see."

Watch now, the great Sage! He gripped his gold-banded cudgel and gave it a shake, and ten thousand beams of colored cloud sprang forth. The horse, seeing the cudgel raised and fearing a blow, took fright; its four hooves flew swift as lightning, and whoosh — it bolted away. The Master, his hands too weak to rein it in, let the brute have its way; up the mountain crag it dashed, until at last it slowed to a heavy, picking stride. Only when his panting had steadied did the Master lift his head and see, far off, a clump of pine-shade with several buildings among it, lofty and imposing indeed. He saw:

> Green cypress hangs above the gate;
> The dwelling nestles near blue hills.
> A few pines softly, slowly sway;
> Some stalks of bamboo, dappled bright.
> By the hedge the wild mums glow with frost;
> Beside the bridge the secret orchids redden in the stream.
> Whitewashed walls of plastered clay,
> A round enclosure laid in brick.
> The high halls grand and richly made,
> The mansion still and clean and calm.
> No ox or sheep, no fowl or hound is seen —
> The autumn harvest done, the farm-work idle now.

The Master had just reined in to gaze unhurried at it when his disciples came up at last. Wujing said, "Master, you didn't tumble from the horse, I hope?" The Elder scolded, "That ruffian Monkey — he frightened my horse! Lucky I could still keep my seat."

Monkey said, smiling apologetically, "Master, don't scold me. It was all Zhu Bajie, who said the horse went too slow, so I made it go a little faster." And the idiot, having run hard chasing the horse, came up puffing and wheezing, muttering and grumbling under his breath: "It's done for, it's done for! With a belly stuck out and a loose waist-band, a load too heavy to hoist up — and now they set me running to and fro after a horse!"

The Elder said, "Disciple, look there to the side — there stands a manor house. We'd do well to beg a night's lodging there." Hearing this, Monkey quickly lifted his head and looked up, and indeed he saw blessed clouds gathered in the upper air, auspicious vapors brimming all about it. He knew at once it was certainly some immortal or buddha working a transformation, but he dared not betray the secret of Heaven, and only said, "Good, good, good — let's go beg a night's lodging."

The Elder hastily dismounted. He saw a gate-tower built with hanging lotus-and-elephant-trunk carvings, painted rafters and sculpted beams. Sha Monk set down his load; Bajie led up the horse and said, "This household is a family of surpassing wealth and substance." Monkey was about to go straight in, but Tripitaka said, "That won't do. You and I are men who have left the household; each of us must avoid all appearance of impropriety, so do not enter uninvited. Let us wait until someone comes out, and then ask for lodging with proper courtesy — that is the way." Bajie tethered the horse and leaned sidewise against the foot of the wall; Tripitaka sat upon a stone drum; Monkey and Sha Monk sat at the edge of the terrace-base. A long while passed and no one came out.

Monkey, being of an impatient nature, sprang up and went in through the gate to have a look. There he found a great three-bayed hall facing south, its blinds and lattices hung high. On the screen-door hung a long horizontal scroll painted with "Mountains of Long Life and Seas of Blessing"; on the gilt-lacquered pillars to either side was pasted a couplet of bright red paper, which read: "Threads of frail willow flutter — evening on the level bridge; / Flecks of snow upon fragrant plum — spring in the little court." In the very center stood an incense-table of polished black lacquer, and upon it an ancient bronze beast-shaped censer. Above were six folding chairs, and on the gable-walls of either side hung four hanging-screens of the four seasons.

Monkey was peering about in this way when suddenly he heard footsteps within the rear door, and out came a woman, neither old nor young, who asked in a soft, charming voice, "Who are you, that you dare intrude upon a widow's gate?" Flustered, the great Sage bowed and bowed, murmuring his apologies: "This humble monk comes from the Land of the East, the Great Tang, sent by imperial decree to the Western Heaven to worship Buddha and seek the scriptures. We are four travelers together. Passing through your precious district, with the daylight already failing, we have come especially to your venerable mansion, good Bodhisattva, to beg a single night's shelter."

The woman, all smiles, welcomed him: "Elder, where are the other three? Pray bring them in." Monkey called out loudly, "Master, please come in." Then Tripitaka, with Bajie and Sha Monk leading the horse and shouldering the load, came in, and saw the woman step out from the hall to receive them. Bajie, with sweet, slanting eyes, stole a look at her — and how was she arrayed? See for yourself:

> She wore a brocaded gown of official green damask,
> Over it a short jacket of pale rose;
> She bound a five-colored, goose-yellow embroidered skirt,
> Below which flashed high-soled flowered shoes.
> Her fashionable coiffure was veiled in black gauze,
> Set off by two-toned coiled-dragon tresses;
> A palace-style ivory comb gleamed vermilion and kingfisher-blue,
> And aslant were thrust two gold-ringed hairpins.
> Her cloud-dark hair was half gone gray, flying like phoenix wings;
> From her ears hung double pendants strung with precious pearls.
> Without rouge or powder she was lovely still,
> Her charm yet that of a young woman's prime.

When the woman had seen the three of them, her delight grew greater still, and with courtesy she invited them into the hall. They made their introductions one by one, and when the greetings were done, she asked them each to be seated and called for tea. From behind the screen there appeared a serving-maid with hair in a coiled knot and trailing silk-locks, bearing a tray of yellow gold and cups of white jade — the fragrant tea breathing warm vapor, the rare fruits shedding a delicate scent. With sweeping colored sleeves and slender spring-bamboo fingers she lifted the jade cups and passed the tea round in offering, bowing to each of them in turn. The tea finished, the woman ordered a vegetarian meal prepared.

Tripitaka raised his hands and asked, "Good Bodhisattva, what is your honored surname? And what is the name of this district?" The woman said, "This is the land of the Western Continent of Cattle-Gift. My maiden family is surnamed Jia, my husband's family Mo. In my youth, by misfortune, my father- and mother-in-law died early, and my husband and I kept up the ancestral estate. We have a fortune of ten thousand strings of cash and a thousand acres of good land. But as fate gave us no son, we had only three daughters. The year before last came a still greater misfortune: I lost my husband too. I have lived a widow, and this year my mourning is fulfilled. There is left only this land and household property, and no kinfolk or relations whatever — only we, a mother and her girls, to take it in hand. To marry out into another's family, I cannot bear to give up the estate. Now that you elders have descended upon us, I think — you are a master and three disciples; we are a mother and three daughters, four of us. It is my wish to keep the estate and take in husbands here, and four of you would suit exactly. I wonder whether your honored intentions would consent or no?"

When Tripitaka heard this, he feigned deafness and played dumb, closed his eyes and stilled his heart, and sat silent without a word in answer.

The woman went on: "My poor house has more than three hundred acres of paddy field, more than three hundred acres of dry field, and more than three hundred acres of hill-land orchard and fruit trees; there are over a thousand yellow water-buffalo, mules and horses in droves, pigs and sheep beyond counting; to the east, south, west, and north, our farmsteads, fortified granges, and pasture-grounds together number some sixty or seventy places; in the household there is grain and rice enough for eight or nine years of unused store, silks and gauzes enough that you could not wear them out in ten years and more, and gold and silver enough that you could not spend it in a lifetime. It is far better than 'hiding the spring behind brocade curtains' — why speak of mere 'two rows of golden hairpins'? If you master and disciples would only turn your hearts and consent to be wedded sons-in-law in our humble home, you could live at ease and enjoy splendor and glory — is that not far better than laboring westward?"

But Tripitaka only sat there as though dull and witless, silent and saying nothing.

The woman said, "I was born in the year of the Boar, on the third day of the third month, in the hour of the cock. My late husband was three years older than I; I am now forty-five. My eldest daughter is named Zhenzhen, and is this year twenty; my second is named Aiai, and is this year eighteen; my third little daughter is named Lianlian, and is this year sixteen — and none of them is yet betrothed to any household. Plain though I am myself, my girls are fortunate enough to have some measure of good looks, and in needlework and embroidery there is nothing they cannot do. Because my late husband had no son, we raised them as if they were boys, and in their childhood we even had them read some Confucian books, so they understand a little of composing verses and matching couplets. Though we dwell in a mountain manor, we are not of the coarse and vulgar sort, and I think they are well matched to you elders. If you will only open wide your hearts, grow out your hair, and become the heads of our household, you shall wear silks and dress in brocade — far better than that earthen begging-bowl and black monk's robe, those straw sandals and rain-cape of woven cloud."

Tripitaka, seated above, was for all the world like a child startled by thunder, like a toad drenched by the rain: he only sat dazed and rigid, the whites of his eyes rolling upward, fallen back in a stupor.

But Bajie, hearing of such wealth, such beauty, found his heart itching past all scratching. Seated in his chair, he was as if a needle were jabbing his backside, twisting left and twisting right, unable to bear it. He came forward and gave the Master a tug, saying, "Master, this lady is telling you something — how can you sit there pretending not to hear? You ought at least to make some answer."

The Master snapped up his head, gave a great cry of "Bah!" and barked Bajie back: "You cursed beast! We are men who have left the household — how should we let our hearts be stirred by wealth, our minds detained by beauty? What manner of religion would that be?"

The woman laughed: "Pitiful, pitiful. What good thing is there in leaving the household?" Tripitaka said, "Lady Bodhisattva, and you who stay in the household — what good thing is there in that?"

The woman said, "Elder, sit, and let me tell you the good of those who stay at home. How shall its worth be shown? There is a poem for proof. It runs:

> In spring we cut fresh gauze and don new silks;
> In summer change to light gauze and admire the green lotus;
> Autumn brings fresh-brewed wine, fragrant from glutinous rice;
> Winter comes, and in the warm chamber our faces flush with drink.
> Through the four seasons there is every kind of plenty;
> At all eight feasts, each rare delicacy in its turn.
> On the wedding-candle night, on brocade laid over silk —
> Far better than to tramp the road and bow to Amitābha."

Tripitaka said, "Lady Bodhisattva, you who stay at home enjoy splendor and receive riches; you have what to wear and what to eat, with sons and daughters gathered round — truly that is good. But you do not know that we who have left the household have a good thing of our own. How shall its worth be shown? There is a poem for proof. It runs:

> To leave the household and set the will is no common thing —
> It overturns the hall of former love and tenderness.
> No outward things give rise to idle gossip of the tongue;
> Within the body there dwells its own good yin and yang.
> Merit complete and conduct fulfilled, we attend the golden gate;
> Seeing our nature, our minds made clear, we return to our old home.
> Far better than at home to crave the taste of blood and flesh,
> And in old age sink down into a stinking sack of skin."

When the woman heard this, she flew into a great rage: "You insolent monk! Were it not that I see you have come so far from the Land of the East, I should have you driven out at once. Here am I, in true and honest heart, wishing to take you in and join you to my household's fortunes — and you turn round and wound me with your words! Even granting you have taken your vows and made your oath never to return to the lay life, surely among your followers my family might take in even one — why are you so stiff and rigid with your Law?"

Seeing her wrathful, Tripitaka could only humble himself, all bows and meekness, and called out, "Wukong, you stay here, then." Monkey said, "From a boy I never knew how to manage such matters — let Bajie stay here." Bajie said, "Brother, don't go planting a man! Let us all reckon it out together at leisure." Tripitaka said, "If you two won't, then let Wujing stay here."

Sha Monk said, "Just listen to what the Master says! This disciple, by the Bodhisattva's persuading, took the vows of conduct and waited for the Master. Since the Master took me in and granted me his teaching, I have followed the Master not yet two whole months, and have not gained even half a measure of merit — how should I dare to scheme after such wealth? I would sooner die and go to the Western Heaven; I will never do so faithless a thing." 

When the woman saw them all refusing and unwilling, she hastily turned and withdrew behind the screen, and slammed the inner door shut with a bang. Master and disciples were left out there with neither tea nor rice, and no one came out again. Bajie, fretting and burning within, grumbled and blamed the Tang Monk: "Master, you really don't know how to handle a thing — you've talked the whole matter dead.
