You ought to have left a little footing for us, just answered vaguely and humored her into giving us a meal, so we'd have one comfortable night out of it. Whether we'd say yes or no tomorrow would still be up to you and me. But now, with the door shut and no one coming out — this cold hearth and dead ashes — how are we to pass the night?"

Wujing said, "Second brother, you go and be a son-in-law in her house." Bajie said, "Brother, don't plant a man — let's reckon it out at leisure." Monkey said, "What is there to reckon? If you're willing, then we'll just have the Master and that woman join as in-laws, and you can be a son-in-law married into her house. A family so rich and full of treasure would surely furnish a dowry, lay on a fine wedding feast — and we'd all get something good out of it. You return to the lay life here — isn't that a thing good for both sides?" Bajie said, "Well, that's all very fine to say, only it'd be a case of me casting off the religious life and then returning to the lay — keeping one wife and taking another." Sha Monk said, "So second brother already has a wife?"

Monkey said, "You don't know him yet. He was originally the son-in-law of old Squire Gao of the Gao Village in the land of Ushas — until old Monkey subdued him. He too once took the Bodhisattva's vows of conduct; helpless against me, he was caught and made a monk, and so cast off his former wife and took up with the Master to journey west and bow to Buddha. He must have been long parted from her, and has begun thinking again of that old business; and now, hearing of this business, he's certainly got the same notion stirring again. Idiot, you go be the son-in-law of this household — only make a few extra bows to old Monkey, and I'll let it pass and not report you."

The idiot said, "Nonsense, nonsense! Everyone here has the same notion — why single out old Pig to be shamed alone? As the old saying goes, 'A monk is a starving ghost in the matter of lust.' Which of you doesn't want it? You all twist and simper and put on airs, and so spoil the whole good thing, till now we can't get sight of so much as tea or water, and there's no one to mind the lamp and fire. Even if we sweat out this one night — that horse must carry someone again tomorrow and tramp the road again; and if it's starved another night, it'll be fit for nothing but skinning. You sit here; let old Pig go and graze the horse a while." 

The idiot hurriedly loosed the halter and dragged the horse out. Monkey said, "Sha Monk, you keep the Master company here while old Monkey goes after him to see where he means to graze the horse." Tripitaka said, "Wukong, go and watch him if you like, but you mustn't keep on mocking him." Monkey said, "I know." The great Sage walked out of the hall, shook himself, and changed into a red dragonfly. Out the front gate he flew, and caught up with Bajie.

The idiot was leading the horse, but where there was grass he would not let it eat; clucking and chuckling, he drove the horse round to the rear door. There he saw the woman with her three daughters standing idle outside the back door, looking at the chrysanthemums for amusement. When the mother and daughters saw Bajie coming, the three girls slipped away inside. The woman stood at the door and said, "Little elder, where are you off to?"

The idiot dropped the halter, stepped up, made a bow, and said, "Mother, I've come to graze the horse." The woman said, "Your master is far too finicky. Were he to take in a son-in-law at my house, wouldn't that beat being a wandering monk and tramping the road to the west?" Bajie laughed: "They are acting on the Tang Emperor's decree, and dare not disobey their sovereign's command, so they won't do this thing. Just now in the front hall they were all planting it on me, and I — well, I'm one to manage those above and serve those below — only I'm afraid Mother thinks my snout too long and my ears too big."

The woman said, "I don't mind that at all. It's only that the house lacks a head; to take one in would do well enough — but I fear my girls may find you a bit ugly." Bajie said, "Mother, you tell your worthy daughters not to be so choosy of a husband. Think of that Tang Monk of mine — handsome enough in person, but really good for nothing. I'm ugly, ugly indeed, but I've a few lines of rhyme to my name." The woman said, "How do they go?"

Bajie said, "Here:

> Though my person is ugly,
> I'm diligent and have my uses.
> If you've a thousand acres of land,
> No need to drive an ox to plow it:
> One pass of my rake will do,
> And the seed comes up in season.
> No rain? I can pray for rain;
> No wind? I can call up wind.
> If the houses seem too low,
> I'll raise them two or three stories higher.
> An unswept floor? I'll sweep it;
> A blocked drain? I'll clear it through.
> All the household's great and small affairs —
> Kicking heaven, dredging wells — I can do them all."

The woman said, "Well, since you can manage the household work, go and talk it over once more with your master; if there's no awkwardness about it, I'll take you in." Bajie said, "No need to talk it over — he's not my father who begot me. Whether I do it or not is up to me alone." The woman said, "Very well, very well; let me speak with my girls." And watch — she slipped inside, and clapped the rear door shut with a bang.

Bajie did not graze the horse at all, but led it back round to the front. Little did he know that the great Sage Sun had heard the whole of it. Beating his wings, Monkey flew back, resumed his true form, and went first to the Tang Monk, saying, "Master, Wuneng has brought the horse back." The Elder said, "Were the horse not led, I feared it might frolic off."

Then Monkey laughed aloud and told over from the beginning all that the woman and Bajie had said. Tripitaka half believed and half doubted it. In a little while the idiot came dragging the horse up and tied it down. The Elder said, "Did you graze the horse?" Bajie said, "There wasn't any good grass — no place to graze the horse." Monkey said, "No place to graze the horse — but a place to lead the horse, eh?"

When the idiot heard these words, he knew the secret was out; and so he hung his head and craned his neck, thrust out his lips and knit his brow, and for a good while said nothing. Then there came a creak — the inner door opened, and out came two pairs of red lanterns and a hand-carried censer, fragrant clouds wreathing thick, girdle-pendants tinkling. The woman led her three daughters out, calling Zhenzhen, Aiai, and Lianlian to come bow before these scripture-seekers. The girls stood ranged in the hall and made their reverence toward the upper seats. Truly they were exquisitely fair; see them:

> Each with moth-brows arched in kingfisher-green,
> Powdered faces breathing spring.
> Bewitching, of nation-toppling beauty;
> Lithe and graceful, stirring the heart.
> Their flowered head-ornaments showed a wealth of charm;
> Their embroidered sashes fluttered, far above the dust.
> Half-smiling, their lips were cherries newly split;
> As they stepped slowly, orchid-and-musk came wafting.
> Their heads were heaped with pearls and kingfisher-jade,
> Trembling beneath countless precious hairpins;
> Their whole bodies breathed a secret fragrance,
> Sweet and delicate with fine threads of flowered gold.
> Why speak of the loveliness of the Chu maidens,
> Or the tender grace of Xi Shi?
> Truly they were the immortal maidens of the Ninth Heaven come down from above,
> The Chang'e of the moon stepping forth from the Cold Palace.

Tripitaka pressed his palms together and bowed his head; the great Sage Sun feigned to take no notice; Sha Monk turned his back away. But look at that Zhu Bajie — his eyes never turned aside, his lustful heart in disorder, his lecherous boldness running riot. He simpered out soft words, murmuring low: "We are honored, fairy maidens, by your descending. Mother, please send the sisters away now." The three girls passed back behind the screen, leaving behind a pair of gauze lanterns.

The woman said, "Will you four elders set your minds to it, and let one of you be matched with my daughter?" Wujing said, "We have talked it over: let the one surnamed Zhu be taken in as son-in-law." Bajie said, "Brother, don't plant me — let's reckon it out with everyone." Monkey said, "What is there left to reckon? You've already settled it all neatly at the back door, and 'Mother' you called her ever so many times — what reckoning is there now? The Master will be the male in-law, this dame the female in-law, old Monkey will stand as guarantor, and Sha Monk as go-between. There's no need even to consult the almanac — today is a lucky day granted by Heaven's grace. Come, bow to the Master and go in to be the son-in-law."

Bajie said, "It won't do, it won't do — how could I bring myself to such a business?" Monkey said, "Idiot, don't put on airs. You called her 'Mother' goodness knows how many times, and now you say it won't do! Hurry and consent — bring us along to drink some wedding wine; that'd be a fine thing." With one hand he gripped Bajie and with the other took hold of the woman, saying, "Mother-in-law, take your son-in-law inside." And the idiot, his feet shuffling, made as if to go that way.

The woman at once called for servant-boys: "Wipe down the tables and chairs, set out the evening meal, and entertain the three in-laws. I'll take the son-in-law to his room." Then she ordered the cook to lay on a banquet, that they might celebrate the wedding next morning. The servant-boys received their orders. The three of them ate their meal, hastily spread their bedding, and lodged for the night in the guest-seats — but of that no more.

Now we tell how Bajie followed his mother-in-law, walking on into the interior, through layer upon layer of rooms past counting, stumbling and bumping along, all the doorsills tripping his feet. The idiot said, "Mother, go a little slower — the way in here is strange to me; lead me along." The woman said, "These are all the storerooms, the treasuries, the milling-rooms, room after room; we've not even reached the kitchen yet." Bajie said, "What a great household!" Stumbling and bumping, turning corners and rounding bends, they walked another good while before reaching the inner halls.

The woman said, "Son-in-law, your senior brother said today is a lucky day granted by Heaven's grace, and so bade you be taken in. But in such haste we've had no time to fetch a diviner of the yin and yang for the bowing-to-the-hall and the bed-strewing rites. You may simply bow eight times to the upper seat." Bajie said, "Mother speaks rightly. Please take the seat of honor, and let me make a few bows — that'll do for the hall-bowing and for thanking the in-laws both, two things in one. Isn't that the tidy way?" His mother-in-law laughed, "Very well, very well — truly a thrifty, capable son-in-law! I'll sit; you bow."

Ah! Through the whole hall the silver candles blazed, and the idiot bowed toward the upper seat. His bows done, he said, "Mother, which of the sisters will you match with me?" His mother-in-law said, "There's just the trouble of it. If I match you with the eldest, I fear the second will be cross; if with the second, I fear the third will be cross; and if with the third, I fear again the eldest will be cross — and so I cannot make up my mind." Bajie said, "Mother, if they're afraid of quarreling, then give them all to me, and there'll be no noise and squabbling to upset the family order." His mother-in-law said, "What a notion! Would you have one man take all three of my daughters?" Bajie said, "Just hear how Mother talks! Which man hasn't his three wives and four concubines? Even were there a few more, your son-in-law would graciously accept them. In my younger years I learned a certain art of long campaigning — I'll warrant I can wait upon each one and keep her well pleased."

The woman said, "No, no. I have here a kerchief; put it over your head to cover your face, and try a 'Heaven-appointed marriage.' I'll have my daughters walk past in front of you; reach out your hands, and whichever one you catch hold of, that one shall be matched to you." The idiot did as she said, took the kerchief, and draped it over his head. There is a poem for proof:

> The dull fool knows not the root of things;
> The sword of lust wounds the body, and in the dark wears him away.
> From of old men trust the rites of the Duke of Zhou —
> And today the bridegroom wears the veil upon his head.

When the idiot had got the kerchief settled in place, he said, "Mother, please have the sisters come out." His mother-in-law called, "Zhenzhen, Aiai, Lianlian — all of you come try the Heaven-appointed marriage, to be matched to your son-in-law." He heard girdle-pendants ringing clear, and orchid-and-musk fragrance, as if fairy maidens were coming and going. The idiot in earnest stretched out his hands to grope for someone, lunging this way and that — to the left he caught nothing, to the right he caught nothing. Back and forth they passed, ever so many girls in motion, yet never could he lay hold of even one. Groping eastward, he embraced a pillar-post; groping westward, he pawed a plank wall. Running both ways till his head spun, he could no longer keep his feet, but only kept tumbling down. Lunging forward, he kicked the door-leaf; staggering back, he ran into the brick wall — stumbling and bumping, he fell until his snout was swollen and his head was bruised blue, and he sat down upon the ground, panting and gasping: "Mother, your daughters are far too nimble and slippery — I can't lay hold of even one! What's to be done, what's to be done?"

The woman lifted the veil from him and said, "Son-in-law, it's not that my daughters are nimble and slippery — it's that they're all giving way to one another, and none will consent to take you." Bajie said, "Mother, since they won't take me, then you take me yourself." The woman said, "What a son-in-law! No sense of high or low — you'd have even your mother-in-law too! These three daughters of mine are most clever of heart and hand; each has knotted a little brocade-bordered, pearl-sewn undershirt. If you can put one of them on, then the one who made it shall take you." Bajie said, "Good, good, good — bring all three out and let me put them on; if I can wear all three, then let all three take me." The woman went back into the room and brought out just one, handing it to Bajie. The idiot stripped off his black brocade-cloth cassock, took the shirt, and put it on his body. But before he could even fasten the belt — flop! — he pitched over and fell to the ground. For it had become several stout ropes, binding him fast and tight. The idiot was in pain past all enduring; and all those people were already nowhere to be seen.

Now we tell how Tripitaka, Monkey, and Sha Monk slept their sleep, and before they knew it the east grew white. Suddenly opening their eyes and lifting their heads to look about, where now was that grand mansion and high hall? There were no carved beams and painted rafters either — they were all sleeping in a grove of pine and cypress. In a fright the Elder hastily called for Monkey. Sha Monk said, "Brother, it's done for, it's done for — we've met with ghosts!" But the great Sage Sun, clear in his own mind, smiled faintly and said, "How do you mean?" The Elder said, "Look where we've been sleeping!" Monkey said, "It's a comfortable enough spot, here beneath the pines. Only there's no telling where that idiot is, suffering for his sins." The Elder said, "Who's suffering?" Monkey laughed: "Yesterday that mother and her daughters — there's no knowing what Bodhisattvas they were — manifested themselves here to test us. They must have departed in the dead of night; it's only poor Zhu Bajie who's left suffering for it."

When Tripitaka heard this, he pressed his palms together in reverence. Then they saw, hanging on an old cypress behind them, a slip of paper fluttering and swaying. Sha Monk hurried to fetch it and bring it to the Master to read, and it was an eight-line hymn:

> The Old Mother of Mount Li had no thought of the mundane;
> The Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea invited her down the mountain.
> Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī were guests as well —
> Transformed into fair women within the grove.
> The holy monk, being virtuous, kept himself free of the worldly;
> But Bajie, lacking meditation, had the common still in him.
> From this day on he must still his heart and mend his ways —
> For if he breeds sloth and slackness, the road ahead is hard.

The Elder, Monkey, and Sha Monk were chanting this hymn aloud when they heard, deep in the grove, a loud voice crying out: "Master! I'm bound to death — save me, save me! I'll never dare again!" Tripitaka said, "Wukong, is that one crying out Wuneng?" Sha Monk said, "It's he indeed." Monkey said, "Brother, pay him no mind — let's just go on." Tripitaka said, "Though that idiot is dull and stubborn of nature, he's an honest, simple-hearted fellow withal, and has some strength in his back; he can carry the baggage. Remember the Bodhisattva's kindness of that day, and let's rescue him to come along with us — surely he'll not dare such a thing again." So Sha Monk rolled up the bedding and put the loads in order; the great Sage Sun loosed the halter and led the horse, and guided the Tang Monk into the grove to look. Ah! This is just to say:

> In upright cultivation one must walk with care;
> Sweep away love and desire, and of itself return to truth.

In the end there is no knowing whether the idiot fared well or ill — so listen to the next chapter for the explanation.

<!-- chapter 24 -->
# Chapter 24: The Mountain of Ten Thousand Years and the Stolen Fruit of Immortality

The three of them pushed through the woods and into the trees, where they found the idiot Zhu Bajie trussed up against a trunk, crying out at the top of his voice, unable to bear his misery. Sun Wukong stepped forward, laughing.

"Well now, my fine son-in-law! It's late in the day and you still haven't risen to thank your bride — and you haven't gone to report your good fortune to the Master, either. Are you still hanging here putting on a show for the crowd? Bah! Where's your mother-in-law now? Where's your darling wife? What a splendid bridegroom you make, strung up and dangling and beaten black and blue."

When the idiot saw him coming with such mockery, he was so ashamed that he ground his teeth and swallowed his pain, not daring to cry out. Sha Monk, when he saw it, could not bear the sight. He set down the luggage, went up, untied the ropes, and brought him down. Bajie could do nothing but kowtow and bow to them, for his shame was past enduring. There is a poem to the tune of "The River Moon" that bears witness:

> Lust is the sword that wounds the body;
> covet it, and disaster surely comes.
> A pretty girl of sixteen, sweetly painted,
> is fiercer than a fiend in armor.
>
> You have but one original treasure,
> and no small profit to add to your purse.
> Guard your capital well and carefully;
> hold fast, and let no wantonness loose.

Now Bajie gathered a pinch of earth, lit incense, and bowed up at the empty sky in worship.

"Do you know who those Bodhisattvas were?" Wukong asked.

"I'd fainted clean away, my head spinning and my eyes a blur," Bajie said. "How was I to know which of them was which?"

Wukong handed him the little slip of paper. When Bajie saw it was a verse of judgment, he was more ashamed than ever.

Sha Monk laughed. "Second brother has such virtues, it seems — virtue enough to move four Bodhisattvas to come and offer themselves in marriage."

"Brother, never bring it up again," said Bajie. "I'm no fit son of man. From this day on I'll never play the fool again. Even if I work my bones to splinters, I'll keep my shoulder to the load and follow the Master to the Western Heaven, and that's all."

"If that's how you talk, then it's well said," said Tripitaka.

So Wukong led the Master back up onto the high road. They had traveled a good long while when suddenly a high mountain barred the way. Tripitaka reined in his horse and stayed his whip.

"Disciples," he said, "there's a mountain ahead. We must go carefully — there may be demons and goblins stirring up trouble, looking to harm our band."

"With the three of us before your horse," said Wukong, "what is there to fear from any demon?" And so the elder pressed on with an easy heart.

There before them rose the mountain, and a fine mountain it was:

> A high peak soaring to the limit,
> a great mass towering grandly.
> Its roots join the veins of Kunlun;
> its summit brushes the Milky Way.
> White cranes come to roost in its junipers and cypresses;
> dark apes hang at times from its vines and creepers.
> Sun lights the clearing groves —
> layer on layer, a thousand strands of red mist coil round;
> wind springs in the shadowed gorges —
> floating, ten thousand banners of bright cloud fly.
> Hidden birds chatter wildly in the green bamboo;
> brocade pheasants spar among the wildflowers.
> See the Thousand-Year Peak, the Five-Blessings Peak, the Lotus Peak,
> lofty and stern, casting their fine bright rays;
> the Ten-Thousand-Year Stone, the Tiger-Fang Stone, the Three-Heavens Stone,
> jutting and glittering, breathing forth auspicious vapor.
> Before the cliffs the grasses are lovely;
> on the ridges the plum blossoms are sweet.
> The thornbushes grow dense and dark;
> the orchids and irises are pure and pale.
> In the deep woods hawks and phoenixes gather a thousand fowl;
> in the ancient grottoes the qilin governs ten thousand beasts.
> The stream-water has feeling —
> winding and curving, it lingers and looks back;
> the ranges are unbroken —
> ridge upon ridge, they circle round of themselves.
> See too the green locust, the spotted bamboo, the blue-black pine,
> swaying for a thousand years, vying in lush splendor;
> the white plum, the red peach, the emerald willow,
> blazing through three months of spring, contending in loveliness.
> Dragons hum and tigers roar; cranes dance and apes cry.
> The river-deer step forth from the flowers;
> the blue simurgh calls to the sun.
> Truly this is an immortal mountain, a land of real blessing —
> Penglai and Langyuan themselves are no more than this.
> See too how the flowers open and fall on the hilltops,
> how the clouds go and come on the ridges and peaks.

Tripitaka, sitting his horse, rejoiced. "Disciple, ever since I started west I've passed through many a mountain and river, all of them craggy and steep and dangerous — but none so fair as this. Its quiet charm is truly out of the ordinary. If we are near the road to Thunderclap and it isn't far, then we'd best make ourselves solemn and dignified to meet the World-Honored One."

Wukong laughed. "Too early, too early! It's nowhere near."

"Elder brother," said Sha Monk, "how far is it to Thunderclap from here?"

"A hundred and eight thousand miles," said Wukong, "and of the ten stages, we haven't even finished one."

"Brother," said Bajie, "how many years' walking before we get there?"

"As for the two of you worthy brothers," said Wukong, "you might do it in ten days or so. As for my going, I could make the trip fifty times in a single day and still see daylight. But as for the Master's walking — don't even think it, don't even think it."

"Wukong," said the Tang Monk, "when do you say we'll arrive?"

"You could walk from childhood to old age," said Wukong, "and from old age back to childhood, and round again a thousand times over, and still find it hard. But if you keep your true nature clear and your will sincere, then the moment you turn your thoughts back upon yourself — that very place is the Spirit Mountain."

"Elder brother," said Sha Monk, "this may not be Thunderclap, but to look at such scenery, surely some good person dwells here."

"Well said," replied Wukong. "There's certainly no evil thing here. This must be the home of some holy monk or company of immortals. Let us stroll along slowly and enjoy ourselves." But of that, no more.

Now this mountain was called the Mountain of Ten Thousand Years. On it stood an abbey called the Five Estates Abbey, and in the abbey lived an Immortal whose Daoist title was Zhen Yuanzi — the Lord of the Origin — and whose common name was the Lord Coeval with the World. From that abbey there came a rare treasure unlike any other: born at the very dividing of primal chaos, the first parting of the murky void, before Heaven and Earth had opened — a divine root that took shape in that age. Of the four great continents under Heaven, only the Five Estates Abbey of the Western Continent of Cattle-Gift produced it. It was called the Grass-Returning Elixir, and also the Ginseng Fruit. Once in three thousand years it flowered; once in three thousand years it set fruit; and only after another three thousand years did it ripen — so that, all told, a single fruit took ten thousand years before it could be eaten. And in all those ten thousand years the tree set only thirty fruits. Each fruit was shaped exactly like a newborn child not yet three days old, with all four limbs complete and all five features in place. If a person had the right karmic fortune and merely smelled one of these fruits, he would live three hundred and sixty years; if he ate one, he would live forty-seven thousand years.

That very day the Great Immortal Zhen Yuan had received a written summons from the Celestial Worthy of the Primordial Beginning, inviting him to the Maitreya Palace in the Highest Pure Heaven to hear a discourse on "The Fruit of the Way of Primal Unity." The wandering immortals who had come forth from this Immortal's school were beyond counting, and even now he had forty-eight disciples, all of them perfected adepts who had attained the Way. On that day he took forty-six of them up to the higher realms to hear the lecture, leaving behind only the two youngest to mind the house: one called Pure Breeze and the other Bright Moon. Pure Breeze was but one thousand three hundred and twenty years old, and Bright Moon had only just turned one thousand two hundred. Zhen Yuanzi instructed the two boys:

"I must not disobey the Great Celestial Worthy's summons; I am off to the Maitreya Palace to hear the discourse. The two of you mind the house carefully. Before many days an old friend of mine will pass this way — do not slight him. You may knock down two of my ginseng fruits and give them to him to eat, as a small token of our old affection."

"Who is our master's old friend?" the two boys asked. "Tell us, if you please, so that we may receive him properly."

"He is the holy monk in the service of the Great Tang court in the Land of the East," said the Immortal. "His Daoist title is Tripitaka — a monk now journeying to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures."

The two boys laughed. "Confucius said: 'Those whose ways differ make no plans together.' We are of the Mystic Gate of Supreme Unity — what acquaintance should we have with such a monk?"

"You don't understand," said the Immortal. "That monk is the reincarnation of the Golden Cicada, the second disciple of the holy ancient one of the West, the Tathagata Buddha. Five hundred years ago I made his acquaintance at the Ullambana Assembly, where he served me tea with his own hands. As a son of the Buddha he showed me honor — and so he is my old friend."

When the two immortal boys heard this, they obeyed their master's command. As the Immortal was about to depart, he charged them once more: "My fruits are limited in number — give him only two, and waste no more."

"When the orchard was opened," said Pure Breeze, "the assembly together ate two, and there are still twenty-eight on the tree. We dare not waste any."

"Though the Tang Tripitaka is an old friend," said the Immortal, "you must guard against any mischief from his followers. Don't let them get wind of it." The two boys received their orders, and the Great Immortal, attended by his throng of disciples, soared aloft and went straight up to the celestial realm.

Now the Tang Monk and his three disciples were rambling about the mountain when, lifting their heads, they saw a cluster of pines and bamboo and several tiers of towers and halls.

"Wukong," said the Tang Monk, "look — what sort of place is that yonder?"

Wukong looked. "That place is no temple — it must be a Daoist abbey. Let's go on a bit; when we reach it we'll know the truth of it."

Before long they came to the gate and looked, and they saw:

> A pine-clad slope, cool and aloof;
> a bamboo path, pure and secluded.
> Coming and going, white cranes usher the drifting clouds;
> up and down, gibbons at times present their fruit.
> Before the gate the pool is broad, the tree-shadows long;
> the rocks have split, and moss-flowers break through.
> The palace halls are arrayed lofty as the Purple Pole;
> the towers and terraces float dim, where rosy vapors fall.
> Truly a land of blessing, a numinous region —
> Penglai's own cloud-grotto.
> Pure and empty, with little of human affairs;
> still and silent, where the heart of the Way is born.
> Blue birds ever bear the Queen Mother's letters;
> purple simurghs forever carry Lord Lao's scriptures.
> Endless the lofty wind of the Way and its Virtue;
> truly the hushed dwelling of the immortals.

Tripitaka dismounted from his saddle, and saw to the left of the mountain gate a stone tablet bearing ten great characters: "The Mountain of Ten Thousand Years, a Land of Blessing — The Five Estates Abbey, a Grotto-Heaven."

"Disciples," said the elder, "this is indeed a Daoist abbey."

"Master," said Sha Monk, "to see such bright and lovely scenery, there must be good folk living within. Let us go in and look. And should we ever return east with our task fulfilled, this too would make a fine sight to remember."

"Well said," replied Wukong. So they all went in together, and over the inner gate they saw a couplet for spring:

> "The dwelling of immortals, eternal life that does not age;
> the home of Daoists, long-lived as Heaven itself."

Wukong laughed. "These Daoists talk big to frighten people. When I, old Sun, made my great uproar in Heaven five hundred years ago, even at the very door of Lord Lao the Most High I never saw such a boast as this."

"Never mind him," said Bajie. "Go in, go in. Perhaps this Daoist has some real virtue — who can say?"

When they came within the second gate, two young boys came bustling out in a hurry to meet them. See how they were dressed:

> Bones pure and spirit fresh, with features fair,
> their hair bound up in tufted knots, the short locks tousled.
> Their Daoist robes, of themselves, wreathe the collar in mist;
> their feather garments, alone, set the sleeves afloat in wind.
> A ringed sash binds them tight in a dragon's-head knot;
> straw sandals are lightly wound with silkworm-throat down.
> Their bearing unusual, no common breed —
> these are the two immortal boys, Pure Breeze and Bright Moon.

The boys made their bows, arching their backs and bending low, and came out to welcome the travelers. "Venerable Master, forgive us for failing to greet you. Pray be seated."

The elder rejoiced, and went with the two boys up into the main hall to look about. It was a great hall of five bays facing south, all fitted with carved lattice screens, bright above and dim below. The immortal boys pushed open the screens and invited the Tang Monk into the hall. There he saw, hanging in the middle of the wall, two great characters worked in five colors: "Heaven and Earth." Beneath them was set a vermilion-lacquered, carved incense table, and on the table a golden censer and vase, with neat sticks of incense laid ready beside the censer.

Tripitaka stepped forward, took up a pinch of incense with his left hand and placed it in the censer, and bowed three times in worship. When he had finished, he turned his head and said, "Immortal boys, your Five Estates Abbey is truly a fairyland of the West. Why do you not make offerings to the Three Pure Ones, the Four Emperors, and all the ministers of the heavens — why do you tend the incense fire only to these two words, 'Heaven and Earth'?"

The boys laughed. "To tell you the truth, Venerable Master — of these two words, the one above is rightly worthy of our reverence; but the one below is not even fit to receive our incense. That one is something our master put up out of flattery."

"What flattery?" asked Tripitaka.

"The Three Pure Ones are our master's friends," said the boys; "the Four Emperors are his old acquaintances; the Nine Luminaries are his juniors; and the Year-Stars are his humble guests."

When Wukong heard this, he laughed until he doubled over.

"Brother," said Bajie, "what are you laughing at?"

"Everyone says old Sun knows how to play tricks," said Wukong. "It turns out this little Daoist boy knows how to bundle up the wind."

"Where is your master?" asked Tripitaka.

"The Celestial Worthy of the Primordial Beginning sent down a summons," said the boys, "and called him to the Maitreya Palace in the Highest Pure Heaven to hear a discourse on 'The Fruit of the Way of Primal Unity.' He is not at home."

When Wukong heard this, he could not hold back, and shouted: "You stinking little Daoist whelps! You don't even know whom you're talking to. Whose face are you playing your tricks before, putting up such a hollow front? Who in that Maitreya Palace is a heaven-immortal of the Supreme Unity, that they'd invite a pair of muddy ox-hooves like your master to go lecture about anything?"

Seeing him fly into a rage, Tripitaka feared the boys would talk back and start a quarrel that would breed trouble, so he said: "Wukong, let's have no contention. Since we've come in, we'll go out again presently, and there'd be no sense in it. As the saying goes, 'An egret won't eat egret's flesh.' Their master isn't home — why throw the place into an uproar? You go out to the gate and tend the horse; Sha Monk, keep watch over the luggage; and Bajie, untie the bundle, take out some rice, borrow their pots and stove, and cook us a meal. When we leave, we'll give them a few coppers for firewood, and that will be that. Each to his own task — and let me rest a while here, and we'll be off as soon as we've eaten." So the three of them each went off to his own duty.

Now Bright Moon and Pure Breeze privately praised the monk to no end, saying: "What a fine monk! Truly a Western lover of holiness come down to the mortal world, his true source undimmed. Our master charged us to receive the Tang Monk and give him the ginseng fruit to eat, in token of old friendship — and also to guard against mischief from his followers. Sure enough, those three have fierce, savage faces and coarse tempers. Lucky for us he's sent them off; for if they'd stayed about, the ginseng fruit would never have come face to face with them at all."

"Brother," said Pure Breeze, "we still don't know whether this monk really is our master's old friend. Let's ask him, lest we make a mistake."

So the two boys came forward again. "May we ask whether the Venerable Master is the Tang Tripitaka, bound from the Great Tang to the Western Heaven for the scriptures?"

The elder returned the courtesy. "I am that humble monk. How do you immortal boys come to know my unworthy name?"

"When our master was setting out," said the boys, "he charged us to go far to meet you. But his carriage came in haste, and so we failed in our welcome. Please be seated, Venerable Master, and let us fetch some tea to offer you."

"I dare not trouble you," said Tripitaka. Then Bright Moon hurried off to his room, brought back a cup of fragrant tea, and offered it to the elder. When the tea was finished, Pure Breeze said: "Brother, we mustn't disobey our master's command. You and I shall go and fetch the fruit."

The two boys took their leave of Tripitaka and went together to their room. One took up a golden mallet, the other a cinnabar tray, and they laid more green cloths to cushion the bottom of the tray. Then they went straight to the ginseng orchard. Pure Breeze climbed up into the tree and struck the fruit with the golden mallet, while Bright Moon waited below, holding up the cinnabar tray to catch it. In a moment two fruits were knocked down and caught in the tray, and the boys carried them straight to the front hall to present.

"Master of Tang," they said, "our Five Estates Abbey lies in a remote corner amid barren hills, and we have nothing worth offering. Here are two humble fruits of the soil, simple country fare, to ease your thirst."

When the elder saw them, he trembled all over and shrank back three feet. "Mercy! Mercy! This very year has been one of good harvests and ripe seasons — how can this abbey suffer such famine as to eat people? These are infants not yet three days old. How are they to ease my thirst?"

Pure Breeze said to himself: "This monk has spent his days in the marketplace of tongues, in the sea of right and wrong, until he's grown a fleshly, mortal eye and can't recognize the rare treasure of us immortals."

Bright Moon stepped up. "Venerable Master, this thing is called the ginseng fruit. There's no harm in eating one."

"Nonsense, nonsense!" said Tripitaka. "Their parents bore them in the womb through who knows how much suffering before they were born. Not three days old, and you'd snatch them up to serve as fruit?"

"It really did grow on a tree," said Pure Breeze.

"Wild talk, wild talk!" said the elder. "How could a tree grow human beings? Take it away — it's no fit thing for a son of man."

When the two boys saw that, push and urge as they might, he would not eat, they had no choice but to take up the tray and go back to their own room. Now the fruits had this strange property: they could not be kept long. Set aside too long, they turned hard and were no good to eat. So the two of them went to their room and, one fruit to each, sat down on the edge of the bed and set to eating with relish.

Aha — but here's the thing of it! Their Daoist room and the kitchen shared a thin party-wall, hard up against each other, so that a soft word spoken on this side was heard at once on the other. Bajie was just then cooking in the kitchen. He had heard from the first the talk of taking the golden mallet and the cinnabar tray, and had marked it in his heart. Then he heard them say that the Tang Monk hadn't recognized the ginseng fruit, and that they had carried it off to their room to eat themselves. He couldn't keep the saliva from running out of his mouth. "How can I get one to taste?" But his body was too clumsy and lumbering, and he couldn't manage it himself — so he waited for Wukong to come, to scheme it out with him. He had no heart for tending the fire at the stove-mouth, but kept poking his head out, craning and peering, slipping out to look.

Before long he saw Wukong leading the horse up; Wukong tied it to a locust tree and was heading straight for the back. The idiot waved his hand wildly: "This way, this way!" Wukong turned and came to the kitchen door. "Idiot, what are you bawling about? I suppose there isn't enough rice — well, let the old monk eat his fill, and we'll beg some more up ahead at the next great house."

"Come in," said Bajie. "It's not that the rice is short. This abbey has a certain treasure — do you know about it?"

"What treasure?" asked Wukong.

Bajie laughed. "Tell you of it, and you'll never have seen it; hand it to you, and you won't even know what it is."

"This idiot's making sport of old Sun," said Wukong. "Five hundred years ago, when I went seeking the Way of the immortals, I roamed to the ends of the sea and the rim of Heaven. What is there I haven't seen?"

"Brother," said Bajie, "have you ever seen the ginseng fruit?"

Wukong started. "That, truly, I've never seen. But I've often heard people say the ginseng fruit is the Grass-Returning Elixir, and that whoever eats it can greatly prolong his life. Where is there any to be had?"

"They have it here," said Bajie. "The boys brought two of them for the Master to eat, but the old monk didn't recognize them — said they were infants not three days old and didn't dare touch them. Those boys are good-for-nothings: since the Master wouldn't eat, they ought to have offered them to us, but instead they kept it from us, and just now in the next room they sat there, one apiece, gobble-gobble, and ate them all up. It set the water fairly flooding in my mouth. How can I get one to taste? I was thinking — you're a nimble fellow. Go into their orchard and steal a few for us to try. How about it?"

"That's easy," said Wukong. "Old Sun will go — I'll have them the moment I reach out." He turned at once to go off in front, but Bajie caught hold of him: "Brother, I heard them say in that room they'd take some 'golden mallet' to knock them down. You've got to manage it properly — don't let the wind get out."

"I know, I know," said Wukong.

The Great Sage worked a spell of invisibility and slipped into the Daoist room to look. But the two boys, having eaten their fruits, had gone up to the hall to talk with the Tang Monk, and were not in the room. Wukong looked all about for the golden mallet, and saw, hanging on the window-lattice, a length of red gold about two feet long and as thick as a finger, with a head at the bottom like a clove of garlic, and an eye at the top through which was threaded a cord of green silk. "This must surely be the thing they call the golden mallet," he said. So he took it down, left the Daoist room, and went straight to the back. He pushed open a pair of doors, lifted his head and looked — ah! It was a flower garden! He saw:

> Vermilion railings and jeweled balustrades,
> winding stone paths and miniature peaks.
> Rare flowers vie in beauty with the bright sun;
> emerald bamboo contends in green against the blue sky.
> Beyond the floating-cup pavilion,
> a bend of green willows trails like smoke;
> before the moon-viewing terrace,
> clusters of tall pines stand splashed with indigo.
> Red and fiery, the pomegranate in its brocade nest;
> green and tender, the embroidered cushion of grass;
> blue and downy, the sand-orchids of jade-green;
> rippling and gentle, the water beside the brook.
> Cinnamon shades the parasol-trees by the golden well;
> brocade locust-trees lean by vermilion rails and jade-stone steps.
> Here are peach blossoms, red and white, of a thousand petals;
> here are autumn chrysanthemums, fragrant and yellow, of the ninth month.
> The rose-trellis sets off the peony pavilion;
> the hibiscus terrace adjoins the herbaceous-peony plot.
> Endless to view: the gentleman-bamboo that braves the frost,
> the high-official pine that defies the snow.
> And more — crane-farms and deer-folds, square ponds and round pools;
> springs that flow like scattered jade, earth-blossoms heaped like gold.
> The north wind makes the plum-flowers burst forth white;
> spring's coming dabs the crabapple red.
> Truly the foremost fairy scene of the human world,
> the chief flowering grove of the West.

Wukong gazed his fill and then saw another tier of doors. He pushed them open and looked — it was a vegetable garden:

> Planted with the vegetables of the four seasons:
> spinach, celery, beet, and gingershoots;
> bamboo-shoots, melons, gourds, and water-bamboo;
> scallions, garlic, coriander, leek, and chive.
> Lotus-root, crown-daisy, and bitter herbs;
> bottle-gourd and eggplant must be set in;
> turnip and radish buried like ram's-heads,
> red amaranth, green cabbage, and purple mustard.

Wukong laughed. "So he's a Daoist who grows his own and eats his own, too."

Passing the vegetable garden, he saw yet another tier of doors. He pushed them open and looked — ah! There in the very center stood a great tree, with truly green and fragrant boughs and shadowy emerald leaves; the leaves were shaped like a plantain's. It rose straight up over a thousand feet high, and its trunk was some seven or eight fathoms around. Wukong leaned at the foot of the tree and looked up, and there on a branch facing south was a single ginseng fruit, exactly like a child. There was a stem at the base of it, and as it hung there at the branch-tip, its hands and feet were moving and its head was nodding and bobbing, and when the wind passed it seemed to make a sound. Wukong was overjoyed and praised it privately: "What a fine thing! Truly rare, truly rare!"

Leaning on the tree, he went *whoosh* and shot up into it — for this monkey had, first and foremost, a gift for climbing trees and stealing fruit. He gave the golden mallet a single tap, and the fruit dropped down with a *plop*. He leapt down after it to look for it — but it was nowhere, utterly gone. He searched all about in the grass, and there was not the faintest trace.

"Strange, strange," said Wukong. "I suppose it has feet and can walk — but even if it ran, it couldn't have jumped over the wall. I know how it is: the local earth-god of this garden won't let old Sun steal his fruit, so he's spirited it away." With that he made the magic sign, recited the sacred word "Om," and compelled the garden's earth-god to appear before him. The earth-god made his bow.

"The Great Sage has summoned this humble spirit — what are your commands?"

"You don't know it," said Wukong, "but old Sun is the most famous chief of thieves under all of Heaven. In years past I stole the Immortal Peaches, filched the imperial wine, and made off with the elixir of the gods, and no one ever dared take a share with me. How is it that today I steal a single fruit of theirs, and you go and snatch away my portion? This fruit grew on a tree — even the birds that fly past in the air ought to have a share of it. If old Sun eats just one of them, what great harm is there? Why, the instant I knocked it down, you scooped it up and away?"

"Great Sage, you wrong this humble spirit," said the earth-god. "This treasure is the possession of an earth-immortal; I am only a ghost-immortal — how would I dare take it? Why, I haven't even the good fortune to give it so much as a sniff."

"If you didn't take it," said Wukong, "then how did it vanish the moment it fell?"

"Great Sage, you know only that this treasure prolongs life," said the earth-god. "You don't know its origins."

"What origins has it?" asked Wukong.

"This treasure flowers once in three thousand years," said the earth-god, "sets fruit once in three thousand years, and ripens only after another three thousand. All told, in ten thousand years it sets but thirty fruits. Whoever has the karma to smell one will live three hundred and sixty years; whoever eats one will live forty-seven thousand years. But it fears the Five Elements, each in its own way."

"How does it fear the Five Elements?" asked Wukong.

"This fruit falls when it meets metal," said the earth-god; "it withers when it meets wood; it dissolves when it meets water; it scorches when it meets fire; and it sinks into the ground when it meets earth. To knock it down you must use a metal implement — only then will it come down. And when it has come down, you must cushion the tray with a silk cloth. If it suffers any contact with wood, it withers, and even eaten it will not prolong life. To eat it you must use a porcelain vessel, dissolving it in clear water before you take it. Meet fire, and it scorches and is good for nothing. And as for meeting earth and sinking in — Great Sage, the moment you knocked it to the ground just now, it bored its way down into the soil. This soil is forty-seven thousand years old; even a steel drill couldn't bore the least bit into it, for it's three or four parts harder than wrought iron. That's why people who eat the fruit gain long life. If the Great Sage doesn't believe it, try striking the ground here and see."

Wukong at once drew out his gold-banded cudgel and struck a single blow. There was a clang, the cudgel bounced back up, and on the earth there was not the slightest mark.

"True enough, true enough," said Wukong. "This rod of mine smashes stone to powder and dents even wrought iron — how is it that this one blow didn't so much as scratch it? In that case I've wronged you. Go on back."

The earth-god then returned to his shrine.

Now the Great Sage had a plan. He climbed up the tree, working the mallet with one hand while with the other he caught up the front hem of his brocade gown to make a pouch and held it ready. Then he threaded through the branches and parted the leaves, knocked down three fruits, and caught them in the fold of his gown. Down from the tree he jumped, and went straight along to the kitchen.

Bajie laughed. "Brother, do you have any?"

"This isn't them?" said Wukong. "Old Sun had them the moment he reached out. We mustn't keep these from Sha Monk, either — give him a call."

Bajie at once beckoned and called: "Wujing, come here." Sha Monk set down the luggage, ran into the kitchen, and said, "Brother, why do you call me?" Wukong opened the fold of his gown. "Brother, look — what's this thing?"

When Sha Monk saw it he said, "It's a ginseng fruit."

"Good for you!" said Wukong. "So you recognize it. Where have you eaten one before?"

"Little brother has never eaten one," said Sha Monk, "but in the old days, when I was Curtain-Lifting Marshal escorting the phoenix-carriage to the Peach Banquet, I often saw the various immortals from beyond the sea offer this fruit to the Queen Mother to wish her long life. See it I have, but eaten it I never have. Brother, may I have a bit to taste?"

"No need to say more — one apiece for us brothers," said Wukong.

So the three of them each enjoyed a fruit. Now Bajie had a deep belly and a wide mouth; and besides, having heard the boys eating earlier, he'd felt the gluttony-worm stirring inside him. So now, the moment he laid eyes on the fruit, he snatched it up, opened wide, and *gulp* — swallowed it whole down his gullet. Then, rolling his eyes shamelessly, he turned to Wukong and Sha Monk: "What were you two eating?"

"The ginseng fruit," said Sha Monk.

"What does it taste like?" asked Bajie.

"Wujing, pay him no mind," said Wukong. "You ate yours first — and now you come asking us?"

"Brother," said Bajie, "I ate it too fast — not like you two, chewing slow and swallowing slow, getting a taste of it. I don't even know whether it had a pit or not; I just bolted it down. Brother — for friendship's sake, see a thing through. You've stirred up my gluttony-worm now — go get me another one, so old Hog can eat it nice and slow."

"Brother," said Wukong, "you don't know when to stop. This thing isn't like rice or noodles, where you can eat your fill once you come by it. In ten thousand years the tree sets only thirty fruits — for us to eat even this one is a great stroke of karmic fortune; it's no trifling thing. Enough, enough, that's plenty." He rose, and through the window-hole he tossed the golden mallet back into the Daoist room, and paid the matter no more heed.

But the idiot kept up his muttering and grumbling. Just then the two Daoist boys came back into their room to fetch tea to serve — and they heard Bajie still grousing: "I didn't get to enjoy that ginseng fruit. It'd be grand to have one more to eat."

When Pure Breeze heard it, he grew suspicious. "Bright Moon, listen — that long-snouted monk is saying he wants 'one more ginseng fruit to eat.' When our master took his leave, he charged us to guard against mischief from these followers. Could it be they've stolen our treasure?"

Bright Moon turned his head. "Brother, this is bad, this is bad! How did the golden mallet come to be lying on the ground? Let's go and look in the orchard."

The two of them hurried off, and found the flower garden standing open. "I shut this gate myself," said Pure Breeze. "How is it open?" They hurried on through the flower garden, and found the vegetable-garden gate open too. They rushed into the ginseng orchard, leaned at the foot of the tree, looked up, and counted; back and forth they counted, every which way, and made it only twenty-two.

"Can you do sums?" asked Bright Moon.

"I can," said Pure Breeze. "Tell me the figures."

"There were thirty fruits to begin with," said Bright Moon. "When our master opened the orchard, two were shared and eaten, leaving twenty-eight. Just now we knocked down two for the Tang Monk to eat, leaving twenty-six. And now only twenty-two remain — so aren't we short four? No question about it, no question — that pack of villains has stolen them. We'll go and curse the Tang Monk for it."

The two of them came out the orchard gate and went straight to the hall, where they pointed at the Tang Monk and railed at him without ceasing — "baldpate" before and "baldpate" behind, a stream of foul and filthy language; thief-faced, rat-brained, stinking this and rancid that, cursing away in a vicious temper. The Tang Monk could not endure it. "Immortal boys, what is all this clamor? Calm yourselves a little. If you've something to say, say it slowly, there's no harm in that — but don't go ranting wild nonsense."

"Are you deaf?" said Pure Breeze. "Or do I talk gibberish you can't understand? You've stolen and eaten our ginseng fruits — how dare you not let me speak of it?"

"What does this ginseng fruit look like?" asked the Tang Monk.

"It's the very thing we brought just now for you to eat," said Bright Moon, "the one you said looked like a child."

"Amitabha!" said the Tang Monk. "The moment I laid eyes on that thing, my heart shook and my gall trembled — how would I dare steal it and eat it? Even if I'd been seized with a craving, I'd never do such a thievish deed. Don't go wronging people unjustly."

"Though you didn't eat it yourself," said Pure Breeze, "you've followers who'd be glad to steal and eat."

"In that case, what you say has some sense," said Tripitaka. "Stop your shouting awhile, and let me question them. If they truly stole it, I'll make them make it good to you."

"Make it good!" said Bright Moon. "Where would you buy more, even if you had the money?"

"Even if there's money and nowhere to buy it," said Tripitaka, "the old saying goes, 'Benevolence and righteousness are worth a thousand pieces of gold.' Have them offer you an apology, and let that be the end of it. And besides, we still don't even know whether it was them or not."

"How could it not be them?" said Bright Moon. "They're in there quarreling over the unfair shares this very moment!"

Tripitaka called out: "Disciples, all of you come here."

Sha Monk heard, and said: "This is bad — the game's up. The old Master is calling us, and the little Daoist boys are cursing away — if the old business hasn't gotten out, then what is it?"

"What an utter disgrace," said Wukong. "But this is no more than a matter of food and drink. If we let it out, then we're confessed as snatchers of mouthfuls — best just deny it."

"Just so, just so," said Bajie. "Brazen it out."

So the three of them had no choice but to leave the kitchen and go up into the hall.

In the end there is no knowing how they were to brazen it out before the boys — so listen to the explanation in the next installment.

<!-- chapter 25 -->
# Chapter 25: The Immortal Zhenyuan Pursues the Pilgrims, and Sun Wukong Wreaks Havoc Upon Five Villages Abbey

Now, the three disciple-brothers came up to the hall and said to their master, "The rice is nearly done. Why have you called for us?"

Tripitaka said, "Disciples, it is not the rice I am asking about. This abbey, it seems, possesses certain ginseng fruit—things shaped like little children. Which of you stole some and ate them?"

"I'm an honest fellow," said Pigsy. "I know nothing of it. I never saw a thing."

"The one who's grinning—that's the one!" cried Clear Wind. "The grinning one, that's him!"

"This old Sun was born with this very grin on his face," Wukong shot back. "Just because you've lost some fruit of yours, am I not even allowed to smile?"

"Disciple, calm your anger," said Tripitaka. "We are people who have left the household life. Do not speak falsehoods, and do not eat food that lies heavy on the conscience. If you truly ate their fruit, then offer them an apology—why deny it so stubbornly?"

Seeing the sense in his master's words, Wukong told the truth. "Master, it is no fault of mine. It was Pigsy who, on the far side of the wall, overheard those two Taoist boys eating some ginseng fruit, and he took a fancy to taste one for novelty's sake. He sent this old Sun to knock down three of them, and we brothers ate one apiece. Well, eaten is eaten—what would you have us do about it now?"

"You stole four of mine," said Bright Moon, "and still this monk says he's no thief!"

"Amitabha!" said Pigsy. "If you stole four, why bring out only three to share—pocketing one ahead of time on the sly?" The simpleton, in his babbling, had given the whole game away.

Now that the two boys had wormed out the truth, their abuse grew fiercer than ever. The Great Sage ground his steel teeth till they rang and rolled his fiery eyes wide; again and again he gripped his golden-banded cudgel, again and again he held himself back. "These boys think it's enough to curse a man to his face," he thought. "Let them have their say. But I'll set them up a scheme with no afterward—I'll fix it so none of them eats a single one again."

Good Wukong! He plucked a single hair from the back of his head, blew on it a breath of immortal air, and called, "Change!" It became a counterfeit Wukong, who took his place beside Tripitaka, alongside Wuneng and Wujing, enduring the boys' tongue-lashing. Meanwhile his true self sent out his spirit, leapt up onto a somersault of cloud, and went straight to the ginseng garden. There he drew out his golden cudgel and—bang!—struck the tree a single blow. Then, summoning that divine strength that can push down hills and shift ranges, he gave the tree a shove and toppled it.

Pity the tree! Its leaves scattered, its branches sprang apart, its roots tore from the soil—and the Taoists' "Grass-Returning Elixir" was cut off at the source. Having pushed the tree over, the Great Sage searched the boughs for fruit, but not so much as half a one could he find. For this treasure, you must understand, falls at the touch of metal: both ends of his cudgel were sheathed in gold, and iron itself is counted among the five metals—so the moment he struck, down they dropped; and once dropped, they sank straight into the earth at its touch. That was why not one fruit remained upon the tree.

"Good, good, good!" he said. "Now everyone's fire is out." He put away his iron cudgel and went straight back to the front. There he shook the hair, drew it back into his body, and rejoined himself. The others, being only common folk of flesh-and-blood eyes, never saw a thing.

Now the immortal boys had cursed and railed for a good long while, until Clear Wind said, "Bright Moon, these monks can certainly take a scolding. We've been cursing them like one scolds a chicken, going at it half this time, and they've never once made a fuss back. Most likely they never stole and ate them after all. Maybe the tree is tall and its leaves are thick, and we miscounted. Let's not curse them for nothing—come, let's go back and check again."

"That's well said," answered Bright Moon. So the two of them went once more into the garden—only to find the tree toppled, its branches splayed, the fruit gone and the leaves down. Terror struck Clear Wind till his legs went soft and he fell flat on his face; Bright Moon's waist gave way and his bones seemed to crumble beneath him. The two of them were frightened clean out of their souls. There is a poem to prove it:

> Tripitaka came west to the Mountain of Ten Thousand Years;
> Wukong cut off the Grass-Returning Elixir there.
> The branches split, the leaves fell, the immortal root lay bare—
> And Bright Moon and Clear Wind grew cold in heart and gall.

The two of them lay sprawled in the dust, their words all jumbled, crying only, "What's to be done? What's to be done? He has ruined the elixir-head of our Five Villages Abbey, cut off the very seed-line of our immortal house! When our master comes home, how shall we two answer him?"

"Brother, don't carry on so," said Bright Moon. "Let us set our caps and robes in order and not alarm those few monks. There's no one else who could have done this—it must surely be that thunder-god-faced, hairy-cheeked wretch. He sent out his spirit and worked his magic and destroyed our treasure. If we have it out with him, the wretch is bound to deny it flatly and quarrel with us; and once the quarrel starts, it'll come to blows. Think now—how could we two ever match his four? Better we go and trick him a little. We'll simply say the fruit is all there, that we miscounted, and turn it around to apologize to him instead. Their rice is already done; when they sit down to eat, we'll serve them a few side dishes besides. Each of them will be holding a bowl—and you stand at the left of the door, I at the right, and slam the door shut, snap the lock to, and bolt every gate behind them. We'll not let them out, but wait for the master to come home, and let him deal with them as he sees fit. The monk is also our master's old acquaintance: if our master pardons him, that's our master's grace to do; and if he does not pardon him, why, we'll have caught the thief all the same—and so we may yet escape the blame for our own fault."

Hearing this, Clear Wind said, "Good reasoning, good reasoning."

The two of them forced up their spirits, mustered a false cheerfulness, and came straight from the back garden up to the hall. There they bowed low before Tripitaka, bending at the waist, and said, "Master, the words we spoke just now were coarse and gave great offense. Don't take it amiss, don't take it amiss."

"What do you mean?" asked Tripitaka.

"The fruit are all there," said Clear Wind. "It was only that the leaves grew high and thick, and we couldn't see clearly. We went just now to count again, and the number is as it always was."

At this Pigsy seized his footing to tease them: "You little boys, too young to know how things are done—you came scolding and railing, mouthing curses for nothing, slandering us falsely. That's no way for honest children to behave."

Wukong understood it all in his heart but said nothing aloud. To himself he thought, "Lies, lies. The fruit are finished, the account is settled—how can they talk like this? They must have some method for bringing the dead back to life."

"If that's how it is," said Tripitaka, "then bring out the rice, and we'll eat and be on our way."

So Pigsy went to dish up the rice while Sandy set out the tables and chairs. The two boys hurried to fetch the side dishes—soy-pickled gourd, soy-pickled eggplant, lees-pickled radish, vinegared green beans, pickled water-chestnut sprouts, and parboiled mustard greens—setting out seven or eight little plates in all for the master and disciples; and they brought out a pot of good tea besides, with two teacups, waiting in attendance on either side. The four of them had no sooner picked up their bowls than the boys, one to each side, slammed the door shut—bang!—and shot home a double-tongued brass lock.

Pigsy laughed. "These boys have got it wrong. Bad customs you have around here—why lock the door to eat your dinner?"

"Quite so, quite so," said Bright Moon. "Eat your dinner first, good or ill, and then we'll open the door."

But Clear Wind cursed them: "You gluttonous, food-stealing bald thieves! You stole and ate my immortal fruit—that's a crime of raiding the melons and fruits of another man's field and garden already; and then you pushed over my immortal tree, ruining the immortal root of our Five Villages Abbey—and still you want to talk back! If ever you reach the West and look upon the face of Buddha, it'll only be after you've turned tail and ridden the wheel of rebirth all over again!"

Hearing this, Tripitaka let his rice bowl fall, and a great stone settled upon his heart. The boys went and locked up the front mountain-gate and the second gate, every one. Then they came back to the door of the main hall and railed with vicious words, "thief" before and "thief" behind, cursing until the sky grew toward evening. Only then did they go to eat their own meal, and after eating retired to their rooms.

Tripitaka reproached Wukong: "You ape's head—time and again you crash into trouble. You stole and ate their fruit; you should have borne their few angry words and let them curse a bit, and that would have been the end of it. But why did you push over their tree besides? If we reason it out by this state of affairs, then should they lodge a complaint, even if your own father were the magistrate, the case still couldn't be argued out."

"Master, don't fret," said Wukong. "The boys have all gone to sleep. We'll just wait until they're sound asleep, and then we'll set out in the night."

"Brother," said Sandy, "all the gates are locked and shut up tight as can be. How are we to get out?"

Wukong laughed. "Never mind, never mind. Old Sun has his own ways."

"As if anyone doubted you had a way," said Pigsy. "You can change into some bug or worm and fly out through the lattice-holes easily enough. But it's hard on us who can't transform—we'll be left here holding the pot and taking the blame."

"If he pulls a trick like that and doesn't take you and me out with him," said Tripitaka, "then I'll start reciting that old-words sutra, and how will he stomach that?"

Hearing this, Pigsy was both worried and amused. "Master, what are you talking about? I've only ever heard that the Buddhist canon has the Śūraṅgama Sutra, the Lotus Sutra, the Peacock Sutra, the Guanyin Sutra, and the Diamond Sutra. I never heard of any 'old-words sutra.'"

"Brother, you don't know," said Wukong. "This band I wear on my crown was bestowed on my master by the Bodhisattva Guanyin. My master tricked me into putting it on, and now it's as though it's taken root—there's no thinking of getting it off. It's called the Tight-Band Spell, also the Tight-Band Sutra. His 'old-words sutra'—that's just this. When he recites it, my head aches, and that's the trick he has to torment me with. Master, don't recite it. I'll surely not fail you—I'll see to it we all get out together."

By the time they had finished talking, the sky was already dark, and without their noticing the moon rose in the east. "Right now there's not a sound in all the world," said Wukong, "and the icy wheel shines clear. This is just the moment to be off."

"Brother," said Pigsy, "no playing ghost-tricks now. The doors are all locked. Where are we to go?"

"Watch my hand," said Wukong. He took the golden cudgel in his grip, worked an "Unlocking Spell," and pointed at the door—and at once there came a rending crash, the double tongues of every lock fell away, and with a clatter the leaves of the doors flew open.

Pigsy laughed. "What skill! Even if you called in a little tinker-smith with his picklock, it wouldn't be half so neat as this."

"What's so wonderful about these doors?" said Wukong. "Even the Southern Gate of Heaven—I'd only have to point, and it would open." Then he asked his master out the door and helped him onto the horse; Pigsy shouldered the luggage, Sandy led the horse, and they made straight along the western road.

"You all go on slowly," said Wukong. "Let old Sun go and see to it that those two boys sleep for a month."

"Disciple," said Tripitaka, "you must not harm their lives—or else you'll have another crime of robbery-with-injury upon you."

"I know," said Wukong. He went back in and came to the door of the room where the boys slept. At his waist he carried sleep-insects—won, as it happens, at the Eastern Gate of Heaven, in a game of guess-fingers with the Heavenly King of Increase and Growth. He fished out two of them, flicked them in through the window-holes, and they flew straight onto the boys' faces. The two fell into a deep, snoring slumber, with no hope of ever waking. Then Wukong stretched out his cloud-stride, caught up with Tripitaka, and they hurried straight on westward along the highway.

All that night the horse never stopped its hooves, and they traveled until the sky lightened. Said Tripitaka, "This ape's head will be the death of me—on account of your appetite you've dragged me through a whole sleepless night."

"Don't keep complaining," said Wukong. "The sky's light now. Just rest a while in that wood by the roadside and nurse your spirit before we go on."

The elder had no choice but to dismount, and he leaned against a pine root, using it for a makeshift meditation seat. Sandy set down the load and dozed; Pigsy pillowed his head on a stone and went to sleep. But the Great Sage had a restless heart all his own—look at him there, leaping among the trees, pulling at the branches, larking about. We'll say no more of the four resting.

Now the Great Immortal had broken up the assembly at the Palace of the Primal Origin, and leading his band of lesser immortals he left the Tushita Heaven, came straight down through the jasper sky, sank his auspicious cloud, and arrived at last before the gate of Five Villages Abbey on the Mountain of Ten Thousand Years. Looking, he saw the abbey gate flung wide and the ground swept clean.

"Clear Wind, Bright Moon are useful boys after all," said the Great Immortal. "Ordinarily, with the sun three poles high, they wouldn't so much as straighten their backs; yet today, with us away, they've actually risen early to open the gate and sweep the ground." All the lesser immortals were pleased.

But when they came up to the hall, the incense was burned out, every human trace was still, and there was no sign of Bright Moon or Clear Wind anywhere. "These two have probably run off with our things while we were away," said the immortals.

"Such a thing is unthinkable!" said the Great Immortal. "Men who cultivate immortality—would they dare such a base-hearted act? Most likely they forgot to shut the gate last night and went off to sleep, and haven't yet woken this morning." The immortals went to the door of the boys' room to look, and indeed the door was shut and the two lay snoring deep. Pound on the door from outside however they would, shout however they would, they could not be roused. The immortals pried off the door-planks and laid hands on the boys to drag them from their beds, but still they would not wake.

The Great Immortal laughed. "Good immortal boys! Men who attain immortality, once their spirit is full, no longer think of sleep—how is it they're this drowsy? Surely someone has worked a trick on them. Quickly, bring water." A boy hurried to fetch half a cup and handed it to the Great Immortal. He recited a spell, took a mouthful of water, and sprayed it on their faces—and at once the sleep-demon was undone.

The two woke up. Suddenly they opened their eyes, rubbed their faces, lifted their heads, and looking about recognized their immortal master, the Lord Coeval-with-the-Age, and all their immortal brethren. In a fluster Clear Wind knocked his head to the ground, and Bright Moon kowtowed, saying, "Master! Your old acquaintance, that monk who came from the east—he's a gang of bandits, and savage in the extreme!"

The Great Immortal laughed. "Don't be frightened. Tell it to me slowly."

"Master," said Clear Wind, "not long after you took your leave that day, there came indeed a Tang monk from the eastern land, with four monks in his company and five mouths counting the horse. Your disciples dared not disobey your command; we asked the reason for their coming, and took down two ginseng fruit to present to them. But that elder, with his common eyes and dull heart, did not recognize the treasure of our immortal house. He said they were children not yet three days old, and would not eat them however we pressed. So your disciples ate one apiece. We never expected that among his followers there were three disciples, and one of them, surnamed Sun, named Wukong the Pilgrim, had already stolen four fruit and eaten them. When your disciples reasoned the matter out with him and spoke a few plain words, he wouldn't have it, and secretly worked a spirit-sending trick. Oh, the bitterness of it!" And reaching this point in their tale, the two boys could not hold back the tears that fell down their cheeks.

"Did the monk beat you?" asked the immortals.

"He didn't beat us," said Bright Moon. "He only knocked over our ginseng tree."

At this the Great Immortal showed no anger at all. "Don't cry, don't cry," he said. "You don't know it, but that one surnamed Sun is himself a Great Monad Scattered Immortal. He once wreaked havoc in the Halls of Heaven, and his divine powers are vast. Since he's knocked over the treasure-tree—would you know those monks again?"

"We'd know them all," said Clear Wind.

"If you'd know them," said the Great Immortal, "then come along with me.—And the rest of you disciples, lay out the instruments of punishment and wait until I return to flog them." The immortals received the order.

The Great Immortal, with Bright Moon and Clear Wind, soared up on auspicious light to pursue Tripitaka, and in an instant they had covered a thousand li. From the edge of his cloud the Great Immortal gazed westward, but saw no sign of the Tang monk. Turning his head to look eastward, he found he had overshot by some nine hundred li and more. For the elder, though his horse never stopped its hooves all night, had gone but a hundred and twenty li; while the Great Immortal's cloud, in one bound, had overshot by more than nine hundred.

"Master," said the immortal boys, "that's the Tang monk, sitting there beneath the tree by the road."

"I've seen him," said the Great Immortal. "You two go back and get the ropes ready; I'll take him myself." So Clear Wind and Bright Moon went on ahead—of which we'll say no more.

The Great Immortal lowered his cloud, shook himself, and changed into a wandering Perfected Man of the Quanzhen sect. And how was he got up?

> He wore a hundred-patched robe and bound it with a Lü-gong cord;
> in his hand he shook a deer-tail whisk and lightly tapped a fisher-drum.
> Three-eared straw sandals graced his feet, a nine-yang kerchief swathed his head;
> the wind blew light and full in his sleeves, and from his lips he sang "The Moon Rides High."

He came straight to the foot of the tree and called out loudly to Tripitaka, "Elder, this poor Taoist salutes you." The elder hurriedly returned the courtesy: "Forgive me for not noticing you sooner, forgive me."

"Where does the elder come from," asked the Great Immortal, "and why do you sit in meditation here on the road?"

"This poor monk," said Tripitaka, "is sent from the Great Tang in the eastern land to fetch scriptures in the Western Heaven. Passing this way, I rest here a moment."

The Great Immortal feigned surprise. "Coming from the east, elder—have you by chance passed through these wild hills of mine?"

"I do not know," said the elder, "which treasure-mountain belongs to the immortal officer?"

"Five Villages Abbey on the Mountain of Ten Thousand Years," said the Great Immortal, "is this poor Taoist's dwelling place."

Hearing this, Wukong—a man with something on his conscience—answered quickly, "No, no. We came up by another road."

The Great Immortal pointed at him and laughed. "You bandit-ape! Whom do you think to deceive? You went into my abbey and knocked over my ginseng-fruit tree, then fled through the night to this place—and still you won't confess! What are you covering up? Don't try to run. Go back at once and return my tree to me."

At these words Wukong's heart flared with rage. He whipped out his iron cudgel and, without a word of explanation, aimed a blow straight at the Great Immortal's head. The Great Immortal twisted his body aside, dodged it, trod his auspicious light, and rose straight into the air. Wukong too mounted his cloud and chased hotly after him. In mid-sky the Great Immortal revealed his true form. And look how he was got up!

> On his head a purple-gold crown; a crane-feather cloak, untouched by care, upon his back.
> Slippers upon his feet; a silken sash bound round his waist.
> His body had the form of a child, his face the bloom of a beautiful woman.
> Three wisps of beard drifted beneath his chin; raven-plume locks lay folded at his temples.
> He met Wukong with no weapon at all—only a jade whisk twirled in his hand.

Wukong, with no high nor low to his blows, flailed wildly with his cudgel. The Great Immortal warded left and parried right with his jade whisk, and held him off through two or three rounds. Then he worked the trick called "Heaven and Earth Within the Sleeve": up in the clouds he let his robe-sleeve open lightly to the wind, and—swish!—swept forward and gathered all four monks and the horse together into a single sleeve.

"This is bad," said Pigsy. "We're all stuffed into a sack."

"Simpleton," said Wukong, "it's no sack. We've been bottled up in his sleeve."

"That's no great matter," said Pigsy. "Let me give it a few digs with my rake and bore a hole in it; we'll slip out the bottom and just say he was careless and didn't sack us up tight, so we tumbled out." The simpleton plied his rake and jabbed away, but he couldn't make it budge: pinch the stuff between your fingers and it felt soft enough, yet strike at it and it was harder than iron.

The Great Immortal turned his auspicious cloud and dropped straight down into Five Villages Abbey, where he took his seat and called for his disciples to bring rope. The lesser immortals attended one and all. And look—from out of his sleeve, just as one plucks out puppets, he drew forth the Tang monk and bound him to a pillar of the eaves before the main hall. Then he drew out the three others and tied one to each pillar. He took out the horse too and tethered it in the courtyard, giving it some hay and fodder, and the baggage he tossed down under the corridor.

Then he said, "Disciples, these monks are men who have left the household life; we may not use sword or spear on them, nor lay axe or halberd to them. Just fetch me out the leather whip and give them a flogging—to vent my spleen for the ginseng fruit." The immortals quickly brought out a whip—not of cowhide, nor of sheepskin, nor of buckskin or calfskin, but a Seven-Stars whip made of dragon-hide, kept soaking there in water. Bidding a strong lesser immortal take it in hand, the Great Immortal was asked, "Master, which one shall I flog first?"

"The Tang monk Tripitaka sets himself up as the elder and won't show respect," said the Great Immortal. "Flog him first."

Hearing this, Wukong thought in secret, "My old monk can't bear a beating. If a flogging should do him harm, isn't that a sin of my making?" He couldn't hold back, and spoke up: "Sir, you've got it wrong. It was I who stole the fruit, I who ate the fruit, and I too who pushed over the tree. Why not flog me first—what's the use of flogging him?"

The Great Immortal laughed. "This bandit-ape has a fierce tongue in his head. Very well then—flog him first."

"How many strokes?" asked the lesser immortal.

"Match it to the number of fruit," said the Great Immortal. "Give him thirty strokes."

The lesser immortal swung up the whip to strike. Fearing the great power of the immortals' arts, Wukong rolled his eyes wide and fixed his gaze to see where the blows would fall. Sure enough, they fell on his legs—so Wukong gave his waist a twist and called, "Change!" His legs became two legs of tempered iron, and he watched to see how the man would flog. Stroke by stroke the lesser immortal laid on thirty, and by then the morning had drawn toward noon.
