The Great Immortal then ordered, "Tripitaka should also be flogged, for being lax in his teaching and letting his wild pupils run riot." So the immortal swung the whip again to strike. Said Wukong, "Sir, you're mistaken again. When the fruit was stolen, my master knew nothing of it—he was up in the hall talking with your two boys, and it was we brothers who did the deed. Even if there's a crime of lax teaching, then as the disciple I ought to take the flogging in his place. Flog me again."

"This bandit-ape," said the Great Immortal, "for all his slyness and crafty mischief, has a touch of filial feeling in him after all. Very well then—flog him instead." The lesser immortal laid on another thirty. Wukong bent his head and looked: his two legs were like bright mirrors, polished gleaming by the blows, and he felt no pain nor itch at all.

By now the sky was drawing toward evening. "Set the whip to soak in water," said the Great Immortal, "and we'll flog them again tomorrow morning." The lesser immortal put away the whip to soak it, and they all returned to their rooms. Their evening fast finished, they all went to their rest—of which we'll say no more.

The elder, tears falling from both eyes, reproached his three disciples: "You've gone and brought down disaster, and dragged me here to suffer for it. How did all this come about?"

"Spare the reproaches," said Wukong. "If there's flogging, I'm flogged first; you took no beating at all, so why turn around and moan?"

"Even though I wasn't flogged," said Tripitaka, "my body still aches from being tied up like this."

"Master," said Sandy, "there are others tied up to bear you company over here."

"None of you make a fuss," said Wukong. "Wait a bit longer and we'll be on the road again."

"There's my brother playing his tricks again," said Pigsy. "Here we are with hempen rope soaked in water, bound tight as tight can be—a far cry from being shut up in the hall, where you used your Unlocking Spell to spring the door and walk out."

"It's no idle boast," said Wukong, "but were it three-strand hempen rope soaked with water, or even a coir hawser thick as a bowl, it would be no more to me than the autumn wind."

While they were still talking, already there was not a sound in all the world—just the hour when the streets of heaven lie hushed and the people are still. Good Wukong! He made his body small—shrank it down—and slipped right out of his bonds. "Master, let's be off."

Sandy was alarmed. "Brother, save us too!"

"Quiet, quiet," said Wukong. He untied Tripitaka, then set loose Pigsy and Sandy, straightened his short cassock, saddled and loaded the horse, took up the baggage from beneath the corridor, and they all went out the abbey gate together. Then he told Pigsy, "Go cut down four willow trees from along that cliff."

"What do you want them for?" asked Pigsy.

"There's a use for them—fetch them, quick." The simpleton had a bit of brute strength; off he went, and one snout, one tree, he rooted up four of them and brought them back in an armful. Wukong snapped off the branch-tips, sent the two brothers back inside, and had them bind the trees to the pillars with the original ropes, just as before. Then the Great Sage recited a spell, bit open the tip of his tongue, and sprayed the blood upon the trees, calling, "Change!" One became the elder, one became himself, and the other two became Sandy and Pigsy—all transformed alike in face and form, so that ask them anything and they would answer, call their names and they would respond.

Only then did the two brothers stretch out their stride and catch up with their master. That whole night, once again, the horse never stopped its hooves, and they put Five Villages Abbey far behind them.

By the time dawn came, the elder was nodding and swaying upon his horse like a mortise-peg. Seeing it, Wukong called out, "Master, this won't do. How can one who's left the household life be so worn out? Old Sun could go a thousand nights without sleep and not know the least bit of weariness. Come, dismount—don't let travelers on the road see you and laugh—and let's rest a while down at the foot of the hill, in some sheltered spot out of the wind, and then go on." So they paused.

We'll say no more of master and disciples halting on the road. Let us tell instead how the Great Immortal rose at daybreak, ate his morning fast, and came out to the hall, ordering, "Bring the whip. Today it's the Tang monk Tripitaka's turn to be flogged." The lesser immortal swung the whip and said to "Tripitaka," "It's you we're flogging." And the willow tree answered, "Flog away." Bang, crash—thirty strokes laid on. Swinging the whip around, he said to "Pigsy," "It's you we're flogging." And the willow tree answered too, "Flog away." When it came to flogging "Sandy," it likewise answered to be flogged. And when it came to flogging "Wukong"—at that moment the real Wukong, off on the road, suddenly gave a shiver and said, "This is bad!"

"What do you mean?" asked Tripitaka.

"I changed those four willow trees into us four, master and disciples," said Wukong. "I reckoned that since they flogged me twice yesterday, they'd not flog me today—but now they're flogging my counterfeit body, and that's why my true self shivers. I'll undo the spell." And in a fluster Wukong recited the spell and withdrew his magic.

Now look at those Taoist boys—seized with terror, they flung down the leather whip and reported, "Master! The first one we flogged was the Tang monk, but this round we've been flogging nothing but willow roots!"

Hearing this, the Great Immortal laughed a cold "ha-ha" and could not stop praising him: "Sun the Pilgrim—truly a fine Monkey King! I had heard how he wreaked havoc in the Halls of Heaven, how they spread nets across the earth and snares across the sky and still could not catch him—and it's true after all. Well enough that you ran off—but how is it you bound some willow trees here to take your name and stand in your place? There'll be no pardoning him. After him!"

At the Great Immortal's word "after him," he soared up on his cloud-head, looked westward, and there were the monks, baggage shouldered and horse whipped on, traveling right along the road. The Great Immortal dropped his cloud-head low and called out, "Sun the Pilgrim, where are you running? Give me back my ginseng tree!"

Pigsy heard it and said, "It's all up—here comes our adversary again."

"Master," said Wukong, "for now wrap up that word 'kindness,' and let us turn a little fierce and savage and finish him off altogether, and so make our escape." Hearing this, Tripitaka trembled and shook and made no answer at all. But Sandy whipped out his treasure-staff, Pigsy raised his rake, and the Great Sage wielded his iron cudgel; all together they pressed forward and surrounded the Great Immortal in mid-air, striking and jabbing wildly. This was a fierce fight indeed. There is a poem to prove it:

> Wukong knew not the immortal Zhenyuan,
> the Lord Coeval-with-the-Age, more wondrous and arcane.
> Three divine weapons plied their fury fierce and free—
> a single deer-tail whisk drifted at its ease.
> Warding left, parrying right, he met them as they came;
> guarding behind, fending before, he turned and turned again.
> By night they went, by morn they came—yet none could break his hold:
> tarrying so, what day would they reach the Western Heaven?

The three disciple-brothers, each plying his divine weapon, attacked all at once; but the Great Immortal merely played his fly-whisk in defense. In less than half a watch he opened his robe-sleeve once more and, as before, gathered the four monks, the one horse, and the baggage all into his sleeve. Then he turned his cloud-head and came back to the abbey, where the immortals received him.

The immortal master took his seat in the hall and again, one by one, drew them out of his sleeve. He bound the Tang monk to a low locust tree at the foot of the steps, Pigsy and Sandy each to a tree on either side, and Wukong he had trussed and thrown down.

"I expect this is for interrogation," said Wukong.

In a little while the binding was all done, and the Great Immortal ordered ten bolts of long cloth fetched out. Wukong laughed. "Pigsy, this gentleman means well—he's bringing out cloth to make us inner sleeves. Save a bit of it and make me a single full robe instead." The lesser immortals carried out the homespun cloth, and the Great Immortal said, "Wrap up the Tang monk Tripitaka, Pigsy, and Sandy in cloth." The immortals stepped forward together and wrapped them.

Wukong laughed. "Good, good, good—they're laying us out for the coffin while we're still alive!" In a moment the wrapping was finished. Then he ordered lacquer brought out. The immortals quickly fetched some of the raw and cooked lacquer they had gathered and dried themselves, and lacquered the three of them over, cloth and all, head to foot—wrapped wholly in cloth and lacquer, with only their heads and faces left out.

"Sir," said Pigsy, "the top end doesn't matter much, but down below you'd best leave a hole, so we can relieve ourselves properly."

Then the Great Immortal ordered a great cauldron carried out. Wukong laughed. "Pigsy—our luck's in! They're carrying out a cauldron; I expect they mean to cook us some rice to eat."

"That'd be all right too," said Pigsy. "Let us eat a bit of rice and at least make handsome, well-fed ghosts of ourselves."

Sure enough, the immortals carried out a great cauldron and set it up at the foot of the steps. The Great Immortal ordered dry firewood stacked and a fierce blaze kindled, saying, "Pour a cauldronful of clear oil and heat it till it boils; then drop Sun the Pilgrim into the oil-cauldron and fry him a turn, to avenge my ginseng tree."

Hearing this, Wukong rejoiced in secret. "This is just to old Sun's liking. I haven't had a bath in all this while, and my skin's gone a bit dry and itchy; a good scalding, however it turns out, would be most obliging of them." In a moment the oil-cauldron was on the boil. But the Great Sage took thought and care, fearing the immortal's arts might be hard to fathom and that he'd find no chance to work his hands in the cauldron. He turned his head and glanced about: there beneath the terrace, to the east, stood a sundial platform, and to the west a stone lion. Wukong gave a leap, rolled over to the west, bit open the tip of his tongue, spat a mouthful upon the stone lion, and called, "Change!" It became his very own likeness, trussed up in a bundle just as he had been. Meanwhile his true spirit issued forth and rose into the clouds, looking down upon the Taoists below.

Now the lesser immortal reported, "Master, the oil-cauldron's boiling through." The Great Immortal ordered, "Carry Sun the Pilgrim down into it." Four immortal boys tried but couldn't lift him; eight came, and still couldn't lift him; another four were added, and still they couldn't lift him.

"This monkey clings to the earth and won't be moved," said the immortals. "Small as he is, he's solid all the same." So they set twenty lesser immortals to heave him up, and pitched him into the cauldron with a great splashing crash, sending up spatters of boiling oil that scalded several blister-raising welts onto the faces of the little Taoists. Then the fire-tending boy cried out, "The cauldron's sprung a leak! The cauldron's sprung a leak!" Before the words were out, the oil had all run dry and the bottom of the cauldron was smashed through—for inside it was a stone lion that had been laid there.

The Great Immortal was furious. "This bandit-ape! What outrageous insolence—working his sleight-of-hand right under my eyes! Well enough that you ran off—but why have you wrecked my stove besides? This bandit-ape there's no holding, for nothing; and even if you caught him it would be like kneading sand or playing with quicksilver, like catching shadows or snatching at wind. Enough, enough, enough—let him go. Now untie the Tang monk Tripitaka instead, change the cauldron for a new one, and fry him a turn to avenge the ginseng tree." And the lesser immortals truly set to work, tearing off the cloth and lacquer.

Up in mid-air Wukong heard it all plainly, and he thought to himself, "My master can't stand it. Once he's in the oil-cauldron, one boil and he's dead, two boils and he's scorched, and by three or five boils he'll be made into a mush of a monk. I'd best go down and save him." Good Great Sage! He dropped his cloud-head, stepped forward with hands folded, and said, "Don't go tearing off the cloth and lacquer and frying my master—wait for me to come down into the oil-cauldron instead."

The Great Immortal started and cursed, "You macaque! How did you work your trick and wreck my stove?"

Wukong laughed. "When you ran up against me, your stove was bound to come to grief—what's that to do with me? I was just about to receive a little of your kindness in oil-broth and oil-water, but I had an urgent call of nature; if I'd let it go in the cauldron, I feared I'd foul your good cooking oil and spoil it for seasoning the dishes. Now that I've thoroughly relieved myself, it's just the right time to go into the cauldron. Don't fry my master—come fry me instead."

Hearing this, the Great Immortal laughed his cold "ha-ha," walked out of the hall, and seized hold of him with one hand.

After all, there's no knowing what words were said, nor truly how he got himself free—so listen to the next chapter told.

<!-- chapter 26 -->
# Chapter 26: The Three Isles and the Sweet Dew of Mercy

A poem says:

> In living in the world, keep the blade upon your heart's intent;
> In cultivating self, recall the mark beside the inch.
> The common saying names the knife the seed of livelihood —
> yet think thrice over, and beware of wrath and fraud.
> The highest gentleman does not contend; so it has been since ancient days,
> and sages carry virtue forward into their own time.
> The strong forever meet a kind more strong than they,
> and in the end all comes to emptiness and naught.

We left off with the Great Immortal Zhenyuan steadying Pilgrim with his hand and saying, "I know your abilities well enough, and I have heard your famous name. But this time you have trampled all reason and cheated your own conscience. Even with your tricks and transformations, you cannot slip from my grasp. I'd pursue you all the way to the Western Heaven, and even before that Buddha of yours, you would still have to restore my ginseng-fruit tree. Don't go playing with your magic powers."

Pilgrim laughed. "What a petty, small-minded gentleman you are! If it's only the tree being made to live again, where's the difficulty in that? Had you said so earlier, we might have spared ourselves all this quarreling."

"If there were no quarrel," said the Great Immortal, "you think I'd let you off so easily?"

"Free my master," said Pilgrim, "and I'll give you back a living tree — how's that?"

"If you truly have such power," said the Immortal, "and can cure the tree back to life, then I'll bow to you eight times and we'll be sworn brothers."

"That's nothing," said Pilgrim. "Let them go, and old Monkey guarantees you'll get your living tree back."

The Great Immortal, judging that he could not escape, at once ordered Tripitaka, Pigsy, and Sandy released. Sandy said, "Master, I don't know what kind of trick big brother is up to."

"What trick?" said Pigsy. "This is what they call a 'kindness shown to your face by a devil.' The tree is dead — can it really be cured back to life? He's putting on a fine smooth show, pretending to go off seeking a remedy for the tree, but really he's just slipping the noose and skipping town. Do you suppose he'll give a thought to you and me?"

"He'd never dare abandon us," said Tripitaka. "Let us ask him where he means to seek the cure." So he called out, "Wukong, how did you trick the Immortal into freeing us?"

"Old Monkey spoke true and honest words," said Pilgrim. "How could I have tricked him?"

"Where will you go to seek the remedy?" asked Tripitaka.

"The ancients said, 'Remedies come from over the sea,'" said Pilgrim. "I mean now to go up to the Great Eastern Ocean, to roam through all the Three Isles and Ten Continents, to seek out the immortal elders and sage patriarchs, and ask for a method of raising the dead and restoring life. I'll guarantee the tree is cured."

"And how long before you return?" asked Tripitaka.

"Three days will do it," said Pilgrim.

"Very well, then," said Tripitaka. "I'll grant you three days as you say. Come back within three days and all is well. But if you are not back after three days, I will recite that little sutra of mine."

"I obey, I obey," said Pilgrim.

Look at him then, hurriedly straightening his tiger-skin kilt and going out the door to face the Great Immortal. "Set your mind at ease, sir. I go and I return. But you must wait well upon my master — three cups of tea and six meals a day, each day, with nothing lacking. If there's the least bit short, old Monkey will settle accounts with you when I'm back, and the first thing I'll do is smash in the bottom of your cooking pot. If his clothes get soiled, see they're rinsed and washed. If his face has gone the least bit sallow, I won't have it; and if he's grown the least bit thin, I'm not stirring from this place."

"Go, go," said the Great Immortal. "I'll certainly not let him go hungry."

Good Monkey King! He hurriedly leapt onto his somersault cloud, took leave of the Five Estates Temple, and went straight up to the Great Eastern Ocean. In mid-air, swift as a lightning bolt, fast as a shooting star, he soon arrived at the fairy region of Penglai. He pressed down the head of his cloud and looked carefully below — truly a splendid place. There is a poem to prove it:

> A great-earth fairyland where ranks of sages dwell,
> Penglai parts and joins, holding down the surging waves.
> The jasper terrace dips its shadow in heaven's cold heart,
> the giant gate's light floats high above the ocean's face.
> Five-hued mist and rosy cloud enfold the jade-toned flutes;
> the ninth empyrean's stars and moon shoot at the golden tortoise.
> The Queen Mother of the Western Pool often comes here,
> bringing many peaches to wish the three Immortals long life.

Pilgrim could not take in all the fairy sights, but went straight into Penglai. As he walked along, he saw, outside the White Cloud Cave, beneath the shade of the pines, three old men gathered round a game of chess. The one watching the board was the Star of Longevity; the two playing were the Stars of Blessing and Emolument. Pilgrim went forward and called, "Old brothers, my respects to you!"

The three stars looked up, brushed aside the chessboard, and returned the bow. "What brings the Great Sage here?"

"I've come especially to play and amuse myself with you," said Pilgrim.

"We heard," said the Star of Longevity, "that the Great Sage had cast off Taoism and turned to Buddhism, that he had spared his life to protect the Tang Monk on the way to the Western Heaven for the scriptures, day after day toiling along the mountain roads. Where would you find the leisure to come amusing yourself?"

"I'll not deceive you, gentlemen," said Pilgrim. "Old Monkey, on his way west, has run into a bit of a snag along the road, and I've come to trouble you over a small matter — I don't know whether you'll oblige me."

"What place is it?" asked the Star of Blessing. "What is the snag? Tell us clearly, and we'll see what can be done."

"It's because I passed Longevity Mountain and the Five Estates Temple, and there I'm held up," said Pilgrim.

The three old men were astonished. "The Five Estates Temple is the fairy palace of the Great Immortal Zhenyuan! Don't tell us you went and stole and ate his ginseng fruit?"

Pilgrim laughed. "And what's so great about stealing and eating it?"

"You monkey, you don't know good from bad!" said the three. "Merely to smell that fruit lets a man live three hundred and sixty years. To eat one lets him live forty-seven thousand years. It's called the Myriad-Years Herb-and-Cinnabar Elixir. Our Way doesn't come near to matching his. He gained it so easily that he can rank his lifespan with Heaven itself, while we must still nourish our essence, refine our breath, preserve our spirit, harmonize the dragon and tiger, seize the Kan and fill the Li — and who knows how much toil it costs us. How can you say his fruit is nothing worth fussing over? In all the world there is only this single numinous root."

"Numinous root, numinous root," said Pilgrim. "I've already gone and snapped that root of his clean through."

"How, snapped the root?" cried the three, alarmed.

"The other day," said Pilgrim, "we were at his temple, but the Great Immortal was not at home — only two young acolytes there to receive my master. They offered my master two ginseng fruits, but my master didn't know what they were and kept insisting they were newborn babies not three days old, and refused over and over to eat. So the boys took the fruits away and ate them themselves, never offering us any. Then old Monkey went and stole three of them, and we three brothers ate them. Those boys, not knowing how high or low to behave, cursed us up and down, before our faces and behind our backs, without stopping. So old Monkey grew angry, gave the tree a single blow with my staff, knocked it over to the ground — all its fruit gone, its boughs split and leaves fallen, its roots torn up and branches wounded, and the thing was already withered dead. The boys, not expecting it, locked us up, but old Monkey wrenched the lock open and we got away. The next morning that gentleman came home, gave chase, and in the back-and-forth our words did not agree, so we fell to fighting him. He gave a flick, spread open his sleeve, and swept all of us up into that one sleeve. He had us bound with rope and cord, flogged and beaten under questioning, and beat us a whole day. That night we escaped again; he overtook us and bagged us up just as before. He carries not an inch of iron on him — only a fly-whisk to parry with — yet we three brothers, with our three kinds of weapons, couldn't so much as touch him. This time he arranged it all over again: he wrapped my master and my two fellow disciples in cloth daubed with lacquer, and set me down in a cauldron of oil. But I worked another escape-trick and got away, and smashed all his cauldrons. Seeing he couldn't hold me, he turned somewhat sour on me — so I had a good talk with him, and got him to release my master and brothers in exchange for my curing the tree alive. Only then will the two households have peace. I remembered that 'remedies come from over the sea,' and so I have come roaming these fairy regions to call on you three old brothers. If you have any remedy for curing the tree, teach me one, to save the Tang Monk from his misery quickly."

When the three stars heard this, their hearts too grew troubled. "You monkey, you don't know people at all. That Zhenyuanzi is the patriarch of the earthbound immortals, while we are merely of the lineage of the celestial spirits. And you, though you've attained the rank of heavenly immortal, are still of the loose, uncounted Grand-Unity sort — you've not entered the true stream. How could you slip out of his hands? If the Great Sage had killed some beast or bird, some insect or scaled creature, a single grain of our millet-cinnabar could bring it back to life. But the ginseng fruit is the root of a fairy tree — how is it to be cured? No remedy, no remedy."

When Pilgrim heard there was no remedy, his brows knit together in twin locks, and his forehead furrowed with a thousand creases. The Star of Blessing said, "Great Sage, if there's no remedy here, there may be one elsewhere — why fall into vexation so soon?"

"To go seeking a remedy elsewhere is easy enough," said Pilgrim. "Even to roam to the corners of the sea and the ends of the sky, to turn through all the thirty-six heavens, would be a small thing. The trouble is that my Elder Tang is strict in his rules and narrow in his patience — he's granted me only three days. If I'm not back after three days, he'll recite that tight-fillet spell."

The three stars laughed. "Good, good, good! If it weren't for this little device to rein you in, you'd be drilling up through the heavens again." Then the Star of Longevity said, "Set your heart at ease, Great Sage; there's no need to fret. That Great Immortal, though he ranks above us, is also an acquaintance of ours. For one thing, it's been long since we parted and we haven't paid him a visit; for another, it's a favor to the Great Sage. Now we three will go together to call on him, and put your case to him, and tell that Tang monk not to recite the tight-fillet spell. Never mind three days or five — we'll only take our leave once you've found a remedy and returned."

"My thanks, my thanks!" said Pilgrim. "Then please, you three old brothers, be on your way, and I'll be off." The Great Sage took leave of the three stars — no more of that.

Now these three stars mounted their auspicious radiance and went at once to the Five Estates Temple. The whole assembly within the temple suddenly heard the cry of cranes across the vast sky — it was the three old men arriving in their glory. And there they saw:

> Filling the sky, dense banks of auspicious light;
> through the cloud-river, billowing waves of fragrance.
> A thousand strands of colored mist guard their feathered robes;
> a single soft cloud upholds their immortal feet.
> The green simurgh flies, the cinnabar phoenix soars,
> their sleeves draw a scented wind that sweeps across the ground.
> Their staffs, hung with dragons, kindle joyous laughter;
> their snowy beards, dripping jade, brush across their breasts.
> Childlike of face, glad and free of all care;
> sturdy of frame, mighty and full of blessing.
> They grasp the star-tallies, add to the sea-house years,
> with gourds at their waists and treasure-talismans.
> Through myriad ages and thousand decades their fortune and life endure;
> through the Ten Continents and Three Isles they lodge as fate provides.
> Often they come to the world to deliver a thousand blessings,
> and each time to mankind they add a hundredfold of fortune.
> Through all of Heaven and Earth, in glory of blessing and emolument,
> blessing and longevity boundless — and now this happy meeting won.

The three old men rode their auspicious light to pay their respects to the Great Immortal; the hall of blessing was all of harmonious air, beyond all measure. When the fairy boy saw them, he hurried to report: "Master, the three Stars from over the sea have come!"

Zhenyuanzi was just then chatting idly with the Tang Monk and his disciples. Hearing the news, he came down the steps to welcome them. When Pigsy saw the Star of Longevity, he went right up and seized hold of him, laughing. "You fleshy-headed old fellow, I haven't seen you in ages — still as carefree as ever, and you didn't even bring a cap along." With that he snatched one of his own monk's caps and slapped it down onto the old man's head, then clapped his hands and roared with laughter. "Good, good, good — this truly is 'adding the cap, advancing in emolument'!"

The Star of Longevity flung the cap to the ground and scolded, "You clumsy lout! What a great oaf, knowing neither high nor low!"

"I'm no clumsy lout," said Pigsy. "It's you lot who are the real lackeys."

"You're the clumsy lout," said the Star of Blessing, "and you dare turn round and call others lackeys?"

Pigsy laughed again. "If you're not somebody's lackeys, then how is it you're called 'Add-Longevity,' 'Add-Blessing,' 'Add-Emolument'?" At this Tripitaka shouted Pigsy down, hurriedly straightened his robes, and made his bows to the three stars.

The three stars greeted the Great Immortal with the courtesy due from juniors, and only then took their seats. Once seated, the Star of Emolument said, "We've long been parted from your honored countenance, and have failed in our respects. Today, because the Great Sage Sun has stirred up trouble on the fairy mountains, we've come especially to call on you."

"Did Pilgrim Sun go to Penglai, then?" asked the Great Immortal.

"He did," said the Star of Longevity. "Because he injured the Great Immortal's cinnabar tree, he came to our place to seek a remedy to cure it. We had no remedy, so he went off to seek elsewhere. But he feared he'd overrun the three-day limit set by the Holy Monk and have the tight-fillet spell recited over him. So we've come — first, to pay our respects; second, to beg an extension of the limit."

Hearing this, Tripitaka answered at once, again and again, "I won't recite it, I won't recite it."

Just as they were speaking, Pigsy came running in again and grabbed hold of the Star of Blessing, demanding fruit to eat. He went groping all through his sleeves, digging about his waist, ceaselessly lifting his robes to search him over. Tripitaka laughed. "What manners are these, Pigsy?"

"It's not bad manners," said Pigsy. "This is what's called 'every turn brings blessing.'" Again Tripitaka shouted at him to get out. The idiot went to the door and stood glaring at the Star of Blessing, fixing him with a furious, unblinking stare.

"You clumsy lout," said the Star of Blessing, "when did I ever do you wrong, that you should hate me so?"

"It's not that I hate you," said Pigsy. "This is called 'turning the head to look back upon blessing.'"

As the idiot came out the door, he spied a young acolyte carrying four tea-spoons, just going to fetch cups and bring fruit and tea. Pigsy snatched them away in one grab, ran up onto the hall, took a little chime in hand, and went banging and beating it about, playing at both ends.

"This monk grows ever more disrespectful," said the Great Immortal.

Pigsy laughed. "It's not disrespect — this is called 'the four seasons of good fortune and celebration.'"

But let us leave Pigsy clowning and carrying on. Let us tell instead how Pilgrim rode his auspicious cloud away from Penglai and soon came to the fairy mountain of Fangzhang — a truly splendid place. There is a poem to prove it:

> Fangzhang towers lofty, a separate heaven of its own,
> where the Palace of the Grand Origin gathers the immortals.
> The purple terrace's light shines on the Three Pure Ones' road;
> the fragrance of flower and tree floats up through five-hued mist.
> The golden phoenix abounds about the coiled-stamen towers;
> who forces the jade-cream to irrigate the mushroom fields?
> Emerald peaches and purple plums newly ripen,
> and the immortals' tidings change again after ten thousand years.

Pilgrim brought down the head of his cloud, but had no heart to enjoy the scenery. As he walked along, he caught only a thick wave of fragrant wind and the cry of a black crane — and there, by that wall, stood an immortal. He saw:

> Filling the sky, ten thousand rays of rosy light appear;
> colored mist drifts and floats, its glow unbroken.
> The cinnabar phoenix holding a flower is fresher still;
> the green simurgh wheels and dances, its cry tender and bright.
> Blessing like the Eastern Sea, longevity like the mountains;
> his face like a young boy's, his body hale.
> In his gourd lie hidden cave-heavens and the deathless elixir;
> at his waist hangs the longevity-script as old as the sun.
> Many a time he has sent down good omens to mankind;
> many a time he has dispelled the world's calamities and woes.
> Emperor Wu once proclaimed him to add to his years of life;
> at the Jasper Pool he attends each Flat-Peach banquet.
> He teaches the host of monks to cast off worldly bonds,
> and points open the great Way, bright as lightning.
> He too has crossed the sea to wish a thousand autumns,
> and often goes to the Spirit Mountain to behold the Buddha's face.
> His holy title is the Great Sovereign Lord of Eastern Florescence,
> the first among the immortal kin of mist and rosy cloud.

Sun Pilgrim went forward with a friendly face, calling out, "Sovereign Lord, my greetings to you!"

The Sovereign Lord hurriedly returned the bow. "Great Sage, forgive my failure to receive you. Pray come to my humble dwelling and take some tea." Taking Pilgrim by the hand, he led him in. It was truly a fairy palace of cowrie gateways, with jasper pools and gem-bright pavilions past all telling. They had just sat down to wait for tea when, from behind a kingfisher screen, there came a young boy. And how was he got up?

> Clad in Taoist robes that flutter with the glint of rosy cloud,
> a silken sash at his waist, its light scattered in tangles.
> On his head a scholar's kerchief patterned with the Dipper's stars;
> on his feet straw sandals for roaming the fairy peaks.
> He has refined the True Origin, sloughed off the husk of self;
> when merit and conduct are complete, joy follows the will.
> He has seen through the source — the essence, breath, and spirit;
> his master knows him true, with never a false stroke.
> Fled from fame, he now rejoices in life without bound;
> the cycle of the sexagenary years cannot constrain him.
> Through winding corridors, up to the treasure-tower he climbs;
> three times he has filched the Flat Peaches of Heaven.
> Out from behind the kingfisher screen, on faint and fragrant cloud —
> this little immortal is none other than Dongfang Shuo.

Seeing him, Pilgrim laughed. "So the little thief is here too! There are no peaches in the Sovereign Lord's place for you to steal and eat."

Dongfang Shuo made a bow toward the high seat and answered, "You old thief, what have you come here for? My master has no elixir of immortality for you to steal and eat."

"Manqian, stop your wild talk," called the Sovereign Lord. "Bring the tea." (Manqian was Dongfang Shuo's Taoist name.) He hurried inside and brought out two cups of tea.

When they had drunk, Pilgrim said, "Old Monkey has come on a matter I wish to lay before you — I don't know whether you'll grant it."

"What matter?" said the Sovereign Lord. "I'll gladly hear your instruction."

"Lately, while escorting the Tang Monk westward, I passed Longevity Mountain and the Five Estates Temple. Because that temple's young acolyte behaved insolently, I lost my temper for a moment and pushed over his ginseng-fruit tree. So we are held up, and the Tang Monk cannot get free. I've come especially to your honored presence to beg the gift of a remedy to cure it. I beseech you, be generous."

"You monkey," said the Sovereign Lord, "with no thought for one thing or another, you go stirring up trouble everywhere. That Zhenyuanzi of the Five Estates Temple, whose holy title is 'Sovereign as Old as the World,' is the patriarch of the earthbound immortals — how could you go and offend him? His ginseng-fruit tree is the Herb-Restoring Elixir; merely to steal and eat the fruit was already a crime, yet you went on to push over the tree as well. Would he ever let that drop?"

"That's just it," said Pilgrim. "We made our escape, but he overtook us and bagged us all up in one sleeve like so many sweat-rags — and that's what galls me. There was nothing for it but to promise to seek a cure for him, and so I've come to beg of you."

"I have a pellet of the Nine-Turn Grand-Unity Restorative Elixir," said the Sovereign Lord, "but it can only cure the living creatures of the world; it cannot heal a tree. A tree is the soul of soil and wood, nourished by Heaven and moistened by Earth. If it were a common mortal fruit-tree, a cure might still be managed. But this Longevity Mountain is a blessed land of the primordial Before-Heaven, and the Five Estates Temple is a cave-heaven of the He Continent, and the ginseng fruit is a numinous root born of the very opening of Heaven and Earth. How could it be cured? No remedy, no remedy."

"Since there's no remedy," said Pilgrim, "old Monkey takes his leave." The Sovereign Lord still wished to keep him for a cup of jade nectar, but Pilgrim said, "The rescue is urgent — I dare not linger." So he mounted his cloud and went on to the sea-isle of Yingzhou — also a splendid place. There is a poem to prove it:

> Pearl-trees, exquisite and fine, shine through the purple mist;
> Yingzhou's palaces and towers join with all the heavens.
> Green hills and emerald waters, the jasper-blossom bright;
> jade nectar, and Kunwu steel hard as iron and stone.
> Five-hued azure cockerels crow to the sea-borne sun;
> thousand-year cinnabar phoenixes drink the vermilion vapor.
> Worldly men never fathom the scene within the gourd —
> beyond all images, the spring light of a billion years.

When the Great Sage reached Yingzhou, he saw, beneath the cinnabar cliffs and pearl-trees, several white-haired, hoary-bearded elders — immortals with childlike faces and crane-feathered temples — playing chess and drinking wine, talking and laughing, singing songs. Truly it was:

Auspicious clouds full of light, lucky vapors floating fragrant. Bright simurghs cried at the cave-mouth; black cranes danced upon the mountaintop. Emerald lotus-root and water-peaches served as relish for the wine; cross-grafted pears and fire-jujubes for a thousand autumns of long life. Each of them heeds no cinnabar summons of the court, yet each is enrolled in the immortals' register. Carefree, they drift with the waves; at ease, they yield to the pure and tranquil. The cycle of the heavens cannot rein them in; the whole of Earth and sky is theirs to roam free. Black gibbons offering fruit follow in pairs, full of lovely affection; white deer holding flowers bow down in couples, full of devoted tenderness.

The old men were just then merry in their feasting when Pilgrim called out in a loud voice, "How about taking me along to play and amuse myself a bit?"

Seeing him, the immortals hurried forward to greet him. There is a poem to prove it:

> The ginseng-fruit tree's numinous root is snapped;
> the Great Sage calls on immortals to seek a wondrous art.
> Winding through cinnabar mist, out from the treasure-grove,
> the Nine Elders of Yingzhou come forward to receive him.

Pilgrim recognized them as the Nine Elders and laughed. "Old brothers, you've it easy here!"

"Great Sage," said the Nine Elders, "had you kept to the straight path in those years and not made havoc of Heaven's palace, you'd be even more at ease than we. But now it's well — we hear you've returned to the true and turned westward to worship the Buddha. How is it you've found the leisure to come here?"

Pilgrim laid out the whole matter of seeking a remedy to cure the tree. The Nine Elders too were greatly alarmed. "You really do go courting disaster — courting disaster! We honestly have no remedy."

"Since there's no remedy," said Pilgrim, "then I'll bid you farewell." The Nine Elders still pressed him to drink the jasper draught and eat the emerald lotus-root. Pilgrim absolutely refused to sit; he only stood and drank one cup of the draught and ate one piece of lotus-root, then hurriedly left Yingzhou and went straight back across the Great Eastern Ocean.

Soon he sighted Potalaka Mountain not far off, so he brought down the head of his cloud and went straight up onto the Potalaka cliff. There he saw the Bodhisattva Guanyin in her purple bamboo grove, expounding the scriptures and preaching the Dharma to the great spirits of the heavens, to Moksha, and to the Dragon Maiden. There is a poem to prove it:

> The sea-lord's city stands high, its lucky vapors dense;
> behold besides the wondrous things, marvels without end.
> Know that beyond the thousand kinds of dim half-seen,
> all issues from the single grade of faint and subtle.
> The Four Sages, in their season, attain the true fruit;
> the Six Common Beings, having heard, escape the cage.
> Shaolin holds another taste of truth besides —
> flower and fruit, fragrant and fair, fill the trees with red.

The Bodhisattva had already seen Pilgrim coming and at once bade the great mountain-guarding spirit go to meet him. The great spirit came out of the grove and called, "Sun Wukong, where are you off to?"

Pilgrim raised his head and shouted, "You bear-monster! Is 'Wukong' a name for the likes of you to be calling? If old Monkey hadn't spared you in the old days, you'd long since have been a corpse-ghost of Black Wind Mountain. Now that you've followed the Bodhisattva, received the good fruit, dwell on this fairy mountain, and constantly hear the teaching of the Dharma — can't you call me even one 'Your Honor'?"

That black bear had indeed attained the true fruit, and now guarded Potalaka in the Bodhisattva's service, styled the Great Spirit — and it was all thanks to Pilgrim. So he could only smile apologetically. "Great Sage, the ancients said, 'A gentleman does not dwell on old wrongs.' Why keep bringing it up? The Bodhisattva sent me to receive you."

At this Pilgrim composed himself in grave reverence, and went with the great spirit into the purple bamboo grove to pay his respects to the Bodhisattva.

"Wukong," said the Bodhisattva, "how far has the Tang Monk traveled now?"

"He has traveled as far as Longevity Mountain in the Western Continent of Cattle-Gift," said Pilgrim.

"On that Longevity Mountain there is a Five Estates Temple, and the Great Immortal Zhenyuan," said the Bodhisattva. "Have you met him?"

Pilgrim bowed his head and said, "It's because of being at the Five Estates Temple. Your disciple did not recognize the Great Immortal Zhenyuan, but injured and destroyed his ginseng-fruit tree and offended him. So he has held up my master, who cannot go forward."

The Bodhisattva, knowing it well, said reproachfully, "You reckless ape, you don't know good from bad! That ginseng-fruit tree of his is a numinous root from the very opening of Heaven and Earth. Zhenyuanzi is the patriarch of the earthbound immortals — even I yield him three parts. How could you go and injure his tree?"

Pilgrim bowed again. "Your disciple truly did not know. That day he was not at home — only two fairy boys attended us. It was Zhu Wuneng who knew he had fruit and wanted one to taste. Your disciple did indeed steal three of them, and we brothers divided and ate them. When the boys found out, they cursed us without end, so your disciple lost his temper and pushed over the tree. The next day he returned and overtook us, bagged us all up in one sleeve, bound us with rope, flogged us with a whip, and beat us under questioning a whole day. We escaped that night, but he overtook us and bagged us again, just as before. Twice and three times — there was truly no escaping. I've already agreed to cure the tree for him, and so I went seeking a remedy over the sea, roaming all the Three Isles, but none of the immortals had the power. And so, with single-hearted devotion, your disciple has come especially to beg of the Bodhisattva, hoping in your mercy you'll graciously bestow a remedy, to save the Tang Monk so he may go west soon."

"Why didn't you come to see me sooner," said the Bodhisattva, "instead of going off to search the isles?"

Hearing this, Pilgrim secretly rejoiced in his heart. "What luck, what luck! The Bodhisattva surely has a remedy!" And he went forward again to beg.

"The sweet-dew water at the bottom of my pure vase," said the Bodhisattva, "is good for curing fairy trees and numinous sprouts."

"Has it ever been tested?" asked Pilgrim.

"It has been tested," said the Bodhisattva.

"What proof is there?" asked Pilgrim.

"In years past," said the Bodhisattva, "the Supreme Lord Lao Tzu once made a wager with me. He pulled off a sprig of my willow, set it in his cinnabar-refining furnace, scorched it dry and crisp, and sent it back to me. I took it and stuck it in my vase, and within a single day and night it grew green twigs and leaves again, just as it was before."

Pilgrim laughed. "What luck indeed, what luck indeed! If a thing scorched and crisped can be cured back to life, how much more a tree merely pushed over — where's the difficulty in that?"

The Bodhisattva instructed her assembly, "Keep watch over the grove; I'll go and return." Then, holding the pure vase in her hand, with the white parrot singing sweetly ahead and the Great Sage following behind, she set out. There is a poem to prove it:

> The jade-tuft and golden form the world can scarcely tell of —
> truly the merciful one who saves from suffering.
> In ages past she met the Buddha-of-No-Defilement;
> to this day she has won a body of efficacious action.
> Through many lives she calmed the waves of desire's sea;
> a single field of heart, free of the smallest dust.
> The sweet dew, long proven a truly wondrous Dharma,
> will surely keep the treasure-tree forever in eternal spring.

Now in the temple the Great Immortal and the three old men were just then in pleasant talk, when suddenly they saw the Great Sage bring down the head of his cloud, calling, "The Bodhisattva is coming — quick, go meet her, go meet her!"

In a flurry, the three stars together with Zhenyuanzi, and Tripitaka with his disciples, all went out together from the treasure-hall to receive her. The Bodhisattva had only just halted her auspicious cloud. First she exchanged words with Zhenyuanzi, then made her courtesies to the three stars, and when the courtesies were done, took the high seat. Before the steps, Pilgrim led the Tang Monk, Pigsy, and Sandy to make their bows, and the various immortals of the temple came forward to pay their respects as well.

"Great Immortal," said Pilgrim, "no need to hesitate. Hurry and set out an incense table at once, and invite the Bodhisattva to go and cure that fruit-tree of yours."

The Great Immortal bowed and thanked the Bodhisattva. "It's such a trifling affair — how could I dare to trouble the Bodhisattva to descend?"

"The Tang Monk is my disciple," said the Bodhisattva, "and Sun Wukong has offended you, sir; it is only right that he make amends for your treasure-tree."

"Since that's so," said the three old men, "there's no need for modest demurrals. Let us all go into the garden, Bodhisattva, and have a look."

The Great Immortal at once ordered the incense table set out and the rear garden swept clean. He invited the Bodhisattva to go ahead, with the three old men following. When Tripitaka and his disciples and all the immortals of the temple came into the garden to look, there lay the tree fallen on the ground, the soil split open and its roots exposed, leaves fallen and branches withered.

"Wukong," called the Bodhisattva, "stretch out your hand." Pilgrim opened his left hand. The Bodhisattva dipped her willow-sprig into the sweet dew of the vase and drew upon Pilgrim's palm a talismanic sign for raising the dead and restoring life, then bade him press it down beneath the tree's roots and watch for the water to come forth as his measure. Pilgrim clenched his fist and thrust it down beneath the roots, and in a moment there welled up a pool of clear spring water.

"That water must not touch any vessel of the Five Elements," said the Bodhisattva. "You must scoop it out with a jade dipper, raise the tree upright, and pour it down from the top. Then the roots and bark will naturally knit together, the leaves will grow and the buds sprout, the branches turn green and the fruit appear."

"Little Taoists," said Pilgrim, "quick, fetch a jade dipper."

"This poor Taoist's humble mountain has no jade dipper," said Zhenyuanzi. "We have only jade tea-bowls and jade wine-cups — will those do?"

"As long as it's a jade vessel that can scoop water, it'll do," said the Bodhisattva. "Bring them and let me see."

The Great Immortal at once bade his young acolytes bring out some twenty or thirty tea-bowls and forty or fifty wine-cups, and they scooped the clear spring out from beneath the roots. Pilgrim, Pigsy, and Sandy hoisted up the tree, propped it upright, and heaped soil about it. Then, bowl by bowl, they offered up the sweet spring in the jade vessels to the Bodhisattva, who sprinkled it on with her willow-sprig, finely and carefully, all the while reciting scriptures and spells in her mouth.

In a little while, when she had sprinkled out all the scooped water, the tree was indeed green again as before, its leaves shading dense and deep, and upon it hung twenty-three ginseng fruits.

The two acolytes Pure Wind and Bright Moon said, "When the fruit went missing the other day, we counted over and over and could only make out twenty-two; now that it's come back to life, how is there one more?"

"'Time reveals a man's heart,'" said Pilgrim. "The other day old Monkey stole only three. One of them fell to the ground, and the Local God told me that this treasure, meeting the soil, sinks into it. Pigsy only kept yelling that I'd cheated and shorted him — that's how the truth leaked out — and the matter dragged on till now, when it's finally come clear."

"The reason I just now used no vessel of the Five Elements," said the Bodhisattva, "is that I knew this thing stands in dread of the Five Elements."

The Great Immortal was overjoyed, and at once ordered the golden mallet brought, and knocked down ten of the fruits. He invited the Bodhisattva and the three old men back to the treasure-hall — first to thank them for their labor, and second to hold a Ginseng-Fruit Assembly. The young immortals arranged tables and chairs, spread out cinnabar trays, and invited the Bodhisattva to take the high seat of honor, the three old men the left seats, the Tang Monk the right seat, and Zhenyuanzi the front seat to keep them company, and each of them ate one. There is a poem to prove it:

> Within Longevity Mountain, an ancient cave-heaven:
> the ginseng ripens once in nine thousand years.
> The numinous root appeared, its sprouts and branches harmed;
> the sweet dew nourished it, and fruit and leaves were whole.
> The three old men, met in joy, are all old friends;
> the four monks, blessed in the meeting, were fated of old.
> From now on, all who eat the ginseng fruit
> shall be immortals of long life, never to grow old.

At this time the Bodhisattva and the three old men each ate one. The Tang Monk, now realizing it was a treasure of the immortal household, also ate one. Wukong and his two brothers each ate one as well; Zhenyuanzi ate one to keep them company, and the immortals of the temple divided one among them.

Then Pilgrim thanked the Bodhisattva and saw her back up to the Potalaka cliff, and sent the three stars straight back to Penglai Isle. Zhenyuanzi then laid out a feast of vegetable dishes and wine and became sworn brothers with Pilgrim. This is the very thing — without a fight there's no acquaintance — and the two households became as one. Master and the four disciples, full of joy and gladness, rested as night fell. And the elder now found that:

Having the karmic bond to eat the Herb-Restoring Elixir, he wins long life — but must yet bitterly endure the monsters' toils.

In the end, how they took their leave the next day — listen to the explanation in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 27 -->
# Chapter 27: The Corpse-Demon Thrice Deceives the Tang Monk; The Holy Pilgrim in Wrath Drives Off the Handsome Monkey King

So it was that the next morning, at first light, Tripitaka and his disciples made ready to press on. But Master Zhenyuan, having sworn brotherhood with Sun Wukong, found the two of them so wholly of one mind and one heart that he would by no means let them go. Again he laid out a feast and pressed his hospitality upon them, so that they lingered five or six days in all. Yet the elder, having tasted of the Herb-of-Return elixir, felt truly as though he had sloughed off his mortal frame and been born anew — clear of spirit, hale of body. His heart was set so hard upon the scriptures that he could not bear to tarry, and at last, there being no help for it, they set out.

Master and disciples took their leave and went their way. Before long there rose up before them a high mountain. Said Tripitaka, "Disciples, there is a steep and perilous range ahead. I fear the horse may not be able to climb it. We must all take the greatest care." Said Wukong, "Set your heart at ease, Master. We shall manage it of ourselves." Good Monkey King — he laid his iron cudgel crosswise before the horse, cut a path open through the mountain, and climbed the high cliffs, gazing out upon a scene that seemed without end:

> Peak upon crag in folded ranks,
> ravine and gully looping round.
> Tigers and wolves move in their packs,
> the roe and stag go troop by troop.
> Countless musk-deer burrow in clusters,
> foxes and hares across the slope gather in swarms.
> Pythons a thousand feet long,
> serpents stretching ten thousand fathoms.
> The great pythons breathe a fog of sorrow,
> the long snakes spit a goblin wind.
> Beside the road the brambles trail and tangle,
> upon the ridge the pine and cedar stand handsome.
> Climbing fig and creeper fill the eye,
> fragrant grasses run to meet the sky.
> Shadows fall toward the dark sea in the north,
> clouds part where the Dipper's handle hangs in the south.
> Through all the ages it holds the old primal breath;
> a thousand peaks loom in ranks, the sunlight cold.

Upon his horse the elder's heart was struck with dread. But the Great Sage put forth his arts: brandishing the iron cudgel, he gave one roaring howl that sent the wolves and reptiles tumbling and scrambling away, and the tigers and leopards fleeing in rout.

Master and disciples entered this mountain, and as they came at last to a rugged, towering place, Tripitaka said, "Wukong, this whole day my belly has gone hungry. Go somewhere and beg us a little vegetarian food to eat." Wukong answered with a forced smile, "Master, how little you understand. Here we are halfway up a mountain — no village before us, no inn behind us. Even with money there is nowhere to buy. Where would you have me look for a meal?"

Tripitaka was displeased, and scolded aloud, "You monkey! Think how you were pinned by the Tathagata inside a stone box at the Mountain of Two Frontiers — your mouth could speak, but your feet could not walk. It was I who saved your life, who laid my hand upon your crown and gave you the vows, and made you my disciple. How is it you will not bestir yourself, but forever harbor a lazy heart?"

Said Wukong, "Your disciple is diligent enough. When have I ever been lazy?"

"If you are so diligent," said Tripitaka, "why will you not beg me a meal? My belly is empty — how am I to travel? Besides, in this place of mountain miasma and pestilent vapors, how shall we ever reach the Thunderclap Monastery?"

Said Wukong, "Master, don't take it amiss, and spare your words. I know your honored temper runs to pride; cross or slight you in the least, and at once you'll be reciting that certain spell. Dismount and sit you down in peace, and let me go find where there are folk and beg a meal."

Then Wukong gave a leap and sprang up into the clouds, shaded his eyes with his hand, and gazed out wide. Alas, the road to the West was utterly desolate — no farmsteads, no walled holds, no human dwellings — a place of many trees and little smoke from any hearth. He looked a long while, and at last, away to the south, he saw a high mountain, and on its sunlit slope a patch of bright red flecks. Wukong brought his cloud down and said, "Master, there's something to eat."

The elder asked what it might be. Said Wukong, "There are no homes hereabouts to beg from, but on that southern mountain is a patch of red — surely ripe wild peaches. I'll go pick a few to stave off your hunger." Tripitaka said gladly, "If a man who has left the household life can have peaches to eat, that is a portion above his deserving." So Wukong took up the alms-bowl, called up his auspicious light, and — watch him! — went tumbling and somersaulting away on a chill, whistling wind, and in a moment was off to the southern mountain to pick peaches; of which no more for now.

Now there is an old saying: "Where the mountain is high, there must be monsters; where the ridge is steep, there spirits are born." And true enough, on this mountain there dwelt a demon, whom the Great Sage's going had startled. Treading the dark wind in the clouds, she looked down and saw the elder sitting upon the ground, and could not contain her joy. "What luck! What luck!" she said. "For years my household and folk have spoken of the Tang monk from the Land of the East, who goes to fetch the Great Vehicle scriptures. He is the very incarnation of the Golden Cicada, the original body of ten lifetimes' cultivation. Whoever eats but a single morsel of his flesh wins long life and immortality. And here, this very day, he has come!"

The demon pressed forward to seize him at once — but she saw that at the elder's left and right hands stood two mighty generals guarding him, and she dared not draw near. Who were these two generals? They were Bajie and Sha Monk. Though neither possessed any very great powers, yet Bajie had once been Marshal Tianpeng of the Heavenly River, and Sha Monk the Curtain-Lifting Captain; the awe and breath of their former rank had not yet wholly faded from them, and so she dared not approach. Said the demon, "Let me toy with him a while, and see what comes of it."

Good demon — she stilled the dark wind, and there in a hollow of the mountain shook her body and transformed, becoming a maiden with a face like the moon and the bloom of flowers, of beauty past telling: brows clear, eyes lovely, teeth white, lips red. In her left hand she carried a little green earthen pot, in her right a green porcelain bottle, and she came straight from the west toward the east, making for the Tang monk:

> The holy pilgrim rests his horse upon the crag,
> when of a sudden a skirted maiden draws near.
> Her kingfisher sleeves sway light, baring jade-shoot fingers;
> her Xiang-silk skirt trails slanting, showing the golden lotus of her feet.
> Sweat dews her powdered face like blossoms holding rain,
> dust brushes her moth-brows like willows wreathed in mist.
> When one looks close and fixes the eye to gaze —
> see, see, she has come right up beside them.

When Tripitaka saw her, he called out, "Bajie! Sha Monk! Wukong said just now that this was a wild and empty place with no people — yet look, here comes someone out yonder!"

Said Bajie, "Master, you and Sha Monk sit still; let old Pig go and have a look." The blockhead set down his nine-toothed rake, smoothed his cassock straight, and went swaggering and swaying along, putting on a refined and scholarly air, straight up to meet her with an oafish, smirking face. And in truth, from afar she was hard to make out, but seen close at hand she was plain enough — that woman was formed like this:

> Ice-flesh hiding bones of jade,
> her collar baring a creamy breast.
> Willow brows heaped with kingfisher dark,
> apricot eyes flashing silver stars.
> A face fair as the moon's own image,
> a nature pure by nature's grant.
> Her form like a swallow nestled in willows,
> her voice like an oriole warbling in the woods.
> Half-opened crabapple cupping the dawn-sun,
> a peony just unfolded, toying with the bright spring.

When Bajie saw how comely she was, the blockhead's earthly passions stirred, and he could not hold his foolish, rambling tongue. He cried, "Lady Bodhisattva, where are you bound? And what is that you carry in your hands?" Plain as day she was a demon, yet he could not tell. The woman answered readily, "Elder, in this green pot is fragrant cooked rice, and in the green bottle is fried wheat-gluten. I have come to this place for no other cause than that I have a vow to fulfill — a vow to feast holy monks."

Hearing this, Bajie's heart was filled with joy. He spun about at once and went galloping back like a pig in a frenzy, to report to Tripitaka: "Master! 'The fortunate man has Heaven's own reward.' You were hungry, and bade my elder brother go beg a meal — and that monkey has gone off heaven-knows-where to pick peaches and play. Eating too many peaches gnaws at the stomach and loosens the bowels. But look — is that not someone come to feast the monks?"

Tripitaka would not believe it. "You great clumsy lout, talking nonsense! We've walked all this stretch and not met one decent soul. Where would a monk-feasting woman spring from?" Said Bajie, "Master — has she not arrived already?"

The moment Tripitaka saw her, he sprang up in haste, pressed his palms together at his breast, and said, "Lady Bodhisattva, where is your honored home? What family are you of? What vow of the heart brings you here to feast the monks?" Plain as day she was a demon, yet the elder too could not tell. Seeing the Tang monk ask after her origins, the demon stood her ground and forged a false tale on the spot, with honeyed words and flowery speech, to cheat and beguile him:

"Master, this mountain is called the White Tiger Ridge, where serpents turn back and beasts take fright. Straight to the west, below, is my home. My father and mother live at home; they read the scriptures and love to do good, and they feast far and near every monk of the road. Because they had no son, they prayed to the gods and worked their merits, and so begot me, their poor daughter. They wished to marry me into another house to raise the family's standing — but then they feared to have no support in their old age, and so took me a son-in-law into the home instead, to keep them in their age and see them to their graves."

Hearing this, Tripitaka said, "Lady Bodhisattva, your words are amiss. The holy classics say: 'While father and mother are living, one does not roam afar; and if one must roam, it must be to a fixed place.' Since you have father and mother at home, and they have taken you a son-in-law besides, and there is a vow to fulfill, it would have been well to send your husband. Why do you walk this mountain yourself, with not even a maidservant to attend you? This is not to keep a wife's proper way."

The woman, smiling sweetly, hastened to answer with pretty words: "Master, my husband is in a hollow on the north side of the mountain, hoeing the fields with a few hired hands. This is the midday meal I have cooked to take to those men to eat. It is only because in this fifth-and-sixth month of high summer there is no one to send, and my parents are aged besides, that I have come to bring it in person. Then of a sudden I met you three travelers from afar, and bethought me how my parents love to do good — and so I would feast these monks with this very food. If you do not scorn it, I would offer it as a poor man's humble gift."

Said Tripitaka, "Amen, amen! I have a disciple gone to pick fruit; he will return presently. I dare not eat. Suppose I, a monk, ate your food, and your husband came to learn of it and scolded you for it — would not the blame for that fall upon this poor monk?"

When the woman saw that the Tang monk would not eat, again her face bloomed like spring, and she said, "Master, ah — that my parents feast the monks is a small thing; but my husband is an even more virtuous man. All his life what he loves is mending bridges and repairing roads, honoring the old and pitying the poor. If he but hears that this food was given for you to eat, then, by the bond of love between us as man and wife, he will hold it dearer by far than common." Yet still Tripitaka would not eat.

But beside him this enraged Bajie past bearing. The blockhead thrust out his snout and grumbled aloud: "There are monks without number under Heaven, but never one so weak and soft as this old monk of mine! Here is food ready before him, and a third of it he will not touch — he must wait for that monkey to come, and split it into four before he'll eat!" And without waiting to argue the matter, with one shove of his snout he overturned the pot, and was about to fall to.

But just then Wukong, having picked a few peaches from the top of the southern mountain, came tumbling back upon a somersault with the alms-bowl in his hands. Opening wide his fiery eyes and golden pupils to look, he knew the woman for a demon. Down went the bowl; out came the iron cudgel, and he aimed a blow straight at her head. The elder, terrified, caught hold of his arm and cried, "Wukong! You come charging up — whom would you strike?"

Said Wukong, "Master, this woman before you — do not take her for a decent person. She is a demon, come to deceive you." Said Tripitaka, "You monkey-head! In your time you had some power of sight; how is it you talk such wild nonsense today? This Lady Bodhisattva has so good a heart as to wish to feast us with this food — how can you say she is a demon?"

Wukong laughed and said, "Master, how should you know? When old Monkey was a demon-king in the Water-Curtain Cave, if ever I had a mind to eat human flesh, this was just my way: I would turn myself into gold or silver, or into a fine mansion, or into a drunken man, or into a woman's charms. And if some lovesick fool grew enamored of me, I would lure him into the cave, and there work my will upon him to my heart's content — steaming him or boiling him to my use; and what I could not finish, I'd dry in the sun against the rainy weather. Master, had I come back a moment late, you would surely have fallen into her snare and met her cruel hand."

But the Tang monk would by no means believe it, and only kept saying she was a good person. Said Wukong, "Master, now I understand you. You saw her good looks, and your earthly passions are surely stirred. If that's truly your meaning, let Bajie fell a few trees, let Sha Monk gather some grass, and I'll play carpenter and put up a little hut here on the spot, where you and she can consummate the match. We'll all break up and go our ways — and would that not be a tidy bit of business? Why go on toiling over mountains, fetching what scriptures and all?"

Now the elder was by nature a soft and gentle man, and he could in no wise stomach such talk. He was so shamed that his shaven scalp flushed crimson clear to his ears.

While Tripitaka stood there in his shame and confusion, Wukong's temper flared again, and he whipped out the iron cudgel and struck full at the demon's face. But the monster had some skill: she worked her "corpse-release method," and when she saw the cudgel coming, she rallied her spirit and slipped away beforehand, leaving a false corpse struck dead upon the ground.

This so terrified the elder that he shook and trembled, and muttered with his lips, "This monkey is utterly without manners! Time and again I counsel him, and he will not heed, but slays a living person for no cause at all!"

Said Wukong, "Master, don't take it amiss. Come and have a look at what's in this pot." Sha Monk supported the elder and brought him near to look — and where was any fragrant rice? It was a pot full of long, tail-dragging maggots; and where was any wheat-gluten? It was a few green frogs and warty toads, hopping all over the ground. Now at last the elder was a third part convinced.

But that could not stop Bajie from his sullen spite. Standing aside, he leaked out eight parts of mischief, egging the master on: "Master, to speak of this woman — she was a farm-wife of these parts, taking food down to the fields, who chanced to meet us on the road. How can he frame her as a demon? Elder brother's cudgel is heavy. He came up and tried his hand with one blow, and unexpectedly beat her to death. Fearing you'd recite that Tight-Fillet spell, he's worked a deliberate eye-blinding trick — turned her into this sort of thing to dazzle your sight, so you won't say the spell."

From this one speech of Tripitaka's came all his ill luck. For he truly believed the blockhead's prodding, and, making the secret sign with his fingers, recited the spell with his lips. Wukong at once cried, "My head! My head aches! Stop, stop — say what you have to say!" Said the Tang monk, "What is there to say? A man who has left the household life must ever be merciful, must never let the kind heart depart from his thoughts — sweeping the floor for fear of harming an ant's life, screening the lamp in pity for the moth. How is it that you act with violence at every step, and have beaten this innocent person to death? What use is it to fetch scriptures? Go back where you came from!"

Said Wukong, "Master, where would you have me go back to?" Said the Tang monk, "I'll not have you for my disciple." Said Wukong, "If you'll not have me for your disciple, I only fear you'll never make your way to the Western Heaven." Said the Tang monk, "My life is in Heaven's keeping. If it's fated that yonder demon should steam me and eat me, or boil me, that cannot be helped. But you — could you ever save me from my appointed end? Be off with you, quick."

Said Wukong, "Master, that I should go is well enough — only I've never yet repaid your kindness." Said the Tang monk, "What kindness have I ever shown you?" Hearing this, the Great Sage knelt down at once and knocked his head upon the ground. "Old Monkey, because I made great havoc in the Heavenly Palace, brought down upon myself the disaster of bodily harm, and was pinned by our Buddha beneath the Mountain of Two Frontiers. By good fortune the Bodhisattva Guanyin gave me the discipline of the vows, and by good fortune you, Master, set my body free. If I do not go up to the Western Heaven at your side, it would show me one who knew a kindness yet did not repay it — no true man — and would make a name to be cursed through ten thousand ages and a thousand autumns."

Now this Tang monk was a holy man of compassion and mercy, and seeing Wukong plead so piteously, his heart relented and turned. "Since you put it so," he said, "I'll forgive you this once more. But never again be insolent. If you go on doing evil as before, I'll recite the spell over and over — twenty times round." Said Wukong, "Thirty times, if you please — only I'll strike no one again." Then at last he served the Tang monk back onto his horse, and offered up the peaches he had picked. The Tang monk ate a few there in the saddle, to stave off his hunger for the while.

Now the demon, it turned out, had escaped with her life and risen into the air; for that one blow of Wukong's had not slain her — she had sent her spirit forth and gone. There in the clouds she gnashed her teeth and silently cursed Wukong: "For years I'd only heard tell of his powers, and today, sure enough, the tale proves no idle one. That Tang monk no longer knew me, and was just about to eat the food. Had he but bent his head and given it a single sniff, I'd have snatched him up in a trice — and would he not be mine? But unlooked-for, that fellow came charging back and broke up my game, and very nearly struck me down with a blow. If I let this monk go, then truly all my labor is for nothing. I'll go down again and toy with him once more."

Good demon — she brought down her dark cloud, and there at the foot of the mountain ahead shook her body and changed, becoming an old woman, fully fourscore years of age, leaning on a crook-headed bamboo staff, coming along with a wail at every step. When Bajie saw her, he cried out in great alarm, "Master, this is bad! That old dame has come looking for someone!" Said the Tang monk, "Looking for whom?" Said Bajie, "The one elder brother beat to death must surely be her daughter — and this is surely her mother, come searching for her!"

Said Wukong, "Brother, don't talk rubbish. That woman was eighteen, and this old dame is eighty. How could she be bearing children sixty years on? It's a sham, beyond doubt. Let old Monkey go and have a look." Good Wukong — he strode up and drew near to look, and the monster was:

> Falsely changed into a granny,
> both temples white as ice and snow.
> Slow and dragging is her gait,
> timid and faltering her step.
> A frail thin body, gaunt and spare,
> a face like a withered cabbage-leaf.
> Her cheekbones jut up high,
> her lips turn down apart.
> Old age is not as youth once was —
> her whole face is creased like a folded lotus-leaf.

Wukong knew her for the demon, and wasting no words upon argument, he raised the cudgel and struck straight at her head. When the monster saw the cudgel rise, she rallied as before, sent her primal spirit forth, slipped her true self away, and left a false corpse struck dead at the side of the mountain road.

The instant the Tang monk saw it, he tumbled in fright from his horse and lay down by the roadside; and without a single further word, he recited the Tight-Fillet spell backward, fully twenty times over. Poor Wukong — his head was squeezed tight as a pinch-waisted gourd, and the pain was past all bearing. He came rolling forward and pleaded, "Master, stop the spell! Whatever you have to say, say it and be done." Said the Tang monk, "What is there to say? A man who has left the household life, whose ear hears words of good, falls not into Hell. I exhort and reform you so — how is it you do nothing but act with violence? You've beaten one innocent to death, and now another! What account is there of this?" Said Wukong, "She was a demon." Said the Tang monk, "This monkey talks nonsense — could there be so very many demons? You are a fellow with no heart turned toward good, a man with a will set on evil. Be gone!"

Said Wukong, "Master, you'd send me off again? Go back I will, if go I must — but there's one thing that doesn't sit right." Said the Tang monk, "What is it that doesn't sit right with you?" Bajie put in, "Master, he wants to divide the baggage with you. He's been a monk in your train these several years — he can't well go back empty-handed. Take a couple of those old worn-out tunics and broken hats out of the bundle and give them to him."

Hearing this, Wukong was so enraged he leapt and stamped. "You sharp-snouted clumsy lout! Old Monkey, all this while keeping faith with the gate of Buddha, has never harbored one hair's-breadth of envy, nor a covetous heart — how should I want to divide any baggage?" Said the Tang monk, "If you've no envy and no greed, then why do you not go?"

Said Wukong, "To tell you the truth, Master, and hide nothing — five hundred years ago, when old Monkey dwelt in the Water-Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, in the full flower of my heroic prime, I subdued the demons of seventy-two caves, and had under my hand forty-seven thousand lesser fiends. On my head I wore a cap of purple gold; on my body a robe of ochre yellow; round my waist a belt of Lantian jade; on my feet cloud-treading boots; and in my hand the As-You-Will Gold-Banded Cudgel. I was truly somebody in my day. But since I passed through the chastening of my sins, shaved my head, and held fast to the upright gate of the monk, and followed you as your disciple, this gold fillet has been clamped upon my head. If I go back now, it would shame me to face the folk of my old home. Master, if you truly want none of me, then recite the Loose-Fillet spell, take this band off, and hand it back to you — slip it onto someone else's head — and I'll be glad and content. That too would be a way to have followed you for a season. Surely there's that much human feeling left between us?"

The Tang monk said in great astonishment, "Wukong, at that time the Bodhisattva secretly gave me only the one scroll of the Tight-Fillet spell — there was never any Loose-Fillet spell at all." Said Wukong, "If there's no Loose-Fillet spell, then you'll have to take me along to walk with you yet." The elder, again at his wits' end, said, "Get up, then. I'll forgive you this once more — but you must not act with violence again." Said Wukong, "I'll not dare. I'll not dare again." And once more he served his master onto the horse, cut the path open, and they went forward.

Now the demon — it turned out Wukong's second blow had not slain her either. There in mid-air the monster heaped praises beyond ceasing upon him: "What a fine Monkey King! He has eyes indeed. Changed as I was, he still knew me. But these monks travel fast; if they pass this mountain and go forty miles down the western slope, they'll no longer be in my domain. And if some demon of another place should snatch him off, it would split the mouths of others laughing, and grind my own heart to pieces. I'll go down and toy with him once more."

Good demon — she pressed down her dark wind, and at the foot of the mountain shook her body and changed, becoming an old man. And truly he was:

> White hair like Pengzu's,
> hoary beard outdoing the Star of Longevity.
> In his ears a chiming of jade chime-stones,
> in his eyes a flickering of golden stars.
> In his hand a dragon-headed staff,
> upon his body a crane-down cloak, light.
> Prayer-beads pinched between his fingers,
> his mouth reciting the "Namo" scripture.

When the Tang monk saw him from his horse, his heart was filled with delight. "Amitabha! The West is truly a land of blessing! That old fellow can scarce make his way up the road, yet for all that he still recites the scriptures." Said Bajie, "Master, don't praise so soon — this is the very root of disaster." Said the Tang monk, "How the root of disaster?" Said Bajie, "Elder brother beat his daughter to death, and beat his old wife to death, and this is surely the old man himself come searching. If we blunder into his arms — Master, you'll have to pay with your life, on a capital charge; old Pig, as accomplice, will be sentenced to the army; and Sha Monk, for crying the orders, will be put to the post-stations. But elder brother will work some vanishing trick and slip away — and won't the three of us be left to carry the pot?"

Hearing this, Wukong said, "This blockhead-root, talking such nonsense, will only frighten the master! Let old Monkey go and have another look." He hid the cudgel close against his body, walked up, faced the monster, and called out, "Old sir, where are you bound? And how is it you walk the road and recite scriptures at once?" The demon mistook her reckoning-mark, taking the Great Sage too for some ordinary fellow, and answered, "Elder, ah — this old man's family has dwelt here for generations. All my life I have loved to do good, to feast monks, to read the scriptures and recite the Buddha's name. By fate I had no son, and begot only a single small daughter, for whom I took a son-in-law into the home. This morning she went to take food down to the fields — I fear she has fallen into a tiger's jaws. My old wife went first to look for her, and has not come back either. I know nothing at all of where they've gone, and so this old man has come out on purpose to search. If indeed their lives have been cut down, there's no help for it; I'll only gather up their bones to carry home, and bury them in the family graves."

Wukong laughed and said, "I'm the very grandsire of all tiger-makers — how is it you've got a ghost tucked up your sleeve, come to fool me? You may deceive everyone else, but you can't deceive me. I know you for a demon." The demon was so struck dumb she could not say a word.

Wukong drew out the cudgel, and reasoned within himself: "If I don't strike her, she'll seem to have made a wind out of nothing; but if I do strike her, I fear the master will recite that certain spell." Then he thought again: "If I don't beat her to death, in some idle moment she'll seize her chance and snatch the master off — and then won't I have to fret and labor all over again to save him? Better to strike. But the moment I lay her dead with one blow, the master will set to reciting the spell. As the old saying goes, 'A tiger, however fierce, won't eat its own cubs.' I'll rely on clever speech and a nimble tongue to coax him round, and then it should be well enough."
