Good Great Sage — he recited a spell, and summoned the local Earth-God of that ward and the Mountain-God of that place, saying: "This demon has come three times to make sport of my master, and this time I mean to beat her to death. Stand witness for me there in mid-air, and let her not escape." The gods heard the command — who would dare disobey? — and stationed themselves in the clouds to watch. Then where the Great Sage's cudgel fell, he struck the demon down, and at last severed her spirit-light.

Upon his horse the Tang monk again shook and trembled with fright, and could not speak. Beside him Bajie laughed again: "Fine Wukong! He's gone clean mad — only half a day on the road, and he's beaten three people to death!" The Tang monk was just about to recite the spell when Wukong rushed up before the horse and cried, "Master, stop, stop! Come and look at her shape." And there it was — a heap of powdery white bones lying there. The Tang monk said in great astonishment, "Wukong, this person has only just died — how is it she's turned into a heap of bones?"

Said Wukong, "She was a stiff corpse, a lurking spirit working its mischief, beguiling men and ruining their root here in this place. I've beaten her dead, and she has shown her true form. There's a line of writing on her spine: she's called the Lady White Bone." Hearing this, the Tang monk was indeed inclined to believe. But that could not stop Bajie from prodding at his side: "Master, his hand is heavy and his cudgel fierce. He's beaten the person dead, and only because he fears that certain spell of yours, he's deliberately worked a change into this shape to blind your eyes." The Tang monk, soft-eared in truth, believed him again, and once more set to reciting. Wukong, unable to bear the pain, knelt by the roadside and could only cry, "Stop, stop! Whatever you have to say, say it quick and be done."

Said the Tang monk, "Monkey-head — is there still more to say? A man who does good is like the grass in a spring garden: you do not see it grow, yet day by day it gains. A man who does evil is like a whetstone: you do not see it wear, yet day by day it wastes away. Here in this wild waste and open country you've beaten three people to death in a row — and still no one denounces you, there's no one to answer for it. But should we come into a city, into a place thronged with people and the smoke of hearths, and you take that mourning-staff of yours and, in some moment past all telling of good from ill, fall to beating people about — and bring down a great calamity — how am I then to save my own skin? Be gone with you!"

Said Wukong, "Master, you wrong me unjustly. This creature was plainly a demon, who truly had it in her heart to harm you. I beat her dead and rid you of the menace — yet you cannot tell it, but believe instead the slanders and cold whispers of that blockhead, and drive me off time and again. As the old saying goes, 'A thing not done past three.' If I do not go now, I'm truly a base and shameless wretch. I'll go, I'll go. Go I will and go I shall — only you'll have no one left under your hand." The Tang monk flared into wrath: "This insolent ape grows more lawless still! By your account, only you are a person — are Wuneng and Wujing, then, not people too?"

When the Great Sage heard him call those two "people," he could not hold back his grief and bitter sorrow, and said to the Tang monk, "Alas! In those days, when you came out from Chang'an, you had Liu Boqin to see you on your road. When you reached the Mountain of Two Frontiers and saved me out, I bowed and took you for my master. I have wound through ancient caves, plunged into deep forests, seized fiends and caught monsters, won Bajie, gained Sha Monk, and tasted a thousand bitter toils and ten thousand hardships. And today, in muddled foolishness behind a wakeful face, you only bid me go back. This is just as it is said: 'When the birds are gone, the bow is hung away; when the hare is dead, the hound is boiled!' Well, well, well — only there's that troublesome Tight-Fillet spell." Said the Tang monk, "I'll recite it no more." Said Wukong, "That's hard to promise. If you come to some place of cruel demons and bitter trials and cannot win free, and Bajie and Sha Monk cannot save you, then in that hour you'll think of me, and cannot keep yourself from reciting it again. Even a hundred thousand miles off, my head would ache. Better, if I'm only to come back to you so, that I never form the intention at all."

Seeing him talk and talk on so, the Tang monk grew the angrier still, and rolled from his saddle to the ground. He bade Sha Monk fetch paper and brush from the bundle, and there by the ravine drew water, ground ink upon a stone, and wrote out a writ of dismissal. Handing it to Wukong, he said, "Monkey-head, take this as proof: I'll not have you for my disciple any longer. If ever I see you again, may I sink into the Avici Hell."

Wukong hastily took the writ and said, "Master, no need to swear oaths. Old Monkey will go." He folded the paper and tucked it in his sleeve, then once more pleaded softly with the Tang monk: "Master, I've followed you for a season, and had the Bodhisattva's instruction besides. Today I'm dismissed halfway, my work unfinished, my merit unwon. I beg you, sit, and receive a bow from me, and then I can go with an easy heart." But the Tang monk turned his back and would not heed him, muttering with his lips, "I'm a good monk; I'll not receive a bad man's courtesies."

Seeing that he would not heed, the Great Sage worked an out-of-body art: he plucked three hairs from the back of his head, blew upon them a breath of immortal air, and cried, "Change!" At once they turned into three more Wukongs, who with his own self made four, surrounding the master on all sides to bow. The elder, dodge left or right as he might, could not escape, and so willy-nilly received a bow.

The Great Sage sprang up, shook his body, drew the hairs back in, and then gave a charge to Sha Monk: "Worthy brother, you are a good man. Only take heed, and guard against Bajie's mischief-making chatter; on the road be more careful still. Should a demon some time seize the master, you must say that old Monkey is his chief disciple — for the bristly fiends of the West, hearing of my powers, will not dare to harm our master." Said the Tang monk, "I'm a good monk; I'll not so much as name a bad man like you. Be gone."

When the Great Sage saw that the elder, thrice over and twice again, would not turn his heart or change his mind, there was no help for it, and he went at last. See him now:

> With tears held back he knocks his head, taking leave of the elder;
> with grief within he lingers, charging Sha Monk to heart.
> One toss of his head, and he wipes it on the grass before the slope;
> with both feet he kicks and overturns the vines upon the ground.
> Up to the sky, down to the earth, he wheels like a turning wheel;
> across the seas, over the hills — first in all the world.
> In a moment his shadow is gone from sight;
> in a flash he speeds back to the road of old.

See him, then — swallowing his anger, he took leave of his master, called up the somersault cloud, and went straight back to the Water-Curtain Cave on the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. All alone, in misery and desolation, he was — when suddenly a roar of water broke upon his ears. Looking out from mid-air, the Great Sage saw that it was the sound of the great tide of the Eastern Ocean at the flood. At the sight of it, he thought once more of the Tang monk, and could not stop the tears from spilling down his cheeks. He stayed his cloud, halted his steps, and only after a long while went on his way.

In the end there is no knowing how this parting and reunion would turn — so listen to the telling in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 28 -->
# Chapter 28: The Demons Gather at the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, and Tripitaka Meets a Fiend in the Black Pine Wood

Now, though the Great Sage had been driven away by the Tang Monk, still he brooded and sighed without end. Soon he sighted the great Eastern Ocean, and he said, "It has been five hundred years since last I traveled this road!" And he beheld the sea-water:

> Smoke and waves rolling, vast billows surging on.
> The smoke and waves roll out to meet the River of Heaven;
> the vast billows surge down to thread the veins of earth.
> When the tide comes raging, the waters flood the curving bays —
> when the tide comes raging it roars like thunder in three months of spring;
> when the waters flood the curving bays it howls like a mad wind through nine days of summer.
> The blessed elder riding his dragon must furrow his brow as he passes;
> the immortal lad astride his crane is troubled, sure enough, again and again.
> Near the shore there is no village, no hamlet;
> beside the water, few fishing boats.
> The waves roll up a thousand years of snow;
> the wind breeds autumn in the sixth month.
> Wild fowl come and go as they please;
> sand-birds sink and float at will.
> No angler stands before the eye;
> only the gull is heard beside the ear.
> Below, the sea-creatures sport in joy;
> at the sky's edge, the passing wild goose grieves.

The pilgrim gave a great leap of his body and bounded across the Eastern Ocean, and soon he came to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. Lowering his cloud-head, he opened his eyes wide and looked about — and upon that mountain there were no flowers, no grass; mist and rosy haze were utterly gone; the peaks and crags had collapsed, the woods and trees were scorched and withered. Do you ask how it came to such a pass? It was only because, when he had made his great uproar in the Palace of Heaven and was hauled up to the upper realm, this mountain was set ablaze and ruined by the Illustrious Sage Erlang at the head of his seven sworn brothers of Mei Mountain. The Great Sage grew doubly miserable. There is an old-style poem, a witness to the ruined mountain's fallen scene, that runs:

> I look back on my immortal hill, and tears fall down in twin streams;
> facing the mountain I grow wretched, and grieve the more.
> Once I thought no harm could come to this mountain;
> only today do I learn that even the earth can be undone.
> How I hate Erlang, who wiped me out;
> how I rage at the petty god who bullied my people.
> In his fury he dug up the graves of your ancient spirits;
> for no cause he broke open your ancestors' tombs.
> The rosy mist that filled the sky is all dispersed;
> the wind and clouds across the ground are scattered thin.
> On the eastern ridge no striped tiger roars;
> on the western hill where now is the white gibbon's cry?
> In the northern gully no fox or hare leaves a track;
> in the southern valley the deer and roebuck have left no shadow.
> The blue stones are burnt to a thousand clods of dirt;
> the emerald sands are turned to a single heap of mud.
> Outside the cave the tall pines all lean and topple;
> before the cliffs the kingfisher-green cypress is grown sparse.
> Cedar, fir, sophora, juniper, chestnut, sandalwood — all scorched;
> peach, apricot, plum, prune, pear, jujube — all gone.
> The cudrania is dead, the mulberry gone — how raise the silkworms now?
> Willows are thin, bamboo is scant — hard for the birds to roost.
> The clever stones of the peaks are turned to dust;
> the springs at the ravine-bottom are dry, all overgrown with weeds.
> Before the cliffs the soil is black, no orchid, no iris;
> beside the road the mud is red, with creeper and vine clinging.
> Where do the flying birds of former days take wing?
> To what mountain did the running beasts of that time flee?
> The leopard scorns this ruined place, the python loathes it;
> the crane shuns it, the snake turns back from the spoiled land.
> Surely it was some evil thought of days gone by
> that brought down such hardship before my eyes today.

While the Great Sage was in the very depth of his grief, he heard, from before a fragrant grassy slope, within a hollow of creeping vetch, a rustling sound — and out leaped seven or eight little monkeys, who swarmed forward in a crowd, surrounded him, and knocked their heads upon the ground. They cried aloud, "Great Sage, Grandfather, have you come home today?" The Handsome Monkey King said, "Why is it you do not frolic and play, but each of you hides and skulks out of sight? I have been here some while, yet saw no trace of you. Why?"

The monkey host, hearing this, each let fall his tears and reported, "Ever since the Great Sage was seized and hauled to the upper realm, we have suffered cruelly at the hunters' hands — truly past enduring. How could we withstand their stiff crossbows and strong bows, their fierce yellow hawks and wicked hounds, their snares and traps, their spears and hooks? And so, each cherishing his own life, none dared show his head to frolic; we only burrowed deep into the caves and fled far to our nests. When hungry, we went to the slope-front to steal grass to eat; when thirsty, we went down to the ravine to sip the clear spring. Just now we heard the Great Sage Grandfather's voice, and so we came especially to meet you — and humbly beg your help and protection." Hearing these words, the Great Sage grew more wretched still. He asked, "How many of you are left upon this mountain?" The monkeys said, "Old and young together, there are but a thousand or so." The Great Sage said, "In my day I had a host of forty-seven thousand demons. Where have they all gone now?"

The monkeys said, "After Grandfather left, this mountain was set alight by Bodhisattva Erlang, and more than half of us were burned to death. We crouched in the wells, we crept into the ravines, we hid beneath the iron-plate bridge, and so we kept our lives. By the time the fire was out and the smoke gone and we came forth, there were no flowers or fruit to feed us, and we could scarcely stay alive, so half of us went off elsewhere. We, this remaining half, have lived in the mountain enduring our hardships. And these two years, the hunters have carried off half of us again."

The pilgrim said, "What do they want with you, that they carry you off?" The monkeys said, "Speak of these hunters and you'll loathe them! Those of us they shoot with arrows or pierce with spears, or poison and beat to death, they take away to skin and bone us — stewed in sauce, steamed in vinegar, fried in oil, parched in salt — and eat us as a relish with their rice. And some of us they catch in nets or snares, taking us alive, and they make us jump through hoops and do tricks, turn somersaults, stand on our heads — and in the streets, to the beating of gongs and the thumping of drums, they make us do every kind of antic for sport."

When the Great Sage heard this, he grew the more enraged, and said, "Who is in charge of affairs in the cave now?" The demons said, "Marshals Ma and Liu, and Generals Beng and Ba, still hold it." The Great Sage said, "Go and let them know I have come." Those little imps rushed in at the gate and reported, "The Great Sage Grandfather has come home!" When Ma, Liu, Beng, and Ba heard the report, they hurried out the gate, knocked their heads, and welcomed him into the cave. The Great Sage took his seat in the middle, and the host of monsters bowed in rows before him and asked, "Great Sage Grandfather, of late we heard you had kept your life and were guarding the Tang Monk to the Western Heaven to fetch scriptures. How is it you do not journey westward, but have come back to your own mountain?"

The Great Sage said, "Little ones, you do not know. That Tang Tripitaka could not tell the worthy from the worthless. All along the road I caught fiends and seized demons for him, spending the whole skill of my life — time and again I slew the monsters; yet he said I was committing violence and doing evil, and would not have me for a disciple. He drove me back home, and wrote out a writ of dismissal as proof, vowing never to use me again."

The monkeys clapped their hands and laughed aloud. "What luck, what luck! Why be a monk? Just come home, and let us frolic together for a few years." They called, "Quick, set out the coconut wine to wash the dust from Grandfather's journey!" The Great Sage said, "Hold off the wine a moment. Let me ask you — these hunters, how often do they come up my mountain?" Ma and Liu said, "Great Sage, no matter the season, they pester us here day after day." The Great Sage said, "Why have they not come today?" Ma and Liu said, "They should be coming presently." The Great Sage gave his orders: "Little ones, all of you go out and gather up for me those crumbled stones on the mountain that the fire baked brittle, and pile them in heaps — twenty or thirty pushed into one pile, or fifty or sixty heaped together — I have a use for them." The little monkeys came on all at once, a whole swarm of them, and in wild confusion gathered many heaps. The Great Sage looked them over and said, "Little ones, all of you go hide inside the cave, and let me work my magic."

The Great Sage climbed to the mountain summit and watched. From the southern half of the slope came the boom-boom of drums and the clang-clang of gongs, and there flashed into view over a thousand men and horses, all bearing hawks and hounds, gripping swords and spears. The Monkey King looked closely at how fierce and dangerous these men came on — fine, valiant fellows, truly bold and brave. Behold:

> Fox-fur covering shoulder and crown,
> brocade silk wrapping waist and breast.
> In their quivers, wolf-fang arrows;
> at their hips, jewel-carved bows hung.
> The men like mountain-searching tigers,
> their horses like ravine-leaping dragons.
> In packs they lead their hounds;
> on every arm a hawk is perched.
> Wicker baskets bearing fire-bombs,
> and Sea-East Falcons set in place.
> A hundred-odd loads of birdlime-poles,
> a thousand hare-forks besides.
> Ox-headed nets to bar the road,
> and Yama-knot nooses of cord.
> All at once they raise a wild halloo,
> scattering out like stars across the sky.

When the Great Sage saw these men spreading up his mountain, his heart filled with great wrath. With his hand he made a magic sign, in his mouth he muttered a spell, and toward the southeast he drew in a breath of air; then, with a whoosh, he blew it out, and it became a furious gale. A fine wind! Behold:

> Raising dust and flinging earth,
> toppling trees and snapping the woods.
> The sea-waves rose like mountains up;
> turbid billows piled ten thousand fold and overran.
> Heaven and earth went dim and reeling;
> sun and moon turned dark and sunk in gloom.
> One blast that shook the pines roared like a tiger;
> then, suddenly, into the bamboo, it sang like a dragon.
> Ten thousand crevices howled in rage — the sky's own breath let go —
> while flying sand and rolling stones wounded men at random.

The Great Sage raised this great wind, and on the wind he sent the crumbled stones flying and whirling in chaos. Pity those thousand-odd men and horses, every one of them —

> Stones struck the crow-heads to powder;
> sand flew, and the sea-horses were all hurt.
> The ginseng and the cassia rushed before the ridge;
> their blood dyed the cinnabar ground.
> The aconite could not return to its native place;
> how should the betel-nut find its way home?
> Their corpses, light as light-powder, lay on the mountain field,
> while the rouge-girl at home looked out and waited.

And there was a poem that said:

> The men dead, the horses dead — how shall they go home?
> Wild ghosts and lonely souls in confusion thick as hemp.
> Pity these brave and bristling captains, these valiant lords —
> who could not tell the worthy from the worthless: their blood dyes the sand.

The Great Sage lowered his cloud-head, clapped his hands, and laughed aloud. "What luck, what luck! Ever since I submitted to the Tang Monk and became a monk, he was forever counseling me, saying, 'A thousand days of doing good, and the good is still not enough; a single day of doing evil, and the evil is more than enough.' Truly there is such a saying. While I followed him, I slew a few monsters, and he blamed me for committing violence. Yet today I come home, and I have finished off this whole crowd of hunters!" He called, "Little ones, come out!" The monkey host, now that the gale had passed, heard the Great Sage's call, and each came leaping forth. The Great Sage said, "Go to the foot of the south mountain and strip the clothes from the hunters who were killed, and bring them home; wash off the bloodstains, and put them on against the cold. Push all the dead men's corpses into the bottomless pool, ten thousand fathoms deep. Drag the fallen horses here, flay off their hides to make boots to wear, and salt down the flesh to eat slowly. Take those bows and arrows, spears and swords, and use them to drill yourselves in the martial arts. And gather up those many-colored banners and standards, and bring them for my use." The monkeys each gave their assent.

The Great Sage took the banners apart, washed them, and pieced them together into a single banner of mingled colors and flowers, and on it he wrote fourteen characters: "Rebuilder of the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, Restorer of the Water-Curtain Cave, Great Sage Equal to Heaven." He raised a pole and hung the banner outside the cave. Day by day he summoned fiends and gathered beasts, stored up fodder and hoarded grain, and never again spoke the two words "the monk." And his good fellowship was great, and his arts were high, so he went to borrow some sweet, life-giving immortal water from the Dragon Kings of the Four Seas, and washed the mountain green again. In front he planted elm and willow; behind, pine and nan-wood; peach, plum, jujube, and prune — nothing was lacking. Carefree and at ease, joyful in his work and settled in his dwelling — but of this no more.

Now we tell how the Tang Monk, listening to crafty counsel and giving free rein to the Mind-Monkey's banishment, climbed into the saddle and mounted his horse. Zhu Bajie opened the road ahead, and Sha Monk shouldered the luggage and went westward. They crossed the White Tiger Ridge, and suddenly came upon a stretch of wooded hills — truly a place of clinging vines and twining creepers, of kingfisher cypress and green pine. Tripitaka called out, "Disciples, the mountain road is rugged and most hard to travel, and the pine forest is thick and clustered, the trees dense and crowded. We must be very careful, for I fear there may be fiends and savage beasts." Now look at that simpleton — he braced up his spirits, told Sha Monk to lead the horse, and himself used his nine-tooth rake to open the way, guiding the Tang Monk straight into the pine wood. As they were going along, the elder reined in his horse and said, "Bajie, I am truly hungry this day. Where can I find some vegetarian food to eat?" Bajie said, "Master, please dismount and wait here; let old Hog go and search." The elder got down from his horse, Sha Monk set down his load, took out the alms-bowl, and handed it to Bajie. Bajie said, "I'm off." The elder asked, "Where are you going?" Bajie said, "Never mind. This trip of mine — I'll bore through ice to fetch fire and find a vegetarian meal; I'll press snow to seek oil and beg up some rice."

Now look at him: he came out of the pine wood and went westward more than ten li, yet never came upon a single house — truly a place where there were wolves and tigers but no human smoke. The simpleton, footsore and weary, mused within himself, "In the years when the pilgrim Sun was about, whatever the old monk wanted, he had at once; today it has fallen to my lot. Truly, as the saying goes, 'Only the householder knows the price of firewood and rice; only the parent knows the grace of bearing a child.' And there's nowhere at all to beg." Then drowsiness came over him, and he thought, "If I go straight back now and tell the old monk there was nowhere to beg, he won't believe I walked all this long way. I must dawdle another hour or two, then go back and report. Well then, well then — let me just have a sleep here in this thicket." So the simpleton tucked his head down into the grass and lay down. He meant only to drowse a little and then get up — but how should one who is footsore from the road do otherwise? Once his head went down, he only snored on and on.

Let us not speak of Bajie sleeping here. We tell rather of the elder in the wood, his ears growing hot and his eyes twitching, his body and mind ill at ease. Quickly he turned and called Sha Monk: "Wukong went to beg for food — why is he not back even at this late hour?" Sha Monk said, "Master, you still don't understand. He saw that here in the west many households feed monks, and his belly is large besides — what does he care about you? He'll come back only when he has eaten his fill." Tripitaka said, "Just so. But if he is over there gorging on alms-food, where shall we find him? The day grows late; this is no place to stay. We must find lodging — that would be best." Sha Monk said, "No great matter, Master. You just sit here, and let me go find him." Tripitaka said, "Just so, just so. Food or no food, let it be — only finding lodging is what matters." Sha Monk took up his treasure-staff and went straight out of the pine wood to look for Bajie.

The elder sat alone in the wood, utterly bored and weary. He could only force up his spirits, leap to his feet, gather the luggage into one place, and tie the horse to a tree. He took off the broad-brimmed hat he wore, planted his pewter staff upright, smoothed his black monk's robe, and strolled at a slow pace through the secluded wood, by way of dispelling his gloom. The elder gazed over all the wild grasses and mountain flowers, but could not bear the clamor of birds returning to roost. Now, that forest was all deep grass and narrow paths, and because his thoughts were tangled and troubled, he took the wrong way. He had come, first, to ease his cares, and second, to find Bajie and Sha Monk; but the two of them had gone by the straight westward road, while the elder, after wandering a while, went off toward the south instead. Coming out of the pine wood, he suddenly raised his head and saw, off in that quarter, a golden light flashing and shimmering, and brilliant vapors rising in clouds. Looking closely, he found it was a precious pagoda, its golden summit shining. It was the light of the setting sun in the west, glancing off that golden roof and making it glow. He said, "Your disciple has no good fortune indeed. Ever since I left the land of the east, I made a vow: at every temple to burn incense, at the sight of every Buddha to bow, at every pagoda I met to sweep the pagoda. Is that shining thing not a precious pagoda of yellow gold? How is it I did not take that road? Below the pagoda there must be a monastery, and in the monastery there must be monks. Let me just go and walk over. As for the luggage and the white horse — I reckon no one travels through this place, so all will be well. If there is a convenient lodging there, I'll wait for the disciples to come, and we'll borrow rest together."

Alas! The elder's ill luck had come upon him at last. Look at him: he strode off and came straight to the pagoda. But behold what he saw:

> Stone cliffs ten thousand fathoms high,
> a mountain so vast it touches the blue empyrean.
> Its roots run deep into the thick earth,
> its peaks are thrust up to the height of heaven.
> On either side, some thousands of assorted trees;
> before and behind, a hundred li and more of twining vines.
> Flowers mirrored on the grass-tips, the wind casting shadows;
> water flowing in the cloudy hollow, the moon without root.
> Fallen timber lies across the deep ravine;
> withered creepers hang knotted upon the bright peak.
> Beneath the stone bridge, a clear spring rolls and rolls;
> upon the terrace-seat, a white powder glows ever bright.
> Seen from afar, it is like the heavenly halls of the Three Isles;
> seen up close, it is like the fairy realm of Penglai.
> Fragrant pines and purple bamboo ring the mountain stream;
> crows and magpies, gibbons and monkeys, thread the steep ridges.
> Outside the cave-gate, the running beasts come and go in rows;
> within the woods, the flying birds emerge and enter in flocks.
> The green, green fragrant grasses are fair;
> the bright, bright wild flowers are in bloom.
> This place is plainly an evil ground —
> and the elder, in his ill luck, came blundering up to it.

The elder stepped forward, and when he had come right beneath the pagoda gate, he saw a mottled-bamboo screen hanging within. He pressed in at the door, lifted the screen, and went on inside. Lifting his head abruptly, he saw upon a stone couch a fiend lying asleep on his side. Do you ask what he looked like?

> A face of indigo-blue, white fangs jutting,
> one great mouth gaping wide.
> On either side, the tangled, bushy temple-locks,
> all of them dyed the color of rouge;
> three or four towering purple whiskers,
> as though they were lychee-shoots in a row.
> A parrot-beak of a nose, arching up;
> eyes like the dawn-star, glittering.
> His two fists like a monk's alms-bowls;
> his two blue feet like the gnarled stumps on a cliff's edge.
> Slung aslant, a pale-yellow robe and curtain,
> finer than a brocaded cassock.
> The blade he carried gleamed with cold light;
> the stone he slept on was smooth and flawless.
> He had marshaled his little imps in their ant-ranks;
> he had sat as old fiend in his wasp-court.
> Look at him — awe-inspiring and stern,
> all crying out together, calling him "Lord."
> He had drunk wine with the moon, making three men of one;
> he had felt the breeze beneath both arms as he tipped his cup of tea.
> Look at him — his spirit-powers are vast indeed:
> with a single blink, he roams the ends of the earth.
> In the wild forest the small birds clamor;
> in the deep thicket lodge the dragon and the snake.
> Where the immortal lads till the fields, white jade is born;
> where the Daoists tend the fire, cinnabar is nourished.
> His little cave-gate, though it cannot reach the Avici Hell,
> houses a hulking fiend — none other than an Ox-Headed Yaksha.

When the elder saw what manner of thing this was, he was so frightened that he started backward a step. His whole body went numb and tingling, his two legs went weak and soft, and he hastily turned to flee. But he had barely turned around when the fiend — whose spirit-sense was truly powerful — flung wide a pair of golden, gleaming demon-eyes and called out, "Little ones, look outside the door — who is that?" One of the little imps stuck out his head, looked outside the door, and saw a bald-headed elder. He ran straight in to report: "Great King, there's a monk outside. Round-headed and full-faced, with two ears hanging to his shoulders; a body of tender, smooth flesh, and a fine, delicate skin — and a very fine monk he is." Hearing this, the fiend gave a roar of laughter and said, "This is what's called 'a fly on a snake's head — food and clothing that comes of its own accord.' You little ones, hurry after him at once and seize him for me. There'll be a rich reward for you here." Those little imps swarmed forward all at once, a whole nest of them. When Tripitaka saw them, though his heart was as anxious as an arrow and his two feet ran as if flying, in the end his heart trembled and his courage failed, his legs went weak and his feet went numb; and besides, the mountain road was rugged, the forest deep, the day far gone — how could he move a step? — and so the little imps hoisted him up bodily and carried him off. Truly it was:

> When the dragon swims in shallow water, the shrimps make sport of him;
> when the tiger comes down to the level plain, the dogs do him insult.
> Even though good deeds meet many a trial and barrier —
> who ever met them as the Tang Monk did, journeying toward the west?

Look — those little imps carried the elder up, set him down outside the bamboo screen, and reported in great delight, "Great King, we've caught the monk and brought him in." The old fiend stole a glance at him too, and saw that Tripitaka held his head erect, his looks majestic — a fine monk indeed. He thought within himself, "So fine a monk as this must be a personage from the upper realm; he's no trifling sort. If I don't put on a show of power, how will he ever yield and submit?" Then all at once, like a fox borrowing the tiger's might, he bristled his red whiskers upright, his blood-red hair stood toward the sky, his eyeballs nearly burst, and with a great roar he cried, "Bring that monk in!" The fiends all answered together with a ringing "Aye!" and shoved Tripitaka straight inside. This was a case of "Under another's low eaves, how dare one not bow the head?" Tripitaka could only press his palms together and pay his respects. The fiend said, "What place are you a monk of? Where do you come from? Where are you going? Speak plainly, and be quick!" Tripitaka said, "I am a monk of the Tang court. By the command of the Great Tang Emperor, I am going to the West to seek out the scriptures and gathas. Passing your honorable mountain, I came especially to the pagoda to pay homage to the holy one, never thinking to disturb your majesty. I beg you to forgive my offense. When I have fetched the scriptures from the west and returned to the land of the east, your high name will be recorded forever." Hearing this, the fiend gave a great "Ho, ho, ho" of laughter and said, "I said you were a personage of the upper kingdom — and so you are. I was just wanting to eat you, and you've come along most conveniently — most conveniently! Otherwise, wouldn't I have let you slip by for nothing? You're meant to be food in my mouth: naturally you'd come crashing in, and now, even if I'd let you go, you couldn't get away; even if you ran, you couldn't escape!" He called to the little imps, "Take that monk away and tie him up." Sure enough, those little imps swarmed forward, wound the elder round with rope and cord, and bound him to the Soul-Fixing Stake.

The old fiend, gripping his blade, asked again, "Monk, how many are there in your party? Surely you didn't dare go up to the Western Heaven all alone?" Seeing him holding the blade, Tripitaka again spoke honestly: "Great King, I have two disciples, called Zhu Bajie and Sha Monk; they have both gone off into the pine wood to beg for food. And there's a load of luggage and a white horse, both left in the pine wood." The old fiend said, "Better luck still! Two disciples, and you that's three, and the horse that's four — enough for a single meal." The little imps said, "Let us go and catch them." The old fiend said, "Don't go out — shut the front gate. When those two have begged their food, they'll surely look for their master to eat; and not finding him, they'll surely come looking right up to my gate. As the saying goes, 'The trade that comes to your door is the easy trade to do.' We'll just catch them at our leisure." So the little imps shut the front gate.

Let us say no more of Tripitaka meeting calamity. We tell rather of Sha Monk, who had come out of the wood to look for Bajie. He went a good ten li or more, and never saw a hamlet or a village. He stood on a high mound, gazing about, when he heard the sound of a man's voice in the grass. Quickly he parted the deep grass with his staff and looked — and there was the simpleton inside, talking in his sleep. Sha Monk grabbed him by the ear and at last woke him, saying, "You fine simpleton! The master sent you to beg for food — did he allow you to sleep here?" The simpleton woke in a fluster and said, "Brother, what time is it?" Sha Monk said, "Get up quick. The master says food or no food it's all one — he's told you and me to go and find lodging."

The simpleton, all dazed and muddled, hefted the alms-bowl, gripped his rake, and went straight back with Sha Monk. When they reached the wood and looked, the master was gone. Sha Monk grumbled, "It's all your fault, you simpleton — failing to beg up any food. A fiend must have carried off the master!" Bajie laughed and said, "Brother, don't talk nonsense. That wood is a clean and elegant sort of place; there's certainly no fiend there. I expect the old monk couldn't sit still and went off somewhere to take the air. Let's go look for him." So the two could only lead the horse, shoulder the load, gather up the broad hat and pewter staff, and go out of the pine wood to search for their master.

This time, too, it was not the Tang Monk's fate to die. When the two of them had searched a while without finding him, they suddenly saw, off to the south, a golden light flashing and shimmering. Bajie said, "Brother, the lucky are simply lucky. Look — the master has gone off to their house. That shining thing is a precious pagoda; who would dare neglect him there? They're surely setting out vegetarian food and keeping him there to enjoy it. We'd better get a move on too, and catch up to have a bit of the meal." Sha Monk said, "Brother, there's no telling good fortune from ill. Let's just go and have a look."

The two of them, bold and bristling, came up to the gate. "Ah! It's shut." And they saw, set crosswise above the gate, a slab of white jade, on which were carved six great characters: "Moon-Wave Cave of Bowl-Hill Mountain." Sha Monk said, "Brother, this is no temple — it's a fiend's cave-dwelling. If our master is here, he won't be a pretty sight." Bajie said, "Brother, don't be afraid. You just tie up the horse and guard the luggage, and let me go and ask after his news." The simpleton lifted his rake, went forward, and shouted, "Open the gate! Open the gate!" The little imp who kept the gate inside opened it, and at the sudden sight of the two of them he hastily drew back and ran in to report, "Great King, trade has come!" The old fiend said, "What trade?" The little imp said, "Outside the cave-gate there's a long-snouted, big-eared monk and an ill-luck-colored monk, come hammering at the gate." The old fiend said in great delight, "That's Zhu Bajie and Sha Monk come searching here. Aha — so he can search, after all! How did he track me right to my gate? Since their faces are fierce and unruly, take care not to slight them." He called, "Bring my armor!" The little imps brought it, and he put it on, gripped his blade in his hand, and went straight out the gate.

Now we tell how Bajie and Sha Monk were waiting before the gate when they saw the fiend come on, fierce and dangerous. Do you ask how he was arrayed?

> A green face, red whiskers, scarlet hair flying;
> golden armor and mail, gleaming and bright.
> A belly-wrap lining his waist, a stone-studded belt;
> a chest-guard lashing his armor, a cloud-walking cord.
> Idle, he stood before the mountain — the wind howled and howled;
> moody, he roamed beyond the sea — the waves surged and surged.
> A pair of indigo-blue, scorched-sinewed hands
> gripping fast the soul-chasing, life-taking blade.
> Would you know this creature's name and surname?
> Sound out the two words, and call him Yellow Robe.

The old fiend Yellow Robe came out the gate and asked, "What region's monks are you, shouting at my door?" Bajie said, "My son, don't you know me? I'm your venerable lord. I'm sent by the Great Tang to the Western Heaven. My master is the imperial brother Tripitaka. If he's inside your house, send him out at once and spare yourself my rake battering its way in!" The monster laughed and said, "Yes, yes, yes — there's a Tang Monk in my house, and I haven't slighted him a bit; I've laid out some buns of human flesh for him to eat. Why don't you come in and have one too — how about it?"

The simpleton actually meant to go in. Sha Monk grabbed him and pulled him back, saying, "Brother, he's tricking you. Since when do you eat human flesh?" Then the simpleton came to his senses, whipped out his rake, and aimed a blow straight at the monster's face; the monster dodged aside and brought up his steel blade to parry and meet him. The two of them each displayed their spirit-powers, leaped onto cloud-heads, and battled it out in mid-air. Sha Monk threw down the luggage and the white horse, raised his treasure-staff, and rushed in haste to join the attack. At that moment two fierce monks and one foul fiend fought a fine battle up in the clouds. Truly it was:

> The staff rose, the blade met it; the rake came, the blade parried.
> One demon-general showed his might;
> two divine monks displayed their transformations.
> The nine-tooth rake was a hero indeed;
> the fiend-quelling staff was fierce and terrible too.
> Front and back, left and right, they came on all at once,
> yet Yellow Robe was plainly unafraid.
> Look at him — his dipped steel blade flashed bright as silver;
> truly his spirit-powers, too, were vast and wide.
> They fought till the whole sky was wreathed in fog and lost in cloud,
> and halfway up the mountain the cliffs crumbled and the ridges cracked.
> One fought for his fame, and would by no means give over;
> one fought for his master, and was utterly without fear.

The three of them went back and forth in mid-air, and after they had fought several tens of rounds, neither side could be told victor or vanquished. Each, holding his own life dear, found it truly hard to disengage and hard to part.

In the end we know not how the Tang Monk was to be rescued; so listen to the next chapter for the explanation.

<!-- chapter 29 -->
# Chapter 29: A Letter Carried Out of Sorrow, and a Monk Who Strode Back to the Mountain

A poem says:

> Vain thoughts need no violent suppression;
> for the True Suchness, why must we strive and seek?
> The Buddha-nature, our own root, is cultivated before the Buddha—
> and how should delusion and awakening stand in any order of before and after?
> Awaken, and in an instant you are made upright;
> stay deluded, and through ten thousand kalpas you sink in the stream.
> If a single thought can join itself to true cultivation,
> the sins and stains as countless as the Ganges sands are wiped away.

Now then. Zhu Bajie and Sha Monk had fought the fiend for some thirty rounds, and still neither side had the better of it. Do you ask why neither could win? If it came to a true contest of skill, then never mind two monks—even twenty of them could not have stood against that demon. It was only because the Tang Monk's allotted span had not yet run out, so that in secret the Dharma-guarding spirits watched over him; and in the air above, the Six Dings and Six Jias, the Guardians of the Five Quarters, the Four Sentinels of the Watches, and the eighteen Protectors of the Faith lent their strength to Bajie and Sha Monk.

But let us leave the three of them at their battle.

Inside the cave the elder wept and grieved, thinking of his disciples, the tears running from his eyes. "Wuneng," he mourned, "in what village have you fallen in with good friends, lingering greedy over their offerings of food? And you, Wujing—you cannot know where to look for him; will you ever find each other? Little do you dream that I have met with a demon, and suffer captivity here. When will I see you again, shake off this great peril, and reach the Spirit Mountain at last?"

In the very midst of his sorrow and distress, he saw a woman come out from within the cave. Steadying herself against the Soul-Fixing Post, she called: "Elder, where have you come from? Why has he bound you here?" Hearing her, the elder peered up through his tears and saw that she was a woman of perhaps thirty years. He answered, "Lady Bodhisattva, there is no need to ask. I am one already doomed to die—I walked in at your gate. If you mean to eat me, then eat me and have done; why ask anything more?"

"I am no eater of men," said the woman. "My home lies more than three hundred li to the west of this place. There stands a city called the Kingdom of Precious Image. I am that king's third princess; my milk-name is Hundred-Flowers Shame. Thirteen years ago, on the night of the fifteenth of the eighth month, while I was out enjoying the moon, this demon swept me up in a gust of wild wind and carried me here. For thirteen years I have been his wife, bearing his children in this place, and not a word of mine has ever gone back to the court. I think of my father and mother, and I cannot see them. From where have you come, that he should have seized you?"

"This poor monk," said Tripitaka, "was sent westward to fetch the scriptures. As I idled along the road I blundered in here by mistake. Now he means to capture my two disciples as well, and steam the whole lot of us to eat."

The princess gave a coaxing smile. "Be easy of heart, elder. Since you are one bound for the scriptures, I can save you. The Kingdom of Precious Image lies along the great road you must take to the West. Carry a letter there for me, and pay my respects to my father and mother—and I will see to it that he spares you."

Tripitaka nodded. "Lady Bodhisattva, if you will but save this poor monk's life, I will gladly be your bearer of letters."

The princess turned quickly to the inner rooms and wrote out a letter home, sealing it fast. Coming back to the post, she loosed the Tang Monk's bonds and put the letter into his hands. Freed at last, he held it up and said, "Lady Bodhisattva, I thank you a thousand times for the gift of my life. On my journey, when I pass through your honored land, I will surely deliver this to the king. But I fear that after so long a span of years your parents may refuse to know me for what I am—what then? Do not blame this poor monk if he should have to tell a small untruth."

"Have no fear," said the princess. "My royal father has no son; he begot only us three sisters. If he sees this letter, he is bound to wish to look upon you."

Tripitaka tucked the letter snugly into his sleeve, thanked the princess, and made to leave by the front. But the princess caught hold of him. "You cannot go out the front way. All the fiends, great and small, are out before the gate waving banners and shouting their war-cries, beating drums and clashing gongs to back up their king against your disciples. Go out by the back gate instead. If the king himself seizes you, at least he will question you first; but I fear the little fiends might catch you, and not knowing good from ill, snatch and tear at you and take your life. Let me go before him and put in a word to smooth the way. Once the king has let you go, wait for some sign from your disciples, then find them and the lot of you can make off together."

Hearing this, Tripitaka knocked his head to the ground in thanks, did exactly as he was bidden, took his leave of the princess, slipped out beyond the back gate, and dared not move on alone, but hid himself among the thorn-brakes.

Now the princess had hatched her clever scheme. She hurried out before the gate and pushed her way through the throng of fiends. From above came the clang and clatter of clashing weapons—for it was Bajie and Sha Monk locked in combat with the fiend in midair. The princess cried out in a piercing voice: "Lord Yellow Robe!"

When the demon king heard the princess call, he flung Bajie and Sha Monk aside, dropped down upon his cloud, gripped his steel blade, and took the princess by the arm. "Wife, what is it you wish to say?"

"My lord," she said, "just now I lay asleep within my gauze curtains, and in a dream I suddenly saw a spirit in golden armor."

"What spirit in golden armor?" the demon asked. "And what did he want at our gate?"

"In my girlhood, while I was still in the palace," she said, "I privately made a certain vow in my heart: that if ever I were matched with a worthy son-in-law as my husband, I would climb the famous mountains, worship at the immortals' shrines, feed the monks and give alms. From the day I was wedded to you, in all our husband-and-wife happiness, I have never once spoken of it. That golden-armored spirit came to claim the unkept vow, and bawled at me till I woke—but it was only an idle dream after all. So I dressed myself in haste and came to tell my lord of it, and never thought to find a monk bound to that post. I beg my lord's mercy: out of regard for my poor wishes, spare that monk, and let it count as my feeding of the monks in fulfilment of the vow. Will my lord consent?"

"Wife," said the fiend, "you fret over nothing at all. What weighty matter is this? If I want to eat men, where can I not scoop up a few to eat? What is a single monk worth here? Let him go."

"My lord," said the princess, "let him out by the back gate."

"What a bother you make of it," said the demon. "If he is to be let go, then let him go—why fuss over back gate or front gate?" Then, taking up his steel blade, he called aloud, "You, Zhu Bajie—come here! It is not that I fear you, or will not fight you; but out of regard for my wife I spare your master. Go quickly to the back gate, find him there, and be off to the West. But if ever you come trespassing on my borders again, there will be no mercy at all."

When Bajie and Sha Monk heard these words, it was as though they had been turned back from the very gate of the dead. In all haste they led the horse, took up the luggage, and scurried off like rats. Rounding the back gate of the Wave-Moon Cave, they called, "Master!" The elder knew their voices and answered from among the thorns. Sha Monk cut a path through the grass, helped his master up, and hurriedly got him onto the horse. As it is said here:

> Cruel and dire, he nearly fell to the blue-faced ghoul;
> but tender of heart, by good fortune, was Hundred-Flowers Shame.
> The great-fish has slipped the golden hook and line—
> tail lashing, head tossing, it rides away upon the waves.

Bajie took the lead at the front, Sha Monk followed behind, and they came out of the pine forest onto the high road. You should have seen the two of them, grumbling and grousing, complaining back and forth, while Tripitaka could only smooth it over between them. At nightfall they sought lodging first; at cockcrow they were up to read the sky. Stage by stage, past long pavilions and short, before they knew it they had covered two hundred and ninety-nine li. Then, lifting their heads with a start, they saw a splendid city before them—and it was the Kingdom of Precious Image. Truly a fine place it was:

> Clouds hang dim and far, the road stretches long;
> though the land lies a thousand li off, its scenes are bounty enough.
> Auspicious vapors and lucky mists enfold it round,
> clear winds and a bright moon beckon and sway.
> The towering, jagged far-off mountains spread out like a painted scroll;
> the babbling, gurgling running streams scatter their crushed jade and gems.
> Land fit for the plow runs ridge on ridge, furrow on furrow;
> grain enough for the table—thick green sprouts and fresh young shoots.
> Anglers at their lines, a few households along the three winding ravines;
> woodcutters gathering fuel, one load between two pepper-crowned peaks.
> Outworks where outworks should be, walls where walls should rise—
> its moat of metal and water stands firm and unbreached;
> home set beside home, household by household,
> each contending only in carefree ease.
> Nine-tiered lofty towers, grand as palace halls;
> terraces ten thousand fathoms high, like banners of brocade.
> There are the Supreme Ultimate Hall, the Flowery Canopy Hall,
> the Incense-Burning Hall, the Hall of Letters,
> the Hall of Proclaiming Government, the Hall of Prolonged Brilliance—
> hall after hall with jade steps and golden stairs,
> ranked with civil caps and martial helms.
> There are the Great Brightness Palace, the Bright-Sun Palace,
> the Palace of Lasting Joy, the Flowery Purity Palace,
> the Establishing-the-Calendar Palace, the Endless Palace—
> palace after palace with bells and drums, pipes and flutes,
> that wash away the boudoir's sorrows and the griefs of spring.
> In the forbidden gardens, dewy blossoms match against tender cheeks;
> along the royal moat, willows in the wind dance with slender waists.
> On the great thoroughfares ride men in coronet and girdle,
> stately of mien, mounted behind five horses;
> in the lonely byways stand men with bow and arrows,
> parting the clouds and mist to skewer a brace of eagles.
> Lanes of flowers and willows, towers of strings and pipes—
> the spring breeze yields nothing to the Bridge of Luoyang.
> The scripture-seeking elder, looking back toward the Great Tang, felt his very liver and gall break with longing;
> the disciples who shared their master's road, resting their burdens at the little post-station, found their dreaming souls dissolve away.

The scenery of the Kingdom of Precious Image was more than the eye could take in. The three of them, master and disciples, put away their baggage and horse and settled to rest at the post-house.

Then the Tang Monk walked on foot to the gate of the court and said to the usher of the palace gate, "There is a monk of the Tang court who has come expressly to seek audience with His Majesty and to have his travel-document countersigned. I beg you to convey the request within."

The Yellow-Gate officer of audiences hurried to the foot of the white-jade steps and reported, "Your Majesty, there is an eminent monk of the Tang court who wishes to see Your Majesty and have his travel-document renewed." When the king learned that the man came from the great country of Tang, and that he was moreover a holy monk from afar, he was greatly pleased and at once granted the audience. "Bid him enter," he commanded. So Tripitaka was ushered up to the golden steps, where he completed the rites of dancing obeisance and crying out the royal acclamations. The civil and military officers ranged on either side could not help sighing, "What manner of man this is from the upper realm—how easy and gracious his ceremony and decorum!"

"Elder," said the king, "on what business do you come into my kingdom?"

"This humble monk," said Tripitaka, "is a follower of Sakyamuni from the Tang court. By the sacred decree of my Son of Heaven I am bound for the West to fetch the scriptures. I carry a travel-document with me, and upon reaching Your Majesty's noble land it is only fitting that I have it countersigned. So, not knowing how I ought to advance or withdraw, I have presumed to disturb the dragon countenance."

"Since you have a travel-document from the Tang Son of Heaven," said the king, "bring it up that I may see it."

Tripitaka raised it up in both hands, unrolled it, and laid it upon the royal table. The document read:

> The Tang Son of Heaven of the Great Tang Kingdom in the Southern Jambudvipa Continent, in obedience to Heaven and in keeping with the cycle of fortune, issues this passport for travel: We humbly consider that We, of meager virtue, have inherited the great foundation. In serving the spirits and governing the people, We have walked as on the edge of an abyss, as upon thin ice, dreading it morning and night. Some while ago, having failed to save the Old Dragon of the Jing River, We were reproached before Our August Sovereign of the Heavenly Court; Our three souls and seven spirits departed in a moment to the shades below, and We were already become a wanderer in the realm of impermanence. But because Our earthly span was not yet spent, We were moved by the lord of the underworld to be released and restored to life. Thereupon We spread abroad great assemblies of merit and built up a Mass for the deliverance of the dead. By grace there appeared the golden body of the Bodhisattva Guanshiyin, Saviour from Suffering, who pointed out that in the West there is a Buddha and there are scriptures, able to ferry over the souls in darkness and release the lonely ghosts. We have therefore specially charged the Dharma-master Xuanzang to journey afar across a thousand mountains and seek out the scriptures and gathas. Should he come to the various kingdoms of the western lands, let them not cut off this bond of goodness, but pass him on according to this document. Such are its necessary contents. On an auspicious autumn day in the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan reign of the Great Tang. The travel-document of the Imperial Presence. (Above it were stamped nine precious seals.)

When the king had read it, he took out his own kingdom's jade seal, set his royal cipher to it, and handed it back to Tripitaka.

Tripitaka gave thanks for the favor, took back his document, and then made a further request: "This poor monk comes, firstly, to have his document countersigned; and secondly, he bears a letter from home to Your Majesty."

The king was overjoyed. "What letter is this?"

"Your Majesty's third princess," said Tripitaka, "was carried off by the Yellow-Robe fiend of the Wave-Moon Cave on Bowl-Top Mountain. This poor monk chanced to meet her, and so she has sent a letter."

At these words the king's eyes brimmed over with tears. "For thirteen years," he said, "since the princess was lost, there is no counting how many civil and military officers I have demoted and dismissed, no counting how many maidservants and eunuchs, within the palace and without, great and small, I have had beaten to death. They could only say that she had walked out of the palace, lost her way, and that there was nowhere to seek her. We questioned the common households throughout the whole city without number, and still there was no trace. Who could have known a demon had carried her off? Hearing these words now, all at once, my heart is wrung, and I weep."

Tripitaka drew the letter from his sleeve and presented it. The king took it, and seeing the two words "All is well," felt his very hands go weak, so that he could not tear it open. He gave the order to summon a Grand Academician of the Hanlin Academy to the hall to read it. The Academician at once came up to the hall. Before the hall stood the civil and military officers; behind it stood the consorts and palace women—all of them inclined their ears to hear. The Academician broke the seal and read aloud. It was written:

> Your unfilial daughter, Hundred-Flowers Shame, bows her head and makes a hundred obeisances before the dragon-and-phoenix hall of her father the king, of great virtue, ten thousand years to him; and beneath the Bright-Sun Palace of her three royal mothers; and before the worthy ministers, civil and military, of the whole court. Your unworthy daughter was fortunate to be entrusted to the queen's palace, and is moved beyond all telling by a thousand kinds of toil and care lavished upon her. I could not exhaust my strength to gladden your faces, nor give my whole heart to the duties of a child. Thirteen years ago, on the fine night and fair hour of the fifteenth of the eighth month, by my royal father's gracious decree, the several palaces set out their banquets to enjoy the splendor of the moon and share together the great gathering of that clear-skied night. In the very midst of our merriment, all unawares a fragrant gust sprang up, and out flashed a demon king with golden eyes, indigo face, and dark-green hair, who seized your daughter, mounted upon an auspicious radiance, and bore me straight off to a wild and lonely place among the mountains, where there was no telling one thing from another. Relying on his strength, the fiend forced me to be his wife. And so, having no choice, I have endured thirteen years, and have borne him two demon sons, every one of them a demon's seed. This is in truth a ruin of all human bonds, a wound to decency and custom, not fit to be set in a letter that only brings shame. But I feared that, after your daughter's death, the matter would never be made plain. Even as I sat nursing my grievance and yearning for my parents, all unlooked-for the holy monk of the Tang court was himself taken captive by the demon king. So your daughter, with falling tears, wrote this letter, and made bold to set him free, entrusting to him this scrap of paper to lay bare the inch of my heart. I humbly beg my royal father to take pity, and send a great general with all speed to the Wave-Moon Cave on Bowl-Top Mountain to seize the Yellow-Robe fiend and bring your daughter back to court—this would be a deep and gracious mercy. Hastily and without due ceremony; the rest I cannot say in writing. Your rebel daughter, Hundred-Flowers Shame, bows her head again and again.

When the Academician had finished reading the letter, the king wept aloud; the three palaces shed tears; the civil and military officers were moved to grief; and there was no one, before or behind, who did not mourn.

The king wept a long while, then asked the two ranks of officers, "Who dares to raise troops and lead an army to take this demon for me and rescue my princess Hundred-Flowers?" He asked it again and again, and not a single man dared answer. They were truly martial generals carved out of wood, civil officials molded out of clay. The king's heart was wrung with vexation, and his tears gushed like a fountain. Then the throng of officers all bowed low together and submitted: "Your Majesty, do not grieve so. The princess was lost; to this day, thirteen years on, there has been no word of her. By chance a holy monk of the Tang court has met her and brought this letter here—and whether it be true we cannot be sure. Moreover we are all of us mortal men on mortal horses; we have studied the books of war and the arts of arms, but we are fit only to draw up battle-lines and pitch camp, to guard the realm from invasion and trespass. That demon is of the kind that comes on clouds and goes in mist; we cannot so much as meet him face to face—how then should we march out to the rescue? Now this scripture-seeker from the eastern land is a holy monk of the upper realm. This monk's Way is lofty enough to make dragon and tiger crouch, his virtue weighty enough to win the awe of ghosts and spirits; he must surely possess the arts of subduing demons. As the old saying goes: 'He who comes to tell of trouble is himself the man of trouble.' Let us then ask this very elder to subdue the demon and rescue the princess—that would be the surest plan of all."

Hearing this, the king turned quickly and entreated Tripitaka: "Elder, if you have the skill, then loose your magic powers, capture the demon, and bring my child home—and you need not go on to the West to worship the Buddha at all. Grow out your hair and keep your head of locks, and I will bind myself to you as a brother, share my dragon throne with you, and we will enjoy wealth and honor together. How would that be?"

Tripitaka hastily made his plea: "This poor monk knows a little of reciting the Buddha's name, but in truth he cannot subdue demons."

"If you cannot subdue demons," said the king, "how do you dare go to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha?"

The elder could not keep it back, and so he brought out his two disciples. "Your Majesty," he reported, "this poor monk alone could hardly have come so far. I have two disciples, well able to open a road where they meet a mountain and to throw a bridge where they meet a river, and so they have brought me safely here."

The king said reproachfully, "You monk, this is most unreasonable. Since you have disciples, why did you not bring them in together to see Us? Had they come to court, even if there were no gift to their liking, there would surely have been a meal of monkish fare to share out."

"This poor monk's disciples are ugly of face," said Tripitaka, "and I dared not bring them unbidden into court, for fear of alarming and harming Your Majesty's dragon person."

The king laughed. "Listen to this monk talk! Surely it cannot be that We should fear them?"

"I dare not say it," said Tripitaka. "My elder disciple is surnamed Zhu, named Wuneng, called Bajie. He has a long snout and protruding tusks, stiff bristles and fan-like ears, a coarse body and great belly, and a wind springs up as he walks. My second disciple is surnamed Sha, with the religious name Wujing. He stands twelve feet tall, his arms broad in three sections; his face is like indigo, his mouth like a basin of blood, his eyes flash and glitter, and his teeth are ranked like driven nails. Such are their two appearances, and that is why I dared not bring them into court of my own accord."

"Since you have described them so," said the king, "what have I to fear? Summon them in." And straightway he sent a golden tablet to the post-house to invite them.

When the idiot heard that they were summoned, he said to Sha Monk, "Brother, you would not have us deliver the letter—and now you see the good of having delivered it. The Master must have handed over the letter, and the king has said, 'The letter-bearer must not be slighted,' and is bound to lay out a banquet to receive him. But the Master has a poor appetite, and out of regard for you and me he has spoken our names, and so has sent the golden tablet to invite us. We'll all have a good meal, and be the better fit to travel tomorrow."

"Brother," said Sha Monk, "whatever the reason may be, shall we go and see?" So they handed over the luggage and horse to the warden of the post-house, took each his own weapon, and followed the golden tablet into court. Coming early before the white-jade steps, they took their stand to left and right, sang out a single salutation up toward the throne, and then never stirred again.

The civil and military officers were every one of them afraid, and all said, "These two monks may be ugly enough—but their coarseness is too gross by far. How is it that, seeing our king, they make no proper kowtow, but after one salutation stand bolt upright on their feet? Strange, strange!" Bajie heard them and said, "Sirs, do not pass judgment. We are just so: at first sight, true enough, we look a little ugly; but watch us a while longer, and we wear quite well to the eye."

The king, seeing how ugly they were, was already startled at heart; and when he heard the idiot speak out so, his courage trembled the more, until he could not keep his seat and tumbled down off the dragon throne. Luckily the attendant officers raised him up. The Tang Monk, in a fluster, fell on his knees before the hall and kept knocking his head, crying, "Your Majesty, this poor monk deserves ten thousand deaths, ten thousand deaths! I told you my disciples were ugly and dared not appear at court, for fear of harming the dragon person—and now truly they have alarmed the royal presence."

Trembling and quaking, the king came forward and helped him up. "Elder, it is well you spoke of it beforehand; had you not, and had I seen them all at once, I should surely have been frightened to death." After a long while the king steadied himself and asked, "Elder Zhu, Elder Sha—which of you is the master at subduing demons?"

The idiot, knowing no better, answered, "Old Zhu can subdue them."

"How will you subdue them?" asked the king.

"I am the Marshal of the Heavenly Reeds," said Bajie. "Only because I broke the laws of Heaven I was cast down into the world below; and now, by good fortune, I have turned to the right path and become a monk. From the time we came hither out of the eastern land, the foremost at subduing demons has been I."

"Since you are a heavenly general come down among mortals," said the king, "you must surely be skilled in transformations."

"I dare not boast," said Bajie, "but I do manage to know a few transformations or so."

"Then transform one for Us to see," said the king.

"Set the subject," said Bajie, "and I'll transform it just to pattern."

"Transform into something large," said the king.

Now Bajie too possessed thirty-six transformations. There before the steps he showed off his skill: pinching his fingers in the magic sign and reciting a spell, he gave a shout—"Grow!"—arched his back, and at once stretched out to a height of eight or nine zhang, for all the world like a Road-Opening Spirit. So terrified were the two ranks of civil and military officers that they shook and trembled, and the whole court, king and ministers alike, stood dumbstruck and dazed. Just then the Hall-Guarding General asked, "Elder, if you grow your body so tall as this, to what height must you grow before there is any limit at all?"

The idiot again let fall some idiot's words: "It depends on the wind. An east wind, well enough; a west wind, I can manage too; but if a south wind springs up, I'll poke the blue sky itself into one great hole."

The king, much alarmed, cried, "Put away your magic—we know now that such are your transformations." Bajie shrank his body down, took on his true form once more, and stood in attendance before the steps.

The king asked again, "Elder, when you go this time, what weapon do you have to do battle with him?"

Bajie drew out his rake from his waist. "Old Zhu uses a nine-toothed rake."

The king laughed. "That can only disgrace your appearance. Here I have whips, batons, melon-maces, hammers, sabers, spears, battle-axes, broadaxes, swords, halberds, lances, sickles—take whichever suits your hand and carry it off. What sort of weapon do you call that rake?"

"Your Majesty does not understand," said Bajie. "This rake of mine, coarse and clumsy as it is, has in truth been my own weapon since boyhood. When I was Marshal in the watery mansion of the Heavenly River, in command of eighty thousand water-troops, I relied wholly on the power of this rake. And now, come down to the mortal world to guard my master, when I meet a mountain I rake through the dens of tigers and wolves, and when I meet water I overturn the lairs of dragons and sea-serpents—all by this rake."

Hearing these words, the king was exceedingly pleased and convinced at heart. At once he commanded the nine ladies of the harem: "Bring out a full flask of the royal wine that We Ourself drink, that We may give the elder a send-off." So a goblet was filled to the brim and offered to Bajie. "Elder," said the king, "this cup of wine is but a token of the toil We lay upon you. When you have caught the demon and brought back Our daughter, there shall be a great banquet to reward you, and a thousand pieces of gold in heartfelt thanks."

The idiot took the cup in his hand. Coarse and rough as the fellow was in his person, in his conduct he showed a touch of refinement: he sang a great salutation toward Tripitaka and said, "Master, by rights this wine should be drunk beginning with you; but since the king has bestowed it upon me, I dare not refuse, so let old Zhu drink first to whet his spirits, the better to catch the demon." The idiot drained it at a draught, then poured a goblet and offered it to his master. "I do not drink wine," said Tripitaka; "you brothers may have it." Sha Monk came forward and took it. Then Bajie summoned a cloud beneath his feet and rose straight up into the air. Seeing this, the king said, "So Elder Zhu can ride the clouds as well!"

When the idiot had gone, Sha Monk likewise drained his wine at a draught and said, "Master, when the Yellow-Robe fiend held you captive, the two of us did battle with him, and could only fight him to a draw. Now Second Brother goes alone, and I fear he is no match for him."

"Just so," said Tripitaka. "Disciple, you had best go and lend him your strength." Hearing this, Sha Monk too leaped up upon a cloud and soared away. The king was thrown into a fluster and caught hold of the Tang Monk. "Elder, do you stay and sit a while with Us—do not go riding off on a cloud as well!"

"Alas, alas," said the Tang Monk, "I cannot go so much as half a step." And so the two of them stayed talking together in the hall—but of that no more.

Now Sha Monk caught up with Bajie and called, "Brother, I've come!"

"Brother," said Bajie, "what have you come for?"

"The Master sent me to lend you a hand," said Sha Monk.

Bajie was delighted. "Well said—and well come. The two of us will put forth our strength together and go catch that monster. Even if it comes to little, we'll at least make a name for ourselves in this kingdom." Just look at them:

> Wreathed in lucky radiance, they take their leave of the kingdom's bounds;
> shrouded in auspicious vapor, they set forth from the capital.
> Bearing the king's command, they come to the mountain cave,
> putting forth their strength with one heart to catch the fiendish thing.

Before long the two of them reached the mouth of the cave and dropped down from their clouds. Bajie drew his rake and, with all his might, struck once at the door of the Wave-Moon Cave, raking a hole in the stone gate as big as a dipper. The little fiends keeping the gate flung it open in terror, and seeing it was those two, ran in to report: "Great king, this is bad! That long-snouted, big-eared monk and that dark-faced, sour-visaged monk have come again, and have battered our gate to pieces!"

The fiend was startled. "This will be Zhu Bajie and Sha the Monk, the two of them. I spared their master—how do they dare come back and batter at my gate?"

"They must have forgotten some article," said the little fiends, "and have come to fetch it."

The old fiend snorted: "Nonsense! Forgotten some article, and dare batter at my gate for it? There must be a reason." In haste he buckled on his harness, gripped his steel blade, and came striding out to ask, "You monks—since I spared your master, how do you dare come back and batter at my gate?"

"You filthy fiend," said Bajie, "you've done a fine piece of work."

"What work?" said the old demon.

"You tricked the third princess of the Kingdom of Precious Image into your cave," said Bajie, "and relying on your strength forced her to be your wife. Thirteen years you've kept her—it's high time you gave her back. I come by the king's command, on purpose to take you. Get inside, quick, and tie yourself up and come out trussed, and spare old Zhu the trouble of laying hands on you."

At these words the old fiend was filled with rage. Just look at him: gnashing his steel teeth till they ground and grated; glaring his round ring-eyes wide; valiant and fierce, he raised his blade; bloody-red, he hacked straight at the head. Bajie dodged aside and met him face-on with the nine-toothed rake; and close behind came Sha Monk, lifting his treasure-staff and rushing up to strike alongside. This bout, fought on the mountaintop, was unlike the one before. Truly it was thus:

> A word amiss, a phrase awry, brings on a man's wrath;
> malice of intent and wounded feeling kindle the fires of rage.
> This demon king with his great steel blade hacks straight at the head;
> that Bajie with his nine-toothed rake meets him face to face.
> Sha Wujing flourishes wide his treasure-staff,
> and the demon king fends off the soldiers of the spirits.
> One ferocious fiend, two holy monks,
> back and forth they go with never a pause.
> This one says, "You cheated the realm—you deserve a death sentence!"
> That one says, "You meddle in idle quarrels, crying injustice!"
> This one says, "By forced wedding of the princess you wronged the state!"
> That one says, "It's no concern of yours—stop your idle wrangling!"
> Reckon it up, and all because of a letter carried home,
> monk and fiend are both at peace no longer.

They had fought before the mountain slope some eight or nine rounds when Bajie began little by little to flag; his rake grew hard to lift, and his strength gave out. Do you ask why he could not stand against the fiend this time? When they first joined battle, the Dharma-guarding spirits, because the Tang Monk was in the cave, had secretly aided Bajie and Sha Monk, so that they could just hold their own to a draw; but this time all the spirits were back in the Kingdom of Precious Image, guarding the Tang Monk, and so the two of them were no match for him.

Said the idiot, "Sha Monk, you go up and fight him a while, and let old Zhu step aside to ease himself." And with that, never minding Sha Monk at all, he bolted off into the wormwood and creeper, the thornbrakes and clinging vines, and, not caring good from ill, burrowed in all in a heap. Never minding that the thorns tore his scalp and the brambles cut his snout and face, he rolled himself down to sleep and dared come out no more—leaving out only half an ear to listen for the sound of the watchman's clapper.

When the fiend saw that Bajie had run off, he made straight for Sha Monk. Caught off guard, Sha Monk was seized by the fiend in one grip and dragged into the cave, where the little fiends bound him hand and foot, all four limbs trussed together like a hog's.

And in the end there is no telling how his life fared—so listen to the explanation in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 30 -->
# Chapter 30: The Demon Profanes the True Law; the Dragon-Horse Remembers the Mind-Monkey

Now, the monster had Friar Sand bound fast, yet he neither killed him nor beat him, nor uttered a single word of abuse. He took up his steel sword, and thought to himself, "This Tang Monk is a man of a great civilized realm — surely he knows propriety and right. He would never have spared his own life and then sent his disciples to seize me. Hah! This must mean that my own wife has somehow sent a letter back to her home country, and word has leaked out. Let me go and question her." And with that the monster, his cruelty rising in him, resolved to kill the princess.

The princess, all unknowing, had just finished her toilet and came stepping forward. There she found the monster glaring, his brows knotted, grinding his teeth in fury. Still she met him with a smiling face. "My lord, what troubles you so?" she asked. The monster spat out a curse: "You dog-hearted, base woman, utterly without human decency! When I first brought you here I never said one harsh word to you. The brocades you wear, the gold you put on, whatever you lacked I went and fetched. Through all four seasons you have had your comforts, every day my love deep upon you. How is it that you think only of your father and mother, and have not the least heart for husband and wife?"

Hearing this, the princess fell to her knees in terror. "My lord! How is it that today you speak of parting?" The monster said, "It is not I who would part — it is you who would part from me! I seized that Tang Monk, meaning to make a meal of him. How is it that, without first telling me, you set him free? It must be that you secretly wrote a letter and bid him carry it for you. Otherwise, how would these two monks come pounding at my gate, demanding that I return you? Is this not your doing?" The princess said, "My lord, you wrong me. When did I ever send any letter?" The old monster said, "Still you talk back! I have one of your accomplices held captive here this very moment — is that not proof?" "Who is it?" she asked. "It is Friar Sand, the Tang Monk's second disciple," said the demon.

Now, when a person comes to a place of death, who will admit to a thing that brings death? She could only deny it to his face. The princess said, "My lord, calm your anger. Let you and me go and question him. If there truly was a letter, then beat me to death and I shall die content. But if there was no letter, would you not have slain me wrongly?"

The monster would hear no more talk. He thrust out one hand, broad as a winnowing-basket and indigo-blue, seized the ten thousand strands of her golden-leafed, jade-branch hair, dragged her forward, and flung her to the ground. Then, grasping his steel sword, he turned to interrogate Friar Sand. "Friar Sand!" he barked. "You two dared to come storming up to my gate. Was it that this woman sent a letter to her country, and the king sent you here?"

Friar Sand, bound there, saw how savage the demon was — how he had flung the princess to the floor and now held the sword ready to kill her.
