And he thought to himself: "It is plain that she did send the letter and saved my master — that is a kindness beyond measure. If I speak the truth, he will kill the princess straightaway, and that would be repaying kindness with injury. Enough, enough! I have followed my master all this while and never rendered him an inch of useful service. Today I am already bound. Let me give this life of mine to repay my master's debt." So he cried aloud: "Monster, do not be so brutish! What letter is there? You wrong this woman and would take her life! We came here to demand the princess for a reason. When you carried off my master to your cave, he saw the princess's face and bearing. Later, when we reached the Kingdom of Precious Image to have our travel-rescript stamped, the king showed us a painted portrait of the princess and went inquiring of her everywhere. He asked my master whether he had seen such a face along the road, and my master spoke of the princess. The king thus knew it was his own child, and bestowed royal wine on us and sent us to seize you and bring the princess home. This is the whole truth — when was there ever any letter? If you mean to kill, then kill old Sand, but do not wrongly harm an innocent woman, for that would grievously offend Heaven's law."

Hearing Friar Sand speak so boldly and grandly, the monster threw down his sword and lifted the princess up in both arms. "It was my own rashness," he said, "I gave you much offense. Do not blame me, do not blame me." He smoothed her black tresses for her, propped up her jeweled coiffure, and with soft, gentle words and a pleasant smiling face cajoled her back inside, and even invited her to sit in the place of honor while he begged her pardon.

Now, the princess was a woman of yielding nature, and seeing him pay her such mistaken courtesies, she softened and changed her heart. "My lord," she said, "if you think on the love of husband and wife, you might loosen Friar Sand's ropes a little." The old demon, hearing this, at once ordered his underlings to untie Friar Sand and chain him up instead. When Friar Sand felt himself unbound and only chained, he rose up and rejoiced secretly in his heart: "The ancients said, 'Do another a kindness, and you do yourself a kindness.' Had I not done him that kindness, why would he have ordered me eased and loosened?"

The old demon then had a banquet laid out to make amends and soothe the princess's fright. When the drinking was half over, the old demon suddenly changed into a bright fresh suit of clothes, took up a precious sword and girt it at his waist, then turned and stroked the princess. "Wife," he said, "stay home and drink your wine, mind the two children, and do not let Friar Sand go. While the Tang Monk is still in that kingdom, I shall go early to claim my kinship." "What kinship will you claim?" she asked. The old demon said, "I'll claim your royal father. I am his son-in-law, he is my father-in-law — how should I not go and acknowledge the bond?"

"You cannot go," said the princess. "Why can I not go?" he asked. The princess said, "My father's kingdom was not won by horse and battle — it is the altar of soil and grain handed down from his ancestors. From boyhood he ascended the throne as crown prince; he has never once gone far from the city gates, and has never seen such a fierce fellow as you. Your countenance and features are so hideous that if he sees you, I fear he'll be frightened, and that would turn out badly. Far better that you do not go to claim the kinship at all." The old demon said, "If that is so, I'll just change into a handsome young man and go." "Then change yourself," she said, "and let me see."

Excellent monster! There at the banquet table he shook his body and changed, and became a comely, dashing young man — and indeed he was born so:

> His form refined and elegant, his frame tall and commanding;
> his speech all courtly grace, his bearing in the very flower of youth.
> In talent like Cao Zhi, who made verse with ease;
> in looks like Pan An, at whom maidens lightly threw their fruit.
> On his head a magpie-tail cap, his dark cloud-hair drawn smoothly up;
> on his body a robe of jade-white gauze, broad sleeves floating in the breeze.
> On his feet black flowered boots, at his waist a phoenix sash agleam.
> Truly a man of marvelous spirit and grace —
> towering over the valleys, a splendid and handsome youth.

The princess, seeing him, was greatly delighted. The demon laughed. "Wife, is this not a fine transformation?" The princess said, "It is good, it is good. When you enter the court, my father, being your kin, will not slight you, but will surely have his civil and military officers keep you to feast. Yet while you drink, take a thousand cares and ten thousand cautions. Do not let your true face show, do not let your horse's hoof slip out, do not let word of it leak — that would not be refined." "No need to instruct me," said the old demon. "I have my own way of managing."

Watch him now ride a cloud, and in a moment he reached the Kingdom of Precious Image. Setting down his cloud, he walked to the outside of the palace gate and said to the gate-keeper, "The Third Son-in-Law has come especially to see His Majesty. I beg you, pass word in." The yellow-gowned usher came before the white jade steps and announced, "Your Majesty, there is a Third Son-in-Law come to see you, now waiting outside the palace gate for your summons."

The king was just then conversing with the Tang Monk. Hearing "Third Son-in-Law," he asked his officials, "I have only two sons-in-law. How is it there's now a third?" The officials said, "The Third Son-in-Law must surely be a demon come." The king said, "Is it well to summon him in?" The elder, alarmed, said, "Your Majesty — as for a demon, one that were not cunning would not be effective. He can know the past and the future; he can mount the clouds and ride the mists. Summon him, and he comes in; do not summon him, and still he comes in. Better to summon him in, and spare ourselves some trouble of words."

The king approved the suggestion and called for the demon to be summoned, and the demon was brought to the golden steps. Like any courtier he performed the rites — dancing and shouting "Long live the king." The officials, seeing how handsome and fair he was, dared not take him for a demon. They were all of fleshly eyes and common mold, and took him for a good man. The king, seeing him so towering and lofty, thought him a pillar fit to save the age, and asked, "Son-in-law, where does your household dwell? Of what region are you a native? When did you wed our princess? And how is it you only come today to claim the kinship?"

The old demon kowtowed. "Sire, your servant is a man of the Moon-Wave Cave on Bowl Mountain, east of the city." The king said, "How far is that mountain from here?" "Not far," said the demon, "only three hundred li." The king said, "Three hundred li — how could my princess have come there to be matched with you?"

The demon, with cunning words and flowery phrases, false feeling and feigned sincerity, answered: "Sire, from my youth I have loved bow and horse, and lived by the hunt. Thirteen years ago, leading a few dozen of my household lads, loosing my hawks and chasing with hounds, I suddenly saw a fierce striped tiger bearing a woman upon its back, making down the mountain slope. Your servant drew his bow and with one arrow brought the tiger down, carried the woman home to my manor, revived her with warm water and broth, and saved her life. When I asked her of what household she was, she never once spoke the two words 'royal princess.' Had she told me at once she was Your Majesty's Third Princess, how would I have dared so deceive my heart as to wed her on my own? I would surely have brought her up to the golden palace and, great or small, sought some office to glorify my person. Only because she said she was a commoner's daughter did your servant keep her at his manor. The maiden was fair, the man was talented; both being willing, we were thus joined, and so have lived these many years.

"At the time of our wedding, I wished to slaughter that tiger and invite all our kin, but it was the princess herself who told me not to kill it. The reason she gave for sparing it was put in a few words, and put so well — she said:

> By Heaven and Earth alone are we made man and wife,
> matched without matchmaker, wedded without witness.
> In a former life the red cord once bound our feet —
> so let the tiger now serve as our go-between.

"On account of these words, I loosed the tiger from its bonds and spared its life. The tiger, carrying its arrow-wound, galloped off with trimming tail. I did not know that, having got its life, it dwelt in those mountains and cultivated itself these several years, refining its body into a spirit, and that it gave itself wholly to bewitching and harming men. I have heard that in years past there were several who went to fetch scriptures, all said to be the Tang Monk come from the Great Tang. I think this tiger must have harmed the Tang Monk, taken his travel-papers, and changed into the very likeness of the scripture-seeker, and now stands in your court deceiving Your Majesty. Sire — the one seated there upon the embroidered stool is exactly that fierce tiger which thirteen years ago bore off the princess. He is no true scripture-seeker at all."

Now watch that yielding-natured king, his foolish, deluded fleshly eyes unable to know a demon: he turned that whole tissue of empty words into solid truth. "Worthy son-in-law," he said, "how do you know this monk to be the tiger that carried off the princess?" The demon said, "Sire, in the mountains I have eaten tiger and worn tiger; I have slept and risen alongside them. How should I not know one?" The king said, "Since you know him, have him show his true form, that I may look." The monster said, "Lend me half a cup of clean water, and I'll make him show his true form." The king ordered an officer to fetch water and hand it to the son-in-law.

The monster took the water in his hand, leaped up, stepped forward, and worked his "Black-Eye Body-Fixing Spell." He recited the incantation and sprayed a mouthful of the water at the Tang Monk, crying, "Change!" The elder's true body was hidden upon the dais, and indeed he was changed into a fierce striped tiger. To the fleshly eyes of king and courtiers, that tiger appeared thus:

> White brow, round head, a flowered body, eyes like lightning.
> Four hooves, straight and towering; twenty claws, hooked and keen.
> Saw-teeth ringed his mouth, sharp ears reaching to his brows.
> Ferocious and stout as a giant cat in shape,
> fierce and mighty as a tawny calf.
> Stiff whiskers stood straight like silver wires;
> his stabbing tongue, blood-red, breathed out a foul vapor.
> Truly a fierce and striped beast,
> gust upon gust of dread power blowing through the precious hall.

At one sight of it the king's soul scattered, his spirit fled. The officials, terrified, all fled and hid. A few bold military officers, leading their generals and lieutenants, rushed forward in a throng and hacked wildly with weapons of every kind. This time — had it not been that the Tang Monk was fated to keep his life and not die — even twenty monks would have been beaten into a pulp. But by good fortune the Guardians of the Days and Hours, the Revealers of Truth, the Officers of Merit, and the Defenders of the Faith were all secretly protecting him from the air above, so that none of those soldiers' weapons could wound him. The officials shouted on until evening, and only then took the tiger alive, chained it with iron ropes, set it in an iron cage, and stored it away in the court chamber.

The king then issued a decree, bidding the Court of Imperial Entertainments lay out a grand banquet to thank the son-in-law for the kindness of his rescue — for otherwise, he said, they had nearly been done to harm by that monk. That evening, when the officials had withdrawn from court, the demon entered the Silver-Peace Hall. Eighteen palace maids and singing-girls were chosen to play and sing and dance and urge the demon to drink and make merry. The monster sat alone at the head of the table, ranged left and right with beauties of lovely form. Watch him take his pleasure and drink until the second watch — when, growing drunk, he could no longer restrain his vile nature. He sprang up, laughed aloud, revealed his true form, and his cruelty bursting out, he reached out his winnowing-basket hand, snatched up one of the girls playing the lute, and with a crunch bit off her head at one mouthful. The other seventeen palace maids fled for their lives, scattering and hiding everywhere. Look at them:

> The palace maids in dread, the singing-girls in alarm.
> The palace maids in dread, like lotus blooms cowering under night-rain;
> the singing-girls in alarm, like peony flowers tossing in the spring wind.
> They smashed their lutes to save their lives,
> tripped over their zithers as they fled.
> Out the door they could not tell north from south,
> leaving the hall they cared not east from west.
> Bruising their jade-fair faces, marring their tender beauty,
> every one ran for her life, each one fled to save the rest.

Those who got out dared not raise an outcry. The night was deep, and they dared not alarm His Majesty. They all huddled beneath the low walls and the eaves, trembling — but of that no more.

Now the monster sat above, pouring and drinking by himself. He would drain a cup, then drag a body over and gnaw two bloody mouthfuls. While he took his pleasure within, the word spread among the people without: "The Tang Monk is a tiger-spirit!" The rumor flew about wildly, until it reached the Golden Pavilion Post-Station. At that hour the station was empty of men; only the white horse stood at its trough, eating grass and fodder. Now this horse was in truth the young Dragon-King of the Western Sea, who for breaking Heaven's law had had his horns sawn off and his scales stripped, been changed into a white horse, and carried the Tang Monk westward to fetch the scriptures. Suddenly hearing men say the Tang Monk was a tiger-spirit, he too thought in his heart: "My master is plainly a good man — surely the demon has changed him into a tiger-spirit and harmed him. What is to be done? What is to be done? My eldest brother has been gone a long time; of Pig and Friar Sand there is no news either." He waited only until the second watch, and then sprang up. "If I do not save the Tang Monk now," he said, "this whole holy work is finished — finished!"

Unable to bear it longer, he snapped clean through his halter, shook off saddle and bridle, leaped up swiftly, and showed his power, becoming a dragon once more as of old. Riding a black cloud, he rose straight into the ninth heaven to look about. There is a poem to prove it:

> Tripitaka came westward to bow to the Honored of the World;
> but on the road there lurked a vile and demon air.
> This night, changed to a tiger, in disaster he was caught —
> and the white horse, dropping his halter, came to save his lord.

The little Dragon-King, hovering in mid-air, saw the Silver-Peace Hall ablaze with lamps and candles — for eight tall candlesticks held eight burning tapers. He lowered his cloud and looked closely, and there was the demon, all alone upon the high seat, drinking by force of magic and eating human flesh. The little dragon laughed: "This wretch is no good. His horse's hoof has slipped, his secret is found out, his scale is off the balance. Is eating men any path to advancement? Yet I do not know what has become of my master, and instead I've met this filthy monster. Let me go and toy with him a while; if I get the upper hand and take the demon, it will not be too late to save my master after."

Good Dragon-King! He shook his body and changed, becoming a palace maid himself — truly her body light and slender, her bearing soft and charming. Quickly she stepped inside and saluted the demon with a blessing: "Son-in-law, do not harm my life. I have come to pour your wine for you." The demon said, "Pour, then." The little dragon took the flagon and poured the wine into his cup, and the wine rose three or five parts higher than the rim, yet never overflowed. This was the little dragon's "Water-Pressing Spell." The monster, seeing it and not knowing what it was, rejoiced in his heart: "You have such a skill?" The little dragon said, "I can pour it higher still." "Pour again, pour again," said the monster. She raised the flagon and poured on as he pleased, and the wine rose on as it pleased, like a thirteen-storied pagoda, peaked and brimming, and not one drop spilled over. The monster stretched out his mouth and drank a cup; then he dragged over a corpse and ate a mouthful. "Can you sing?" he asked. The little dragon said, "I know a little." And she sang a small tune, true to its melody and rhyme, then offered another cup. "Can you dance?" the monster asked. "I know a little," said the little dragon, "but my hands are bare, and the dance is not pretty to see." The monster lifted his robe, unfastened the precious sword at his waist, drew it from the sheath, and handed it to the little dragon.

The little dragon took the sword, and with care, there before the banquet table — three up and four down, five left and six right — set going a flowery sword-play. The monster watched, his eyes agape. Then the little dragon cast off the flourishes and aimed a chop straight at the demon. Excellent monster! He twisted aside and dodged it, then in a flurry snatched up one of the tall candlesticks and parried the precious sword. Now that candlestick was forged of wrought iron, and with its handle weighed eighty or ninety catties. The two of them went out of the Silver-Peace Hall, and the little dragon resumed his true form, rode up his cloud, and joined battle with the demon in mid-air. This was a fine fight in the dark. How was it seen?

> The one a monster born of Bowl Mountain;
> the other a true dragon banished from the Western Sea.
> One loosed his radiance, like white lightning spat forth;
> one bred his fierce vigor, like red clouds bursting out.
> One was like a white-tusked old elephant come among men;
> one like a golden-clawed wildcat flown down to the mortal world.
> One a jade pillar propping up the sky;
> one a golden beam bridging the seas.
> The silver dragon flew and wheeled; the yellow fiend tumbled and rolled.
> Left and right the precious sword knew no rest;
> back and forth the tall candlestick never ceased.

The two of them battled in the clouds for eight or nine rounds. Then the little dragon's hands grew weak and his sinews went numb, while the old fiend was strong of body and stout of power. The little dragon could hold out no longer, and flung his sword to cut down the demon. But the demon had a trick for catching swords: with one hand he caught the precious sword, and with the other hurled down the candlestick to strike. The little dragon could not parry in time, and was hit on his hind leg. In panic he dropped his cloud, and thanks only to the Imperial Water River was his life saved, for the little dragon plunged headlong into the water. The demon pursued and sought him but could not find him, and so, taking up his precious sword and his candlestick, he returned to the Silver-Peace Hall and went on drinking and sleeping as before — but of that no more.

Now the little dragon lay hidden at the bottom of the water. For half an hour he heard no sound, and only then, gritting his teeth and bearing the pain in his leg, did he leap up. Treading the black cloud, he went straight back to the post-station, changed again into his old form as the horse, and crouched beneath the trough. Pitiful — his whole body was wet, and his leg bore a wound. At that hour:

> The Will-Horse and Mind-Monkey were both scattered and lost;
> the Metal-Sire and Wood-Mother both withered and fallen.
> The Yellow Dame was wounded, all parted and astray —
> with the Way and its virtue dwindling, how could the work be wrought?

Let us say no more of Tripitaka's calamity nor of the little dragon's defeat. Now Zhu Bajie, after parting from Friar Sand, had buried his head in a clump of grass and rooted himself out a pig's wallow. That nap lasted clean through to midnight before he woke. When he woke he could not tell where he was. He rubbed his eyes, steadied his wits, and cocked his ear to listen. Ah! Truly the mountains were so deep no dog barked, the wilds so empty few cocks crowed. He saw the stars shift and the Dipper turn — it must be about the third watch — and he thought: "If I want to go back and rescue Friar Sand, truly 'a single thread makes no cord, and one hand alone cannot clap.' Enough, enough — let me go into the city and see my master, get the king's leave, then pick out some bold men and horses to help old Pig come rescue Friar Sand tomorrow."

The blockhead hurriedly rode his cloud and went straight back into the city. In a moment he reached the post-station. By then men were still and the moon was bright. He searched the two corridors but could not find his master; he saw only the white horse lying there, its whole body wet, with a spot the size of a plate, blue and bruised, on its hind leg. Bajie cried out in alarm: "Double bad luck! This dead thing has not even been traveling — how come there's sweat on his body and a bruise on his leg? Some villains must have robbed my master and beaten the horse to harm."

The white horse recognized Bajie, and suddenly spoke with human speech, calling out, "Brother!" The blockhead was so startled he fell flat, then scrambled up and made to run outside. But the white horse stretched out its body and seized his black robe in its mouth. "Brother," it said, "do not be afraid of me." Bajie, trembling, said, "Younger brother, how is it you've taken to speaking today? If you speak, there must surely be some great misfortune."

The little dragon said, "Do you know that our master is in trouble?" Bajie said, "I do not." The little dragon said, "You do not. You and Friar Sand showed off your powers before the king, thinking to overthrow the demon and beg merit and reward. But you never reckoned the demon's skill was great and your own arts wanting, so you could not master him. By rights, one of you should have come back to bring word — yet there was no news at all. The demon changed into a handsome scholar, broke into the court, and claimed kinship with the king. He has changed our master into a fierce striped tiger, who was seized by the assembled officers and is now chained in an iron cage in the court chamber. When I heard of this misery, my heart was as if cut by knives. You two were not here these two days and did not know, and I feared for his life at any moment; so I had no choice but to change into my dragon's body to go and rescue him. But when I got to the court, I could not find my master. And when I came to the outside of the Silver-Peace Hall, I met the demon, and I changed into the form of a palace maid to fool the monster. The monster bid me dance with the sword for him to watch, so I took my chance and cut at him once. But he dodged it at once, and lifting up the tall candlestick in both hands, he beat me back. I flung the sword at him again, but he caught the sword, hurled down the candlestick, and struck me once on the hind leg. So I dived into the Imperial Water River and escaped with my life. The blue on my leg is from the blow of his candlestick."

Bajie said, "Is there truly such a thing?" The little dragon said, "Would I be fooling you?" Bajie said, "What's to be done? What's to be done? Are you able to move?" The little dragon said, "And if I can move, what of it?" Bajie said, "If you can move, then move on down to the sea! Let old Pig carry the baggage off to Gao Village, go back to the furnace, and be a son-in-law again."

Hearing this, the little dragon bit fast onto his long gown and would not let go, and could not hold back the tears falling from his eyes. "Brother," he said, "by all means do not give way to sloth." Bajie said, "And if I'm not slothful, then what? Brother Sand has already been taken by him; I am no match for him in a fight. If I don't break up the company now, what am I waiting for?"

The little dragon brooded a long while, then said through fresh tears, "Brother, do not talk of breaking up the company. If you would save our master, you have only to go and fetch one person." Bajie said, "Whom would you have me fetch?" The little dragon said, "Make haste, ride your cloud back to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, and invite our eldest brother, Sun the Pilgrim. He still has the great power to subdue demons. He will surely save our master, and avenge for you and me this defeat as well."

Bajie said, "Brother, let's fetch someone else. That monkey and I are a bit at odds. Back on White Tiger Ridge, when he killed that White-Bone Lady, he blamed me for egging the master on to recite the Tightening-Fillet Spell. I only meant it as a joke — I never thought the old monk would take it in earnest and start chanting, and so drove him away home. I don't know how angry he is with me; he certainly won't be willing to come. And if even one word goes amiss between us, that mourning-staff of his is heavy — if, not knowing my place, I catch a few blows, how would I live through it?"

The little dragon said, "He will certainly not beat you. He is a Monkey-King of benevolence and righteousness. When you see him, do not say the master is in trouble — only say, 'The master is thinking of you.' Lure him along. When he comes here and sees this state of things, he is sure to be indignant, and will certainly contend with that demon. He'll be sure to take the demon and rescue our master." Bajie said, "Very well, very well. Since you are so wholehearted, if I do not go I'd seem the heartless one. I'll go this once. If the Pilgrim truly will come, I'll bring him along; but if he won't come, then do not look for me — I shan't come back either." The little dragon said, "Go, go — he is sure to come."

So the blockhead truly gathered up his rake, hitched up his gown, leaped aloft, trod the cloud, and went straight eastward. This time too it was that the Tang Monk was fated to live. The blockhead met a fair following wind, spread out his two ears like a pair of sails, and was soon across the Eastern Ocean. Setting down his cloud — and before he knew it the sun had risen — he entered the mountains to seek the way.

Just as he was going along, he suddenly heard voices. Looking closely, Bajie saw that it was the Pilgrim, gathered together with a host of his fellow spirits in a mountain hollow. He was seated on a great rock cliff, and before him were more than twelve hundred monkeys, ranked and ordered, crying, "Long live the Great Sage, Grandfather!" Bajie said, "What enjoyment, what enjoyment! No wonder he was unwilling to be a monk and only wanted to come home — so there were all these good things here: such a great estate, and so many little monkeys to wait on him. If old Pig had a mountain like this, I wouldn't be a monk either. Well, now that I'm here, what shall I do? I really must see him."

The blockhead was a little afraid of him, and dared not show himself openly, so he slipped along by the grassy cliff-side, slipping and sliding, and squeezed in among the twelve or thirteen hundred monkeys, kowtowing along with them. But the Great Sage Sun sat high, and his eye was sharp and cunning; he saw him plainly, and asked: "In that ranked company, the one bowing all out of order — that's some foreign fellow. Where's he come from? Bring him up." The words were scarcely out when the little monkeys swarmed like bees and pushed Bajie up, pressing him down to the ground.

The Pilgrim said, "Where are you from, foreigner?" Bajie, hanging his head, said, "I wouldn't presume — thank you for asking. I'm no foreigner; I'm an old acquaintance, an old acquaintance." The Pilgrim said, "All the monkeys of my Great-Sage company are of one same look. Your mug is shaped quite differently, your features rather lumpish — you must be a demon from somewhere else. Since you're from elsewhere, if you wish to enlist under me, you must first present a written application of your particulars and report your name, and then I'll keep you here to be mustered in with the ranks. If I haven't enrolled you, how dare you bow here all out of order?"

Bajie, head down and snout puckered, said, "For shame — so you put on this face for me! You and I were brother disciples for several years, and now you make as if you don't know me, calling me some foreigner." The Pilgrim laughed: "Lift your head and let me look." The blockhead thrust his snout upward. "Look, then," he said. "You may not know me, but surely you know the snout." The Pilgrim could not help laughing: "Zhu Bajie." Hearing himself named, the blockhead bounced up in a single roll and cried, "That's right, that's right! I'm Zhu Bajie." And he thought to himself, "Since he knows me, it'll be easy to talk."

The Pilgrim said, "Why aren't you off fetching scriptures with the Tang Monk, but here instead? You must have offended the master, and he's banished you back. If there's any letter of dismissal, hand it here and let me see." Bajie said, "I never offended him; there's no letter of dismissal, and he never drove me away." The Pilgrim said, "If there's no letter of dismissal and he never drove you off, then why have you come to me?" Bajie said, "The master is thinking of you, and sent me to fetch you." The Pilgrim said, "He neither invited me nor thinks of me. That day he swore an oath to Heaven and wrote a letter of dismissal in his own hand — how would he now be willing to think of me, or willing to send you so far to invite me? I most certainly won't go."

Bajie made up a lie on the spot, saying quickly, "It's true he's thinking of you, true he's thinking of you." The Pilgrim said, "How was he thinking of me?" Bajie said, "The master was riding along on the horse and called out, 'Disciple!' I didn't hear, and Friar Sand pretended to be deaf. So the master thought of you, and said we were no good, said you were a clever, quick-witted fellow — when he called you'd always answer, ask one thing and you'd answer ten. Because he thought of you so, he sent me especially to invite you. Pray go and make the journey: first, you'll not disappoint his longing hope; second, you'll not waste my coming all this way."

Hearing this, the Pilgrim leaped down from the cliff, took Bajie by the hand, and said, "Worthy brother, you've put yourself to trouble coming so far. Come and play a while with me." Bajie said, "Brother, this place is far on the road; I fear the master's looking out for us, and we'll be late. I'll not play." The Pilgrim said, "You've come all this way once — look over my mountain scenery, won't you?" The blockhead dared not stubbornly refuse, and had to go along with him a while.

The two of them went hand in hand, the whole crowd of little fiends following behind, up to the very summit of the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit. A fine mountain! Since the Great Sage had come home, in these few days he had set it all in order, restored fresh as new. There one saw:

> Green as carved kingfisher-jade, high as if scraping the clouds.
> All around, tigers couched and dragons coiled;
> on every side, much crying of apes and calling of cranes.
> At dawn the clouds sealed the mountaintop;
> at dusk the sun hung among the trees.
> The flowing water murmured, chiming like jade pendants;
> the ravine springs dripped, sounding like a jasper zither.
> Before the mountain, cliffs and crags and sheer walls;
> behind the mountain, flowers and trees in lush abundance.
> Above it joined the basin where the Jade Maidens wash their hair;
> below it linked the diverted waters of the River of Heaven.
> Heaven and Earth wrought its beauty to rival Penglai;
> the pure and the turbid bred it into a true grotto-heaven.
> The cunning brush of the painter could scarcely depict it;
> the immortals' own deft minds could not draw it out.
> Exquisite, the strange rocks; strange, the exquisite rocks;
> exquisite their gathered hues upon the ridge and peak.
> When the sunlight stirred, a thousand strands of purple splendor;
> when the auspicious vapor swayed, ten thousand shafts of rosy cloud.
> A grotto-heaven, a blessed land, exists among men —
> all over the mountain, new trees and new flowers.

Bajie looked his fill and could not exhaust it, and was filled with delight. "Brother," he said, "what a fine place! Truly it's the first famous mountain under heaven." The Pilgrim said, "Worthy brother, could one pass one's days here?" Bajie laughed: "Listen to my brother talk! A treasure-mountain is a grotto-heaven, a blessed land — how can you speak of merely 'passing the days'?"

The two of them talked and laughed a good while, then went down the mountain. There by the roadside were several little monkeys holding up purple-glistening grapes, sweet-scented pears and dates, golden loquats, and bright-red bayberries, kneeling beside the path and crying, "Great-Sage Grandfather, please come to your morning meal." The Pilgrim laughed: "My brother Pig has a great stomach, and fruit won't do for his meal. Well, well — don't scorn the poor fare; make do and eat a few as a snack." Bajie said, "My stomach may be great, but when in the country, do as the country does. Hand them here, hand them here — I'll eat a few and taste the new ones."

The two of them ate the fruit, and gradually the sun climbed high. The blockhead, fearing he'd delay the rescue of the Tang Monk, kept urging him on: "Brother, the master is yonder looking out for you and me. I beg you, let's go quickly, you and I." The Pilgrim said, "Worthy brother, pray come into the Water-Curtain Cave and play a while." Bajie firmly declined: "I'm much obliged for your kind feeling, brother, but the master has waited long; no need to trouble going into the cave." The Pilgrim said, "If that's so, I dare not detain you long. Let us part right here." Bajie said, "Brother — you're not going?" The Pilgrim said, "Where would I go? Here, Heaven cannot constrain me, Earth cannot govern me; I'm free and at ease. If I don't play here, what's the good of being a monk? I'm not going — go along yourself. But pass word to the Tang Monk: since he's driven me off, let him think no more of me."

Hearing this, the blockhead dared not press him hard, only fearing he'd rouse his temper and earn a couple of strokes of the staff. So, with no choice, he muttered his farewell, found the road, and went off. When the Pilgrim saw him gone, he at once dispatched two nimble little monkeys to follow Bajie and listen to what he might say. Truly, no sooner had the blockhead got down the mountain, not three or four li along, than he turned his head, pointed back at the Pilgrim, and cursed aloud: "This monkey — won't be a monk, would rather be a demon! This baboon — I came in good faith to invite him, and he won't go. Well, if you won't, then you won't!" He walked a few steps, and cursed a few more. The two little monkeys hurried back and reported: "Great-Sage Grandfather, that Zhu Bajie isn't very honest. He walks a bit, then curses a few times." The Pilgrim flew into a great rage and cried, "Bring him here!" The whole pack of monkeys came flying over the ground, overtook Bajie, knocked him sprawling, grabbed his bristles and pulled his ears, dragged his tail and tugged his hair, and hauled him back.

What treatment was in store for him, and whether his life would be spared or lost — listen to the explanation in the next chapter.

<!-- chapter 31 -->
# Chapter 31: The Brotherly Bond, and the Cunning Capture of the Yellow-Robed Fiend

Bound in brotherhood, the heart is whole; the Dharma returns to its true nature.
When metal yields and wood is tamed, the right fruit ripens; the Mind-Monkey and the Wood-Mother together compose the elixir's root.
Together they climb toward the Land of Perfect Bliss; together they arrive at the Gateway of Non-Duality.
The scriptures are the great road of cultivation; the Buddha is matched to one's own original spirit.
Brother and brother meet to seal a threefold pact; demon and fiend in their hues answer to the Five Elements.
Cut away the lures of the six gates, and at once you reach the Great Thunderclap Monastery.

Now, that idiot Zhu Bajie had been seized by the whole pack of monkeys — hoisted up, dragged about, hauled this way and that until his black cassock was ripped clean through. Muttering and grumbling to himself, he moaned, "It's finished, it's finished. This time I'm in for a beating that'll kill me."

Before long they reached the mouth of the cave. The Great Sage sat upon the stone cliff and cursed down at him: "You bran-stuffed, blockheaded oaf! You'd already gone on your way — so why did you curse me behind my back?"

Bajie knelt on the ground and said, "Brother, I never cursed you. If I cursed you, may I chew my own tongue out at the root. I only said that since you wouldn't come, I'd go report to Master myself. How would I dare curse you?"

Wukong said, "How can you fool me? When I tug my left ear upward, I can hear the talk of the gods in the Thirty-Three Heavens; when I tug my right ear downward, I can hear the Ten Kings of the Underworld and their judges going over their ledgers. You cursed me as you walked along — do you think I didn't hear?"

Bajie said, "Brother, I know how sly and rat-witted you are. You surely changed yourself into some little thing and followed me to listen."

Wukong shouted, "Little ones! Pick out the big cudgels. First give him twenty whacks across the shins to greet him, then twenty across the back to send him off — and after that I'll see him on his way with my own iron rod."

Bajie, terrified, kowtowed and pleaded, "Brother — for Master's sake, I beg you, spare me!"

Wukong said, "I do recall that Master is a kind and righteous man."

Bajie went on, "Brother, if not for Master's sake, then for the sake of the Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea — spare me!"

When Wukong heard the Bodhisattva mentioned, three-tenths of his heart softened. He said, "Brother, since you put it that way, I'll not beat you. But speak the plain truth and don't lie to me. Where has Tang Monk run into trouble, that you've come here to trick me?"

Bajie said, "Brother, there's no trouble at all — I simply missed you."

Wukong cursed, "You beatable, worthless creature — still you try to bluff me! I, old Sun, returned in body to the Water-Curtain Cave, but my heart follows the scripture-seeking monk. That Master meets danger at every step, calamity at every turn. Tell me at once, and spare yourself the beating."

Hearing this, Bajie kowtowed and confessed, "Brother — I'll be honest, I came to fetch you, meaning to keep it hidden from you. I never expected you'd be this uncanny. Spare me the beating, and let me up so I can speak."

Wukong said, "Very well — get up and talk." The monkeys let go their hold. The idiot sprang to his feet and kept glancing nervously to either side.

Wukong said, "What are you staring at?"

Bajie said, "Just checking that the road there is wide and open — good for running."

Wukong said, "And where would you run to? I'd even give you three days' head start, yet old Sun has the skill to fetch you back. Speak quickly — if this rouses my temper, I'll never spare you."

Bajie said, "I'll hold nothing back from you, brother. After you left, Sha Monk and I escorted Master onward. We came to a forest of black pines, where Master dismounted and bade me go beg for vegetarian food. I walked a long way and found not a single household; worn out, I lay down in the grass for a little nap. But Sha Monk, parting from Master, came looking for me. You know how restless Master is — he wandered alone through the trees, enjoying the scenery. Coming out of the wood, he saw a golden pagoda shining with light, and took it for a monastery. He didn't expect that beneath the pagoda dwelt a fiend named Yellow Robe, who seized him.

"Later, when Sha Monk and I returned to search, we found only the white horse and the baggage — no Master. We followed the trail to the cave mouth and did battle with that monster. As it happened, Master had a savior within: the third princess of the Kingdom of Precious Image, whom the fiend had carried off. She wrote a letter to her family and entrusted it to Master to deliver, and so found a way to set him free. When he reached the capital and handed over the letter, the king begged Master to subdue the fiend and bring back the princess. Brother — you know it — can that old monk subdue any fiend? The two of us went back to fight it, but the monster's powers are vast and we never reckoned on them; it captured Sha Monk too. I fled defeated and hid in the grass.

"Then the monster changed into a handsome scholar, entered the court, claimed kinship with the king, and turned Master into a tiger. By great good fortune the white dragon-horse revealed its dragon-body by night and went searching for Master. It never found him, but came upon the fiend drinking in the Silver-Peace Hall. The horse changed into a palace maid, poured the fiend's wine, and danced with a sword, meaning to seize the moment and cut him down — but instead the fiend struck its leg with the great Hall-Lamp and wounded it. It was the horse that sent me to fetch you, brother. It said: 'Your elder brother is a man of benevolence and honor, and an honorable man bears no grudge for old wrongs — he will surely come to save Master from this one trial.' So I beg you, brother, remember the old saying, *Once a man is your teacher for a day, he is your father for life* — and by all means, go and save him!"

Wukong said, "You idiot — when I took my leave, I charged you again and again: 'If any fiend should seize Master, you have only to say that old Sun is his eldest disciple.' Why did you not speak of me?"

Bajie thought to himself, "Begging him won't move him half so well as goading him. Let me prick his pride a little." So he said, "Brother — it would have been better not to mention you at all. It was only because I did mention you that the fiend grew utterly outrageous."

Wukong said, "What do you mean?"

Bajie said, "I told it: 'Fiend, don't be insolent — don't harm my master. I have an elder brother called Sun the Pilgrim. His powers are vast, and he is a master at subduing demons. When he comes, he'll leave you without so much as a patch of earth to be buried in.' But the monster, hearing this, grew all the angrier and cursed: 'What sort of thing is this Sun the Pilgrim, that I should fear him? If he comes, I'll flay off his skin, draw out his sinews, gnaw his bones, and eat his heart. Lean as that monkey is, I'll still chop him to a hash and boil him in oil!'"

When Wukong heard this, he was so enraged he scratched his ears and rubbed his cheeks, leaping about in a fury. "Who dares curse me like this?"

Bajie said, "Calm your anger, brother — it was that Yellow-Robed Fiend who cursed so, and I'm only repeating it for you to hear."

Wukong said, "Worthy brother, get up. It isn't that I wouldn't have gone. But since the fiend dares curse me, I cannot but subdue him — I'll go with you. Five hundred years ago, when I made my great havoc in Heaven, every god and general in all the skies, seeing me, bowed and bent his back and called me Great Sage, every one of them. This insolent fiend dares curse me to my face and behind my back. I'll go and take him, hack his corpse into ten thousand pieces, and so repay the insult! That done, I'll come straight back."

Bajie said, "Just so, brother. Only go and take the fiend and avenge yourself — and whether you come back after or not is entirely as you please."

Then the Great Sage sprang down from the cliff, dashed into the cave, stripped off his fiend's garb, straightened his brocade cassock, cinched his tiger-skin kilt, took up his iron rod, and marched straight out the gate. The whole troop of monkeys, alarmed, barred his way and cried, "Grandfather Great Sage, where are you going? Take us along to romp for a few years — that would be fine, too."

Wukong said, "Little ones, what nonsense is this. In this matter of guarding Tang Monk, all Heaven above and Earth below know that Sun Wukong is Tang Monk's disciple. He did not drive me back at all — he sent me home to look in on you, sent me home to enjoy myself at ease. It's only because of this affair now. You must all keep careful watch over our home and estate. Plant the willows and pines in their season, and let nothing fall to ruin. When I've gone back and seen Tang Monk safe and fetched the scriptures back to the Land of the East, then, my task complete, I'll return and share with you the joys of our natural state."

The monkeys, each and all, received his command.

Then the Great Sage joined hands with Bajie and mounted the clouds. They left the cave, crossed the Great Eastern Ocean, and reached the western shore, where they brought their cloud-light to rest. Wukong called, "Brother, walk slowly here a while and wait — let me go down into the sea and cleanse my body."

Bajie said, "We're hurrying along the road — what's all this washing about?"

Wukong said, "You wouldn't understand. Ever since I went home, these few days have left some smell of fiend-haunt about me. Master loves cleanliness, and I'm afraid he'll find me distasteful."

It was only now that Bajie understood Wukong was acting from a heart wholly sincere, with no other thought behind it.

In a moment the washing was done, and they mounted the clouds again to press westward. Soon they saw the golden pagoda shining. Bajie pointed and said, "Isn't that the home of the Yellow-Robed Fiend? Sha Monk is still inside."

Wukong said, "Stay in the air. Let me go down and look at how things stand before the gate, the better to meet the fiend in battle."

Bajie said, "Don't bother — the fiend's not at home."

Wukong said, "I know."

Fine Monkey King! He brought his auspicious light down and went straight to the cave mouth to look about. There he saw two little boys at play, swinging crook-headed clubs to knock a fur ball and snatch at the hole — at their games. One looked about ten years old, the other eight or nine. While they were at their sport, Wukong rushed up — never minding whether they were the Zhang family's or the Li family's — seized one by the topknot, and lifted him bodily across. The child took such a fright that he raged and wept, cursing and crying all at once. This startled the little fiends of the Wave-Moon Cave, who hurried in to report to the princess: "Madam — some stranger has carried off the two young masters!" (For those two children were the offspring the princess had borne to the fiend.)

Hearing this, the princess rushed out the cave gate, and there she saw Wukong holding the two children, standing high upon the cliff and making as if to dash them down below. Terrified, she cried out shrilly, "You fellow! I have nothing to do with you — why have you carried off my sons? Their father is a fearsome creature, and should any harm come to them, he will never let it rest with you."

Wukong said, "Don't you know me? I am Sun Wukong the Pilgrim, eldest disciple of Tang Monk. I have a younger brother, Sha the Monk, in your cave. Go and set him free, and I'll give you back these two children. Two for one — that's still a bargain for you."

Hearing this, the princess hurried inside, drove off the little fiends guarding the doors, and with her own hands untied Sha Monk. Sha Monk said, "Princess, do not untie me — for I fear that when the fiend comes home and demands his prisoner of you, you'll be dragged into trouble and suffer for it."

The princess said, "Reverend, you are my benefactor. You argued my family letter for me and saved my life — so I have taken care to set you free. And as it happens, outside the cave gate there is your elder brother, Sun Wukong, who has come and bids me release you."

Ah! The moment Sha Monk heard those three words — "Sun Wukong" — it was as if cream had been poured over his head, as if sweet dew had moistened his heart. At once a joy was born in him, his whole breast filled with spring; it was not like hearing that some man had come, but like picking up a slab of gold and jade. See him shake out his sleeves and stride out the gate! He saluted Wukong and said, "Brother, you truly have descended from Heaven. I beg you, save me!"

Wukong laughed and said, "You little Sha-monk — when Master chants the Tight-Fillet spell, would you ever speak a kind word for me? All your fine talk about guarding Master — why aren't you walking the westward road, but squatting here? What for?"

Sha Monk said, "Brother, no more of that. An honorable man does not reproach what is past. We are defeated generals — we cannot speak of valor. Save me, save me, I beg you."

Wukong said, "Come up here." And Sha Monk leapt up onto the stone cliff.

Now, Bajie, hovering in the air, saw Sha Monk come out of the cave and at once brought his cloud-head down, calling, "Brother Sha — bear up, bear up!" Sha Monk looked round and said, "Second brother, where did you come from?"

Bajie said, "Yesterday I was beaten in the fight. By night I went into the city and met the white horse, and learned that Master was in danger — bewitched by the Yellow-Robed Fiend's magic into a tiger. The white horse and I took counsel together, and so I went to fetch elder brother."

Wukong said, "Idiot, never mind reunions now. Take these two children, each of you carry one, and go first into the city of Precious Image to goad that fiend out, while I deal with him here."

Sha Monk said, "Brother, how are we to goad him?"

Wukong said, "The two of you ride up on a cloud and stand above the Hall of Golden Bells. Without a word of warning, dash these children down before the white-jade steps. If anyone asks who you are, just say, 'We are the Yellow-Robed Fiend's children, carried off by the two of us.' When the fiend hears it, he's bound to come back — and then I won't have to enter the city to fight him. For if I battled him within the city walls, there'd be clouds spewed and mist breathed, dust flung and earth tossed, and the court, the officials, and the common folk would all be thrown into fear and disorder."

Bajie laughed and said, "Brother — whenever you do a thing, you stick us with the worst of it."

Wukong said, "How have I stuck you with anything?"

Bajie said, "These two children you've snatched are already scared witless; in a moment their voices will be too hoarse to cry, and a little after that they'll surely die. If we take them and dash them down, smashing them into meat patties, will the fiend let us go once he catches up? He'll certainly demand the two of us pay with our lives. And you'll come off clean, with not even a witness against you — isn't that sticking us with it?"

Wukong said, "If he lays hold of you, then the two of you just fight him back here. Here the battleground is broad and open, and here I'll be waiting to deal with him."

Sha Monk said, "Just so, just so — what elder brother says makes good sense. Let us go." And the two of them, leaning on their bold spirits, took the children away.

Wukong then leapt down from the cliff and went to stand beneath the pagoda gate. The princess said, "You monk — you have no faith or honor at all. You said that if I freed your brother you'd give me back my children. Now your brother is freed, yet you keep my children still and come back to my gate — what for?"

Wukong said, smiling courteously, "Princess, don't take it ill. You've been here a great many years; I'm only taking your sons to go and meet their grandfather."

The princess said, "Monk, don't be rude. My Yellow-Robed lord is not like other folk. If you've frightened my children, you'll have to soothe their fright for them."

Wukong laughed and said, "Princess — born as we all are between Heaven and Earth, how can a man so easily be said to have committed a crime?"

The princess said, "I understand such things."

Wukong said, "You're a woman of the inner chambers — what would you understand?"

The princess said, "From childhood I was raised in the palace and taught by my parents. I recall the old books say: 'Of the five punishments and their three thousand offenses, none is greater than unfilial conduct.'"

Wukong said, "Then you are precisely an unfilial person. For it is written: 'My father begot me, my mother nourished me. Alas, my father and mother — they bore me in toil and pain.' Therefore filial piety is the source of all conduct, the root of every good. How is it, then, that you keep company with a fiend and never once think of your father and mother? If this is not the crime of being unfilial, what is?"

When the princess heard this upright speech, for a long while her ears burned and her face flushed, and she was ashamed beyond all measure. At last the words burst from her: "Reverend, your words are most good. How could I not think of my parents? It was only that this fiend snatched me away and beguiled me here; his commandments are strict, my own steps are hindered, the road is long and the mountains far, and there was no one through whom to send word. I wished to take my own life, but feared my parents would suspect I had run off, and the matter would never be made clear. So, having no choice, I dragged out this poor remnant of life — truly the greatest sinner between Heaven and Earth." So saying, her tears welled up like a spring.

Wukong said, "Princess, you needn't grieve. Zhu Bajie told me you wrote a letter that saved my master's life, and that in your letter too you showed your longing for your parents. Old Sun, having come, will surely take the fiend for you, bring you back to court to see your sovereign, find you another fine match, and let you serve your parents to their old age. What do you say to that?"

The princess said, "Monk, don't go seeking your death. Yesterday those two fine champions, your fellow disciples, couldn't even prevail over my Yellow-Robed lord. And you — a scrawny ghost all sinew and little bone, looking for all the world like a crab with all your bones grown on the outside — what skill have you, that you dare talk of taking a fiend?"

Wukong laughed and said, "You've no eye for people, and can't tell a man when you see one. As the common saying goes: 'A bladder, big as it is, weighs nothing; a steelyard-weight, small as it is, presses down a thousand catties.' Those two of mine are all bulk and no use: they brace against the wind as they walk, they waste cloth when they dress, hollow at the heart for kindling, soft at the loins beneath the crown, and no good at all once the meal's been eaten. As for old Sun — small I may be, but I'm tightly knit."

The princess said, "Have you truly such skill?"

Wukong said, "My skill you've never seen. I'm a perfect master at subduing fiends and supremely able to quell monsters."

The princess said, "Don't go misleading me, now."

Wukong said, "I'll certainly not mislead you."

The princess said, "Since you can subdue fiends and quell monsters — how will you take him now?"

Wukong said, "Go off and hide yourself for now; don't stay here before my eyes. For when he comes, it'll be hard to move freely against him — I only fear that you, grown too fond of him, won't bear to see him harmed."

The princess said, "How should I be too fond of him? That I've lingered here so long is only because I had no choice."

Wukong said, "You've been husband and wife with him thirteen years — how should there be no feeling? If I see him, I'll not toy with him: every blow of the rod a real blow, every strike of the fist a real strike. I must beat him down before you can return to court to see your sovereign."

The princess did indeed do as Wukong told her, and went off to a quiet place to hide. (And it was likewise that her marriage-bond was fated to end, and so she met the Great Sage's coming.)

The Monkey King, having hidden the princess away, gave his body a shake and changed himself into the very likeness of the princess, then went back into the cave to wait for the fiend.

Now, Bajie and Sha Monk carried the two children to the Kingdom of Precious Image and dashed them down before the white-jade steps. Pitiful — they were smashed flat as meat-pancakes, fresh blood spurting, bones shattered to powder. The whole court of officials, terrified, reported: "Disaster, disaster — two men have been hurled down from the sky!" Bajie cried out in a great voice, "Those children are the Yellow-Robed Fiend's sons — carried off and brought here by old Zhu and Brother Sha!"

The fiend was still in the Silver-Peace Hall, his wine-stupor not yet slept off. Just then, dreaming in his sleep, he heard someone call his name, rolled over, raised his head, and looked — and there in the clouds were Zhu Bajie and Sha the Monk, hooting and shouting. The fiend thought to himself: "Zhu Bajie I could expect — but Sha Monk I bound up at home. How did he get out? How would my wife consent to free him? And how could my children fall into his hands? This must be Zhu Bajie's trick, because he couldn't get me out to fight him, contriving this stratagem to snare me. If I own up to this bait, then I'm in for a brawl with him. Ai — and I'm still aching from the wine! Suppose he gets in a blow at me with his rake — wouldn't that wipe out all my prestige and let him see through my secret? Let me first go home and look — whether they're my children or not — and there'll be time enough to talk with him after." Fine fiend! Without even taking leave of the king's audience, he turned to the mountain forest and went straight to the cave to look into the matter.

By this time the court already knew he was a fiend. For that night he had eaten one of the palace maids, and seventeen others had escaped with their lives; at the fifth watch they had reported the whole affair to the king. And because he had now departed without taking leave, all the more was it known he was a monster. The king set many officials to keep watch over the false tiger — but of that no more.

Now, the fiend went straight back to the cave mouth. When Wukong saw him coming, he laid a snare for him: squeezing his eyes, he let the tears fall pattering down like rain, stamped his feet and beat his breast, wailing of Heaven and earth, sobbing bitterly there in the cave. For the moment the fiend could not tell, and came up and embraced him, saying, "Wife, what is the matter, that you grieve so?"

The Great Sage spun his ghost-tale and shaped his false words, and weeping streams of tears, lamented: "My lord — as the saying goes, 'A man with no wife has no master of his goods; a woman with no husband finds her life come to nothing.' Yesterday you went to court to claim kinship — why did you not come back? This morning Zhu Bajie carried off Sha Monk and snatched away our two children too. I pleaded bitterly, but he would not relent. He said he'd take them to court to meet their grandfather. Half a day now, and no sign of the children — I know not whether they live or die. And you not come home either — how could I bear to give them up? That is why I could not stop my heartbroken weeping."

Hearing this, the fiend flew into a great rage. "Were they truly my children?"

Wukong said, "They were indeed — carried off by Zhu Bajie."

The fiend, raging, leapt about. "It's finished, finished. My children have been dashed to death by him; they cannot be alive now. The only thing left is to fetch those monks and make them pay with their lives to avenge my sons. Wife, weep no more. How do you feel in your heart now? Let me see to a cure for it."

Wukong said, "I'm not ill — it's only that I can't bear to lose the children, and weeping so has left me with a pain in my heart."

The fiend said, "That's no great matter. Get up — I have here a treasure. Just rub it a little over the painful spot, and the pain will stop. But be careful — don't flick it with your thumb; if you flick it with your thumb, it will reveal my true form."

When Wukong heard this, he laughed inwardly: "This vile fiend is honest enough — without any torture he's confessed of his own accord. Once he brings out the treasure, I'll give it a flick and see what kind of fiend he is." The fiend, leading Wukong by the hand, went deep into the cave's most hidden, sealed recess. Then from his mouth he spat out a treasure, about the size of an egg — a śarīra relic, an exquisite inner elixir. Wukong rejoiced in his heart: "What a fine thing! No telling how many sessions of sitting went into this, how many years of trial in the refining, how many turns of pairing male and female to forge this inner-elixir relic. Today, by great karmic fortune, it has met old Sun." The monkey took it in hand — but where was there any sore spot? On purpose he rubbed it about, and then flicked it once with his finger. The fiend, alarmed, snatched at it with both hands. But think — that monkey was wonderfully quick, and gulped the treasure down into his belly in one swallow. The fiend clenched his fist and struck; Wukong blocked it with one hand, wiped his face once over, and revealed his true form, calling out: "Fiend, no more of your insolence! Now look hard — do you know who I am?"

Seeing him, the fiend started in great fright: "Yah! Wife — how is it you've put on this kind of face?"

Wukong cursed, "I'll smash you, you vile fiend! Who's your wife? You don't even know your own ancestor!"

The fiend suddenly began to recall: "I seem to half-know you."

Wukong said, "I'll not strike you yet — look again."

The fiend said, "Your face does seem familiar, but for the moment I can't call up your name. Who are you, really, and where did you come from? Where have you knocked my wife flat and stowed her, that you come to my home to cheat me of my treasure by deceit? Truly insolent, truly hateful!"

Wukong said, "So you don't know me after all. I am Tang Monk's eldest disciple, Sun Wukong the Pilgrim. I am your old ancestor of five hundred years ago."

The fiend said, "There's no such thing, no such thing. When I seized Tang Monk, I knew only that he had two disciples, called Zhu Bajie and Sha Monk — whoever spoke of anyone surnamed Sun? You're some monster come from who-knows-where, come here to swindle me."

Wukong said, "I did not come with those two. My master, because old Sun was forever beating fiends and had killed a great many, and he being a man of mercy and goodness, drove me back — and so I was not traveling the road with them. It is you who don't know your ancestor's name and surname."

The fiend said, "You're a poor sort of fellow indeed. Driven off by your master as you were, what sort of face have you to come showing yourself before people again?"

Wukong said, "You vile fiend — how should you know that 'Once a man is your teacher for a day, he is your father for life'? That 'between father and son there is no grudge that outlasts a single night'? You harmed my master — how should I not come to save him? Harming him might be one thing — but you also cursed me behind my back and to my face. What do you say to that?"

The fiend said, "When did I ever curse you?"

Wukong said, "Zhu Bajie told me."

The fiend said, "Don't believe him. That Zhu Bajie has a sharp snout and a knack for old-wife gossip — how can you listen to him?"

Wukong said, "Enough of this idle talk. Just consider: today old Sun has come to your home, and you've treated your far-traveled guest poorly. Though you've no wine or feast to offer, you do have a head. Quick — stretch your head over here and let old Sun give it one blow of the rod by way of tea."

When the fiend heard talk of being struck, he laughed aloud: "Sun the Pilgrim, you've miscalculated. Since you mean to fight, you ought not to have followed me in here. I have a hundred and more fiends, big and small; though you were all hands over, you'd never beat your way out my gate."

Wukong said, "No nonsense. Never mind a hundred-odd — were there thousands or tens of thousands, I'd only need to mark each one out clear and beat them one by one, no blow wasted, till I'd wipe out your root and leave no trace."

Hearing this, the fiend hastily passed the order, and the fiends from before the mountain and behind it, the monsters inside the cave and out, were all mustered, each gripping a weapon, and they blocked the three or four layers of doors close-packed, letting no one through. Seeing it, Wukong's heart filled with joy. With both hands he gripped his rod and shouted: "Change!" — and changed into three heads and six arms. He gave the golden-hooped rod a flourish and made it three golden-hooped rods. See him wield three rods in six hands, beating his way through — just like a tiger loosed among sheep, a hawk among the hens of the coop! Pitiful, those little fiends: those his rod touched had heads smashed to powder; those it grazed bled like running water. Back and forth, lengthwise and across, he went as into a place where no one stood against him.

Only one old fiend was left, who chased out the gate and cursed: "You vile ape, what an utter rogue you are! How dare you come to a man's door and bully his household?" Wukong quickly turned his head, beckoned with his hand, and said, "Come on, come on — to beat you down, that's the real achievement!" The fiend raised his precious sword and slashed straight at his head; fine Wukong drew his iron rod and met him face to face. This battle, upon the mountaintop, half in cloud and half in mist — they fought:

> The Great Sage's powers were vast; the fiend's own arts ran high.
> This one leveled crosswise his rod of raw iron;
> that one held up aslant his sword of quenched steel.
> Lazily the sword rose, bright as a glowing dawn-cloud;
> lightly the rod parried, like a colored cloud adrift.
> To and fro they guarded their crowns, turning many a time;
> over and over their whole bodies wheeled round and round.
> One shifted his features with the wind;
> the other stood his ground and rocked his frame.
> That one opened wide his fiery eyes and stretched his ape-long arm;
> this one flashed bright his golden pupils and bent his tiger-waist.
> You come, I go, the weapons crossing in war,
> sword meeting rod, rod parrying sword, neither yielding.
> The Monkey King's iron staff followed the Three Stratagems;
> the monster's steel sword kept to the Six Secret Teachings.
> One, long skilled in his arts, was lord of fiends;
> the other, lavish in his powers, guarded Tang Monk.
> The fierce Monkey King grew fiercer still;
> the heroic monster grew the more heroic.
> Heedless of life or death they fought in the air,
> all for Tang Monk's far-off worship of the Buddha.

The two of them battled some fifty or sixty bouts, with neither victor nor vanquished. Wukong rejoiced inwardly: "This vile fiend — that sword of his can actually hold off old Sun's rod. Let old Sun feint an opening and see whether he can spot it." Fine Monkey King! With both hands he raised his rod and assumed the posture of "The Tall Probing Horse." The fiend, not knowing it was a ruse, saw the gap, brandished his sword, and rushed straight in to slash low; whereupon Wukong swiftly shifted to "The Great Centered Level," knocked his sword aside, and then with the move "Stealing Peaches Beneath the Leaves" brought the rod down on the fiend's very crown — and beat him clean away into no shadow, no trace.

Quickly drawing back the rod to look, he saw no sign of the fiend. Wukong was greatly astonished: "Why, my lad — he couldn't even take a beating, and beaten he's vanished! If he were truly beaten dead, there'd at least be some pus and blood — how is there not the least trace of him? He must have fled." Hastily he sprang up into the clouds to look, but on every side there was no stir or sound. "These two eyes of old Sun's see everything everywhere at a single sweep — how could he have slipped off so nimbly? Now I see. The fiend said he half-knew me; he must be no mere mortal monster, but very likely a spirit come down from Heaven."

In a fit of anger the Great Sage could no longer hold himself in. Gripping his iron rod, he turned a somersault and leapt straight up to the Southern Gate of Heaven. This so alarmed the deities Pang, Liu, Gou, and Bi, and Zhang, Tao, Deng, and Xin, and the rest, that they bent their backs and bowed on either side, daring not to bar his way, and let him pass through the Heaven-gate straight to below the Hall of Universal Brightness. There the Four Grand Preceptors — Zhang, Ge, Xu, and Qiu — asked, "Great Sage, what brings you here?"

Wukong said, "While guarding Tang Monk, I came to the Kingdom of Precious Image, where a fiend had deceived the king's daughter and harmed my master. Old Sun fought it in single combat; but in the midst of the battle the fiend vanished. I think it is no mortal monster, but most likely a spirit from Heaven, and I have come to investigate — what fiend-deity has slipped away?"

Hearing this, the Preceptors went into the Hall of Divine Mists and reported to the throne. By command they made inquiry: the Nine Luminaries, the Twelve Branches, the Five Dippers of the East, West, South, North, and Center, the host of stars of the River of Heaven, the Five Sacred Peaks and Four Great Rivers — all the gods and saints of all Heaven were present in the skies, and not one had dared leave his post. Then they checked, outside the Palace of the Dipper and Ox, the Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions — and, strange to tell, there were only twenty-seven; the Star of Kui alone was missing. The Preceptors reported back to the throne: "Kui, the Wood-Wolf, has gone down to the mortal world."

The Jade Emperor said, "How long has he been absent from Heaven?"

The Preceptors said, "He failed four roll-calls. Roll is called once every three days; it is now thirteen days."

The Jade Emperor said, "Thirteen days in Heaven is thirteen years in the world below." At once he ordered his own bureau to recall him to Heaven.

The twenty-seven mansion-officers received the decree, went out the Heaven-gate, and each chanted spells to rouse the Star of Kui. Now where do you suppose he had hidden himself? He was the very god-general whom the Great Sage had beaten and frightened during his great havoc in Heaven; so he had darted into a mountain ravine to skulk from the calamity, and the water-vapor had veiled his fiend-cloud — which is why Wukong had not been able to find him. Hearing his own bureau's officers chant the spells, he at last dared show his head and went up with them to Heaven. The Great Sage barred the Heaven-gate, meaning to strike him, but happily the other stars dissuaded him, and they brought the fiend before the Jade Emperor. From his waist the fiend drew out his golden tablet and, below the hall, kowtowed and confessed his crime.

The Jade Emperor said, "Kui, the Wood-Wolf — the upper realm has boundless splendid sights, which you did not stay to enjoy, but stole away to a single quarter of the world below. Why?"

The Kui mansion kowtowed and reported: "Your Majesty, pardon your servant his crime worthy of death. The princess of the Kingdom of Precious Image is no ordinary mortal. She was once a jade maiden who tended the incense in the Hall of Spreading Fragrance. Because she wished to have a secret union with me — and I, fearing to defile the splendid precincts of the Heavenly Palace — she, longing for the mortal world, first descended below and was reborn within the royal palace. I, not failing the earlier tryst, changed into a fiend, took a famed mountain for my own, carried her off to my cave-dwelling, and was matched with her as husband and wife for thirteen years. 'Every sip and every peck — none but is fore-ordained.' Now, through the Great Sage's coming here, the matter is accomplished."

Hearing this, the Jade Emperor took back the golden tablet and demoted him to tend the fire for Lord Lao Zi in the Tushita Palace — kept on his stipend but set to labor; should he earn merit, his post would be restored, and should he earn none, his punishment would be the heavier.

When Wukong saw the Jade Emperor deal thus with him, his heart was glad. He made a great bow toward the throne and, turning to the assembled gods, said, "Gentlemen, I've put you to trouble." The Preceptors laughed: "That monkey is still such a country boor. We've collected his fiend-deity for him, and instead of giving thanks for Heaven's grace, he just makes a bow and withdraws." The Jade Emperor said, "So long as he gives us no trouble and leaves Heaven in peace, that is our good fortune."

The Great Sage brought down his auspicious light and went straight back to the Wave-Moon Cave on Bowl Mountain. He sought out the princess and recounted to her, just as it was, the tale of the star who, longing for the mortal world, had come down — and of the fiend's capture. Just then he heard Bajie and Sha Monk calling loudly from mid-air: "Brother! If there are fiends, leave a few for us to beat!"

Wukong said, "The fiends are utterly wiped out."

Sha Monk said, "Since the fiends are all destroyed, there's nothing left to hinder us — let's bring the princess into the court. Don't open your eyes, brothers — let's use the earth-shrinking art."

The princess heard only a rushing of wind in her ears, and in an instant was carried straight back into the city. The three of them brought the princess up onto the Hall of Golden Bells. She reverently saluted her royal father and mother and met again her sisters, and all the officials came to pay their respects. Then the princess reported: "It is thanks to the boundless powers of the Reverend Sun that the Yellow-Robed Fiend was subdued and your handmaid restored to her country."

The king asked, "What sort of fiend was Yellow Robe?"

Wukong said, "Your Majesty's son-in-law was the Star of Kui from the upper realm, and your beloved daughter was a jade maiden who tended the incense, who out of longing for the mortal world came down among men. This is no small matter — it was all karma from a former life, and these marriage-ties were destined to be. The fiend was taken when old Sun went up to the Heavenly Palace and reported to the Jade Emperor, who, finding that he had missed four roll-calls and been thirteen days in the world below — which is thirteen years, for one day in Heaven is a year below — at once sent his own bureau's stars to recall him to Heaven and demoted him to do penance and earn merit in the Tushita Palace. And old Sun has thus saved your beloved daughter."

The king thanked Wukong for his great kindness and bade them, "Go now and see to your master." The three of them went straight down from the hall and, with the officials, came to the audience-chamber, where they carried out the iron cage and loosed the false tiger from its chains. To everyone else he looked a tiger; to Wukong alone he looked a man. For the master had been bound fast by the fiend's sorcery and could not move, though his mind was clear — only his mouth and eyes were hard to open.

Wukong laughed and said, "Master — you're such a fine monk; how have you got yourself up in this hideous shape? You blamed me for being violent and doing evil, and drove me away. You meant to be wholly bent on goodness — so how have you suddenly worked yourself into a face like this?"

Bajie said, "Brother — save him, save him; don't keep nettling him so."

Wukong said, "You instigated everything — you're his favorite, fine disciple. If you won't save him, what do you come seeking old Sun for? I told you to begin with: once I'd subdued the fiend and avenged the curse against me, I'd go straight back."

Sha Monk came forward and knelt: "Brother — the ancients said, 'If you won't look at the monk's face, look at the Buddha's.' Since elder brother has come this far, I beg you, save him. If we could have saved him ourselves, we'd never have dared come so far to invite you."

Wukong took him by the hand and raised him up: "How could I ever mean in my heart not to save him? Quick — fetch water." Bajie flew like a shooting star to the post-house, fetched the baggage and the horse, took out the purple-gold alms-bowl, filled it half with water, and handed it to Wukong. Wukong took the water in hand, chanted the true words, and spewed a mouthful straight over the tiger's head — and the sorcery withdrew, the tiger-shape dissolved.

The elder showed forth his original body. Steadying his spirit and opening his eyes, he knew it for Wukong at last. He grasped him close and said, "Wukong — where have you come from?" Sha Monk, standing in attendance to either side, set forth the whole affair in order: how they had invited Wukong, how he subdued the fiend, saved the princess, dissolved the tiger-spell, and the matter of returning to court — all of it told through. Tripitaka thanked him without end: "Worthy disciple — it is thanks to you, thanks to you! On this journey, may we reach the West early and return straight to the Land of the East to report to the Tang Emperor; yours shall be the foremost merit."

Wukong laughed and said, "Say no more, say no more — only don't chant that certain thing, and I'll be deeply moved by your kind regard."

When the king heard these words, he again pressed his thanks upon all four of them. A vegetarian feast was prepared and the Eastern Pavilion thrown wide open. The master and disciples received the royal favor, took their leave of the king, and went westward. The king, too, led his many officials to see them far on their way. Truly it was:

> The sovereign returns to his precious hall and sets his realm at peace;
> the monks depart for the Thunderclap to seek the Buddha-Patriarch.

And in the end, what further matters lay ahead, and when they would reach the Western Heaven — that you must hear told in the chapter to come.

<!-- chapter 32 -->
# Chapter 32: The Spirit of the Day Brings Warning on Flat-Top Mountain, and Wood Mother Meets Disaster at Lotus Cave

Now that the Tang Monk had recovered Sun Wukong, master and disciples were once more of one heart and one body, and together they pressed on toward the West. Since rescuing the princess in the Kingdom of Precious Elephant, they had been escorted out the western gate by king and ministers alike. Of the road there is no need to speak in full — hunger met with food and thirst with drink, lodging at night and traveling at dawn. And just then it happened to be the season of the third month of spring. At that time of year:

> A light breeze stirs the willows, green as threads of silk,
> A scene so fair it begs to be set down in verse.
> The season hurries the birds to song,
> Warmth coaxes the blossoms open,
> And fragrance spreads across the earth.
> To the courtyard of flowering crab-apple come paired swallows —
> Truly the time to savor spring.
> Red dust and purple lanes, silken robes and sounding strings,
> Plucking the wildflowers, passing the wine-cup round.

As master and disciples journeyed on, drinking in the sights, a mountain rose up to block their way. Said the Tang Monk, "Disciples, be careful. There's a high mountain ahead, and I fear there may be tigers and wolves lying in wait." Wukong replied, "Master, a man who has left the household life should not speak as a householder does. Don't you recall what the Crow's-Nest Monk said in his *Heart Sutra* — 'The mind without hindrance: being without hindrance, there is no fear, and one is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions'?
