It comes down only to this: 'Sweep the grime from the mind, wash clean the dust from the ears. He who will not endure the bitterest of bitterness can never become the man above all men.' Don't let yourself worry. As long as old Sun is here, even if the very sky should come crashing down, I can keep you safe — so what's a tiger or a wolf to us?" The Elder reined his horse back and said,

> "In that year I took the imperial command and left Chang'an,
> Mindful only of going west to bow before the Buddha's face.
> In the land of the Sariras, golden images glow with color;
> Within the pagoda towers, the jade brow-mark gleams.
> I seek to the ends of the earth nameless waters,
> And cross every land to a mountain I never reach.
> On and on through layered mists and rolling waves —
> When will this body of mine ever find rest?"

When Wukong heard this, he laughed aloud and said, "If you want your body at rest, where's the difficulty in that? Once the work is accomplished, all ties will be cut and all phenomena will be empty. At that moment, naturally and of itself — won't your body be at rest then?" Hearing this, the Elder could only take joy and forget his cares. He loosened the rein and urged on the white horse, gathering the bridle and pressing the jade dragon forward.

Master and disciples climbed up the mountain, and it was steep beyond measure — truly towering and craggy. A fine mountain:

> Lofty, soaring ridges; sharp, whittled peaks.
> Below the winding deep ravines, beside the lonely sheer cliffs.
> Below the winding deep ravines you hear only the splash and gurgle of a water-python rolling its body over;
> Beside the lonely sheer cliffs you see only the steep-shouldered tiger lashing its tail as it bursts from the woods.
> Look up — the summits jut so high they pierce the blue heavens;
> Turn your eyes — the gorges sink so deep they border the green void.
> Climbing up, it is like ladders, like footstools;
> Going down low, it is like moats, like pits.
> Truly it is a strange and grotesque peak-and-ridge land,
> Truly a chain of jagged, whittled cliff-walls.
> On the peak-and-ridge heights, the herb-gatherer dreads to set foot;
> Before the whittled cliff-walls, the woodcutter can scarcely advance an inch.
> Wild rams and wild horses dart about like shuttles;
> Cunning hares and mountain oxen are drawn up as if in battle array.
> So high it screens the sun and blots out the stars,
> And here and there one meets monstrous beasts and gray wolves.
> The grassy paths are tangled and dim, hard for a horse to pass —
> How shall one ever reach the Thunderclap and behold the Buddha-King?

The Elder reined in his horse and gazed at the mountain. Just where the going was hardest, he saw, standing upon a slope of green sedge, a woodcutter. And how was he got up? Listen:

> On his head a battered old indigo felt hat;
> On his body a coat of coarse black wool.
> The battered old indigo felt hat, screening mist and shading sun — a rare sight indeed;
> The coarse black wool coat, joy enough to forget all care — a man seldom met with.
> In his hand a sharp steel axe, ground bright;
> His blade has felled the dry wood, bound tight in a bundle.
> Spring colors hang at his eaves, serene through all four seasons;
> The idle ease beyond his body is calm as the three stars of evening.
> To his old age he passes content with his lot —
> What glory or disgrace has ever touched this mountain?

And that woodcutter:

> Was felling rotten brushwood there before the slope,
> When suddenly he met the Elder coming from the east.
> He stilled his stroke and set down his axe and came out of the trees,
> Hurrying his steps up onto the rocky cliff.

In a sharp, loud voice he called out to the Elder: "You there, Elder, journeying west — hold a moment! I have a word to offer you. On this mountain there is a band of poisonous fiends and savage monsters, who feed precisely on travelers like you, passing east and west." When the Elder heard this, his soul flew from him and his wits scattered; trembling, he could no longer sit steady in his carved saddle. He turned his head at once and hurriedly called to his disciples, "Did you hear what that woodcutter reports? He says this mountain has poisonous fiends and savage monsters! Who dares go and question him about the particulars?" Said Wukong, "Set your mind at ease, Master. Let old Sun go and get the whole story out of him."

What a fine Wukong! He strode out and made straight up the mountain. To the woodcutter he called "Elder Brother," and offered a respectful greeting. The woodcutter returned the courtesy and said, "Elder, what brings you all to this place?" Said Wukong, "I'll not hide it from you, Brother — we are sent from the Land of the East to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. The one on the horse is my master, and he's rather faint of heart. Just now you were good enough to warn us of some poisonous fiends and savage monsters, so I've come to ask you straight: how many years' standing has this fiend, and how many years' standing has this monster? Is he an old hand, or a mere fledgling? Be so kind, Brother, as to tell me honestly, so that I may have the mountain god and the local earth-spirit hand him over and pack him off."

Hearing this, the woodcutter threw back his head and laughed at the sky: "So you're a mad monk after all!" Said Wukong, "I'm not mad — this is plain honest talk." The woodcutter said, "If it's honest talk, how do you dare speak of having him handed over and packed off?" Said Wukong, "Since you stand here puffing up his fearsome power, talking such wild nonsense, blocking the road to bring us warning — surely you must be kin to him? If not kin, then a neighbor; if not a neighbor, then a friend." The woodcutter laughed, "You ruffian of a mad monk, you've no sense at all! Here I come out of pure good will, on purpose to warn you so you'll keep your guard up morning and night as you travel — and you turn it round and lay the blame on me! And never mind that I don't even know where the demons came from — suppose I did know: how would you dare have him 'handed over'? Handed over to where?"

Said Wukong, "If he's a Heaven-fiend, hand him to the Jade Emperor; if he's an Earth-fiend, hand him to the Earth Bureau. Those of the West belong to the Buddha, those of the East to the Sage; those of the North are handed to the True Warrior, those of the South to the Fire Virtue. If he's a flood-dragon spirit, hand him to the Lord of the Sea; if he's a ghostly haunt, hand him to King Yama. Each has his own quarter and direction. Old Sun is known to folk everywhere — I'll issue a single writ and have him packed off overnight at a run."

The woodcutter could not hold back a cold, mocking laugh: "You ruffian of a mad monk! No doubt you've roamed about the country and learned a few tricks of charms and water-spells, fit only to drive off goblins and bind ghosts — but you've never yet run up against monsters as vicious and venomous as these." Said Wukong, "How do you reckon they're so vicious and venomous?" The woodcutter said, "This mountain road runs some six hundred *li* across, and its name is Flat-Top Mountain. In the mountain is a cave called Lotus Cave. In the cave are two demon chiefs. They have painted likenesses and drawn portraits, meaning to seize monks; they have copied out names and looked up surnames, meaning to eat the Tang Monk. If you'd come from anywhere else it might be well enough — but if you carry so much as the single word 'Tang,' you may give up all thought of getting through, of getting through at all." Said Wukong, "We are precisely from the Tang court." The woodcutter said, "Then he means to eat you, sure enough." Said Wukong, "What luck, what luck! Only I wonder — how does he go about eating us?" The woodcutter said, "How would you like him to eat you?" Said Wukong, "If he eats the head first, that's still some sport; but if he eats the feet first, then it's a wretched business." The woodcutter said, "What do you mean, head first? What do you mean, feet first?" Said Wukong, "You've never gone through it, that's clear. If he eats the head first, one bite and it's off — I'm already dead, and however he fries or stews or boils or simmers me, I'll feel no pain. But if he eats the feet first, gnawing the ankle-bones, chewing the leg-shanks, eating up to the waist-joint, and I'm still in too much of a hurry to die — won't I be suffering bit by bit, piece by piece? That's why it's a wretched business." The woodcutter said, "Monk, he hasn't all that much leisure. He simply seizes you, ties you up in his steamer-basket, and steams you whole to eat." Wukong laughed, "Better and better! At least the pain won't be unbearable — only a bit of stifling discomfort to put up with." The woodcutter said, "Monk, don't make light with your tongue. These demons carry five treasures about them, and their magic powers are vast beyond all measure. Even were you the jade pillar that props up the sky, the golden beam that spans the sea, if you meant to see the Tang monk safely through, you'd still have to faint dead away a time or two." Said Wukong, "Faint how many times?" The woodcutter said, "You'd have to faint three or four times." Said Wukong, "No matter, no matter. In a single year we faint seven or eight hundred times, so these three or four are easily come by — we'll faint them off and be done."

What a great Sage — wholly without fear, his whole heart bent only on guarding the Tang Monk! He left the woodcutter behind, strode back, and came straight to the front of the horse on the mountain slope. "Master," he said, "there's nothing much to it. There may be a little goblin or two, but it's only that the folk hereabouts are timid and let it weigh on their hearts. With me here, what's there to fear? On we go, on we go." Hearing this, the Elder could only set his heart at ease and follow on. But just then, the woodcutter was nowhere to be seen. Said the Elder, "How is it that the woodcutter who brought us warning has vanished?" Bajie said, "Our luck's run low — we've gone and met a ghost in broad daylight." Said Wukong, "I expect he's ducked into the woods to look for firewood. Let me go take a look."

What a great Sage! He opened wide his fiery eyes and golden pupils and scanned across the whole mountain and over every ridge — but there was no trace of the man. Suddenly he lifted his head and looked up into the clouds, and there he saw it was the Spirit of the Day on guard. At once he leaped upon his cloud to overtake him, cursed him a few times for a "hairy demon," and said, "Why didn't you come and speak your piece plainly, instead of changing yourself like that and putting on a show for old Sun?" In a fluster the Spirit made his bow and said, "Great Sage, I was late in bringing the warning — forgive me, forgive me. These monsters truly have vast powers and many transformations. Only by your own cunning and skill, by the working of your divine wit, can you carefully guard your master. Should you grow even a trifle slack, the road to the Western Heaven you may as well forget." Hearing this, Wukong dismissed the Spirit with a shout, fixed the matter firmly in his heart, pressed down his cloud-head, and came straight up the mountain. There he saw the Elder, with Bajie and Sha Monk clustered round, pressing forward.

Now he thought to himself in secret: "If I tell my master the Spirit's words exactly as they were, he's no good for it — he'll start crying for certain. And if I don't tell him truly but lead him along blind, then, as the old saying goes, 'Newly into the reed marsh, one knows not its depth.' Should the demons carry him off, won't it be old Sun who has all the worry again? Let me make a little use of Bajie first. I'll send him out ahead to do a round with the monster. If he can beat him, that's one merit to his credit; and if he hasn't the skill and the monster seizes him, it'll be soon enough for old Sun to go and rescue him then — and it'll let me show off my talents and make a name." So he was reckoning with himself, asking his own heart of his heart: "Only I fear Bajie is lazy and won't stick his neck out, and the master has a soft spot for him too. Let old Sun rein him in a little and bridle him."

What a great Sage! Watch him work a piece of trickery: he rubbed and rubbed at his eyes until he had squeezed out a few tears, then went straight up toward his master. When Bajie saw him, he called out at once, "Sha Monk! Set down the load, get out the baggage — let the two of us divide it up." Said Sha Monk, "Second Brother, divide it for what?" Bajie said, "Divide it up! You go back to the Flowing-Sands River and be a monster again, and old Hog will go back to Gao Village to look in on the wife. We'll sell the white horse, buy a coffin, and send the master off to his rest. Everyone scatters — who's still going to the Western Heaven?" The Elder, hearing this from horseback, said, "You blockhead! We're walking along well enough — why are you talking nonsense again?" Bajie said, "It's your son talking nonsense. Don't you see Sun Wukong coming back over there crying? He's a hero who can bore through Heaven and dig into Earth, who fears neither the axe's blow nor the fire's burn nor the cauldron of boiling oil — and now he's put on a cap of grief and comes blubbering, tears streaming. That mountain must be sheer and steep, the monsters fierce and savage. Soft, feeble folk like us — how are we ever to get through?" The Elder said, "Stop your nonsense for now and let me ask him a word, to see what he says." So he asked, "Wukong, whatever there is to talk over, let's do it face to face — why are you fretting all by yourself? Putting on this weeping-bag face — are you trying to scare me with a paper tiger?"

Wukong said, "Master, just now the one who brought us warning was the Spirit of the Day on guard. He says the demons are fierce and savage, and the going here is hard. Sure enough, the mountain is high and the road is steep, and we can't go forward — let's go some other day." Hearing this, the Elder was struck with dread and terror, and clutched at Wukong's tiger-skin kilt: "Disciple, of our three stages of road we've already walked a stage and a half — why do you speak words of turning back and regret?" Wukong said, "It's not that I'm not giving my whole heart to it. I only fear the demons are many and our strength is slight, our company few and alone. As the saying goes, 'Even a lump of iron — once in the furnace, how many nails can it make?'" The Elder said, "Disciple, you have a point — truly one man alone is hard pressed. The art of war says, 'The few cannot withstand the many.' But here I still have Bajie and Sha Monk, both my disciples. Marshal and command them as you please — let them be your defending generals and helping hands, joining strength and uniting hearts to sweep the mountain paths clean and lead me over. Won't we all then attain the true fruit?"

So all of Wukong's writhing and squirming had been only to coax these few words out of the Elder. He wiped away his tears and said, "Master, if we're to get over this mountain, then Zhu Bajie must agree to two things of mine — only then have we three parts in ten of getting through. But if he won't heed my words and take a turn in my place, there's not half a part of hope of passing." Bajie said, "Brother, if we're not going, let's just scatter — don't drag me into it!" The Elder said, "Disciple, just ask your elder brother what it is he wants you to do." So the idiot truly said to Wukong, "Brother, what is it you want me to do?" Said Wukong, "The first task is to watch over the master; the second is to go scout the mountain." Bajie said, "Watching the master means sitting still, and scouting the mountain means walking. You don't mean to have me sit a while, then walk, then walk a while, then sit? How could I tend to both at once?" Wukong said, "I'm not telling you to do both together — just take on one and have done." Bajie laughed again, "That can be arranged, then. But I don't know what 'watching the master' is like, or what 'scouting the mountain' is like. Explain them both to me first, and let me pick the more suitable one to do." Said Wukong, "As for watching the master: when the master goes to relieve himself, you wait on him; when the master wants to walk, you support him; when the master wants his vegetarian meal, you go beg the alms. And if he's gone the least bit hungry, you're to be beaten; if his face has gone the least bit sallow, you're to be beaten; if his frame has grown the least bit thin, you're to be beaten." Bajie took fright: "That's hard, hard, hard! Waiting on him and supporting him is no great matter; even carrying him on my back without ever setting him down would still be easy. But suppose you send me into the villages to beg alms — on these western roads they won't know I'm a scripture-pilgrim monk; they'll only take me for a half-grown stout hog come out of the hills, and a whole crowd of them with pitchforks and brooms will surround old Hog and knock him down, haul him home and butcher him, salt him down to keep for New Year — won't that be a plague of an end?" Said Wukong, "Go scout the mountain, then." Bajie said, "And what's scouting the mountain like?" Wukong said, "You go into this mountain and find out how many monsters there are, what mountain it is, what cave it is, so we can get safely past." Bajie said, "That's a small matter — old Hog will go scout the mountain." And the idiot hitched up his robe, leveled his nine-tooth rake, and, bold and bristling, strode straight into the deep mountains; full of swagger he charged up the high road.

At his side Wukong could not hold back a snickering cold laugh. The Elder scolded him, "You wretched ape! Toward your brothers you've not the least tenderness or pity, but always nurse a jealous heart. You've put on this cunning show, all clever words and a fawning face, to dupe him into going off to scout the mountain — and then you stand here laughing at him." Said Wukong, "I'm not laughing at him — there's flavor in this laugh. You watch: Bajie, going off like this, will certainly not scout the mountain, nor dare to face a monster. There's no telling where he'll go to skulk and hide for a while, then make up a lie to fool us with." The Elder said, "How can you know that about him?" Wukong said, "I reckon he's just so. If you don't believe it, let me follow him and take a look, and have a listen: first, to back up his hand in subduing demons; second, to see whether he has any sincere heart to bow before the Buddha." The Elder said, "Good, good, good — only don't go playing tricks on him." Wukong promised, and went straight up the mountain slope. There he gave his body a shake and changed himself into a tiny gnat-moth. Truly he changed himself light and deft — only look at him:

> Wings thin, he dances on the wind without effort;
> Waist tapering, fine and small as a needle.
> Threading the cattails, brushing the grass, passing through flower-shade,
> Swift as a shooting star, and swifter still.
> Eyes bright and clear and gleaming,
> Voice and breath faint and all but mute.
> Of all the insect kind he is the smallest,
> Yet slender, graceful, deep in his cunning.
> Many an idle day he rests in the quiet woods —
> His whole body cannot be seen,
> A thousand eyes could not find him out.

With a hum he flew off on his wings, overtook Bajie, and lit at the root of the bristles behind his ear. The idiot only kept trudging along, never dreaming there was someone on him. After seven or eight *li* of road, he flung down his rake, turned his head about, and, glaring back toward the Tang Monk, jabbed his fingers and waved his hands and railed: "You flabby old monk, you pinching Protector of the Horses, you weak-faced Sha Monk — there you all sit at your ease, having tricked old Hog into tramping the roads! We're all fetching scriptures, all hoping to win the true fruit — yet it's me alone they send off to scout some mountain. Ha ha ha! Knowing there are monsters, you skirt round and away, and even that's not the half of it — but you send me to go looking for them! What rotten luck. I'll just go somewhere to sleep, sleep a good one, and go back and give them some muddled answer — just say I scouted the mountain, and that'll settle the account." And so the idiot, on a sudden stroke of cunning, shouldered his rake and walked on, until in a hollow of the mountain he came on a bend of red grass on a slope. In he burrowed, with his rake spread out a flat bed on the ground, and down he rolled to sleep. Stretching his back with a stretch, he said, "Pleasant! Even that Protector of the Horses can't be as easy and free as I am."

Now all the while, Wukong, at the root of his ear, had heard every single word. He could not help flying up to play him another trick. Again he gave his body a shake and changed himself into a woodpecker. Only look:

> An iron beak, sharp and pointed, glossy red;
> Kingfisher plumage, gaudy bright and gleaming.
> A pair of steel claws, keen as nails.
> What of a hungry belly, when the woods are still?
> Best he loves the dry rotten stumps,
> And most he scorns the bare, lonely old trees.
> Round eyes, forked tail, a nimble, capricious nature,
> And his rat-a-tat sound is fine to hear.

This bird was neither large nor small — on the scale it would weigh but two or three ounces. Red-copper beak, black-iron feet, with a flick of his wings he came swooping down. Bajie had toppled over and was sound asleep, when the bird gave him a sharp jab — *tchak!* — right on the lip.

The idiot scrambled up in a fright, bawling, "Monsters! Monsters! Something speared me and got away — my lip hurts something terrible!" He reached up to feel, and out oozed the blood. He said, "Confound it — I've had no joyful event, so how have I come to hang out a red banner on my lip?" Looking at his bloody hand, muttering and grumbling, he peered all about on both sides, but there was no stir of anything. He said, "No monster at all — so what speared me?" Then, lifting his head to look up, he saw it was a woodpecker, flying there in mid-air. The idiot ground his teeth and cursed, "You dead thing! It's bad enough the Protector of the Horses bullies me — now you come to bully me too! I see how it is. He surely doesn't take me for a man at all — he just takes my snout for a length of black rotten dead wood with worms breeding inside, and came hunting worms to eat, and so gave me that one peck. Let me tuck my snout into my breast and sleep." And the idiot rolled over and lay down to sleep again as before. Wukong flew over once more and gave him another peck behind the ear. The idiot scrambled up in alarm: "This dead thing — what a torment you are to me! This must be his nest, where he lays his eggs and broods his young, and he's afraid I'll take it over, so he keeps pestering me like this. Enough, enough, enough — I won't sleep here." Shouldering his rake, he made straight out of the red grass slope and found the road and walked on. And wasn't Sun Wukong delighted to bits — the Handsome Monkey King was nearly toppled over laughing. Said Wukong, "That clod, with both eyes wide open, can't even recognize his own people."

What a great Sage! He gave his body another shake and changed back into a gnat-moth, and lit behind Bajie's ear, never leaving his body. The idiot went into the deep mountains, and after another four or five *li*, he saw in a hollow of the hills three squarish slabs of blue-green stone, each as broad as a tabletop. The idiot set down his rake and made a great deep bow to the stones. Wukong laughed to himself in secret: "That idiot! The stones aren't people, can't talk, can't return a courtesy — what's he bowing to them for? Isn't that a blind business?" But it turned out the idiot was treating the stones as the Tang Monk, Sha Monk, and Wukong — the three of them — and rehearsing before them. He said, "When I get back this time and see the master, if he asks whether there are monsters, I'll say there are monsters. If he asks what mountain it is, then — if I say it's made of mud, or made of earth, or beaten of tin, or cast of bronze, or steamed of dough, or pasted of paper, or drawn with a brush, they'll all say I'm being an idiot; if I talk that way, it'll just prove me an idiot all the more. I'll only say it's a stone mountain. If he asks what cave, I'll likewise just say a stone cave. If he asks what gate, I'll say it's an iron-leaf gate studded with nails. If he asks how far it is inside, I'll just say there are three layers within. And if he searches it out thoroughly and asks how many nails are on the gate, I'll just say old Hog was in too much of a flurry to count them right. With all this made up neat and ready, I'll go fool that Protector of the Horses." And the idiot, having patched it all together, dragged his rake and set straight back along the road.

How was he to know that Wukong, behind his ear, had heard every bit of it clearly? When Wukong saw him turning back, he beat his two wings and got back ahead of him, resumed his true form, and presented himself to the master. The master said, "Wukong, you've come back — how is it Wuneng is not yet seen returning?" Wukong laughed, "He's over there making up his lies — he'll be along directly." The Elder said, "His two ears cover his eyes — he's a dull, stupid fellow. What lies could he make up? It's you cooking up some spook-tale again to slander him." Said Wukong, "Master, you do nothing but cover for him. This is talk with proof to match." And he told it all in advance — how Bajie had burrowed into the grass to sleep, been woken by the woodpecker's peck, bowed to the stones, and concocted the whole story of a stone mountain, a stone cave, an iron-leaf gate, and monsters within.

He had scarcely finished when, before long, the idiot came walking up. Still afraid of forgetting his lies, he came with his head down, conning them over under his breath. Wukong gave a shout: "Idiot! What are you reciting there?" Bajie pushed up his ears and looked about: "Have I reached the place already?" Then the idiot came forward and knelt down. The Elder lifted him up: "Disciple, you've had a hard time of it." Bajie said, "Just so. Of all men, the road-walker and the mountain-climber have the hardest time of all." The Elder said, "Are there monsters, then?" Bajie said, "There are monsters, there are monsters — a whole heap of monsters!" The Elder said, "And how did they send you back?" Bajie said, "They called me Grandfather Hog and Great-Uncle Hog, laid out some bean-curd soup and vegetarian fare and had me eat a good meal, and said they'd line up flags and drums and see us safely over the mountain." Said Wukong, "I expect he fell asleep in the grass and that's a bit of dream-talk." Hearing this, the idiot shrank two inches in fright: "Father! When I was sleeping, how would you know it?" Wukong came forward and seized him fast: "Come here and let me question you." The idiot panicked again, and trembling all over said, "Question away and have done — what's all the grabbing and pulling for?" Said Wukong, "What mountain is it?" Bajie said, "A stone mountain." "What cave?" "A stone cave." "What gate?" "An iron-leaf gate studded with nails." "How far inside?" "Three layers within." Wukong said, "You needn't say any more — the second half I remember exactly. But for fear the master won't believe it, let me say it in your stead." Bajie said, "The cheek of you! You never even went — what do you know of any of it, that you'd say it for me?" Wukong laughed, "'And if asked how many nails are on the gate, just say old Hog was in too much of a flurry to count them right.' Isn't that it?" And down went the idiot in a flustered kneel. Wukong said, "And bowing to the stones as though they were the three of us, asking and answering yourself — isn't that it? And saying besides, 'Once I've got my lies made up neat, I'll go fool that Protector of the Horses' — isn't that it?" The idiot at once fell to knocking his head on the ground: "Brother, when I went to scout the mountain, you didn't go and follow me to listen, did you?"

Wukong railed at him: "You chaff-stuffed blockhead! At so crucial a spot I send you to scout the mountain, and off you go to sleep! If the woodpecker hadn't pecked you awake, you'd be there sleeping still. And the moment you were woken, you cook up a whopping great lie like this — won't that ruin the whole business? Stick out your ankle, quick — five strokes of the rod to fix it in your memory." Bajie took fright: "That mourning-staff of yours is heavy — a graze of it peels the skin, a brush of it bruises the sinew. If you strike five, that's the death of me." Wukong said, "You're afraid of being beaten — then why did you tell lies?" Bajie said, "Brother, just this once — I'll never dare again." Wukong said, "One offense gets three strokes." Bajie said, "Father! I couldn't stand half a stroke." Helpless and out of all resource, the idiot clutched the master: "Put in a good word for me." The Elder said, "When Wukong said you'd made up lies, I still didn't believe it; but now that it's turned out so, you really do deserve a beating. Yet just now, in crossing this mountain, we're short of hands to send about — Wukong, let him off for the present, and beat him once we're over the mountain." Said Wukong, "The ancients say, 'To go along with one's parents' wishes is called great filial piety.' Since the master says don't beat you, I'll let you off for now. You go back and scout the mountain again — and if you tell one more lie and bungle the business, I'll not spare you so much as a single stroke."

So the idiot had to scramble up and go again. Watch him charge up the high road — but a suspicious heart breeds phantom devils, and at every step he fancied it was Wukong transformed, dogging him; so at every thing he saw, he at once suspected it was Wukong. After seven or eight *li*, he saw a tiger come running across the mountain slope, and he wasn't even afraid, but raised his rake and said, "Brother, come to listen for lies again? This time I'm not making any up." Walking on, the mountain wind came on very fierce, and with a *whoosh* it blew down a withered tree that came rolling right up before him. He stamped his feet and beat his breast: "Brother! What's the meaning of this? The moment I say I dare not make up lies, you go and change into some tree to come hit a man?" Going on ahead, he saw a white-necked old crow caw-cawing straight overhead, calling several times running, and he said again, "Brother, shame on you, shame on you! I said I won't make up lies and I won't — what are you forever changing into an old crow for? Have you come to listen?" Now this time, in fact, Wukong had not followed him at all; it was only that the idiot, frightening and bewildering himself, suspected and second-guessed at every turn, so that wherever he went he supposed it was Wukong on his trail. But of the idiot's fright and suspicions, no more for now.

Now to tell of that mountain, which was called Flat-Top Mountain, and that cave, which was called Lotus Cave. In the cave were two demons: one called the Great King Golden Horn, the other called the Great King Silver Horn. Golden Horn was sitting in his place, and he said to Silver Horn, "Brother, how long is it since we scouted the mountain?" Silver Horn said, "It's been half a month." Golden Horn said, "Brother, go today and scout it for me." Silver Horn said, "What's the scouting for today?" Golden Horn said, "You don't know. I've lately heard that the Tang court of the Land of the East has sent an imperial younger brother, the Tang Monk, west to bow before the Buddha. A party of four, called Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Monk, with the horse five mouths in all. Find out whereabouts he is and catch him for me." Silver Horn said, "If we want to eat men, there's nowhere we can't grab a few. If these monks have reached this far, let them go on by." Golden Horn said, "You don't understand. In the year I came out from the Heavenly Realm, I often heard people say: the Tang Monk is the Elder Golden Cicada come down to the mortal world, a good man of ten lifetimes' cultivation, his primal yang not once spilt; whoever eats his flesh will have his years prolonged and live forever." Silver Horn said, "If eating his flesh can prolong our years and make us immortal, then why bother sitting in meditation, or building up merit, or refining the dragon and the tiger, or mating the female and the male? We ought just to eat him. Let me go and catch him." Golden Horn said, "Brother, you're a bit hasty — don't be in such a hurry. If you go out the door and, never minding good or bad, drag in every monk you meet, suppose it's not the Tang Monk — that wouldn't be right at all. I remember what they look like; I once had their master and disciples painted in likeness and drawn in portrait. Take them with you, and whenever you meet a monk, check them against these and verify." Then he told over, one by one, which man bore which name. Silver Horn took the portraits and learned the names, then went out of the cave, mustered thirty little fiends, and came up the mountain to patrol.

Now to tell of Bajie, whose luck was out. Just as he was walking along, head-on he ran into the band of demons, who blocked his way and demanded, "What man comes there?" Only then did the idiot lift his head, push up his ears, and see they were monsters — and he panicked, thinking in his heart, "If I say I'm a scripture-pilgrim monk, they'll snatch me up." So he only said he was a traveler passing through. The little fiends reported back, "Great King, it's a passing traveler." Among the thirty little fiends, some knew him and some did not. One at the side, who had been listening to the pointers and instructions, said, "Great King, this monk looks like the Zhu Bajie in the picture." He called for the spirit-portrait to be hung up. When Bajie saw it, he started in great alarm: "No wonder I've felt so out of spirits all this while — it turns out they've carried off a likeness of my very soul!" A little fiend held it up on a spear-point, and Silver Horn pointed with his finger: "This one riding the white horse is the Tang Monk; this hairy-faced one is Sun Wukong —" Bajie heard and said, "City God! It's all the same to me if you leave me out of it — a hog's-head and the three sacrificial beasts, and twenty-four portions of pure offering!" Muttering away under his breath, he kept making vows. The monster went on, "This black tall one is Sha Monk, and this long-snouted, big-eared one is Zhu Bajie." Hearing himself named, the idiot took fright and tucked his snout into his breast to hide it. The monster called, "Monk, stick out your snout!" Bajie said, "I've a congenital ailment — it won't stick out." The monster ordered the little fiends to hook it out with a hook. Frightened, Bajie thrust out his snout and said, "What petty manners! There — isn't this it? If you want to look, just look — what's the hooking for?"

The monster knew it was Bajie, drew his treasure-sword, and came forward to hack. The idiot raised his nine-tooth rake to block it and said, "My boy, no insolence — mind the rake!" The monster laughed, "This monk took his orders halfway through life." Bajie said, "Good son, you've some wit about you. How did you ever know that your old man left the household life only midway?" The monster said, "Since you know how to use that rake, you must have been digging the ground in somebody's garden plot and stolen this rake of his away." Bajie said, "My boy, what would you know of this rake of your old man's? It's no common ground-digging rake. This is it:

> Giant teeth cast like the claws of a dragon,
> Dressed in mottled gold to the shape of a tiger.
> Should it meet a foe, a cold wind scatters down;
> Should it grapple in combat, fire-flames spring up.
> It can rid the Tang Monk of obstacle and bar,
> And on the western road seize the demons and spirits.
> Swung about, its mist and haze blot out sun and moon;
> Raised up, its dusky clouds darken the Dipper and stars.
> It topples Mount Tai, and tigers take fright;
> It overturns the great sea, and old dragons quail.
> For all your tricks, you monster,
> One stroke of this rake leaves nine bloody holes."

Hearing this, the monster would by no means give way. He plied his Seven-Star sword, loosed his full repertoire of strokes, and went at it with Bajie, back and forth, fighting in the mountain some twenty rounds without victory falling to either side. Bajie worked himself into a fury and met him at the risk of his life. The monster, seeing him flap his ears, spray sticky slobber, and brandish his rake, roaring and bellowing all the while, was after all a little daunted, and at once turned his head and called up the little fiends to set on all together. Had it been one against one, all might still have been well; but seeing the little fiends all rush in at once, Bajie lost his nerve, could not fend them off, broke ranks, turned tail, and ran. But the ground was uneven, and not having watched it closely, all at once he was tripped by a tangle of trailing vine and went stumbling head over heels. He picked himself up and was just making off when another little fiend, lying flat on the ground, grabbed him by the heel, and *thump!* — down he went again, a dog gobbling muck. The whole pack caught up and pinned him, seizing his bristle-mane, hauling his ears, dragging his legs, pulling his tail, and lugging and heaving carried him off into the cave. Alas! It was just as the saying goes:

> A body's demon-nature is hard to wipe out,
> And the myriad disasters that breed are not easily cleared away.

After all, there is no telling whether Zhu Bajie kept his life or no — so listen to the next chapter for the explanation.

<!-- chapter 33 -->
# Chapter 33: The False Way Beguiles the True Nature; the Primal Spirit Aids the Original Heart

Now the demon carried Pigsy into the cave and announced, "Brother, I've caught one and brought him in." The old monster rejoiced. "Bring him here and let me see." The second monster said, "Is this not him?" The old monster replied, "Brother, you've grabbed the wrong one. This monk is good for nothing." At that Pigsy stuck out his snout and spoke up. "Great King, if the monk is good for nothing, then turn him loose and let him go. It's not fitting to mistreat a fellow." But the second monster said, "Brother, don't release him. Useless though he is, he still belongs to the Tang Monk's party — they call him Zhu Bajie. Let's soak him for now in the clear-water pool out back. Once the bristles have soaked loose from his hide, we'll salt him down, dry him in the sun, and keep him to eat with our wine on a cloudy day." Hearing this, Pigsy groaned, "What rotten luck — I've blundered into a monster who deals in salted pork and cured ham!" The little fiends hauled Pigsy in and flung him into the water. Let us leave him there.

Now Tripitaka sat upon the slope, his ears burning and his eyelid twitching, his whole body ill at ease. He called out, "Wukong, why is it that Wuneng has gone off to scout this mountain and stayed away so long without returning?" Sun Wukong said, "Master, you still don't understand his heart." Tripitaka asked, "What heart has he?" Wukong answered, "Master, if there were a monster on this mountain, he could not advance half a step — he'd surely raise a great commotion and come running back to report to me. Since there's been no such alarm, I reckon the road is quiet and clear, and he has simply gone straight on ahead." Tripitaka said, "But if he has truly gone on, where shall we meet up with him again? This is wild, open mountain country — not like the streets and wells of some town or market." Wukong said, "Don't fret, Master. Climb back on your horse. That idiot is somewhat lazy; he's bound to be plodding along slowly. Give the horse a touch of the whip and we'll certainly catch him, and all go on together." So indeed Tripitaka mounted, Sandy shouldered the luggage, and Wukong led the way up the mountain.

Meanwhile the old monster called again to the second. "Brother, since you've already caught Pigsy, then the Tang Monk is surely near. Go scout the mountain once more, and mind you don't let him slip past." The second monster said, "At once, at once." And see how he hastily mustered fifty little fiends and went up the mountain to patrol. As they marched, they saw auspicious clouds drifting and a haze of good omen circling in the air. The second monster said, "The Tang Monk is coming." The fiends asked, "Where is the Tang Monk?" The second monster said, "Over a good man's head, auspicious clouds cast their glow; over an evil man's head, black vapors surge to heaven. That Tang Monk was once the Elder Golden Cicada come down into the mortal world — a good man of ten lifetimes' cultivation — and so these auspicious clouds drift about him." But none of the fiends could see them. The second monster pointed with his finger. "Is that not he?" At that moment Tripitaka, upon his horse, gave a sudden shiver. The monster pointed again, and again the monk shivered. Three times in a row he pointed, and three times in a row the monk shivered. Uneasy in heart and spirit, Tripitaka said, "Disciples, why do I keep shivering so?" Sandy said, "Shivering like that is probably an attack of indigestion." Wukong said, "Nonsense. The Master is passing through deep mountains and steep ridges, so naturally he's cautious and starting at shadows. Don't be afraid, don't be afraid — let old Monkey clear the road ahead with my cudgel and steady your nerves."

Good Wukong! He whipped out his cudgel and before the horse spun through several flourishes — three up and four down, five left and six right — running through all the strategies of the Six Secret Teachings and the Three Strategies, and putting forth his magic powers. The elder, watching from his horse, saw a display the like of which is rare in the whole realm and altogether absent from the world. Wukong cleaved open the road and pressed straight on — and very nearly frightened that monster to death. For the fiend, watching from the mountaintop, lost his soul and his wits, and cried out, "For years I've heard tell of Sun the Pilgrim, and only today do I learn the rumors weren't empty — it's all really true!" The fiends crowded forward. "Great King, why puff up another man's spirit and snuff out your own prestige? Whom are you praising?" The second monster said, "Sun the Pilgrim's magic powers are vast — that Tang Monk is not for him to eat." The fiends said, "Great King, if you've no means to take him, let a few of us go report to the eldest king, summon all the soldiers great and small of our cave, deploy them in formation, and join hearts and strength as one — where could he run to then?" The second monster said, "You've never seen that iron cudgel of his — it carries a valor that ten thousand men could not withstand. Our cave has no more than four or five hundred soldiers; how could they endure a single blow of his?" The fiends said, "If that's how it stands, and the Tang Monk can't be eaten, then haven't we grabbed Pigsy by mistake? Let's send him back, then." The second monster said, "Caught him we did, and not by mistake; but to send him back would not be wise either. The Tang Monk is to be eaten in the end — it's only that we can't manage it just yet." The fiends asked, "On this reckoning, must we wait several more years?" The second monster said, "It won't take years. As I see it, that Tang Monk can be plotted for only by gentle means, never seized by force. To try to lay hands on him by show of strength — we'd not get so much as a whiff of him. He can only be moved by kindness; once we've coaxed his heart to chime with mine, then within that kindness we'll lay our scheme, and so we'll have him." The fiends said, "If the Great King has settled on a plan to take him, may we be of use?" The second monster said, "Go back, each of you, to your own stockades — but breathe not a word of this to the eldest king. If he's stirred up, word will surely leak and spoil my scheme. I have a magic of my own and shifting shapes by which I can take him." And the fiends dispersed.

Then alone he leapt down the mountain, and there beside the road shook himself and changed into an aged Daoist priest. And how was he got up? Behold:

> A star-crown gleaming bright,
> hoary crane-white hair all tousled and loose;
> feathered robe girt with an embroidered sash,
> cloud-treading shoes trimmed with tawny brown.
> His spirit clear, his eyes bright as an immortal's,
> his frame hale, his body light as a man of great age.
> Speak not of the Azure-Ox Daoist —
> he outshone even the Plain-Tablet sage.
> A false image he fashioned, true as the true,
> a feigned feeling he molded, real as the real.

There by the great road he played a Daoist with a broken leg, his foot all running with blood, groaning and moaning, crying only, "Save me! Save me!"

Now Tripitaka, leaning on the strength of Sun the Great Sage and of Sandy, came joyfully forward. Just as they were traveling on, they heard the cry, "Master, save a man!" Hearing it, Tripitaka said, "Mercy! Mercy! In this lonely wilderness of mountains, with not a village or cottage on any side — who is it that cries out? It must be someone struck down with fright by tigers or leopards, wolves or vipers." The elder reined his fine horse about and called, "Whoever is in distress, come forth!" The monster came crawling out of the brush, and before the elder's horse knocked his head on the ground bang after bang. Seeing from his horse that here was a Daoist, and one well on in years, Tripitaka could not bear it. He dismounted at once and lifted him, saying, "Rise, please rise." The monster said, "It hurts, it hurts, it hurts." Letting go his hands and looking closer, Tripitaka saw the blood streaming from the man's foot. Alarmed, he asked, "Sir, where have you come from? And how did you come to injure your honorable foot?" The monster, with crafty words and flowery speech, with feigned feeling and counterfeit sincerity, replied, "Master, west of this mountain there stands a pure and secluded abbey — I am a Daoist of that abbey." Tripitaka said, "If you do not stay in your own abbey, tending the incense fires and practicing the rites of the scriptures, why are you wandering idly out here?" The fiend said, "The day before yesterday a patron's household in the southern hills invited a company of Daoists to perform a star-quelling rite and scatter blessings, and we came away late — my disciple and I traveling along together. As we reached a deep defile, suddenly a mottled fierce tiger fell upon us and carried my disciple off in its jaws. Trembling and with nowhere to flee, I took a tumble on a slope of jumbled rocks, hurt my leg, and lost the way home. Today, by great heavenly fortune, I have met with you, Master. I beg you, of your boundless mercy, save my life. If I can but reach the abbey, I would pawn my very body and sell my life to repay so deep a kindness." Hearing him, Tripitaka took it all for truth and said, "Sir, you and I are both men of a single life. I am a monk, you a Daoist; our robes and caps differ, but the principle of cultivation is one and the same. If I did not save you, I'd be no member of the religious orders. Save you I will — but you cannot walk the road, can you?" The monster said, "I can't so much as stand up. How am I to walk?"

Tripitaka said, "Well then, well then — I can still walk; I'll yield you my horse to ride a stretch, and when we reach your abbey you can return it to me." The monster said, "Master, I'm moved by your deep kindness, but my hip and thigh are broken in the fall, and I cannot ride a horse." Tripitaka said, "Quite right." He called to Sandy, "Lash the luggage onto my horse, and you carry him a stretch." Sandy said, "I'll carry him." But the monster hastily turned his head, threw him a glance, and said, "Master, I've been so frightened by that fierce tiger that the sight of this ill-omened, dark-faced master frightens me all the more — I dare not have him carry me." Tripitaka called, "Wukong, you carry him." Wukong answered briskly, "I'll carry him, I'll carry him." So the fiend fixed upon Wukong, contentedly insisting that he do the carrying, and would say no more. Sandy laughed and said, "What a no-eyed old Daoist! Won't let me carry him, perversely wants the other to. The moment that one's out of the Master's sight, on some three-pointed crag he'll dash your guts clean out of you!"

Hearing this, Wukong laughed under his breath. "You filthy fiend, how dare you come and provoke me? Ask yourself how many years old Monkey has been in the world! These ghostly tales of yours might fool the Tang Monk — but do you think you can fool me too? I know you for a monster of this mountain, and I reckon you mean to eat my master. But my master is no common sort — is he yours to eat? If you'd eat him, then at least you'd best hand over more than half the share to old Monkey." When the fiend heard Wukong muttering, he said, "Master, I'm the son and grandson of a good family, who became a Daoist. Today, by misfortune, I've met with the peril of tigers and wolves — I am no monster." Wukong said, "If you fear tigers and wolves, why don't you recite the Northern Dipper Scripture?" Tripitaka, just then mounting his horse, heard these words and scolded, "You wretched ape! 'To save one life surpasses building a seven-storied pagoda.' Just carry him and have done — why all this talk of the 'Northern Dipper Scripture' and the 'Southern Dipper Scripture'?" Hearing this, Wukong said, "This rascal is in luck! My master is a kind and charitable man — though fair without, he's somewhat thorny within. If I refuse to carry you, he'll blame me. Carry you I shall, but I must lay things straight with you first: if you need to make water or worse, tell me beforehand. If it comes dribbling down my spine, the stink is unbearable, and it'll foul my clothes — and there's no one to wash them." The monster said, "A man of my age — don't I understand your meaning?" Then Wukong hauled him up, slung him onto his back, and together with the elder and Sandy made for the highroad westward. Over the uneven heights and hollows of the mountain Wukong walked slowly and with care, letting the Tang Monk go on ahead.

They had gone scarcely three or four miles when the Master and Sandy descended into a hollow of the hills, so that Wukong could no longer see them. In his heart he grumbled, "The Master, old as he is, still understands nothing of how things stand. On so long a road, even an empty load feels heavy in the hand — I could fling it down for spite — and yet he sets me to carrying this monster. Never mind that he's a monster; even were he an honest man, at this age he might well be dead already. I'll just dash him to death — why carry him?" Now just as the Great Sage was reckoning to dash him down, that monster knew it, and being skilled in spell-craft, he worked a magic to move mountains and overturn seas. Right there on Wukong's back he made the secret signs and pronounced the true words, and dispatched the whole of Mount Sumeru through the air to come crashing down upon Wukong's head. The Great Sage, startled, tilted his head aside, and the mountain pressed down upon his left shoulder and arm. He laughed and said, "My boy, what spell of heavy-bodies is this you've worked to crush old Monkey? This is nothing to fear — only that a balanced load is easy to bear, and a lopsided one hard to endure." The fiend said, "One mountain won't hold him down." So again he chanted the spell and dispatched Mount Emei through the air to press upon him. Wukong tilted his head aside once more, and it came to rest on his right shoulder and arm. See him then, bearing two great mountains, hurrying like a shooting star after the Master! The fiend, watching, was so terrified that his whole body broke out in sweat and ran wet from head to foot. "He can actually carry mountains!" Steeling himself again, he pronounced the true words and dispatched Mount Tai through the air to crash straight down upon Wukong's head. Then the Great Sage's strength went soft and his sinews went numb, and meeting this spell of Mount Tai pressing on his crown, he was so crushed that the Three Corpse-spirits within him shrieked and red blood spurted from his seven orifices.

Fine monster! Having used his magic to crush Wukong, he rode swiftly on the long wind to overtake Tripitaka of Tang, and from amid the clouds reached down a hand to snatch the man off his horse. In a panic Sandy flung down the luggage, whipped out his demon-quelling staff, and met him head-on to block the way. The monster lifted up a seven-star sword and came on to meet him face to face. It was a fine combat:

> The seven-star sword, the demon-quelling staff —
> ten thousand glints of golden light flashing like lightning.
> This one, with round eyes, fierce as the Black God of Death;
> that one, with iron face, truly the Curtain-Rolling General.
> The monster, before the mountain, showed his full power,
> his whole heart bent on seizing Tripitaka of Tang;
> this one strove with all his might to guard the true monk,
> his whole heart resolved to die before he'd let go.
> The two of them spat clouds and belched fog up to the heavenly palace,
> tossed earth and raised dust to veil the very Dipper.
> They fought till the single red sun went pale and lost its light,
> and the whole wide world of heaven and earth grew dim and reeling.
> Back and forth they grappled eight or nine rounds —
> and beyond all expectation, Sandy was defeated.

The monster was exceedingly fierce. Wielding his precious sword, he sent its flourishes whirling down like shooting stars, until he had worn Sandy weak and unable to ward him off. Sandy turned to flee — but the fiend pressed in on his staff at once, swung out his great hand, seized Sandy and clamped him under his left armpit; with his right hand he took Tripitaka off the horse, hooked the luggage with his toes, opened his mouth and bit down on the horse's mane; then, working his fetching-magic, he carried the whole lot of them off in a gust of wind into the Lotus-Flower Cave, crying out in a piercing voice, "Brother! I've caught all the monks and brought them here!"

When the old monster heard this, he was overjoyed and said, "Bring them here and let me see." The second monster said, "Are these not they?" The old monster said, "Worthy brother — bah! You've grabbed the wrong ones again!" The second monster said, "You said to catch the Tang Monk." The old monster said, "That's so — this one is indeed the Tang Monk. But you still haven't caught that capable one, Sun the Pilgrim. We must catch him first — only then is it well to eat the Tang Monk. If we haven't caught him, don't lay a hand on his people. That Monkey King's magic powers are vast and his transformations are many; if we ate his master, would he take it lying down? He'd come kicking up a din at our gate, and we could forget all hope of peace and quiet." The second monster laughed. "Brother, you do overmuch to flatter the man! To hear you praise him, he's rare in heaven and altogether absent on earth. As I see it, he's only just so — no great prowess at all." The old monster said, "Have you caught him?" The second monster said, "I've already dispatched three great mountains to crush him beneath them, so that he can't shift an inch. That's how I came to fetch the Tang Monk and Sandy here, horse, luggage and all." Hearing this, the old monster's heart was filled with joy. "Fortune, fortune! With that fellow pinned down, the Tang Monk is at last the meat in our mouths." He called to the little fiends, "Quick, set out wine, and let me pour your Second Great King a cup for his merit." The second monster said, "Brother, don't drink yet. Tell the little ones to fish Pigsy up out of the water and hang him up." So they hung Pigsy in the eastern corridor, Sandy on the west side, and the Tang Monk in the middle; the white horse they led to the trough, and the luggage they stowed away inside.

The old monster laughed. "Worthy brother, fine work — twice over you've caught three monks. But although Sun the Pilgrim is pinned under the mountains, we still need to contrive some means to bring him here as well, to add to the steamer — only then will it be well." The second monster said, "Elder brother, please be seated. To take Sun the Pilgrim, there's no need for us to stir ourselves — we need only send two little fiends with two of our treasures to pack him up and bring him in." The old monster said, "Which treasures shall we send?" The second monster said, "My purple-gold red gourd and your mutton-fat jade vase." The old monster brought out the treasures and said, "Which two shall we send?" The second monster said, "Send the two — Fine-Spirit and Clever-Bug." He gave them their orders: "You two take these treasures and go straight to the topmost peak of the high mountain. Turn the bottom toward heaven and the mouth toward earth, and call out once, 'Sun the Pilgrim.' If he answers, he's already packed inside. Straightaway paste on the slip that reads 'By order of the Most High Lord Lao, hurry, hurry, as the statute commands' — and in a single hour and a quarter he'll dissolve into pus." The two little fiends knocked their heads in obedience, took up the treasures, and set out to catch Wukong. Let us leave them.

Now the Great Sage, pinned by the monster's magic beneath the roots of the mountains, in his suffering thought of Tripitaka, in his calamity yearned for the holy monk. In a piercing voice he cried, "Master! Think back to when you came to the Mountain of Two Frontiers and peeled away the sealing slip — old Monkey escaped his great affliction and took up the gate of religion. Grateful for the Bodhisattva's bestowal of the holy decree, you and I dwelt together and cultivated together, shared the same karma and the same form, the same seeing and the same knowing. Little did I think that, coming to this place, we'd meet such a demon-barrier, and I'd be crushed under his dispatched mountains. Pity, oh pity! My death is deserved enough — but it's hard on Sandy and Pigsy, and on the little dragon who turned himself into our horse. This is just the saying: 'A great tree calls down the wind, and the wind shakes the tree; a man strives for high fame, and fame is the death of the man.'" Having sighed, his tears fell like rain.

This soon startled the mountain god, the local earth-spirit, and the host of Guardian deities of the Five Quarters. The Golden-Headed Guardian gathered them and asked, "Whose mountain is this?" The earth-spirit said, "It's ours." "And who is it you've crushed beneath it?" The earth-spirit said, "We don't know who." The Guardian said, "So you don't know, after all. The one crushed here is the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, Sun Wukong the Pilgrim, who five hundred years ago raised his great uproar in the Palace of Heaven. He has now turned to the true fruit and become the Tang Monk's disciple. How could you lend your mountain to a demon to crush him? You're as good as dead. If one day he frees himself and gets out, will he spare you? At the very lightest, the earth-spirit would be charged with manning a relay post and the mountain god with banishment to the army — and we ourselves would draw a grave charge of dereliction." Then the mountain god and earth-spirit grew afraid and said, "We truly didn't know, didn't know. We only heard that demon chant his mountain-moving spell, and so we shifted the mountains over. Who would have guessed it was the Great Sage Sun?" The Guardian said, "Don't be afraid just yet. The statute says: 'He who acts in ignorance does not bear the guilt.' Let me work this out with you — release him, but don't let him fall to beating us." The earth-spirit said, "That'd be unreasonable — release him, and then he beats us?" The Guardian said, "You don't understand. He has an As-You-Will Gold-Banded Cudgel, exceedingly fierce: whatever it strikes dies, whatever it grazes is wounded; one tap snaps the sinews, one brush flays the skin."

The earth-spirit and mountain god, fear in their hearts, conferred with the Guardians of the Five Quarters, and then came to the gate of the triple-peaked mountain and called, "Great Sage — the mountain god, the earth-spirit, and the Guardians of the Five Quarters come to see you." Good Wukong! Though the tiger is lean, the hero's heart remains; his bearing was naturally lofty, his voice clear and ringing as he said, "What do you want with me?" The earth-spirit said, "We report to the Great Sage: we will move away the mountains and beg the Great Sage to come out, and pardon us small spirits our discourtesy." Wukong said, "Move away the mountains, and I won't beat you." Then he barked, "Up and away!" — just like an official issuing a command. The deities chanted the true words and the spell, and dispatched the mountains back each to its proper place, and set Wukong free. Wukong sprang up, shook off the dirt, tightened his skirts, and from behind his ear drew out the cudgel. He called to the mountain god and the earth-spirit, "All of you stick out your ankle-bones — each take two strokes to start with, and let old Monkey work off his vexation." The deities were aghast. "Just now the Great Sage said he'd pardon our offense — how is it that the moment you're out you've changed your tune and want to beat us?" Wukong said, "Fine earth-spirit, fine mountain god — you say you don't fear old Monkey, yet you fear a monster?" The earth-spirit said, "That demon's magic powers are vast, his sorcery high and strong; he chants the true words and the spell and presses us into service in his cave, one of us standing duty in turn each day."

When Wukong heard the words "standing duty," his heart was shaken too. He raised his face to heaven and cried aloud, "O blue Heaven, O blue Heaven! Ever since the primal chaos first divided, since heaven opened and earth was sundered, the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit gave birth to me. I too sought out enlightened masters far and wide and was given the secret arts of long life. Think of me — shifting shapes upon the wind, subduing tigers and quelling dragons, raising my great uproar in the Palace of Heaven, styled the Great Sage — yet never did I cow the mountain god and earth-spirit into servitude. Today this lawless demon — how dare he summon the mountain god and earth-spirit to be his slaves and stand duty in turn for him? O Heaven! Since you gave birth to old Monkey, why did you also give birth to such a creature as this?"

Just as the Great Sage was sighing thus, he saw a rosy glow come blazing toward him out of a hollow of the hills. Wukong said, "Mountain god, earth-spirit — since you stand duty in this cave, what is that thing giving off the light?" The earth-spirit said, "That's the demons' treasures shining. Likely some fiend has come bearing treasures to subdue you." Wukong said, "Now this will be good sport! Let me ask you — who has dealings with him in that cave?" The earth-spirit said, "What he loves is to refine elixirs and decoct medicines; what he delights in is Complete-Reality Daoists." Wukong said, "No wonder, then, that he changed into an old Daoist and tricked my master away. Since that's how it is — I'll mark you all down for a beating, and you may go back. Let old Monkey catch him himself." And the host of deities all rose into the sky and dispersed.

Then the Great Sage shook himself and changed into an old True Man. And how was he got up? Behold:

> His hair done up in twin coiled knots,
> his body clad in a hundred-patch robe;
> in his hand he tapped fisher-drum and clappers,
> at his waist hung the Lü Patriarch's cord.
> Slantwise he lounged beside the great road,
> waiting on purpose for the little fiends.
> In a moment the fiends arrived —
> and the Monkey King slyly laid his trap.

Before long the two little fiends came up. Wukong stretched out the gold-banded cudgel, and the fiends, off their guard, tripped on it and went sprawling flat. Scrambling up, they finally caught sight of Wukong and clamored, "Insolence, insolence! If it weren't that our Great King reveres you religious folk, we'd settle accounts with you!" Wukong said with a smile, "Settle what accounts? Daoist meeting Daoist — we're all one family." The fiends said, "Why were you sleeping here, that you tripped us up?" Wukong said, "When the little Daoist lads meet me, an old Daoist, they should give me a tumble for a meeting-gift." The fiend said, "Our Great King's meeting-gift takes only a few taels of silver — how is it that with you, a tumble is the meeting-gift? You must come from some other district's customs — you're certainly no Daoist of these parts." Wukong said, "Truly I'm not. I come from Mount Penglai." The fiend said, "Mount Penglai is the sea-isle realm of the immortals." Wukong said, "If I'm not an immortal, who is?" At that the fiends turned their anger to delight and came forward, saying, "Old immortal, old immortal — we are creatures of fleshly eyes and common mold, who could not recognize you; our words gave offense — pardon us, pardon us." Wukong said, "I don't blame you. As the old saying goes, 'An immortal's body treads not common ground.' How were you to know? Today I've come to your mountain to deliver some worthy soul to become an immortal and attain the Way. Which of you is willing to follow me?" Fine-Spirit said, "Master, I'll follow you." Clever-Bug said, "Master, I'll follow you."

Wukong, knowing well, asked as though he did not, "Where do you two come from?" The fiends said, "We've come from the Lotus-Flower Cave." "And where are you bound?" The fiends said, "By our Great King's command, we're off to catch Sun the Pilgrim." Wukong said, "To catch whom?" The fiends said again, "To catch Sun the Pilgrim." Wukong said, "Would that be the Sun the Pilgrim who follows the Tang Monk to fetch the scriptures?" The fiend said, "The very one, the very one — do you know him too?" Wukong said, "That monkey is rather rude. I know him, and I've a grudge against him myself. I'll go catch him along with you — that'll be lending you a hand." The fiend said, "Master, there's no need for your help. Our Second Great King has some sorcery — he's dispatched three great mountains to crush him beneath them so he can't shift a step, and sent us two to fetch treasures to pack him up." Wukong said, "What treasures?" Fine-Spirit said, "Mine is the red gourd, his is the jade vase." Wukong said, "How do you pack him up with them?" The little fiend said, "We turn the bottom of the treasure toward heaven and the mouth toward earth, and call out to him once. If he answers, he's packed inside; then we paste on a slip reading 'By order of the Most High Lord Lao, hurry, hurry, as the statute commands,' and in a single hour and a quarter he dissolves into pus." Hearing this, Wukong was secretly alarmed in his heart. "How fearsome, how fearsome! When the Duty-God on watch brought word that day, he said there were five treasures — these are two of them. I wonder what the other three may be?" Wukong said with a laugh, "You two — lend me the treasures to have a look." The little fiends, knowing nothing of the trick, drew the two treasures from their sleeves and handed them over to Wukong with both hands. Seeing them, Wukong rejoiced in secret. "Splendid things, splendid things! If I just give my tail a flick, I'll go whisking up and away — and reckon them a gift to old Monkey." But then he thought again, "No, no. To snatch and run would only ruin old Monkey's good name. That would be called daylight robbery." So he handed them back, saying, "You still haven't seen my treasure." The fiend said, "What treasure has the master? Lend it to us common folk to look at, that it may ward off calamity."

Good Wukong! He reached down, plucked a hair from his tail, gave it a pinch, and called, "Change!" — and it changed into a great purple-gold red gourd a foot and seven inches long. He took it out from his waist and said, "Behold my gourd!" Clever-Bug took it in hand, examined it, and said, "Master, this gourd of yours is big and shapely, fine to look at — only it's of no use." Wukong said, "How of no use?" The fiend said, "Each of these two treasures of ours can hold a thousand people." Wukong said, "What's so rare about a thing that packs in people? My gourd packs in the whole of heaven itself." The fiend said, "It can pack in heaven?" Wukong said, "Truly it packs in heaven." The fiend said, "I fear it's a lie. Pack heaven up and show us, then we'll believe; otherwise we'll never believe you." Wukong said, "If heaven vexes me, in a single month I often pack it up seven or eight times; if it doesn't vex me, then half a year may pass and I won't pack it once." Clever-Bug said, "Brother, a treasure that packs up heaven — let's trade for it." Fine-Spirit said, "His packs up heaven; why should he be willing to swap it for ours that only packs up people?" Clever-Bug said, "If he won't, we can throw in this jade vase to boot." Wukong rejoiced in secret. "Gourd for gourd, and the jade vase thrown in besides — one of mine for two of theirs; truly that suits very well." He stepped forward, took hold of Clever-Bug, and said, "Will you trade if it packs up heaven?" The fiend said, "If it packs up heaven, we'll trade; if I won't trade, I'm your son." Wukong said, "Well then, well then — I'll pack it up for you two to see."

Good Great Sage! He bowed his head, made the secret signs, chanted a spell, and summoned the Day-Wandering Spirit, the Night-Wandering Spirit, and the Guardians of the Five Quarters: "Go at once and report for me to the Jade Emperor. Say old Monkey has turned to the true fruit and is guarding the Tang Monk on the road to the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures; that the way is barred by a high mountain and the master has met bitter affliction; that I mean to lure the demons into trading away that treasure of theirs. With a thousand and ten thousand prostrations, I beg that Heaven be lent to old Monkey to be packed up and shut away for half an hour, to help bring this off. And if there's so much as a single word of refusal, I'll come up to the Hall of Numinous Mists and set sword and spear to work."

The Day-Wandering Spirit went straight in through the Southern Gate of Heaven, below the Hall of Numinous Mists, and reported it all to the Jade Emperor. The Jade Emperor said, "This wretched ape-head — his words are without manners. Before, Guanyin came and asked that he be released to guard the Tang Monk, and We here further dispatched the Guardians of the Five Quarters and the four Duty-Gods to protect him in turn. Now he wants to borrow Heaven to pack it up — can Heaven be packed up?" Just as He was saying it could not be done, out from the ranks stepped the Third Prince Nezha and reported, "Your Majesty, Heaven can be packed up." The Jade Emperor said, "How is Heaven to be packed up?" Nezha said, "From the first division of the primal chaos, the light and pure became Heaven, the heavy and turbid became Earth. Heaven is a single mass of pure vapor sustaining the jasper palaces and gates of the heavens; reasoned out, it truly cannot be packed up. But Sun the Pilgrim is guarding the Tang Monk westward to fetch the scriptures — this is indeed what is called a karmic blessing high as Mount Tai, a fortune of goodness deep as the sea — and today we ought to help him bring it off." The Jade Emperor said, "What help would you give?" Nezha said, "I pray a decree be handed down. Let me go to the Northern Gate of Heaven and borrow from Zhenwu his black-eagle banner; unfurl it once above the Southern Gate of Heaven, and it will shut away sun, moon, and stars. Face to face one won't see a man; clutch at white and one won't see black — so we'll dupe the fiends into believing Heaven really has been packed up, and help Wukong bring it off." Hearing this, the Jade Emperor said, "Let it be as you have proposed." Receiving the decree, the prince went to the Northern Gate of Heaven, saw Zhenwu, and reported it all. The Patriarch at once handed the banner to the prince.

Quickly a Wandering Spirit descended in haste to the Great Sage's ear and said, "Prince Nezha has come to lend his aid." Wukong raised his face and looked — and saw auspicious clouds curling round, and there indeed was the deity. He turned his head back to the little fiends and said, "Let's pack up heaven." The little fiends said, "If you're going to pack it, then pack it — why keep fiddling and dawdling like passing a stubborn stool?" Wukong said, "I was just now working my spirit and chanting the spell." The little fiends both opened their eyes wide to watch how he would pack up heaven. Then Wukong flung the false gourd up into the air. Now think — this was a thing made from a single hair; how much could it weigh? Caught by the wind on the mountaintop, it went drifting and tumbling about for a full half-hour before it came down. And up at the Southern Gate of Heaven, Prince Nezha snapped open the black banner with a rustle and shut away sun, moon, and stars together. Truly, heaven and earth seemed dyed in ink, the cosmos painted over with indigo. The two little fiends cried out in alarm, "Just now when we were talking it was barely midday — how is it suddenly dusk?" Wukong said, "Once heaven's packed up, you can't tell the hours apart — why wouldn't it be dusk?" "But why so utterly black?" Wukong said, "Sun, moon, and stars are all packed inside — there's no light left without; how could it not be black?" The little fiends said, "Master, whereabouts are you speaking from?" Wukong said, "Am I not right here before you?" The little fiends reached out and felt for him, saying, "We only hear you speak — we can't see your face at all. Master, what kind of place is this?" Wukong fooled them again. "Don't move your feet. This is the shore of the Bohai Sea. If you lose your footing and fall in, you won't reach the bottom in seven or eight days!" The little fiends cried out in alarm, "Stop, stop, stop — let heaven loose again! Now we understand it's packed up just so. If you keep at it any longer and we tumble into the sea, we'll never get home."

Good Wukong! Seeing that they'd taken it for the truth, he chanted the spell again, stirring the prince, who rolled up the banner — and at once the sunlight stood at high noon. The little fiends laughed. "Marvelous! Marvelous! Such a fine treasure — if we didn't trade for it, we'd truly be no sons fit to keep a household." Then Fine-Spirit handed over the gourd, Clever-Bug brought out the jade vase, and together they passed them to Wukong; and Wukong handed the false gourd over to the little fiends in exchange. The treasures traded, he then carried the business through to the very end. He plucked a hair from below his navel, blew on it a breath of immortal air, and changed it into a copper coin. He called, "Little lads, take this coin and go buy a sheet of paper." The little fiends said, "What for?" Wukong said, "I'll write you out a deed of contract. You've traded these two people-packing treasures for one heaven-packing treasure of mine; lest a man's heart prove uneven, and lest in the long years to come there be any going-back-on-it or inconvenience, we'll write this out, each to keep a copy as proof." The little fiends said, "There's neither brush nor ink hereabouts — what deed shall we write? Let's swear an oath with you instead." Wukong said, "How shall we swear?" The little fiends said, "We've swapped our two people-packing treasures for your one heaven-packing treasure; if we go back on it, may we be struck with plague through all four seasons of the year." Wukong laughed and said, "I'll certainly never go back on it; and if I do, may I likewise be struck with plague through your four seasons."

Having sworn the oath, Wukong gave a leap of his body, gave his tail a flick, and sprang up before the Southern Gate of Heaven, where he thanked Prince Nezha for the merit of his banner-waving aid. The prince returned to his palace to render his report, and sent the banner back to Zhenwu — but of that no more. Wukong stood upright there amid the heavens and looked down at the two little fiends.

After all, there's no knowing how things were to be settled; so listen to the next chapter told.
